        The relative bar complex over the universal curve 𝜋 : M 𝑔,1 → M 𝑔 has ﬁber cohomology concentrated
    in the center 𝑍 (A): the Koszul property forces all higher ﬁber cohomology to vanish, and the degree-zero
    identiﬁcation 𝐻 0 = 𝑍 (A) holds because a bar-degree-0 cocycle is an element whose OPE with every
    ﬁeld is regular –- the deﬁning property of a central element. The center forms a local system ZA on M 𝑔 .
    Verdier self-duality of the center equips 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , ZA ) with a (−1)-shifted symplectic structure in the
    sense of Pantev–Toën–Vaquié–Vezzosi, and Verdier duality A ↔ A ! splits the ambient complex into
    complementary Lagrangian halves:

                                    𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , ZA ) ≃ Q 𝑔 (A) ⊕ Q 𝑔 (A ! ) ,

    the deformation complex of A and the obstruction complex of its dual. The Lagrangian condition
    ⟨Q 𝑔 (A) , Q 𝑔 (A ! )⟩ = 0 means that every ﬁrst-order deformation of A at genus 𝑔 is annihilated
    by the obstruction map of A ! .
        Clutching along the boundary divisors of M 𝑔 –- the stable-graph strata where the curve degenerates
    –- organizes the genus tower into a single modular deformation. A cyclic 𝐿∞ -algebra structure on the
    deformation complex Def cyc (A), constructed from the Fay trisecant identity on FM compactiﬁcations,
    supports a universal Maurer–Cartan element

    Verdier duality gives Θ A ↦→ Θ A ! .
        The chiral Hochschild cohomology 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) of a principal W-algebra at generic level is poly-
    nomial: ℂ[ Θ1 , . . . , Θ𝑟 ] with deg Θ𝑖 = 𝑚𝑖 + 1 where 𝑚1 , . . . , 𝑚𝑟 are the exponents of 𝔤. At critical

    ℂ[ Θ1 , . . . , Θ𝑟 ]. The Koszul duality functor acts on Hochschild cohomology via the Connes periodicity
    operator 𝑆 .
       The construction has two genuinely different specializations because the logarithmic propagator on a
    curve interacts with two distinct algebraic structures.
          On the commutative (E∞ -chiral) side, the Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 is the ﬁrst nontrivial example.

      The current 𝐽 ( 𝑧 ) with OPE 𝐽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝐽 (𝑤 ) = 𝑘 /( 𝑧 −𝑤 ) 2 gives a bar element 𝐽 ⊗ 𝐽 ⊗ 𝜂12 ∈ 𝐵 ; the bar
      differential produces Res𝜖 =0 [ 𝜖 𝑑𝜖 ] = 0 (triple pole, no residue). The level 𝑘 is invisible at genus 0
                                           −3

      and appears at genus 1 as curvature 𝜅 = 𝑘 . Every feature of the general theory –- Arnold nilpotence,
      Verdier duality, complementarity, the 𝐴ˆ-genus, the Hodge bundle correction –- is already present and
      computable.
          On the braided (E1 -chiral) side, the Yangian 𝑌 (𝔤) is the ﬁrst nontrivial example. The RTT presen-
      tation 𝑅12 ( 𝑢−𝑣 ) 𝑇1 ( 𝑢) 𝑇2 ( 𝑣 ) = 𝑇2 ( 𝑣 ) 𝑇1 ( 𝑢) 𝑅12 ( 𝑢−𝑣 ) replaces commutativity with the Yang–Baxter
      equation, and the bar differential acts on ordered conﬁguration spaces. Koszul duality inverts the 𝑅-
      matrix: 𝑌 (𝔤) !  𝑌𝑅 −1 (𝔤). The derived Drinfeld–Kohno theorem –- that E1 -factorization categories of
      Yangians and quantum groups are equivalent on the evaluation locus –- is proved for the evaluation-
      generated core at all simple Lie types. For lattice vertex algebras 𝑉Λ , sectorwise ﬁniteness of the Λ-graded
      bar complex bypasses thick generation entirely, yielding unconditional factorization equivalences for all
      even positive-deﬁnite lattices.
          Explicit computations, occupying half this volume, cover the Heisenberg algebra (the E∞ atom), free
      fermions and the 𝑏𝑐 - 𝛽𝛾 Koszul pair (Com-Lie duality incarnate), aﬃne Kac–Moody at Feigin–Frenkel
      dual levels with the oper space emerging at critical level, the Virasoro algebra with its 𝑐 ↔ 26 − 𝑐
      complementarity, principal W-algebras through Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction with complete stage-4 OPE
      structure constants for 𝑊4 , ADE lattice algebras with their quantum deformations, and Yangians with
      Mittag-Leﬄer stabilization of the RTT bar-cohomology tower. Bar cohomology dimensions, genus free
      energies through 𝑔 = 10, Koszul dual Hilbert series, and modular characteristics are computed for every
      family.

• B̄(A) denotes the geometric bar complex
• 𝐵¯ ch (A) denotes the abstract chiral bar complex (when distinction needed)
• 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) = 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is the compactified configuration space
• 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) are the logarithmic 1-forms
• E∞ -chiral, E1 -chiral, P∞ -chiral refer to curve-based chiral factorization levels (Definition 2.8.1ff.); bare
  E𝑛 refers to the little-disks/topological axis on real 𝑛-manifolds. A complex curve therefore enters the
  topological ladder at 𝑛 = 2, not 𝑛 = 1 (Remark 2.8.7)
Chapter 1


Introduction

The Heisenberg algebra is the minimal commutative atom that already displays the full modular bar-cobar
mechanism in computable form: the bar differential can be written down explicitly, Verdier duality is visible
without auxiliary generators, the genus-1 defect is scalar, and the genus tower closes to the 𝐴ˆ-series. What
Heisenberg cannot see is ordered factorization: there is no nontrivial braid reversal and no 𝑅-matrix to
invert. That omission is structural. The Yangian supplies the first genuinely braided example on the E1 side.
    The subject of this monograph is the bar construction for chiral algebras on algebraic curves. The starting
point is a simple geometric observation: place elements 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑛 of a chiral algebra A at points 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧𝑛
on a smooth curve 𝑋 , extract residues of the operator product expansion along the boundary divisors of
the Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), and assemble the results into a graded coalgebra 𝐵 (A).
The Arnold relation among triple collisions forces 𝑑 2 = 0: the bar complex is a factorization coalgebra on
Ran( 𝑋 ).
    This construction, carried out for every major family of chiral algebras –- Heisenberg, free fermions,
𝛽𝛾 systems, affine Kac–Moody at arbitrary level, Virasoro, principal W-algebras, lattice vertex algebras,
Yangians –- is the engine of chiral Koszul duality. The bar construction is the categorical logarithm: its
kernel is the logarithmic form 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ), and it maps the multiplicative OPE structure to the
nilpotent bar differential with 𝑑 2 = 0. At genus 0, this logarithm is single-valued and specializes to classical
operadic Koszul duality.
    At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the logarithm acquires monodromy from the period structure of the curve, the prop-
agator acquires corrections from the Hodge bundle over M 𝑔 , the bar differential develops curvature
  2 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 whose coefficient 𝜅 (A) is the infinitesimal generator of this monodromy, and the genus
𝑑fib               𝑔
tower organizes into a modular deformation whose generating function is the 𝐴ˆ-genus. Throughout,
nilpotence is the logarithm of periodicity: the nilpotent data ( 𝑑 2 = 0, 𝜅 , the bar differential) determine the
periodic data (modular transformations, periodicity of bar cohomology, the monodromy representation)
via exponentiation (Remark 6.0.1).
    The examples are arranged so that the geometry appears before its braided refinement. The first four
examples stay on the commutative E∞ face, where unordered configurations, curvature, and complemen-
tarity are already visible. The lattice and Yangian previews are included to show where that picture stops
being sufficient: once ordering becomes mathematical data, one leaves the Heisenberg world and enters
the braided E1 face.
• The Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 (§1.1–§1.12) carries the full vertical structure: the bar complex at genus 0,
  the Arnold relation, the Koszul dual, bar-cobar inversion, genus-1 curvature, the 𝐴ˆ-genus generating
  function, and the complementarity of quantum corrections. Every theorem of Part I is instantiated here.
• Free fermions and the 𝛽𝛾 system (§1.14) exhibit the Lie–Com duality of chiral algebras: the fermion,
  governed by a simple pole, is Koszul dual to the 𝛽𝛾 system. This is the chiral incarnation of the classical




                                                         47
48                                                                               Chapter 1. Introduction


  Lie! = Com duality, and it clarifies the distinction between Koszul duality, bosonization, and level-
  shifting.
• Affine Kac–Moody algebras (§1.15) introduce both simple and double poles. The bar differential acquires
  a bracket component from the simple pole and a curvature component from the double pole; neither is
  individually a differential. The Borcherds identity, coupling both pole orders, replaces the Jacobi identity.
  The PBW spectral sequence emerges as the correct computational tool, and the Feigin–Frenkel involution
  𝑘 ↔ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ is revealed as Koszul duality.
• W-algebras (§1.16) arise from Kac–Moody via Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction and test the theory against
  derived constructions. Composite fields such as Λ =: 𝑇 𝑇 : − 103 𝜕 2𝑇 introduce quartic OPE poles; the
  PBW spectral sequence does not automatically degenerate. Koszul duality commutes with DS reduction,
  extending the Feigin–Frenkel involution to the full W-algebra tower.
• Lattice vertex algebras (§1.17) bring E1 -monoidal structure from the braiding. Cocycle deformations
  produce quantum lattice algebras, and the E1 bar-cobar adjunction inverts the quantum parameter:
  𝜀 ↦→ 𝜀 −1 .
• Yangians (§1.17) realize the 𝑅 ↔ 𝑅 −1 duality in factorization form. Through factorization homology, the
  chiral Koszul duality of the Yangian recovers the Drinfeld–Kohno equivalence between KZ monodromy
  and quantum group representations.

Grading and desuspension accounting
The bar complex uses cohomological grading and desuspension. The current 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) has conformal
weight | 𝛼 | = 1. Under desuspension, the bar complex element 𝑠 −1 𝛼 has cohomological degree shifted
by +1:
                                       deg( 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ) = | 𝛼 | + 1 = 2.
A degree-𝑛 bar element involves ( 𝑛 + 1) desuspended currents and an 𝑛-form, giving total cohomological
degree
                        ( 𝑛 + 1) · deg( 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ) + deg( 𝜂 ) = 2( 𝑛 + 1) + 0 = 2𝑛 + 2,
where the logarithmic forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 carry form-degree 1 but cohomological degree 0 in the bar complex grading.
The bar differential has | 𝑑res | = +1 in cohomological degree.
  For a degree-1 element, the data is:

                                two desuspended currents:       𝑠 −1 𝛼 ( 𝑧1 ) ⊗ 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ( 𝑧2 ) ,
                                                                    𝑑𝑧1 − 𝑑𝑧2
                                one logarithmic 1-form:     𝜂12 =             .
                                                                     𝑧1 − 𝑧2

Remark 1.1.1 (Where the OPE data goes). The map 𝑑res : 𝐵¯ 1ch → 𝐵¯ 0ch = ℂ sends each pair of currents to the
constant 𝑘 . On ℙ1 , where 𝐻 1 ( 𝑋 ) = 0, the kernel of 𝑑res on 𝐵¯ 1 is trivial: every element maps to a nonzero
multiple of the vacuum. At higher genus, zero modes of 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) along cycles of Σ 𝑔 contribute nontrivially to
ker( 𝑑res ), producing 𝐻 1  𝐻 1 ( Σ 𝑔 , ℂ) (Theorem 18.11.2).

Sign conventions for the bar differential at degree 2
Before computing, we fix signs. The bar differential is a sum over boundary strata:

where 𝜕𝐷 𝑖𝑗 restricts to the divisor 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 = { 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 } and extracts the OPE coefficient, and 𝜎 ( 𝑖, 𝑗 ) is the
Koszul sign arising from permuting the desuspended elements past each other.
    For degree-2 elements with three desuspended currents 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ( 𝑧1 ) ⊗ 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ( 𝑧2 ) ⊗ 𝑠 −1 𝛼 ( 𝑧3 ), the Koszul sign

shift 1), hence is even in the graded sense. Moving even-degree elements past each other produces sign
(−1) 2·2 = +1. Consequently, for the Heisenberg algebra (single even generator), all Koszul signs from
the coalgebra coproduct are +1. The signs in the bar differential come entirely from the orientation of the
logarithmic forms on the boundary strata.
Term-by-term computation of 𝑑 res
The element (1.4) lives on 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ), whose boundary divisors are 𝐷12 , 𝐷23 , and 𝐷13 . The bar differential

Alternative basis and the role of 𝐷 13
To see that the vanishing of 𝐷13 above was a feature of the basis choice, consider the alternative degree-2
element 𝛼 ⊗3 ⊗ 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 . The Arnold relation (1.9) below gives

                             𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 = − 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 − 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = − 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂31 .

Computing 𝑑res on this element, the stratum 𝐷13 does contribute (with coefficient +𝑘 ), but the stratum
𝐷12 picks up an additional sign. The computation of 𝑑res 2 = 0 on any basis element requires the full Arnold

relation, not just pairwise cancellation. This is the essential content: the Arnold relation is the universal
identity guaranteeing 𝑑 2 = 0.
    The cancellation is not an accident. It is an instance of a general identity on the logarithmic forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 .
Proposition 1.2.1 (Arnold relation; [proved]). For any three distinct points 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 , 𝑧3 ∈ 𝑋 , the
logarithmic forms satisfy:
                            𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 + 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = 0                             (1.9)
in Ω2log ( 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 )).

Proof. The identity 𝑧1 −1 𝑧2 · 𝑧2 −1 𝑧3 + 𝑧2 −1 𝑧3 · 𝑧3 −1 𝑧1 + 𝑧3 −1 𝑧1 · 𝑧1 −1 𝑧2 = 0 follows from partial fractions: the
three terms have total numerator ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) + ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) + ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) = 0. Taking 𝑑 log of each factor and
wedging produces (1.9).

   The Arnold relation forces 𝑑 2 = 0 on the bar complex. At degree 2, the two paths from 𝐵¯ 2 to 𝐵¯ 0
through 𝐵¯ 1 correspond to the two ‘‘boundary of boundary’’ strata in 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ): 𝐷12 ∩ 𝐷23 and 𝐷13 ∩ 𝐷23 .
The Arnold relation ensures these two paths contribute with opposite signs, so they cancel.
   More precisely: the differential 𝑑 on the bar complex is a sum of residue maps along all collision divisors.
When 𝑑 is applied twice, each pair of successive collisions defines a codimension-2 stratum of 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ). By
Stokes’ theorem on manifolds with corners, 𝑑 2 = 0 if and only if the boundary of the boundary vanishes,
which is precisely the Arnold relation on the logarithmic forms.
Remark 1.2.2 (The Arnold relation as factorization coherence). The identity (1.9) is the fundamental co-
herence relation of factorization algebras: the bar complex is well-defined because Arnold holds, Verdier
duality exchanges bar and cobar because Arnold is self-dual, and the genus tower extends over M 𝑔 because
Arnold lifts to boundary strata of the FM operad. In the operadic language, (1.9) defines the gravity operad
Grav = HyCom! , and the genus-0 bar-cobar adjunction is operadic Koszul duality.

1.3     The bar complex at all degrees — 𝑑 2 = 0
The pattern continues. At degree 𝑛, the bar complex element is

                                  𝛼 ( 𝑧1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝛼 ( 𝑧𝑛+1 ) ⊗ 𝜂𝑖1 𝑗1 ∧ · · · ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑛 𝑗𝑛
and the bar differential extracts OPE data at each collision divisor. Because the Heisenberg OPE has no
simple pole, the bracket component 𝑑bracket of the bar differential vanishes identically. Only the curvature
component 𝑑curvature (which extracts the double-pole coefficient) is nonzero.
    Before stating the general theorem, we carry out the degree-3 computation in full detail. This is the
first degree where the cancellation mechanism for 𝑑 2 = 0 involves pairs of Arnold relations, revealing the
pattern that persists at all higher degrees.

1.3.1  Explicit degree-3 computation (𝑛 = 3, four points)
A degree-3 bar element lives on 𝐶 4 ( 𝑋 ) with four points 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 , 𝑧3 , 𝑧4 and involves a 3-form in the logarithmic

This is the ‘‘chain’’ basis element, where the logarithmic forms link consecutive pairs 1–2, 2–3, 3–4.
Boundary strata of 𝐶 4 ( 𝑋 )

Assembling 𝑑 res at degree 3
Only the three ‘‘adjacent’’ strata 𝐷12 , 𝐷23 , 𝐷34 contribute. The three ‘‘non-adjacent’’ strata 𝐷13 , 𝐷24 , 𝐷14

Clean verification of 𝑑 2 = 0 via Arnold pairs
Rather than tracking the intermediate expressions through relabeling, we verify 𝑑 2 = 0 structurally. The
bar differential 𝑑 = 𝑑res satisfies 𝑑 2 = 0 if and only if every codimension-2 boundary stratum of 𝐶 4 ( 𝑋 )
contributes zero. The codimension-2 strata are of two types:
Type I: nested collisions 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ∩ 𝐷𝑗 𝑘 (three points 𝑧 𝑖 , 𝑧𝑗 , 𝑧 𝑘 collide in sequence). These contribute via
the composition 𝜕𝐷𝑗 𝑘 ◦ 𝜕𝐷 𝑖𝑗 : first 𝑧 𝑖 collides with 𝑧𝑗 , then the collision point collides with 𝑧 𝑘 . The reverse
order 𝜕𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ◦ 𝜕𝐷𝑗 𝑘 gives the same codimension-2 stratum with opposite orientation. By the Arnold relation
on the triple ( 𝑧 𝑖 , 𝑧𝑗 , 𝑧 𝑘 ), these two contributions cancel.
   For the four-point configuration, the nested triples are: (1, 2, 3), (2, 3, 4), (1, 2, 4), (1, 3, 4), (2, 3, 4). Each
produces one Arnold-relation cancellation.
Type II: disjoint collisions 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ∩ 𝐷 𝑘𝑙 where { 𝑖, 𝑗 } ∩ { 𝑘, 𝑙 } = ∅. For four points, the only such stratum
is 𝐷12 ∩ 𝐷34 (simultaneous collision 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 and 𝑧3 = 𝑧4 ). The two orderings 𝜕𝐷34 ◦ 𝜕𝐷12 and 𝜕𝐷12 ◦ 𝜕𝐷34
commute (they act on disjoint pairs), and the sign from the form restriction ensures they cancel. Explicitly,
for the form 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂34 :
• 𝜕𝐷12 then 𝜕𝐷34 : consume 𝜂12 (sign +1), leaving 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂34 ; then consume 𝜂34 (sign −1 from moving past
  𝜂23 ). Net: (−1).
• 𝜕𝐷34 then 𝜕𝐷12 : consume 𝜂34 (sign +1 by cyclic permutation), leaving 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 ; then consume 𝜂12 (sign
  +1). Net: (+1).
The two orderings produce opposite signs:

                             𝜕𝐷34 ◦ 𝜕𝐷12 ( 𝜉3 ) + 𝜕𝐷12 ◦ 𝜕𝐷34 ( 𝜉3 ) = 𝑘 2 · (−1 + 1) = 0.

   Since every codimension-2 stratum contributes zero (Type I by Arnold, Type II by sign cancellation),
we conclude:

The adjacency pattern
The degree-3 computation reveals a structural feature. For the chain basis element 𝛼 ⊗4 ⊗ 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂34 ,
only ‘‘adjacent’’ strata (those 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 where 𝜂𝑖𝑗 appears as a factor in the wedge) give nonzero contributions
to 𝑑 . The non-adjacent strata 𝐷13 , 𝐷24 , 𝐷14 all vanish by form-squaring ( 𝜂 ∧ 𝜂 = 0). This adjacency
pattern persists at all degrees for the chain basis: the differential on 𝛼 ⊗ ( 𝑛+1) ⊗ 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 ∧ · · · ∧ 𝜂𝑛,𝑛+1
1.4. The twisting morphism: the propagator as algebraic map                                                     57


receives contributions only from 𝐷12 , 𝐷23 , . . . , 𝐷𝑛,𝑛+1 , producing an alternating sum of 𝑛 terms with
signs +1, −1, +1, −1, . . .
    For a general basis element (not the chain basis), all strata can contribute, and 𝑑 2 = 0 requires the
full Arnold relation. The chain basis is special precisely because it diagonalizes the ‘‘adjacency’’ of the
logarithmic forms.

1.5      Reading off the Koszul dual
The bar coalgebra 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) carries a coproduct determined by the OPE. On the single cogenerator 𝛼 ∗ ∈ 𝐵¯ 1 ,
there is nothing to decompose:
                                          Δ ( 𝛼∗) = 𝛼∗ ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ 𝛼∗ .
This is the definition of a primitive element. Every element of 𝐵¯ 1 is primitive, and the double-pole residue
is symmetric under 𝑧 𝑖 ↔ 𝑧𝑗 , so the coproduct is cocommutative at all degrees. The bar coalgebra is also
conilpotent (Theorem 6.2.27): every element is eventually annihilated by iterated reduced coproducts. By
the Milnor–Moore theorem (characteristic zero, conilpotent, cocommutative), such a coalgebra is the
universal enveloping coalgebra of its primitives. For H𝑘 the space of primitives is one-dimensional, so:
                               𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 ) ≃ coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ) ,    𝑉 ∗ = Span{ 𝛼 ∗ } .

   (i) Dualize (graded linear dual): coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ) ∨  Symch (𝑉 ∗ ), the free commutative algebra in one
       generator –- the Koszul dual algebra H𝑘! .

         ering the original algebra (Theorem 6.12.1).

Dualizing changes the category (coalgebra → algebra, coLie → Sym); cobar stays in the algebra category
and produces a resolution. Both originate from 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ), but they point in opposite algebraic directions –-
and this is the Com! = Lie duality made concrete.
   The level 𝑘 determines a curvature element 𝑚0 = −𝑘 · 𝜔 ∈ Sym2 (𝑉 ∗ ), encoding the central extension.

Remark 1.5.2 (The canonical twisting morphism for Heisenberg). The Koszul duality above is witnessed

Remark 1.5.3 (Three different ‘‘dualities’’). Three distinct operations must not be confused: (1) Koszul

correspondence Rep(H𝑘 ) ≃ Rep(F ⊗2 ). Only (1) is the subject of this monograph.

1.6      Bar-cobar inversion — Theorem B in action
The bar construction and the cobar construction form an adjoint pair Ω ⊣ 𝐵 between augmented chiral
algebras and conilpotent chiral coalgebras (Chapter 6). The counit of this adjunction

                                          𝜀 : Ωch 𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 ) −−→ H𝑘
                                                              ∼

is a quasi-isomorphism: the bar-cobar round trip recovers the original algebra.

The double-pole coefficient 𝑘 passes through the bar-cobar cycle without loss:

The bar differential extracts 𝑘 as a residue (§1.1); the bar cohomology stores it in the central class 𝑐𝑘

1.7.2  Curvature: 𝑑fib    2 ≠ 0 at genus 1

Compute the bar differential on 𝐸𝜏 using the elliptic propagator (1.14). The B-cycle monodromy of 𝐺𝜏

This shift is the genus-1 curvature.
Theorem 1.7.2 (Genus-1 curvature; [proved]). For H𝑘 on 𝐸𝜏 , the fiberwise differential satisfies
                                                       2
                                                     𝑑fib = 𝑘 · 𝜔1 · id

where 𝜔1 = 𝑐1 (𝔼) ∈ 𝐻 2 (M 1 ) is the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle on the moduli space of elliptic
curves.
    The proof is the direct computation: the B-cycle monodromy of the elliptic propagator contributes a
phase 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖𝑘 to the parallel transport of bar complex elements. Squaring the differential, the two B-cycle
transports contribute a factor (−2 𝜋 𝑖 ) 2 that, after integration over M 1 , produces the Hodge class 𝜔1 = 𝑐1 (𝔼)
with coefficient 𝑘 . The detailed computation appears in Theorem 8.13.3.
    The fiberwise differential has ceased to be strictly square-zero.
    At genus 0, the bar complex was a genuine chain complex ( 𝑑02 = 0) and its cohomology was well-defined.
At genus 1, the bar complex is curved: 𝑑fib 2 = 𝑘 · 𝜔 is proportional to the level. The curvature vanishes only
                                                        1
at 𝑘 = 0, where the Heisenberg algebra degenerates.
Remark 1.7.3 (Physical meaning of curvature). The curvature 𝑑fib    2 = 𝑘 · 𝜔 is the conformal anomaly: 𝑘

M 1 measures the obstruction to consistent definition on all elliptic curves.

1.9     Why the ordinary derived category fails
The curvature 𝑑fib 2 = 𝑘 · 𝜔 means that the genus-1 bar complex is not a chain complex in the ordinary
                              1
sense: it does not live in the derived category 𝐷 (Vect). It lives in the coderived category 𝐷 co (Vect) of
Positselski [171].
                                                                                                2 ≠ 0 is simply
    The distinction is subtle but essential. In the ordinary derived category, a complex with 𝑑fib
undefined. In Positselski’s framework, a curved differential graded (co)algebra –- one where 𝑑fib  2 =𝑚 ≠0
                                                                                                          0
for some curvature element 𝑚0 –- has a well-defined coderived category in which:
   (i) The bar-cobar adjunction still holds (as an adjunction of curved (co)algebras).
  (ii) The notion of ‘‘acyclic’’ is refined: a curved complex can be coacyclic (contractible in the coderived
       sense) without being acyclic in the ordinary sense.
 (iii) The bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) → A holds in the coderived category when it fails in
       the ordinary derived category.
    The Heisenberg algebra at 𝑘 ≠ 0 is the simplest object that forces us out of the ordinary derived category.
At 𝑘 = 0, 𝑑fib2 = 0 and the ordinary derived category suffices; at 𝑘 ≠ 0, the curvature is nonzero and only

the coderived category gives the correct homological algebra.
    This is not an abstract concern. The genus-1 bar complex of H𝑘 with 𝑘 ≠ 0 is ‘‘acyclic’’ in the naïve sense
(its homology with respect to 𝑑fib is zero, since 𝑑fib   2 ≠ 0 means the notion of ‘‘homology’’ is undefined),

but it is not coacyclic in Positselski’s sense –- it carries genuine invariants (the Hodge class 𝜔1 , the partition
function 1/ 𝜂 ( 𝜏 )) that are invisible to ordinary homological algebra but visible in the coderived category.
    The general theory of bar-cobar duality in the coderived setting is developed in Chapter 6
(Theorem 9.1.39).

1.12     Complementarity — Theorem C in action
The Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 and its Koszul dual H𝑘! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) form a Koszul pair. Their genus- 𝑔
quantum corrections are complementary.
Theorem 1.12.1 (Quantum complementarity for Heisenberg; [proved]). For the Koszul pair
(H𝑘 , Symch (𝑉 ∗ )) at genus 𝑔 :

                                 𝑄 𝑔 (H𝑘 ) + 𝑄 𝑔 (H𝑘! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(H𝑘 ))

where 𝑄 𝑔 denotes the genus- 𝑔 quantum correction (the obstruction to extending the genus-0 bar-cobar
quasi-isomorphism to genus 𝑔 ), and Z(H𝑘 ) is the center local system on M 𝑔 .
     At genus 1:
• The Heisenberg deformation space is one-dimensional, generated by the level 𝑘 .
• The obstruction space of Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) is also one-dimensional, generated by the curvature 𝑚0 = −𝑘 · 𝜔.
• Together, they span 𝐻 ∗ (M 1 , Z(H𝑘 ))  ℂ2 .
   The complementarity is controlled by Verdier duality on M 𝑔 : the bar complex computes deforma-
tions, the cobar complex computes obstructions, and Verdier duality exchanges them. What H𝑘 sees as a
deformation (varying the level 𝑘 ), its Koszul dual sees as an obstruction (the curvature 𝑚0 ), and vice versa.
1.13. The characteristic hierarchy in the Heisenberg frame                                                     67


   This is Theorem C (Theorem 8.14.12) for the Heisenberg case. The general theorem establishes com-
plementarity for all Koszul chiral algebra pairs, with the ambient space 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z) carrying a shifted-
symplectic pairing from Verdier duality on the center local system.

1.13    The characteristic hierarchy in the Heisenberg frame
Everything computed in this chapter –- the bar complex, the Koszul dual, the curvature at each genus,
the free energy tower, the complementarity –- assembles into a characteristic hierarchy with three proved
layers: a scalar package, an ambient/spectral shadow, and a full homotopy completion (Theorem 8.18.72).
Deﬁnition 1.13.1 (Characteristic hierarchy for Heisenberg). The Heisenberg frame exhibits the following
characteristic data:
   (i) The proved scalar characteristic data 𝜅 (H𝑘 ) = 𝑘 (Theorem 8.18.30), which determines the entire
       scalar modular package: obs 𝑔 = 𝑘 · 𝜆 𝑔 for all 𝑔 ≥ 1.
  (ii) The proved ambient complementarity complex

                                              𝐻H𝑘 := 𝑅Γ M 𝑔 , ZH𝑘
                                                                        


       Verdier duality then provides the shifted-symplectic structure needed for complementarity
       (Theorem 8.14.12).

1.14     Free fields and the Lie–Com duality
The Heisenberg algebra has a single bosonic current with a double pole. The free fermion has a single
fermionic current with a simple pole:
                                                           1
                                       𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜓 (𝑤 ) =       + regular.
                                                          𝑧−𝑤
68                                                                                      Chapter 1. Introduction


Two differences from Heisenberg: the pole order drops from 2 to 1, and the statistics change from bosonic
to fermionic. Each has an independent algebraic consequence.
    Pole order. The simple pole means the bar differential 𝑑 = 𝑑bracket has no curvature component –- it is
entirely bracket-type. At degree 1, it extracts the simple-pole residue Res 𝑧 =𝑤 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜓 ( 𝑤 ) = 1, a scalar.
    Statistics. The Koszul sign rule acts on the bar complex: when 𝜓 is fermionic (| 𝜓 | = 1), two desus-
pended cogenerators in 𝐵¯ 2 satisfy 𝜓 ∗ ⊗ 𝜓 ∗ = −𝜓 ∗ ⊗ 𝜓 ∗ under transposition, forcing antisymmetry. The
coproduct on 𝐵¯ (F ) is therefore co-antisymmetric: the bar coalgebra is a coLie coalgebra, and the Koszul
dual algebra is the commutative algebra Com. This is Lie! = Com, visible in the OPE: the self-pairing
𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜓 (𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) is antisymmetric under 𝑧 ↔ 𝑤 (fermionic), encoding Lie structure.
    Contrast with Heisenberg: 𝛼 is bosonic (| 𝛼 | = 0), so the desuspended cogenerators commute, the
bar coalgebra is cocommutative (coLie → Sym), and the Koszul dual is Symch (𝑉 ∗ ). The statistics of the
generators, not the pole order, determine the operadic type.
Theorem 1.14.1 (Free fermion bar complex; see Theorem 18.1.3; [proved]). The bar complex 𝐵 (F )
of the free fermion is acyclic: 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵 (F )) = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 1, with 𝐻 0 = ℂ. In particular, F is chiral Koszul.
   Acyclicity is the strongest form of the Koszul property: no cohomological obstruction at any degree.
For Heisenberg, 𝐻 2 ( 𝐵 (H𝑘 )) = ℂ · 𝑐𝑘 ≠ 0 (Theorem 1.3.1) –- the double-pole curvature creates a class
that obstructs acyclicity. The free fermion, having only a simple pole, has no such obstruction.
The Koszul dual: the 𝛽𝛾 system. The Koszul dual of the free fermion is the 𝛽𝛾 system, a chiral algebra
with two bosonic generators 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) of weight 1 and 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) of weight 0. Compute the OPE directly:

    The W-algebra example demonstrates that chiral Koszul duality is compatible with the fundamental
derived operations of conformal field theory. Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction, which constructs W-algebras
from Kac–Moody algebras as BRST cohomology, is a derived functor in the sense of homological algebra;
the fact that it commutes with the bar construction means that the entire Koszul duality machine descends
through this derivation. The composite field phenomenon, far from obstructing the theory, enriches it: the
PBW spectral sequence acquires non-trivial higher differentials that encode the normal-ordering structure
of conformal field theory.

1.17     The braided world: lattice algebras and Yangians
Every chiral algebra considered so far –- Heisenberg, free fermions, Kac–Moody, W-algebras –- is E∞ -
chiral: its operations are commutative and local, configuration spaces 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) are unordered, and Verdier
duality on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) exchanges bar and cobar. We now pass to chiral algebras with E1 -monoidal structure,
where the operations are associative but not commutative. This change of algebraic type, internal to chiral
geometry on a fixed curve, opens the door to quantum groups.
Lattice vertex algebras. Let Λ be an even lattice with bilinear form ⟨−, −⟩ and cocycle 𝜀 : Λ × Λ → {±1}.
The lattice vertex algebra 𝑉Λ𝜀 is built from a Heisenberg sector (one current 𝛼 𝑖 ( 𝑧 ) per basis vector of Λ ⊗ ℂ,
with double-pole OPE) together with vertex operators 𝑒 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) for each 𝛼 ∈ Λ, satisfying

antisymmetric ( 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ ), the algebra acquires E1 -monoidal structure: the bar complex

uses ordered configuration spaces 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), and the coproduct is no longer cocommutative.

   The passage from E∞ -chiral (Heisenberg) to E1 -chiral (Yangian) is an internal change of algebraic type
within chiral geometry on a fixed curve: from commutative/local factorization on unordered configuration
spaces to associative/nonlocal factorization on ordered configuration spaces. It is not the passage from
curves to higher-dimensional manifolds. A separate topological ladder is governed by little-disks 𝐸𝑛 -algebras
on real 𝑛-manifolds; for a complex curve the relevant topological index is 𝑛 = 2, not 𝑛 = 1. Chapter 15
develops that distinct topological framework.

 The four theorems, the genus tower, and the modular characteristic package point toward a unified theory.

 1.18.2    The operadic architecture
 The genus tower of §1.11 is organized by an operadic structure that we now make visible in the Heisenberg
 example.
76                                                                             Chapter 1. Introduction


Genus 0: HyCom ↔ Grav
The Arnold relation (Proposition 1.2.1) is the defining relation of the gravity operad Grav, which governs
the genus-0 bar complex. Its Koszul dual is the hypercommutative operad HyCom, which governs the cobar
complex. The genus-0 bar-cobar adjunction

                                       𝐵¯ : AlgHyCom ⇄ coAlgGrav : Ω

is an instance of operadic Koszul duality (Getzler–Kapranov [32]). For Heisenberg:
• H𝑘 is a HyCom-algebra (the chiral operations are commutative and local).
• 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) is a Grav-coalgebra (the bar differential is controlled by the Arnold relation).
• The cobar Ω 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) ≃ H𝑘 recovers the original algebra (§1.6).
    The two operads are dual incarnations of a single structure: HyCom( 𝑛) = 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝑀 0,𝑛+1 ) (cohomology
of genus-0 moduli), and Grav( 𝑛) = 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝑀 0,𝑛+1 ) ! (Koszul dual grading). The genus-0 bar complex is the
Grav-coalgebra structure, and the collision differential 𝑑02 = 0 follows from the Grav relations (= Arnold).
Genus 1: the elliptic operad
At genus 1, the moduli space M 1,𝑛 enters. The bar complex on an elliptic curve acquires fiberwise curvature
  2 = 𝑘 · 𝜔 (§1.7). Operadically, the genus-1 structure is governed by the elliptic operad: the collection

In Chapter 1, we saw the bar complex, Koszul duality, genus-1 curvature, and the 𝐴ˆ-genus tower for the

    Part I is the proved modular Koszul core: it establishes these results in full generality while marking the
exact boundary beyond which the full modular homotopy theory remains programmatic.
    Its governing claim is that on a curve the bar-cobar transform is already modular: genus enters through
the same configuration-space logarithm, Verdier duality, and clutching formalism that define genus-0
duality, so the genus tower is internal to the transform rather than an external correction.
    The argument proceeds through four stages: classical Koszul duality is the point-level shadow; config-
uration spaces provide the geometric kernel; bar-cobar duality and Verdier intertwining give the genus-0
equivalence; higher genus internalizes the same construction through Hodge-theoretic curvature and
modular-operadic clutching. The proved spine consists of Theorem A (bar-cobar duality intertwined with
Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 )), Theorem B (higher-genus inversion on the Koszul locus, with coderived per-
sistence off it), Theorem C (Lagrangian complementarity of deformation and obstruction), Theorem Dscal
and Theorem DΔ (the scalar and spectral characteristic layers), the higher-genus PBW entry theorem for
affine Kac–Moody, Virasoro, and principal finite-type W-algebras, and the universal Maurer–Cartan class
Θ A constructed by Theorem 8.18.72.
Chapter 2


Introduction

2.1    A geometric synthesis
The subject has two irreducible entry points. The Heisenberg atom (E∞ ) realizes symmetric configurations,
genus-tower curvature, complementarity, and the full scalar characteristic package. The Yangian atom (E1 )
realizes ordered configurations, 𝑅-matrix inversion, the evaluation locus, and the Drinfeld–Kohno ladder.
Every other family–-Kac–Moody, Virasoro, W-algebras, lattice vertex algebras–-lies between these two
poles. Chapters 6 and 8 establish Theorems A–D and the universal Maurer–Cartan package Θ A ; Part II
computes the standard families; Chapter 34 records the boundary between proved core and frontier.
    Theorems A–D, Lagrangian complementarity, the scalar and spectral characteristic packages, uncondi-
tional modular Koszulity for the standard interacting families, and the universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ A
(Theorem 8.18.72) are proved. The live frontier–-MC3 (factorization DK/KL beyond the evaluation-
generated core), MC4 (infinite-generator limits for W∞ and Yangian towers), and downstream MC5–-is
recorded in Chapter 34.

Guide to the reader
Three entry points.
(a) Fast route via the Heisenberg frame. Chapter 1 → Chapter 6 → Chapter 8 → Chapter 34. This path
    reaches the four main theorems with a single example and no Lie-theoretic prerequisites beyond 𝔰𝔩 2 .
(b) Complete theory. Part I (Chapters 1–8) read linearly, followed by the examples of Part II in any order.
(c) Braided/Yangian entry. Definition 2.8.3 → Chapter 24. This path foregrounds the E1 -factorization
    side: ordered configurations, 𝑅-matrices, and the DK ladder.

Part structure.
           Part               Character                                          Reading advice
           I Theory           Foundational; definitions, proofs, main theorems   Read linearly
           II Examples        Modular; each family self-contained                Read selectively
           III Connections    Perspective; physics, concordance, frontier        Read for context

Semantic levels. Every major statement is tagged at one of three levels (Convention 2.9.1): H-level
(homotopy-native, ∞-categorical), M-level (model-level, dg/bar-complex), S-level (shadow, cohomologi-
cal/numerical). Proofs operate at M-level; theorems are stated at H-level where possible; examples compute
S-level invariants. These tags are not ornamental: they prevent conflation of a dg model computation with
a model-independent theorem.

2.3    The selection principle
The bar construction of §2.2 is a geometric machine. Take a D 𝑋 -module 𝑉 equipped with a meromorphic
pairing 𝜇 : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉 ⊠ 𝑉 ) → Δ! (𝑉 ) (the OPE), place sections at points of the Fulton–MacPherson
compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), and extract residues along boundary divisors. The output is a graded object
𝐵 𝑋 (𝑉 , 𝜇) with a candidate differential 𝑑 = 𝑑internal + 𝑑residue + 𝑑dR .
   The question that governs the theory is:

             For which algebraic inputs (𝑉 , 𝜇) does the FM bar construction produce 𝑑 2 = 0?

Remark 2.3.1 (Classical vs. chiral selection). The bar construction asks the same question at every level of
geometry:

                        Base           Condition for 𝑑 2 = 0       Selected objects
                        Point          Jacobi identity             Lie algebras
                        Curve 𝑋        Borcherds identity          Chiral algebras
                        𝑋 over M 𝑔     + period corrections        Modular Koszul algebras

Each row is forced by the geometry of the next: the Jacobi identity handles triple collisions when all poles
are simple; on a curve, multiple pole orders mix at the codimension-2 strata of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), and the Borcherds
identity is the unique condition that makes this mixing consistent; at higher genus, period corrections
from the Hodge bundle restore 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0. Chiral algebras are what configuration space geometry accepts;
modular Koszul algebras are what the genus tower accepts.

2.4     The four theorems
The four theorems are not four parallel achievements. They are four determinations of the categorical
logarithm: existence, inversion, branch structure, and leading coefficient.
   Chapter 1 exhibits them before braiding enters. Chapter 24 shows what becomes new once ordered
factorization is part of the structure. Theorem A is proved in Chapter 6; Theorems B, C, D in Chapter 8.
• Theorem A (Geometric bar-cobar duality, Theorem 9.1.39). The bar functor

  composes into chiral twisting morphisms (A0 , Theorem 9.1.8), bar concentration (A1 , Theorem 9.1.38),
  and Verdier-geometric duality (A2 , Theorem 9.1.39). A BRST interpretation requires a specified state
  complex and a compatible map from the chiral construction. The Virasoro square and the augmentation
  obstruction are given in Chapter 30.
• Theorem B (Bar-cobar inversion, Theorem 8.17.4). On the Koszul locus, the counit Ω 𝑋 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) −
                                                                                                        ∼

  becomes curved; the failure is measured by Θ A (2.4). The displayed counit concerns the stated bar–cobar
  construction. A BRST resolution also requires its state-space comparison.
• Theorem C (Deformation-obstruction complementarity, Theorem 8.14.12). The ambient complex

At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ A measures the failure of strict commutativity;

(Chapter 30), and in every example of Part II.
    The Koszul locus is the convergence radius of the categorical logarithm. Off this locus, the coderived
category (Positselski [171]) provides analytic continuation: the curved bar complex is acyclic in the ordinary
derived category but retains its full homotopical content in the coderived category–-as the logarithm is
trivial on a simply-connected domain but carries monodromy on a multiply-connected one.

2.6     The total space
The nilpotence-periodicity correspondence becomes geometric in the total space of the universal configu-
ration fibration:
                                      𝜋 : 𝐶 𝑛 (C𝑔 ) −→ M 𝑔 .
Its fiber over [ Σ 𝑔 ] is 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ). The boundary has two types of divisors:
(a) Collision divisors 𝐷 𝐼 (vertical): marked points collide on a fixed smooth curve. These produce the bar
    differential.
(b) Degeneration divisors 𝛿Γ (horizontal): the curve acquires a node. These produce the period corrections
    that restore 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0.
At genus 0, only type (a) exists and the Arnold relation alone gives 𝑑02 = 0. At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, both coexist.

the period corrections live in 𝔼∨ ⊠ 𝔼. The scalar trace yields

2.7     Architecture
Remark 2.7.1 (Five geometric ingredients). Modular Koszul duality rests on five geometric ingredients. The
first four belong to the commutative (E∞ ) face; the fifth to the associative (E1 ) face.
90                                                                           Chapter 2. Introduction


   (i) Three-point collision. The Arnold relation (2.2) is factorization coherence: fusing three insertions
       does not depend on the order of pairwise collisions. The genus-0 seed.
  (ii) Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 ). 𝔻Ran 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) ≃ 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A ! ) (Theorem 9.1.39)–-the Koszul dual as theo-
       rem, not definition-by-analogy.
 (iii) Genus-1 curvature. 𝑑fib2 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 · id (Theorem 8.13.16). The natural home is Positselski’s
                                              1
       coderived category: quantum corrections are a change of ambient category, not extra terms.
 (iv) Clutching of stable curves. The genus tower is compatible with boundary clutching via the modular
       operad (Theorem 12.13.25). The combinatorics is stable graphs, not trees, and Θ A (Theorem 34.12.3,
       proved by Theorem 8.18.72) is compatible with clutching, trace, and Verdier duality.
  (v) Associative structure. The Yangian 𝑌 (𝔤) is E1 -chiral (Definition 2.8.3): its bar complex uses ordered
       configuration spaces, and Verdier duality acts by 𝑅-matrix inversion 𝑅 ↦→ 𝑅 −1 (Theorem 24.2.2).
       The sign flip ℏ ↦→ −ℏ replaces the Feigin–Frenkel involution.

In the Heisenberg algebra, only pieces (i)–(iv) are active, and they already force the full commuta-
tive/modular package: Arnold ensures 𝑑 2 = 0; Verdier produces H𝑘! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ); the genus-1 period
integral creates curvature 𝜅 = 1/𝑘 ; clutching assembles the genus tower.
In the Yangian, piece (v) becomes unavoidable. Ordered configurations, 𝑅-matrix inversion on the module
category, and the derived Drinfeld–Kohno bridge (Theorem 24.9.7) are not embellishments of the Heisen-
berg picture but the first genuinely braided determination of the same configuration-space mechanism.
The subject begins with Heisenberg because one should first see the mechanism before braiding enters,
and it extends to Yangian because the ordered world introduces a genuinely new geometric feature rather
than a different subject.

2.8     Dictionary: chiral algebra types and Koszul dualities
Collision geometry on a curve forces three levels of algebraic structure–-commutative (E∞ ), associative
(E1 ), semiclassical (P∞ )–-each carrying its own Koszul duality.
Deﬁnition 2.8.1 (E∞ -chiral algebra = vertex algebra). Throughout, 𝑘 = ℂ and 𝑋 is a smooth algebraic curve.
The ambient ∞-category is D-mod( 𝑋 ), equipped with the chiral tensor product ⊗ ch [2, §3.4]. Duality
means Verdier duality 𝔻 of holonomic D-modules (Remark 2.8.2).
    An E∞ -chiral algebra on 𝑋 is a commutative algebra in (D-mod( 𝑋 ) , ⊗ch ) (cf. [43, §5.1]). Equivalent
formulations: (a) D 𝑋 -module with chiral Lie bracket [2, §3.3]; (b) vertex algebra [10, §3.7] for 𝑋 = 𝔸1 ;
(c) factorization algebra on Ran( 𝑋 ) (Definition 4.10.3).
Remark 2.8.2 (Verdier versus linear duality). 𝔻(M) is the Verdier dual D-module, not the naïve linear
dual Hom𝑘 (M , 𝑘 ). The Koszul dual A ! is constructed via Verdier duality on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) (Theorem 6.3.32).
Deﬁnition 2.8.3 (E1 -chiral algebra = nonlocal vertex algebra). An E1 -chiral algebra on 𝑋 is an associative
(but not necessarily commutative) algebra over the associative chiral operad Assch (Definition 2.8.4): a D 𝑋 -
module A with binary chiral operation 𝜇 : A ⊗ ch A → Δ! A satisfying 𝜇 ◦ ( 𝜇 ⊗ id) = 𝜇 ◦ (id ⊗ 𝜇) but
not necessarily skew-symmetry. In vertex algebra language, a nonlocal vertex algebra (Li [134]; cf. [43, §4.1];
Beilinson–Drinfeld [2, Theorem 3.4.9]; Francis–Gaitsgory [26]).
Deﬁnition 2.8.4 (The associative chiral operad). The associative chiral operad Assch on 𝑋 is the non-Σ
chiral operad with Assch ( 𝑛) = Δ!( 𝑛 ) 𝜔 𝑋 , supported on the small diagonal without Σ𝑛 -action. Quadratic
presentation: Assch = Freech ( 𝜇)/( 𝜇 ◦1 𝜇 = 𝜇 ◦2 𝜇).

within the same operadic type.

Deﬁnition 2.8.6 (P∞ -chiral algebra = chiral Poisson). A P∞ -chiral algebra is an E∞ -chiral algebra with a

Remark 2.8.7 ( 𝐸𝑛 terminology). The subscripts E∞ , E1 , P∞ refer to the factorization level inside the BD
chiral tensor category. Bare 𝐸𝑛 and E𝑛 refer to little-disks algebras [43, §5.1]. An E1 -chiral algebra on a curve
is not a topological 𝐸1 -algebra; the suffix ‘‘-chiral’’ is load-bearing.
   The hierarchy E∞ -chiral ⊂ P∞ -chiral ⊂ E1 -chiral. Deformation quantization passes from P∞ to E1 .
Bar-cobar duality operates at each level: E∞ computes factorization homology; E1 connects to Yangians and
quantum groups (Chapter 24).
Remark 2.8.8 (Operadic hierarchy and conﬁguration spaces). The hierarchy is organized by the geometry
of insertion points:

     Algebra type              Operad                   Configuration space          Koszul exchange
     Heisenberg, KM, Vir, W    E∞ (comm.)               𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) unordered           type exchange A ↔ A !
     Lattice VOA               E∞ with E1 sublattice    𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) with monodromy      type exchange + screening
     Yangian 𝑌 (𝔤)             E1 (assoc.)              Conf ord
                                                              𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) ordered        𝑅-matrix inversion
     Elliptic QG               modular deformation      Conf on 𝐸𝜏                   elliptic 𝑅-inversion

The progression from E∞ to E1 is not ‘‘more generality’’; it is a change in the geometry of collision, from
symmetric to ordered, with correspondingly different Koszul exchange mechanisms.

2.9     Conventions
Convention 2.9.1 (Semantic levels: homotopy, model, shadow). H-level (homotopy/native). The statement
in the stable ∞-category of factorization (co)algebras on Ran( 𝑋 ), or in the associated formal moduli /
shifted-symplectic language. Defined up to contractible ambiguity.
M-level (model). An explicit dg / 𝐿∞ / filtered complex. The geometric bar complex 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) =
(𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā) , 𝑑 ) built from configuration space integrals on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is the canonical model.
S-level (shadow). The cohomological, Ext, numerical, or generating-function consequence: bar cohomol-
ogy dimensions, Hilbert series, 𝜅 (A), free energies 𝐹𝑔 (A).
Notation.
• ≃ : equivalence in the homotopy/∞-categorical sense (H-level).
•  : strict isomorphism of chosen dg models (M-level).
• = : definition or literal equality only.
The proved results (Remark 2.1) are proved at M-level and stated at H-level.
Model independence. Any two admissible dg presentations are connected by a contractible space of
quasi-isomorphisms (Proposition 6.2.52).
Convention 2.9.2 (Regime tags). Four regimes, in order of increasing generality:
  (i) Quadratic. Simple poles only; 𝑑02 = 0; Theorems A–D hold without qualification. Heisenberg, free
      fermions, lattice VOAs.
                         2 = 𝜅 · 𝜔 ; 𝐷 2 = 0. 𝔤
 (ii) Curved-central. 𝑑fib                    b𝑘 at non-critical level, Virasoro with 𝑐 ≠ 0.
                                  𝑔     𝑔
 (iii) Filtered-complete. Complete filtration with gr 𝐹 A quadratic Koszul. W-algebras via DS reduction,
       deformation quantizations.
 (iv) Programmatic. Stratum II (Remark 2.1); stated as conjectures. Derived DK, 𝔼𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 2.
The four regimes correspond to increasing monodromy of the categorical logarithm: single-valued, scalar
curvature, filtered convergence, full structure.
Convention 2.9.3 (Standing assumptions). (SA1) Ground field ℂ. All vector spaces, algebras, and cate-
      gories are over ℂ.
(SA2) Cohomological grading: | 𝑑 | = +1. See Appendix H.
(SA3) Formal power series in completed tensor products. Configuration space integrals converge abso-
      lutely on FM compactifications (Theorem 5.5.16).
(SA4) Smooth projective geometrically connected curves over ℂ.
(SA5) Completed chiral algebras at genus 𝑔 ≥ 1 (Appendix P).

The Fourier seed

The bar construction is a one-dimensional non-abelian Fourier transform. Its kernel is the logarithmic
propagator on configuration spaces; its output is a factorization coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ). Four explicit evalu-
ations of increasing complexity–-a point, two curves, and one non-abelian family–-exhibit the transform
before the general theory of Chapter 6.

3.3      Specialization to a point
Theorem 3.3.1 (Specialization; [proved]). Let 𝑋 = Spec 𝑘 . Then:
   (i) 𝐶 𝑛 (Spec 𝑘 ) = Spec 𝑘 for all 𝑛.
  (ii) Ω• ( 𝐶 𝑛 , log 𝐷 ) = 𝑘 (no forms, no propagator).
 (iii) 𝑑dR = 0 and 𝑑res reduces to the binary bracket differential.
 (iv) 𝐵 𝑋 (A) reduces to 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā , 𝑑bracket ), the classical bar construction of Loday–Vallette [135, §2.2].

Proof. Items (1)–(3) are immediate: Spec 𝑘 has no nontrivial configuration geometry. For (4), the general
three-component differential 𝑑 = 𝑑int + 𝑑res + 𝑑dR collapses to 𝑑int + 𝑑res when 𝑋 = Spec 𝑘 . The residue
3.4. The four properties                                                                                   103


component 𝑑res at 𝑋 = Spec 𝑘 extracts only the leading OPE coefficient, which on a point is the binary
product. The result is the classical bar construction 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā , 𝑑2 ) with the standard bar differential.

Remark 3.3.2. The entire theory of operadic Koszul duality (Loday–Vallette [135]) is the zero-dimensional
shadow of the chiral bar-cobar theory. Every classical theorem–-bar-cobar adjunction, Koszul criterion,
PBW theorem–-lifts to a genus-sensitive statement on curves, with the configuration space geometry
providing the lift.

3.4    The four properties
Theorem 3.4.1 (The four properties of the Fourier transform; [proved]). The bar construction 𝐵 𝑋 ,
viewed as a non-abelian Fourier transform, has four structural properties corresponding to Theorems A–D
of this monograph:
(A) Intertwining. 𝔻Ran ◦ 𝐵 𝑋 ≃ 𝐵 𝑋 ◦ (−) ! (Theorem 9.1.39). Verdier duality intertwines the bar of A
    with the bar of the Koszul dual A ! .
                                                 ∼
(B) Inversion. On the Koszul locus, Ω ( 𝐵 (A)) −−→ A (Theorem 8.17.4). The cobar construction inverts
    the transform.
(C) Plancherel. 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) ≃ 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 A ) (Theorem 8.14.12). The deformation and obstruc-
    tion complexes form complementary Lagrangians.
(D) Characteristic function. 𝜅 (A) determines the genus expansion; its generating function is the 𝐴ˆ-genus
    (Theorem 8.18.30).

Chapter 4


Algebraic foundations and bar constructions

This chapter fixes the operadic prerequisites for the bar-cobar adjunction 𝐵¯ ⊣ Ω.

4.1     Classical Koszul duality
4.1.1  Quadratic algebras and Koszul duality
Deﬁnition 4.1.1 (Quadratic algebra). A graded algebra 𝐴 = 𝑇 (𝑉 )/ 𝐼 is quadratic if:
   (i) 𝑉 is a graded vector space (generators)
  (ii) 𝐼 ⊂ 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 is a subspace of relations in degree 2
 (iii) The defining ideal is ( 𝐼 ) generated by 𝐼
We write 𝐴 = 𝐴 (𝑉 , 𝑅) where 𝑅 ⊂ 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 are the relations. The algebra carries a canonical augmentation

4.1.3   Koszul pairs: precise definition
Deﬁnition 4.1.5 (Koszul pair). A pair of quadratic algebras ( 𝐴1 , 𝐴2 ) is a Koszul pair if:
   (i) 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴1 ) ≃ 𝐴!2 (as coalgebras)
  (ii) 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴2 ) ≃ 𝐴!1 (as coalgebras)
 (iii) Ω ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴1 )) ≃ 𝐴1 (cobar inverts bar)
 (iv) Ω ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴2 )) ≃ 𝐴2 (cobar inverts bar)
Deﬁnition 4.1.6 (Koszul locus). An augmented chiral algebra A (Definition 4.3.3) lies on the Koszul locus
if the bar coalgebra 𝐵 𝑋 (A) is formal: quasi-isomorphic to its cohomology, which is concentrated in bar
degree 1.
    Formality is the convergence condition for the categorical logarithm. Four equivalent formulations
(Theorem 9.1.25):
(a) Spectral: the PBW spectral sequence, induced by the conformal weight filtration on 𝐵 𝑋 (A), degen-
    erates at 𝐸2 .
                                                           ∼
(b) Resolution: the cobar–bar counit Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵 𝑋 (A)) −     → A is a quasi-isomorphism.
(c) Concentration: 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵 𝑋 (A)) is concentrated in bar degree 1.
(d) Acyclicity: the twisted tensor product 𝐵 𝑋 (A) ⊗𝜋 A ! , formed with the universal twisting morphism 𝜋
    (Proposition 4.1.12(i), Definition 4.1.11), is acyclic.
Off the Koszul locus, the bar complex is curved and lives in the coderived category (Appendix P.11.2); the
logarithm has monodromy.
The chiral analogue is not defined by bar-cobar inversion directly. Instead, Chapter 9 introduces a chiral
twisting datum (Definition 9.1.1) and a Koszul twisting morphism (Theorem 9.1.8) as antecedent recogni-
tion data; bar-cobar identifications are then proved as consequences on the Koszul locus. The full chiral
Koszul pair is Definition 9.1.14 (previewed in §4.1.5 below); the E1 -chiral version appears in Theorem 9.5.4;
the modular (higher-genus) refinement is Definition 8.18.7 (Chapter 8).
Remark 4.1.7 (Two phenomena). Conditions (1)–(2) establish Koszul duality: bar of 𝐴1 produces the dual
coalgebra to 𝐴2 , and vice versa. Conditions (3)–(4) establish bar-cobar inversion: Ω ◦ 𝐵¯ is homotopy
equivalent to the identity. These are logically independent.

sense of Definition 4.1.5:
   (i) (Sym(𝑉 ) , Λ (𝑉 ∗ )) — commutative and exterior algebras

   The chiral enhancement appears in Chapter 1 (Heisenberg, double pole), §18.1 (free fermions, simple

4.1.5    Chiral Koszul pairs: preview
Definition 4.1.5 extends to chiral algebras (Definition 4.3.3) via a two-step formulation: the construction of
bar and cobar exists for all augmented chiral algebras (Definition 9.1.1), while the Koszul recognition criterion
identifies when these constructions yield resolutions (Definition 9.1.3; full treatment: Definition 9.1.14,
Chapter 9).
   The chiral Koszul pair structure has three layers (cf. Definition 9.1.14, Chapter 9):
  (i) Construction layer: For every augmented chiral algebra A, the bar construction 𝐵¯ ch (A) and cobar
      construction Ωch ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)) exist as objects (Definition 9.1.1).
  (ii) Recognition layer: A chiral twisting datum (A , C , 𝜏, 𝐹• ) satisfying PBW degeneration and acyclicity
       of twisted tensor products provides antecedent Koszul recognition data (Definition 9.1.3).
 (iii) Theorem layer: For a chiral Koszul pair (A1 , A2 ), Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39) proves 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) ≃
       A2! and Ωch (A 𝑖! ) ≃ A 𝑖 as consequences of the recognition data, not as definitions.
Off the Koszul locus, the bar-cobar object persists only in the completed coderived category
(Appendix P.11.2).
   The correspondence between twisting morphisms and GLZ Maurer–Cartan elements is Proposi-
tion 4.1.16(iii).

4.1.6    Twisting morphisms: the fundamental object
The single algebraic structure underlying bar-cobar duality, Koszul resolutions, and the modular genus
tower is the convolution dg Lie algebra Hom( 𝐶, 𝐴); its Maurer–Cartan elements are the twisting mor-
phisms. We give the classical theory ([135, §2.1–2.3]) before the chiral generalization (Chapter 9); the modular
extension appears in Remark 4.1.14.
Deﬁnition 4.1.9 (Convolution dg Lie algebra). Let ( 𝐶, Δ, 𝑑𝐶 ) be a conilpotent dg coalgebra and ( 𝐴, 𝜇, 𝑑 𝐴 )
a dg algebra. The convolution algebra Hom( 𝐶, 𝐴) is the graded vector space of all linear maps 𝐶 → 𝐴,
equipped with:
   (i) the convolution product 𝑓 ★ 𝑔 := 𝜇 ◦ ( 𝑓 ⊗ 𝑔 ) ◦ Δ;
  (ii) the differential 𝜕 ( 𝑓 ) := 𝑑 𝐴 ◦ 𝑓 − (−1) | 𝑓 | 𝑓 ◦ 𝑑𝐶 ;
 (iii) the Lie bracket [ 𝑓 , 𝑔 ] := 𝑓 ★ 𝑔 − (−1) | 𝑓 | | 𝑔 | 𝑔 ★ 𝑓 .
The triple (Hom( 𝐶, 𝐴) , [−, −] , 𝜕 ) is a dg Lie algebra [135, Proposition 2.1.1].
Deﬁnition 4.1.10 (Twisting morphism). A twisting morphism 𝜏 : 𝐶 → 𝐴 is a degree-+1 linear map (degree
−1 in the homological convention of [135]) satisfying the Maurer–Cartan equation in the convolution
algebra (Definition 4.1.9):

                  𝜕 ( 𝜏 ) + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0,      i.e.,   𝑑 𝐴 ◦ 𝜏 + 𝜏 ◦ 𝑑𝐶 + 𝜇 𝐴 ◦ ( 𝜏 ⊗ 𝜏 ) ◦ Δ𝐶 = 0.           (4.1)

The set of all twisting morphisms is Tw( 𝐶, 𝐴) := MC(Hom( 𝐶, 𝐴)) [135, §2.1].

Remark 4.1.17 (Complementarity of the two approaches). The GLZ algebraic framework provides concep-
tual clarity for quadratic algebras; the geometric framework of this monograph extends to non-quadratic
examples (Virasoro, W-algebras, Yangian) via configuration space integrals, at the cost of more involved
compactification and convergence analysis.

4.2       Symmetric sequences and operads
We work in V = Chℂ , cochain complexes over ℂ with cohomological grading (| 𝑑 | = +1) and Koszul sign
rule (Convention 2.9.3).
Deﬁnition 4.2.1 (Symmetric sequence). A symmetric sequence is a collection 𝑃 = { 𝑃 ( 𝑛)}𝑛 ≥0 where each
𝑃 ( 𝑛) is an object of V equipped with a right action of the symmetric group 𝑆𝑛 . Morphisms of symmetric
sequences are collections of 𝑆𝑛 -equivariant maps. When V carries a differential structure, we require that
the 𝑆𝑛 -action commutes with differentials.

defined by:

where 𝑗 : 𝑋 2 \ Δ ↩→ 𝑋 2 is the complement of the diagonal and Δ! = Δ∗ ◦ D 𝑋 → 𝑋 2 is the D-module
pushforward. The three axioms are:
   (i) Locality: 𝜇 factors through 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ –- the product is meromorphic with poles only along the diagonal.
  (ii) Associativity: the Borcherds identity –- the unique algebraic condition under which the FM bar
       construction produces 𝑑 2 = 0 (§2.3).
 (iii) Unit: an embedding 𝜔 𝑋 ↩→ A (the vacuum).
Axiom (ii) is the selection principle: it is not imposed by fiat but forced by the boundary stratification of
𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) (§2.3).
    An augmented chiral algebra carries a splitting 𝜀 : A → 𝜔 𝑋 of the unit; the augmentation ideal is Ā =
ker( 𝜀 ). The operator product expansion 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑏 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑛 ≥0 𝑐𝑛 ( 𝑤 )/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 𝑛+1 is the mode expansion
                                                           P
of 𝜇. The chiral bracket { 𝑎, 𝑏 } = 𝑐0 extracts the simple-pole residue; the full product 𝜇 involves all pole
orders (Convention 6.0.4). The complete formulation, with the twisting datum needed for the Koszul
pair structure, is Definition 9.1.1 (Chapter 9).
Theorem 4.3.4 (Chiral algebras on Ran space; [proved]). (Beilinson–Drinfeld [2, Chapter 3])
  A chiral algebra A on 𝑋 (Definition 4.3.3) determines a D-module FA on Ran( 𝑋 ) satisfying:
   (i) Factorization: FA ( 𝑆 ⊔ 𝑇 ) = FA ( 𝑆 ) ⊗ FA (𝑇 )
  (ii) Compatibility with embeddings
 (iii) D-module structure encoding OPEs
   The bar-cobar duality acts on these sheaves on Ran space, realizing NAP duality for factorization
algebras.
Deﬁnition 4.3.5 (Operad). An operad 𝑃 is a monoid for the composition product: composition maps
𝛾 : 𝑃 ( 𝑘 ) ⊗ 𝑃 ( 𝑖1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑃 ( 𝑖𝑘 ) → 𝑃 ( 𝑖1 + · · · + 𝑖𝑘 ) and unit 𝜂 : 𝕀 → 𝑃 (1), satisfying associativity and
𝑆𝑛 -equivariance. In V = Chℂ , all structure maps are chain maps.
Deﬁnition 4.3.6 (Cooperad). A cooperad is a comonoid for the composition product, with structure maps
dual to those of an operad. Explicitly, we have decomposition maps Δ : 𝐶 ( 𝑛) → ( 𝐶 ◦ 𝐶 ) ( 𝑛) and a counit
𝜖 : 𝐶 → 𝕀 satisfying coassociativity and coequivariance axioms.

with composition given by substitution of multilinear operations. This is the fundamental example moti-

4.4.1   The fundamental bar-cobar isomorphism
Remark 4.4.3 (Operadic Koszul pairs). The operadic version of Definition 4.1.5 replaces algebras by operads,
generator duality by collection duality, and relation orthogonality by the operadic Koszul dual cooperad
𝑃 ! = maximal sub-cooperad of F 𝑐 (𝑉 ∗ ) cogenerated by 𝑅⊥ (see Chapter 9 for the chiral analog).
Example 4.4.4 (Com-Lie: the prototypical Koszul pair). For the commutative and Lie operads:
• Generators: 𝜇 ∈ Com(2) (commutative product) and ℓ ∈ Lie(2) (Lie bracket)
• Pairing: ⟨ 𝜇, ℓ ⟩ = 1 (canonical pairing between symmetry and antisymmetry)
• Bar-cobar isomorphisms:

                      𝐵 (Com) ≃ coLie (partition complex gives Lie cooperad)
                        𝐵 (Lie) ≃ coCom (Chevalley–Eilenberg gives Com cooperad)
                     Ω (coLie) ≃ Com (cobar reconstructs commutative structure)
                   Ω (coCom) ≃ Lie (cobar reconstructs Lie structure)

  Concretely: the bar complex of the commutative operad is the chain complex of the partition lattice,
whose homology is precisely the Lie operad (with sign).
Remark 4.4.5 (Two levels of Koszul duality). Koszul duality operates at two distinct levels:
 (a) Operadic level: the operad 𝑃 itself has a Koszul dual cooperad 𝑃 ! = 𝑃 ¡,∗ (e.g. Com! = Lie). This
     governs the type of algebraic structure.
4.5. The operadic bar-cobar duality                                                                        113


(b) Algebraic level: a 𝑃 -algebra 𝐴 has a bar coalgebra 𝐵 ( 𝐴) (the Koszul dual coalgebra; Convention 6.0.3).
    This governs the speciﬁc duality for a given algebra.
In the chiral setting, both levels are active simultaneously. The operadic structure supplies the geometry
(FM compactification, Arnold relation, logarithmic forms); the algebraic structure supplies the OPE data
(generators, relations, pole orders). The bar construction weaves them together: it places OPE data on the
operadic geometry and extracts residues. The result is a factorization coalgebra that encodes both the type
of structure (commutative, associative, Lie) and the specific algebra A. Inversion holds on the Koszul locus
(Definition 4.1.6).

4.7     Quadratic operads and Koszul duality
Deﬁnition 4.7.1 (Quadratic operad). A quadratic operad has the form 𝑃 = Free( 𝐸 )/( 𝑅) where 𝐸 is a
collection of generating operations in arity 2, 𝑅 ⊂ Free( 𝐸 ) (3) consists of quadratic relations, and ( 𝑅) is
the operadic ideal generated by 𝑅.
Deﬁnition 4.7.2 (Koszul dual cooperad). The Koszul dual cooperad 𝑃 ! is the maximal sub-cooperad of
the cofree cooperad 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 𝐸 ∨ ) cogenerated by the orthogonal relations 𝑅⊥ ⊂ ( 𝑠 −1 𝐸 ∨ ) ⊗2 , where the
orthogonality is with respect to the natural pairing induced by evaluation.
Deﬁnition 4.7.3 (Koszul operad). An operad 𝑃 is Koszul if the canonical map Ω ( 𝑃 ! ) → 𝑃 is a quasi-
isomorphism. Equivalently, the Koszul complex 𝐾• ( 𝑃 ) = 𝑃 ! ◦ 𝑃 with differential induced by the cooperad
and operad structures is acyclic in positive degrees.

4.8     Derivation of Com-Lie duality
Theorem 4.8.1 (Com-Lie Koszul duality; [proved]). We have canonical isomorphisms of operads:

                                      Com!  Lie      and    Lie!  Com

At the cooperad level, 𝐵 ( Com) ≃ coLie and 𝐵 ( Lie) ≃ coCom. Moreover, both Com and Lie are Koszul
operads with quasi-isomorphisms:
                                              ∼                         ∼
                                  Ω (coLie) −
                                            → Com,        Ω (coCom) −
                                                                    → Lie

Proof via partition lattices. By Theorem 12.13.38, 𝐵 ( Com) ( 𝑛) ≃ 𝑠 𝑛−1 𝐶˜∗ ( Π 𝑛 ) ⊗ sgn𝑛 .
   Classical results of Björner–Wachs [9] and Stanley [14] establish that the reduced homology of Π 𝑛 is:
• The order complex | Π 𝑛 | has dimension 𝑛 − 3 (maximal chains in Π 𝑛 have length 𝑛 − 3)
• 𝐻˜ 𝑘 ( Π 𝑛 ) = 0 for 𝑘 ≠ 𝑛 − 3 (homology concentrated in the top degree)
• The 𝑆𝑛 -representation on 𝐻˜ 𝑛−3 ( Π 𝑛 ) is Lie ( 𝑛) ⊗ sgn𝑛 where Lie ( 𝑛) is the Lie representation
4.9. The quadratic dual and orthogonality                                                                    115


   The geometric realization | Π 𝑛 | is homotopy equivalent to a wedge of ( 𝑛 − 1)! spheres of dimension
𝑛 − 3, with the 𝑆𝑛 -action on the top homology given by the Lie representation tensored with the sign.
   For Com-Lie duality, the bar construction gives:

                                       𝐵 ( Com) ( 𝑛) ≃ 𝑠 𝑛−1 𝐶˜∗ ( Π 𝑛 ) ⊗ sgn𝑛

         𝐻∗ ( 𝐵 ( Com) ( 𝑛)) ≃ 𝑠 𝑛−1 𝐻˜ 𝑛−3 ( Π 𝑛 ) ⊗ sgn𝑛 = 𝑠 𝑛−1 Lie ( 𝑛) ⊗ sgn𝑛 ⊗ sgn𝑛 = 𝑠 𝑛−1 Lie ( 𝑛)

Since this is concentrated in a single degree, the bar complex is formal and we obtain 𝐵 ( Com) ≃ coLie,
where the arity-dependent shift 𝑠 𝑛−1 is absorbed into the cooperadic convention coLie ( 𝑛) := 𝑠 𝑛−1 Lie ( 𝑛)
(LV12, §7.2). Applying Ω yields Ω (coLie) ≃ Com.
   The dual statement Lie!  coCom follows by Schur–Weyl duality, using the characterization of Lie as
the primitive part of the tensor coalgebra.

Alternative proof via generating series. The Poincaré series of the operads satisfy:

                                                𝑃Lie ( 𝑥 ) = − log(1 − 𝑥 )

dual pairs, providing an independent verification of the duality.

4.10        Factorization algebra axioms: verification
4.10.1      Motivation
Construction 4.10.1 (Conﬁguration space realization). A factorization algebra F on a manifold 𝑀 assigns
to each open 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑀 a vector space F (𝑈 ) satisfying F (𝑈 ⊔ 𝑉 )  F (𝑈 ) ⊗ F (𝑉 ) and the colimit
reconstruction

                  F (𝑈 ) = colim ( 𝑥1 ,...,𝑥𝑛 ) ∈ 𝐶𝑛 (𝑈 ) F (disk around 𝑥1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ F (disk around 𝑥𝑛 )

over the configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) = {( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑛 ) ∈ 𝑀 𝑛 : 𝑥 𝑖 ≠ 𝑥𝑗 }. Factorization algebras on ℝ𝑛 are
equivalent to 𝐸𝑛 -algebras [43, Theorem 5.4.5.9].

4.10.2      Weiss topology and factorization algebras
The cosheaf condition defining factorization algebras requires a topology finer than the ordinary open-
cover topology. The correct notion, introduced by Weiss [123] in the context of manifold calculus and
adopted by Costello–Gwilliam [27], is the following.
Deﬁnition 4.10.2 (Weiss cover). Let 𝑀 be a topological space. A collection {𝑈𝑖 } 𝑖 ∈ 𝐼 of open subsets of 𝑀
is a Weiss cover of an open 𝑉 ⊂ 𝑀 if every ﬁnite subset 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑉 is contained in some single 𝑈𝑖 .
   The Weiss topology on Opens( 𝑀 ) is the Grothendieck topology whose covering families are exactly
the Weiss covers. A prefactorization algebra that satisfies descent for the Weiss topology is a factorization
algebra.

with values in V consists of:
   Data.

                                         𝜇𝑉𝑈1 ,...,𝑈𝑛 : F (𝑈1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ F (𝑈𝑛 ) → F (𝑉 ) .

      (FA1) Functoriality. The assignment 𝑈 ↦→ F (𝑈 ) is a functor from Opens( 𝑀 ) to V:

4.10.4    Chiral algebras as factorization algebras
Theorem 4.10.4 (Chiral algebras are factorization algebras; [proved]). (Beilinson–Drinfeld [2,
Theorem 3.4.9, §3.4.10–3.4.12])
    Let 𝑋 be a smooth algebraic curve over ℂ. Every chiral algebra A on 𝑋 in the sense of [2, §3.3] determines
a factorization algebra of D-modules on Ran( 𝑋 ) satisfying axioms (FA1)–(FA5). More precisely, the
functor
                                 A ↦−→ FA ,          FA (𝑈 ) = Γ (𝑈 , A) ,
defines an equivalence between the category of chiral algebras on 𝑋 and the category of factorization
algebras of D-modules on Ran( 𝑋 ).
Remark 4.10.5 (Categorical distinction). Although Theorem 4.10.4 establishes an equivalence of categories,
the two notions have different signatures and live in different ambient categories:
• A chiral algebra (Definition 4.3.3) is a D 𝑋 -module on the curve 𝑋 equipped with a chiral product 𝜇.
• A factorization algebra (Definition 4.10.3) is a cosheaf on Ran( 𝑋 ) with multiplicative structure.
The bar construction (Chapter 6) produces a factorization coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ) (Convention 6.0.3): it
lives on the factorization side of the equivalence. When the chiral perspective is needed (e.g. for the OPE,
the pole decomposition, the Borcherds identity), we work with the chiral product 𝜇; when the geometric
perspective is needed (e.g. for Verdier duality, factorization homology, the Ran-space structure), we work
with the factorization coalgebra 𝐵 𝑋 (A). The equivalence of Theorem 4.10.4 ensures that no information
is lost in the translation.

             Multiplicativity (FA2)           Factorization isomorphism      [2, (3.4.4.2)]
             Coherence (FA3)                  Higher compatibilities         [2, Proposition 3.4.2]
             𝑆𝑛 -equivariance (FA5)           Equivariant structure          [2, §3.4]
             Chiral product 𝜇                 Chiral operation 𝜇ch           [2, §3.3.1]
             Configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )     𝑛-th stratum of Ran( 𝑋 )       [2, §3.4.10–3.4.12]

      The translation proceeds as follows:
   (i) BD’s factorization isomorphism A|𝑈1 ⊔···⊔𝑈𝑛  A|𝑈1 ⊠ · · · ⊠ A|𝑈𝑛 ([2, (3.4.4.2)]) is precisely our
       axiom (FA2), with ⊠ the external tensor product of D-modules on disjoint opens reducing to the
       ordinary tensor product on global sections.
  (ii) Coherence of the factorization isomorphisms ([2, Proposition 3.4.2]) gives axiom (FA3).
 (iii) The 𝑆𝑛 -equivariance built into BD’s definition ([2, §3.4]) gives axiom (FA5).
 (iv) Axioms (FA1) and (FA4) are the presheaf and unit conditions, which are part of the D-module
       structure.
   The remaining content of this monograph–-in particular the bar-cobar constructions via configuration
space integrals on Fulton–MacPherson compactifications–-provides an explicit geometric realization of
the factorization structure, which is not contained in [2].

4.10.5      Gluing formulas and excision
Theorem 4.10.7 (Excision property; [proved]). (Costello–Gwilliam [27, §6.3]; Lurie [43, Theo-
rem 5.5.3.11])
   Let F be a factorization algebra on 𝑀 , and let 𝑀 = 𝑈 ∪ 𝑉 be a Weiss cover (i.e., every finite subset of
𝑀 is contained in 𝑈 or in 𝑉 ). Then there is a natural equivalence:

                                       F ( 𝑀 ) ≃ F (𝑈 ) ⊗ F (𝑈 ∩𝑉 ) F (𝑉 )

where the tensor product is the derived pushout over F (𝑈 ∩ 𝑉 ).
   For locally constant factorization algebras ( 𝐸𝑛 -algebras), excision holds more generally for collar-gluing
decompositions of manifolds, without the Weiss hypothesis [43, Theorem 5.5.3.11].

Proof. This is a special case of the cosheaf property for Weiss covers (Theorem 4.10.8 below) applied to the
two-element Weiss cover {𝑈 ,𝑉 }. The pushout diagram

                                              𝑈 ∩𝑉             𝑉


                                                 𝑈             𝑀

in Opens( 𝑀 ) is sent by F to a pushout in the target category by the descent condition for Weiss covers.
4.10. Factorization algebra axioms: verification                                                             119


4.10.6    Cosheaf property
Theorem 4.10.8 (Factorization algebras are cosheaves for Weiss covers; [proved]). (Costello–
Gwilliam [27, Theorem 6.3.1])
    A prefactorization algebra F on 𝑀 is a factorization algebra if and only if it satisfies the cosheaf property
for Weiss covers: for every Weiss cover {𝑈𝑖 } 𝑖 ∈ 𝐼 of an open 𝑉 ⊂ 𝑀 (Definition 4.10.2), the natural map
                                                             ∼
                                       hocolim𝐶ˇ ( {𝑈𝑖 } ) F −−→ F (𝑉 )

is an equivalence, where the homotopy colimit is taken over the Čech nerve of the Weiss cover.
Remark 4.10.9 (Weiss covers versus ordinary covers). Ordinary open covers detect only single-point behavior.
Weiss covers ensure every finite configuration is witnessed by a single open, so the cosheaf condition for
Weiss covers is exactly equivalent to (FA1)–(FA5) with descent [27, Proposition 6.3.4].

Configuration spaces

The propagators 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) from the Heisenberg bar complex (Chapter 1) live on Fulton–
MacPherson compactifications; the Arnold relations among triple collisions force 𝑑 2 = 0.

5.1      Fulton–MacPherson compactification
The Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) adds boundary divisors encoding all collision patterns.
Verdier duality exchanges logarithmic forms (bar) and distributions (cobar), realizing 𝔻Ran 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) ≃
𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A ! ) at the chain level.

5.1.1     Explicit construction
Deﬁnition 5.1.1 (Conﬁguration space at genus 𝑔 ). For a Riemann surface Σ 𝑔 of genus 𝑔 , the configuration
space of 𝑛 distinct ordered points is:

                           𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) = {( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑛 ) ∈ Σ𝑛𝑔 | 𝑥 𝑖 ≠ 𝑥𝑗 for all 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 }
      This is an open dense subset of Σ𝑛𝑔 , with complement the ‘‘fat diagonal’’ Δ =                𝑖 <𝑗 Δ 𝑖𝑗 .

5.1.2  The Fulton–MacPherson compactification across genera
The configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) is non-compact. The Fulton–MacPherson compactification [12] resolves
this by iterated blow-ups along diagonals, recording collision rates and angles in exceptional divisors. For a
logarithmic variant on punctured and nodal curves, see Mok [210].
5.1.2.1 Iterated blow-up construction
Theorem 5.1.2 (Fulton–MacPherson compactification at genus 𝑔 [12]; [proved]). There exists a
canonical smooth compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) constructed via iterated blow-ups. More precisely:
  (i) There is a natural open embedding

       with dense image.
  (ii) The compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) is smooth and proper over ℂ; as a blow-up of the smooth projective
       variety Σ𝑛𝑔 along smooth centers, it is itself a smooth projective variety.
 (iii) The complement 𝐷 = 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) \ 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) is a normal crossing divisor, i.e., locally analytically isomor-
       phic to coordinate hyperplanes.
 (iv) The boundary admits a natural stratification:

      | 𝑆𝑗 | ≥ 2.

5.1.2.2 Boundary stratification and stable curves
At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the boundary has additional structure beyond just point collisions:
Theorem 5.1.4 (Boundary strata of M 𝑔 ,𝑛 [143, 144]; [proved]). For the Deligne–Mumford–
Knudsen moduli space M 𝑔,𝑛 (which serves as the universal compactified configuration space), the
boundary 𝜕 M 𝑔,𝑛 consists of:
124                                                                     Chapter 5. Configuration spaces


   (i) Collision strata: 𝐷 𝑆 where points in subset 𝑆 collide (as in genus 0)
  (ii) Degeneration strata: 𝐷 Γ where the curve degenerates to a stable nodal curve of genus 𝑔 with dual
       graph Γ
    The Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) of a ﬁxed smooth curve Σ 𝑔 has only collision strata
–- no curve degeneration occurs. The degeneration strata appear when one works with the universal family
over M 𝑔 , i.e., when the underlying curve is allowed to vary and degenerate.

Proof. There is a natural forgetful map:

                                                 M 𝑔,𝑛 −−→ M 𝑔

that forgets the marked points and stabilizes. Over the interior M 𝑔 , the fiber 𝜋 −1 ( [ Σ 𝑔 ]) is the FM com-
pactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ). The full boundary 𝜕 M 𝑔,𝑛 decomposes according to two mechanisms.
     (1) Collision strata. For a subset 𝑆 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑛} with | 𝑆 | ≥ 2, the stratum 𝐷 𝑆 parameterizes configura-

divisor 𝐷 𝑆  𝐶 | 𝑆 | (ℂ) × 𝐶 𝑛− | 𝑆 |+1 ( Σ 𝑔 ), which records the relative positions and directions of approach
of the colliding points. This is exactly the genus-0 construction applied to a local coordinate neighborhood
of the collision point, and the resulting strata have normal crossings (Theorem 5.1.11).
     (2) Degeneration strata. These arise from the boundary of M 𝑔 , not from point collisions. A boundary

Remark 5.1.7 (Connection to moduli of stable curves). For a fixed smooth curve Σ 𝑔 , stabilization gives a
map 𝜋 : 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) → M 𝑔,𝑛 sending ( 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 ) ↦→ [ Σ 𝑔 ; 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 ] st . Its image lies in the closure of
the locus of curves isomorphic to Σ 𝑔 , and over boundary strata the bubble tree structure maps to the
nodal curve structure. This underlies the modular properties of chiral correlators and the identification of
conformal anomalies with failure of sections to extend over the boundary.

5.1.3     Stratification
5.1.3.1 Incidence relations and poset structure
Deﬁnition 5.1.12 (Stratiﬁcation poset). Define a partial order on partitions 𝜋 ∈ Π𝑛≥2 :

                          𝜋 ≤ 𝜋 ′ ⇐⇒ every part of 𝜋 is contained in some part of 𝜋 ′

      Equivalently: 𝜋 ≤ 𝜋 ′ means " 𝜋 is a refinement of 𝜋 ′ ."
      The boundary strata satisfy:
                                           𝐷 𝜋 ⊆ 𝐷 𝜋 ′ ⇐⇒ 𝜋 ≤ 𝜋 ′
where 𝐷 𝜋 ′ is the closure of 𝐷 𝜋 ′ .
Example 5.1.13 (Poset for 𝑛 = 3). For 𝑛 = 3, the partitions (with at least one part of size ≥ 2) are:
• 𝜋1 = (12|3): points 1,2 collide, 3 separate

• 𝜋2 = (13|2): points 1,3 collide, 2 separate
• 𝜋3 = (23|1): points 2,3 collide, 1 separate
• 𝜋4 = (123): all three collide
   The partial order:
                                                 𝜋1 , 𝜋2 , 𝜋3 < 𝜋4
(any pairwise collision is refined by the triple collision)
   The closure relations:

                                                𝐷 𝜋1 = 𝐷 𝜋1 ∪ 𝐷 𝜋4
                                                𝐷 𝜋2 = 𝐷 𝜋2 ∪ 𝐷 𝜋4
                                                𝐷 𝜋3 = 𝐷 𝜋3 ∪ 𝐷 𝜋4

   Geometrically: the triple collision 𝐷 𝜋4 lies in the closure of each pairwise collision divisor.

Proof. The closure relation follows from the blow-up construction:
• 𝐷 𝜋 corresponds to collision pattern 𝜋 (certain groups of points colliding)
• 𝐷 𝜋 includes limits where colliding groups merge further

  𝜋′ > 𝜋
     For codimension: if 𝜋 ′ > 𝜋 , then 𝜋 ′ has fewer parts, meaning more points have collided. Each additional
collision increases codimension by 1 (locally, it is one more equation 𝜖𝑗 = 0).
     For intersections: 𝐷 𝜋1 ∩ 𝐷 𝜋2 ≠ ∅ requires configurations satisfying both collision patterns simul-
taneously. This is possible iff the patterns are compatible, i.e., there is a common refinement 𝜋3 with
𝜋1 , 𝜋2 ≤ 𝜋3 .

• The open stratum of 𝐷 𝑆 fibers over 𝐶𝑛− | 𝑆 |+1 ( Σ 𝑔 ) (the collision center replaces the cluster) with fiber
  𝐶 | 𝑆 | (ℂ)/ℂ∗ (the FM screen modulo scaling)

5.1.4  Logarithmic differential forms
Deﬁnition 5.1.17 (Logarithmic forms). The forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) that served as propagators in the
Heisenberg bar complex (§1.1) are the simplest instances of the following class.
  A differential 𝑘 -form 𝜔 on 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) has logarithmic poles along 𝐷 if:
   (i) 𝜔 is smooth on the interior 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )
  (ii) Near each divisor 𝐷 𝛼 defined locally by { 𝑓𝛼 = 0}, we have:
                                                              𝑑𝑓𝛼

        where 𝛼 is a ( 𝑘 − 1)-form and 𝛽 is a 𝑘 -form, both smooth up to 𝐷 𝛼
      The sheaf of logarithmic 𝑘 -forms is denoted:

                                                 Ω𝑘              (log 𝐷 )
                                                    𝐶 𝑛 (Σ 𝑔 )

Remark 5.1.18 (Multi-logarithmic extension). On codimension-𝑘 strata where 𝑘 boundary divisors
𝐷 𝑆1 , . . . , 𝐷 𝑆𝑘 intersect, logarithmic forms restrict to multi-logarithmic forms with logarithmic poles
along each component simultaneously. Since 𝐷 is a normal crossing divisor (Theorem 5.1.2(3)), the sheaf
Ω𝑘 (log 𝐷 ) is locally free, so multi-logarithmic extension across higher-codimension strata is automatic.
