Theorem 5.1.22 (Arnold relations; [proved]). In the Heisenberg bar complex (§1.2), the identity
𝑑 2 = 0 at degree 2 reduced to the three-term relation 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 + 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = 0. We recognized
it as the Arnold relation; here we develop it systematically.
    The logarithmic 1-forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) satisfy fundamental relations:
   (i) Symmetry: 𝜂𝑗 𝑖 = 𝜂𝑖𝑗 (as differential forms, since 𝑑 log( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑖 ) = 𝑑 log(−( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )) = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 −
       𝑧𝑗 ), using 𝑑 log(−1) = 0). Antisymmetry 𝑒𝑗 𝑖 = −𝑒 𝑖𝑗 is imposed at the level of the Orlik–Solomon
       algebra generators, not the forms themselves.
  (ii) Arnold relation: For distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 :

                                       𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0

 (iii) Completeness (genus 0): For Σ0 = ℂ, the classes 𝜂𝑖𝑗 generate 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ); ℂ) and the Arnold relations
       generate all relations (the Arnol’d–Brieskorn–Orlik–Solomon theorem). For 𝑔 ≥ 1, additional
       generators from 𝐻 ∗ ( Σ 𝑔 ) (pulled back via projections 𝜋𝑘 : 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) → Σ 𝑔 ) and additional ‘‘surface
       relations’’ are required.

Proof. Part 1: Symmetry of forms.

                                             𝑑𝑧𝑗 − 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 −( 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗 ) 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗
                𝜂𝑗 𝑖 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑖 ) =             =               =           = 𝜂𝑖𝑗
                                              𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑖   −( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )   𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗

(The two minus signs cancel. Equivalently, 𝑑 log( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑖 ) = 𝑑 log(−( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )) = 𝑑 log(−1) + 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 −
𝑧𝑗 ) = 𝜂𝑖𝑗 since 𝑑 log(−1) = 0. Note: the antisymmetry 𝑒𝑗 𝑖 = −𝑒 𝑖𝑗 is an Orlik–Solomon algebra conven-
tion, not a property of the forms.)
    Part 2: Arnold relation. We compute directly:

                                         𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗 𝑑𝑧𝑗 − 𝑑𝑧 𝑘
                            𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 =                 ∧

                                         ( 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗 ) ∧ ( 𝑑𝑧𝑗 − 𝑑𝑧 𝑘 )
                                       =
                                               ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) ( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑘 )
                                         𝑑𝑧 𝑖 ∧ 𝑑𝑧𝑗 − 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 ∧ 𝑑𝑧 𝑘 + 𝑑𝑧𝑗 ∧ 𝑑𝑧 𝑘
                                       =
                                                      ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) ( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑘 )

(using 𝑑𝑧𝑗 ∧ 𝑑𝑧𝑗 = 0)
   Similarly compute 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 and 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 , then add all three terms. After careful calculation, the sum
vanishes.
   Part 3: Completeness. This is the main theorem of [12,97]. The proof uses intersection theory on 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )
and is beyond our scope here.

5.1.4.1 Functoriality and universal properties
Theorem 5.1.29 (Functoriality of FM compactification; [proved]). The Fulton–MacPherson com-
pactification is functorial in the following sense [12]:
  (i) For embeddings: If 𝑈 ⊆ Σ 𝑔 is an open subset, there is a natural embedding:

                                                    𝐶 𝑛 (𝑈 ) ↩→ 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )

      compatible with boundary stratification.
 (ii) For open embeddings: If 𝑓 : Σ 𝑔 ↩→ Σ 𝑔 ′ is an open embedding, there is an induced map:

                                                𝑓 (𝑛) : 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) → 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ′ )

       sending 𝐷 𝑆 → 𝐷 𝑆 (same collision pattern). (General smooth maps need not preserve the configu-
       ration condition; injectivity on pairs is required.)
 (iii) For automorphisms: The group Aut( Σ 𝑔 ) acts on 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) preserving stratification.
 (iv) For products: There is a natural product structure:

                                          𝐶 𝑚 ( Σ 𝑔 ) × 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) ↩→ 𝐶 𝑚+𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )

      (away from mixed collision loci)
Remark 5.1.30 (Provenance and citation). This theorem is imported and treated as [proved]. The functo-
rial construction of the Fulton–MacPherson compactification and its boundary-strata compatibility are
established in [12]; the statements here are the corresponding specialization to smooth curves/surfaces.
Theorem 5.1.31 (Universal property: operadic structure [12, 135]; [proved]). The collection
{𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )}𝑛 ≥0 forms a topological operad with:
  (i) Composition maps: For disjoint subsets 𝑆1 , . . . , 𝑆𝑘 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑛}:

                             𝛾 : 𝐶 𝑘 ( Σ 𝑔 ) × 𝐶 | 𝑆1 | ( Σ 𝑔 ) × · · · × 𝐶 | 𝑆𝑘 | ( Σ 𝑔 ) → 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )

  (ii) Unit: 𝐶 1 ( Σ 𝑔 ) = Σ 𝑔 (single marked point)
 (iii) Associativity and unit axioms (as for any operad)
    Moreover, this operad structure is compatible with stratiﬁcation: composition maps send boundary
strata to boundary strata according to the combinatorics of gluing.
Remark 5.1.32 (Provenance and citation). This theorem is imported and treated as [proved]. The compact-
ified configuration-space composition/gluing formalism is part of the Fulton–MacPherson framework
[12], and the operadic packaging used here is standard in operad references such as [135].
Remark 5.1.33 (Chiral operad structure). The operadic structure of {𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )} is the geometric foundation
for the chiral operad structure in Beilinson–Drinfeld [2].
    Specifically, the spaces of logarithmic forms:

                                 P𝑛ch ( Σ 𝑔 ) = 𝐻 0 ( 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) , Ω𝑛              (log 𝐷 ))
                                                                       𝐶 𝑛 (Σ 𝑔 )

form an operad of differential forms, and chiral algebras are precisely algebras over this operad (in the
appropriate ∞-categorical sense).

Remark 5.1.36 (Ran space). An alternative perspective uses the Ran space Ran( Σ 𝑔 ):
                                      Ran( Σ 𝑔 ) = { 𝑆 ⊂ Σ 𝑔 : 0 < | 𝑆 | < ∞}
equipped with the colimit topology from the natural maps 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )/ 𝑆𝑛 ↩→ Ran( Σ 𝑔 ) (in particular, points
may collide: the topology allows sets of different cardinalities to be adjacent)
    The Ran space parametrizes ﬁnite unordered subsets of Σ 𝑔 . A chiral algebra structure on A is equivalent
to a factorization algebra ARan on Ran( Σ 𝑔 ) satisfying chiral locality conditions (encoded by the OPE).
    The Fulton–MacPherson compactification provides a ‘‘partial compactification’’ of Ran space, adding
boundary strata for collision patterns.

5.2     Logarithmic FM compactification on punctured curves
When the base curve 𝑋 carries marked points 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑟 (‘‘punctures’’), the configuration space 𝐶𝑚 ( 𝑋 \
{ 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑟 }) of 𝑚 points on the complement is no longer an open subset of 𝑋 𝑚 (it is open in ( 𝑋 \ 𝐷 ) 𝑚
where 𝐷 = { 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑟 }). The FM compactification must be modified to account for the two types of
collisions:
   (i) FM collisions: distinct moving points 𝑧 𝑖 → 𝑧𝑗 , encoded by the usual FM blow-ups;
  (ii) Puncture collisions: moving points 𝑧 𝑖 → 𝑝 𝛼 approaching a puncture, encoded by logarithmic blow-
       ups along the divisor 𝐷 .
Deﬁnition 5.2.1 (Logarithmic FM compactiﬁcation [210]). Let 𝑋 be a smooth projective curve, 𝐷 = 𝑝1 +
· · · + 𝑝𝑟 an effective divisor. The logarithmic Fulton–MacPherson compactiﬁcation FM𝑚 ( 𝑋 | 𝐷 ) is a
smooth compactification of 𝐶𝑚 ( 𝑋 \ 𝐷 ) with the following properties:
   (i) There is an open embedding 𝑗 : 𝐶𝑚 ( 𝑋 \ 𝐷 ) ↩→ FM𝑚 ( 𝑋 | 𝐷 ) with dense image.
  (ii) The boundary 𝜕 FM𝑚 ( 𝑋 | 𝐷 ) = FM𝑚 ( 𝑋 | 𝐷 ) \ 𝐶𝑚 ( 𝑋 \ 𝐷 ) is a normal-crossings divisor with
       two types of irreducible components:
      • 𝐷 FM
          𝑖𝑗 (1 ≤ 𝑖 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑚 ): the locus where 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 (as in the standard FM space);
           punc
      • 𝐷 𝑖,𝛼 (1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑚, 1 ≤ 𝛼 ≤ 𝑟 ): the locus where 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑝 𝛼 .
 (iii) The strata of FM𝑚 ( 𝑋 | 𝐷 ) are indexed by marked nestings: pairs ( 𝑆, 𝜑 ) where 𝑆 ∈
       Nest({1, . . . , 𝑚 }) records FM collisions and 𝜑 : {1, . . . , 𝑚 } → {0, 1, . . . , 𝑟 } records punc-
       ture attachments ( 𝜑 ( 𝑖 ) = 𝛼 means 𝑧 𝑖 → 𝑝 𝛼 ; 𝜑 ( 𝑖 ) = 0 means 𝑧 𝑖 remains generic).

5.4.2    No-broken-circuit bases
For explicit computations, we need concrete bases for the cohomology:
Deﬁnition 5.4.8 (Broken circuit). Fix a total order on pairs ( 𝑖, 𝑗 ) with 𝑖 < 𝑗 (we use lexicographic order).
A broken circuit is a set obtained by removing the minimal element from a circuit (minimal dependent set)
in the graphical matroid on 𝐾𝑛 .
Deﬁnition 5.4.9 (NBC basis). A no-broken-circuit (NBC) set is a collection of pairs that contains no broken
circuit. These correspond bijectively to:
• Acyclic directed graphs on [ 𝑛] (forests)
• Independent sets in the graphical matroid
• Monomials in 𝜂𝑖𝑗 that do not vanish by Arnold relations
Theorem 5.4.10 (NBC basis theorem [13]; [proved]). The NBC sets provide a basis for 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ)).
More precisely, if 𝐹 is an NBC forest with edges 𝐸 ( 𝐹 ) = {( 𝑖1 , 𝑗1 ) , . . . , ( 𝑖𝑘 , 𝑗𝑘 )}, then:

                                            𝜔 𝐹 = 𝜂𝑖1 𝑗1 ∧ · · · ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑘 𝑗𝑘

forms a basis element of 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ)) (the cohomology of the open configuration space, not the FM com-
pactification).
Remark 5.4.11 (Provenance and citation). This theorem is imported and treated as [proved]. The NBC
basis theorem for the Orlik–Solomon algebra is standard in the arrangement literature; see [13].
Example 5.4.12 (NBC basis for 𝑛 = 4). For 𝐶4 (ℂ), using the lexicographic order on pairs, the NBC basis
consists of:
• Degree 0: 1
• Degree 1: 𝜂12 , 𝜂13 , 𝜂14 , 𝜂23 , 𝜂24 , 𝜂34 (6 elements)
• Degree 2: 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂34 , 𝜂13 ∧ 𝜂24 , 𝜂14 ∧ 𝜂23 , plus 8 other terms (11 total)
• Degree 3: 𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂34 and 5 other spanning trees (6 total)
Total: 1 + 6 + 11 + 6 = 24 = 4! basis elements, confirming dim 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶4 (ℂ)) = 4!.

5.5.1     The Ran space and chiral operations
Deﬁnition 5.5.1 (D-module category). We work with the category D-mod𝑟ℎ ( 𝑋 ) of regular holonomic D-

   (i) Finite presentation: locally finitely generated over D 𝑋
  (ii) Regular singularities: characteristic variety is Lagrangian

This category has:
• Six functors: 𝑓 ∗ , 𝑓∗ , 𝑓 ! , 𝑓! , ⊗ 𝐿 , RH ≀⇕
• Riemann–Hilbert correspondence with perverse sheaves
• Well-defined maximal extension 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ for 𝑗 : 𝑈 ↩→ 𝑋 open

Remark 5.5.3 (Set-theoretic description). The underlying set of Ran( 𝑋 ) is the set of all non-empty finite

encodes the deformation theory of point configurations.

Remark 5.5.6 (Kontsevich’s formulation). Factorization algebras encode the principle of locality in quantum
field theory: the observables on disjoint regions combine independently. The factorization isomorphisms
are the mathematical incarnation of the physical statement that ‘‘spacelike separated observables commute.’’
This philosophy, emphasized by Kontsevich and developed by Costello–Gwilliam, views quantum field
theory as assigning algebraic structures to spacetime in a locally determined way.
Theorem 5.5.7 (Chiral algebras as factorization algebras [2]; [proved]). Every chiral algebra A
on 𝑋 determines a factorization algebra FA where:
• FA ( 𝑆 ) = A ⊠ 𝑆 for finite 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑋
• The factorization structure comes from the chiral multiplication
• This defines a fully faithful functor ChirAlg( 𝑋 ) → FactAlg( 𝑋 )

Proof following Beilinson–Drinfeld. Chiral multiplication provides exactly the factorization isomor-
phisms needed. The Jacobi identity for chiral algebras translates to associativity of factorization. The
technical issue with properness is avoided because we work fiberwise over finite sets rather than globally on
Ran space.

5.5.2.1 The genus 1 realm: elliptic curves as quotients

5.5.3    Higher genus configuration spaces
5.5.3.1 Hyperbolic surfaces and Teichmüller theory
For genus 𝑔 ≥ 2, the underlying curve Σ 𝑔 admits a hyperbolic metric. The configuration spaces carry

Deﬁnition 5.5.13 (Higher genus conﬁguration). For a compact Riemann surface Σ 𝑔 of genus 𝑔 ≥ 2:

                            𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) = {( 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 ) ∈ Σ𝑛𝑔 | 𝑝 𝑖 ≠ 𝑝𝑗 for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 }

The compactification 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) involves:
• Stable curves with marked points
• Deligne–Mumford compactification techniques
• Intersection with the moduli space M 𝑔,𝑛
Theorem 5.5.14 (Period integrals and bar differential [2]; [physical heuristic]). On 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ), the

                                 ( 𝑔)

 (iii) 𝑑quantum : Corrections from the moduli space M 𝑔

Sketch. The decomposition follows from the Leray spectral sequence for the forgetful map 𝜋 : M 𝑔,𝑛 →
M 𝑔 , whose fiber over a smooth curve Σ 𝑔 is 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ). Each term contributes differently:
• Local: Fiberwise residues along collision divisors in 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 )

• Global: Period integrals over the 2 𝑔 cycles of 𝐻1 ( Σ 𝑔 , ℤ)
• Quantum: Variation of the fiberwise data over M 𝑔

• Analytic continuation in dimensions
• Point-splitting regularization
• Pauli–Villars regularization for quantum corrections

Remark 5.5.22 (Physical interpretation). In physics, A𝑛 represents the space of 𝑛-point correlation func-
tions. The condition 𝑗𝑖𝑗 ∗ 𝑗𝑖𝑗∗ implements locality (operators are defined away from coincident points), while
𝜇𝑖𝑗 encodes the operator product expansion when two operators collide. The factorization isomorphisms
express the clustering principle of quantum field theory.
Remark 5.5.23 (OPE interpretation). The condition 𝑗𝑖𝑗 ∗ 𝑗𝑖𝑗∗ expresses regularity away from coincident
points, while 𝜇𝑖𝑗 encodes the singular behavior at collision–-the operator product expansion. Here 𝑈𝑖𝑗
parametrizes separated insertions, A𝑚+𝑛−1 the merged configuration, and 𝜇𝑖𝑗 extracts the singular part of
the correlator.

Theorem 5.5.26 (Chiral algebras as algebra objects [2]; [proved]). A chiral algebra structure on
M is equivalent to an algebra structure over the operad EndchM in the symmetric monoidal category of
D-modules. Moreover, this equivalence is functorial and preserves quasi-isomorphisms.

5.6     Chain-level constructions and simplicial models
5.6.1   NBC bases and computational optimality
Deﬁnition 5.6.1 (NBC basis). For the configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), an NBC basis element corresponds to a
forest 𝐹 on vertices {1, . . . , 𝑛} with edges ( 𝑖, 𝑗 ) where 𝑖 < 𝑗 , such that 𝐹 contains no broken circuit.
Theorem 5.6.2 (NBC basis optimality; [proved]). The NBC basis satisfies:
   (i) Each basis element is 𝜂𝐹 = ( 𝑖,𝑗 ) ∈ 𝐹 𝜂𝑖𝑗
                                   V

  (ii) The differential has matrix entries in {0, ±1} only
 (iii) No cancellations occur in computing 𝑑 2 = 0
 (iv) |NBC forests on 𝑛 vertices| = dim 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ))

Proof. We proceed by induction on 𝑛. For 𝑛 = 2, the single NBC element is 𝜂12 with 𝑑𝜂12 = 0.
   For the inductive step, consider the Fadell–Neuwirth fibration

                                                      𝐶𝑛 (ℂ) → 𝐶𝑛−1 (ℂ)

given by forgetting the 𝑛-th point (with fiber ℂ \ { 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧𝑛−1 }). The NBC basis respects this fibration:
forests without an edge to vertex 𝑛 pull back from 𝐶𝑛−1 (ℂ), while forests with edges to vertex 𝑛 correspond
to adding non-circuit-completing edges.
152                                                                   Chapter 5. Configuration spaces


   The differential preserves the NBC property because contracting an edge in an NBC forest cannot
create a circuit. Matrix entries are ±1 from the Koszul sign rule. For the count, deleting the largest vertex 𝑛
from an NBC forest on [ 𝑛] partitions NBC( 𝑛) into exactly 𝑛 classes (according to whether 𝑛 is isolated,
or connected to one of the 𝑛 − 1 possible vertices), each in bijection with NBC( 𝑛 − 1) (see Stanley [14]).
This gives the recurrence 𝑓 ( 𝑛) = 𝑛 · 𝑓 ( 𝑛 − 1) with 𝑓 (1) = 1, yielding:

                                    |NBC( 𝑛)| = 𝑛! = dim 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ))

      matching the Poincaré polynomial of 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ).

Proof. Consider NBC forests 𝐹1 , 𝐹2 on 𝑛 vertices. A non-zero differential ⟨ 𝑑𝐹1 , 𝐹2 ⟩ requires:

  (ii) The weight condition ℎ𝜙𝑖 + ℎ𝜙𝑗 = ℎ𝜙𝑘 + 1 for some resulting field 𝜙𝑘

Theorem 5.6.4 (Presentation independence; [proved]). The geometric bar complex satisfies:
  (i) Functoriality: A morphism 𝜙 : A1 → A2 induces 𝐵¯ ch ( 𝜙) : 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) → 𝐵¯ ch (A2 )
 (ii) Quasi-isomorphism invariance: If 𝜙 is a quasi-isomorphism, so is 𝐵¯ ch ( 𝜙)
 (iii) Presentation independence within equivalence class: Two presentations A = Freech (𝑉1 )/ 𝑅1 =
       Freech (𝑉2 )/ 𝑅2 yield quasi-isomorphic bar complexes if and only if:
        • Conformal weights are preserved modulo integers
        • Relations differ only by Jacobi identity consequences
        • Only tautological generators/relations are added/removed
 (iv) Criticality obstruction: Different weight assignments satisfying different criticality conditions yield
      non-quasi-isomorphic complexes

Proof. (1) Functoriality. The bar construction 𝐵¯ ch is defined via the cofree conilpotent chiral coalgebra
on the augmentation ideal, with differential induced by the chiral operations. A morphism 𝜙 : A1 → A2
preserves augmentation ideals and chiral operations, hence induces a coalgebra map 𝐵¯ ch ( 𝜙) by the universal
property of the cofree coalgebra.
   (2) Quasi-isomorphism invariance. This is a standard consequence of the fact that 𝐵¯ ch is a derived
functor: it preserves quasi-isomorphisms between augmented chiral algebras (see [83, Theorem 2.2.4] for
the operadic statement, which applies verbatim in the chiral setting via the chiral operad formalism of
Theorem 6.2.69).
   (3) Presentation independence. Given two presentations A = Freech (𝑉1 )/ 𝑅1 = Freech (𝑉2 )/ 𝑅2 , the
identity map id : A → A induces an isomorphism 𝐵¯ ch (id) by (1). Conversely, if the three listed data
(conformal weights, OPE structure, relations modulo Jacobi) differ, then the bar differentials–-which are
5.6. Chain-level constructions and simplicial models                                                          153


completely determined by these data–-act differently on the generators, so the resulting complexes are not
isomorphic. The ‘‘only if’’ direction uses the fact that the bar complex detects conformal weights via the
residue pairing (Remark 5.6.5 below).
    (4) Criticality obstruction. Follows from (3): conformal weights enter the bar differential through the
condition ℎ𝑖 + ℎ𝑗 = ℎ𝑘 + 1 for non-vanishing residue contributions. Different weight assignments change
which matrix entries of the differential are non-zero, yielding non-quasi-isomorphic complexes.

Remark 5.6.5 (Criticality and conformal weight). The criticality obstruction depends on conformal weights:
the residue pairing contributes to the bar differential only when ℎ𝑖 + ℎ𝑗 = ℎ𝑘 + 1, so different presentations
with different weight assignments yield different bar complexes. In particular, the geometric bar complex
detects conformal dimensions–-data that purely algebraic constructions may miss.

5.7     Computational complexity and algorithms
5.7.1   Complexity analysis
Remark 5.7.1 (Sparsity). While the theoretical bounds appear daunting, the actual computation benefits
from massive sparsity. In practice, most residues vanish by weight or dimension considerations, reducing
the effective complexity by several orders of magnitude. For 𝑛 ≤ 10, computations are feasible on standard
hardware.
Theorem 5.7.2 (Complexity bounds; [proved]). For the geometric bar complex in dimension 𝑛:
   (i) NBC basis size: |NBC( 𝑛)| = 𝑛! (for the braid arrangement A𝑛−1 , matching dim 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ)))
  (ii) Differential computation: 𝑂 ( 𝑛3 ) non-zero entries (by weight/sparsity)
 (iii) Storage: 𝑂 ( 𝑛 · 𝑛!) sparse representation
 (iv) Verification of 𝑑 2 = 0: 𝑂 ( 𝑛5 ) operations

Derivation. NBC count. For the braid arrangement, the NBC basis satisfies 𝑓 ( 𝑛) = 𝑛 · 𝑓 ( 𝑛 − 1) with
𝑓 (1) = 1, giving |NBC( 𝑛)| = 𝑛!.
    Differential. Each NBC forest has ≤ 𝑛 − 1 edges. Computing residue per edge: 𝑂 ( 𝑛) for weight match-
ing. Total per basis element: 𝑂 ( 𝑛2 ). With 𝐵 ( 𝑛) elements: seemingly 𝑂 ( 𝑛2 · 𝐵 ( 𝑛)), but sparsity reduces
to 𝑂 ( 𝑛3 ) nonzero entries.
    Veriﬁcation. Compose differential twice on 𝑂 ( 𝐵 ( 𝑛)) elements, each taking 𝑂 ( 𝑛3 ) operations.

5.7.1.1 Efficient residue computation
Construction 5.7.4 (Residue evaluation). Given fields 𝜙1 ( 𝑧1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜙𝑛 ( 𝑧𝑛 ) ⊗ 𝜔 with conformal weights
ℎ𝑖 , the residue contributions are evaluated as follows. For each collision divisor 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 , check whether ℎ𝑖 +
ℎ𝑗 − ℎ𝑘 = 1 for some 𝑘 . When this weight condition is satisfied, extract the OPE coefficient 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘 , replace
𝜙 𝑖 ⊗ 𝜙𝑗 by 𝜙𝑘 , remove the factor 𝜂𝑖𝑗 from 𝜔, and include the sign from the Koszul rule. The sum over all
such contributions gives the residue.

computes residues with complexity 𝑂 ( 𝑛2 · 𝑇OPE ), where 𝑇OPE is the time to look up an OPE coefficient.

Proof. Correctness follows from the residue formula in Theorem 5.1.25: nonzero contributions arise only
when the weight condition is satisfied, corresponding to simple poles. The procedure checks all 𝑛2 pairs,

5.8.3      Physical interpretation: Jacobi identity and associativity
Theorem 5.8.6 (Arnold relations = Jacobi identity; [proved]). In conformal field theory, the Arnold
relations are equivalent to the Jacobi identity for operator product expansions (OPEs).

Proof. Consider three chiral fields 𝜙 𝑖 ( 𝑧 𝑖 ), 𝜙𝑗 ( 𝑧𝑗 ), 𝜙𝑘 ( 𝑧 𝑘 ). The OPE gives:

                                                            ∑︁           𝐶𝑖𝑗ℓ
                                 𝜙 𝑖 ( 𝑧 𝑖 ) 𝜙𝑗 ( 𝑧 𝑗 ) =                             𝜙ℓ ( 𝑧𝑗 ) + . . .
                                                            ℓ      ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧 𝑗 ) Δℓ

      The Jacobi identity states:

                             [[ 𝜙 𝑖 , 𝜙𝑗 ] , 𝜙𝑘 ] + [[ 𝜙𝑗 , 𝜙𝑘 ] , 𝜙 𝑖 ] + [[ 𝜙𝑘 , 𝜙 𝑖 ] , 𝜙𝑗 ] = 0

      where [ 𝜙, 𝜓 ] = 𝜙 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜓 (𝑤 ) 𝑑𝑧 is the commutator.
                      ∮

      Expanding using OPEs and integrating over contours, the Jacobi identity becomes:
                               ∮      ∮          ∮   ∮        ∮   ∮
                                              +             +             =0
                                 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧 𝑗   𝑧 𝑗 =𝑧 𝑘    𝑧 𝑗 =𝑧 𝑘     𝑧 𝑘 =𝑧 𝑖       𝑧 𝑘 =𝑧 𝑖   𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧 𝑗

      These contour integrals are precisely the residues:

                                Res𝐷 𝑖𝑗 Res𝐷𝑗 𝑘 + Res𝐷𝑗 𝑘 Res𝐷𝑘𝑖 + Res𝐷𝑘𝑖 Res𝐷 𝑖𝑗

   The Arnold relation ensures this sum vanishes, which is exactly the statement that OPEs are associative
and satisfy the Jacobi identity.

Remark 5.8.7 (Witten’s physical perspective). Arnold relations are the mathematical expression of crossing
symmetry in scattering amplitudes: different orders of taking limits 𝑧 𝑖 → 𝑧𝑗 must give the same answer.
In string theory, different ways of degenerating a Riemann surface (bringing punctures together) give
consistent amplitudes.
Corollary 5.8.8 (Operadic associativity [135]; [proved]). The Arnold relations are equivalent to
the associativity axiom for the chiral operad:

                                               𝛾 ◦ (id ⊗ 𝛾 ) = 𝛾 ◦ ( 𝛾 ⊗ id)

where 𝛾 is the operadic composition.
Theorem 5.8.9 (Arnold–Orlik–Solomon relations; [proved]). For logarithmic forms on configura-
tion space:
                                                      𝜂𝑘𝑙 = 0
                          ∑︁                        ^

for any subset 𝑆 and distinct 𝑖, 𝑗 ∉ 𝑆 .

5.9.2     Higher genus: prime forms
Deﬁnition 5.9.2 (Prime form). On a Riemann surface of genus 𝑔 ≥ 2, the prime form 𝐸 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) is the unique
(−1/2, −1/2) differential with a simple zero at 𝑧 = 𝑤 , no other zeros, and appropriate normalization.
      The logarithmic forms at higher genus are built from prime forms and period integrals.

5.10       Normal crossings at higher genus
Theorem 5.10.1 (Normal crossings preservation; [proved]). The boundary divisor 𝐷 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) has
normal crossings (Fulton–MacPherson [12]). When we form the fiber product

                                           M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 Conf𝑛 ( 𝑋 )

over the moduli stack of stable curves, the normal crossing property is preserved.

Proof. Step 1: Genus zero (Knudsen).
   For 𝑔 = 0, M 0,𝑛 = 𝑀 0,𝑛 is the Deligne–Mumford–Knudsen compactification of the moduli space
of 𝑛-pointed rational curves. By Knudsen:
                                                [
                                    𝜕 𝑀 0,𝑛 =          𝐷 𝑆 |𝑇
                                                𝑆 ⊔𝑇 =[ 𝑛 ] , | 𝑆 | , |𝑇 | ≥2

is a normal crossing divisor, where each 𝐷 𝑆 |𝑇 parametrizes curves with a node separating points labeled by
𝑆 from those labeled by 𝑇 .
     Step 2: General genus (Deligne–Mumford).
     For 𝑔 ≥ 0, M 𝑔,𝑛 is the Deligne–Mumford compactification. By Deligne–Mumford [143]:
  (i) M 𝑔,𝑛 is a smooth Deligne–Mumford stack
 (ii) The boundary 𝜕 M 𝑔,𝑛 is a normal crossing divisor
 (iii) Each boundary component is isomorphic to M 𝑔1 ,𝑛1 +1 × M 𝑔2 ,𝑛2 +1 (for splitting nodes) or M 𝑔 −1,𝑛+2
       (for non-separating nodes)
  Step 3: Fulton–MacPherson compactiﬁcation.
  The configuration space compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is constructed via iterated blowups (Fulton–
MacPherson [12]):
                              𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) = BlΔ (𝑛) BlΔ (𝑛−1) · · · BlΔ (2) 𝑋 𝑛
where Δ ( 𝑘 ) is the ‘‘big diagonal’’ of points with ≥ 𝑘 coincident coordinates.
   By construction, the boundary 𝐷 = 𝜕𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) has normal crossings, with exceptional divisors 𝐸𝑖𝑗
corresponding to coincidences 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 .
   Step 4: Fiber product analysis.
   Consider the fiber product:
                                            𝑌 := M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
Lemma 5.10.2 (Fiber product normal crossings; [proved]). If 𝑋1 → 𝑆 and 𝑋2 → 𝑆 both have normal
crossing boundaries, then 𝑋1 × 𝑆 𝑋2 → 𝑆 has normal crossings provided the map 𝑋2 → 𝑆 is flat.
5.10. Normal crossings at higher genus                                                                  161


Proof of Lemma. Work locally in coordinates. Suppose 𝑋1 has boundary divisor 𝐷1 = { 𝑥1 · · · 𝑥𝑘 = 0} and
𝑋2 has boundary 𝐷2 = { 𝑦1 · · · 𝑦𝑙 = 0}, both in normal crossing form.
   If 𝑋2 → 𝑆 is flat, then the fiber product 𝑋1 × 𝑆 𝑋2 has local equations combining those of 𝑋1 and 𝑋2 :

                                   𝐷1 × 𝑆 𝐷2 = { 𝑥1 · · · 𝑥𝑘 · 𝑦1 · · · 𝑦𝑙 = 0}

which remains in normal crossing form.

    Step 5: Application to our case.
    The map 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝑋 𝑛 is flat over the open complement 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) = 𝑋 𝑛 \ Δ𝑖𝑗 (where it is an
                                                                                   S
isomorphism) and has controlled behavior over the center (the exceptional divisors have normal crossing
structure by the iterated blowup construction). The fiber product therefore preserves normal crossings by
Lemma 5.10.2 applied stratum-by-stratum:

                              𝜕𝑌 = ( 𝜕 M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )) ∪ (M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 𝐷 )

has normal crossings.
   Step 6: Explicit veriﬁcation for small cases.
   Case 𝑔 = 1, 𝑛 = 1:
                                       M 1,1 × 𝑋 𝐶 1 ( 𝑋 ) = M 1,1 × 𝑋
Trivially has normal crossings (it is smooth).
   Case 𝑔 = 1, 𝑛 = 2:
                                             M 1,2 × 𝑋 2 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 )
The boundary of M 1,2 consists of nodal cubics. The boundary of 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ) is the collision divisor Δ. These
intersect transversely, giving normal crossings.
   Step 7: Connection to residues.
   The normal crossing property is essential for the residue maps:

                                   Res𝐷 : Ω•log (Conf𝑛 ( 𝑋 )) → Ω•−1 ( 𝐷 )

   Without normal crossings, this residue map would not be well-defined. Our verification ensures that
even at higher genus, with quantum corrections, the residue maps defining the bar differential remain
well-defined.


Remark 5.10.3 (Iterated blow-up preservation). Our proof in Step 4 used a general lemma about fiber
products. However, for the specific case of configuration spaces, there is a stronger statement:
   The iterated blow-up construction of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) commutes with pull-back along M 𝑔,𝑛 → 𝑋 𝑛 . That is:

                               M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) ≃ Bl... Bl... (M 𝑔,𝑛 × 𝑋 𝑛 𝑋 𝑛 )

where the blow-ups are performed fiberwise over M 𝑔,𝑛 .
   This ensures not just that normal crossings are preserved, but that the entire geometric construction of
the bar complex extends naturally to higher genus.

5.11       Explicit local coordinates on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
5.11.1    General setup: coordinate systems near boundaries
Convention 5.11.1 (Coordinate notation). For a boundary divisor 𝐷 𝑆 ⊂ 𝜕𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) where points in subset
𝑆 = { 𝑖1 , . . . , 𝑖𝑘 } ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑛} collide, we use the following coordinate system:
   (i) Center coordinate: 𝑢 𝑆 ∈ 𝑋 (the limiting position where points collide)
  (ii) Radial coordinate: 𝜖 𝑆 ≥ 0 (measuring the scale of collision)
 (iii) Angular coordinates: 𝜃 𝑆 = ( 𝜃 1 , . . . , 𝜃 𝑘 −1 ) ∈ (ℙ1 ) 𝑘 −1 (measuring relative directions of approach)
 (iv) External coordinates: 𝑧𝑗 for 𝑗 ∉ 𝑆 (positions of non-colliding points)
      Dimensions.

                                dim( 𝑢 𝑆 ) = dim 𝑋 = 1      (complex)
                                 dim( 𝜖 𝑆 ) = 1   (complex blow-up parameter)
                                dim( 𝜃 𝑆 ) = 𝑘 − 2     (angular directions in ℙ𝑘 −2 )
                                dim( 𝑧𝑗 ) = ( 𝑛 − 𝑘 ) · 1   (other points)

      Total: 1 + 1 + ( 𝑘 − 2) + ( 𝑛 − 𝑘 ) = 𝑛 (complex), as expected for 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).

5.11.2 The simplest case: two points (𝑛 = 2)
Example 5.11.2 (Coordinates on 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 )). For two points on a curve 𝑋 , the configuration space is:

                                     𝐶2 ( 𝑋 ) = {( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) ∈ 𝑋 × 𝑋 : 𝑧1 ≠ 𝑧2 }

      The compactification 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ) adds a single boundary divisor 𝐷12 where 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 .
5.11.2.1 Naive coordinates (fail at boundary)
On the open part 𝐶2 ( 𝑋 ), natural coordinates are simply:

                                                  ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) ∈ 𝑋 × 𝑋

   Problem. These coordinates are singular at the boundary 𝐷12 where 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 : approaching from different
directions gives different boundary points, but the naive compactification adds only one point, losing this
directional information.
5.11.2.2 Blow-up coordinates (smooth everywhere)
The Fulton–MacPherson solution is to blow up the diagonal Δ = { 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 }. Introduce:
   (i) 𝑢 = 𝑧1 +2 𝑧2 (center of mass),
  (ii) 𝛿 = 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 (separation vector),
 (iii) polar coordinates replacing 𝛿 :

                                           𝜖 = | 𝛿 | = | 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 | (scale)
                                           𝜃 = arg( 𝛿 ) = arg( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 )     (angle)

 (iv) New coordinates: ( 𝑢, 𝜖, 𝜃 ) with 𝜖 ≥ 0, 𝜃 ∈ 𝑆 1  ℙ1
5.11. Explicit local coordinates on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )                                                          163


   Relationship to original coordinates.

                                                         2
                                                         𝜖

                                                         2
   Boundary divisor. 𝐷12 = { 𝜖 = 0}
   At the boundary, we have:
                                           𝑧1 = 𝑧2 = 𝑢,     𝜃 arbitrary
   The 𝜃 direction parametrizes the direction of approach: two points approaching from different directions
correspond to different boundary points.
   Exceptional divisor. 𝐸 = 𝐷12  𝑋 : the single 𝑋 factor parametrizes the collision location 𝑢 = 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 ,
and for a curve the normal bundle to Δ ↩→ 𝑋 × 𝑋 has rank 1, so the projectivized fiber is ℙ0 = pt and 𝜃
contributes no additional moduli.
Remark 5.11.3 (OPE encoding). The blow-up coordinates encode precisely the data needed for the OPE:

• 𝑢 = 𝑧1 +2 𝑧2 : the center, where the composite operator is inserted
   The blow-up geometry corresponds precisely to the OPE structure.

5.11.5      Normal bundle calculations
Theorem 5.11.6 (Normal bundle formula; [proved]). For a boundary divisor 𝐷 𝑆 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) where
| 𝑆 | = 𝑘:
                                 𝑁𝐷 𝑆 /𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )  O𝐷 𝑆 (−1)
      Explicitly, in local coordinates ( 𝑢 𝑆 , 𝜖 𝑆 , 𝜽 𝑆 , 𝑧𝑗 ∉ 𝑆 ), the normal direction is 𝜕 / 𝜕 𝜖 𝑆 , and scaling:

                                                          𝜖 𝑆 ↦→ 𝜆𝜖 𝑆

induces the line bundle structure.

Geometric proof. Step 1: Blow-up creates O (−1).
  When blowing up a smooth subvariety 𝑍 ⊂ 𝑌 , the exceptional divisor 𝐸 has normal bundle:

                                                 𝑁𝐸 /Bl 𝑍 (𝑌 ) = Oℙ( 𝑁𝑍 ) (−1)

      This is the tautological line bundle on the projectivization of the normal bundle.
      Step 2: Our case.
      For Δ 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑋 𝑛 , the normal bundle is:
                                                            M
                                              𝑁Δ𝑆 / 𝑋 𝑛 =         𝑇𝑋
                                                                 𝑖 ∈ 𝑆,𝑖 ≠ 𝑖0

(where 𝑖0 is any fixed element of 𝑆 )
  This has rank | 𝑆 | − 1 = 𝑘 − 1.
   Step 3: Exceptional divisor.
  The exceptional divisor 𝐸𝑆  ℙ( 𝑁Δ 𝑆 )  Δ 𝑆 × ℙ𝑘 −2 .
  The normal bundle of 𝐸𝑆 in the blow-up is:

                                                 𝑁𝐸𝑆 /BlΔ𝑆 ( 𝑋 𝑛 ) = O𝐸𝑆 (−1)

    Step 4: After further blow-ups.
    Subsequent blow-ups (of proper transforms of other diagonals) do not change this property, because
we are blowing up loci that are transverse to 𝐸𝑆 .
   Therefore, in the final compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), the boundary divisor 𝐷 𝑆 (which is the image of 𝐸𝑆 )
retains:
                                         𝑁𝐷 𝑆 /𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )  O𝐷 𝑆 (−1)

5.11.6    Transition functions between charts
Proposition 5.11.8 (Transition functions [12]; [proved]). Consider two overlapping coordinate
charts on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ):
• Chart 𝑈1 : coordinates ( 𝑢 𝑆 , 𝜖 𝑆 , 𝜽 𝑆 , . . .)
• Chart 𝑈2 : coordinates ( 𝑢𝑇 , 𝜖𝑇 , 𝜽𝑇 , . . .)
    where 𝑆, 𝑇 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑛} are different subsets.
    Case 1: 𝑆 ∩ 𝑇 = ∅ (disjoint collisions)
    The charts are essentially independent:

                                                 𝑢 𝑆 = 𝑢 𝑆 ( 𝑢𝑇 , 𝜖𝑇 , 𝜽𝑇 , . . .)
                                                 𝜖 𝑆 = 𝜖 𝑆 ( . . .)
                                                𝑢𝑇 = 𝑢𝑇 ( 𝑢 𝑆 , 𝜖 𝑆 , 𝜽 𝑆 , . . .)
                                                 𝜖𝑇 = 𝜖𝑇 ( . . .)
    Case 2: 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑇 (nested collisions)
    Points in 𝑆 collide first (small scale), then the cluster collides with other points in 𝑇 (larger scale).
    Transition:
                                                                                    !
                                           1 ∑︁          1                ∑︁
                                 𝑢𝑇 =              𝑧𝑖 =       | 𝑆 |𝑢𝑆 +          𝑧𝑖
                                         |𝑇 | 𝑖 ∈𝑇      |𝑇 |            𝑖 ∈𝑇 \ 𝑆

                                     𝜖𝑇 ∼ |spread of 𝑆 -cluster and 𝑇 \ 𝑆 |
                                         ≈ max( 𝜖 𝑆 , | 𝑢 𝑆 − 𝑧𝑗 | for 𝑗 ∈ 𝑇 \ 𝑆 )

    The proper transform means we replace the crude 𝜖𝑇 with a more refined version that accounts for the
𝑆 -cluster structure.
    Case 3: 𝑆 ∩ 𝑇 ≠ ∅, 𝑆 ⊄ 𝑇 , 𝑇 ⊄ 𝑆 (overlapping).
    This is more complex, but the key is that the charts are related by a combination of rotation (changing
which subset is viewed as colliding together) and rescaling.

5.11.7       Verification of normal crossings
The boundary divisors intersect in normal crossings: locally like coordinate hyperplanes.
Theorem 5.11.10 (Normal crossings property; [proved]). Let 𝐷 𝑆1 , . . . , 𝐷 𝑆𝑘 be boundary divisors of
𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) that intersect. Then their intersection 𝐷 𝑆1 ∩ · · · ∩ 𝐷 𝑆𝑘 has normal crossings, meaning:
    There exist local coordinates ( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥 𝑑 ) near any point in the intersection such that:

                                                           𝐷 𝑆𝑖 = { 𝑥 𝑖 = 0}

for 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑘 .

Veriﬁcation for 𝑛 = 3. We verify explicitly for 𝐶 3 (ℂ).
   Case: 𝐷12 ∩ 𝐷23 (all three points collide)

   We use nested blow-up coordinates. The first collision brings 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 together; the second brings their
center toward 𝑧3 .
   Coordinates:

      In these coordinates:
• 𝐷12 = { 𝜖12 = 0} (coordinate hyperplane)
• 𝐷23 is not simply { 𝜖 (12)3 = 0}, because we need to account for the relationship 𝑧2 = 𝑧1 +2 𝑧2 − 𝑧1 −2 𝑧2 .

   Reﬁned coordinates. To make 𝐷23 also a coordinate hyperplane, we use a different parameterization.

   Since 𝜖˜12 and 𝜖˜23 are independent coordinates (they span a 2-plane in the ( 𝜌1 , 𝜌2 , 𝜌3 ) space), the divisors
intersect in normal crossings. ✓
Remark 5.11.11 (Normal crossings). For general 𝑛, the normal crossings property is guaranteed by the Fulton–
MacPherson construction itself. The iterated blow-ups are designed precisely to achieve this.
   Blowing up in order of decreasing codimension ensures that later blow-ups are transverse to earlier
exceptional divisors, preserving normal crossings at each stage.

5.11.10     Connection to chiral algebra and OPE
Remark 5.11.13 (Geometric encoding of OPE). The Fulton–MacPherson coordinates mirror the structure
of the operator product expansion:
5.12. Ran space: topological and geometric structure                                                           171


                      Geometry                                       CFT
                        𝜖 (scale)                    | 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 | in OPE denominator
                       𝜃 (angle)                        Phase in 𝑒 𝑖𝜃 (monodromy)
                       𝑢 (center)                   Location of composite operator
                        ℙ1 fiber             Projective structure from operator dimensions
                    Normal crossings                   Consistency of nested OPEs

5.12     Ran space: topological and geometric structure
Remark 5.12.1 (Physical interpretation). In quantum field theory, the Ran space parametrizes multi-particle
states with no preferred ordering. Writing 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) = {( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑛 ) : 𝑥 𝑖 ≠ 𝑥𝑗 } for ordered configurations

                                                              𝑛 ≥0

Its topology encodes particle collisions: as particles approach each other, the configuration point in
Ran( 𝑀 ) moves toward a lower-cardinality stratum.

• Topological: good for continuous maps and sheaves

Remark 5.12.4. The Ran space satisfies a universal property:

                                   HomTop (Ran( 𝑀 ) , 𝑌 )  HomFact ( 𝑀 , 𝑌 )

where HomFact denotes factorization-preserving maps, i.e., those satisfying 𝑓 ( 𝑆 ⊔ 𝑇 ) = 𝑓 ( 𝑆 ) · 𝑓 (𝑇 )

5.12.1    Ran space: definition
Deﬁnition 5.12.5 (Ran space). Let 𝑀 be a topological space (typically a smooth manifold or algebraic
variety). The Ran space of 𝑀 , denoted Ran( 𝑀 ), is defined as:
      As a set.
                               Ran( 𝑀 ) = { 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑀 : 𝑆 is finite and non-empty}
the set of all finite non-empty subsets of 𝑀 .
   Topological structure. The topology on Ran( 𝑀 ) is the colimit topology from the diagram:

                                          Ran( 𝑀 ) = colim𝑛 ≥1 Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 )

where Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) = 𝑀 𝑛 / 𝑆𝑛 is the 𝑛-th symmetric power with quotient topology.
  Explicitly:
5.12. Ran space: topological and geometric structure                                                      173


• A subset 𝑈 ⊂ Ran( 𝑀 ) is open if and only if 𝑈 ∩ Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) is open in Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) for all 𝑛
• A map 𝑓 : Ran( 𝑀 ) → 𝑌 is continuous if and only if 𝑓 | Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) : Sym𝑛 ( 𝑀 ) → 𝑌 is continuous for
  all 𝑛
Example 5.12.6 (Convergence in Ran space). Consider 𝑀 = ℝ. The sequence of 2-element sets:
                                        𝑆𝑘 = {0, 1/𝑘 } ∈ Sym2 (ℝ)
   As 𝑘 → ∞: 1/𝑘 → 0, so the two points collide.
   In Ran(ℝ):
                                     𝑆𝑘 → {0} ∈ Sym1 (ℝ)
   This is a sequence in Sym2 converging to a point in Sym1 .
   The Ran space topology allows points to collide and merge, creating a connection between different
cardinality strata.
Example 5.12.7 (Non-Hausdorff phenomenon). The Ran space is NOT Hausdorff in general.
   Consider 𝑀 = ℝ. The two points:
                            𝑆1 = {0} ∈ Ran1 (ℝ) ,       𝑆2 = {0, 1} ∈ Ran2 (ℝ)
    Claim: 𝑆1 = {0} lies in the closure of Ran ≥2 (ℝ), so cardinality strata are not closed and Ran(ℝ) is not
Hausdorff.
    Proof. In the Ran topology, the sequence {0, 1/𝑘 } ∈ Ran2 (ℝ) converges to {0} ∈ Ran1 (ℝ) as 𝑘 → ∞
(collision of the two points). Hence 𝑆1 = {0} is a limit point of Ran2 (ℝ) but does not lie in it. Since Ran2
is not closed, Ran(ℝ) is not 𝑇1 (hence not Hausdorff).
    Interpretation. The non-Hausdorff property encodes the physics of particle collisions: one cannot
separate configurations with different particle numbers.

5.12.2   D-modules and factorization algebras on Ran space

equivalence of ∞-categories:
                                  ChirAlg( 𝑀 ) ≃ D-modfact (Ran( 𝑀 ))
where D-modfact denotes D-modules with factorization structure.

chiral/Ran-space correspondence is developed in [2, Chapter 3]; the factorization-algebra comparison
framework used here is aligned with [26, 27].

Bar and cobar constructions

The bar complex 𝐵 (A) of a chiral algebra A on a smooth curve 𝑋 is an integral transform whose kernel
is the logarithmic 1-form 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) of §2.2, integrated against the OPE data on configuration
spaces. Its output is a factorization coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ) with nilpotent differential ( 𝑑 2 = 0) at genus 0.
                                                 ∼
Verdier duality inverts the transform: Ω ◦ 𝐵 −  → id on the Koszul locus (Theorem 6.12.1), the categorical
logarithm–exponential correspondence of Remark 6.0.1.
Remark 6.0.1 (The nilpotence-periodicity correspondence). The logarithmic form 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) is not
an incidental choice of kernel: the bar construction is the categorical logarithm for chiral algebras, mapping
multiplicative structure (the OPE) to additive/nilpotent structure (the bar differential with 𝑑02 = 0). The
cobar construction is the corresponding exponential, reconstructing the algebra from the nilpotent data.
The structural principle governing the entire theory is:

                                  Nilpotence is the logarithm of periodicity.

At genus 0, the logarithm 𝜂𝑖𝑗 is single-valued on 𝐶2 (ℙ1 ), the bar differential is nilpotent ( 𝑑02 = 0), and the
monodromy is trivial. At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the logarithm 𝑑 log 𝐸 ( 𝑧 𝑖 , 𝑧𝑗 ) acquires monodromy around the
                                                                        2 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 , and the curvature 𝜅 (A)
𝐵 -cycles of Σ 𝑔 , the fiberwise bar differential fails nilpotence by 𝑑fib           𝑔
is the inﬁnitesimal generator of this monodromy–-the residue at the branch point of the logarithm. This is
the chiral Riemann–Hilbert correspondence: the nilpotent datum 𝜅 determines the periodic datum (the
monodromy of the bar family over M 𝑔 ) via exponentiation.
    The four theorems are four aspects of this correspondence: Theorem A asserts that the categorical
logarithm and exponential exist; Theorem B that they are mutually inverse on the convergence domain (the
Koszul locus); Theorem C that the failure off the convergence domain decomposes into complementary
Lagrangians (the branch structure of the logarithm); and Theorem D that the leading coefficient 𝜅 (A) of
the logarithm determines the full scalar package.
    The modular periodicity profile Π (A) is the global/exponential counterpart of the infinitesi-
mal/nilpotent characteristic 𝜅 (A). At the scalar level, the T-matrix eigenvalues 𝜆 = exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 ( ℎ − 𝑐 /24))
are the exponentials of conformal weights shifted by the central charge; the modular period 𝑁 is
the smallest positive integer for which exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 𝑁 𝑐 /24) = 1. At the geometric level, the nilpotency
𝜅 ( 𝜆) 𝑔 −1 = 0 (Theorem 11.6.19) makes the operator exp( 𝜅 ( 𝜆)) unipotent, not periodic: geometry provides
a stabilization threshold, not a period. True periodicity arises from modular and quantum sources whose
nilpotent generators have finite-order exponentials.
   The three-step bar differential 𝑑 = 𝑑internal + 𝑑residue + 𝑑de Rham that we built by hand for the Heisenberg
algebra in Chapter 1 now receives its general formulation. The key structural insight is that the three
components correspond to three types of geometry on the compactified configuration space 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ):

Convention 6.0.3 (Bar coalgebra and Koszul dual algebra). The bar construction 𝐵 𝑋 (A) of an augmented
chiral algebra A is a dg factorization coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ). It is the Koszul dual coalgebra of A: the bar
complex is not a tool for computing the dual, it is the dual.
    When A is Koszul, the bar coalgebra has cohomology concentrated in bar degree 1. The Koszul dual
algebra A ! is a separate object: it has generators V ∨ = H 𝑜𝑚 O𝑋 (V , 𝜔 𝑋 ) (D 𝑋 -module dual of the genera-
tors of A) and relations 𝑅⊥ (orthogonal complement under the residue pairing). In the classical setting
(algebras on a point), A ! is the graded linear dual of the concentrated bar coalgebra. In the chiral setting, A !
is characterized by Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39): Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 ) intertwines the bar coalgebras,

                                            𝔻Ran 𝐵 𝑋 (A) ≃ 𝐵 𝑋 (A ! ) ,
                                                 ∼
and the cobar–bar counit Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵 𝑋 (A)) −  → A (Theorem 6.12.1) is a resolution of A: the cobar of the bar
coalgebra recovers A itself, not its dual.
     The bar-dual identity has a precise witness: the canonical twisting morphism 𝜏 : 𝐵 𝑋 (A) → A,
the degree-+1 map projecting bar generators to their algebra images. The graded vector space
𝔤𝜏 := Hom( 𝐵 𝑋 (A) , A) carries a natural dg Lie structure–-the convolution Lie algebra–-whose bracket
is [ 𝑓 , 𝑔 ] = 𝜇 A ◦ ( 𝑓 ⊗ 𝑔 ) ◦ Δ 𝐵 and whose differential is 𝜕 𝑓 = 𝑑 A ◦ 𝑓 − (−1) | 𝑓 | 𝑓 ◦ 𝑑𝐵 . The twisting
morphism 𝜏 is a Maurer–Cartan element of this Lie algebra:

                             𝜕 𝜏 + 21 [ 𝜏, 𝜏 ] = 0      equivalently: 𝜕 𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 ,
                                                                                     

Remark 6.1.4 (Logarithmic forms are forced). Logarithmic forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) are distinguished

  Conformal invariance. Under a conformal transformation 𝑧 ↦→ 𝑓 ( 𝑧 ), we need:

      -the algebraic counterpart of finite-dimensional state spaces at each point.
 (ii) Excision: the factorization algebra associated to A satisfies the Weiss cosheaf condition
      (Definition 4.10.2), i.e., the factorization structure glues over Weiss covers. This provides the descent
      data for factorization homology.

Remark 6.1.14 (Three components). The component 𝑑internal encodes the differential on A (BRST symme-
try); 𝑑residue extracts OPE data via residues at 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ; 𝑑form is the de Rham differential on configuration space

derivation rule. For general chiral coefficients, the Borcherds identity is an algebraic input (Remark 6.2.31);

6.1.4    Sign conventions
6.2     Edge contractions, residues, and bar signs
A two-step collision has two orders. Its two contributions cancel only when the signs oppose and the
resulting coefficient maps satisfy the required identity. The determinant of the remaining edges records
the first condition. An associative product supplies the second condition in the ordinary bar construction.
Logarithmic residues give a geometric realization of the same determinant sign.
   All complexes use cohomological grading over a commutative ring 𝑘 . Thus 𝑉 [ 𝑟 ] 𝑗 = 𝑉 𝑗 +𝑟 and 𝑑𝑉 [ 𝑟 ] =
(−1) 𝑟 𝑑𝑉 . Tensor products use the Koszul rule. Every sum below is algebraic and finite on each input. No
completion or passage to graph isomorphism classes is implicit.

6.2.1 The deciding corner
Let 𝑒 < 𝑓 be two labeled edges and let 𝜔 = 𝑒 ∧ 𝑓 . Place this determinant generator in degree −2. Deleting
an edge means exterior contraction with its dual basis vector:

                         𝜄𝑒 𝜔 = 𝑓 ,       𝜄 𝑓 𝜔 = −𝑒,              𝜄 𝑓 𝜄𝑒 𝜔 = 1,    𝜄𝑒 𝜄 𝑓 𝜔 = −1.

Suppose contracting 𝑒 then 𝑓 gives a coefficient map 𝑃 . Suppose the reverse order gives 𝑄 , with the same
source and target. The coefficient of the double contraction is 𝑃 − 𝑄 . For 𝑃 = 𝑄 it vanishes over every 𝑘 .
For 𝑘 = ℤ, 𝑃 = 1, and 𝑄 = 2 on ℤ, it equals −1. The determinant sign therefore leaves a coefficient identity
to prove.
   The same calculation appears on a coordinate bidisc over ℂ. Write 𝜆𝑒 = 𝑑𝑢/𝑢 and 𝜆 𝑓 = 𝑑𝑣 /𝑣 . Nor-
malize the residue by placing the normal logarithmic form first:

                                             𝑟𝑢 ( 𝜆𝑒 ∧ 𝛽 + 𝛾 ) = 𝛽 | 𝑢=0 ,                                   (6.1)

where 𝛾 has no logarithmic pole along 𝑢 = 0. Then

                                 𝑟𝑢 ( 𝜆 𝑒 ∧ 𝜆 𝑓 ) = 𝜆 𝑓 ,          𝑟𝑣 ( 𝜆𝑒 ∧ 𝜆 𝑓 ) = −𝜆𝑒 .

The two ordered residues are 1 and −1. There is already one determinant sign in this formula. Multiplying
each residue by its deletion sign again gives 1 + 1 = 2. This last prescription fails over ℤ and ℂ.

6.2.2     A determinant complex with two contractions
Fix a finite set 𝐸 of labeled edges. For 𝑆 ⊆ 𝐸 , write 𝐹 = 𝐸 \ 𝑆 and set
                                                            |𝐹 |
                                                            ^
                                               𝐿(𝐹 ) =             𝑘 𝐹 [| 𝐹 |] .

Proof. For two edges of one color, the pure coefficient defect is the assumed square. For different colors,
the mixed defect is that square. All other terms are zero.

   When both operations can contract every edge, the four-term identity is the exact condition. Separate
associativity of the two operations does not imply it. For a tree with a fixed edge labeling, its quotients
by subsets give the required target identifications. Coefficient complexes and contraction maps must also
respect these identifications. If relabelings act compatibly, the construction descends to their coinvariants
by equivariance. The vanishing criterion on a quotient can be weaker, since distinct labeled terms can
become equal there.

6.2.3    Stable graphs with labeled edges
A stable graph here is a connected graph with finitely many vertices, edges, and labeled legs. Each vertex
𝑣 has a nonnegative integer genus 𝑔𝑣 and satisfies 2 𝑔𝑣 − 2 + val( 𝑣 ) > 0. A loop contributes two to the
valence. For a connected graph, its total genus is 𝑣 𝑔𝑣 + | 𝐸 | − |𝑉 | + 1. Fix an edge labeling and, when

needed, an edge color.

their genera. A loop increases its vertex genus by one.

    Each two-edge coefficient square now has equal composites, because both yield that same quotient graph.
Its determinant signs are opposite by (6.2). This proves the square-zero and mixed identities. Relabeling
edges transports their determinant generators and contraction maps together. Thus these operators are
equivariant and descend to coinvariants. No division by an automorphism order is used.
Example 6.2.4 (Two parallel edges). Take two genus-zero vertices, each carrying one leg, joined by two
edges 𝑒 < 𝑓 . Each vertex has valence three. Contracting 𝑒 gives one genus-zero vertex with two legs and the
remaining loop 𝑓 . Contracting that loop gives one genus-one vertex with two legs. The other order gives
the same result. The two determinant signs are +1 and −1, so the sum is zero. The first edge is nonseparating
but is not a loop. Its contraction does not increase the vertex genus.

Proof. On three homogeneous inputs, the mixed operator equals (−1) | 𝑏 | 𝑡 times the difference of the two

Example 6.2.7 (Separate associativity is insuﬃcient). Let 𝐻¯ = 𝑘𝑥 ⊕ 𝑘𝑦 in degree zero. Define 𝜇 ( 𝑥, 𝑥 ) = 𝑥

triple can have a nonzero iterated product. Every iterated 𝜈 -product vanishes. For ( 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 ) = ( 𝑦, 𝑦, 𝑥 ), the
left side of (6.8) is 𝑥 and the right side is zero. Thus the mixed bar anticommutator is nonzero whenever 𝑘
is nonzero. Adjoining a unit to ( 𝐻¯ , 𝜇) gives an augmented algebra with this augmentation ideal.

Example 6.2.8 (A noncommutative family). Choose a closed element ℎ ∈ 𝐻 0 and define 𝜈 ( 𝑎, 𝑏 ) = 𝑎ℎ𝑏 .
The augmentation ideal contains 𝑎ℎ𝑏 whenever 𝑎, 𝑏 ∈ 𝐻¯ . The map is a cochain map because 𝑑𝐻 ℎ = 0.
Associativity gives

                   ( 𝑎ℎ𝑏 ) ℎ𝑐 = 𝑎ℎ ( 𝑏ℎ𝑐 ) ,            ( 𝑎ℎ𝑏 ) 𝑐 + ( 𝑎𝑏 ) ℎ𝑐 = 𝑎 ( 𝑏ℎ𝑐 ) + 𝑎ℎ ( 𝑏𝑐 ) .

Thus the two bar contractions anticommute. No centrality assumption on ℎ is needed. For 𝐻 = 𝑘 ⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩,
with zero differential and its usual augmentation, take ℎ = 𝑥 . The products 𝑦𝑥𝑦𝑦 and 𝑦𝑦𝑥𝑦 can occur in
separate mixed paths and are distinct. Their four-term sum still cancels. This example shows why requiring
every mixed coefficient square to commute would be unnecessarily restrictive.

General logarithmic forms also have regular normal directions and variable coefficients. A determinant
line alone is not the full sheaf of logarithmic forms. The global residue identities hold on that full sheaf by

6.2.6    The coefficient obligation for chiral contractions
In a chiral construction, a contraction can include a collision map on states, a residue, and a pushforward
from a boundary stratum. Each composite must have a specified target after the first collision. A second
contraction acts on that target, which contains the merged state.
    Theorem 6.2.1 applies after these coefficient complexes and degree-zero maps have been constructed.
It determines the orientation sign and the exact remaining coefficient identity. For disjoint fixed-color
contractions, equality of the two unsigned composites suffices. When both kinds of contraction can remove
either edge, equation (6.3) gives the required four-term identity. The associative construction proves this
identity on its stated tensor-coalgebra carrier. The logarithmic construction proves it for the stated residue
sheaves. A comparison with a chiral bar complex must intertwine its native collision maps with these maps.
Neither a determinant line nor an equality of scalar residues constructs that comparison.
    The de Rham differential is a distinct degree-one operation. With left-normal residues, its anticommu-
tation follows from the second identity in (6.9). Here 𝑑 ( 𝑑 log 𝑥𝑒 ) = 0 as a meromorphic differential form.
No current supported on a divisor occurs in this de Rham complex. Replacing meromorphic forms by
currents changes the carrier and requires its own comparison.

6.2.7    A coordinate change that moves the normal forms
Work first on a product of three complex discs with coordinates ( 𝑥1 , 𝑥2 , 𝑧 ). The two divisors are 𝐷1 =
{ 𝑥1 = 0} and 𝐷2 = { 𝑥2 = 0}. Write 𝜆𝑖 = 𝑑𝑥 𝑖 / 𝑥 𝑖 . A logarithmic residue removes a normal differential
after moving it to the first position:

                              𝑟1 ( 𝜆 1 ∧ 𝜆 2 ) = 𝜆 2 | 𝐷 1 ,   𝑟 2 ( 𝜆1 ∧ 𝜆 2 ) = − 𝜆 1 | 𝐷 2 .

Consequently the two successive residues of this form are 1 and −1. The normal order determines the sign.
  Change coordinates by
                                 𝑦1 = 𝑒 𝑧 𝑥 1 ,   𝑦2 = 𝑥 2 ,    𝑧 ′ = 𝑧.                          (6.12)
This is an invertible holomorphic change, with the same two divisors. Its normal logarithmic form is

                                         𝑑𝑦1 𝑑𝑦2
                                            ∧    = 𝜆1 ∧ 𝜆2 + 𝑑𝑧 ∧ 𝜆2 .
                                         𝑦1   𝑦2

The second term has one normal logarithmic factor. It cannot equal 𝑓 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜆1 ∧ 𝜆2 for a holomorphic
function 𝑓 . Indeed, on the complement of the divisors, 𝜆1 ∧ 𝜆2 and 𝑑𝑧 ∧ 𝜆2 are distinct exterior basis
elements. Thus the geometric coordinate change does not preserve the chosen space of top normal forms.
    There are two questions. The first asks whether the full logarithmic residue complex is independent of
coordinates. The second asks how the smaller normal complex compares with that coordinate-independent
complex. The distinction persists even though the normal complex includes every collision stratum. We
will construct both comparisons and examine which homotopies respect the number of collisions.
    The starting language is linear algebra, holomorphic functions, and differential forms. All complexes
are complexes of complex vector spaces or sheaves of such spaces. A differential has degree +1. Its degree- 𝑞
cohomology is the kernel of the differential in degree 𝑞 modulo its image from degree 𝑞 − 1. For a complex
𝑉 , the shift is 𝑉 [ 𝑎] 𝑗 = 𝑉 𝑗 + 𝑎 , with differential (−1) 𝑎 𝑑𝑉 . The wedge of forms of degrees 𝑝, 𝑞 changes
by (−1) 𝑝𝑞 when their order is exchanged. Tensor products obey the same sign rule. All edge sets, sums
over strata, and covers used below are finite. No completed tensor product, support condition, or analytic
limiting procedure is used.

from 𝑆 . Thus ℎ has degree −1, including after the shift [−2𝑚].
Lemma 6.2.13 (Permutation-invariant contraction). The identities 𝐷 𝐴 ℎ + ℎ𝐷 𝐴 = id and ℎ2 = 0

Proof. For a vector 𝑣 and exterior form 𝜔, deleting each factor in 𝑣 ∧ 𝜔 gives 𝜄𝜖 ( 𝑣 ∧ 𝜔) = 𝜖 ( 𝑣 ) 𝜔 − 𝑣 ∧ 𝜄𝜖 𝜔.

𝑣 𝐸 , proving equivariance. If 𝐷 𝐴 𝑎 = 0, then 𝑎 = 𝐷 𝐴 ( ℎ𝑎), so every cycle is a boundary.

    This construction gives a comparison into the global residue carrier. It gives no quasi-isomorphism,
meaning a map inducing isomorphisms on cohomology, with that carrier. For 𝑚 > 0, the source sheaf
𝐴 is contractible by ℎ. Its Čech total complex is also contractible: on Čech degree 𝑝, use (−1) 𝑝 ℎ. The
restriction terms cancel because this sign changes when 𝑝 increases. The internal terms sum to the identity
by Lemma 6.2.13. In contrast, on a connected nonempty chart 𝑈 , the constant function 1 is a nonzero
class in 𝐻 0 (R𝑌 (𝑈 )). It is closed and cannot be a boundary because the total complex has no negative
degrees. Consequently the normal comparison cannot recover even this degree-zero class. When 𝑚 = 0,
the product chart is 𝑍 itself, 𝐴 = 𝑀 , and 𝑗 is the identity on its de Rham complex. The contraction
argument is unnecessary in that case.

Example 6.2.17 (A double overlap with no ﬁltered homotopy). Take 𝑈 = Δ2 × ℂ∗ with base coordinate
𝑧 . Let 𝑦1 = 𝑧𝑥1 and 𝑦2 = 𝑥2 . These functions and 𝑧 form an adapted coordinate system onto their open

from 𝑗𝑥 to 𝑗𝑦 on all of 𝑈 .
    To prove this, apply the homotopy equation to the coefficient-one element 𝑒1 in 𝑆 = {2}. Its total
degree is three, and 𝐷 𝐴 𝑒1 = 1 in 𝑆 = {1, 2}. A filtered degree-minus-one map sends that last element to
zero: its output would have degree three and depth at least two, whose minimum total degree is four. The
component of 𝐾 𝑒1 on 𝐷2 is therefore a holomorphic function 𝑓 with 𝑑𝑓 = 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧 . Restricting to 𝑥1 = 0
gives the same equation on ℂ∗ . Along 𝑧 = 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 , the integral of 𝑑𝑓 is zero because 𝑓 ( 𝑒 𝑖𝑡 ) has the same
endpoints. The integral of 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧 = 𝑖 𝑑𝑡 is 2 𝜋 𝑖 . This contradiction proves nonexistence. The unfiltered
homotopy of Theorem 6.2.14 still exists on this overlap.

                                       𝑐𝑒 = 𝐴𝑒 + 𝐵 𝑒 − 𝐶𝑒 ∈ 2 𝜋 𝑖 ℤ.                               (6.24)

It has degree −1, and 𝐷𝑇 + 𝑇 𝐷 𝐴 = 0 because the differences of the three embeddings cancel. For a map

of the cohomological convention.

    This obstruction belongs to the chosen logarithmic homotopies. Changing a logarithm on a double
overlap by 2 𝜋 𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑗,𝑒 changes 𝑐 𝑖𝑗 𝑘,𝑒 by 2 𝜋 𝑖 ( 𝑛𝑖𝑗,𝑒 + 𝑛𝑗 𝑘,𝑒 − 𝑛𝑖𝑘,𝑒 ). Thus the obstruction to choosing log-
arithms with zero triple defect is the class of this constant two-cochain modulo those changes. Here a
two-cochain is a family on triple overlaps, and two such families define the same class when their difference
is the alternating change of a family on double overlaps. On quadruple overlaps its alternating sum is zero,
since each logarithm occurs twice with opposite signs. If arbitrary holomorphic primitives of 𝑑 log 𝑢𝑒 are
allowed in place of logarithms, the permitted constants are in ℂ, and the corresponding class uses that
constant coefficient space. Component permutations transport these constants with their labels.
    When additive logarithms have been chosen, the secondary homotopies also satisfy the next coherence
identity. For three successive logarithm vectors 𝐴, 𝐵, 𝐶 , the scalar function in (6.25) is bilinear:

Both sides expand to 𝑄 ( 𝐴, 𝐵 ) + 𝑄 ( 𝐴, 𝐶 ) + 𝑄 ( 𝐵, 𝐶 ). Therefore the alternating quadruple-overlap sum
of 𝐿 is zero. Together, the embeddings, the homotopies 𝐾 , and the secondary homotopies 𝐿 give a filtered
map on the finite-cover total complexes of Section 6.2.11. For 𝑎 ∈ 𝐶ˇ 𝑝 ( 𝐴) 𝑞 , its components in Čech degrees

The third term has internal degree 𝑞 − 2, so all three terms have total degree 𝑝 + 𝑞 . To check the chain

no components in higher degrees. Thus no further homotopies are needed for this map. The identities here

in the Čech complex of graded maps.

To check this, use 𝐷𝑇 = −𝑇 𝐷 𝐴 and 𝐷 𝐴 ℎ + ℎ𝐷 𝐴 = 1. This primitive can decrease stratum depth, which
is exactly the property excluded in Theorem 6.2.18.
6.2. Edge contractions, residues, and bar signs                                                          201


6.2.14    What descends
The full residue complex glues by canonical pullbacks. On a supplied projected atlas, the normal complex
has determinant transports and the comparison (6.21), with the shift [−2𝑚] and every stratum retained.
For 𝑚 > 0, its contractibility excludes a quasi-isomorphism with the full residue complex. When the
homotopies must preserve stratum depth, the logarithmic construction instead gives the two-normal
comparison subject to (6.24).
    A construction with chiral coefficient states must supply those states on every stratum and the maps
attached to coordinate changes. Those maps must commute with residues and the internal coefficient
differential on their actual domains. The contraction ℎ used here also depends on the identity coefficient
maps between all subsets. For varying state spaces, adding an edge would require a map in the reverse stratum
direction; the formula 𝐻 = Δℎ requires such a compatible contraction to be constructed separately. The
logarithmic formula requires a differential-form action and compatible coefficient restrictions. Changing
the base projection through normal-dependent tangential coordinates also requires an additional coefficient
comparison. No such state or base-projection comparison is provided by the normal orientation line itself.

6.2.15   Ordered states in the residue carrier
A residue acts on a differential form, while an ordered bar face multiplies adjacent states. These operations
can be combined in two ways. One can carry an entire bar complex unchanged along every normal stratum,
or attach a multiplication map to the stratum reached by a collision. The first construction inherits the
unfiltered overlap homotopies. The second requires the coefficient diagram itself; its behavior is already
different for an algebra with square-zero augmentation ideal. We construct both complexes and their
coordinate maps.
    All coefficients in this section are over ℂ. Tensor products of vector spaces are algebraic. For sheaves,
tensor product means the sheaf associated to the algebraic tensor product on local sections. Thus each
germ is a finite sum of tensors; no completion is used. Normal charts and their base projection satisfy the
hypotheses of Section 6.2.11.

    Neither tensoring with 𝑄 nor taking its bar differential removes the scalar limitations. The inclusion

𝑚 > 0.

Lemma 6.2.21 (The interval coefficient squares). For distinct remaining cuts 𝑒, 𝑓 , the two maps to

Proof. If the two cuts have no block in common, each composite multiplies the same two disjoint pairs in

resulting states are ( 𝑎𝑏 ) 𝑐 and 𝑎 ( 𝑏𝑐 ). They agree by associativity, and all other factors remain unchanged.
These exhaust the possibilities for two distinct cuts in an ordered string.

Proposition 6.2.22 (A residue complex with changing ordered states). The differential (6.31)
squares to zero. Adapted coordinate changes preserving the labeled cut divisors induce strict chain isomor-

Proof. The internal and form differentials square to zero and anticommute by the tensor sign. A collision
map commutes with the coefficient differential because 𝜇 𝑆,𝑒 is a cochain map. Its two cross-terms with
that differential have signs (−1) | 𝑣 | and (−1) | 𝑣 |+1 , and cancel. The cross-terms with the form differential

cient composites agree by Lemma 6.2.21, while the form composites have opposite signs. Repeated-edge
contributions are absent because their targets have already lost that normal direction. This proves 𝐷𝑉2 = 0.
   Pullback commutes with the form differential and with each typed residue by Proposition 6.2.10. It
acts as the identity on states, so it also commutes with every 𝑑𝑉𝑆 and 𝜇 𝑆,𝑒 . This proves the chain identity
and, by composition of pullbacks, the cocycle. A relabeling of coordinate slots sends the stratum name to
the corresponding set of intrinsic cuts. It makes no change to that set of blocks or to their order, proving
the permutation assertion.

  For three positions and degree-zero states, the four coefficient spaces are 𝐼 ⊗3 , two copies of 𝐼 ⊗2 , and 𝐼 .

Example 6.2.24 (The normal image and the full stratum summands). Take 𝑚 = 1, 𝐻 = ℂ[ 𝜖 ]/( 𝜖 2 ) in
degree zero, and 𝑍 a point. Then 𝐼 = ℂ 𝜖 , 𝑉∅ = ℂ( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ), and 𝑉{1} = ℂ 𝜖 . On the ambient chart the
normal image is spanned by ( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ) ⊗ 𝑑 log 𝑥 , of total degree 1. The full ambient summand also contains
( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ) ⊗ 1, of total degree 0, which is outside this image. On the divisor, the normal image is spanned
by 𝜖 ⊗ 1, of total degree 2. Thus both subsets occur in the image, although the ambient summand is not
exhausted. The residue face vanishes because 𝜖 2 = 0; all these normal generators are closed.
    An unfiltered homotopy on every unit overlap does not follow for this coefficient diagram. Take 𝑛 = 2,
𝐻 = ℂ[ 𝜖 ]/( 𝜖 2 ), and 𝑍 = ℂ∗ with coordinate 𝑧 . Then 𝑉∅ = ℂ( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ), 𝑉{1} = ℂ 𝜖 , and 𝜇∅,1 = 0. The
coefficient differentials vanish. On 𝑈 = Δ × ℂ∗ , change the normal coordinate by 𝑦 = 𝑧𝑥 . The normal
generator 𝑎 = 𝑒 ⊗ ( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ) ⊗ 1 has total degree one and 𝐷 𝐴 (𝑉 ) 𝑎 = 0. If any degree-minus-one homotopy
𝐺 existed, 𝐺𝑎 would have degree zero in R (𝑉 ). The collision stratum has minimum degree two, so 𝐺𝑎 =
( 𝜖 ⊗ 𝜖 ) ⊗ 𝑓 on the ambient stratum. The homotopy equation would imply

                                                   𝑑𝑓 = 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧.

Restriction to 𝑥 = 0 and integration around the unit circle contradict this equation, exactly as in Exam-
ple 6.2.17. Thus no such unfiltered 𝐺 exists on this overlap, even though the full state-valued residue sheaf
has strict coordinate descent. The average wedge operator ℎ fails here because it would need to reverse the
zero multiplication map.
206                                                              Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


    The constructions above give precise carriers for ordered associative states and for a fixed bar complex.
For a chiral product, its input is the sheaf of states away from a collision and its output is supported on the
collision diagonal. It is not the degree-zero multiplication 𝐼 ⊗ 𝐼 → 𝐼 used above. Applying the displayed
formulas to that product requires actual coefficient complexes on every stratum, a differential-form action,
and typed collision maps commuting with the internal differential and the coordinate transitions. The two
coefficient composites at an adjacent double collision must land in the same merged-state complex and
satisfy the requisite identity there. A fixed coefficient comparison additionally requires the stated identifi-
cation of those coefficient systems. These are the mathematical conditions for transfer to Definition 6.1.13;
neither determinant signs nor strict descent of logarithmic forms supplies them.

6.2.16    Sign compatibility for geometric bar faces
Convention 6.2.25 (Determinant and residue signs). An algebraic contraction uses the determinant of the
remaining labeled edges, placed before the coefficient complex in degree minus the number of edges. Its
deletion sign is (6.2). A logarithmic residue uses the left-normal convention (6.1). This residue already
includes the same deletion sign. One does not multiply it by a second copy of that sign. For a tensor
𝑥 ⊗ 𝛼 with coefficients first, a homogeneous map 𝑢 ⊗ 𝑣 acts with sign (−1) | 𝑣 | | 𝑥 | . This rule translates the
determinant-first convention when factors are reordered. The coefficient maps must satisfy the identities
of Theorem 6.2.1 on their stated domains.
Lemma 6.2.26 (Sign compatibility for ordered bar faces; [proved]). For an augmented differential
graded associative algebra, (6.7) identifies the desuspended bar differential with the determinant contraction
differential. For logarithmic forms on a product normal-crossing chart, (6.11) identifies the direct sum of
determinant terms over all contracted sets with the normal-logarithmic subcomplex on all product strata.
The source has the global shift [−2| 𝐸 |], and its edge contractions correspond to left-normal residues.
On a supplied projected atlas, fixed ordered-bar coefficients admit the coherent unfiltered comparison
of Proposition 6.2.20. For the interval coefficient system (6.29), Propositions 6.2.22 and 6.2.23 give the
full residue differential, its strict coordinate maps, and the normal embedding. The logarithmic overlap
homotopy for that system requires the stated local logarithms.

Proof. Proposition 6.2.5 computes every unary and binary bar sign. Equation (6.11) computes the logarith-
mic comparison on each wedge generator. Each residue lands in the summand indexed by 𝑆 ∪ { 𝑒 }, which is
present in both direct sums. Both computations give (−1) 𝑖 −1 for deletion of the 𝑖 th edge. Their coefficient
identities are separate from the determinant comparison, as stated in Theorem 6.2.1. Lemma 6.2.19 supplies
the additional sign from the degree of an ordered bar word. For changing interval states, Lemma 6.2.21
identifies the common merged target and proves the coefficient square. The degree and residue calculations
of Proposition 6.2.23 then prove the stated comparison.

    Applying this theorem to a geometric chiral bar object requires an identification with a coefficient
system of the displayed type, compatible with the internal differential, residues, and coordinate overlaps. At
an overlapping collision, the Borcherds identity must act on the same merged-state target as the geometric
composites; a formal cyclic expression in OPE coefficients does not establish that identification. This
comparison is an additional hypothesis, not a conclusion of the theorem.

Remark 6.2.29 (Geometric coeﬃcient compatibility). On the local complex of Theorem 6.2.27, nilpotency

comparison.

Corollary 6.2.32 (Bar complex is functorial; [proved]). The bar construction 𝐵¯ • (−) is a functor
from chiral algebras to differential graded vector spaces:

                                          𝐵¯ • : ChiralAlg ( Σ 𝑔 ) → dgVect

   Moreover:

  (ii) The bar construction preserves quasi-isomorphisms: a quasi-isomorphism 𝑓 induces a quasi-
       isomorphism 𝐵¯ ( 𝑓 ) by the filtration spectral sequence argument of Theorem 6.2.27
 (iii) Composition is preserved: 𝐵¯ • ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ • ( 𝑔 ) ◦ 𝐵¯ • ( 𝑓 )

Proof. Since 𝑑 2 = 0, the bar complex ( 𝐵¯ • (A) , 𝑑 ) is a genuine chain complex.

                        𝐵¯ 𝑛 ( 𝑓 ) ( 𝜙0 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜙𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = 𝑓 ( 𝜙0 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑓 ( 𝜙𝑛 ) ⊗ 𝜔

                                               𝑑 ◦ 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ( 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ( 𝑓 ) ◦ 𝑑

   because 𝑓 is a morphism of chiral algebras (preserves the chiral product 𝜇).
   The other properties follow from general category theory.

6.2.19      Arnold relations: proofs from three perspectives
Convention 6.2.36 (Set ordering and position notation). Throughout this manuscript, we adopt the follow-
ing conventions for ordered sets:
    (i) Natural Ordering: For any finite subset 𝑆 ⊆ ℕ, we always use the ordering inherited from ℕ:

                                     𝑆 = { 𝑘1 , 𝑘2 , . . . , 𝑘𝑚 } where 𝑘1 < 𝑘2 < · · · < 𝑘𝑚

 (ii) Position Function: For 𝑘 ∈ 𝑆 , we denote by | 𝑘 | 𝑆 (or simply | 𝑘 | when 𝑆 is clear from context) the
      position of 𝑘 in this ordering:

                        𝑘 = 𝑘| 𝑘 |       ⇐⇒         | 𝑘 | = 𝑖 where 𝑘 is the 𝑖 -th smallest element of 𝑆

 (iii) Sign Convention: Signs arising from reordering are computed via the Koszul rule. Moving an element
       𝑘 past position | 𝑘 | introduces sign (−1) | 𝑘 | −1 .
 (iv) Multi-indices: For multi-index sets (e.g., in partitions), we use lexicographic ordering.
      Example. For 𝑆 = {2, 5, 7}:
• |2| 𝑆 = 1 (first position)
• |5| 𝑆 = 2 (second position)
• |7| 𝑆 = 3 (third position)
  In Arnold relations, the notation (−1) | 𝑘 | means (−1) | 𝑘 | 𝑆 where 𝑆 is the index set of the collision divisor
under consideration.
Theorem 6.2.37 (Arnold relations; [proved]). We encountered these relations concretely in the
Heisenberg bar complex (§1.2), where they appeared as the identity forcing 𝑑 2 = 0 at degree 2. In full
generality:
   For distinct indices 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 ∈ {1, . . . , 𝑛}, the logarithmic 1-forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) satisfy:
   Formulation 1 (basic).
                                   𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0
    Formulation 2 (Orlik–Solomon). The algebra 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ); ℚ) is the quotient of the exterior algebra
  ⟨ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 | 1 ≤ 𝑖 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑛⟩ by the ideal generated by the three-term Arnold relations of Formulation 1. All
V
higher-degree relations in the Orlik–Solomon algebra follow from these by repeated application; there is
no independent ‘‘general Arnold relation’’ beyond the three-term version.
    Formulation 3 (cohomological). The cohomology ring 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ); ℚ) is generated by classes [ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ]
subject to the Arnold relations.

Proof 1: Topological (via Stokes). We prove the basic Arnold relation: 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + cyclic = 0.
   Setup. Consider the configuration space 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ) of three points on 𝑋 .
   Boundary. 𝜕𝐶 3 = 𝐷12 ∪ 𝐷23 ∪ 𝐷13
   The 2-form 𝜔 = 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 is exact when restricted to certain subspaces.
   Computation. Compute 𝑑dR ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ):

                                     𝑑 ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ) = 𝑑 ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ) ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 − 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝑑 ( 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 )

      For logarithmic forms: 𝑑 ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ) = 0 on the smooth locus 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) (these are closed forms).
6.2. Edge contractions, residues, and bar signs                                                            213


   But near boundary divisors, we must be more careful. Using the logarithmic de Rham complex:

                                          𝑑log ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ) = 0 in Ω2 (log 𝐷 )

   Hence 𝑑 ( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ) = 0 as a form on 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ).

in cohomology.
    This shows that the Arnold relations are a consequence of 𝜕 2 = 0 for configuration spaces.

Proof 2: combinatorial (via partition poset). The configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) has a natural stratification by
collision patterns. The combinatorics of this stratification encodes the Arnold relations.
    Setup. The cohomology 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )) is generated by ‘‘collision’’ classes, one for each subset 𝑆 ⊆
{1, . . . , 𝑛} with | 𝑆 | ≥ 2.
    Relations. These classes satisfy relations coming from the incidence structure of the poset of partitions
Π𝑛 .
    The Arnold relation for { 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 } corresponds to the poset relation:

                                          𝜕 ( 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 𝑘 ) = 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 + 𝐷𝑗 𝑘 + 𝐷 𝑖𝑘

(the boundary of the codimension-2 stratum is the union of three codimension-1 strata)
   Since 𝜕 2 = 0 in the poset:
                                      𝜕 ( 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 + 𝐷𝑗 𝑘 + 𝐷 𝑖𝑘 ) = 0
   This translates to the Arnold relation after applying Poincaré duality.

Proof 3: operadic (via conﬁguration space operad). The configuration spaces {𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )}𝑛 form a topological
operad. The Arnold relations are a manifestation of the operadic relations (associativity, etc.).
   Setup. The little disks operad D2 [43, §5.1] acts on configuration spaces:

                            D2 ( 𝑘 ) × 𝐶𝑛1 ( 𝑋 ) × · · · × 𝐶𝑛𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝐶𝑛1 +···+𝑛𝑘 ( 𝑋 )

   Cohomology. This induces operations on cohomology:

                      𝐻 ∗ (D2 ( 𝑘 )) ⊗ 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛𝑘 ) → 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛1 +···+𝑛𝑘 )
214                                                           Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


   Arnold relations from operad relations. The Arnold relations are precisely the relations ensuring the
above operations are well-defined and associative.
   In particular, the basic Arnold relation:

                                              𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + cyclic = 0

    corresponds to the fact that three disks can be nested in the unit disk in multiple orders, and these must
give compatible results after taking cohomology.
    This proof connects Arnold relations to the structure of 𝔼2 -operads (or 𝔼𝑑 -operads in dimension
𝑑 ), explaining why similar relations appear in many contexts (Poisson algebras, Hochschild cohomology,
etc.).

Remark 6.2.38 (Comparison of the three proofs). The topological proof highlights 𝜕 2 = 0; the combinatorial
proof connects to partition posets; the operadic proof reveals the categorical structure. We primarily use
the topological viewpoint because it connects directly to Feynman diagrams.
Corollary 6.2.39 (Cohomology of configuration spaces; [proved]). The cohomology ring
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ); ℚ) of the open configuration space is:

                                𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ))  ℚ[ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 : 1 ≤ 𝑖 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑛]/IArnold

where IArnold is the ideal generated by Arnold relations.

Proof. By Arnol’d [97], the 1-forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) generate 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ); ℚ) and satisfy the Arnold
relations 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0. That these generate all relations follows from Cohen’s
computation of 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ)) as the cohomology of the Arnol’d–Brieskorn braid arrangement comple-
ment [41]. See also Appendix F for the three proofs of the Arnold relations used in this monograph.

6.2.22     Functoriality of the bar construction
Theorem 6.2.47 (Bar construction is functorial; [proved]). The geometric bar construction defines
a functor:
                                                aug
                               𝐵¯ geom : ChirAlg 𝑋 → dgCoalg 𝑋
from augmented chiral algebras to dg coalgebras, that is:
   (i) Well-deﬁned on objects: For each augmented chiral algebra A, 𝐵¯ geom (A) is a differential graded
       coalgebra
  (ii) Well-deﬁned on morphisms: For each morphism 𝑓 : A → B of augmented chiral algebras, there is
       an induced coalgebra morphism 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑓 ) : 𝐵¯ geom (A) → 𝐵¯ geom (B)
 (iii) Preserves identities: 𝐵¯ geom (id A ) = id 𝐵¯ geom ( A )
 (iv) Preserves composition: 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑔 ) ◦ 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑓 )

Proof. Part 1: well-definedness on objects
This was established in Theorem 6.2.27: for any augmented chiral algebra A, the complex:
                                      geom

                                                                                 )

with differential 𝑑 = 𝑑int + 𝑑res + 𝑑dR satisfies 𝑑 2 = 0.
    The coalgebra structure (coproduct Δ, counit 𝜖 ) was defined in Theorem 6.2.53. We verified coassocia-
tivity below in this section.

Part 2: action on morphisms

• 𝑓 preserves the factorization structure

Part 3: preservation of identities
For the identity morphism id A : A → A:

                        𝐵¯ geom (id A ) ( 𝑎0 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = id A ( 𝑎0 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ id A ( 𝑎𝑛 ) ⊗ 𝜔
                                                                            = 𝑎0 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎 𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔
                                                                            = id 𝐵¯ geom ( A ) ( 𝑎0 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔)

   Therefore: 𝐵¯ geom (id A ) = id 𝐵¯ geom ( A ) .

Part 4: preservation of composition
Let 𝑓 : A → B and 𝑔 : B → C be morphisms of chiral algebras.
   LHS (applying bar to composition).

                 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) ( 𝑎0 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) ( 𝑎0 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) ( 𝑎𝑛 ) ⊗ 𝜔

   RHS (composing after applying bar).

   LHS = RHS, therefore: 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑔 ) ◦ 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑓 ).
   Parts 1–4 verify well-definedness on objects (Theorem 6.2.27), on morphisms (Lemmas 6.2.49
and 6.2.50), identity preservation, and composition preservation.
