Corollary 6.2.51 (Natural transformation property; [proved]). A commutative diagram of chiral
algebras induces a commutative diagram of bar complexes: if 𝑘 ◦ 𝑓 = 𝑔 ◦ ℎ in ChirAlg 𝑋 , then 𝐵¯ ( 𝑘 ) ◦
𝐵¯ ( 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) ◦ 𝐵¯ ( ℎ) in dgCoalg 𝑋 . This is immediate from functoriality.
Proposition 6.2.52 (Model independence; [proved]). Let A be a chiral algebra on 𝑋 . Any two
admissible1 dg presentations of the bar object B 𝑋 (A) are connected by a contractible space of quasi-
isomorphisms. In particular, any two such models give canonically isomorphic cohomology, spectral se-
quences, and generating functions.
Proof. Both presentations are cofibrant-fibrant objects in the model structure on conilpotent dg coalgebras
over Ran( 𝑋 ) (Positselski [171], Theorem 8.1). Cofibrant-fibrant replacements in this model structure are
unique up to a contractible space of weak equivalences: the mapping space Map( 𝐵 1 , 𝐵 2 ) between two such
replacements is contractible whenever both compute the same homotopy object. The configuration-space
model 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) is cofibrant by freeness of the coalgebra generators and fibrant by the Cousin filtration
(Theorem 8.15.6). Any other admissible model shares these properties by the same arguments, whence the
mapping space between them is contractible.

6.2.23      Coalgebra structure
Theorem 6.2.53 (Bar coalgebra; [proved]). The bar complex carries a natural coalgebra structure:
                                      Δ : 𝐵¯ geom (A) → 𝐵¯ geom (A) ⊗ 𝐵¯ geom (A)
induced by the diagonal map 𝑋 → 𝑋 × 𝑋 .
Proof. Define Δ on tensors by summing over ordered bipartitions of the input index set and restricting
the logarithmic form to the corresponding boundary factorization stratum, as in the explicit formula used
in Theorem 6.2.54. This defines a morphism 𝐵¯ geom (A) → 𝐵¯ geom (A) ⊗ 𝐵¯ geom (A).
   Coassociativity of this coproduct is proved in Theorem 6.2.54; counit compatibility is proved in Theo-
rem 6.2.55. Hence the stated coproduct gives a coalgebra structure on 𝐵¯ geom (A).

is a differential graded coalgebra.

Proof. This assembles Theorem 6.2.27 ( 𝑑 2 = 0), Theorem 6.2.54 (coassociativity of Δ), and Theorem 6.2.55

Remark 6.2.57 (Geometric meaning of coassociativity). Coassociativity says the order of splitting does not
matter: ( Δ ⊗ id) ◦ Δ (split, then split left) equals (id ⊗ Δ) ◦ Δ (split, then split right). Geometrically,
corners of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) where multiple divisors intersect can be approached from different directions, giving
consistent boundary data.
Theorem 6.2.58 (Differential is coderivation; [proved]). The differential 𝑑 on 𝐵¯ (A) is a coderiva-
tion:
                                Δ ◦ 𝑑 = ( 𝑑 ⊗ id + id ⊗ 𝑑 ) ◦ Δ
Proof. The coderivation identity Δ ◦ 𝑑 = ( 𝑑 ⊗ id + id ⊗ 𝑑 ) ◦ Δ is verified for each component of
𝑑 = 𝑑int + 𝑑res + 𝑑dR separately.
    For 𝑑int : the internal differential acts on each tensor factor 𝜙 𝑖 independently, and the deconcatenation
coproduct Δ ( [ 𝑎1 | · · · | 𝑎𝑛 ]) = 𝑛𝑖=0 [ 𝑎1 | · · · | 𝑎𝑖 ] ⊗ [ 𝑎𝑖 +1 | · · · | 𝑎𝑛 ] splits the tensor factors. The Leibniz

Remark 6.2.60 (Orientation and edge signs). The smooth complex configuration space has a canonical
real orientation. Its edge determinant 𝐿 ( 𝐸 ) is a separate graded line, whose signs record the order of
collision contractions. A further coefficient line at positive genus requires its own definition and compatible
contraction maps. It is not supplied by the real orientation of the configuration space.

Lemma 6.2.63 (Orientation of a corner; [proved]). At a transverse intersection of two boundary
hypersurfaces of an oriented real manifold with corners, the two induced boundary orientations are opposite.
For a simple normal crossing divisor in a complex manifold, the analogous sign occurs in the ordered wedge
of its logarithmic normal forms.

Proof. Let 𝑛𝑒 , 𝑛 𝑓 be outward normal vectors. The two boundary conventions write the ambient orientation
as 𝑛𝑒 ∧ 𝑛 𝑓 ∧ 𝜔𝑒𝑓 and 𝑛 𝑓 ∧ 𝑛𝑒 ∧ 𝜔 𝑓 𝑒 . Equality implies 𝜔𝑒𝑓 = − 𝜔 𝑓 𝑒 . For logarithmic forms, interchange
𝑑 log 𝑥𝑒 and 𝑑 log 𝑥 𝑓 instead. Their wedge changes sign once. The real outward-normal convention and the
logarithmic residue convention have distinct domains, and each gives the stated two-order comparison.
6.2. Edge contractions, residues, and bar signs                                                                  225


Lemma 6.2.64 (Residue properties; [proved]). On the direct sum of logarithmic forms over labeled
strata, the component 𝑟𝑒 is zero after 𝑒 has been removed. It satisfies 𝑟𝑒2 = 0 and 𝑟𝑒 𝑟 𝑓 + 𝑟 𝑓 𝑟𝑒 = 0 for distinct
components. It also satisfies 𝑟𝑒 𝑑dR + 𝑑dR 𝑟𝑒 = 0.

Proof. The first assertion follows from the source and target of 𝑟 𝑆,𝑒 . The other assertions are (6.9). These
identities concern geometric residues. Coefficient contractions obey the separate identities in (6.3).

6.2.26       Explicit residue computations
Remark 6.2.68 (Sign conventions: comparison with Loday–Vallette). Our sign conventions for the bar
construction follow the geometric approach, which differs slightly from the operadic conventions in Loday–
Vallette [83].
   The differences are as follows.
   (i) Koszul sign rule: We use the geometric Koszul rule where moving a differential form of degree 𝑝 past
       an operator of degree 𝑞 introduces (−1) 𝑝𝑞 .
  (ii) Residue orientation: Our residues include an orientation factor from the normal bundle to collision
       divisors. This introduces signs when collision divisors intersect.
 (iii) Suspension: Loday–Vallette use operadic suspension 𝑠 : 𝑉 → 𝑠𝑉 with | 𝑠 | = 1. We work with
       geometric forms directly, so suspension is implicit in the degree shift of Ω𝑛 (log 𝐷 ).
   Translation between conventions.
         Loday–Vallette (Operadic)                          Ours (Geometric)
         𝑑𝑜 𝑝 ( 𝑠𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑠𝑎𝑛 )                         𝑑 𝑔𝑒𝑜𝑚 ( 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔𝑛 )
         Sign: (−1) | 𝑎1 |+···+| 𝑎𝑖 −1 |                    Sign: (−1) 𝜖𝑖 (from form degree)
         Suspension degree | 𝑠𝑎𝑖 | = | 𝑎𝑖 | + 1             Form degree | 𝜔 | = 𝑛
226                                                                  Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


   The two conventions agree up to an overall normalization constant (which can be absorbed into the
definition of the pairing).
   The nine-term proof of 𝑑 2 = 0 (Theorem 6.2.27) uses geometric signs throughout. Translating to
operadic conventions via the dictionary above preserves 𝑑 2 = 0.

6.3       The geometric cobar complex
6.3.1     Motivation: reversing the prism
Remark 6.3.1 (Inverse prism principle). If the bar construction acts as a prism decomposing chiral algebras
into their spectrum, the cobar construction acts as the inverse prism, reconstructing the algebra from its
spectral components. Geometrically: the bar extracts residues at collision divisors (analysis), the cobar
integrates over configuration spaces (synthesis), and their duality is the residue-integration pairing on
logarithmic forms.
   Physical intuition (Witten). The bar complex encodes off-shell amplitudes with infrared cutoffs
(compactification provides the cutoff); the cobar complex encodes on-shell propagators with ultraviolet
regularization (delta functions provide the regulator); the bar-cobar pairing computes S-matrix elements
by integrating off-shell wavefunctions against on-shell propagators.
   Geometric picture (Kontsevich).

                                        Bar                                Cobar
                    Space       Compactified 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )                 Open 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
                   Forms       Logarithmic (residues)         Distributional (delta functions)
                  Operation       Extract (analyze)                  Insert (synthesize)
                  Boundary     Normal crossing divisors            Diagonal singularities
                   Physics         Off-shell states                On-shell propagators

6.3.2      Distribution theory prerequisites

space:

consisting of smooth, compactly supported functions. This is equipped with the inductive limit topology
from exhaustion by compact sets.

Remark 6.3.7. The definition says: to build the cobar of a coalgebra C, ﬁrst form the bar of its dual algebra
C ∨ , then apply Verdier duality on the conﬁguration space. Concretely, the bar uses 𝑗∗ (maximal extension
across diagonals) and logarithmic forms; the cobar uses 𝑗! (extension by zero) and distributional sections.
This is precisely the exchange effected by Verdier duality: 𝔻 ◦ 𝑗∗  𝑗! ◦ 𝔻 (Lemma 6.3.9).

Lemma 6.3.8 (Holonomicity of the bar complex; [proved]). Let A be a chiral algebra on a smooth
projective curve 𝑋 , finitely generated over D 𝑋 with regular singularities. Then for each 𝑛 ≥ 0:
 (a) The 𝑛-th bar component 𝐵¯ ch (A) is a regular holonomic D-module on the Fulton–MacPherson
                                   𝑛
    compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).
(b) The bar differential 𝑑bar : 𝐵¯ 𝑛ch (A) → 𝐵¯ 𝑛ch−1 (A) is a morphism of holonomic D-modules.

Proof. Step 1: External tensor product. Since A is a holonomic D 𝑋 -module by hypothesis, the external
tensor product A ⊠𝑛 is a holonomic D 𝑋 𝑛 -module [33, Theorem 3.2.3].
    Step 2: Pullback to the FM compactiﬁcation. The blowdown morphism 𝜋 : 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝑋 𝑛 is proper and
birational, so 𝜋 ! A ⊠𝑛 is a holonomic D𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) -module [33, Theorem 3.2.3].
    Step 3: Logarithmic extension. The bar sheaf on the open configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is 𝑗 ∗ 𝜋 ! A ⊠𝑛 ⊗
Ωlog ( 𝐷 ), where 𝑗 : 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) ↩→ 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is the inclusion and 𝐷 = 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) \ 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is a normal crossings
  ∗

divisor (Theorem 5.1.2). The logarithmic differential forms Ω∗log ( 𝐷 ) define a regular integrable connection
on the NCD complement, so 𝑗∗ of the resulting regular holonomic module on 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is regular holo-
nomic on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) by Deligne’s regularity theorem [33, Theorem 5.2.17]. This identifies 𝐵¯ 𝑛ch (A) as a regular
holonomic D𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) -module.
    Step 4: Bar differential. The bar differential 𝑑bar = 𝑑internal + 𝑑residue + 𝑑form (Definition 6.1.13). The
internal differential 𝑑internal is induced by the chiral algebra structure, which is a D 𝑋 -module morphism
by definition. The form differential 𝑑form is the de Rham differential on Ω∗log ( 𝐷 ), which is a D-module
morphism. The residue differential 𝑑residue = 𝐷 Res𝐷 is the composition of restriction to a boundary
                                                   P
divisor 𝐷 followed by the trace map, both of which are morphisms of D-modules [195, Chapter 4]. Hence
𝑑bar is a morphism of holonomic D-modules.

Lemma 6.3.9 (Verdier duality exchanges extensions; [proved]). Let 𝑌 be a smooth variety, 𝑈 ↩−
                                                                                            →𝑌
an open inclusion with complement a normal crossings divisor, and M a holonomic D𝑈 -module. Then
there is a canonical isomorphism in the derived category of holonomic D𝑌 -modules:

                                         𝔻𝑌 ( 𝑗∗ M)  𝑗! 𝔻𝑈 (M) .

Proof. This is a standard consequence of the theory of holonomic D-modules; we recall the argument for
completeness. By adjunction, 𝑗∗ is right adjoint to 𝑗 ∗ and 𝑗! is left adjoint to 𝑗 ! . For 𝑗 an open inclusion
we have 𝑗 ! = 𝑗 ∗ , so:
                                              𝑗! ⊣ 𝑗 ∗ ⊣ 𝑗∗ .
Verdier duality exchanges left and right adjoints: for any holonomic M on 𝑈 ,

                               𝔻𝑌 ( 𝑗∗ M) = 𝔻𝑌 ( 𝑗∗ 𝔻𝑈 𝔻𝑈 M)  𝑗! (𝔻𝑈 M)

where the last step uses the identity 𝔻𝑌 ◦ 𝑗∗ ◦ 𝔻𝑈  𝑗! , which holds because 𝑗∗ preserves holonomicity
(the complement is a normal crossings divisor) and Verdier duality is involutive on the holonomic category
[33, Theorem 2.6.1].

Remark 6.3.12 (Resolution of delta-function products). A classical objection to the distributional cobar is that
products of delta distributions may be ill-defined: for instance, the product 𝛿 ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) · 𝛿 ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) requires
a renormalization choice in the analytic category. The intrinsic definition (Definition 6.3.6) dissolves this
objection entirely: the cobar is defined as a Verdier dual in the D-module category, where compositions of
234                                                            Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


D-module morphisms are governed by the calculus of nearby and vanishing cycles. The normal crossings
condition on the boundary divisor 𝐷 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) ensures that all relevant compositions are transversal,
hence well-defined without renormalization.
    The distributional representation (Theorem 6.3.10) is a consequence–-it tells us how the intrinsic D-
module object looks when evaluated on test sections, but the differential and its nilpotence are established
at the D-module level, where no analytic subtleties arise.

Theorem 6.3.16 (Cobar differential; [proved]). The cobar differential is a degree +1 operator:

Remark 6.3.18 (Duality with bar 𝑑 2 = 0 proof). The structure of this proof mirrors exactly the bar 𝑑 2 = 0
proof from Section 6.2.17:

                   Bar (Section 6.2.17)                              Cobar (this section)
                   Residues at divisors                              Delta functions at diagonals
                   Compactified space 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )                      Open space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
                   Logarithmic forms                                 Distributional currents
                   Stratification by collisions                      Singular support on diagonals
                   Arnold–Orlik–Solomon relations                    Arnold relations for distributions
                   Extract (analyze)                                 Insert (synthesize)

   This duality is the mathematical incarnation of the bar-cobar adjunction. The proofs are dual under
Verdier duality.

6.3.5    Sign conventions for cobar operations
Convention 6.3.19 (Cobar sign system). The cobar complex inherits signs from three sources:
   Koszul signs (from grading). The standard Koszul sign rule (Appendix H).
   Symmetry signs (from permutations). The symmetric group 𝔖𝑛 acts on 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) and C ⊠𝑛 . For 𝜎 ∈ 𝔖𝑛
and elements 𝑐1 , . . . , 𝑐𝑛 :

                                 𝜎 ( 𝑐1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑐𝑛 ) = (−1) 𝜖 ( 𝜎 ,𝑐 ) 𝑐 𝜎 (1) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑐 𝜎 ( 𝑛 )
where 𝜖 ( 𝜎 , 𝑐 ) is the Koszul sign for moving graded elements according to 𝜎 .
   Distributional signs (from convolution). When convolving distributions, there are signs from interchang-
ing integrals:                                       ∫
                                   ( 𝐾1 ∗ 𝐾2 )( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) =            𝐾1 ( 𝑧, 𝑢) 𝐾2 ( 𝑢, 𝑤 ) 𝑑𝑢

Interchanging the order introduces sign (−1) | 𝐾1 | · | 𝐾2 | .
Lemma 6.3.20 (Sign consistency for cobar differential; [proved]). The sign conventions above ensure
that for any two operations in the cobar differential, the double application produces consistent signs that
allow cancellations in the 𝑑 2 = 0 proof.
6.3. The geometric cobar complex                                                                           241


Proof. Consider the prototypical case: applying 𝑑extend twice. This inserts two delta functions 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )
and 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑘 − 𝑧ℓ ).
   Case 1: Disjoint collisions ( 𝑖, 𝑗 ) ∩ ( 𝑘, ℓ ) = ∅
   The delta functions commute with sign:

                        𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) ∧ 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑘 − 𝑧ℓ ) = (−1) 1·1 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑘 − 𝑧ℓ ) ∧ 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )

  The sign (−1) 1·1 = −1 comes from both delta functions being 1-forms (in the distributional sense).
Summing over orderings ( 𝑖 < 𝑗, 𝑘 < ℓ ) vs ( 𝑘 < ℓ , 𝑖 < 𝑗 ) gives cancellation.
  Case 2: Nested collisions (e.g., 𝑖 = 𝑘, 𝑗 ≠ ℓ )
  We have:
                        𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) ∧ 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧ℓ ) = (−1) 𝛿 ( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧ℓ ) ∧ 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧ℓ )
   This is the distributional analog of the Arnold relation. Caveat: products of delta functions supported
on intersecting submanifolds require wavefront set conditions for rigorous definition; the argument
here is heuristic. The rigorous proof of 𝑑 2 = 0 for the cobar complex is provided by Verdier duality
(Corollary 6.3.11).
                                                                                   2
   In all cases, the signs are chosen so that the Arnold relations hold, ensuring 𝑑extend = 0.

Theorem 6.3.25 (Fermion-boson Koszul duality; [proved]). [Regime: quadratic (Convention 2.9.2).]
The 𝛽𝛾 system is the Koszul dual of free fermions. This is the chiral analog of the classical
Sym(𝑉 ) ↔ Λ (𝑉 ∗ ) Koszul duality (see Part II for the complete bar-cobar computation).
  The Koszul duality correspondence exchanges:
   (i) Relations: anticommuting fields { 𝜓 , 𝜓 } = 0 ↔ symplectic bosons [ 𝛽, 𝛾 ] = 1; exterior relation
       𝜓 ⊠ 𝜓 = 0 ↔ symplectic pairing ⟨ 𝛽, 𝛾 ⟩ = 𝑧1 −1 𝑧2 .
  (ii) Algebra structure: exterior algebra Λ∗ ( 𝜓 ) ↔ polynomial-type algebra; bar complex 𝐵¯ (F ) =
       Λ∗ ( 𝜓 , 𝜕𝜓 , . . .) ↔ 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) with symplectic differential.
 (iii) Statistics: fermionic ↔ bosonic.

6.3.7   Physical interpretation: on-shell propagator and Feynman-rule tem-
        plates
Conjecture 6.3.27 (Cobar elements as on-shell propagator templates; [physical heuristic]). Elements of the
cobar complex Ωch (C) should be read as algebraic shadow data for on-shell propagators in the sense of
quantum field theory.
    Precise statement. For a chiral coalgebra C corresponding to a 2d CFT, elements 𝐾 ∈ Ω𝑛 (C) are
distributions satisfying:
   (i) Ultraviolet behavior: Singularities along diagonals { 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 } encode short-distance behavior (UV
       divergences).
  (ii) On-shell condition: The cobar differential 𝑑cobar ( 𝐾 ) = 0 should model the equations of motion (e.g.,
       □ 𝜙 = 0 for free fields).
 (iii) S-matrix elements: The cohomology 𝐻 ∗ ( Ωch (C)) should model physical on-shell scattering ampli-
       tudes.
246                                                                   Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


Remark 6.3.28 (Evidence: Physical explanation). Step 1: Cobar as Green’s-function template
  A propagator 𝐺 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) in QFT is a Green’s function satisfying:

                                       (□ 𝑧 − 𝑚2 ) 𝐺 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) = 𝛿 (2) ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )

   This is the Green’s-function template in which 𝐺 extends across the diagonal 𝑧 = 𝑤 as a distribution
with a delta function singularity. In the conjectural cobar/QFT dictionary this is modeled by:

                                                𝑑extend ( 𝐺 ) = 𝛿 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )

   Step 2: Cobar differential as equations-of-motion template
   For a field 𝜙 satisfying equations of motion □ 𝜙 = 0, the propagator 𝐺 satisfies:

                                                      𝑑cobar ( 𝐺 ) = 0

   This is the template for the on-shell condition. Elements in the cohomology 𝐻 ∗ ( Ωch ) should therefore
be read as algebraic shadows of on-shell propagators.
   Step 3: 𝐴∞ operations as Feynman-rule template
   The operation 𝑛𝑘 in the cobar 𝐴∞ structure should model tree-level 𝑘 -point correlation functions:

                              ⟨ 𝜙 ( 𝑧1 ) · · · 𝜙 ( 𝑧 𝑘 )⟩ = 𝑛𝑘 ( 𝐺, . . . , 𝐺 ) ( 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑘 )

   The 𝐴∞ relations encode (all at genus zero, hence tree-level):
• 𝑛2 = binary vertex (standard product)
• 𝑛3 = ternary vertex (measures failure of strict associativity)
• 𝑛𝑘 = 𝑘 -ary vertex (higher associahedra corrections)
Loop corrections (genus 𝑔 ≥ 1) arise from the higher-genus bar complex, not from higher 𝑛𝑘 at genus zero.
  This gives the conjectural algebraic template for genus-zero Feynman rules.
Remark 6.3.29 (Scope). Conjecture 6.3.27 is tagged [physical heuristic] because the identification of cobar
elements with on-shell propagators requires external physics input (equations of motion, path integral
measure) that lies outside the algebraic framework of this monograph.
   Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type VII (physics-dictionary). The conjecture treats cobar com-
plex elements as algebraic shadow data for QFT on-shell propagators, with the 𝐴∞ operations furnishing
the genus-zero Feynman-rule template.

6.3.8   Verdier duality on bar and cobar
Theorem 6.3.32 (Bar-cobar Verdier; [proved]). [Regime: quadratic, genus-0 (Convention 2.9.2).]
  There is a perfect pairing:

• 𝜔bar ∈ Γ ( 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , A ⊠𝑛 ⊗ Ω∗log ) is a bar element (logarithmic form on compactified space)
• 𝐾cobar ∈ D ′ ( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , C ⊠𝑛 ) is a cobar element (distribution on open space)

• The integration is well-defined because logarithmic forms pair with distributions

   Properties of the pairing.
   (i) Perfect pairing: Non-degenerate in both arguments (by Lemma 6.3.8: each graded piece is a holo-
       nomic D-module on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), hence has finite-dimensional stalks, and Verdier duality for holonomic

 (iv) Verdier duality: This realizes Ωch (C) ≃ 𝔻( 𝐵¯ ch (A ! ))

Proof. Step 1: Well-deﬁnedness of the pairing
   Logarithmic forms on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) restrict to distributional forms on 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ). Explicitly, near a divisor

Corollary 6.3.33 (Bar-cobar mutual inverses; [proved]). Let A be an augmented chiral algebra
on a smooth curve 𝑋 , valued in holonomic D-modules (Convention 2.9.1), and let C be an augmented
chiral coalgebra. Assume:
  (i) A is chiral Koszul: the bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A) has cohomology concentrated in a single degree
       (Definition 9.1.14);
  (ii) Conilpotence or completion: either 𝐵¯ ch (A) is conilpotent, or A is complete with respect to its aug-
       mentation ideal (§6.8.2).
Then the bar and cobar functors are mutually quasi-inverse:

      The quasi-isomorphisms are induced by the Verdier pairing (Theorem 6.3.32).

Proof. Consider the coradical filtration 𝐹• on 𝐵¯ ch (A), where 𝐹𝑛 is spanned by elements of tensor degree
≤ 𝑛. The associated spectral sequence has 𝐸1 = 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 (gr 𝑝 Ωch ( 𝐵¯ ch (A))).
                                              𝑝,𝑞

    Under hypothesis (i), the Koszulity condition ensures that 𝐸2 collapses: the only nonzero column is
 𝑝 = 0, where it gives A.
    Convergence of the spectral sequence is guaranteed by hypothesis (ii): conilpotence ensures the filtration
is exhaustive with finite-length iterated coproducts, so the cobar differential involves only finite sums. In
the completed regime, convergence follows from the completeness of the 𝐼 -adic topology.
    The unit 𝜂 : A → Ωch ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)) is induced by the Verdier pairing (Theorem 6.3.32) and is a quasi-
isomorphism by the spectral sequence argument. The counit argument is dual.

6.3.9      Kontsevich formality and chiral bar construction
Theorem 6.3.38 (Kontsevich formality (1997); [proved]). [35] For any smooth manifold 𝑀 , there
exists an 𝐿∞ quasi-isomorphism:
                                                                        ∼

                                                                 → 𝐷poly ( 𝑀 )

from polyvector fields to polydifferential operators, given by configuration space integrals:
                                                          ∑︁    ∫
                                 U𝑛 ( 𝛾1 , . . . , 𝛾𝑛 ) =    𝑤Γ        𝜔Γ
                                                      Γ ∈ 𝐺𝑛    𝐶 𝑛,𝑚 (ℍ)

where 𝐺𝑛 = admissible graphs, 𝑤 Γ = combinatorial weights, and 𝜔Γ involves propagators 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )
and angle forms 𝑑𝜃 𝑖 .
Remark 6.3.39 (Relation to chiral bar construction). Kontsevich’s formality is the prototype for our con-
struction: replace ℝ𝑑 with a Riemann surface 𝑋 , polyvector fields with A, 𝐶 𝑛 (ℍ) with 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), and 𝐿∞
with curved 𝐴∞ . Both realize a duality (deformation quantization resp. Koszul duality) via configuration
space integrals.
Remark 6.3.40 (Costello–Gwilliam factorization algebras). Our construction extends [27]: Vol. 1 develops
factorization homology on manifolds, Vol. 2 treats quantum corrections and curved 𝐴∞ in QFT. We
specialize to complex curves (essential for chiral structure) and use configuration geometry rather than the
BV formalism.
Remark 6.3.41 (Cobar summary). The geometric cobar is Verdier-dual to the bar (Section 6.2.17): the
three-component differential, nine-term 𝑑 2 = 0 verification, and Arnold relations all mirror their bar
counterparts.

isomorphic to a Čech-type complex:

where 𝔘 = {𝑈𝜎 } is the open cover of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) by coordinate charts and FC is the factorization algebra
associated to C.

Proof. The factorization algebra FC on 𝑋 is defined by the assignment 𝑈 ↦→ FC (𝑈 ) = Ω (C|𝑈 ), with
factorization structure maps FC (𝑈1 ) ⊗ FC (𝑈2 ) → FC (𝑈1 ⊔ 𝑈2 ) for disjoint opens, given by the cobar
product. This is a cosheaf on the Ran space Ran( 𝑋 ), hence in particular a precosheaf on 𝑋 .
   Step 1: Cover and nerve. Choose a cover 𝔘 = {𝑈𝜎 } 𝜎 ∈ 𝑆 of 𝑋 by coordinate discs. The configuration space
𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) inherits an open cover 𝔘 ( 𝑛 ) = {𝑈𝜎1 × · · · × 𝑈𝜎𝑛 ∩ 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )}. The FM compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is
covered by the closures 𝑈𝜎1 × · · · × 𝑈𝜎𝑛 together with boundary coordinate charts at collision strata. The
nerve of this cover computes the Čech complex 𝐶ˇ • (𝔘 , FC ).
   Step 2: Čech-de Rham comparison. On each chart 𝑈𝜎 , the factorization algebra FC |𝑈𝜎 is computed by the
cobar complex with local coordinates. The cobar differential 𝑑Ω on 𝑈𝜎 uses the coproduct Δ̄ of C together
with the local propagator 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ). On overlaps 𝑈𝜎 ∩ 𝑈𝜏 , the transition data is encoded by
the change-of-coordinate forms, which are 𝜕¯-exact on the holomorphic curve 𝑋 .
   The cobar complex Ωch (C) computes global sections of FC via integration of local cobar elements
against logarithmic forms on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ). This is precisely the Čech-de Rham double complex: the Čech
direction glues local cobar data across charts, while the de Rham direction is the cobar differential.
   Step 3: Quasi-isomorphism. Since 𝑋 is a smooth algebraic curve, the FM compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is a
smooth variety with normal crossings boundary (Theorem 5.1.11). The cover 𝔘 ( 𝑛 ) can be chosen to be a
Leray cover: each finite intersection 𝑈𝜎1 ∩ · · · ∩ 𝑈𝜎𝑘 is either empty or contractible (being an intersection
254                                                                            Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


of coordinate discs in 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )). For a Leray cover of a smooth variety, the Čech-to-derived-functor spectral
sequence degenerates at 𝐸1 , giving:

                                      𝐻ˇ 𝑝 (𝔘 , FC )  𝐻 𝑝 ( 𝑋 𝑛 , FC ) .
The right-hand side is the factorization homology 𝑋 FC , which by the Costello–Gwilliam equivalence
                                                     ∫

(cf. [27]) agrees with the cobar cohomology 𝐻 ∗ ( Ωch (C)).

Theorem 6.3.45 (Cobar as free chiral algebra; [proved]). As a graded chiral algebra (forgetting
the differential), the cobar construction Ωch (C) is the free chiral algebra generated by 𝑠 −1 C̄, where C̄ =
ker( 𝜖 : C → 𝜔 𝑋 ). The differential 𝑑Ω is the unique derivation extending the reduced comultiplication
Δ̄ : C̄ → C̄ ⊗ C̄ (this is essential data: Ωch (C) is a DG chiral algebra, not merely a free algebra).
Proof. By construction (Definition 8.2.14), the underlying graded chiral algebra of Ωch (C) is Freech ( 𝑠 −1 C̄),
the free chiral algebra generated by 𝑠 −1 C̄ as a D 𝑋 -module. The universal property of free algebras then
gives: for any chiral algebra A and graded D 𝑋 -module morphism 𝑓 : 𝑠 −1 C̄ → A, there exists a unique
chiral algebra morphism 𝑓˜ : Freech ( 𝑠 −1 C̄) → A extending 𝑓 .
   It remains to verify that 𝑑Ω is a derivation. Since Freech is left adjoint to the forgetful functor, a derivation
on a free algebra is determined by its restriction to generators. The restriction 𝑑Ω | 𝑠 −1 C̄ equals the desus-
pended reduced comultiplication 𝑠 −1 Δ̄ : 𝑠 −1 C̄ → ( 𝑠 −1 C̄) ⊗2 ↩→ Freech ( 𝑠 −1 C̄), which is a well-defined map
of D 𝑋 -modules. The Leibniz extension to all of Ωch (C) is unique, giving 𝑑Ω as the unique derivation
extending Δ̄.

6.4     Precise distribution spaces
Deﬁnition 6.4.1 (Distribution space). The space Dist( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , C ⊠𝑛 ) consists of distributional sections with:
• Prescribed singularities along diagonals
• Growth conditions at infinity
• Appropriate transformation under 𝔖𝑛
Theorem 6.4.2 (Topology; [proved]). The distribution space Dist( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , C ⊠𝑛 ) is a complete locally

𝜙. By the Banach-Alaoglu theorem, bounded subsets of the distribution space are weak-∗ precompact.

Remark 6.4.3 (Regularization methods). When distributional products arising in the cobar differential
require regularization, three standard methods are available:
   (i) Dimensional regularization: analytic continuation in dimension 𝑑 = 𝑑0 − 𝜖 ;
  (ii) Principal value prescription: P.V. 𝑓 ( 𝑧 )/ 𝑧 𝑑𝑧 ;
                                         ∫

 (iii) Hadamard ﬁnite parts: extracting the finite part of a divergent integral.
For the cobar construction in the chiral setting, no regularization is needed at genus 0 because the distribu-
tional products are convolutions with delta functions supported on smooth submanifolds (the diagonals
Δ𝑖𝑗 ⊂ 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )), and such convolutions are well-defined by the calculus of wavefront sets [84]: the conormal
bundles 𝑁 ∗ Δ𝑖𝑗 do not intersect the wavefront set of the coalgebra coproduct, which is supported along
the diagonals themselves. At higher genus, the propagator acquires distributional corrections requiring the
regularization methods listed above; see the genus- 𝑔 analysis in Theorem 8.17.4.

6.4.1    Poincaré–Verdier duality realization
Theorem 6.4.5 (Bar-cobar as Poincaré–Verdier duality; [proved]). The bar and cobar construc-

                                                    ∫

  The duality has the following structure:
• Logarithmic forms on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) (bar) are dual to distributions on 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) (cobar)
• Residues at divisors (bar) are dual to principal value integrals (cobar)
• Collision divisors (bar) correspond to extension loci (cobar)
• The duality exchanges extraction (analysis) with reconstruction (synthesis)

6.5     Genus 1 contributions: central extensions in the bar-
        cobar complex
Everything constructed so far lives on a ﬁxed curve 𝑋 . The bar differential is a residue on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ); the cobar
differential inserts delta functions on 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ); Verdier duality exchanges the two. None of this involves the
moduli of curves.
    Now let the curve vary. Replace 𝑋 by a family 𝜋 : X → 𝑆 over a base 𝑆 , and ask: how does the bar
complex change as 𝑋 moves in M 𝑔 ? At genus 0 the answer is: it does not –- there are no moduli. At genus 1,
the propagator 𝐾 (1) = 𝜃 1′ / 𝜃 1 depends on the modular parameter 𝜏 , and the bar differential acquires a
6.5. Genus 1 contributions: central extensions in the bar-cobar complex                                              261


correction. This correction is the central extension: curvature 𝑚0 = 𝜅 (A) emerges because the trace of
the OPE around the 𝐴-cycle of the torus is nonzero. The central charge, invisible at genus 0, is the first
shadow of the universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ A .

6.5.1    Central extensions at genus 1: intuition
6.5.1.1 Physical picture
Consider the Heisenberg vertex algebra with generators 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) , 𝑎∗ ( 𝑧 ) satisfying:
                                                                           𝜅
                                             [ 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) , 𝑎∗ ( 𝑤 )] ∼
                                                                       ( 𝑧 − 𝑤)2
where 𝜅 is the central charge.

                       OPE               1                                         Tr
        Genus 0                                                  Genus 1
                                                                                                    ∮ 𝜅 𝑑𝑧
                                    ( 𝑧 −𝑤 ) 2                                                             𝑧2
                                           residue                                                         residue
                                       0                                                               𝜅
                             explanation                                                     explanation

                             Tree-level: no cycles                                      One-loop: central charge

    The double pole 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 in the OPE produces different behavior at each genus: at genus 0, residues
at 𝑧 = 𝑤 give derivatives of delta functions that integrate to zero over the sphere; at genus 1, the trace
Tr( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ ) around the 𝑆 1 cycle picks up the 𝜅 coefficient as a non-vanishing residue.
    This is the first manifestation of the principle that central extensions are intrinsically one-loop phenom-
ena.
6.5.1.2 Absence at genus 0
Consider the genus 0 bar differential on A ⊗ A:

                                  𝑑 (0) ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ) = 𝜇 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ) − 𝑎 ⊗ 𝟙 − 𝟙 ⊗ 𝑏
where 𝜇 is the OPE product.
   For central terms: 𝜇 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ ) ∼ 𝜅 · 𝟙
   But 𝑑 (0) ( 𝜅 · 𝟙) = 𝜅 · 𝟙 − 𝜅 · 𝟙 − 𝜅 · 𝟙 = −𝜅 · 𝟙
   So the cocycle 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ − 𝜅 · 𝟙 satisfying 𝑑 (0) (· · · ) = 0 would require 𝜅 = 0. The central charge cannot
appear at genus 0.

                               𝑐1 = Tr( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ ) − 𝜅 · 𝟙 ∈ 𝐶1(1) (A) ⊗ 𝐶1(1) (A)

Theorem 6.5.1 (Central charge cocycle; [proved]). [Regime: curved-central (Convention 2.9.2).]
  The element 𝑐1 satisfies:
                                          𝑑 (1) 𝑐1 = 0
and represents the central extension in 𝐻1(1) (A).
   Moreover, the class [ 𝑐1 ] is:
• Non-trivial: [ 𝑐1 ] ≠ 0 in homology
• Universal: independent of the choice of cycle on 𝕋 2
• Generates: all genus 1 central phenomena factor through [ 𝑐1 ]

Proof. The differential 𝑑 (1) at genus 1 includes:
   (i) Standard bar differential (as at genus 0)
  (ii) New term: Contraction around the 𝑆 1 cycle
   Computing:

            𝑑 (1) [Tr( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ )] = Tr[ 𝜇 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ )] − Tr( 𝑎) ⊗ Tr( 𝑎∗ )
                                = Tr[ 𝜅 · 𝟙] − 0      (Tr( 𝑎) = Tr( 𝑎∗ ) = 0 for non-vacuum modes)
                                =𝜅·𝟙       (normalized trace: Tr(𝟙) = 1)

   Therefore: 𝑑 (1) [Tr( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ ) − 𝜅 · 𝟙] = 0.

6.5.5   Comparison with physical literature
Our construction recovers known results from physics:
• Kac–Moody algebras: The level 𝑘 of a Kac–Moody algebra is precisely the central charge 𝜅 appearing in
  our genus 1 cocycle
• Virasoro central charge: For the Virasoro vertex algebra, the central charge 𝑐 appears as Tr( 𝐿𝑚 ⊗ 𝐿𝑛 )
  with 𝑚 + 𝑛 = 0
• 𝑊 -algebras: For 𝑊 -algebras (following Arakawa), higher-weight central charges appear at genus 1 in
  traces of higher-weight operators

6.5.6    Genus 1 summary
                     Algebra                  Physics                  Bar-Cobar
                     Central extension        One-loop correction      Genus 1 cocycle
                     Central charge 𝜅         Quantum parameter        Trace coefficient
                     Level of Kac–Moody       UV divergence            𝐻2(1) class
                     Virasoro 𝑐               Conformal anomaly        Tr(𝑇 ⊗ 𝑇 )

Remark 6.5.4 (Functoriality). The entire construction is functorial: a morphism A → B of vertex algebras
preserving central charge induces:
                                          𝐶•(1) (A) → 𝐶•(1) (B)
respecting the central extension cocycles. This is the Grothendieck perspective: genus 1 phenomena are
determined by functoriality from genus 0 data plus the choice of torus.

   (i) For the matter-ghost BRST system, the obstruction vanishes when 𝑐matter = 26 (cancellation with

Corollary 6.5.11 (Recognition principle; [proved]). A chiral coalgebra C is in the essential image of
B̄ if and only if its cobar Ωch (C) is a chiral algebra (not just 𝐴∞ ).

Proof. The bar-cobar adjunction (Theorem 6.3.46) provides unit and counit maps for any augmented chiral
algebra and any conilpotent coalgebra. On the Koszul locus (Definition 9.1.14), the counit 𝐵¯ ( Ω (C)) → C
is a quasi-isomorphism (Theorem 9.1.39), which identifies C as the bar of its cobar. This holds precisely
when Ω (C) has strict (not homotopy) chiral algebra structure.

6.6     Relationship between bar-cobar and Koszul duality
For a chiral Koszul pair (A1 , A2 ), the bar of one is the Koszul dual coalgebra of the other, and Verdier
duality on Ran( 𝑋 ) provides the equivalence. The Koszul property –- diagonal Ext vanishing in the (bar
degree, weight) bigrading –- is the condition under which this equivalence descends from the coderived
category to the ordinary derived category.

6.6.1   Precise formulation of the relationship
Remark 6.6.1 (Criteria for chiral Koszul pairs –- updated recollection). Recall from Definition 9.1.14 that a
chiral Koszul pair is specified by antecedent recognition data: a chiral twisting datum, a Koszul twisting mor-
phism, compatible filtrations, and Verdier-compatible dual coalgebras. The bar/cobar quasi-isomorphisms
are then proved consequences (Theorem 9.1.8 and Theorem 9.1.39), not part of the definition.
Remark 6.6.2 (Bar-cobar vs. Koszul: the fundamental distinction). Always true (for any augmented chiral
algebra A):
• 𝐵¯ : A → 𝐵¯ (A) exists and 𝑑 2 = 0 (Theorem 6.2.27)
• Ω : 𝐵¯ (A) → Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) exists and 𝑑 2 = 0 (Theorem 6.3.17)
   These are constructions–-they work for any augmented algebra.
   On the Koszul locus only (chiral Koszul pairs, Deﬁnition 9.1.14):
• The counit Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −
                            ∼
                            → A is a quasi-isomorphism (Theorem 9.1.39)
• 𝐵¯ (A1 ) ≃ A2! as chiral coalgebras (Theorem 9.1.38)
   Off the Koszul locus, Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) still exists but the counit need not be a quasi-isomorphism; the
bar-cobar object represents A in the completed coderived category 𝐷 co (-CoMod) of Positselski
(Theorem 8.17.4(b)).
Theorem 6.6.3 (Necessary conditions for chiral Koszul duality [26]; [proved]). For (A1 , A2 ) to
form a chiral Koszul pair, the following must hold:
   (i) Both algebras are finitely generated over D 𝑋
  (ii) The bar complexes have finite-dimensional cohomology in each degree
 (iii) There exists a non-degenerate pairing ⟨−, −⟩ : 𝐵¯ (A1 ) ⊗ 𝐵¯ (A2 ) → 𝜔 𝑋

6.6.2    Diagram of relationships
The relationship between bar, cobar, and Koszul duality can be summarized:

6.6.3      Examples illustrating the distinction
Example 6.6.4 (Heisenberg: level shift required). Bar-cobar inversion gives Ω ( 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 )) ≃ H𝑘 automatically,
while Koszul duality yields H𝑘! ≃ Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) with curvature 𝑚0 = −𝑘 𝜔 (cf. §18.22). These are distinct
statements: bar-cobar inverts H𝑘 , but the Koszul dual is a different type of algebra (commutative vs. Lie).
See Part II.

forces the boundary integral to cancel term by term. The detailed bookkeeping across all boundary strata is
carried out in the proof of Theorem 8.14.12, Steps 3–4.

6.8     Curved Koszul duality and I-adic completion
Not all chiral algebras are quadratic. Many examples of interest–-Virasoro, higher W-algebras, 𝑊∞ –-require
curved structures or infinite-dimensional presentations. For these, the strict finite-type bar-cobar theorem
no longer applies directly. One must separate the proved M-level completed shadows that control curvature
and complementarity from the stronger H-level realization problem for an actual dual factorization object.
To treat even the model-level question, we must introduce:
• Curved structures: Allowing 𝜇0 ≠ 0 (failure of d² = 0)
• Completion: I-adic topology ensuring convergence
• Filtered structures: More general than curved (Gui–Li–Zeng)
   We follow Gui–Li–Zeng [91].

6.8.1  Curved 𝐴∞ algebras: definitions
Deﬁnition 6.8.1 (Curved 𝐴∞ algebra). A curved 𝐴∞ algebra is a graded vector space 𝐴 with operations:

                                               { 𝜇𝑛 : 𝐴⊗ 𝑛 → 𝐴}𝑛 ≥0

of degree 2 − 𝑛, satisfying the curved 𝐴∞ relations:

                                       (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝜇𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝜇 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0
                                 ∑︁
                                 𝑟 + 𝑠 +𝑡 =𝑛
                                𝑟,𝑡 ≥0, 𝑠 ≥0

   Key differences from ordinary 𝐴∞ :
   (i) 𝑛 = 0 is allowed: 𝜇0 : ℂ → 𝐴 is the curvature
  (ii) 𝑛 = 1: 𝜇21 = [ 𝜇0 , −], so 𝜇1 is a differential only modulo curvature
 (iii) 𝑛 ≥ 2: Higher operations as usual
Remark 6.8.2 (Curvature, backreaction, and 𝑑 2 ). (i) The curvature is 𝑚0 := 𝜇0 (1) ∈ 𝐴2 .
  (ii) 𝜇21 ( 𝑎) = 𝜇2 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎) − 𝜇2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚0 ): the total bar differential always satisfies 𝑑bar
                                                                                            2 = 0; curvature mani-

       fests in the internal 𝐴∞ structure.
 (iii) In physics, backreaction is the same phenomenon: the BRST operator 𝑄 = 𝜇1 satisfies 𝑄 2 ≠ 0, with
       the obstruction measured by 𝑚0 .
 (iv) A curved 𝐴∞ algebra is strictiﬁable iff 𝑚0 is central (Theorem 6.8.3) and the curvature class is gauge-
       trivial in the completed filtration.
Theorem 6.8.3 (Curvature as 𝜇 1 -cycle; [proved]). For a curved 𝐴∞ algebra ( 𝐴, 𝜇0 , 𝜇1 , 𝜇2 , . . .), the
curvature element satisfies:
  (i) 𝜇1 ( 𝜇0 ) = 0 (the curvature is a 𝜇1 -cycle);
 (ii) 𝜇21 = [ 𝜇0 , −] 𝜇2 , where [ 𝜇0 , 𝑎] 𝜇2 := 𝜇2 ( 𝜇0 , 𝑎) − 𝜇2 ( 𝑎, 𝜇0 ) is the inner derivation.
In particular, 𝜇1 fails to be a differential precisely when 𝜇0 is not central with respect to 𝜇2 . For chiral
algebras (which are graded-commutative), [ 𝜇0 , −] 𝜇2 = 0 automatically, so the curvature enters through
higher operations ( 𝜇3 , 𝜇4 , . . . ) or via the completed tensor product.

Remark 6.8.36 (Attack route for the 𝑊∞ factorization target). The reduction chain from Proposition 6.8.35

Proposition 6.8.37 (Higher-spin ideal criterion for principal-stage 𝑊∞ quotients; [proved]).
Let F∞ be a separated complete factorization algebra on a curve, topologically generated by fields 𝑊 ( 𝑠 ) of
conformal weights 𝑠 ≥ 2. For each 𝑁 ≥ 2, let 𝐼> 𝑁 F∞ denote the closed factorization ideal generated by
the fields 𝑊 ( 𝑠 ) with 𝑠 > 𝑁 . Assume:
   (i) the differential, translation operator, and factorization products preserve each ideal 𝐼> 𝑁 F∞ ;
  (ii) modulo 𝐼> 𝑁 F∞ , the OPE of the generators 𝑊 (2) , . . . ,𝑊 ( 𝑁 ) closes among those same generators;
 (iii) the quotient factorization algebra F≤ 𝑁 := F∞ / 𝐼> 𝑁 F∞ admits a chiral envelope or equivalent dg
       model quasi-isomorphic to the principal stage 𝑊𝑁 ; and
 (iv) the quotient maps F≤ 𝑁 +1 ↠ F≤ 𝑁 intertwine the principal-stage truncation tower.
Then the quotients {F≤ 𝑁 } 𝑁 ≥2 define a principal-stage quotient system in the sense of Definition 6.8.32.
Consequently, Proposition 6.8.34, Proposition 6.8.33, and Corollary 6.8.30 apply.
   In particular, the remaining W∞ construction problem is to prove that the higher-spin generators above
stage 𝑁 define stable factorization ideals whose quotients recover the theorematic principal stages.

Proof. Assumptions (1)–(4) supply closed factorization ideals, closed OPE, finite-stage identification with
𝑊𝑁 , and compatibility with the principal-stage tower. This is exactly the data required by Definition 6.8.32.
The stated comparison results then follow from Proposition 6.8.34, Proposition 6.8.33, and Corollary 6.8.30.

                                              𝑛 ≥0

the curved 𝐴∞ structure:
                                                   ∑︁
                         𝜇𝑛𝛼 ( 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑛 ) =    𝜇𝑛+𝑘 ( 𝛼 ⊗ 𝑘 , 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑛 )

   The twisted structure ( 𝐴, { 𝜇𝑛 }) is again a curved 𝐴∞ algebra, with new curvature:

   If 𝛼 is an MC element, then 𝜇0𝛼 = 0, so the twisted structure is uncurved.
Remark 6.8.139 (Physical interpretation). MC elements correspond to vacua (different ground states of
the theory), deformations (continuous families parametrized by the MC equation), and obstructions (failure
of the MC equation means curvature persists).

6.8.7    Summary and comparison table

                             Table 6.1: Quadratic, curved, and filtered structures

               Property                  Quadratic                Curved              Filtered
               Curvature 𝜇0                  0                     ∈ Z(A)             Multiple
               Completion needed?           No                   Sometimes            Usually
               Koszul dual exists?          Yes            Yes (with completion)     Sometimes
               Example                   Heisenberg               Virasoro              W3

   The hierarchy is therefore:
                                      Quadratic ⊂ Curved ⊂ Filtered
  Each level requires more sophisticated technology (completion, filtered cooperads), but also captures
more examples from physics and representation theory.

6.9     Curved 𝐴∞ structures: strict vs. homotopy nilpotence
For chiral algebras A with quantum corrections at genus 𝑔 , the curvature 𝜇0 controls two distinct squares:
  (i) Algebraic: 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = [ 𝜇0 , 𝑎]. When 𝜇0 ∈ 𝑍 (A), this vanishes for all 𝑎, so 𝑚1 is a strict differential
      on A. All standard chiral algebras (Heisenberg, Kac–Moody, Virasoro, W-algebras) satisfy this
      because their central extensions are central.
 (ii) Geometric: 𝑑fib 2 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 ≠ 0 whenever 𝜅 (A) ≠ 0 (Convention 8.0.2). Even when 𝜇 is
                                       𝑔                                                                    0
      central, the fiberwise bar differential over M 𝑔 is not nilpotent–-its failure is controlled by the scalar
      invariant 𝜅 (A).
The total corrected differential 𝐷 𝑔 absorbs the geometric curvature and satisfies 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0 unconditionally
(Theorem 8.15.13).

6.9.1     Mathematical foundations: three regimes
The three regimes below correspond to the first three levels of the regime hierarchy (Convention 2.9.2):
quadratic (Regime I), curved-central (Regime II), and filtered-complete (Regime III). The fourth level
(programmatic) lies beyond the scope of the present chapter.

Remark 6.9.4 (What if 𝜇0 ∉ 𝑍 (A)?). If the curvature is not central, then:
                                                   2

                  2 = 0 up to homotopy.
and we only have 𝑑bar
   This leads to:
• Homotopy coherent structures (Lurie, Higher Topos Theory)
• Spectral sequences that may not degenerate
• Obstruction theories with non-closed obstructions
• Need for 𝐴∞ or 𝐿∞ structures at all levels
   However, all our examples (Heisenberg, Kac–Moody, Virasoro, W-algebras) have central curvature, so
we obtain strict nilpotence. See Remark 6.9.5 for the precise mechanism.
Remark 6.9.5 (Central curvature in vertex operator algebras). For vertex operator algebras, the vacuum
axiom guarantees that the vacuum vector 1 ∈ 𝑉 is central: 𝑌 (1, 𝑧 ) = id𝑉 . In the curved 𝐴∞ framework,
the curvature element 𝜇0 arising from the genus- 𝑔 quantum correction is proportional to 1 (it equals the
central charge or level times 1; see Examples 6.9.7–6.9.10). Since 1 acts by the identity on every module, 𝜇0
lies in 𝑍 (A), and Theorem 6.9.3 yields 𝑑bar2 = 0 strict.

    For more general chiral algebras without a vacuum axiom –- for instance, chiral algebras on higher-
dimensional varieties, or non-unital factorization algebras –- the curvature need not be central, and 𝑑 2 = 0
may hold only up to homotopy. Similarly, chiral algebras arising from field theories with non-central
anomalies (such as gravitational anomalies that act non-trivially on the operator algebra) fall outside the
scope of Theorem 6.9.3.
6.9.1.3 Regime III: general homotopy coherent ( 𝑑 2 ∼ 0 via homotopy)
Deﬁnition 6.9.6 (Homotopy coherent differential). A homotopy coherent differential on a graded space 𝑉
consists of:
• 𝑑1 : 𝑉 → 𝑉 [1] (the ‘‘differential’’)
• ℎ : 𝑉 → 𝑉 [−1] (a homotopy)
• Satisfying: 𝑑12 = [ 𝑑1 , ℎ] (not zero, but homotopic to zero)
• Plus higher coherence homotopies ℎ2 , ℎ3 , . . . ad infinitum
   This is the setting of Lurie’s (∞, 1)-categories [92], derived algebraic geometry (Toën–Vezzosi, Lurie),
and non-curved 𝐴∞ or 𝐿∞ structures.
   We do not need this level of generality for the chiral algebras studied in this monograph, since their
curvature elements are central (see Remark 6.9.5 below).

crossings divisor with strata indexed by dual graphs Γ. Codimension-2 strata arise from refinements Γ′ → Γ
of dual graphs. The fundamental topological identity 𝜕 2 = 0 on the stratification of M 𝑔,𝑛 states that each
codimension-2 stratum appears with opposite signs from the two codimension-1 strata that contain it. This
is equivalent to the modular operad axiom: the composition in the modular operad is associative.
   Step 2: Genus-0 nilpotence ( 𝑑02 = 0). This is Theorem 6.9.11: the Arnold relations (Theorem 6.2.37)
provide the codimension-2 cancellation on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) = M 0,𝑛+1 .

Remark 6.9.14. The distinction between strict and homotopy nilpotence has significant consequences:
    Computations. Strict nilpotence allows direct cohomology computation (Theorem 6.9.12); homotopy
nilpotence requires spectral sequences that may not degenerate.
    Convergence. Strict nilpotence ensures the bar-cobar adjunction (Theorem 6.3.46) works without com-
pletion (for quadratic algebras); homotopy nilpotence necessitates completion (Theorem 6.8.5), with
attendant convergence issues.
    Physics. Strict nilpotence means quantum corrections are controlled by central charges (Theorem 6.7.1);
homotopy nilpotence requires full renormalization group analysis.
    Good news. Vertex operator algebras (with the standard vacuum axiom) and chiral algebras arising from
unitary CFT have central curvature (Remark 6.9.5; see also Theorem 6.9.12), so we are in the strict regime.

6.9.5   Connection to literature
6.9.5.1 Gui–Li–Zeng (2022)
In [91], Gui–Li–Zeng develop the theory of curved Koszul duality for chiral algebras. Their key result:
Theorem 6.9.15 (GLZ, Theorem 5.3; [proved]). For a quadratic chiral algebra A with central curva-
ture 𝜇0 ∈ 𝑍 (A):
  (i) The Koszul dual A ! exists as a curved cooperad
332                                                            Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


  (ii) The bar-cobar adjunction holds: Ω ( 𝐵 (A)) ≃ A
 (iii) The equivalence is an isomorphism in the derived category
      Our Theorem 6.9.3 provides the geometric realization of their algebraic result.
6.9.5.2 Francis–Gaitsgory
Francis–Gaitsgory [26] prove that factorization algebras satisfy a bar-cobar duality. Their result:
Theorem 6.9.16 (FG, Theorem 7.2.1; [proved]). For a factorization algebra F on a curve 𝑋 :

                                          Fact( 𝑋 , Ω ( 𝐵 (F ))) ≃ F

    Combined with our explicit bar construction (Definition 6.1.13), this confirms that our geometric bar
differential has the correct homological properties.
6.9.5.3 Costello–Gwilliam
In [96], Costello–Gwilliam use curved structures to study BV quantization with anomalies, renormaliza-
tion in perturbative QFT, and effective field theories with central charges.
    Their MC equation (Definition 3.2.1.1 in [96]) is:
                                                   1
                                              𝛿 𝐼 + {𝐼 , 𝐼 } = 0
                                                   2
for the quantum effective action 𝐼 .
    This is our equation (6.9.2.4) in the field theory context.
    The connection is that central charges in QFT correspond to central curvature in chiral algebras; both
ensure that quantum corrections do not destroy associativity/nilpotence.

6.9.7    Perspectives on strict nilpotence
6.9.7.1 Physical perspective
Associativity of the OPE algebra reflects locality: the OPE ( 𝐴𝐵 ) 𝐶 = 𝐴 ( 𝐵𝐶 ) follows from the consistency
of correlation functions as operators approach each other. Quantum corrections (loop diagrams) do not
break locality, so they enter as central charges that modify the normalization but preserve associativity. For
example, in 2D CFT, the central charge 𝑐 in the Virasoro OPE

                                                                𝑐 /2
                                         𝑇 ( 𝑧 )𝑇 ( 𝑤 ) =             +···
                                                            ( 𝑧 − 𝑤)4
is a quantum correction (zero classically) that is central and therefore does not affect the Jacobi identity.
6.9.7.2 Geometric perspective
Kontsevich’s formality theorem [36] shows that:
                                                        ∼
                                     Poly• ( 𝑀 ) [[ 𝑡 ]] −
                                                         → Dpoly• ( 𝑀 ) [[ 𝑡 ]]

via explicit configuration space integrals.
    The integrals:                                     ∫
                                                𝑈Γ =               𝜔Γ
                                                        𝐶𝑛 (ℝ𝑑 )
over configuration spaces satisfy:

                                              𝑈Γ · (boundary terms) = 0
                                        ∑︁
                                          Γ

by Stokes’ theorem.
   This is our strict nilpotence 𝑑 2 = 0. The Arnold relations are the genus-0 case of this pattern.
   At higher genus, the same Stokes argument works because curvature terms are central and do not
interfere with the boundary calculations.
6.9.7.3 Computational verification
Nilpotence holds degree by degree: 𝑑 2 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ) = 0 by direct calculation (degree 2), 𝑑 2 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 ) = 0
using Arnold relations (degree 3), and similarly through degree 5 using extended Arnold relations. The
centrality of 𝜇0 is used at each stage.

6.9.7.4 Functorial perspective
Strict nilpotence also follows from functoriality:
Theorem 6.9.20 (Functoriality of bar construction; [proved]). The bar construction:

                                          𝐵 : ChAlgcentral → Coalg

is a functor from chiral algebras with central curvature to coalgebras, characterized by the universal property:

                               HomCoalg ( 𝐵 (A) , 𝐶 ) ≃ HomChAlg (A , Ω ( 𝐶 ))
                                             2 = 0 by the universal property.
      This adjunction automatically implies 𝑑bar

Proof. The proof assembles three previously established results into the claimed adjunction.
    Functoriality. By Theorem 6.2.47, the bar construction 𝐵 is functorial: a morphism 𝑓 : A → B of
chiral algebras induces 𝐵 ( 𝑓 ) : 𝐵 (A) → 𝐵 (B) compatible with the coalgebra structures. The category
ChAlgcentral consists of chiral algebras whose curvature 𝜇0 lies in the center 𝑍 (A).
    Adjunction. The bar-cobar adjunction 𝐵 ⊣ Ω is established in Theorem 6.3.46. For a coalgebra 𝐶 and a
chiral algebra A, a coalgebra map 𝜙 : 𝐵 (A) → 𝐶 determines a chiral algebra map 𝜙˜ : A → Ω ( 𝐶 ) by the
universal property of the tensor coalgebra: 𝜙 restricts to a map on cogenerators 𝜙¯ : 𝑠 A → 𝐶¯ , and 𝜙˜ = 𝑠 −1 𝜙¯
is the corresponding algebra map. Conversely, 𝜙˜ : A → Ω ( 𝐶 ) extends uniquely to 𝜙 : 𝐵 (A) → 𝐶 by
the cofree property of the tensor coalgebra.
    𝑑 2 = 0 from the adjunction. The bar differential 𝑑𝐵 on 𝐵 (A) satisfies 𝑑𝐵2 = 0 when the curvature 𝜇0 is
central: by Theorem 6.9.3, the centrality 𝜇0 ∈ 𝑍 (A) implies that the curvature-induced term [ 𝜇0 , −] in 𝑑𝐵2
vanishes identically. From the Grothendieck perspective, this is automatic: 𝑑𝐵 is the unique coderivation
on 𝐵 (A) whose projection to cogenerators recovers the chiral algebra structure maps. The condition
𝑑𝐵2 = 0 is equivalent to the 𝐴∞ relations on A, which reduce to the associativity of the chiral product
when 𝜇0 is central (the curved 𝐴∞ relations 𝑚𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝑚 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0 collapse because the terms
                                              P
involving 𝑚0 = 𝜇0 commute with everything).

Remark 6.9.21 (Dependencies). This proof uses three ingredients:
(D1) Concrete bar-functor functoriality (Theorem 6.2.47).
(D2) The bar-cobar adjunction framework (Theorem 6.3.46).
(D3) Central curvature implies strict nilpotence (Theorem 6.9.3).
      Once centrality of 𝜇0 ensures the adjunction exists, the nilpotence 𝑑 2 = 0 follows formally.

6.9.8      Strict versus homotopy nilpotence
Remark 6.9.22 (Strict vs homotopy nilpotence). For chiral algebras A arising from vertex operator algebras
(satisfying the vacuum axiom 𝑌 (1, 𝑧 ) = id) or from conformal field theories whose anomalies are central,
           2 = 0 strictly at all genera. The ingredients are: (1) the curvature 𝜇 is proportional to the
we have 𝑑bar                                                                        0
vacuum 1, hence central by the vacuum axiom (Remark 6.9.5); (2) Arnold relations ensure 𝑑residue 2    = 0;
(3) the Leibniz rule gives the anticommutation of 𝑑internal and 𝑑residue ; (4) the modular operad boundary
relations on M 𝑔,𝑛 extend this to all genera (Theorem 6.9.12).
    This covers all standard examples (Heisenberg, Kac–Moody, Virasoro, 𝑊 -algebras, free field systems).
For non-unital chiral algebras or theories with non-central anomalies, 𝑑 2 = 0 may hold only up to homo-
topy.

6.11.1      Chiral CDG-coalgebras
Deﬁnition 6.11.1 (Chiral CDG-coalgebra). A chiral CDG-coalgebra over a smooth curve 𝑋 is a triple
( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) where:
   (i) 𝐶 is a graded chiral coalgebra on 𝑋 : a graded D 𝑋 -module equipped with a comultiplication Δ : 𝐶 →
       𝐶 ⊗ch 𝐶 (defined via configuration space splitting maps, cf. Theorem 6.2.73), a counit 𝜀 : 𝐶 → 𝜔 𝑋 ,
       coassociativity, and the counit axioms.
  (ii) 𝑑 : 𝐶 → 𝐶 is a homogeneous endomorphism of degree 1 that is an odd coderivation: the composition
       Δ ◦ 𝑑 = ( 𝑑 ⊗ id + id ⊗ 𝑑 ) ◦ Δ holds, and 𝜀 ◦ 𝑑 = 0 on 𝐶 >−2 (the counit annihilates 𝑑 except
       possibly in the lowest degree).
 (iii) ℎ : 𝐶 → 𝜔 𝑋 is a homogeneous linear functional of degree 2 (the curvature), satisfying:
         a) 𝑑 2 ( 𝑐 ) = ℎ ∗ 𝑐 − 𝑐 ∗ ℎ for all 𝑐 ∈ 𝐶 , where ℎ ∗ 𝑐 denotes the coaction of the curvature (defined
            via the comodule structure of 𝐶 over itself);
         b) ℎ ◦ 𝑑 ( 𝑐 ) = 0 for all 𝑐 ∈ 𝐶 (the curvature is a cocycle for the coderivation 𝑑 ).
When ℎ = 0, we recover an ordinary DG chiral coalgebra.

holds for 𝐵¯ ch (A) when A is finitely generated over D 𝑋 ), Homch ( 𝐶, 𝑃 )  𝐶 ∗ ⊗ ch 𝑃 where 𝐶 ∗ =
Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝐶, 𝜔 𝑋 ) is the graded dual. In this finite-type case, contramodules over 𝐶 are equivalent to com-
plete modules over the dual algebra 𝐶 ∗ , recovering the correspondence between conilpotent comodules
and complete modules already used in Theorem 9.6.2.
Remark 6.11.7 (No cohomology for CDG-comodules). Since 𝑑 2 ≠ 0 in a CDG-comodule (when ℎ ≠ 0),
there is no notion of cohomology. This is the fundamental reason why the ordinary derived category
is inadequate at higher genus: one cannot define acyclic objects via vanishing cohomology. The correct
substitute is the coderived category (Definition 6.11.12).

6.11.3  Chiral cotensor and cohomomorphism complexes
Deﬁnition 6.11.8 (Chiral cotensor product). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a chiral CDG-coalgebra, 𝑁 a right chiral CDG-
comodule, and 𝑀 a left chiral CDG-comodule. The chiral cotensor product 𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 is the equalizer:

                   𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 = ker 𝜌 ⊗ch id − id ⊗ch 𝜆 : 𝑁 ⊗ch 𝑀 ⇒ 𝑁 ⊗ch 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑀
                                                                                                      

in the category of graded D 𝑋 -modules. The differential on 𝑁 ⊗ch 𝑀 restricts to 𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 (this uses the
compatibility of coactions with differentials), and the restricted differential has 𝑑 2 = ℎ 𝑁 ∗ (−) − (−) ∗
ℎ 𝑀 on the cotensor product, making 𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 a complex (i.e., 𝑑 2 = 0) precisely when ℎ 𝑁 = ℎ 𝑀 (the
curvatures match), which holds when 𝑁 and 𝑀 are CDG-comodules over the same CDG-coalgebra 𝐶 .
Deﬁnition 6.11.9 (Chiral cohomomorphisms). For left chiral CDG-comodules 𝐿 and 𝑀 over 𝐶 , the chiral
cohomomorphism complex is:

                 Cohom𝐶ch ( 𝐿, 𝑀 ) = { 𝑓 ∈ Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝐿, 𝑀 ) : 𝜆 𝑀 ◦ 𝑓 = (id𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑓 ) ◦ 𝜆 𝐿 }

with differential ( 𝑑𝑓 ) ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑑 𝑀 ( 𝑓 ( 𝑥 )) − (−1) | 𝑓 | 𝑓 ( 𝑑 𝐿 ( 𝑥 )). This differential has a zero square (using the
CDG-comodule axioms), making Cohom𝐶ch ( 𝐿, 𝑀 ) an honest complex.
Deﬁnition 6.11.10 (Chiral contratensor product). For a right chiral CDG-comodule 𝑁 and a left chiral
CDG-contramodule 𝑃 over 𝐶 , the chiral contratensor product 𝑁 ⊙𝐶ch 𝑃 is the coequalizer:

                            𝑁 ⊙𝐶ch 𝑃 = coker 𝑁 ⊗ch Homch ( 𝐶, 𝑃 ) ⇒ 𝑁 ⊗ch 𝑃
                                                                                             

where the two maps are 𝜌 ⊗ ch 𝜋 𝑃 and id 𝑁 ⊗ ch 𝜋 𝑃 . The induced differential on 𝑁 ⊙𝐶ch 𝑃 has zero square
by the same curvature cancellation as for the cotensor product.
Lemma 6.11.11 (Adjunction; [proved]). There is a canonical isomorphism of complexes:

                  Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 , 𝑉 )  Cohom𝐶ch 𝑀 , Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝑁 ,𝑉 )
                                                                            

for any graded D 𝑋 -module 𝑉 , and dually:

                           Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 , 𝑃 )  Hom D 𝑋 (𝑉 , Homch ( 𝐶, 𝑃 ))

establishing Φ𝐶 ⊣ Ψ𝐶 (see Definition 6.11.18 below).

Proof. Both isomorphisms are instances of the tensor-hom adjunction in the chiral category. For the
first: an element of the left side is a D 𝑋 -linear map 𝑓 : 𝑁 □𝐶ch 𝑀 → 𝑉 . By the universal property of
the equalizer, this is equivalent to a D 𝑋 -linear map 𝑓˜ : 𝑁 ⊗ ch 𝑀 → 𝑉 that equalizes the two coac-
tion maps. By the chiral tensor-hom adjunction (which holds for holonomic D 𝑋 -modules by [2, Propo-
sition 3.4.6]), 𝑓˜ corresponds to a map 𝑀 → Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝑁 ,𝑉 ) that is 𝐶 -colinear, i.e., an element of
Cohom𝐶ch ( 𝑀 , Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝑁 ,𝑉 )). The second isomorphism is analogous.

6.11.4     Coderived and contraderived categories
Deﬁnition 6.11.12 (Coderived and contraderived categories). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a chiral CDG-coalgebra.
   Exact triples. An exact triple of left chiral CDG-comodules is a short sequence 0 → 𝐿 → 𝑀 → 𝑁 →
0 that is exact in the abelian category of graded 𝐶 -comodules (with closed, degree-zero morphisms). The
analogous notion applies to CDG-contramodules.
338                                                          Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


    Coacyclic objects. A left chiral CDG-comodule 𝑀 is coacyclic if it belongs to the minimal thick subcat-
egory of Hot( 𝐶 -comodch ) that contains the totalizations of all exact triples and is closed under infinite
direct sums. Denote by Acyclco ( 𝐶 -comodch ) the thick subcategory of coacyclic CDG-comodules.
    Contraacyclic objects. A left chiral CDG-contramodule 𝑃 is contraacyclic if it belongs to the minimal
thick subcategory of Hot( 𝐶 -contrach ) that contains the totalizations of all exact triples and is closed under
infinite direct products. Denote by Acyclctr ( 𝐶 -contrach ) the thick subcategory of contraacyclic CDG-
contramodules.
    The exotic derived categories.

                      𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) := Hot( 𝐶 -comodch ) / Acyclco ( 𝐶 -comodch )
                      𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contrach ) := Hot( 𝐶 -contrach ) / Acyclctr ( 𝐶 -contrach )

Remark 6.11.13 (Comparison with ordinary derived category). When ℎ = 0 (genus 0), CDG-comodules are
ordinary DG-comodules and one can also form the standard derived category 𝐷 ( 𝐶 -comodch ) by localizing
at acyclic objects (those with 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝑀 ) = 0). In general, Acyclco ⊃ Acycl, so 𝐷 co is a quotient of 𝐷 . When 𝐶
has finite homological dimension (e.g., when A is Koszul with finite global dimension), the two categories
coincide (Positselski [171, §4.5]). When ℎ ≠ 0, the standard derived category is trivial (no cohomology
exists), while 𝐷 co retains rich structure.

6.11.5  Injective comodules and projective contramodules
Deﬁnition 6.11.14 (Cofree chiral CDG-comodule). For a graded D 𝑋 -module 𝑉 , the cofree graded chiral
𝐶 -comodule on 𝑉 is:
                                         𝐽 (𝑉 ) := 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑉
with coaction Δ ⊗ch id𝑉 : 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑉 → 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 . The CDG-comodule differential is 𝑑 𝐽 (𝑉 ) ( 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑣 ) =
𝑑 ( 𝑐 ) ⊗ 𝑣 , and the curvature relation 𝑑 2𝐽 (𝑉 ) = ℎ ∗ (−) is inherited from 𝐶 .
Proposition 6.11.15 (Injective and projective resolutions; [proved]). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a conilpotent
chiral CDG-coalgebra with finite-dimensional graded pieces.
(a) For any left chiral CDG-comodule 𝑀 , the cofree chiral comodule 𝐽 ( 𝑀 ) = 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑀 is injective in
    the abelian category of graded 𝐶 # -comodules (where 𝐶 # denotes 𝐶 with forgotten differential and
    curvature).
(b) For any left chiral CDG-contramodule 𝑃 , the free chiral contramodule 𝐹 ( 𝑃 ) = Homch ( 𝐶, 𝑃 ) is
    projective in the abelian category of graded 𝐶 # -contramodules.
(c) The homotopy categories admit semiorthogonal decompositions: the coderived category
    𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) is equivalent to the homotopy category of CDG-comodules with injective
    underlying graded comodules, and 𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contrach ) is equivalent to the homotopy category of
    CDG-contramodules with projective underlying graded contramodules.

tensor-hom adjunction in the chiral category: Hom𝐶 # ( 𝑀 , 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 )  Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝑀 ,𝑉 ), and the functor
Hom D 𝑋 (−,𝑉 ) is exact on holonomic D 𝑋 -modules (since holonomic modules have finite length).
   Part (b). Dual to (a): for an exact sequence 0 → 𝑃 → 𝑄 → 𝑅 → 0 of graded 𝐶 # -contramodules,
Hom𝐶 # (Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) , −) is exact because Hom𝐶 # (Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) , 𝑃 )  Hom D 𝑋 (𝑉 , 𝑃 ).

    Part (c). For any CDG-comodule 𝑀 , the cobar resolution provides a functorial injective resolution:

Corollary 6.11.17 (Contractibility of coacyclic injectives; [proved]). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a conilpo-
tent chiral CDG-coalgebra with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and let 𝑀 be a chiral CDG-comodule
with injective underlying graded 𝐶 # -comodule. Then 𝑀 is coacyclic if and only if it admits a contracting
homotopy: a degree −1 graded 𝐶 # -comodule endomorphism 𝑠 : 𝑀 → 𝑀 satisfying

                                         𝑑𝑀 ◦ 𝑠 + 𝑠 ◦ 𝑑𝑀 = id 𝑀 .                                         (6.43)

Proof. If such an 𝑠 exists, then id 𝑀 = 𝑑Hom ( 𝑠 ) in the CDG Hom-complex of Proposition 6.11.16 (with
𝑀 = 𝑁 ), so 𝑀 is null-homotopic and a fortiori coacyclic.
340                                                       Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


    Conversely, suppose 𝑀 is coacyclic with injective underlying graded comodule. By the semiorthogonal
decomposition in Proposition 6.11.15(c), 𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) is equivalent to Hot( 𝐶 -comodch
                                                                                            inj ). A coacyclic
object that already has injective underlying comodule represents the zero object in this homotopy category,
hence is null-homotopic: there exists a degree −1 closed morphism 𝑠 with 𝑑Hom ( 𝑠 ) = id 𝑀 . Expanding
via (6.42) gives (6.43).

6.11.6  The correspondence functors
Deﬁnition 6.11.18 (Functors Φ𝐶ch and Ψ𝐶ch ). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a chiral CDG-coalgebra.
• For a left chiral CDG-contramodule 𝑃 , define Φ𝐶ch ( 𝑃 ) to be the left chiral CDG-comodule whose
  underlying graded D 𝑋 -module is the chiral contratensor product 𝐶 ⊙𝐶ch 𝑃 . Concretely, Φ𝐶ch ( 𝑃 ) is a
  quotient of 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑃 ; the comodule structure comes from the comultiplication on the left factor 𝐶 , and
  the differential is induced by the differentials on 𝐶 and 𝑃 via the standard formula for the tensor product
  of graded D 𝑋 -modules with differentials.
• For a left chiral CDG-comodule 𝑀 , define Ψ𝐶ch ( 𝑀 ) to be the left chiral CDG-contramodule whose
  underlying graded D 𝑋 -module is Hom𝐶ch ( 𝐶, 𝑀 ) = Cohom𝐶ch ( 𝐶, 𝑀 ). The contramodule structure
  comes from the comultiplication on 𝐶 , and the differential is induced from 𝑑𝐶 and 𝑑𝑀 .
These define DG-functors:

                              Φ𝐶ch : DG( 𝐶 -contrach ) −→ DG( 𝐶 -comodch ) ,
                              Ψ𝐶ch : DG( 𝐶 -comodch ) −→ DG( 𝐶 -contrach ) .

Lemma 6.11.19 (Key properties of Φ 𝐶ch and Ψ𝐶ch ; [proved]). (a) Φ𝐶ch is left adjoint to Ψ𝐶ch on the ho-
     motopy categories.
(b) Φ𝐶ch maps the free graded contramodule Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) to the cofree graded comodule 𝐶 ⊗ch 𝑉 , for
     any graded D 𝑋 -module 𝑉 .
 (c) Ψ𝐶ch maps the cofree graded comodule 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 to the free graded contramodule Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ).
(d) Φ𝐶ch maps projective graded contramodules to injective graded comodules, and Ψ𝐶ch maps injective
     graded comodules to projective graded contramodules.

Proof. Part (a). The adjunction Φ𝐶ch ⊣ Ψ𝐶ch follows from the standard isomorphism Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝐶 ⊗ch
𝑉 , 𝑃 )  Hom D 𝑋 (𝑉 , Homch ( 𝐶, 𝑃 )) (the chiral tensor-hom adjunction), which makes Φ𝐶ch left adjoint
to Ψ𝐶ch as DG-functors (Lemma 6.11.11).
    Parts (b) and (c). The free graded contramodule on 𝑉 is Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) = Hom D 𝑋 ( 𝐶,𝑉 ). Then:

                              Φ𝐶ch (Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 )) = 𝐶 ⊙𝐶ch Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) .

By the contramodule-comodule correspondence at the graded level (cf. the example in Positselski [171, §5.1]),
the contratensor product of 𝐶 with the free contramodule on 𝑉 is canonically isomorphic to the cofree
comodule 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 . In the chiral setting, this isomorphism follows from the tensor-hom adjunction for
D 𝑋 -modules:

      𝐶 ⊙𝐶ch Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 )  coker 𝐶 ⊗ch Homch ( 𝐶, Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 )) ⇒ 𝐶 ⊗ch Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 )
                                                                                                      

                              𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 ,
6.11. Chiral coalgebra homological algebra                                                                341


where the last step uses the counit of the adjunction ev : Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) ⊗ch 𝐶 → 𝑉 and the coassociativity
of 𝐶 . Part (c) is the dual computation.
   Part (d). Combine (b)–(c) with Proposition 6.11.15(a)–(b): free graded contramodules are projective
and cofree graded comodules are injective, so Φ𝐶ch sends projective objects to injective objects and vice
versa.

6.11.7   The chiral comodule-contramodule correspondence
Theorem 6.11.20 (Chiral comodule-contramodule correspondence; [proved]). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑, ℎ) be a
conilpotent chiral CDG-coalgebra on a smooth curve 𝑋 with finite-dimensional graded pieces. The derived
functors

                             𝕃 Φ𝐶ch : 𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contrach ) −→ 𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) ,
                            ℝΨ𝐶ch : 𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) −→ 𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contrach )

are mutually inverse equivalences of triangulated categories.

Proof. The proof follows Positselski [171, §5.2], with the ordinary tensor product replaced by the chiral
tensor product ⊗ch and exactness properties established via the geometry of D 𝑋 -modules on configuration
spaces. We verify each step.
   Step 1: Derived functors. By Proposition 6.11.15(c), the contraderived and coderived categories

                                  𝐷 ctr ( 𝐶 -contrach ) ≃ 𝐾proj ( 𝐶 -contrach ) ,
                                  𝐷 co ( 𝐶 -comodch ) ≃ 𝐾inj ( 𝐶 -comodch )

are equivalent to the homotopy categories of CDG-contramodules (resp. CDG-comodules) with pro-
jective (resp. injective) underlying graded module. The left derived functor 𝕃 Φ𝐶ch restricts to projective
contramodules; ℝΨ𝐶ch restricts to injective comodules.
    Step 2: Mutual inverse on generators. By Lemma 6.11.19(b)–(c), Φ𝐶ch sends the free graded contramodule
Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ) to the cofree graded comodule 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 , and Ψ𝐶ch sends 𝐶 ⊗ ch 𝑉 back to Homch ( 𝐶,𝑉 ).
These are the generating objects for the respective categories (any CDG-comodule has an injective resolution
by cofree comodules, and any CDG-contramodule has a projective resolution by free contramodules, by
Proposition 6.11.15).
    Step 3: Equivalence on full triangulated subcategories. We claim that the restrictions of Φ𝐶ch and Ψ𝐶ch to
the full triangulated subcategories

                                 Hot( 𝐶 -contrach                     ch
                                               proj ) ⊂ Hot( 𝐶 -contra ) ,

                                  Hot( 𝐶 -comodch                   ch
                                               inj ) ⊂ Hot( 𝐶 -comod )

are mutually inverse equivalences.
   To see this, observe that the unit and counit natural transformations

                              𝜂 : id → Ψ𝐶ch ◦ Φ𝐶ch ,         𝜀 : Φ𝐶ch ◦ Ψ𝐶ch → id

are isomorphisms on free contramodules and cofree comodules (Step 2). Since these objects generate
the respective homotopy categories (every object is built from generators by shifts, cones, and countable
(co)products), and both Φ𝐶ch and Ψ𝐶ch preserve exact triangles and countable (co)products, the natural
342                                                          Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


transformations 𝜂 and 𝜀 are isomorphisms on all objects with projective (resp. injective) underlying graded
structure.
    Step 4: Descent to exotic derived categories. To pass from the full homotopy categories to 𝐷 co and 𝐷 ctr ,
we verify that Φ𝐶ch maps contraacyclic CDG-contramodules to coacyclic CDG-comodules, and Ψ𝐶ch maps
coacyclic CDG-comodules to contraacyclic CDG-contramodules.
    For Φ𝐶ch : since Φ𝐶ch is a left adjoint, it preserves (all) colimits, in particular coproducts and cokernels. A
contraacyclic CDG-contramodule is built from totalizations of exact triples and direct products. Now, Φ𝐶ch
preserves exact triples (being a left adjoint of an exact functor, hence right exact; and by Lemma 6.11.19(d)
it sends projective contramodules to injective comodules, so the left derived functor is exact). The image
of a totalization under Φ𝐶ch is a totalization, and the image of a direct product is computed using the cofree
resolution from Step 2. Thus Φ𝐶ch preserves contraacyclic → coacyclic. The argument for Ψ𝐶ch is dual.
    Step 5: Conclusion. Combining Steps 3 and 4: 𝕃 Φ𝐶ch and ℝΨ𝐶ch are well-defined triangulated functors
between 𝐷 ctr and 𝐷 co , they are mutually inverse on the generating subcategories (projective contramodules
↔ injective comodules), and both categories are compactly generated by finite-dimensional objects (using
conilpotency and finite-type grading; the argument parallels Positselski [171, §5.5], with the key input that any
graded 𝐶 -comodule is the union of its finite-dimensional subcomodules, which holds for conilpotent chiral
coalgebras because the conformal weight grading bounds the coaction filtration). By the uniqueness of
extensions of equivalences from compact generators to the full compactly generated category (cf. [171, §5.5]),
the equivalence extends to all objects.

Remark 6.11.21 (Hypotheses). The two key hypotheses–-conilpotency and finite-type grading–-are satisfied
by 𝐶 = 𝐵¯ ch (A) whenever A is a finitely generated chiral algebra with finite-dimensional conformal
weight spaces (which includes all Koszul chiral algebras arising in this monograph: Kac–Moody, Virasoro,
𝑊 -algebras, Heisenberg, free fields, and Yangians). Conilpotency was established in Theorem 7.4.3(4);
finite-type grading follows from the finite-generation hypothesis on A.

6.11.8    Application: the Positselski equivalence for chiral algebras
The chiral comodule-contramodule correspondence yields the derived module category equivalence at all
genera.
Theorem 6.11.22 (Positselski equivalence for chiral algebras; [proved]). For a Koszul chiral algebra
A on a smooth curve 𝑋 with curved bar complex 𝐶 = 𝐵¯ ch (A) (a conilpotent chiral CDG-coalgebra by

between the coderived category of conilpotent chiral A-comodules and the contraderived category of chiral
A ! -contramodules.

categories provide the correct framework.

Remark 6.11.24 (Relation to genus-0 module Koszul duality). At genus 0, the curvature ℎ = 0, so CDG-
comodules reduce to DG-comodules, the coderived category reduces to the ordinary derived category, and

                               𝐷 𝑏 (Modcompl (A)) ≃ 𝐷 (CoModconil (A ! )) .
The virtue of the coderived/contraderived framework is that it provides the correct generalization to
                                  ( 𝑔)
genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, where the curvature 𝑚0 ≠ 0 makes the ordinary derived category trivial.
344                                                         Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


Remark 6.11.25 (The role of the conﬁguration space geometry). The proof of the chiral comodule-
contramodule correspondence (Theorem 6.11.20) uses the geometry of configuration spaces in three
places:
   (i) Exactness of the chiral tensor product. The tensor-hom adjunction for holonomic D 𝑋 -modules
       on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) ensures that cofree comodules are injective and free contramodules are projective
       (Proposition 6.11.15).
  (ii) Conilpotency from conformal weight. The conformal weight grading on 𝐵¯ ch (A) (inherited from A)
       ensures conilpotency (Theorem 7.4.3(4)), which is needed for the compact generation argument in
       Step 5 of the proof.
 (iii) Finite-dimensionality from holonomicity. The holonomicity of the bar complex on each configuration
       space stratum (Lemma 6.3.8) ensures finite-dimensional graded pieces, which is needed for the duality
       between contramodules and complete modules (Remark 6.11.6).
These geometric inputs are specific to the chiral setting and have no analogue in Positselski’s ground-field
framework.

                                          𝜓 : Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −→ A

induced by the bar-cobar adjunction is a quasi-isomorphism, not merely an isomorphism in cohomology.
   More precisely:
   (i) The map 𝜓 is a morphism of chiral algebras (respects all structure)
  (ii) At each genus 𝑔 , the genus- 𝑔 component:

       is a quasi-isomorphism
