Scope. The Koszul hypothesis is essential: for admissible-level affine algebras and minimal-model Virasoro/W-
algebras the bar spectral sequence has nontrivial higher differentials and the counit 𝜓 is not a quasi-
isomorphism (see Remark 20.12.4 and 12.7.22). In those regimes one must work with the completed or
coderived bar-cobar correspondence (Corollary 6.3.33, §6.8.2).
Dependency-closed proof. We verify each numbered clause by previously established results in this chapter.
 (D1) Morphism of chiral algebras. The map 𝜓 is the counit of the bar-cobar adjunction from Theo-
      rem 6.3.46; therefore it is canonical and respects the algebraic structure by functoriality of bar and
      cobar (Theorem 6.2.47, Theorem 6.12.11).
(D2) Genuswise quasi-isomorphism. The genus-0 base case is proved independently by Theorem 6.2.27
      and Theorem 9.3.7; equivalently, it is the implication (i)⇒(ii) of the fundamental theorem of chiral
      twisting morphisms (Theorem 9.1.8). The genus- 𝑔 components 𝜓 𝑔 for 𝑔 ≥ 1 are quasi-isomorphisms
      by induction on genus via Theorem 6.12.8, item (2), together with the higher-genus inversion package
      (Theorem 8.17.4).
(D3) Full genus-graded convergence and quasi-isomorphism. This is Theorem 6.12.8, item (3), which iden-
      tifies the completed genus series 𝜓 = 𝑔 ≥0 ℏ2 𝑔 −2 𝜓 𝑔 and proves convergence.
                                             P

(D4) Spectral sequence statement. Existence and explicit page description are exactly Theorem 6.12.6; col-
      lapse for Koszul input is Theorem 6.12.7.
Combining (D1)–(D4) gives all four clauses of the theorem.
Remark 6.12.2 (Relation to the fundamental theorem A0 ). At genus 0, Theorem 6.12.1 is a consequence of
the fundamental theorem of chiral twisting morphisms (Theorem 9.1.8): the counit Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A)) → A
being a quasi-isomorphism is one of the four equivalent characterizations of Koszulity established there.
The present theorem extends this to all genera via the genus induction of clause (D2).
Remark 6.12.3 (Quasi-isomorphism of chain complexes vs chiral algebras). The distinction is between two
levels of structure:
    Chain complex quasi-isomorphism. A chain map 𝜓 : 𝐶 • → 𝐷 • inducing an isomorphism 𝐻 • ( 𝜓 ) :
          
𝐻 • (𝐶 ) −→ 𝐻 • ( 𝐷 ) on cohomology. This is the standard notion; a ‘‘homology isomorphism’’ and a
‘‘quasi-isomorphism’’ are the same thing at the chain complex level.
    Chiral algebra quasi-isomorphism. An 𝐴∞ (or chiral algebra) morphism 𝜓 : A → B whose linear
component 𝜓1 : A → B is a chain complex quasi-isomorphism. Such a map preserves the full 𝐴∞ structure
up to coherent homotopy. The distinction matters: A chain complex quasi-isomorphism tells us only about
𝐻 • and need not respect multiplicative or 𝐴∞ structure, whereas a chiral algebra quasi-isomorphism gives
a full equivalence in the derived category of chiral algebras, preserving all homotopy-theoretic information.
For Koszul duality, the map Ω ( 𝐵 (A)) → A must be a quasi-isomorphism of chiral algebras, not merely
of chain complexes, to establish derived equivalences.
    Example. Consider a dga ( 𝐶 • , 𝑑, 𝜇) with:
                                                     0
                                     ··· → 0 → ℂ −
                                                 → ℂ → 0 → ···
   This has 𝐻 0 = ℂ, 𝐻 𝑖 = 0 for 𝑖 ≠ 0.
   Compare with the algebra ( 𝐷 • , 0, 𝜈 ) = (ℂ, 0, 0) in degree 0. The projection 𝜋 : 𝐶 • → 𝐷 • is a quasi-
isomorphism of chain complexes (both have 𝐻 0 = ℂ), but 𝜋 does not respect the multiplication ( 𝜋 need
not intertwine 𝜇 and 𝜈 at the chain level). To obtain a quasi-isomorphism of algebras, one must work with
𝐴∞ morphisms, which encode the higher homotopies relating the two multiplicative structures.

Lemma 6.12.5 (Associated graded; [proved]). The associated graded of the bar-cobar filtration is:

                                        Gr 𝑝 Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) = Ω 𝑝 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑝 (A))

Proof. By definition of associated graded:

                                       Gr 𝑝 = 𝐹 𝑝 / 𝐹 𝑝+1 = Ω 𝑝 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑝 (A))

   The full differential on Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) decomposes as 𝑑 = 𝑑internal + 𝑑bar + 𝑑cobar , where 𝑑internal preserves
the filtration degree (it acts within each tensor factor), 𝑑bar preserves or lowers filtration degree (collisions
reduce arity), and 𝑑cobar raises filtration degree by 1 (comultiplication increases cobar arity). On the asso-
ciated graded Gr 𝑝 = 𝐹 𝑝 / 𝐹 𝑝+1 , only the ﬁltration-preserving component survives: 𝑑cobar maps 𝐹 𝑝 into

𝑑gr = 𝑑internal , which is the 𝑑0 differential of the spectral sequence (cf. Theorem 6.12.6).

6.12.5      The counit of the adjunction
Proposition 6.12.10 (Counit is quasi-isomorphism; [proved]). The counit of the bar-cobar adjunc-
tion:
                                     𝜖 : 𝐵¯ ( Ω (C)) −→ C
for a chiral coalgebra C is also a quasi-isomorphism (dual statement).

Proof. By Verdier duality (Theorem 6.3.32), the counit 𝜖 C : 𝐵¯ ch ( Ωch (C)) → C is the Verdier dual of
the unit 𝜂 A ! , which is a quasi-isomorphism by Theorem 6.3.46. Since Verdier duality on the Fulton–
MacPherson compactifications preserves quasi-isomorphisms (Theorem 6.3.32), the result follows.

 Remark 6.12.13 (Scope and limitations). The hypotheses above are essential:
 • Without finite generation, the bar construction may produce unbounded complexes.
 • Without conilpotence, the cobar series Ω (A ! ) = 𝑛 ≥1 A !⊗ 𝑛 may not converge, and the functor Ω is
                                                    L
   not well-defined.
 • For non-quadratic algebras, one must replace A ! by its nilpotent completion (Appendix P) and work
   with pro-nilpotent comodules.
 Even in ordinary algebra, Koszul duality yields equivalences between speciﬁc subcategories, not the entire
 derived category without finiteness conditions; cf. Beilinson–Ginzburg–Soergel [5].
 Remark 6.12.14 (Physical signiﬁcance). From the physics perspective, the distinction between homology
 isomorphism and quasi-isomorphism corresponds to:
     A homology isomorphism gives only on-shell equivalence: physical states match, but one cannot com-
 pute scattering amplitudes or access quantum corrections. A full quasi-isomorphism gives off-shell equiva-
 lence: the entire QFT matches, correlation functions and amplitudes are computable, quantum corrections
 are encoded in the higher homotopies, and the path integral measure is determined. This is why establishing
 the quasi-isomorphism–-not just the homology isomorphism–-is essential for physical applications.

 6.14        The Ran-space perspective
The ∞-categorical framework of factorization algebras on Ran( 𝑋 ) provides the conceptual home for the
bar-cobar adjunction.
 Remark 6.14.1 (From conﬁguration spaces to Ran space). The configuration spaces 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) and their FM com-
 pactifications 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) are finite-dimensional approximations to the Ran space Ran( 𝑋 ) = colim𝑛 𝑋 𝑛 /Σ𝑛 ,

                                                                             L
 on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), assembles into a single object on Ran( 𝑋 ). The bar differential, given by residues at collision
 divisors (Definition 6.1.13), becomes the factorization structure map: when two points collide, the OPE
 produces the ‘‘fusion’’ of the corresponding tensor factors.
     In this language, the Arnold relations that ensure 𝑑 2 = 0 (Theorem 6.2.27) are the coherence conditions
 for the factorization algebra axiom: the result of a three-point collision does not depend on the order in
 which pairs collide, because the relevant boundary strata of 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ) are related by the Arnold relation
 𝜔12 ∧ 𝜔23 + 𝜔23 ∧ 𝜔31 + 𝜔31 ∧ 𝜔12 = 0.
 Remark 6.14.2 (Verdier duality as the engine of Koszul duality). The bar-cobar adjunction

                             𝐵¯ 𝑋 : Algaug (Fact( 𝑋 )) ⇄ CoAlgconil (Fact( 𝑋 )) : Ω 𝑋

 is controlled by Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 ). The key identification is:

                                            𝔻Ran 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) ≃ 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A ! ) .

Remark 6.14.3 (Curvature and coderived categories). When curvature is present–-i.e., when the genus-1

The ordinary derived category of A-modules is then the wrong quotient: it erases the distinction between
                       2 ≠ 0’’ and ‘‘acyclic because of genuine exactness.’’

    The correct ambient category is the coderived category D co (A) in the sense of Positselski [171]. In this
category, a curved complex ( 𝑀 , 𝑑 𝑀 ) with 𝑑 𝑀 2 = 𝜅 · id

between the coderived category of modules and the contraderived category of comodules. On the Koszul
locus–-where the curvature vanishes or is absorbed into the differential–-the coderived and derived cat-
egories agree, and the equivalence reduces to Corollary 6.12.12. Off this locus, the coderived formalism
captures the ‘‘acyclic-but-not-contractible’’ phenomena that higher-genus curvature creates.
    This perspective clarifies the physical meaning of curvature: the cosmological constant Λ ∼ 𝜅 (A)
in the AdS3 /CFT2 correspondence (Conjecture 34.10.13) is the obstruction to reducing the coderived
category to the derived category. Anomaly cancellation at 𝑐 = 26 (𝜅 = 0) is precisely the condition under
which the coderived and derived categories agree, i.e., under which the string theory is ‘‘on-shell’’ in the
derived-categorical sense.
    The bar-cobar adjunction for chiral algebras is now fully constructed: the bar differential is a residue on
Fulton–MacPherson compactifications, 𝑑 2 = 0 follows from the Arnold relations, and Verdier duality on
Ran( 𝑋 ) intertwines bar and cobar (Theorem 6.3.32). For Koszul pairs, the adjunction is an equivalence
(Theorem 9.1.39). This is the genus-0 theory. Everything built so far lives on configuration spaces of the
fixed curve 𝑋 , with no reference to moduli of curves.

cobar counit Ω 𝐵¯ (A) → A is the Fourier inversion formula.

datum that organizes the M-level constructions.

6.15     The categorical logarithm
The constructions of this chapter–-bar, cobar, Verdier intertwining, bar-cobar inversion, factorization
homology–-are not independent results. They are aspects of a single structure: the categorical logarithm
for factorization algebras on algebraic curves. In this section we develop this identification systematically,
extracting from it both the conceptual unity of the four main theorems and concrete predictions for
higher-genus theory.

Remark 6.15.2 (The logarithmic kernel). The fact that the bar construction uses a logarithmic kernel 𝜂𝑖𝑗 =
𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) is the surface manifestation of the categorical identification. The classical logarithm of a
product is a sum: log( 𝑧1 𝑧2 ) = log 𝑧1 + log 𝑧2 . The bar differential implements precisely this: the OPE (a
product structure at colliding points) is converted, via the residue Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 ( 𝜇ch · 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ), into a sum (the bar
differential is a sum over pairwise collisions). The kernel 𝜂 is the infinitesimal version of this conversion.

6.15.2    The Taylor expansion of the logarithm
The PBW spectral sequence of a chiral algebra A (Definition 9.1.14) is the Taylor expansion of the categorical
logarithm.
   More precisely: the weight filtration on the bar complex 𝐵 (A) = 𝑛 ≥0 ( 𝑠 −1 A) ⊗ 𝑛 induces a spectral
                                                                         L
sequence
                           𝐸1 = 𝐻 𝑞 gr 𝑝 𝐵 (A) =⇒ 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 ( 𝐵 (A)) .
                              𝑝,𝑞                    

In the exp/log framework, the filtration degree 𝑝 is the order of the Taylor expansion: the 𝑝-th filtered piece
𝐹 𝑝 𝐵 (A) retains contributions from at most 𝑝 points in configuration space, i.e., the first 𝑝 terms of the
logarithmic series. The differential 𝑑1 on the 𝐸1 -page extracts the leading term of the logarithm (the binary
OPE residue); higher differentials 𝑑𝑟 capture higher-order corrections from 𝑟 -fold collisions.
Proposition 6.15.3 (Convergence criterion; [proved] Theorems 6.12.7 and 6.12.1). The categorical
logarithm converges–-meaning exp ◦ log = id–-if and only if the PBW spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 .
The 𝐸2 degeneration is equivalent to:
   (i) The chiral algebra A lies on the Koszul locus (Definition 9.1.14);
  (ii) The Taylor expansion has finitely many nonzero corrections at each filtration degree: the logarithm
       is ‘‘polynomial’’ in the filtration variable;
358                                                        Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


 (iii) The counit 𝜓 : Ω𝐵 (A) → A is a quasi-isomorphism (Theorem 6.12.1).
Off the Koszul locus, the Taylor series diverges in the ordinary derived category. The coderived category
(§6.11.4) provides the analytic continuation: it is the completion of the derived category that makes the
divergent logarithm well-defined, exactly as the maximal analytic continuation of log 𝑧 requires passage
from ℂ× to its universal cover.
Remark 6.15.4 (Convergence radius from OPE data). The analogy with power series provides a heuristic
for the following conjectural expectation: the convergence radius of the categorical logarithm should be
computable from the input data. For the classical logarithm log(1 + 𝑧 ) = (−1) 𝑛+1 𝑧 𝑛 /𝑛, the radius is
                                                                                 P
determined by the growth rate of the coefficients. For the categorical logarithm, the ‘‘coefficients’’ are the
OPE residues, and the ‘‘growth rate’’ is the complexity of multi-point collisions.
    In concrete terms: Kac–Moody algebras have first-order OPE poles (linear growth), and the categorical
logarithm converges (Theorem 34.9.1). The Virasoro algebra has a second-order pole from the central term,
but the Sugawara constraint tames the growth, and convergence holds (Theorem 9.1.35). For non-Koszul
algebras (e.g., admissible-level affine algebras), the OPE singularity structure generates higher differentials
in the spectral sequence–-the Taylor coefficients grow too fast for convergence. A precise bound relating
the OPE pole orders to the convergence radius of the categorical logarithm is a natural target for future
work.

6.15.3   Additivity and the branch structure
The fundamental property of any logarithm is that it converts products to sums. For the categorical loga-
rithm, this is the content of the complementarity theorem.
Proposition 6.15.5 (Additivity of the categorical logarithm; [proved] Theorem 8.14.12). Let
(A , A ! ) be a Koszul pair. The quantum corrections to the bar complex satisfy

                                 𝑄 𝑔 (A) + 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 A ) .

In the exp/log framework, this is the statement logcat (A ⊗ A ! ) = logcat (A) + logcat (A ! ): the logarithm
of the Koszul product is the sum of the logarithms, and the right-hand side is the total logarithmic data
logcat (A ⊗ A ! ) computed from the center 𝑍 A via the Hodge cohomology of M 𝑔 .
    The Lagrangian decomposition 𝐶 𝑔 (A) = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) is the decomposition of the total log-
arithm into its two branches: the sheet associated to A and the sheet associated to its Koszul dual. The
pairing between them is the monodromy acquired when analytically continuing from one branch to the
other.
Remark 6.15.6 (The categorical Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula). For the classical logarithm,
log( 𝑒 𝑋 𝑒𝑌 ) = 𝑋 + 𝑌 + 21 [ 𝑋 , 𝑌 ] + · · · (the BCH formula). The categorical analogue is the twisted tensor
product decomposition: for an extension 0 → A ′ → A → A ′′ → 0 of chiral algebras, the bar complex
decomposes as 𝐵 (A) ≃ 𝐵 (A ′′ ) ⊗𝜏 𝐵 (A ′ ), where the twisting cochain 𝜏 encodes the extension data
through iterated brackets, in direct analogy with the commutator corrections of BCH. This follows from
the standard filtered bar construction applied to the extension filtration, and the twisting cochain 𝜏 can be
computed order by order from the connecting maps of the extension. A systematic development of the
categorical BCH, including explicit formulas for the first correction terms and their geometric content, is
deferred to §6.8.6.

6.15.5 The characteristic hierarchy as logarithmic data
The modular package ( 𝜅, Δ, Θ, Π ) of a chiral algebra is the data of the categorical logarithm, organized by
order:
Level 1: Scalar logarithmic data. The modular characteristic 𝜅 (A) is the leading coefficient of the cate-
         gorical logarithm–-the residue of the curvature. Its exponential is the scalar period 𝑁 : the smallest
         integer for which exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 𝑁 𝑐 /24) = 1. This is the content of Theorem D (Theorem 8.18.30).
Level 2: Spectral logarithmic data. The spectral discriminant Δ (A) encodes the eigenvalues of the
         monodromy of the categorical logarithm. Its exponential is the periodicity profile Π (A): the
         collection of periods of individual T-matrix eigenvalues 𝜆𝑖 = exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 ( ℎ𝑖 − 𝑐 /24)).
360                                                        Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


Level 3: Full logarithmic data. The universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ A ∈ 𝐻 2 (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 A )
         (Theorem 8.18.72) is the complete categorical logarithm: it encodes all genus- 𝑔 correc-
         tions to the bar differential. Its exponential is the full modular automorphy of A: the action of
         Γ 𝑔 on the conformal blocks, i.e., the modular functor.
The hierarchy is controlled by a single principle: each level is the leading term of the next. The scalar char-
acteristic 𝜅 is the trace of the spectral data Δ; the spectral data is the eigenvalue decomposition of the full
data Θ. In the language of complex analysis: 𝜅 is the winding number of the logarithm, Δ is the set of
periods, and Θ is the full multi-valued function.

6.15.6    Visible theorems
The exp/log identification makes certain results visible that would otherwise have no natural formulation:
 (1) Categorical Torelli. If the monodromy of the categorical logarithm (the higher-genus corrections to
     the bar differential, encoded in Θ A ) determines A up to quasi-isomorphism, this is a categorical Torelli
     theorem. It follows from bar-cobar inversion (Theorem 6.12.1) plus the fact that the curvature deter-
     mines the flat connection up to gauge equivalence on a simply connected base: since the Teichmüller
     space is contractible, the flat bar family is determined by its curvature, i.e., by 𝜅 (A).
(2) Functional equation. The complementarity theorem (Theorem 8.14.12) is the functional equation of
     the categorical logarithm: it relates logcat (A) and logcat (A ! ) through the total data 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 A ),
     exactly as the functional equation of the Riemann 𝜁 -function relates 𝜁 ( 𝑠 ) and 𝜁 (1 − 𝑠 ) through the
     Γ-factor.
(3) Acyclicity of the trivial algebra. For the unit (trivial) chiral algebra A = 𝑘 , the bar complex 𝐵 ( 𝑘 )
     is acyclic: 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵 ( 𝑘 )) = 𝑘 concentrated in degree 0. In the exp/log framework this is log(1) = 0: the
     logarithm of the multiplicative identity is the additive identity.
(4) Convergence radius from OPE poles. The Koszul locus should be characterized by the singularity
     structure of the OPE: the convergence radius of the categorical logarithm equals the inverse of the
     growth rate of multi-point OPE singularities, in analogy with the Cauchy–Hadamard formula.
(5) Screening as infinitesimal generator. In the lattice setting (Construction 17.11.19), the screening
     charges 𝑄 𝑖 with 𝑄 𝑖2 = 0 are the infinitesimal generators of the categorical logarithm; the quan-
     tum group relations 𝑒 𝑖𝑁 = 0 at 𝜁 = 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖 / 𝑁 are their 𝑁 -th powers; and the representation category
     Rep(𝔲 𝜁 (𝔤)) carries the periodic (exponential) structure. The passage 𝑄 2 = 0 → 𝑒 𝑁 = 0 is literally
     exponentiation: the root of unity 𝜁 = exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 / 𝑁 ) is the monodromy of the categorical logarithm
     around the 𝑁 -th root.

6.15.7    The monograph as construction of a categorical logarithm
Taken at full depth, the four main theorems are the four fundamental properties of any logarithm:
• Theorem A (existence): the categorical logarithm and exponential exist, as a pair of adjoint functors
  between augmented factorization algebras and conilpotent factorization coalgebras.
• Theorem B (invertibility): on the convergence domain (the Koszul locus), exp ◦ log = id, and the
  logarithm faithfully encodes its input.
• Theorem C (branch structure): the failure of convergence off the Koszul locus decomposes into com-
  plementary Lagrangians–-the two branches of the multi-valued logarithm–-and the total logarithmic
  data is the sum of the two branches.
• Theorem D (leading coefficient): the leading coefficient 𝜅 (A) of the logarithmic expansion determines
  the full scalar package, just as the leading coefficient of log(1 + 𝑧 ) = 𝑧 + · · · determines the local behavior.
   Every open problem in the monograph is a question about this logarithm. The five master conjectures
are five aspects of one question: what is the categorical logarithm for factorization algebras on algebraic
curves, completely?
• MC1: does the logarithm converge? (PBW concentration)
• MC3: what is the convergence domain? (thick generation in category O)
• MC4: does the logarithm extend to infinite rank? (stability of towers)
• MC5: does the physical logarithm (BRST) equal the mathematical one (bar)? (BV–BRST identification)
• Periodicity: what is the monodromy group of the categorical logarithm?
These are not five separate programmes. They are five windows onto a single object.

6.15.8    From tree-level to modular homotopy theory
The constructions of this chapter are tree-level: the bar differential is indexed by collisions on a single smooth
curve, and the operadic compositions are indexed by planar rooted trees. Three levels of homotopy-algebraic
structure emerge as one opens the genus filtration.
Deﬁnition 6.15.9 (Tree-level operadic homotopy theory). A tree-level operadic homotopy theory for a cyclic
operad 𝑃 is an ∞-category H with homotopy-coherent 𝑃 -action: operations 𝑚𝑇 indexed by 𝑃 -decorated
rooted trees 𝑇 , satisfying the operadic master equation 𝑇 𝑚𝑇 = 0 up to coherent homotopies. The
                                                         P
bar-cobar constructions of this chapter produce such a theory for 𝑃 = Comch or 𝑃 = Assch .
Deﬁnition 6.15.10 (Modular homotopy theory, abstract). A modular homotopy theory for a modular op-
erad 𝑀 is an ∞-category H with homotopy-coherent 𝑀 -action: operations 𝑚Γ indexed by 𝑀 -decorated
stable graphs Γ (graphs with genus labels 𝑔𝑣 at each vertex, satisfying 𝑣 𝑔𝑣 + 𝑏1 ( Γ) = 𝑔 ), compatible with
                                                                       P
separating and nonseparating clutching (Definition 2.5.1).
Remark 6.15.11 (The formal step is small; the existence problem is hard). Replacing rooted trees by stable
graphs is the only combinatorial change from tree-level to modular homotopy theory. The formal gen-
eralization is immediate. What is not immediate is existence: constructing the operations 𝑚Γ for graphs
with loops requires integration over M 𝑔,𝑛 , which produces curvature ( 𝑑fib2 ≠ 0) and demands the full

Maurer–Cartan package Θ A . This is the content of Chapter 8.
362                                                          Chapter 6. Bar and cobar constructions


      In Chapter 8, the curve itself varies over M 𝑔 , and the bar differential acquires curvature: the genus- 𝑔
                ( 𝑔)
correction 𝑚0 is a section of the obstruction sheaf on M 𝑔 , controlled by a single universal Maurer–Cartan
class Θ A . The passage from this chapter to the next is the passage from operadic to modular Koszul duality
–- from the combinatorics of associahedra to the geometry of the Deligne–Mumford compactification
–- or, in the language of the categorical logarithm, the passage from the single-valued to the multi-valued
regime.

7.1    The circularity problem
Problem 7.1.1 (Independent construction of Koszul dual). In defining chiral Koszul duality, we face a circular
definition issue:
   Claim.
                                              𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) ≃ A2!
    The circularity. The dual A2! is typically ‘‘defined’’ as the Koszul dual cooperad–-but no independent
construction as a chiral coalgebra has been given, no first-principles proof that the bar construction defines
a dg coalgebra that is this dual exists, and for non-quadratic cases the classical orthogonality criterion
𝑅1 ⊥ 𝑅2 does not apply.
    What is needed. An intrinsic definition of A2! using only A2 ; a proof that A2! is inherently a coalgebra;
a geometric identification of 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) with this dual; and an extension to non-quadratic and curved cases
via nilpotent completion.

7.3       Verdier duality on configuration spaces
Setup 7.3.1 (Conﬁguration space duality). Let 𝑋 be a smooth curve (or more generally, an 𝑛-dimensional
manifold). The configuration space of 𝑘 points is:

                             𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) = {( 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑘 ) ∈ 𝑋 𝑘 : 𝑧 𝑖 ≠ 𝑧𝑗 for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 }

   Its Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) is a smooth manifold with corners, with boundary
divisors parametrizing collision patterns.

Remark 7.3.3 (Algebraic vs. analytic Verdier duality). Theorem 7.3.2 uses ‘‘Verdier duality’’ in two senses
that must be carefully distinguished:
  (i) Algebraic (D-module) Verdier duality. The functor 𝔻alg = RH 𝑜𝑚 (−, 𝜔𝐶 [dim]) acts on holo-
                                                                                        𝑘
      nomic D-modules on 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑋 ). It exchanges 𝑗! and 𝑗∗ extensions (Lemma 6.3.9). This is the sense
      used in Definition 6.3.6 to construct the cobar complex intrinsically.
              Chapter 7. Non-abelian Poincaré duality and the construction of Koszul dual
366                                                                            cooperads


  (ii) Analytic (Borel–Moore) Verdier duality. On the real manifold underlying 𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ), Poincaré–
       Lefschetz duality identifies 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶 𝑘 ) with 𝐻𝑐𝑑 −∗ ( 𝐶𝑘 ), realized concretely by the integration pairing
       of logarithmic forms against distributional currents.
The bridge between (1) and (2) is the Riemann–Hilbert correspondence: applying the de Rham functor
to holonomic D-modules produces constructible sheaves, and the algebraic duality 𝔻alg becomes the
topological Verdier duality on constructible complexes [195]. See Theorem 6.3.10 for the analytic realization
as a consequence of the algebraic statement.

Example 7.3.5 (Heisenberg specialization). For the Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 with generator 𝐽 ( 𝑧 ), The-
orem 7.3.4 reduces to: the residue Res 𝑧1 =𝑧2 𝐽 ( 𝑧1 ) 𝐽 ( 𝑧2 ) 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) = 𝑘 on the bar side is dual to

Remark 7.3.6 (Analytic framework). The computation above is formal: the expression 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )
is not well-defined as a pointwise product of distributions, since 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) has a singularity
precisely at the support of 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ). The correct framework is Verdier duality as a functor on constructible
sheaves (see [154, Exposé XVIII]): the pairing is defined at the level of the derived category 𝐷 𝑐𝑏 ( 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑋 )) via
the proper push-forward theorem, not by pointwise multiplication. The formula above is a shorthand for
the sheaf-theoretic adjunction, and the passage from line 1 to line 2 is justified by the localization triangle
for the pair ( 𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) , 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ) rather than by literal integration of a distribution against a singular function.

7.4.1      Verification of coalgebra axioms
Theorem 7.4.3 (Coalgebra structure via NAP; [proved]). The construction of A ! via Verdier duality
yields a well-defined conilpotent chiral coalgebra:
   (i) Coassociativity: ( Δ ⊗ id) ◦ Δ = (id ⊗ Δ) ◦ Δ.
  (ii) Counit: ( 𝜖 ⊗ id) ◦ Δ = id = (id ⊗ 𝜖 ) ◦ Δ.
 (iii) Coderivation (graded): Δ ( 𝑑 ( 𝑐 )) = 𝑑 ( 𝑐 (1) ) ⊗ 𝑐 (2) + (−1) | 𝑐 (1) | 𝑐 (1) ⊗ 𝑑 ( 𝑐 (2) ).
                                            P

 (iv) Conilpotency: For each 𝜙∗ ∈ A ! , there exists 𝑁 such that Δ ( 𝑁 ) ( 𝜙∗ ) = 0.

Proof via geometric stratiﬁcations. Part 1: Coassociativity.
   The coproduct Δ : A ! → A ! ⊗ A ! arises from the geometric map:
                                                [
                                  𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) →          𝐶| 𝐼 | ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶| 𝐽 | ( 𝑋 )

   The composition ( Δ ⊗ id) ◦ Δ corresponds to:

                                    𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝐶 | 𝐼 | ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶 | 𝐽 | ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶 | 𝐾 | ( 𝑋 )

for 𝐼 ⊔ 𝐽 ⊔ 𝐾 = [ 𝑘 ].
   This is manifestly independent of how we bracket the split ( 𝐼 ⊔ 𝐽 ) ⊔ 𝐾 vs. 𝐼 ⊔ ( 𝐽 ⊔ 𝐾 ), giving
coassociativity.
    Part 2: Counit property.

   The counit 𝜖 : A ! → 𝜔 𝑋 corresponds to the projection:

                                                 𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝑋

selecting a single point (say, the first).
    The composition ( 𝜖 ⊗ id) ◦ Δ corresponds to:
                               Δ                          𝜖 ×id
                     𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) −
                              → 𝐶1 ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶𝑘 −1 ( 𝑋 ) −−−→ 𝑋 × 𝐶𝑘 −1 ( 𝑋 )  𝐶𝑘 −1 ( 𝑋 )

   This is the identity on 𝐶𝑘 −1 ( 𝑋 ), verifying the counit axiom.
   Part 3: Coderivation property.
   The coproduct Δ on A ! is the Verdier dual of the chiral product on A:

                                              Δ : A! → A! ⊗ A!

   Geometrically, this corresponds to:

                                       𝑑 : 𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑋 ) →

where 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 is the collision divisor.
  The coderivation property:
                                        Δ ◦ 𝑑 = ( 𝑑 ⊗ id + id ⊗ 𝑑 ) ◦ Δ
   follows from the identity:

               (split then collide) = (collide then split on left) + (collide then split on right)

    This is the combinatorial identity for configuration space strata, which holds because boundary divisors
satisfy:                                                     [
                                            𝜕 ( 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑋 )) =   𝐷𝜎

with compatible orientations.
    Part 4: Conilpotency.
    The chiral coalgebra A ! is conilpotent because it inherits a weight grading from the conformal weight
grading on A. Since A is graded by conformal weight with finite-dimensional graded pieces, A ! inherits a
dual weight grading. The coproduct strictly increases total weight, so the iterated coproduct Δ ( 𝑁 ) vanishes
on elements of weight ≤ 𝑁 .
    This can also be seen from the bar construction perspective: once Theorem 7.5.1 identifies A ! ≃ 𝐵¯ ch (A),
conilpotency is manifest because 𝐵¯ ch (A) is filtered by bar degree and the coproduct (deconcatenation)
strictly increases the number of tensor factors, ensuring Δ ( 𝑁 ) = 0 on bar degree ≤ 𝑁 .

strata { 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 }. The precise formulation requires working with D-modules or perverse sheaves
on 𝐶3 ( 𝑋 ) rather than literal products of delta distributions (the naive products 𝛿 ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) 𝛿 ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ),
𝛿 ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) 𝛿 ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ), 𝛿 ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) 𝛿 ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) are each well-defined as distributions on ℂ3 , but they are all
supported on the full diagonal { 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 = 𝑧3 } and sum to 3𝛿123 ≠ 0, so the Arnold relation is not preserved
by naive Verdier duality at the level of distributions). The correct dual statement is that the Verdier dual of
the Arnold relation, viewed as a relation in 𝐻 2 ( 𝐶3 ( 𝑋 )), yields the corresponding relation in the homology
𝐻2𝑛−2 of the Borel–Moore compactification.

𝑅𝑗∗ (Theorem 7.3.2), identifying logarithmic forms on the compactification with distributional forms on

the level of differential forms, since residues (bar operations) and delta functions (cobar operations) are
Verdier duals.

8.2.2.2 Distributions vs. differential forms: the dual picture
While the bar complex uses differential forms on compactified configuration spaces, the cobar complex
uses distributions on open configuration spaces. This duality is the distributional manifestation of the
intrinsic Verdier-dual definition (Definition 6.3.6); see Theorem 6.3.10 for the precise identification.

8.2.3      Bar-cobar exchange
8.2.3.1 Chain/cochain level precision
Theorem 8.2.18 (Chain-level vs. homology-level structure; [proved]). Let (A , { 𝑚𝑘 }) be an 𝐴∞
chiral algebra.
   (i) Chain level. The full 𝐴∞ structure { 𝑚𝑘 } 𝑘 ≥1 is preserved, all operations are computable via configu-
       ration space integrals, and homotopies have geometric meaning as forms on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).
  (ii) Homology level. The homotopy transfer theorem (Appendix K) produces a minimal 𝐴∞ structure
       { 𝑚𝑘𝐻 } on 𝐻 ∗ (A) with 𝑚1𝐻 = 0. The product 𝑚2𝐻 descends to homology (it is strictly associative
       if A is formal). However, the transferred higher operations 𝑚𝑘𝐻 for 𝑘 ≥ 3 are in general non-trivial:
       they are the Massey products, encoding obstructions to formality.
 (iii) What is lost. The explicit chain-level homotopies { ℎ𝑛 } (the contracting data) are lost in the passage
       to homology. For a Koszul algebra, formality ensures 𝑚𝑘𝐻 = 0 for 𝑘 ≥ 3; for a non-Koszul algebra,
       the 𝑚𝑘𝐻 carry essential information that cannot be recovered from 𝑚2𝐻 alone.

Proof. Step 1: Construction of the SDR. The bar complex B̄(A) is a chain complex of D 𝑋 -modules, graded
by bar degree 𝑛 and conformal weight ℎ. Since we work over a field (Convention 2.9.1), the splitting lemma
(Lemma K.2.3) furnishes a strong deformation retract:
                              𝑝
          ( B̄(A) , 𝑑bar )            ( 𝐻 ∗ ( B̄(A)) , 0)          ℎ : B̄𝑛 → B̄𝑛−1 ,         id − 𝜄 𝑝 = 𝑑bar ℎ + ℎ 𝑑bar .
                              𝜄

The SDR is constructed by choosing, at each conformal weight ℎ, a complement to ker( 𝑑 ) in B̄ℎ : de-
                                           ∼
compose B̄ℎ = 𝐻ℎ ⊕ 𝐵 ℎ ⊕ 𝐶ℎ where 𝑑 : 𝐶ℎ − → 𝐵 ℎ is an isomorphism (boundaries and ‘‘extra cycles’’).
Then:
• 𝜄 : 𝐻ℎ ↩→ B̄ℎ includes the harmonic representatives;
• 𝑝 : B̄ℎ ↠ 𝐻ℎ projects along 𝐵 ℎ ⊕ 𝐶ℎ ;
• ℎ : 𝐵 ℎ → 𝐶ℎ is the inverse of 𝑑 | 𝐶ℎ , and ℎ | 𝐻ℎ = ℎ | 𝐶ℎ = 0.

The side conditions 𝑝𝜄 = id, ℎ2 = 0, 𝑝ℎ = 0, ℎ𝜄 = 0 follow immediately.
  Step 2: Transferred operations via the tree formula. The homotopy transfer theorem (Theorem K.2.1,
Construction K.3.1) produces 𝐴∞ operations { 𝑚𝑘𝐻 } on 𝐻 ∗ ( B̄(A)) given by:

(Kadeishvili [180]; Construction K.3.1).
   Step 3: Chain level vs. homology level. At chain level, the associator satisfies:

                                𝑚2 ( 𝑚2 ⊗ id) − 𝑚2 (id ⊗ 𝑚2 ) = 𝑑bar ( ℎ3 ) + 𝑚3 ,

where ℎ3 is the associating homotopy. In homology, 𝑑bar ( ℎ3 ) = 0, so [ 𝑚2 ] is strictly associative: the
homotopy ℎ3 is lost. The obstruction transfers to the Massey product 𝑚3𝐻 via (8.5). For 𝑘 ≥ 4, the tree
formula produces 𝑚𝑘𝐻 from 𝐶𝑘 planar binary trees (e.g., 𝐶4 = 5 trees for 𝑚4𝐻 ; see Computation 29.5.9 for
the Virasoro case).
    Step 4: Vanishing for Koszul algebras. If A is Koszul, the bar spectral sequence concentrates 𝐻 ∗ ( B̄(A))
on a single line (Corollary 9.1.36). The SDR may then be chosen compatible with the bigrading, so that ℎ
preserves bar degree and shifts internal (conformal weight) degree. Every tree with 𝑛 ≥ 3 leaves contributing
to 𝑚𝑛𝐻 would produce an operation of bidegree incompatible with the Koszul line, forcing 𝑚𝑛𝐻 = 0. Thus,
for Koszul A, the minimal model has only 𝑚2𝐻 and is strictly associative. (This vanishing is weaker than
formality in the sense of Deligne–Griffiths–Morgan–Sullivan.)

   Commutative side.

      Lie side.

• Higher 𝑚𝑘 encode coherent homotopies (generally non-trivial)
• Non-trivial 𝐴∞ structure (contrast with Com)

                                       Lie

      The difference in these compactifications determines the 𝐴∞ structure.

8.2.7.4 Example: 𝛽 𝛾 system deformation
Proposition 8.2.37 ( 𝛽 𝛾 deformations; [proved]). The 𝛽𝛾 system admits a 1-parameter family of

with residue along the diagonal, deforms the stress tensor by 𝑇 ↦→ 𝑇 + 𝑡 𝜕 ( 𝛽𝛾 ). This shifts the conformal
weights of 𝛽 and 𝛾 by +𝑡 and −𝑡 respectively (since [ 𝐿0 , 𝛽 ] = (1+𝑡 ) 𝛽 and [ 𝐿0 , 𝛾 ] = −𝑡 𝛾 in the deformed
algebra), while preserving the 𝛽𝛾 OPE (which has only a simple pole, unaffected by the contact deforma-
tion). The MC equation 𝑑𝛼 + 21 [ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] = 0 is satisfied because 𝜔contact is closed on 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ) and the bracket
[ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] = 0 vanishes (the 𝛽𝛾 system is abelian at the level of the deformation, since 𝜔contact ∈ 𝐻 1 ( 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ))
is one-dimensional and any 1-form squares to zero in the Lie bracket).

of 𝐾6 are products 𝐾𝑖 × 𝐾𝑗 with 𝑖 + 𝑗 = 7, and each such stratum contributes a composition 𝑚𝑖 ◦𝑘 𝑚𝑗 .
The signs are determined by the Koszul sign rule on desuspended generators as in the general case.

8.3.5    Interpretation
8.3.5.1 Algebraic meaning
The commutation relation [ 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑎𝑛∗ ] = 𝜅𝑚𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0 is an algebraic property of the Heisenberg vertex algebra
and does not change with genus. What the genus 2 geometry modifies is the bar complex differential: the
propagator’s regular part introduces new terms in the bar differential, giving rise to a curved 𝐴∞ structure
with curvature 𝑚0 ≠ 0 controlled by Siegel modular forms:

                                  𝑚0(2) = 𝜅 2 𝑐4 · 𝐸4 ( Ω) + 𝑐6 · 𝐸6 ( Ω) + · · ·
                                                                                     

where 𝑐4 , 𝑐6 are computable constants depending on the normalization of the bar complex.
8.3.5.2 Geometric meaning
The Eisenstein series 𝐸4 , 𝐸6 generate 𝑀∗ ( Γ2 ) and arise as Chern classes of tautological bundles on M2 .
The genus-2 bar complex 𝐶•(2) (A) is a sheaf on M2 ; pulling back along M2,2 → M2 gives the OPE
corrections.
8.3.5.3 Physical meaning
In CFT, 𝑍 2 = M |det Im Ω | − 𝑐 /2 , ⟨ 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎∗ ( 𝑤 )⟩2 ∝ | 𝐸 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 )| −2Δ , and the OPE is the operator limit
                ∫
                   2
𝑧 → 𝑤 of this correlator.
   The 𝐸4 , 𝐸6 terms are two-loop quantum corrections to the bar complex curvature, appearing in the regular
part of the propagator and manifesting as curved 𝐴∞ structure.

8.3.6    Generalization to higher weight operators
8.3.6.1 Virasoro at genus 2
The Virasoro OPE 𝑇 ( 𝑧 )𝑇 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ ( 𝑧 𝑐−/2𝑤 ) 4 + (2𝑧𝑇−(𝑤𝑤))2 + 𝜕𝑇𝑧 −(𝑤𝑤 ) is genus-independent (the pole orders are
fixed by ℎ𝑇 = 2). At genus 2, the two-point correlation function acquires modular corrections:

                                                        𝑐 /2
                              ⟨𝑇 ( 𝑧 )𝑇 ( 𝑤 )⟩2 =             + 𝑓 ( Ω) + 𝑂 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )
                                                    ( 𝑧 − 𝑤)4

where 𝑓 ( Ω) = 𝑐 · 𝐸4 ( Ω) + · · · is a regular function encoding the genus 2 geometry. In the bar complex,
these corrections contribute to the curvature 𝑚0(2) and to the higher operations 𝑚𝑘(2) .
8.3.6.2 𝑊 -algebras at genus 2
Following Arakawa’s theory, the genus- 𝑔 correlation functions of a 𝑊 -algebra with generators 𝑊 ( 𝑘 )
of weight 𝑘 involve Siegel modular forms 𝐶𝑗( 𝑘 ) ( Ω) depending on the period matrix Ω ∈ H 𝑔 . The OPE
singularity structure (pole orders ≤ 2𝑘 ) remains genus-independent, but the correlation functions’ regular
parts depend on Ω.
    The pattern: genus 𝑔 introduces Siegel modular forms of weight ≤ 𝑔 ( 𝑔 + 1)/2, matching the dimension
of the Siegel upper half-space H 𝑔 (not M 𝑔 , whose dimension is 3 𝑔 − 3; these coincide for 𝑔 ≤ 3 but differ
for 𝑔 ≥ 4 due to the Schottky problem).

8.3.8  Computational summary
To compute genus 2 corrections 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) · 𝑏 (𝑤 ) for vertex operators 𝑎, 𝑏 :
   (i) Draw all 2-loop Feynman diagrams with external legs at 𝑧, 𝑤 .
  (ii) Assign the genus-2 propagator 𝐺Σ2 ( 𝑧 𝑖 , 𝑧𝑗 ) to each internal line.
 (iii) Integrate over Σ2 using theta function identities and residues.
 (iv) Regularize via the holomorphic anomaly equation and minimal subtraction.
  (v) Integrate over M2 by expanding in Eisenstein series.
 (vi) Extract the OPE by taking the 𝑧 → 𝑤 limit and expanding in ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) − 𝑘 .
The corrections are proportional to 𝜅 2 𝐸2𝑘 ( Ω).

8.3.9    Connection to string theory
The genus-2 OPE corrections have a string-theoretic interpretation: Σ2 is the worldsheet, the amplitude
⟨𝑉𝑎 ( 𝑧 )𝑉𝑎∗ ( 𝑤 )⟩Σ2 is the genus-2 string amplitude, the OPE is the factorization limit 𝑧 → 𝑤 , and the
Eisenstein series arise from summing over intermediate states.
Remark 8.3.2 (Formality). The genus-2 bar-cobar complex realizes the formality theorem: the induced
★-product is the quantization of the classical OPE Poisson structure, with corrections given by Eisenstein
series (a consequence of 𝐸2 collapse on the Koszul locus; see Proposition 8.17.12).
Remark 8.3.3 (Higher genera). At genus 𝑔 ≥ 3, modular forms of weight ≤ 𝑔 ( 𝑔 + 1)/2 appear, with
relations from gluing equations along boundary strata of M 𝑔 . All structures are determined by genus-
0 data and modular invariance (Witten; see Remark 8.0.5 for the precise reformulation in terms of the
parameter-source chain).

8.4     The fundamental theorem: genus-zero base case
Remark 8.4.1 (Summary of Theorem A –- see Theorem 9.1.39). The genus-zero bar-cobar duality
(Theorem 9.1.39, Chapter 9) establishes: for a chiral Koszul pair (A1 , A2 ) (Definition 9.1.14), the unit
and counit of the bar-cobar adjunction are quasi-isomorphisms, and the bar functor is intertwined with
Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 ). The counit is a quasi-isomorphism only on the Koszul locus; off this locus it
persists in the completed coderived category.

Remark 8.4.6 (Origin of the shift by 2). The uniform shift [2] in (8.6) arises from the bigraded structure of

8.5     Higher-genus configuration spaces
8.5.1   The genus stratification philosophy
Remark 8.5.1 (Genus as quantum number). The genus 𝑔 organizes corrections: genus 0 is classical ( 𝑑 (0)2 =
0 exactly), genus 1 produces central extensions, and genus 𝑔 ≥ 2 introduces modular structures.
   This parallels the loop expansion in quantum field theory:
                                   𝑍 = 𝑍 tree + ℏ 𝑍 1-loop + ℏ2 𝑍 2-loop + · · ·
with 𝑔 playing the role of loop number.

8.5.2   Configuration spaces at arbitrary genus
Deﬁnition 8.5.2 (Higher-genus conﬁguration space). Let Σ 𝑔 be a closed Riemann surface of genus 𝑔 . The
𝑛-point configuration space is:
                           𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) = {( 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 ) ∈ Σ𝑛𝑔 : 𝑝 𝑖 ≠ 𝑝𝑗 for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 }

    The Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) (Theorem 5.1.29) is constructed by iteratively
blowing up all diagonals Δ 𝐼 = { 𝑝 𝑖 = 𝑝𝑗 : 𝑖, 𝑗 ∈ 𝐼 }, adding exceptional divisors 𝐷 𝐼 with normal crossing
structure, and extending to stable pointed curves when points collide.
    The boundary stratification consists of:
• Collision divisors: 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 where 𝑝 𝑖 → 𝑝𝑗 on the same component
                           sep
• Separating divisors: 𝐷 𝐼 | 𝐽 where Σ 𝑔 → Σ 𝑔1 ⊔ 𝑝∗ Σ 𝑔2 with 𝑔1 + 𝑔2 = 𝑔
• Non-separating divisors: 𝐷 non𝛾 where a cycle 𝛾 ∈ 𝐻1 ( Σ 𝑔 ) is pinched
Remark 8.5.3 (Dimension count). The configuration space has complex dimension:
                                       dimℂ 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) = 𝑛 · dim Σ 𝑔 = 𝑛
However, we must account for the moduli:
                                          dimℂ M 𝑔,𝑛 = 3 𝑔 − 3 + 𝑛

The universal family over M 𝑔 with fiber 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) has total dimension (3 𝑔 − 3) + 𝑛, which equals dim M 𝑔,𝑛 .
Indeed, M 𝑔,𝑛 can be identified with this universal configuration space.

8.5.3   The moduli space M 𝑔,𝑛
Deﬁnition 8.5.4 (Deligne–Mumford compactiﬁcation). The moduli space M 𝑔,𝑛 parametrizes stable 𝑛-
pointed curves of genus 𝑔 :
                                   [ Σ 𝑔 ; 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 ] ∈ M 𝑔,𝑛
where stability requires Σ 𝑔 to be a connected nodal curve with 2 𝑔𝑖 − 2 + 𝑛𝑖 > 0 on every component 𝐶𝑖
and finite automorphism group.
8.5. Higher-genus configuration spaces                                                                    405


Theorem 8.5.5 (Structure of M 𝑔 ,𝑛 [143, 144]; [proved]). The Deligne–Mumford compactification
satisfies:
  (i) M 𝑔,𝑛 is a proper Deligne–Mumford stack of dimension 3 𝑔 − 3 + 𝑛
 (ii) The interior M 𝑔,𝑛 parametrizes smooth curves (smooth Riemann surfaces)
 (iii) The boundary 𝜕 M 𝑔,𝑛 is a normal crossing divisor
 (iv) Each boundary stratum corresponds to a dual graph Γ

Proof. By Deligne–Mumford [143] and Knudsen [144]: (1) Properness follows from stable reduction: any
family of smooth curves over a punctured disk extends uniquely to a stable curve over the closed disk. (2) The
interior M 𝑔,𝑛 is smooth, with local coordinates provided by Teichmüller theory (quadratic differentials).
(3) Boundary strata correspond to degenerations: separating nodes ( Σ 𝑔 → Σ 𝑔1 ∪ Σ 𝑔2 ) and non-separating
nodes (pinching a cycle), classified by dual graphs Γ. (4) Local models near boundary divisors are products
of smooth divisors, giving normal crossing structure [144].

8.5.4    Fibration structure
Theorem 8.5.6 (Universal curve fibration [144]; [proved]). There exists a universal curve:

                                              𝜋 : C 𝑔,𝑛+1 → M 𝑔,𝑛

such that:
• The fiber over [( Σ 𝑔 ; 𝑝1 , . . . , 𝑝𝑛 )] is Σ 𝑔 with 𝑛 marked points removed
• Sections 𝜎𝑖 : M 𝑔,𝑛 → C 𝑔,𝑛+1 give the marked points
• The relative dualizing sheaf 𝜔𝜋 = 𝜔 C 𝑔,𝑛+1 /M 𝑔,𝑛 is relatively ample
   The configuration space sits in this fibration:
                                                         (𝑛)
                                         𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) ⊂ C 𝑔,𝑛+1 → M 𝑔,𝑛

where the superscript ( 𝑛) denotes the 𝑛-fold fiber product over M 𝑔,𝑛 .

Remark 8.5.10 (Summary of the genus-2 case). The pattern is universal: the holomorphic cyclic sum vanishes
by the Fay identity (Step 1), the non-holomorphic correction produces the Arakelov form (Step 2), and
cross-terms cancel by type. The only genus-dependent input is the period matrix Ω ∈ ℌ 𝑔 .

General case 𝑔 ≥ 3. The proof follows the same three-step strategy as the genus-2 case, using the Fay trise-
cant identity at arbitrary genus.

Proof via spectral sequence. Consider the Leray spectral sequence for the universal configuration space
fibration:
                                           𝜋 : C 𝑔,𝑛 → M 𝑔
where C 𝑔,𝑛 is the relative Fulton–MacPherson compactification of 𝑛 points on the universal curve over M 𝑔 .
The fiber over [ Σ 𝑔 ] ∈ M 𝑔 is 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ).
    Step 1: Fiberwise differential. On each fiber 𝐶 𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ), the differential 𝑑 (0) is the genus-zero bar differential
using residues at collision divisors. By Theorem 6.2.27, ( 𝑑 (0) ) 2 = 0.
    Step 2: Base contributions. The differential 𝑑 (1) arises from the Gauss–Manin connection on the local
system 𝑅 𝑞 𝜋∗ (A ⊠𝑛 ⊗ Ω∗log ) over M 𝑔 . The compatibility { 𝑑 (0) , 𝑑 (1) } = 0 follows from flatness of the
Gauss–Manin connection (Stokes’ theorem applied fiberwise).
    Step 3: Higher corrections. Terms 𝑑 ( 𝑘 ) for 𝑘 ≥ 2 arise from the Leray filtration: 𝑑 ( 𝑘 ) maps 𝐹 𝑝 → 𝐹 𝑝+𝑘
in the filtration by base degree. The relations ensuring 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0 (e.g., { 𝑑 (0) , 𝑑 (2) } + ( 𝑑 (1) ) 2 = 0) follow
from the associativity of the Leray filtration and the exactness of the total complex.

8.8      Genus 1: the elliptic bar complex
8.8.1       Motivation: where quantum corrections begin
At genus 0, the bar differential satisfies 𝑑02 = 0 exactly, the propagator is the rational function ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −1 ,
and there are no moduli. At genus 1, all three change: the propagator becomes the elliptic function 𝜃 1′ ( 𝑧 −
𝑤 | 𝜏 )/ 𝜃 1 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 | 𝜏 ), the modular parameter 𝜏 parametrizes a one-dimensional moduli space, and the fiber-
wise differential acquires curvature 𝑑fib   2 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 proportional to the central charge. This single step –-
                                                         1
from genus 0 to genus 1 –- is the birth of the modular theory.
   In the language of Remark 6.0.1: at genus 0 the logarithm 𝜂 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) is single-valued and
nilpotence is exact; at genus 1 the logarithm 𝑑 log 𝜃 1 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 | 𝜏 ) acquires monodromy 2 𝜋 𝑖 around the 𝐵 -
cycle (since 𝜃 1 ( 𝑧 + 𝜏 | 𝜏 ) = −𝑒 − 𝜋 𝑖𝜏 −2𝜋 𝑖 𝑧 𝜃 1 ( 𝑧 | 𝜏 )), and this monodromy is the exponential of the nilpotence
defect 𝜅 · 𝜔1 . The birth of the modular theory is the birth of non-trivial monodromy of the categorical
logarithm.

Theorem 8.8.12 (Nilpotency at genus 1; [proved]). For the Heisenberg algebra on 𝐸𝜏 , we saw in §1.7

   The genus-1 differential satisfies:

  (ii) Genus-1 corrections (from 𝐸2 )

Proof. Write 𝐷1 = 𝑑𝑟 + 𝑑𝑒 + 𝑑𝑚 for the residue, elliptic, and modular components. Expanding

({ 𝑑𝑟 , 𝑑𝑒 }, { 𝑑𝑟 , 𝑑𝑚 }, { 𝑑𝑒 , 𝑑𝑚 }).
     Term 1: 𝑑𝑟2 = 0. The residue differential 𝑑𝑟 at genus 1 extracts residues at the collision divisors of
𝐶 𝑝+1 ( 𝐸𝜏 ), exactly as at genus 0. The proof of Theorem 6.2.27 applies verbatim: disjoint pairs anticommute,
overlapping pairs cancel by the Borcherds identity (which is a property of the chiral algebra, not of the
curve), and repeated pairs give Res2𝐷 𝑖𝑗 = 0.
     Term 2: 𝑑𝑒2 = 0. The elliptic differential 𝑑𝑒 acts via the Weierstrass 𝜁 -function 𝜁 ( 𝑧 | 𝜏 ) =
𝜗1′ ( 𝑧 | 𝜏 )/ 𝜗1 ( 𝑧 | 𝜏 ), which is the genus-1 propagator. The operator 𝑑𝑒 is a D-module endomorphism:
it multiplies by 𝜁 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 | 𝜏 ) 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 and sums over pairs. Since 𝑑𝑒 acts by multiplication by a 1-form on
configuration space, 𝑑𝑒2 involves the wedge product 𝜁 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 ∧ 𝜁 ( 𝑧 𝑘 − 𝑧ℓ ) 𝑑𝑧 𝑘 . For 𝑖 ≠ 𝑘 , these
anticommute and cancel in the ordered sum. For 𝑖 = 𝑘 , we get 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 ∧ 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 = 0. Hence 𝑑𝑒2 = 0.
     Term 3: 𝑑𝑚     2 = 0. The modular differential 𝑑 is proportional to 𝜕¯ = 𝜕 / 𝜕 𝜏¯ , acting on the ℂ[ 𝜏, 𝜏¯ ]

   All six terms vanish, so 𝐷12 = 0.

8.9     Genus 2
8.9.1    The genus 2 case
Remark 8.9.1 (Genus 2 vs higher genus). Genus 2 is the first case with period matrices, spin structures (16
characteristics), hyperelliptic involution, and the Schottky problem. For 𝑔 ≥ 3, the full Teichmüller theory
is needed.

   (i) 𝐸 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) is a (−1/2, −1/2) differential in ( 𝑧, 𝑤 )

Remark 8.9.7 (Computational challenge). Computing 𝐸 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) requires normalizing holomorphic differ-
entials, computing the period matrix, evaluating theta functions (convergent for Im( Ω) ≫ 0), and taking
gradients. The procedure is intensive but algorithmic.

8.10       Genus 3: beyond hyperelliptic
8.10.1     The transition at genus 3
Remark 8.10.1 (Generic vs special curves). At genus 2, every curve is hyperelliptic. At genus 3, the hyperelliptic
locus H3 ⊂ M3 has dimension 2 𝑔 − 1 = 5, while dim M3 = 3 𝑔 − 3 = 6, so the generic genus-3 curve is
not hyperelliptic. By Noether’s theorem, a generic genus-3 curve is a smooth plane quartic, canonically
embedded in ℙ2 . For 𝑔 ≥ 3, the hyperelliptic locus has codimension 𝑔 − 2 in M 𝑔 .
   For the bar complex, this means genus-2 propagators can be expressed via the Weierstrass ℘-function,
whereas genus 3 requires the full theta function machinery on Jac( Σ3 ) = ℂ3 /Λ.

(Riemann’s bitangent theorem).

8.11     The genus spectral sequence
The genus-by-genus bar complexes assemble into a single spectral sequence whose 𝐸1 page is the genus-
stratified bar cohomology, whose differentials are the clutching maps along boundary divisors of M 𝑔 , and
whose 𝐸∞ page computes the full chiral homology. The collapse page depends on the family: 𝐸1 for Kac–
Moody (by CE acyclicity of the associated graded); 𝐸2 for Virasoro and W-algebras (the DS reduction
of the 𝐸1 -collapsed KM spectral sequence introduces one additional differential from the BRST operator
𝑄DS , shifting the collapse by one page; see Theorem 12.11.1).

8.12       Moduli space cohomology and quantum obstructions
8.12.1     Cohomology of M 𝑔,𝑛
Theorem 8.12.1 (Mumford–Morita–Miller classes [150]; [proved]). The cohomology ring
𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 , ℚ) is generated by:
  (i) Tautological classes:
         • 𝜆𝑖 ∈ 𝐻 2𝑖 (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) (Chern classes of Hodge bundle)
         • 𝜓𝑖 ∈ 𝐻 2 (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) (first Chern classes of cotangent lines at marked points)
         • [ Δ 𝐼 ] ∈ 𝐻 2 (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) (boundary divisor classes, codimension 1)
  (ii) Generators in low genus:

                                      𝐻 ∗ (M 0,𝑛 ) = ℚ[ 𝜓1 , . . . , 𝜓𝑛 ]/(relations)
                                       𝐻 ∗ (M 1,1 ) = ℚ[ 𝜆1 ]/( 𝜆12 )
                                        𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 ) ⊃ ℚ[ 𝜆1 , . . . , 𝜆 𝑔 ] for 𝑔 ≥ 2

Remark 8.12.2 (Provenance and citation). This theorem is imported and treated as [proved]. Standard
descriptions of tautological generators and low-genus cohomology structure for M 𝑔,𝑛 are classical in the

8.13.5  Verification: obstruction squares to zero
Theorem 8.13.9 (Nilpotence of obstruction ( 𝑔 ≤ 2); [proved]). For any augmented chiral algebra A
and genus 𝑔 ≤ 2, the genus- 𝑔 obstruction satisfies:

                                    (obs 𝑔 ) 2 = 0     in 𝐻 4 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑔 (A) , 𝑍 (A))

   This is a consistency condition ensuring the curved 𝐴∞ structure is well-defined.

Proof. For 𝑔 ≤ 2, nilpotence follows from dimensional vanishing. By Theorem 8.13.16, obs 𝑔 is proportional
to the Hodge class 𝜆 𝑔 , which lies in 𝐻 2 𝑔 (M 𝑔 , ℚ) (Table 8.1). The cup product (obs 𝑔 ) 2 therefore lies in
𝐻 4 𝑔 (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A) ⊗2 ). Since dimℝ M 𝑔 = 6 𝑔 − 6, this cohomology group vanishes whenever 4 𝑔 > 6 𝑔 − 6,
i.e., when 𝑔 < 3. Case by case: 𝑔 = 0: obs0 = 0 by convention (the genus-0 bar complex has no curvature),
so (obs0 ) 2 = 0; 𝑔 = 1: (obs1 ) 2 ∈ 𝐻 4 (M 1 ), but dimℝ M 1 = 2, so 𝐻 4 = 0; 𝑔 = 2: (obs2 ) 2 ∈ 𝐻 8 (M 2 ),
but dimℝ M 2 = 6, so 𝐻 8 = 0.

Remark 8.13.11 (Comparison with the dimensional argument). For 𝑔 ≤ 2, Theorem 8.13.9 established 𝜆2𝑔 = 0
by the weaker observation that CH2 𝑔 (M 𝑔 ) = 0 when 2 𝑔 > 3 𝑔 − 3, i.e., 𝑔 < 3. Mumford’s relation is
strictly stronger: it proves 𝜆2𝑔 = 0 for all genera, including 𝑔 = 3 (where 𝜆32 ∈ CH6 (M 3 ) with dim M 3 = 6,
so the dimensional argument fails) and all 𝑔 ≥ 4.

ch(𝔼 ⊕ 𝔼∨ ) being concentrated in degree 0, since 𝔼 ⊕ 𝔼∨ = HdR     1 has trivial Chern character. Via the New-

ton identities relating power sums to elementary symmetric functions, all 𝜆-class products are determined
by the Bernoulli-number weighted traces ch𝑘 (𝔼) = 𝐵 𝑘 · 𝜅𝑘 /𝑘 ! (where 𝜅𝑘 are the Miller–Morita–Mumford
classes), giving the full multiplicative structure of the obstruction ring.

Remark 8.13.21 (Universality principle). The factorization obs 𝑔 = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝑔 holds at the cohomology-class

Corollary 8.13.22 (Additivity of the obstruction coefficient; [proved]). For Koszul chiral algebras
A, B such that A ⊗ B is Koszul:

                                        𝜅 (A ⊗ B) = 𝜅 (A) + 𝜅 (B) .

In particular, obs 𝑔 (A ⊗ B) = obs 𝑔 (A) + obs 𝑔 (B) for all 𝑔 ≥ 1.

Proof. The singular part of the OPE of A ⊗ B is the sum of the singular parts of A and B (the tensor
product acts on disjoint sets of fields). The genus-1 curvature, which determines 𝜅 by Theorem 8.13.16, is
therefore additive. Since the Faber–Pandharipande integral 𝜆FP 𝑔 is linear in 𝜅 , the factorization (8.14) gives
obs 𝑔 (A ⊗ B) = ( 𝜅 (A) + 𝜅 (B)) · 𝜆 𝑔 = obs 𝑔 (A) + obs 𝑔 (B).

Example 8.13.23. For a rank- 𝑑 lattice vertex algebra 𝑉Λ = H1⊗ 𝑑 , additivity gives 𝜅 (𝑉Λ ) = 𝑑 · 𝜅 (H1 ) = 𝑑 ,
confirming the Master Table entry (Table 27.1). For the 𝑏𝑐 – 𝛽𝛾 system, 𝜅 ( 𝑏𝑐 ⊗ 𝛽𝛾 ) = 𝑐 /2 + (−𝑐 /2) = 0
(since 𝜅 ( 𝛽𝛾 ) = −𝜅 ( 𝑏𝑐 ) by Theorem 26.7.1).

Theorem 8.13.31 (Grothendieck group of Koszul chiral algebras; [proved]). Let KCA denote the
category of Koszul chiral algebras with tensor product ⊗. The obstruction coefficient defines a group
homomorphism
                                      𝜅 : 𝐾0 (KCA, ⊗) → (ℚ, +)
from the Grothendieck group to the rationals. This homomorphism is:
   (i) Surjective: the Heisenberg family H𝜅 achieves any 𝜅 ∈ ℚ;
  (ii) Non-injective: the kernel contains all algebras at critical level (𝜅 = 0);
 (iii) Compatible with Koszul duality: for Kac–Moody algebras, 𝜅 (A ! ) = −𝜅 (A), so the Koszul involu-
       tion acts as negation on the image.

Proof. Additivity is Corollary 8.13.22. The unit 1 (trivial algebra) has 𝜅 (1) = 0. Surjectivity follows from
𝜅 (H𝑞 ) = 𝑞 for 𝑞 ∈ ℚ. Non-injectivity: the Feigin–Frenkel center 𝔷(b   𝔤− ℎ∨ ) is a non-trivial Koszul algebra
with 𝜅 = 0. Part (iii) is Theorem 8.13.16(ii).

Deﬁnition 8.13.32 (Uncurved quotient). The uncurved quotient of the category KCA is the localization

                                         KCAunc := KCA[ 𝜅 −1 (0)]

at the full subcategory of algebras with 𝜅 = 0. Objects of KCAunc are equivalence classes of Koszul chiral
algebras modulo critical-level algebras: A ∼ B if A ⊗ C ≃ B ⊗ C ′ for some C , C ′ with 𝜅 = 0. By
Theorem 8.13.31, the obstruction coefficient 𝜅 is a complete invariant on 𝐾0 (KCAunc ).

Proof via Serre duality. Step 1: Serre duality on moduli space.

                           𝐻 𝑖 (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) ∗  𝐻 3 𝑔 −3− 𝑖 (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A ! ) ⊗ 𝜔 M 𝑔 )

   Step 4: Non-degeneracy.
   The pairing is non-degenerate by Poincaré duality on M 𝑔 .
   Therefore, obstructions and deformations are mutually dual.

Proposition 8.13.36 (Obstruction lifting criterion; [proved]). A Koszul chiral algebra A at genus
𝑔 lifts to genus 𝑔 + 1 (i.e., obs 𝑔 +1 (A) = 0 in the appropriate obstruction group) if and only if 𝜅 (A) = 0.
Equivalently:
   (i) If 𝜅 ≠ 0, the bar complex has nontrivial curvature at every genus 𝑔 ≥ 1;
  (ii) If 𝜅 = 0, the bar complex is uncurved at all genera simultaneously.
There is no intermediate case: the genus-1 obstruction determines all higher-genus obstructions.
Proof. By Theorem 8.13.16, obs 𝑔 = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝑔 with 𝜆 𝑔 ≠ 0 for all 𝑔 ≥ 1 (the Hodge class is nonzero). Thus
obs 𝑔 = 0 for some 𝑔 iff 𝜅 = 0 iff obs 𝑔 = 0 for all 𝑔 .
Remark 8.13.37 (Dichotomy from the universal class). The 0/∞ dichotomy is geometric: Θ A = 𝜅 · 𝜂 ⊗ Λ
(Theorem 8.18.36) either vanishes identically or is nonzero at every genus. The MC equation couples all
genera simultaneously –- there is no mechanism for Θ to ‘‘turn off’’ at a single genus while remaining
active elsewhere. Anomaly cancellation (𝜅 = 0) is the homotopy-algebraic incarnation: the bar complex is
uncurved precisely when the universal MC element is trivial.
Remark 8.13.38 (𝜅 as Chern–Simons level). For affine Kac–Moody 𝔤      b𝑘 , the obstruction coefficient 𝜅 =
( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) 𝑑 /(2ℎ∨ ) is proportional to the shifted level 𝑡 = 𝑘 + ℎ∨ , which is the level of the associated
3d Chern–Simons theory. The genus- 𝑔 free energy 𝐹𝑔 = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝐹𝑔 𝑃 then becomes a tautological integral
over M 𝑔 weighted by the Chern–Simons level. This connects the bar-complex obstruction theory to
the Witten–Reshetikhin–Turaev invariants of 3-manifolds: the free energy 𝑔 𝐹𝑔 ℏ2 𝑔 −2 is the asymptotic

expansion of the Chern–Simons partition function on Σ 𝑔 × 𝑆 1 . The universal MC class Θb𝔤min = 2𝑡ℎ· 𝑑∨ 𝜂 ⊗ Λ

(Theorem 8.18.36) is proportional to 𝑡 = 𝑘 + ℎ∨ , the Chern–Simons level: the bar-complex curvature
is the homotopy-algebraic shadow of the Chern–Simons action, and Θ = 0 at critical level recovers the
uncurved phase where the CS partition function is topological.

8.14. The complementarity theorem                                                                            445


8.14     The complementarity theorem
8.14.1    Physical and mathematical motivation
Remark 8.14.1 (Physical perspective: Witten’s insight). In conformal field theory, consider a chiral algebra
A and compute its partition function on a genus- 𝑔 Riemann surface Σ 𝑔 :
                                                ∫
                                     𝑍 𝑔 [A] =        ⟨A⟩Σ 𝑔 · 𝑒 − 𝑆 [ Σ 𝑔 ]
                                                    M𝑔

   At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, quantum corrections split into deformations (marginal operators) and obstructions
(anomalies). The complementarity theorem asserts: what A sees as obstruction, its Koszul dual A ! sees as
deformation, and vice versa.
Remark 8.14.2 (Kodaira–Spencer action on tautological classes). The center 𝑍 (A) acts on 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 ) ( 𝜆-
classes, 𝜓 -classes, boundary classes) via the Kodaira–Spencer map 𝜌 : 𝑍 (A) → End( 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 )), and the
eigenspace decomposition gives 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ).
Remark 8.14.3 (Algebraic perspective: Grothendieck’s functoriality). Since (A ! ) ! ≃ A, any functor on
Koszul pairs must satisfy 𝐹 (A) ⊕ 𝐹 (A ! ) = universal object. The complementarity theorem identifies
this universal object as 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)): the decomposition is direct, exhaustive, and functorial.
Remark 8.14.4 (Computational perspective: Heisenberg at genus 1). For H𝜅 at genus 1: 𝐻 ∗ (M 1,1 ) = ℚ ⊕ ℚ𝜆,
𝑄1 (H𝜅 ) = ℂ · 𝜅 (central extension), 𝑄1 (H𝜅! ) = ℂ · 𝜆 (curved structure), and 𝑄1 ⊕ 𝑄1! = 𝐻 0 ⊕ 𝐻 2 = ℂ2 .

8.14.2    Statement of the theorem
Deﬁnition 8.14.5 (Deformation-obstruction complexes: H-level). Let (A , A ! ) be a chiral Koszul pair on 𝑋 .
The ambient complex at genus 𝑔 is

                                        C 𝑔 (A) := 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) ,

where Z(A) is the center local system. The Verdier involution 𝜎 acts on C 𝑔 (A) as a cochain-level en-
domorphism with 𝜎 2 = id (Theorem 6.3.32). Define the deformation-obstruction complexes as homotopy
eigenspaces:

              Q 𝑔 (A) := fib( 𝜎 − id : C 𝑔 → C 𝑔 ) ,       Q 𝑔 (A ! ) := fib( 𝜎 + id : C 𝑔 → C 𝑔 ) .      (8.18)

The cohomological shadows (S-level) are defined by:

                       𝑄 𝑔 (A) := 𝐻 ∗ (Q 𝑔 (A)) = ker( 𝜎 − id | 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A))) ,                       (8.19)
                      𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) := 𝐻 ∗ (Q 𝑔 (A ! )) = ker( 𝜎 + id | 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A))) .

Remark 8.14.6 (H/M/S layers; Convention 2.9.1). The homotopy fibers (8.18) are the H-level objects; the
explicit cochain models ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) , 𝐷 𝑔 ) are the M-level presentations; and the kernel decomposition (8.19)
is the S-level shadow. The standard involution-splitting lemma in characteristic 0 (an involution on a
complex splits it into homotopy eigenspaces whose direct sum recovers the original) makes the passage
from H to S automatic.
Lemma 8.14.7 (Involution splitting in characteristic 0; [proved]). Let 𝑉 be a cochain complex over
a field of characteristic ≠ 2, and let 𝜎 : 𝑉 → 𝑉 be a cochain involution ( 𝜎 2 = id, 𝜎 ◦ 𝑑 = 𝑑 ◦ 𝜎 ). Then:
446                                                                              Chapter 8. Higher genus


(a) The homotopy eigenspaces 𝑉 + := fib( 𝜎 − id) and 𝑉 − := fib( 𝜎 + id) split 𝑉 in the homotopy
                           ∼
    category: 𝑉 + ⊕ 𝑉 − −−→ 𝑉 .
(b) On cohomology: 𝐻 ∗ (𝑉 ) = ker( 𝜎 − id) ⊕ ker( 𝜎 + id).
(c) If ⟨−, −⟩ is a cochain-level pairing on 𝑉 with ⟨ 𝜎 𝑥, 𝜎 𝑦 ⟩ = −⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩ (anti-symmetric under 𝜎 ), then
    𝑉 + and 𝑉 − are isotropic for ⟨−, −⟩; if the pairing is non-degenerate, they are Lagrangian.
Proof. The projectors 𝑝± := 21 (id ± 𝜎 ) are cochain maps with 𝑝+ + 𝑝 − = id, ( 𝑝± ) 2 = 𝑝± , and 𝑝+ ◦ 𝑝 − =
0. Part (a): the inclusion im( 𝑝+ ) ⊕ im( 𝑝 − ) ↩→ 𝑉 is a quasi-isomorphism by direct-sum decomposition,
and im( 𝑝± ) ≃ fib( 𝜎 ∓ id) via the standard cone identification. Part (b) follows by applying 𝐻 ∗ to (a).
Part (c): for 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝑉 + we have 𝜎 𝑥 = 𝑥 , 𝜎 𝑦 = 𝑦 , so ⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩ = ⟨ 𝜎 𝑥, 𝜎 𝑦 ⟩ = −⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩, hence ⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩ = 0.
Maximality is immediate from the direct-sum decomposition.

Theorem 8.14.12 (Quantum complementarity as Lagrangian polarization; [proved]). [Regime:
curved-central (Convention 2.9.2)].
The Heisenberg complementarity of §1.12 generalizes to a Lagrangian polarization. Let (A , A ! ) be a
chiral Koszul pair on a smooth projective curve 𝑋 over ℂ, with A a sheaf of chiral algebras in the sense

H-level (homotopy). For each genus 𝑔 ≥ 0:
448                                                                         Chapter 8. Higher genus


  (i) Homotopy Lagrangian decomposition. Verdier duality induces a cochain-level pairing ⟨−, −⟩𝔻
      on C 𝑔 (A) of cohomological degree −(3 𝑔 −3), anti-symmetric under the Verdier involution 𝜎 . By

                                    C 𝑔 (A) ≃ Q 𝑔 (A) ⊕ Q 𝑔 (A ! ) ,

 (iii) Functoriality. The decomposition is natural in morphisms of Koszul pairs and compatible with the
       conformal weight and cohomological degree gradings.

Remark 8.14.13 (Elementary model presentation; Convention 2.9.2). Step B (M-level): The homotopy
eigenspace Q 𝑔 (A) = fib( 𝜎 − id) is modeled by im( 𝑝+ ) with 𝑝+ = 21 (id + 𝜎 ) on 𝐶 𝑔 = 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)).
The Lagrangian property is ⟨ 𝑝+ 𝑥, 𝑝+ 𝑦 ⟩ = 0 (Lemma 8.14.7(c)). Taking cohomology gives the S-level
decomposition H 𝑔 = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ); model independence (Proposition 6.2.52) lifts to H-level. For
the Heisenberg atom at genus 1: 𝑄 1 = 𝐻 0 , 𝑄 1! = 𝐻 2 .
Remark 8.14.14 (Comparison with literature). Beilinson–Drinfeld [2, Chapter 4] proved the 𝑔 = 0 case;
we extend to 𝑔 ≥ 1. Gui–Li–Zeng [91] (curved Koszul duality for non-quadratic operads) is applied here to
the chiral setting. Costello–Gwilliam [27] (factorization homology for TFTs) is the topological analogue
of our holomorphic construction. Arakawa [124] (W-algebra representation theory) is explained by our
complementarity at critical level.
Remark 8.14.15 (Homotopy-native formulation). The complex C 𝑔 (A) = 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) carries a (−1)-
shifted symplectic structure (PTVV [253]). The decomposition C 𝑔 ≃ Q 𝑔 (A) ⊕ Q 𝑔 (A ! ) is a Lagrangian
fibration with 𝜎 acting as anti-symplectomorphism; the tangent and obstruction complexes are Serre dual.
The S-level eigenspace decomposition is the decategorification.

8.14.3   Strategy of proof: overview
The proof has three major parts, each consisting of multiple steps:
8.14. The complementarity theorem                                                                             449


             Part I      Spectral Sequence Construction (Steps 1-4)
                         Construct spectral sequence relating bar complex to moduli space co-
                         homology
                         Show genus stratification gives filtration
                         Compute 𝐸2 page in terms of fiber cohomology
                         Identify limit 𝐸∞ with quantum corrections
             Part II     Verdier Duality on Fibers (Steps 5-6)
                         Prove Verdier duality for configuration space compactifications
                         Show duality interchanges A and A ! spectral sequences
                         Establish perfect pairing between 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )
             Part III    Decomposition and Complementarity (Steps 7-10)
                         Analyze center action on moduli space cohomology
                         Decompose into eigenspaces for 𝑍 (A) action
                         Prove direct sum property (intersection vanishes)
                         Verify exhaustion (dimension count matches)

   The proof uses the following ingredients:
• Leray spectral sequence for fibration 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) × M 𝑔 → M 𝑔
• Poincaré–Verdier duality on configuration spaces 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
• Kodaira–Spencer map relating deformations of complex structure to cohomology
• Riemann–Roch theorem for Hodge bundle on M 𝑔
• Arnold–Orlik–Solomon relations ensuring 𝑑 2 = 0
    While each ingredient is classical, their synthesis to prove complementarity for chiral algebras at all genera
is new: quantum corrections live in moduli space cohomology, and Koszul duality acts as an involution on
this cohomology.

   In summary: the geometric content of the eigenspace decomposition is the 𝑗∗ /𝑗! dichotomy. Bar
cochains of A on the FM compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) are sections of 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ A ⊠𝑛 : they extend across the bound-
ary with logarithmic poles (the 𝑗∗ -extension, which permits growth along boundary divisors). Cobar
cochains of A–-equivalently, bar cochains of A ! –-are sections of 𝑗! 𝑗 ∗ (A ! ) ⊠𝑛 : they have compact support
away from the boundary (the 𝑗! -extension, which forces vanishing along boundary divisors). The Verdier in-
volution exchanges 𝑗∗ and 𝑗! (Lemma 6.3.9), hence exchanges A-contributions and A ! -contributions. The
identification of the +1-eigenspace with 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and the −1-eigenspace with 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) then follows from the
Verdier intertwining 𝔻Ran 𝐵¯ (A) ≃ 𝐵¯ (A ! ) (Theorem 6.3.32): at the level of centers, 𝜎 (Z(A)) = Z(A ! ),
so 𝜎 acts as +1 on 𝑗∗ -extended classes from A and as −1 on 𝑗! -extended classes from A ! .
   More precisely, the anti-commutativity (8.23) ensures that the Kodaira–Spencer deformation maps 𝑉 +
to 𝑉 − and vice versa. If 𝛼 ∈ 𝑉 + , then
                                   𝜎 (∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) 𝛼 ) = −∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) ( 𝜎 𝛼 ) = −∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) 𝛼
so ∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) 𝛼 ∈ 𝑉 − . This confirms that the two eigenspaces carry genuinely different deformation-theoretic
content.
Lemma 8.14.30 (Obstructions vs. deformations; [proved]). In the decomposition of Lemma 8.14.29:
   (i) Elements of 𝑄 𝑔 (A) = 𝑉 + correspond to obstructions to extending A from genus 𝑔 − 1 to genus 𝑔
  (ii) Elements of 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝑉 − correspond to deformations of A ! at genus 𝑔
 (iii) What A sees as obstruction, A ! sees as deformation
Proof of Lemma 8.14.30. The bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) computes obstruction classes: a class 𝛼 ∈
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A)) represents a cohomological obstruction to extending the genus-( 𝑔 −1) structure to
genus 𝑔 . By Lemma 8.14.20, these are precisely the 𝐸∞ terms of the spectral sequence, which lie in 𝑉 + by
the previous lemma.
   Conversely, the bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A ! ) computes obstructions for A ! , which correspond to defor-
mations of A by Koszul duality: the deformation complex of A is quasi-isomorphic to the obstruction
complex of A ! (Theorem 9.3.7). These lie in 𝑉 − .
   Step 9: Intersection vanishes (direct sum).

Lemma 8.14.32 (Exhaustion property; [proved]). The quantum correction spaces exhaust the moduli
space cohomology:
                    dim 𝑄 𝑔 (A) + dim 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))

Proof of Lemma 8.14.32. Since 𝜎 2 = id on the finite-dimensional vector space 𝑉 = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)), the
minimal polynomial of 𝜎 divides 𝑡 2 − 1 = ( 𝑡 − 1) ( 𝑡 + 1). Over ℂ, every vector decomposes uniquely into
±1 eigenvectors via the projectors 𝜋 + = 21 (id + 𝜎 ) and 𝜋 − = 21 (id − 𝜎 ). Therefore:
                                   𝑉 = 𝑉 + ⊕ 𝑉 − = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )
and in particular dim 𝑉 + + dim 𝑉 − = dim 𝑉 .
    Veriﬁcation at small genera.
    Genus 0: M 0 = pt, so dim 𝐻 ∗ = 1. The involution 𝜎 acts as +1 on 𝐻 0 (identity class), giving 𝑄 0 (A) =
ℂ, 𝑄 0 (A ! ) = 0. Dimension check: 1 + 0 = 1.
    Genus 1: dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 1,1 ) = 2 ( 𝐻 0 ⊕ 𝐻 2 ). For the Heisenberg algebra: 𝑄 1 (H𝜅 ) = ℂ · 𝜅 (central exten-
sion, eigenvalue +1) and 𝑄 1 (H𝜅! ) = ℂ · 𝜆 (curvature, eigenvalue −1). Dimension check: 1 + 1 = 2.
    Genus 2: dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 ) = 8 (Poincaré polynomial 1 + 3𝑡 2 + 3𝑡 4 + 𝑡 6 ). The involution 𝜎 splits 𝐻 ∗
into ±1-eigenspaces whose dimensions depend on the chiral algebra through the 𝑗∗ /𝑗! extension data. For
self-dual algebras (e.g., Vir0 ), Corollary 8.14.48 gives dim 𝑉 + = dim 𝑉 − = 4. For all Koszul chiral algebras
A with trivial center, dim 𝑄 2 (A) + dim 𝑄 2 (A ! ) = 8. Detailed genus-2 complementarity dimensions are
verified in Part II (§26.4.7).

   This completes Step III. Combining Steps 7–10, we have shown:
   (i) Kodaira–Spencer map via Gauss–Manin connection (Step 7), with anti-commutativity 𝔻 ◦ ∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) =
       −∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) ◦ 𝔻
  (ii) Verdier involution 𝜎 with 𝜎 2 = id (Step 8)
 (iii) Direct sum: 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ∩ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 0 as eigenspaces of 𝜎 (Step 9)
 (iv) Exhaustion: 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) because 𝜎 2 = id (Step 10)
   Therefore:
                                 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))
   This completes the proof of Theorem 8.14.12.

Proposition 8.14.33 (Verdier pairing and Lagrangian eigenspaces; [proved]). Let (A , A ! ) be a
chiral Koszul pair and let 𝑉 = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)).
  (i) Verdier duality on the center local system Z(A) induces a non-degenerate bilinear pairing
                                              ⟨−, −⟩𝔻 : 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 → ℂ
      of cohomological degree −(3 𝑔 − 3) (the shift coming from dimℂ M 𝑔 = 3 𝑔 − 3).
8.14. The complementarity theorem                                                                             463


  (ii) The Verdier involution 𝜎 is an anti-involution for this pairing: ⟨ 𝜎 ( 𝑣 ) , 𝜎 ( 𝑤 )⟩𝔻 = −⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 for all
       𝑣, 𝑤 ∈ 𝑉 .
 (iii) Consequently, the eigenspaces 𝑉 + = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and 𝑉 − = 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) are Lagrangian with respect
       to ⟨−, −⟩𝔻 : the pairing restricts to zero on each eigenspace, and 𝑉 = 𝑉 + ⊕ 𝑉 − is a Lagrangian
       polarization.

Proof. Part (i). The center local system Z(A) on M 𝑔 is a constructible sheaf, and Verdier duality gives
a perfect pairing 𝐻 𝑘 (M 𝑔 , Z) ⊗ 𝐻 (3 𝑔 −3) − 𝑘 (M 𝑔 , 𝔻Z) → ℂ. The Koszul pairing identifies 𝔻Z(A) 
Z(A ! )  Z(A) (the last isomorphism by Theorem 8.14.12, Step 7), so the pairing lands on 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 .
Non-degeneracy follows from Verdier duality for constructible sheaves on the smooth Deligne–Mumford
stack M 𝑔 .
    Part (ii). The Verdier involution 𝜎 is defined by 𝜎 = 𝔻 ◦ KS, where KS is the Kodaira–Spencer iso-
morphism (Theorem 8.14.26) and 𝔻 is Verdier duality. Since 𝔻2 = id on constructible sheaves and the
Kodaira–Spencer map satisfies the anti-commutativity 𝔻 ◦ ∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) = −∇𝜅𝑧 ( 𝑣 ) ◦ 𝔻 (Step 7 of the proof of The-
orem 8.14.12), the involution 𝜎 reverses the sign of the pairing: ⟨ 𝜎 ( 𝑣 ) , 𝜎 (𝑤 )⟩𝔻 = ⟨𝔻𝑣, 𝔻𝑤 ⟩𝔻 = −⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 ,
where the last step uses the anti-commutativity property.
    Part (iii). For 𝑣, 𝑤 ∈ 𝑉 + (eigenvalue +1): ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 = ⟨ 𝜎 ( 𝑣 ) , 𝜎 (𝑤 )⟩𝔻 = −⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 , so ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 = 0. The
same argument applies to 𝑉 − . Since 𝑉 = 𝑉 + ⊕ 𝑉 − and the pairing is non-degenerate on 𝑉 , the subspaces
𝑉 + and 𝑉 − are maximal isotropic, i.e., Lagrangian.
Remark 8.14.34 (Lagrangian interpretation of complementarity). The decomposition of Theorem 8.14.12
is a Lagrangian polarization: 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) are complementary Lagrangians for the Verdier pairing.
This extends to a (−1)-shifted symplectic structure in the PTVV sense (Theorem 34.12.1).

Proposition 8.14.36 (PTVV Lagrangian embedding; [proved]). For a chiral Koszul pair (A , A ! )
and 𝑔 ≥ 2, the cochain complex 𝐶 𝑔 := 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) carries a (−(3 𝑔 −3))-shifted symplectic struc-
ture in the sense of Pantev–Toën–Vaquié–Vezzosi [253], and 𝑄 𝑔 (A), 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) embed as complementary
Lagrangians in the PTVV sense.
8.14. The complementarity theorem                                                                           465


Proof. Shifted symplectic structure. For a cochain complex 𝑉 with a non-degenerate symmetric pairing
⟨−, −⟩ : 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 → ℂ[ 𝑛], the associated linear derived affine scheme V := Spec(Sym(𝑉 ∗ )) carries an
𝑛-shifted symplectic structure: the pairing defines a constant 2-form of degree 𝑛 on V, and the closure
condition 𝑑dR 𝜔 = 0 is automatic for a constant form on a linear space [253, Example 1.4]. Non-degeneracy
of the pairing translates to non-degeneracy of the 2-form. The Verdier pairing on 𝐶 𝑔 (Proposition 8.14.33(i))
is a non-degenerate symmetric pairing of degree −(3 𝑔 −3), so 𝐶 𝑔 carries a (−(3 𝑔 −3))-shifted symplectic
structure.
    PTVV Lagrangian conditions. A Lagrangian in a linear 𝑛-shifted symplectic space (𝑉 , 𝜔) is a subcom-
plex 𝐿 ↩→ 𝑉 satisfying [253, Definition 2.8]:
(a) Isotropy: 𝜔 | 𝐿 = 0 (the pairing restricts to zero on 𝐿 ).
(b) Non-degeneracy: the induced map 𝐿 → (𝑉 / 𝐿 ) ∨ [ 𝑛] is a quasi-isomorphism.
For 𝐿 = 𝑄 𝑔 (A):
• Condition (a) is Proposition 8.14.33(iii): ⟨𝑣, 𝑤 ⟩𝔻 = 0 for 𝑣, 𝑤 ∈ 𝑄 𝑔 (A).
• Condition (b): Since 𝐶 𝑔 = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) (Theorem 8.14.12), we have 𝐶 𝑔 /𝑄 𝑔 (A)  𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ), and
  the induced map 𝑄 𝑔 (A) → 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) ∨ [−(3 𝑔 −3)] is a quasi-isomorphism: the Verdier pairing restricted
  to 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊗ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) is perfect of degree −(3 𝑔 −3) by (8.20).
The same argument applies with A and A ! exchanged.

(Kontsevich [35], Costello–Gwilliam [27]) is here made precise for chiral algebras.

8.14.8    Corollaries and physical interpretation
Conjecture 8.14.41 (Physical interpretation; [physical heuristic]). In conformal field theory language, the
Complementarity Theorem states:
• Central charges in one theory ↔ Curved algebra structure in dual theory
  Example: The level 𝜅 in Heisenberg H𝜅 appears as central extension, while in the Koszul dual CE(𝔥− 𝜅 )
  (curved commutative algebra) it appears as curvature 𝜇0 = −𝜅 · 𝜔 ≠ 0.
• Marginal deformations in A ↔ Obstructions in A !
  Example: Deforming the Kac–Moody level 𝑘 → 𝑘 + 𝛿 𝑘 is obstructed in 𝔤    b𝑘 but free in the W-algebra
  W (𝔤).
• Quantum corrections split between electric and magnetic sectors
  Example: In N = 4 SYM under topological twist, instanton corrections split between Coulomb branch
  (A) and Higgs branch (A ! ) moduli.
Remark 8.14.42 (Scope of Conjecture 8.14.41). This corollary is labeled [physical heuristic] because a complete
proof requires: (a) the identification of cohomological obstructions in the bar complex with BRST anoma-
lies in the physical theory, which is established for 𝑔 = 0 (Beilinson–Drinfeld) but requires Costello’s
renormalization formalism [168] at 𝑔 ≥ 1; (b) the N = 4 example requires constructing the Kapustin–
Witten twist as a chiral Koszul pair, which is beyond the scope of this monograph. The first two bullet points
are proved for specific examples (Heisenberg at genus 1 in Example 8.14.53, Kac–Moody in Example 8.14.54).
    Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type VII (physics-dictionary). The conjecture asserts that
quantum complementarity (Theorem 8.14.12) reproduces established physics identifications (central charge
8.14. The complementarity theorem                                                                   467


duality, marginal-obstruction exchange, electric-magnetic splitting) when applied to specific CFT Koszul
pairs.
Corollary 8.14.43 (Modular properties; [proved]). The decomposition 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) is
compatible with the natural Sp(2 𝑔, ℤ) action on 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 ) (modular group for genus- 𝑔 curves).
  Explicitly, for 𝛾 ∈ Sp(2 𝑔, ℤ):

                          𝛾 · ( 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )) = 𝑄 𝑔 ( 𝛾 · A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 ( 𝛾 · A ! )

where 𝛾 · A denotes the chiral algebra obtained by modular transformation.

Proof of Corollary 8.14.43. The modular group acts on M 𝑔 by automorphisms. Since the complementarity
decomposition is functorial (property 3 of Theorem 8.14.12), it commutes with the modular action.
   Modular forms therefore appear in:
• Partition functions of chiral algebras (transformed under Sp(2 𝑔, ℤ))
• Elliptic genera (combinations of characters transforming as modular forms)
• Quantum corrections at genus 𝑔 ≥ 1 (parametrized by modular forms)


Corollary 8.14.44 (Uniqueness of quantum corrections; [proved]). Given genus- 𝑔 corrections
𝑄 𝑔 (A) for a chiral algebra A, the Koszul dual corrections 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) are uniquely determined by:
                                                                      ∨
                                𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))/𝑄 𝑔 (A)

where the dual is taken with respect to Verdier duality.
  This identification is constructive.

Proof of Corollary 8.14.44. By the direct sum property (Lemma 8.14.31) and exhaustion (Lemma 8.14.32),
we have:
                                 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )
   Thus:
                                  𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))/𝑄 𝑔 (A)
as vector spaces.
    By Verdier duality (Corollary 8.14.25):

                                              𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝑄 𝑔 (A) ∨

   Combining these gives the stated formula.
   The algorithm is: compute 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)), compute 𝑄 𝑔 (A) via the bar spectral sequence, and take
the Verdier-orthogonal complement. See Examples 8.14.53 and 8.14.54.

Corollary 8.14.45 (Vanishing results; [proved]). If A has no quantum corrections at genus 𝑔 ,
meaning 𝑄 𝑔 (A) = 0, then:
                              𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))
468                                                                               Chapter 8. Higher genus


   Conversely, if both 𝑄 𝑔 (A) = 0 and 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 0, then:

                                             𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) = 0

meaning the center acts trivially on moduli space cohomology.

Proof of Corollary 8.14.45. First statement: By the decomposition theorem:

                                   𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) = 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )

   If 𝑄 𝑔 (A) = 0, then 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)).
   Second statement: If both vanish, then by exhaustion:

                         0 = dim 𝑄 𝑔 (A) + dim 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A))

   Thus 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) = 0.

Remark 8.14.46 (Examples of vanishing). At genus 0: 𝑄 0 (A) = ℂ, 𝑄 0 (A ! ) = 0 (tree-level, no obstruc-
tion). For TFTs: 𝑄 𝑔 (A) = 0 for all 𝑔 . For 𝑏𝑐 – 𝛽𝛾 : opposite obstructions cancel in the complementarity
sum (Theorem 26.7.1), but individual 𝑄 𝑔 need not vanish.
