Remark 8.14.50 (Signiﬁcance). For self-dual A: (i) dim 𝑄 𝑔 = 21 dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 ), shared by Vir0 and
𝑌 (𝔤); (ii) at the critical level, the complementarity decomposition partitions 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Fun(Op𝔤∨ )), bridg-
ing chiral Koszul duality and geometric Langlands; (iii) different self-dual algebras give different Verdier
splittings of the same cohomology group.
Conjecture 8.14.51 (String theory interpretation; [physical heuristic]). In topological string theory, the com-
plementarity theorem explains:
• A-model/B-model duality: The A-model chiral algebra and B-model chiral algebra are Koszul dual, with
  quantum corrections satisfying complementarity.
• Large 𝑁 duality: At large 𝑁 (genus expansion parameter), the planar ( 𝑔 = 0) contributions of one
  theory match the non-planar ( 𝑔 ≥ 1) contributions of the dual theory.
• Gopakumar–Vafa invariants: The generating function for Gopakumar–Vafa invariants packages both
  𝑄 𝑔 (A) and 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) into a single modular form.
Remark 8.14.52 (Scope of Conjecture 8.14.51). Labeled [physical heuristic] because: (a) A/B-model Koszul
pair identification requires [103]; (b) large 𝑁 duality is physics input; (c) Gopakumar–Vafa integrality is
open. The mathematical content is that Theorem 8.14.12 applied to the conjectural Koszul pair yields these
identifications.

8.14.11  Higher genus: genus 2 explicit computations
Example 8.14.57 (Heisenberg at genus 2). Setup: For genus 𝑔 = 2, the moduli space has dimension dim M 2 =
3. The cohomology is:
                                 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 ) = ℚ[ 𝜆1 , 𝛿0 , 𝛿1 , 𝜆2 ]/(relations)
where 𝜆1 ∈ 𝐻 2 is the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle, 𝛿0 , 𝛿1 ∈ 𝐻 2 are the boundary divisor classes,
and 𝜆2 ∈ 𝐻 4 is the second Chern class of the Hodge bundle.
   The Poincaré polynomial is:

                                    𝑃𝑡 ( 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 )) = 1 + 3𝑡 2 + 3𝑡 4 + 𝑡 6

   Genus-2 quantum corrections for Heisenberg:

                                      𝑄2 (H𝜅 ) = ℂ · 𝜅 2 ⊕ ℂ · [ 𝜅, 𝜆1 ]

   The first term 𝜅 2 corresponds to the genus-2 contribution from two independent genus-1 handles
(product structure). The second term [ 𝜅, 𝜆1 ] is a genuine genus-2 effect (interaction between handles).
   Dual corrections:                                                ∨
                                  𝑄2 (H𝜅! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 )/𝑄2 (H𝜅 )
   Computing dimensions:

                           dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 ) = 8      (sum of Poincaré polynomial)
                            dim 𝑄 2 (H𝜅 ) = 2
                            dim 𝑄 2 (H𝜅! ) = 8 − 2 = 6

   The complementarity holds: 𝑄 2 (H𝜅 ) ⊕ 𝑄 2 (H𝜅! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 2 ).

8.14.12  Algorithmic computation of quantum corrections
We conclude with a practical algorithm for computing 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and verifying complementarity.
Remark 8.14.58 (Computing quantum corrections). Given a chiral algebra A on a curve 𝑋 of genus 𝑔 , the
quantum correction space 𝑄 𝑔 (A) is computed as follows (see Remark 8.7.4 for notation).
   (i) Compute the center 𝑍 (A) = { 𝑧 ∈ A : [ 𝑧, 𝑎] = 0 for all 𝑎 }.
  (ii) Construct the bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) = 𝑛 Γ ( 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 𝑔 ) , A ⊠𝑛 ⊗ Ω∗log ).
                                                L

 (iii) Compute the total corrected differential 𝐷 𝑔 on 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) (Theorem 8.7.3), which includes fiberwise
      collision residues, the Gauss–Manin connection, and modular corrections. This differential satisfies

  Step 3 (BD 3.4.12): Prove acyclicity via Cousin filtration. The key ingredients:

Remark 8.15.2 (Requirements for higher genus). To extend to higher genus, we must ensure:
   (i) The factorization structure persists: A (𝑈 ⊔ 𝑉 ) ≃ A (𝑈 ) ⊗ A (𝑉 )
  (ii) Normal crossings are maintained in the boundary divisors
 (iii) Descent data are compatible with moduli stack stratification
 (iv) Quantum corrections (from 𝐻 1 ( Σ 𝑔 , ℂ), the period data of the fiber curve) preserve acyclicity

8.15.2    The universal curve and relative Ran space
At higher genus, we work over the moduli stack M 𝑔 .
Construction 8.15.3 (Relative Ran space). Let 𝜋 : C𝑔 → M 𝑔 be the universal curve of genus 𝑔 . The relative
Ran space is:
                                   𝑅 (C𝑔 /M 𝑔 ) := colim𝑛 ≥0 (C𝑔 ) ( 𝑛 ) /M 𝑔
where (C𝑔 ) ( 𝑛 ) = C𝑔𝑛 \ {diagonals} is the configuration space of 𝑛 distinct points.
  Fiber over a point. For [ Σ 𝑔 ] ∈ M 𝑔 , the fiber is:
                                        𝑅 (C𝑔 /M 𝑔 )| [ Σ 𝑔 ] = 𝑅 ( Σ 𝑔 )
the ordinary Ran space of the Riemann surface Σ 𝑔 .
Proposition 8.15.4 (Factorization over moduli; [proved]). For disjoint open sets 𝑈 ,𝑉 ⊂ Σ 𝑔
varying in families over M 𝑔 :
                               A (𝑈 ⊔ 𝑉 ) ≃ A (𝑈 ) ⊗ OM 𝑔 A (𝑉 )
The factorization is O M 𝑔 -linear.

Proof. The chiral product 𝜇 : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (A ⊠ A) → Δ∗ A is a morphism of D-modules defined locally on 𝑋
(Beilinson–Drinfeld [2], §3.4). For disjoint open sets 𝑈 ,𝑉 ⊂ Σ 𝑔 , the factorization isomorphism A (𝑈 ⊔
𝑉 ) ≃ A (𝑈 ) ⊗ A (𝑉 ) depends only on the restriction of A to 𝑈 ⊔ 𝑉 and the factorization isomorphism
of the D-module structure. Since 𝑈 ∩ 𝑉 = ∅, no global data (periods, modular parameter) enters: the
isomorphism is determined by the local chiral product and the D-module structure on each open set. The
base O M 𝑔 -linearity follows because the family 𝜋 : C𝑔 → M 𝑔 is a smooth family of curves, and the relative
D-module structure on A over M 𝑔 ensures all structure maps are O M 𝑔 -linear.

The parameters 𝑡𝑘 vary independently as [ Σ 𝑔 ] moves in the Siegel upper half-space ℌ 𝑔 , so the vanishing

                                   𝑑𝑘 𝑑𝑙 + 𝑑𝑙 𝑑𝑘 = 0 for all 1 ≤ 𝑘, 𝑙 ≤ 𝑔.

This is the operator-level manifestation of the Lagrangian isotropicity 𝛾𝑘 · 𝛾𝑙 = 0 of the 𝐴-cycle subspace
in 𝐻1 ( Σ 𝑔 , ℤ): the Riemann bilinear relations connect iterated period integrals of the Cauchy kernel to
the symplectic intersection pairing, and restricting to a Lagrangian subspace forces all anticommutators to
vanish.
    (Note: The two vanishings 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0 and 𝑑fib  2 ≠ 0 are not in tension; they are the two faces of the chiral

Riemann–Hilbert correspondence (Remark 8.0.3). The holomorphic propagator deﬁnes a ﬂat connection on
the universal cover of Σ 𝑔 . The Arakelov propagator deﬁnes the single-valued but curved projection to Σ 𝑔 itself.
The total corrected differential 𝐷 𝑔 lives in the ﬂat gauge; the ﬁberwise differential 𝑑fib lives in the curved
gauge. The passage 𝑑fib ⇝ 𝐷 𝑔 is the chiral exponential map.)

Remark 8.15.14 (Curved twisting morphisms at higher genus). At genus 0, the universal twisting morphism
𝜏 : 𝐵¯ (A) → A satisfies the flat Maurer–Cartan equation 𝑑𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 (Corollary 9.1.9, Remark 9.1.10).
At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the propagator acquires monodromy and the twisting morphism becomes curved:

                                          𝑑𝜏 𝑔 + 𝜏 𝑔 ★ 𝜏 𝑔 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 𝑔 .                                 (8.26)

The curvature 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 𝑔 is the Arakelov (1, 1)-form weighted by the modular characteristic
(Theorem 8.5.9): it measures the failure of the single-valued propagator to satisfy the Arnold relation at
genus 𝑔 .
     The three propagators in the table of Step 4 above correspond to three twisting morphisms: 𝜏0 (classical,
flat MC), 𝜏 𝑔hol (holomorphic, flat MC via the Fay identity), and 𝜏 𝑔Ar (Arakelov, curved MC with curvature 𝜅 ·
𝜔 𝑔 ). The total corrected differential 𝐷 𝑔 corresponds to 𝜏 𝑔hol ; the fiberwise differential 𝑑fib corresponds to
𝜏 𝑔Ar . The passage between them is the chiral exponential map.
     The three incarnations descend through the H/M/S hierarchy:
• H-level. The universal MC class Θ A ∈ MC(𝔤mod   A ) assembles all genera into a single modular twisting
  cochain (Remark 8.18.35).
• M-level. At each genus, the three twisting morphisms in the table above are explicit dg maps, with the
  curved MC equation (8.26) encoding the Arakelov defect.
• S-level. The scalar shadow is 𝜅 (A) · 𝜆 𝑔 ∈ 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 ) (Theorem 8.13.16): one number per genus, deter-
  mined by the genus-1 curvature alone.

8.16.1   Three levels of duality
Deﬁnition 8.16.1 (Three duality structures). We work with three dualities simultaneously.
    Verdier duality (geometric). For 𝑋 a smooth variety of dimension 𝑑 , Verdier duality is 𝔻 𝑋 : 𝐷 𝑐𝑏 ( 𝑋 ) →
𝐷 𝑐𝑏 ( 𝑋 ) op , 𝔻 𝑋 (F ) = 𝑅H 𝑜𝑚 (F , 𝜔 𝑋 [ 𝑑 ]). It satisfies 𝔻2𝑋 ≃ id, Poincaré duality
                              𝑅Γ𝑐 ( 𝑋 , 𝔻 𝑋 F ) ≃ 𝑅 Hom( 𝑅Γ𝑐 ( 𝑋 , F ) , ℂ) ∨ ,
and compatibility with proper pushforward 𝔻𝑌 ◦ 𝑓∗ ≃ 𝑓! ◦ 𝔻 𝑋 .
   Ayala–Francis duality (topological). For an 𝐸𝑛 -algebra 𝐴 and manifold 𝑀 , 𝑀 𝐴 ≃ 𝔻 𝑀 ( − 𝑀 𝐴∨ ),
                                                                                 ∫                ∫

                                 ∫ dual and  ∫ − 𝑀 denotes the opposite orientation. This satisfies oriented

   Linear duality (algebraic). For vector spaces, 𝑉 ∨ = Hom(𝑉 , ℂ).

8.16.2    The de Rham functor: bridge between geometry and topology
Deﬁnition 8.16.2 (de Rham functor). The de Rham functor:

                                  DR : 𝐷 𝑏 ( 𝐷 -mod( 𝑋 )) → 𝐷 𝑏 (Vectℂ )

is defined by taking global sections followed by de Rham cohomology:

                                    DR(M) = 𝑅Γ ( 𝑋 , Ω•𝑋 ⊗ D 𝑋 M)

   For a right D 𝑋 -module M, this computes the de Rham cohomology with coefficients in M.
Proposition 8.16.3 (DR preserves duality structures; [proved]). The de Rham functor is compati-
ble with duality in the following sense:

                                      DR(𝔻 𝑋 M) ≃ DR(M) ∨ [− 𝑑 ]

where 𝑑 = dim 𝑋 and (−) ∨ is linear duality.

Remark 8.16.9. This compatibility theorem ensures the construction is not ad hoc. It shows:
   (i) Geometric bar-cobar (via configuration space integrals and Verdier duality)
  (ii) Topological factorization homology (via 𝐸∞ operads and Ayala–Francis)

Remark 8.16.15 (Compatibility with chiral Koszul duality). The geometric construction (Verdier duality on
configuration spaces) and the topological construction (Ayala–Francis duality on factorization algebras)
produce equivalent results.
    Without this compatibility, we could not be sure that the ‘‘dual coalgebra’’ we construct geometrically
is the same as the ‘‘Koszul dual’’ in the abstract algebraic sense.
    The theorem provides the bridge: geometric duality via 𝐷 -modules corresponds to topological duality
via factorization homology, both giving the same Koszul dual algebra.
   With Verdier duality and Ayala–Francis compatibility established, the bar-cobar adjunction at higher
genus can be inverted on the Koszul locus.

8.17     Bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism at higher genus
Lemma 8.17.1 (Open-stratum quasi-isomorphism; [proved]). Let 𝑈𝑔 ⊂ M 𝑔 be the open stratum of
smooth genus- 𝑔 curves. The restriction

                                    𝑗 𝑔∗ 𝜓 𝑔 : 𝑗 𝑔∗ Ω 𝑔 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑔 (A)) −→ 𝑗 𝑔∗ A 𝑔

is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof. On 𝑈𝑔 , the bar differential is computed by residues along collision divisors (Section 8.6.2), and the
cobar differential is the dual diagonal-distribution differential. Fiberwise this is exactly the Verdier duality
pairing used in Theorem 6.3.32, so each geometric fiber of 𝑗 𝑔∗ 𝜓 𝑔 is a quasi-isomorphism.
   The cone 𝐶 = Cone( 𝑗 𝑔∗ 𝜓 𝑔 ) is therefore a complex of constructible sheaves on 𝑈𝑔 whose stalk coho-
mology vanishes at every geometric point (by the fiberwise quasi-isomorphism just established). Con-
structibility of 𝐶 is inherited from that of the fiber cohomology sheaves on 𝑈𝑔 (established in the proof
of Theorem 8.14.18, Step 2). The cohomology sheaves H 𝑞 ( 𝐶 ) are therefore constructible sheaves on the
smooth connected stack 𝑈𝑔 whose stalks H 𝑞 ( 𝐶 ) 𝑠 = 𝐻 𝑞 ( 𝐶𝑠 ) = 0 vanish at every geometric point 𝑠 . A
constructible sheaf on a connected base whose stalks are all zero is the zero sheaf (see [154, Exposé IX,
Théorème 2.14]); hence H 𝑞 ( 𝐶 ) = 0 for all 𝑞 , which means 𝐶 is acyclic and 𝑗 𝑔∗ 𝜓 𝑔 is a quasi-isomorphism
on 𝑈𝑔 .

Lemma 8.17.2 (Boundary-stratum compatibility of 𝜓 𝑔 ; [proved]). For every boundary stratum
𝐷 Γ ⊂ 𝜕 M 𝑔 indexed by a stable graph Γ, the restricted map

                                   𝜓 𝑔 | 𝐷Γ : Ω 𝑔 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑔 (A))| 𝐷Γ −→ A 𝑔 | 𝐷Γ

is a quasi-isomorphism, provided the higher-genus inversion statement is known for all genera < 𝑔 .

Proof. By Proposition 8.15.9 and Lemma 8.15.10, restriction of the bar data to 𝐷 Γ factorizes over nodal
gluings into tensor products of lower-genus pieces. Functoriality of bar-cobar inversion (Theorem 6.12.11)
identifies 𝜓 𝑔 | 𝐷Γ with the corresponding tensor product of lower-genus inversion maps.
8.17. Bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism at higher genus                                                        491


    Every vertex genus in Γ is strictly smaller than 𝑔 : in the separating case, 𝑔 = 𝑔1 + 𝑔2 with 𝑔1 , 𝑔2 ≥ 0
and each 𝑔𝑖 < 𝑔 (note: one component may have genus 0, which is the base case of the induction); in the
non-separating case, the single vertex has genus 𝑔 − 1 < 𝑔 . In either case, the induction hypothesis applies
to each vertex. Tensor products of quasi-isomorphisms are quasi-isomorphisms by the Künneth formula
for factorization algebras at nodes: the factorization tensor product at a node is computed fiberwise over
the normalization, reducing to the plain tensor product of chain complexes over the ground field, which
preserves quasi-isomorphisms by Künneth. This yields the claim.

Lemma 8.17.3 (Extension across boundary; [proved]). Let 𝑋 be a stack with open-closed decomposi-
tion 𝑋 = 𝑈 ⊔ 𝑍 (with 𝑗 : 𝑈 ↩→ 𝑋 , 𝑖 : 𝑍 ↩→ 𝑋 ). For a morphism of complexes 𝑓 : 𝐾 → 𝐿 on 𝑋 , if
𝑗 ∗ 𝑓 and 𝑖 ∗ 𝑓 are quasi-isomorphisms, then 𝑓 is a quasi-isomorphism.
Proof. Let 𝐶 = Cone( 𝑓 ). It suffices to prove 𝐶 is acyclic. From 𝑗 ∗ 𝑓 and 𝑖 ∗ 𝑓 quasi-isomorphisms, 𝑗 ∗ 𝐶
and 𝑖 ∗ 𝐶 are acyclic. Apply the localization triangle
                                                                   +1
                                      𝑗! 𝑗 ∗ 𝐶 −→ 𝐶 −→ 𝑖∗ 𝑖 ∗ 𝐶 −→ .

Both outer terms are acyclic, hence 𝐶 is acyclic. Therefore 𝑓 is a quasi-isomorphism.

Lemma 8.17.5 ( 𝐸2 collapse at higher genus; [proved]). For a Koszul chiral algebra A on a genus- 𝑔

Proof. The PBW filtration is a filtration by chiral algebras, and the Koszulness hypothesis ensures that the
associated graded is a Koszul complex in the classical sense. The 𝑑𝑟 differential for 𝑟 ≥ 2 maps between PBW-

on the associated graded) forces these maps to have zero source or zero target. This is Corollary 9.1.36, Step 4,
applied fiberwise over M 𝑔 : on each geometric fiber (a fixed smooth or stable curve), the collision differential
is genus-0 type, and the genus- 𝑔 quantum corrections live in higher Leray degrees, contributing only to
𝑑𝑟 for 𝑟 ≥ 2; since 𝐸2 is already concentrated on the diagonal by Koszul concentration, these higher
differentials vanish.

8.17.1   Factorization homology descent: the homotopy-native proof

homotopy-theoretic perspective is not merely convenient but necessary.

8.18       Koszul duality across genera
The genus-0 Koszul duality Ω ( 𝐵¯ (0) (A)) ≃ A extends to a tower indexed by genus. We record the struc-
tural framework here; a key structural question is whether the Koszul property (diagonal Ext vanishing)
propagates from genus 0 to higher genus. For the standard examples at generic parameters, the PBW argu-
ment of Proposition 8.18.13 gives an affirmative answer; at special parameters (e.g. admissible levels), the
question remains open.

8.18.3   Modular Koszul chiral algebras: the definition
A modular Koszul chiral algebra is the natural object for which the categorical exp/log correspondence
(Remark 6.0.1) holds at all genera: the bar functor (categorical logarithm) and cobar functor (categorical
exponential) are mutually inverse on the Koszul locus, the curvature is controlled by a universal scalar, and
the full modular package admits the logarithmic-to-exponential hierarchy of Remark 8.18.29. Equivalently,
it is the natural object for which all four main theorems hold simultaneously. We give a homotopy-native
version (Definition 8.18.7) and a concrete dg model (Definition 8.18.9).
Deﬁnition 8.18.7 (Modular Koszul object –- homotopy form). Let 𝑋 be a smooth projective curve over ℂ. A
modular Koszul object on 𝑋 is an augmented factorization algebra A ∈ Algaug (Fact( 𝑋 )) equipped with:
 (D1∞ ) A bar object B 𝑋 (A) ∈ CoAlgconil (Fact( 𝑋 )) in the homotopy category of factorization coalge-
        bras.
(D2∞ ) A dual object A ! .
(D3∞ ) A filtered cyclic deformation object Def cyc (A) (Definition 11.5.11), and (when constructed) a
        genus-completed Maurer–Cartan datum Θ A (Theorem 34.12.3 for the non-scalar part).
(D4∞ ) A center local system ZA on M 𝑔,• (or the appropriate modular parameter stack), whose global
        sections house the obstruction classes.
(D5∞ ) A spectral discriminant Δ A ( 𝑥 ) = det(1 − 𝑥 𝑇rec ) (Theorem 34.12.6).
(D6∞ ) A periodicity proﬁle Π (A) = ( 𝑀A , 𝑄 A , 𝐺 A ) (Remark 10.5.10).
satisfying the antecedent axioms:
(MK1∞ ) (Koszulity.) The weight filtration on B 𝑋 (A) makes it Koszul on the associated graded.
(MK2∞ ) (Verdier intertwining.) 𝔻Ran B 𝑋 (A) ≃ B 𝑋 (A ! ) as homotopy factorization coalgebras, functo-
        rially over M 𝑔,𝑛 .
(MK3∞ ) (Modular deformation.) The genus tower arises from a filtered Maurer–Cartan deformation
        of B 𝑋 (A), whose scalar shadow is obs 𝑔 = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜆 𝑔 (Theorem 8.13.16).

Remark 8.18.10 (Axioms versus consequences). Only MK1–MK3 are part of the definition. MK4 and MK5
are theorematic consequences proved later (Theorems 8.17.4 and 8.14.12) and are not axioms. For modular
Koszul chiral algebras with simple Lie symmetry, MK6 and MK7 are further theorematic consequences of
MC2 full resolution (Lemma 8.18.73). MK8 is the remaining ordered-factorization frontier.
Remark 8.18.11 (Logical structure). The definition separates hypotheses (MK1–MK3) from consequences
(MK4–MK5). The hypotheses are checkable conditions on the chiral algebra and its genus tower; the
consequences are theorems: MK4 (inversion) is proved by Theorem 8.17.4 and MK5 (complementarity) by
Theorem 8.14.12, both from MK1–MK3. There is no circularity: the axioms are genuinely antecedent to the
theorems. The dg axioms MK1–MK3 present the homotopy axioms (MK1∞ ), (MK2∞ ), and (MK3∞ ) of
Definition 8.18.7. For simple Lie symmetry, Lemma 8.18.73 adds MK6–MK7 as theorematic consequences
without enlarging the antecedent axiom list.
Remark 8.18.12 (Extended consequences and remaining ordered frontier). The full modular homotopy
package adds three consequences:
(MK6) (Universal MC control.) Θ A ∈ MC(Def cyc (A) ⊗    b G mod ) (Theorem 8.18.34).
(MK7) (Verdier/clutching compatibility.) 𝜉 ( Θ A ) = Θ A ★ Θ A and 𝔻( Θ A ) = Θ A ! .

(MK8) (E1 -ordered face.) Spectral 𝑅-matrix and A∞ -Yang–Baxter data (Proposition 24.3.4).
For simple Lie symmetry, MK6–MK7 follow from Theorem 8.18.72 (Lemma 8.18.73). MK8 remains
programmatic.

  (i) the diagonal block on conformal weight ℎ can only come from weight-2 states, hence only from the

   The finite calculation of the weight-triangular mechanism applies for the first higher-spin case W3
through conformal weight 8, together with the principal generator weights for the finite-type families 𝐴1 ,

Theorem 8.18.24 (Universal PBW enrichment-killing for chiral algebras with conformal vector;
[proved]). [Regime: curved-central (Convention 2.9.2).]
   Let A be a chiral algebra defined by local OPE relations, admitting a PBW filtration by conformal
weight, and satisfying:
 (a) the augmentation ideal 𝑉¯A is positively graded: every homogeneous state has conformal weight ℎ ≥
    ℎmin > 0;
(b) among all generators, exactly one has conformal weight 2, namely the stress tensor 𝑇 , with 𝑇(1) = 𝐿0 .
Then for every genus 𝑔 ≥ 1 and every conformal weight ℎ, the genus-enrichment summand of the PBW
spectral sequence satisfies
                                 𝑑2PBW E ∗,ℎ = ℎ · id 𝑀ℎ ⊗ id 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) ,
                                              𝑔

and similarly on the antiholomorphic factor. Consequently the entire genus-enrichment is killed by the 𝐸3
page. In particular, for families satisfying hypotheses (a)–(b), axiom MK3 is reduced to a separate later-page
and extension analysis after this 𝐸3 -page vanishing.
   Suppose further that A satisfies:
 (c) the Lie symmetry algebra 𝔤 of A is semisimple: there exists a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 acting on
     each enrichment module 𝑀ℎ through the (0)-products of the generators, compatible with the PBW
     filtration.
Then the genus-enrichment is universally killed by 𝑑2PBW , with no separate later-page or extension analysis
required. Precisely: for every genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, 𝐸∞ ( 𝑔 ) = 𝐸∞ (0).
508                                                                              Chapter 8. Higher genus


Proof. The enrichment factorization (8.29) holds for any chiral algebra defined by local OPE relations: at
each conformal weight ℎ,
                                     E ∗𝑔,ℎ  𝑀ℎ ⊗ℂ 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) ,
because the 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) forms are smooth across collision divisors and enter as passive multiplicative factors.
   The 𝑑2PBW differential on the enrichment is induced by the (1)-products of the generators. A generator
of conformal weight 𝑠 has (1)-product shifting conformal weight by 𝑠 − 2. By hypothesis (b), the stress
tensor 𝑇 is the unique generator with 𝑠 = 2, so it is the unique generator whose (1)-product preserves
conformal weight. Every other generator has 𝑠 ≠ 2 and therefore shifts the weight-grading: its contribution
appears on a page of the PBW spectral sequence different from the one where the weight-preserving 𝑇(1)
acts. Concretely, generators with 𝑠 > 2 contribute on earlier pages (weight-raising terms, already accounted
for on 𝐸1 ), while generators with 𝑠 < 2 contribute on later pages (weight-lowering terms, appearing on 𝐸3
or beyond).
   Consequently, the 𝑑2PBW differential on the enrichment at conformal weight ℎ is controlled entirely
by 𝑇(1) = 𝐿0 :
                                      𝑑2PBW E ∗,ℎ = ℎ · id 𝑀ℎ ⊗ id 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) .
                                             𝑔

Since ℎ ≥ ℎmin > 0, this map is an isomorphism, killing the entire genus- 𝑔 enrichment on the 𝐸3 page.
The weight-lowering contributions from generators with 𝑠 < 2 now act on zero (the enrichment is already
dead) and cannot create new classes.
   The antiholomorphic factor 𝐻 0,1 ( Σ 𝑔 ) is handled identically. Bounded-below convergence ((iii) of
Theorem 9.1.25) then shows that once later differentials and extension classes are ruled out by family-
specific input, the genus- 𝑔 and genus-0 𝐸∞ pages agree. Under hypotheses (a)–(b) alone, the theorem
proves only the common 𝐸3 -page vanishing mechanism.
   Part (c): semisimple symmetry gives universal 𝐸2 collapse.
   Assume additionally hypothesis (c): 𝔤 is semisimple and acts on each 𝑀ℎ through the (0)-products.
Decompose 𝑀ℎ = 𝑀ℎ𝔤 ⊕ 𝑀ℎnon-triv into 𝔤-invariant and non-trivial summands.
   Non-trivial summands. The 𝑑1PBW differential (Lie bracket residue from the (0)-products of the genera-
tors) acts on the enrichment through the 𝔤-module factor 𝑀ℎnon-triv , leaving the 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) factor unchanged.
The enrichment complex at weight ℎ restricted to the non-trivial summand is

                                 𝐶 ∗ (𝔤, 𝑀ℎnon-triv ) , 𝑑CE ⊗ℂ 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) .
                                                           


By the Whitehead–Chevalley–Eilenberg vanishing theorem, 𝐻 𝑞 (𝔤, 𝑁 ) = 0 for all 𝑞 ≥ 0 and any finite-
dimensional 𝔤-module 𝑁 with no trivial summand, since 𝔤 is semisimple. Therefore the non-trivial en-
richment is acyclic already at the 𝐸2 page:

                                            𝐸2∗,ℎ ( 𝑔 )enr, non-triv = 0.

   Invariant summands. The surviving 𝔤-invariant enrichment classes live in 𝑀ℎ𝔤 ⊗ 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ). On these,
the 𝑑2PBW differential acts through 𝑇(1) = 𝐿0 as proved above: the conformal vector is the unique weight-2
generator, and its (1)-product gives 𝐿0 | 𝑀 𝔤 = ℎ · id. Since ℎ ≥ ℎmin > 0, this is an isomorphism, and the
                                           ℎ
𝔤-invariant enrichment is killed at the 𝐸3 page.
   No later differentials or extension ambiguity. The two mechanisms are complementary and exhaustive:
every enrichment class belongs to either the 𝔤-non-trivial summand (killed by Whitehead at 𝐸2 ) or the 𝔤-
invariant summand (killed by 𝐿0 invertibility at 𝐸3 ). No residual classes survive to later pages, and there are
8.18. Koszul duality across genera                                                                       509


no extension ambiguities because the enrichment is zero on the 𝐸3 page. By bounded-below convergence
((iii) of Theorem 9.1.25), 𝐸∞ ( 𝑔 ) = 𝐸∞ (0) unconditionally.
    The antiholomorphic factor is handled identically.

Remark 8.18.25 (Scope of the universal PBW theorem). Hypotheses (a)–(b) of Theorem 8.18.24 capture
the common unique-weight-2 mechanism behind the Virasoro and principal W degenerations. KM uses
the independent Whitehead–Casimir–Killing mechanism (Theorem 8.18.19). Non-principal W-algebras
(Bershadsky–Polyakov, hook-type, N = 1, 2) satisfy (a)–(b); when the Levi factor of 𝔤 𝑓 is semisimple,
hypothesis (c) gives unconditional enrichment-killing at all genera. For W∞ , hypotheses (a)–(b) hold
at each finite stage; the completed MK3 statement is part of the MC4 package. The structural input is
the enrichment factorization 𝑀ℎ ⊗ 𝐻 1,0 ( Σ 𝑔 ) (8.29), which separates local OPE data from global curve
topology.

Explicit construction of the universal class
The abstract existence statement becomes concrete through the minimal cyclic 𝐿∞ model. The result is
a closed-form formula for Θ A that reduces the full homotopy datum to the Lie bracket of 𝔤, the scalar
𝜅 (A), and the Hodge classes 𝜆 𝑔 .

by additivity.

Remark 8.18.47 (Resolution of Hypothesis (MC2-2)). Proposition 8.18.46 resolves MC2-2 conditionally

−𝑦 , so 𝐸 𝑔 is 𝜎 -stable and
                                           𝐸 𝑔 = ℂ 𝑥 ⊕ ℂ𝑦 = 𝐿 𝑔 ⊕ 𝐿 !𝑔 .
Again by Proposition 8.14.33, the pairing vanishes on each of the two lines individually. The assumed
non-vanishing of ⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ⟩𝔻 therefore makes the restriction of the pairing to 𝐸 𝑔 non-degenerate.

Proposition 8.18.50 (One-channel PTVV / anti-involution criterion; [proved]). In the setting
of Proposition 8.18.49, fix a 𝜎 -stable Verdier-nondegenerate plane

Choose the projector model of Remark 8.14.13: a cochain model 𝐶 𝑔 for C 𝑔 (A) with strict involution 𝜎 ,
projectors 𝑝± := 21 (id ± 𝜎 ), and eigenspace subcomplexes 𝐶 𝑔± := im( 𝑝± ) ⊂ 𝐶 𝑔 . Then the following are

  (i) there exists a perfect 𝜎 -stable subcomplex 𝐸 𝑔• ⊂ 𝐶 𝑔 whose projector pieces

      satisfy
                                       𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐸 𝑔•,+ ) = 𝐿 𝑔 ,       𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐸 𝑔•, − ) = 𝐿 !𝑔 ,
      and whose inclusions 𝐸 𝑔•,± ↩→ 𝐸 𝑔• are complementary Lagrangian embeddings in the PTVV sense
      for the restricted Verdier pairing;
 (ii) there exist perfect subcomplexes L 𝑔 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑔+ and L!𝑔 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑔− such that:
       (a)
                                            𝐻 ∗ (L 𝑔 ) = 𝐿 𝑔 ,         𝐻 ∗ (L!𝑔 ) = 𝐿 !𝑔 ;
       (b) the restricted Verdier pairing vanishes on each summand:

                                            ⟨L 𝑔 , L 𝑔 ⟩𝔻 = 0,         ⟨L!𝑔 , L!𝑔 ⟩𝔻 = 0;

       (c) the cross pairing induces quasi-isomorphisms
                                   ∼                                          ∼
                              L 𝑔 −−→ (L!𝑔 ) ∨ [−(3 𝑔 −3)] ,           L!𝑔 −−→ (L 𝑔 ) ∨ [−(3 𝑔 −3)] .

In particular, once the cohomological one-channel Verdier plane is isolated, the remaining H-level step is
reduced to constructing perfect one-channel subcomplexes in the ±-projector sectors and checking the
PTVV non-degeneracy quasi-isomorphism.

Proof. (i) ⇒ (ii). Set
                                         L 𝑔 := 𝐸 𝑔•,+ ,        L!𝑔 := 𝐸 𝑔•, − .
The cohomology identities are part of the hypothesis. Since the inclusions 𝐸 𝑔•,± ↩→ 𝐸 𝑔• are PTVV La-
grangian, their restricted pairings vanish. By Lemma 8.14.7, the projector decomposition gives

                                               𝐸 𝑔•  𝐸 𝑔•,+ ⊕ 𝐸 𝑔•, − ,

so 𝐸 𝑔• / 𝐸 𝑔•,+  𝐸 𝑔•, − and 𝐸 𝑔• / 𝐸 𝑔•, −  𝐸 𝑔•,+ . For a linear shifted symplectic complex, the PTVV non-
degeneracy condition is exactly the statement that the induced map from one Lagrangian summand to
the shifted dual of the quotient is a quasi-isomorphism (Proposition 8.14.36), which is therefore the cross-
pairing quasi-isomorphism in (ii)(c).
   (ii) ⇒ (i). Since 𝐶 𝑔+ ⊕ 𝐶 𝑔− ↩→ 𝐶 𝑔 is the projector splitting of Remark 8.14.13, the direct sum

                                             𝐸 𝑔• := L 𝑔 ⊕ L!𝑔 ⊂ 𝐶 𝑔
8.18. Koszul duality across genera                                                                            523


is a perfect 𝜎 -stable subcomplex, and its projector pieces are exactly L 𝑔 and L!𝑔 . Condition (ii)(a) gives the
required cohomology lines. Condition (ii)(b) is the PTVV isotropy condition for each inclusion into 𝐸 𝑔• ,
while condition (ii)(c) is the PTVV non-degeneracy condition, again by Proposition 8.14.36. Thus the two
inclusions are complementary PTVV Lagrangian embeddings.
    It remains to identify the anti-involution. For 𝑥, 𝑥 ′ ∈ L 𝑔 and 𝑦, 𝑦 ′ ∈ L!𝑔 , the projector model gives
𝜎 ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑥 and 𝜎 ( 𝑦 ) = −𝑦 , hence

                               𝜎 ( 𝑥 + 𝑦 ) , 𝜎 ( 𝑥 ′ + 𝑦 ′ ) 𝔻 = 𝑥 − 𝑦, 𝑥 ′ − 𝑦 ′ 𝔻 .

The same-summand pairings vanish by (ii)(b), so only the cross terms remain:

                    𝑥 − 𝑦, 𝑥 ′ − 𝑦 ′ 𝔻 = −⟨ 𝑥, 𝑦 ′ ⟩𝔻 − ⟨𝑦, 𝑥 ′ ⟩𝔻 = − 𝑥 + 𝑦, 𝑥 ′ + 𝑦 ′ 𝔻 .

Therefore 𝜎 | 𝐸 𝑔• is anti-symplectic, so 𝐸 𝑔• is precisely the desired one-channel H-level PTVV / anti-involution
lift.

Remark 8.18.70 (Frontier consequence for MC2). Proposition 8.18.45 turns MC2 into a three-package
frontier: (1) construct the cyclic 𝐿∞ model Def cyc (A); (2) realize the modular-operadic clutching package
over M 𝑔,• ; (3) identify the one-channel genus- 𝑔 obstruction with the tautological line via clutching/trace
isolation, then reduce through the Verdier/Koszul Lagrangian plane, PTVV lift, chain-model seeds, root-
string transfer, and a single scalar comparison (Propositions 8.18.48 through 8.18.69). Once packages (1)–(2)
exist, package (3) is a finite reduction to one normalized scalar check.

projective curve 𝑋 with non-degenerate invariant form and simple Lie symmetry 𝔤, all three hypotheses of

clutching, and Verdier properties. In particular, MC2 is fully proved.

Remark 8.18.99 (Non-examples and boundaries). Not modular Koszul: (i) KM at admissible levels
(inversion fails); (ii) Virasoro minimal models (singular-vector quotient, MK1 may fail); (iii) logarithmic
algebras (W ( 𝑝), non-semisimple). The coderived category (Positselski [171]) is the correct framework; see
§34.12.
    The four main theorems are proved.
    Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39): the bar-cobar adjunction is an equivalence for Koszul pairs, intertwined
with Verdier duality on Ran( 𝑋 ).
    Theorem B (Theorem 8.17.4): on the Koszul locus the counit is a quasi-isomorphism at every genus;
off this locus the bar-cobar object persists in the coderived category with curvature measured by Θ A .
    Theorem C (Theorem 8.14.12): the ambient moduli cohomology H 𝑔 (A) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) carries
a shifted-symplectic pairing from Verdier duality, and the deformation and obstruction spaces of a Koszul
pair embed as complementary Lagrangians.
    Theorem Dscal (Theorem 8.18.30): the scalar invariants of the modular characteristic hierarchy are deter-
mined by a single number 𝜅 (A), which is universal (controls all genera), additive (a group homomorphism
under tensor product), anti-symmetric under duality, and whose vanishing is anomaly cancellation.
8.18. Koszul duality across genera                                                                          555


   Theorem DΔ (Theorem 8.18.32): the spectral discriminant is a separately proved non-scalar invariant.
   The full universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ A (Theorem 8.18.34) is now established by Theorem 8.18.72,
completing the modular characteristic hierarchy.
   These are five aspects of a single object: the modular Koszul chiral algebra (Definition 8.18.9). Every
chiral algebra in Part II will be verified as an instance of this structure. The computations that follow –- bar
cohomology, genus expansions, discriminants, complementarity sums –- are not isolated calculations but
invariants of the modular characteristic package CA = ( Θ A , 𝜅 (A) , Δ A , Π A , H A ) (Definition 8.18.27).
What one algebra sees as deformation, its dual sees as obstruction: this is the Lagrangian principle at work,
algebra by algebra, genus by genus.

Chiral Koszul duality

9.1     From the Heisenberg example to general twisting data
The bar complex of H𝑘 (Chapter 1, Theorem 1.5.1) produces the coalgebra 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) ≃ coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ), whose
cohomology gives the Koszul dual algebra H𝑘! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ). The bar-cobar counit Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (H𝑘 )) −−→
                                                                                                         ∼

H𝑘 is a quasi-isomorphism (recovering the original algebra, not its dual). Two structural features make this
work:
  (i) The twisted tensor product 𝐾𝜏𝐿 (H𝑘 , coLiech (𝑉 ∗ )) is acyclic–-the twisting morphism
      𝜏 : coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ) → H𝑘 solves the Maurer–Cartan equation.
 (ii) The PBW filtration on H𝑘 produces an associated graded that is quadratic-Koszul in the classical
      sense.
   These two properties–-acyclicity of twisted tensor products and classical Koszulness of the associated
graded–-are the recognition criteria for chiral Koszulness. The point is not that the chiral algebra itself is
quadratic (it is not), but that the PBW filtration by bar-length makes the leading-order structure quadratic-
Koszul (Theorem 9.1.25). These criteria apply equally to the Virasoro algebra (quartic pole in the 𝑇 𝑇
OPE), W-algebras (poles of arbitrarily high order), and Yangians (spectral-parameter relations), none of
which admit a quadratic presentation.

9.1.1   Construction layer: twisting data
Before imposing any Koszulness hypothesis, we record the constructions that exist for every augmented
chiral algebra. The bar construction 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) and cobar construction Ω 𝑋 (C) are defined in Chapter 6
for any augmented A and any conilpotent complete coalgebra C. The Koszul property is a recognition
criterion on these constructions, not a prerequisite for their existence.
Deﬁnition 9.1.1 (Chiral twisting datum). A chiral twisting datum on a smooth curve 𝑋 is a quadruple
(A , C , 𝜏, 𝐹• ) consisting of:
   (i) an augmented chiral algebra A ∈ Factaug ( 𝑋 );
  (ii) a conilpotent complete factorization coalgebra C ∈ CoFactconil,comp ( 𝑋 );
 (iii) a degree +1 morphism 𝜏 : C → A satisfying the Maurer–Cartan equation 𝑑𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 in the
       convolution dg Lie algebra;
 (iv) an exhaustive bounded-below filtration 𝐹• on A, C, 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A), and Ω 𝑋 (C), compatible with all
       structure maps.
Associated to 𝜏 are the twisted tensor products

        𝐾𝜏𝐿 (A , C) := (A ⊗ C , 𝑑 A + 𝑑 C + 𝑑𝜏𝐿 ) ,     𝐾𝜏𝑅 (C , A) := (C ⊗ A , 𝑑 C + 𝑑 A + 𝑑𝜏𝑅 ) .

Deﬁnition 9.1.3 (Chiral Koszul morphism). A chiral twisting datum (A , C , 𝜏, 𝐹• ) is Koszul if:
   (i) both 𝐾𝜏𝐿 (A , C) and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 (C , A) are acyclic;
  (ii) the associated graded (gr A , gr C , gr 𝜏 ) is quadratic/Koszul in the ordinary operadic sense;
 (iii) the filtration converges strongly on 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) and Ω 𝑋 (C).
Remark 9.1.4 (Construction versus resolution). For every augmented chiral algebra A, the bar 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) and
cobar Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A)) exist as constructions. But the counit Ω 𝑋 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A)) → A is a quasi-isomorphism
only when 𝜏 is a Koszul morphism (Theorem 6.12.1). Off the Koszul locus, the bar-cobar object persists in
the provisional coderived category Dco
                                     prov ( 𝑋 ) (Appendix P.11.2), not in the ordinary derived category. This is
the chiral/factorization analogue of the fundamental theorem of twisting morphisms [135, Theorem 2.3.1].
      The following lemmas make the mapping-cone identifications explicit, as required for Theorem 9.1.8.

twisting datum. There is a natural identification of chain complexes

                                         𝐾𝜏𝐿 (A , C) ≃ Cone( 𝜀𝜏 ) [−1]

where 𝜀𝜏 : Ω 𝑋 (C) → A is the canonical counit. In particular, 𝐾𝜏𝐿 is acyclic if and only if 𝜀𝜏 is a quasi-
isomorphism.

Proof. Decompose the total differential on A ⊗ b C as 𝑑 A + 𝑑 C + 𝑑𝜏𝐿 . The 𝑑𝜏𝐿 component acts as the cobar
differential on the C-factor and as the 𝜀𝜏 -induced augmentation on the A-factor. The resulting complex
is exactly the mapping cone of 𝜀𝜏 : Ω 𝑋 (C) → A shifted by [−1]: the rows of the double complex are
A ← A ⊗ C ← A ⊗ C ⊗2 ← · · · , which is the bar-type resolution of the augmentation map. This is the
chiral analogue of [135, Lemma 2.2.5].

Lemma 9.1.6 (Right twisted tensor product as mapping cone; [proved]). Under the same hypotheses,
there is a natural identification
                                  𝐾𝜏𝑅 (C , A) ≃ Cone( 𝜂𝜏 ) [−1]
where 𝜂𝜏 : C → 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) is the canonical unit. In particular, 𝐾𝜏𝑅 is acyclic if and only if 𝜂𝜏 is a weak
equivalence.

Proof. Dual to Lemma 9.1.5: the 𝑑𝜏𝑅 component on C b ⊗ A acts as the bar differential on the A-factor and
as the 𝜂𝜏 -induced augmentation on the C-factor, identifying 𝐾𝜏𝑅 with Cone( 𝜂𝜏 ) [−1].
9.1. From the Heisenberg example to general twisting data                                                   559


Lemma 9.1.7 (Filtered comparison; [proved]). Let (A , C , 𝜏, 𝐹• ) be a chiral twisting datum whose
filtration is exhaustive, complete, and bounded below. If 𝜀𝜏 is a quasi-isomorphism, then:
(a) the associated graded datum (gr A , gr C , gr 𝜏 ) is a classical Koszul datum;
(b) both twisted tensor products 𝐾𝜏𝐿 and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 are acyclic.

Proof. Filter 𝜀𝜏 by 𝐹• . Since the filtration is bounded below and complete, the spectral sequence converges
strongly (Eilenberg–Moore). The associated graded gr 𝜀𝜏 is a quasi-isomorphism between graded objects,
which by [135, Theorem 3.2.1] identifies gr 𝜏 as a classical Koszul morphism. Classical Koszulity gives
acyclicity of the associated graded twisted tensor products. Strong convergence then lifts this to acyclicity
of 𝐾𝜏𝐿 and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 themselves.

Theorem 9.1.8 (Fundamental theorem of chiral twisting morphisms; [proved]). [Regime:
quadratic (Convention 2.9.2).]
This is the chiral analogue of [135, Theorem 2.3.1]. For a chiral twisting datum (A , C , 𝜏, 𝐹• )
(Definition 9.1.1), the following are equivalent:
   (i) 𝜏 is a chiral Koszul morphism (Definition 9.1.3).
  (ii) The canonical counit 𝜀𝜏 : Ω 𝑋 (C) → A is a quasi-isomorphism.
 (iii) The canonical unit 𝜂𝜏 : C → 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) is a weak equivalence of conilpotent complete factorization
       coalgebras.
 (iv) Both twisted tensor products 𝐾𝜏𝐿 (A , C) and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 (C , A) are acyclic.

Proof. The equivalence follows the same logical structure as the classical case [135, Theorem 2.3.1], adapted
to the chiral/factorization setting.
     (i)⇒(iv): By definition (Definition 9.1.3, condition 1).
     (iv)⇒(ii): By Lemma 9.1.5, 𝐾𝜏𝐿 ≃ Cone( 𝜀𝜏 ) [−1]. Acyclicity of 𝐾𝜏𝐿 is therefore equivalent to 𝜀𝜏 being
a quasi-isomorphism.
     (iv)⇒(iii): By Lemma 9.1.6, 𝐾𝜏𝑅 ≃ Cone( 𝜂𝜏 ) [−1]. Acyclicity of 𝐾𝜏𝑅 is therefore equivalent to 𝜂𝜏 being
a weak equivalence.
     (ii)⇒(i): By Lemma 9.1.7: filter Ω 𝑋 (C) by cobar degree; the quasi-isomorphism of 𝜀𝜏 implies classical
Koszulity of the associated graded datum and acyclicity of the twisted tensor products. The convergence
hypothesis (Definition 9.1.3, condition 3) ensures the spectral sequence converges strongly.
     (iii)⇒(i): Filter 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A) by bar degree. The weak equivalence of 𝜂𝜏 implies, by the bar-degree analogue of
Lemma 9.1.7, that the associated graded datum (gr A , gr C , gr 𝜏 ) is classically Koszul. Strong convergence
of the bar-degree spectral sequence (ensured by the completeness and bounded-below hypotheses of the
filtration 𝐹• ) then lifts acyclicity of the associated graded twisted tensor products to acyclicity of 𝐾𝜏𝐿 and
𝐾𝜏𝑅 .

Remark 9.1.10 (Why the MC equation is Stokes’ theorem). The Maurer–Cartan equation 𝑑𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0
is not an imposed axiom. It is forced by the geometry of 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ). The convolution ( 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 ) ( 𝑥 ) = 𝜇 ◦ ( 𝜏 ⊗
𝜏 ) ◦ Δ ( 𝑥 ) evaluates the two-point OPE: it extracts the residue of the propagator 𝜂12 at the collision divisor
𝐷12 ⊂ 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ), then multiplies in A. The term 𝑑𝜏 computes the Stokes boundary on 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ). The MC
equation says: on the compactiﬁed two-point conﬁguration space, the propagator residue is exact. At three
points, this becomes the Arnold relation. At 𝑛 points, 𝑑bar  2 = 0.

    At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the propagator acquires monodromy, the Stokes argument picks up a curvature term
𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 𝑔 , and 𝜏 becomes curved (Remark 8.15.14).

  products acyclic.

  𝐻 0  C.
• A2 : geometric bar-cobar duality (Theorem 9.1.39): for a chiral dual pair, Verdier duality intertwines bar

A0 is the Koszul recognition theorem; A1 extracts the dual coalgebra; A2 links two Koszul data via Verdier
geometry.

9.1.2   The concept of chiral Koszul pairs: precise formulation
To handle non-quadratic examples, we extend the notion of Koszul pairs beyond the quadratic setting. The
defining property is a set of recognition criteria–-checkable conditions on the pair–-from which the full
bar-cobar identification follows as a theorem. No quasi-isomorphism statement is built into the definition
itself.
Deﬁnition 9.1.14 (Chiral Koszul pair). A chiral Koszul pair on a smooth projective curve 𝑋 is a pair of
chiral Koszul data (Definition 9.1.1, Definition 9.1.3)

                                    (A1 , C1 , 𝜏1 , 𝐹• ) ,   (A2 , C2 , 𝜏2 , 𝐹• )

equipped with Verdier-compatible identifications

                                   𝔻Ran (C1 ) ≃ C2 ,         𝔻Ran (C2 ) ≃ C1 ,

compatible with the twisting morphisms and filtrations. In this situation we write A2 ≃ A1! and A1 ≃ A2! .
These are antecedent hypotheses: the twisting data (Definition 9.1.1), the Koszulness condition
(Definition 9.1.3), and Verdier compatibility can all be verified without invoking bar-cobar duality itself.
Theorem 9.1.39 then proves the full bar-cobar identification as a consequence.
Standard construction. For the standard examples, the Koszul pair is constructed as follows: C𝑖 = 𝐵¯ 𝑋 (A 𝑖 )
with the canonical twisting morphism, 𝐹• is the PBW filtration (Theorem 9.1.25), acyclicity follows from
spectral sequence degeneration, and Verdier compatibility from Theorem 6.3.32. The Heisenberg pair
(H𝑘 , Symch (𝑉 ∗ )) is the prototype (§1.5).
Example 9.1.15 (Heisenberg specialization). For the Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 at level 𝑘 ≠ 0, Definition 9.1.14
yields the Koszul pair (H𝑘 , Symch (𝑉 ∗ )), where H𝑘 is Liech -type (generated by a single bosonic field 𝑎 ( 𝑧 )
with OPE 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑘 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 ) and Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) is Comch -type–-the chiral incarnation of classical
Lie–Com duality. Theorem 9.1.39 yields 𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 ) ≃ Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) ! : the bar complex 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) was computed
degree by degree in §1.1–§1.3, producing exactly the commutative Koszul dual (§1.5). Because H𝑘 is abelian,
the PBW spectral sequence (Theorem 9.1.25) is trivial and the Koszul complex 𝐾𝜏 (H𝑘 , Symch (𝑉 ∗ )) is
manifestly acyclic.

9.1.3     Filtered states and chain maps
A filtration records the leading part of a differential, but it does not determine the differential or a com-
parison map. For current algebras, three operations must be distinguished: filtering the full state space,
taking sections of the collision sheaves, and lifting a graded map. We construct the filtration and the lifting
equations separately. The obstruction already occurs in a complex with two basis vectors.
   All complexes are cohomologically graded over ℂ, with differential of degree 1. Tensor products of
vector spaces are algebraic, and 𝐶 [ 𝑘 ] 𝑛 = 𝐶 𝑛+𝑘 . A degree- 𝑎 map 𝑢 : 𝐶 → 𝑇 has differential 𝜕𝑢 = 𝑑𝑇 𝑢 −
(−1) 𝑎 𝑢𝑑𝐶 . Thus a chain map has degree zero and satisfies 𝜕𝑢 = 0.
9.1.3.1 A graded map that has no chain lift
An increasing filtration on a complex 𝐶 consists of subcomplexes 𝐹𝑝 −1 𝐶 ⊆ 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 , with 𝐹−1 𝐶 = 0. It is
exhaustive if every element belongs to some 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 . Its graded piece is gr 𝑝 𝐶 = 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 / 𝐹𝑝 −1 𝐶 . A filtered map
sends 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 into 𝐹𝑝𝑇 .
Example 9.1.17 (The ﬁrst lifting obstruction). Let 𝐶 0 = 𝑇 0 = ℂ 𝑥 and 𝐶 1 = 𝑇 1 = ℂ 𝑧 . Give both spaces
the filtration 𝐹0 = ℂ 𝑧 , 𝐹1 = ℂ 𝑥 ⊕ ℂ 𝑧 . Set 𝑑𝐶 = 0, while 𝑑𝑇 𝑥 = 𝑧 and 𝑑𝑇 𝑧 = 0. Both associated graded
differentials vanish, so their graded complexes and first cohomology pages agree. Any degree-zero map
inducing the identity on the graded pieces must send 𝑥 to 𝑥 and 𝑧 to 𝑧 . The chain equation on 𝑥 would
then give 𝑧 = 0, a contradiction.
    Equivalently, use the decreasing filtration 𝐺 0 = 𝐶 , 𝐺 1 = ℂ 𝑧 , 𝐺 2 = 0. Then 𝑥 has filtration index zero
and 𝑧 has index one. The target has a nonzero first page differential [ 𝑥 ] ↦→ [ 𝑧 ], whereas the source has
none. Putting 𝑥 in increasing order 𝑁 and 𝑧 in order zero moves the same obstruction to order 𝑁 . Every
earlier differential then vanishes.

    There is another distinction between states and an augmentation ideal. An augmentation of a unital
current vertex algebra to the trivial vertex algebra ℂ1 must preserve its products and vacuum. The first cur-

kills the currents, preservation of this product implies 0 = 𝑘𝜅 ( 𝑎, 𝑏 ). At nonzero level and nonzero 𝜅 , such
an augmentation does not exist. The positive-energy vector subspace above is therefore not automatically
a chiral augmentation ideal. A curved or relative bar construction requires its specified coefficient and

Lemma 9.1.20 (Symbols of tensor coefficients). For filtered complex vector spaces with 𝐹−1 = 0, the
canonical map
                            gr 𝑝1 𝐴1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ gr 𝑝𝑏 𝐴𝑏 −→ gr 𝑝 ( 𝐴1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝐴𝑏 )
                    M
                        𝑝1 +···+ 𝑝𝑏 = 𝑝

is an isomorphism. The same assertion holds for tensor products of sheaves over their coefficient ring if
their filtrations split locally through each finite order. If all coefficient maps and differentials are filtered,
the isomorphism intertwines their symbols.

Proof. Choose complements 𝐴𝑖,𝑟 to 𝐹𝑟 −1 𝐴𝑖 in 𝐹𝑟 𝐴𝑖 . Up to order 𝑝, the tensor product is the direct sum of
the tensors with 𝑟𝑖 ≤ 𝑝. Quotienting by order 𝑝 − 1 leaves precisely 𝑟𝑖 = 𝑝. The resulting map sends
                  P                                                         P
a tensor of classes to the class of its tensor, so it is independent of the complements. Local splittings give
the identical argument for sheaves. Their canonical maps agree on overlaps and therefore glue. Applying
any filtered map before or after passing to classes gives the same element, proving compatibility.

   For chiral coefficients, the actual input includes state sheaves away from collisions and maps to diagonal-
supported targets. These maps need not be multiplication of two vectors in a fixed fiber. To apply the
preceding lemma to a chiral bar model, one must supply the full coefficient sheaves, their localized or
extended domains, and their typed collision maps. Each map must preserve (9.2), including every lower-
pole and regular contribution selected by its test form. The coordinate transitions, coefficient connection
566                                                                        Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


and twisting terms must preserve the same filtration. Their symbols must be compared with the proposed
graded differential on those same sheaves. Flatness of the state fibers does not construct any of these maps.
   For current pairs, the regular normally ordered product has order two, the bracket coefficient has order
one, and the central coefficient has order zero. Consequently the leading operator in the order filtration is
determined by the test-form residue and its degree in state order. It is not determined by the order of the
OPE pole. A bracket that lowers state order appears in a lower filtration component, rather than in the
order-preserving differential.

   This lemma specifies the algebraic signs and filtration requirements for a twisting term. In a chiral model,
the coproduct, coefficient action and twisting map must have their actual sheaf domains and diagonal

only if that defect acts by zero.
9.1.3.5 Sections and their graded lifting obstruction
Let K 𝑛 be a sheaf with filtration 𝐹𝑝 K 𝑛 , and use honest global sections 𝐾 𝑛 = Γ (𝑌 , K 𝑛 ). Set 𝐹𝑝 𝐾 𝑛 =
Γ (𝑌 , 𝐹𝑝 K 𝑛 ). The natural map

                                      gr 𝑝 Γ (𝑌 , K 𝑛 ) −→ Γ (𝑌 , gr 𝑝 K 𝑛 )                              (9.4)

is injective, but need not be surjective. For a global symbol 𝑠 , choose local lifts 𝑎𝑖 on a cover 𝑈𝑖 . The
differences 𝑎𝑗 − 𝑎𝑖 belong to 𝐹𝑝 −1 K 𝑛 and satisfy the cocycle equation on triple intersections. Changing
the lifts changes this cocycle by a coboundary. Its class vanishes, possibly after refining the cover, exactly
when the lifts can be adjusted to glue. This gives the exact obstruction to surjectivity of (9.4). Here a
degree-one Čech class means such overlap cocycles modulo coboundaries and refinement.
Example 9.1.23 (A locally split ﬁltration with no global lift). For algebraic sheaves on ℙ1 with homogeneous
coordinates [ 𝑋 : 𝑌 ], use
                                             (−𝑌 ,𝑋 )              ( 𝑋 ,𝑌 )
                            0 −→ O (−2) −−−−−−→ O (−1) ⊕2 −−−−−→ O −→ 0.

The two sections 𝑋 , 𝑌 never vanish together, so the sequence is exact and locally split. Filter the middle
bundle by 𝐹0 = O (−2) and 𝐹1 = O (−1) ⊕2 . Every graded piece is locally free. Nevertheless, Γ (O (−1) ⊕2 ) = 0,
while Γ (O) = ℂ.
    The failure can be computed without a dimension formula for sheaf cohomology. On 𝑋 ≠ 0, write
𝑧 = 𝑌 / 𝑋 and choose the lift (1, 0) in the 𝑋 −1 frame. On 𝑌 ≠ 0, choose (0, 1) in the 𝑌 −1 frame, which
becomes (0, 𝑧 −1 ) on the overlap. Their difference (−1, 𝑧 −1 ) equals 𝑧 −1 (− 𝑧, 1). Thus the obstruction is
𝑧 −1 in the 𝑋 −2 frame of O (−2). Coboundaries lie in ℂ[ 𝑧 ] + 𝑧 −2 ℂ[ 𝑧 −1 ], which has no 𝑧 −1 coefficient.
The class is nonzero. The same transition description shows that a global section of O (−1) would lie in
ℂ[ 𝑧 ] ∩ 𝑧 −1 ℂ[ 𝑧 −1 ] = 0.
   Replacing Γ by a Čech or derived section complex changes the carrier. Such a change can be useful,
but it requires its own comparison with the stated native complex. Even exhaustive sheaf filtrations need
not give exhaustive filtrations on global sections without a uniform finite order for each section. Both
conditions must therefore be checked on the chosen section carrier.
9.1.3.6 A filtered criterion with its exact hypotheses
Theorem 9.1.24 (Filtered acyclicity). Let ( 𝐾 , 𝑑 ) have an exhaustive increasing filtration with 𝐹−1 𝐾 =
0 and 𝑑𝐹𝑝 ⊆ 𝐹𝑝 . If 𝐻 𝑛 (gr 𝑝 𝐾 ) = 0 for every 𝑝, then 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐾 ) = 0. No finite-dimensionality or completion
assumption is needed. If a filtered chain map 𝑓 : 𝐶 → 𝑇 has a quasi-isomorphism on associated graded
complexes, it is a quasi-isomorphism.

Proof. A cycle 𝑥 has finite order 𝑝. Its symbol is a graded cycle, hence the differential of a symbol of degree
𝑛 − 1. Choose a lift 𝑦 ∈ 𝐹𝑝 𝐾 𝑛−1 of that primitive. Then 𝑥 − 𝑑𝑦 has order at most 𝑝 − 1. Repeat until
order −1, which is zero. The finite sum of the chosen 𝑦 is a primitive for 𝑥 .
568                                                                       Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


    For the map assertion use Cone( 𝑓 ) 𝑛 = 𝑇 𝑛 ⊕ 𝐶 𝑛+1 with differential 𝐷 ( 𝑦, 𝑥 ) = ( 𝑑𝑇 𝑦 + 𝑓 𝑥, − 𝑑𝐶 𝑥 )
and the sum filtration. Its graded complex is the cone of gr 𝑓 and is acyclic. The first assertion makes the full
cone acyclic. For a target cycle 𝑦 , a primitive of ( 𝑦, 0) expresses its class as 𝑓 [ 𝑥 ], proving surjectivity. If 𝑥 is

proving injectivity.

Theorem 9.1.25 (PBW criterion on a supplied chiral coefficient complex). Let 𝐾 = 𝐵¯ ch (A) ⊗𝜏 A
denote a specified native cochain complex, including its full state sheaves, section functor, collision maps
and twisting differential. Assume the following conditions.
   (i) Its state-order filtration is (9.2) on every coefficient tensor and includes all collision strata with
       their grading shifts. The actual differential and transitions preserve it. The tensor symbol maps are
       isomorphisms on the supplied coefficient sheaves.
  (ii) After the prescribed section functor, the graded symbol complex has a specified, order-preserving
       chain isomorphism or quasi-isomorphism to a graded complex 𝐾0 whose positive-degree cohomology

       only of state vector spaces.
 (iii) On the chosen global section carrier, the filtration is exhaustive, 𝐹−1 𝐾 = 0, and the global symbol

Then 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐾 ) = 0 for 𝑛 > 0. Thus this specified native Koszul complex is acyclic in the degrees required
for chiral Koszulness.

Proof. The first condition defines a filtered cochain complex on the stated carrier. The third condition
identifies its graded section complex with the sections of the symbol complex. In the second condition, the
comparison and vanishing are understood on this same section carrier, so they give 𝐻 𝑛 (gr 𝑝 𝐾 ) = 0 for
every 𝑝 and 𝑛 > 0. Theorem 9.1.24 applies. In particular, no finite-dimensional state count is substituted
for a global section comparison or a filtration bound.

    The classical polynomial resolution is one possible graded complex, but it must be identified by an
actual map. For a vector space 𝑉 with basis 𝑥 𝑖 , put 𝑃 = Sym(𝑉 ) ⊗ Λ ( 𝑒 𝑖 ), with | 𝑥 𝑖 | = 0, | 𝑒 𝑖 | = −1 and
𝑑𝑒 𝑖 = 𝑥 𝑖 . The differential extends by the graded Leibniz rule and squares to zero. The degree-minus-one
derivation ℎ defined by ℎ ( 𝑥 𝑖 ) = 𝑒 𝑖 and ℎ ( 𝑒 𝑖 ) = 0 satisfies 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 = 𝑁 on monomials of total polyno-
mial and exterior length 𝑁 . Indeed its anticommutator is a degree-zero derivation fixing every generator.
Consequently ℎ/ 𝑁 contracts every positive length, leaving only the constant class. Each expression is finite
even for an infinite basis. This proves polynomial Koszul exactness internally, but supplies no map from a
localized chiral coefficient complex to 𝑃 .

Lemma 9.1.31 (The algebraic operator domain). The linear current term and the normal-ordered cubic
term define locally finite degree-one, energy-zero operators on 𝑀 ⊗ F . The same holds after adding the
stated charge term.

Proof. For 𝑣 ∈ 𝑀ℎ , the modes with 𝑚 > ℎ annihilate 𝑣 . For 𝑚 ≤ 0, the ghost 𝑐 𝑎,𝑚 annihilates a fixed
exterior monomial unless that monomial contains 𝑏 𝑎,𝑚 . Thus the linear sum has finitely many nonzero
terms on every pure tensor.
    In a normal-ordered cubic monomial, all annihilators act before all creators. Every annihilator must
match one of the finitely many occupied creation variables of the input. Their indices therefore range over
a finite set. The Lie grading gives 𝑚𝑘 = 𝑚𝑖 + 𝑚𝑗 , so each cubic term has total energy zero. Its creation
energies are nonnegative, and their sum equals the energy removed by the annihilators. Only finitely many
creation variables have energy at most that fixed sum, including the finite-dimensional zero-mode space.
If a term has no annihilators, its creators all have energy zero, giving the same finiteness conclusion. This
proves local finiteness on each exterior monomial and hence on every algebraic input. The operator degrees
follow from | 𝑐 | = 1 and | 𝑏 | = −1.

   The square-zero identity is a separate condition on these actual operators. It depends on the coefficient
action, central generators and polarization. On a completion allowing infinitely many excitations, the
preceding algebraic proof does not establish continuity or convergence.

   The example does not identify a general chiral bar complex with either target. It shows why a pro-
posed semi-infinite comparison must specify its central treatment and differential before computing a
page. Likewise, conformal energy does not identify the full ghost space with exterior powers of the zero
modes. Positive-energy creation operators remain in its graded pieces. Discarding them requires a proved
contraction or another comparison map.
9.1.3.10 The native comparison and its descent conditions
Suppose the full native bar complex 𝐶 and a specified square-zero semi-infinite target 𝑇 have been con-
structed. Their filtrations must be defined on all state, form and ghost factors. A proposed initial map
must be a chain map 𝑓0 : gr 𝐶 → gr 𝑇 on those actual carriers. An isomorphism to the cohomology of a
finite-dimensional Lie algebra is not such a construction. Given 𝑓0 , equations (9.5)–(9.6) state exactly what
each higher collision or mode correction must solve. If their obstructions vanish compatibly, they give the
actual map 𝐹 . If 𝑓0 is a quasi-isomorphism and the stated algebraic or complete filtration hypotheses hold,
the cone construction supplies its inverse and homotopies. These are conditional conclusions about the
specified native objects.
    If a sheaf or differential-operator comparison is required, the corrections must belong to the correspond-
ing complex of morphisms. The vector-space splittings in (9.7) need not preserve coefficient multiplication,
differential operators or restriction maps. One may use that formula in such a category only when the
displayed projections and homotopies have those compatibilities. Otherwise the obstruction must be solved
in that smaller morphism complex.
    For local maps 𝐹𝑖 on a cover, a first overlap homotopy has degree −1 and must satisfy

                                              𝜕 𝐻𝑖𝑗 = 𝐹𝑗 − 𝐹𝑖 .

The triple-overlap difference 𝐻𝑗 𝑘 − 𝐻𝑖𝑘 + 𝐻𝑖𝑗 is closed. For the total differential 𝛿 + (−1) 𝑟 𝜕 in Čech
degree 𝑟 , the next required map has degree −2 and satisfies

                                      𝜕 𝐾𝑖𝑗 𝑘 = −( 𝐻𝑗 𝑘 − 𝐻𝑖𝑘 + 𝐻𝑖𝑗 ) .

Closedness follows by applying 𝜕 and cancelling the three differences of 𝐹𝑖 . Existence of 𝐾 requires that
closed map to be a boundary. Further overlaps give the analogous equations in lower internal degrees.
Strict descent requires the maps themselves to agree on overlaps; homotopy-coherent descent instead uses
these additional maps and a specified total section complex. Neither replaces the underived global sections
silently.
    Thus the remaining native construction consists of filtered collision and twisting operators on the
full state sheaves, the global symbol comparison, and a specified polarized semi-infinite differential. One
574                                                                   Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


must then provide 𝑓0 and solve its filtered and overlap equations in the required coefficient category. The
state-level PBW basis, the polynomial Koszul contraction, and an identification of first pages do not supply
these maps.
Remark 9.1.33 (State symbols and the chiral coeﬃcient complex). The polynomial contraction above proves
exactness of a classical polynomial Koszul resolution. Applying it to a native chiral complex requires the
symbol map and global-section hypotheses of Theorem 9.1.25. The current and Virasoro state bases supply
the state filtration. They do not identify the full collision sheaves or their differential with that polynomial
resolution.

Theorem 9.1.38 (Bar concentration for Koszul pairs; [proved]). [Regime: quadratic on the Koszul
locus (Convention 2.9.2).]
   Let (A1 , A2 ) be a chiral Koszul pair (Definition 9.1.14). Then the augmented bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ),
equipped with its bigrading by bar degree 𝑝 and bar-differential cohomological degree 𝑞 , satisfies:
                     𝐻 𝑝,𝑞 ( 𝐵¯ ch (A1 )) = 0 for 𝑞 ≠ 0,         𝐻 𝑝,0 ( 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ))  (A2! ) 𝑝 .
Equivalently, 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) ≃ A2! in the derived category of graded chiral coalgebras, where A2! carries its
internal grading concentrated in bar-differential degree 0. In particular, the natural map 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) → A2!
is a quasi-isomorphism of graded chiral coalgebras.
Proof. Filter 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) by bar degree. By the PBW criterion (Theorem 9.1.25), the associated graded is the
classical Koszul complex of gr 𝐹 A1 , which is acyclic in positive degrees by hypothesis. Corollary 9.1.36
then gives dim 𝐻 𝑛 = dim(A2! )𝑛 . It remains to show that 𝐻 0 ( 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ))  A2! as coalgebras, not merely
as graded vector spaces. The twisting morphism 𝜏 : 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) → A2 satisfies the Maurer–Cartan equa-
tion 𝜕 ( 𝜏 ) + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 in the chiral convolution algebra Hom( 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) , A2 ) (Definition 9.1.3), so the
twisted tensor products 𝐾𝜏𝐿 (A1 , C1 ) and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 (C1 , A1 ) are well-defined chain complexes (twisted differ-
entials square to zero by the MC equation). These are acyclic by hypothesis. Now 𝜏 induces a coalgebra
map 𝜏∗ : 𝐻 0 ( 𝐵¯ ch (A1 )) → A2! that preserves comultiplication: the bar comultiplication Δ 𝐵¯ on 𝐻 0 is
intertwined with the Koszul dual coalgebra structure on A2! via the convolution product defining 𝜏 .
Acyclicity of 𝐾𝜏𝐿 and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 upgrades this map from a graded comparison to a coalgebra isomorphism (the
chiral analogue of [135, Theorem 2.3.1]; the identical argument applies because acyclicity of the Koszul
complexes is the only input beyond the MC equation, and both hold in the chiral setting by Lemma 6.3.8
and Theorem 9.1.8).

Koszul dual is the RTT algebra for 𝑅 −1 .
   For the Yang 𝑅-matrix, 𝑅 −1 ( 𝑢) = (1 − ℏ 𝑃 /𝑢) −1 ; since 𝑃 2 = id, the geometric series gives

to the exterior algebra (i.e., Sym! = ). Both limits are consistent.

Proposition 9.2.2 (Yangian Koszulness for all simple 𝔤; [proved]). For every simple Lie algebra 𝔤,
the Yangian 𝑌 (𝔤) in the RTT presentation is Koszul: the bar spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 and the
quadratic dual computed above is the true Koszul dual.

Proof. This follows from the Polishchuk–Positselski PBW criterion [198, Ch. 4] applied to 𝑌 (𝔤). The
three hypotheses are verified as follows.
  (i) PBW basis. Molev [72] establishes a PBW basis for 𝑌 (𝔤) in the RTT presentation for every simple 𝔤:
      ordered monomials in the generators {𝑇𝑖𝑗( 𝑟 ) } form a vector space basis, and the associated graded
      is the polynomial algebra Sym(𝑉 ) with 𝑉 = 𝑟 ≥0 End(ℂ 𝑁 ) 𝑟 , 𝑁 = dim 𝑉0 the dimension of the
                                                     L
      chosen fundamental representation. This gives a flat deformation from 𝑌 (𝔤) to Sym(𝑉 ).
  (ii) Quadraticity. The RTT relation (24.1) is quadratic in the generators 𝑇𝑖𝑗( 𝑟 ) , so 𝑌 (𝔤) is a quadratic
       algebra in the sense of Polishchuk–Positselski.
 (iii) Local ﬁniteness. Each level component 𝑉𝑟 = span{𝑇𝑖𝑗( 𝑟 ) } has dimension 𝑁 2 = (dim 𝑉0 ) 2 , which is
       finite and independent of 𝑟 . Since the RTT relation is homogeneous of degree 𝑟 + 𝑠 in the level grad-
       ing, the quadratic algebra is locally finite in a non-negative connected grading. This holds uniformly
       for all simple 𝔤 –- no case-by-case verification is needed.
The Polishchuk–Positselski criterion then gives: the PBW flat deformation from 𝑌 (𝔤) to Sym(𝑉 ) transfers
acyclicity of the Koszul complex 𝐾 (Sym(𝑉 )) = Sym(𝑉 ) ⊗ (𝑉 ∗ ) to acyclicity of 𝐾 (𝑌 (𝔤)), proving
                                                               V
Koszulness.

9.3     The three-stage construction: resolving the circularity
9.3.1   The circularity problem
Problem 9.3.1 (Circularity in Koszul duality). In stating " 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) ≃ A2! ", we face a logical gap:
   (i) We have not given an independent deﬁnition of A2! as a chiral coalgebra
  (ii) We have not proven that A2! satisfies coalgebra axioms
 (iii) We have not constructed the quasi-isomorphism 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) −
                                                                 ∼
                                                                 → A!      2

   For quadratic algebras, the classical orthogonality criterion 𝑅1 ⊥ 𝑅2 suffices. But for non-quadratic
algebras (Virasoro, W-algebras, affine Yangian), this fails completely.
Remark 9.3.2. A chiral coalgebra encodes how fields decompose rather than how they compose. The
coproduct Δ : C → C ⊠ C describes how one insertion splits into two–-the inverse of the chiral product.

9.3.3    Stage 2: verification of coalgebra axioms
Theorem 9.3.5 (Coalgebra structure on A 2! ; [proved]). The structure (A2! , Δ, 𝜖, 𝑑! ) defined in Defi-
nition 9.3.3 satisfies:
   (i) Coassociativity: ( Δ ⊠ id) ◦ Δ = (id ⊠ Δ) ◦ Δ
  (ii) Counit axiom: ( 𝜖 ⊠ id) ◦ Δ = id = (id ⊠ 𝜖 ) ◦ Δ
 (iii) Coderivation property: Δ ◦ 𝑑! = ( 𝑑! ⊠ id + id ⊠ 𝑑! ) ◦ Δ
 (iv) Nilpotence: 𝑑!2 = 0
   Therefore, A2! is a chiral coalgebra in the sense of Beilinson–Drinfeld.

-it is part of the universal property defining ‘‘cofree’’.

splittings into three factors.

Remark 9.3.6. Theorem 9.3.5 exhibits the characteristic feature of Koszul duality: associativity of the
algebra A2 is equivalent to nilpotence of the coalgebra differential 𝑑! . Algebraic structure on one side
translates to cohomological structure on the dual side.

Lemma 9.3.8 (Completion convergence; [proved]). For chiral algebras satisfying:
• Finite generation over D 𝑋
• Polynomial growth of structure constants
• Formal smoothness: dim 𝐻 ∗ (A , A) < ∞
   The completion converges and:
                                                 𝐵¯\

Proof of Lemma. The conilpotent ﬁltration on 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) is:

                                         𝐹𝑛 = { 𝑐 ∈ 𝐵¯ : Δ̄ ( 𝑛 ) ( 𝑐 ) = 0}

   Geometrically: 𝐹𝑛 consists of forms with "≥ 𝑛 nested collisions".
   The estimates are as follows:
• Finite generation ⇒ dim( 𝐼 𝑛 ∩ 𝐵¯ 𝑘 ) bounded by a polynomial in 𝑛, 𝑘
• Polynomial growth ⇒ Structure constants | 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 | ≤ 𝑃 ( 𝑚) for some polynomial 𝑃
• Formal smoothness ⇒ Hochschild cohomology controls deformations
   We verify the Mittag-Leﬄer condition for the inverse system { 𝐵¯ / 𝐼 𝑛 }: for each fixed bar degree 𝑘 and
each internal (conformal weight) degree ℎ, the component 𝐵¯ 𝑘,ℎ is finite-dimensional. Indeed, finite gen-
eration over D 𝑋 ensures that the space of sections Γ ( 𝐶 𝑘+1 ( 𝑋 ) , A ⊠( 𝑘+1) ⊗ Ω∗log ) in each conformal
weight is a finitely generated D 𝑋 -module, hence finite-dimensional after taking global sections on the
proper variety 𝐶 𝑘+1 ( 𝑋 ). The 𝐼 -adic filtration 𝐼 𝑛 ∩ 𝐵¯ 𝑘,ℎ is therefore a descending chain of subspaces of
a finite-dimensional vector space, which necessarily stabilizes: for each ( 𝑘, ℎ), there exists 𝑁 ( 𝑘, ℎ) such
that 𝐼 𝑛 ∩ 𝐵¯ 𝑘,ℎ = 𝐼 𝑁 ( 𝑘,ℎ ) ∩ 𝐵¯ 𝑘,ℎ for all 𝑛 ≥ 𝑁 ( 𝑘, ℎ). This is precisely the Mittag-Leffler condition for
the inverse system { 𝐵¯ 𝑘,ℎ / 𝐼 𝑛 }𝑛 ≥0 , which ensures lim1 = 0 and the inverse limit is exact (cf. Weibel [110],
                                                         ←−
Proposition 3.5.7).

   This completes the proof of Theorem 9.3.7.

Remark 9.3.9 (Frontier completion package). The completion convergence argument above is the finite-
stage precursor to the systematic completion framework developed in Appendix P. The present chapter
treats only the case where the bar complex is finite-dimensional in each bidegree; the full 𝐼 -adic comple-
tion theory, including the Mittag-Leffler exhaustion and the derived-limit control needed for infinite-type
algebras, belongs to the frontier package of that appendix. The theorematic core of this chapter does not
depend on the frontier hypotheses of Appendix P.
Corollary 9.3.10 (Circularity-free Koszul duality; [proved]). Let A be a chiral algebra on a
smooth curve 𝑋 satisfying:
  (i) A = 𝑇chiral (V)/( 𝑅) is finitely generated over D 𝑋 ,
  (ii) the OPE structure constants satisfy polynomial growth: | 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 | ≤ 𝑃 ( 𝑚) for a polynomial 𝑃 ,
586                                                                    Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


 (iii) A is formally smooth: dim 𝐻ch
                                   ∗ (A , A) < ∞.

Then there exists a chiral coalgebra A ! , defined without reference to the bar construction, together with a
natural quasi-isomorphism of differential graded chiral coalgebras

                                               Φ : 𝐵¯ ch
                                                               ∼
                                                    \    (A) −−→ A !

where 𝐵¯ ch
       \    (A) is the 𝐼 -adic completion of the geometric bar complex. The construction of A ! and the
proof of Φ being a quasi-isomorphism are logically independent of each other: the dependency chain is

              (V , 𝑅, 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 ) =⇒ (A ! , Δ̄, 𝑑! ) =⇒ 𝑑!2 = 0 =⇒ Φ is a quasi-isomorphism.

For non-quadratic chiral algebras (Virasoro, 𝑊 -algebras, Yangians), the 𝐼 -adic completion is essential: the
uncompleted bar complex is not quasi-isomorphic to A ! .

Proof. The proof proceeds through three logically independent stages, each relying only on the output of
the preceding stage and on configuration space geometry.
Stage 1: Intrinsic construction of A ! .
   Given only the presentation data (V , 𝑅) and the OPE structure constants 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 , we define A ! as in
Definition 9.3.3:
• The underlying D 𝑋 -module is the cofree chiral coalgebra 𝑇chiral
                                                                  𝑐    (V ∨ ), where V ∨ = H𝑜𝑚 O𝑋 (V , 𝜔 𝑋 ).
• The reduced coproduct Δ̄ is the universal deconcatenation coproduct on the cofree coalgebra.
• The differential 𝑑! is the unique coderivation determined on cogenerators by dual OPE data:
                                              ∑︁
                               𝑑! ( 𝜙∗𝑖 ) = −     𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 · ( 𝜙𝑗∗ ⊠ 𝜙∗𝑘 ) ⊗ 𝜂 ⊗ ( 𝑚 −1)
                                              𝑗,𝑘,𝑚 ≥1

  where 𝜂 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) is the standard logarithmic 1-form on 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ).
This definition uses only the data of A (generators, relations, structure constants) and makes no reference
to the bar construction.
Stage 2: Veriﬁcation of coalgebra axioms.
    We must verify four properties, each using only the output of Stage 1 and the geometry of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).
    Coassociativity. The coproduct Δ̄ is coassociative by the universal property of the cofree coalgebra
  𝑐
𝑇chiral (V ∨ ): both ( Δ̄ ⊠ id) ◦ Δ̄ and (id ⊠ Δ̄) ◦ Δ̄ equal the universal decomposition into ordered partitions
of tensor factors.

    The geometric meaning is as follows. Each summand corresponds to a codimension-2 boundary stratum
𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ℓ ⊂ 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ) where three points collide. The three codimension-1 divisors 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 , 𝐷𝑗 ℓ , 𝐷 𝑖ℓ meeting

iterated residues that constitutes 𝑑!2 = 0.
    We emphasise that this verification uses only:
• associativity of the OPE (an intrinsic property of A),
• the boundary geometry of 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ) (Arnold relations).
It does not invoke the bar construction, nor any notion of ‘‘Koszul pair.’’

Logical independence. We record that the argument is circularity-free:
9.4. Explicit calculations: W-algebras and beyond                                                           589


• Stage 1 defines A ! using only (V , 𝑅, 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘,𝑚 )–-no bar construction.
• Stage 2 verifies coalgebra axioms using only OPE associativity and the boundary geometry of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )–-no
  comparison map.
• Stage 3 constructs Φ and proves it is a quasi-isomorphism using Verdier duality and spectral sequences–-
  taking (A ! , 𝑑!2 = 0) as input from Stage 2, never invoking the definition of A ! through the bar construc-
  tion.
The non-quadratic case (Virasoro, 𝑊𝑁 , Yangian) is handled uniformly via 𝐼 -adic completion; the uncom-
pleted statement 𝐵¯ ch (A) ∨ ≃ A ! (bar coalgebra dualizes to the Koszul dual algebra) holds only in the
quadratic case, where 𝐼 -adic and discrete topologies coincide.

Remark 9.3.11 (Comparison with classical Koszul duality). When A is quadratic with relations 𝑅 ⊂
𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (V ⊠2 ), the weight filtration on 𝐵¯ ch (A) is bounded and the spectral sequence of Stage 3d collapses at
𝐸2 . In this case A ! is the classical quadratic dual; no completion is needed, and Corollary 9.3.10 reduces to
the Ginzburg–Kapranov theorem for operads.
    The algebra-coalgebra mirror governs the construction of the dual. For algebras, the Koszul dual is a
quotient of the free algebra: one imposes the orthogonal relations 𝑅⊥ to obtain A ! = 𝑇chiral (V ∨ )/( 𝑅⊥ ).
For coalgebras, the Koszul dual is a sub-coalgebra of the cofree coalgebra: one selects the maximal sub-
coalgebra of 𝑇 𝑐 (V ∨ ) cogenerated by 𝑅⊥ . These are dual operations–-quotients of free objects correspond
to sub-objects of cofree objects under the general principle that relations in an algebra become corelations
in a coalgebra–-and the distinction is forced by the reversal of arrows: a quotient of 𝑇 (V) is a coequalizer,
while a sub-coalgebra of 𝑇 𝑐 (V ∨ ) is an equalizer.
    The configuration space machinery is essential for the non-quadratic case, where the spectral sequence
may not degenerate and the 𝐼 -adic completion is required to ensure convergence.

9.5     The E1 -chiral Koszul duality theorem
The preceding sections developed the bar-cobar adjunction and Koszul pairs for E∞ -chiral algebras (vertex
algebras), where the underlying operad is the commutative chiral operad Comch . The associative case
treats algebras over the associative chiral operad Assch (Definition 2.8.4). This is the setting of nonlocal
vertex algebras (Definition 2.8.3), and the resulting Koszul duality is self-dual by Proposition 2.8.5. The
∞-categorical bar-cobar formalism for algebras over operads that underlies the construction is developed
in [43, §3.1].
596                                                                   Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


9.5.1     Augmented and pro-nilpotent E1 -chiral algebras
Deﬁnition 9.5.1 (Augmented E1 -chiral algebra). An E1 -chiral algebra A is augmented if it is equipped
with a morphism of E1 -chiral algebras 𝜀 : A → 𝜔 𝑋 (the unit chiral algebra). The augmentation ideal is
Ā := ker( 𝜀 ).
Deﬁnition 9.5.2 (Pro-nilpotent and conilpotent). An augmented E1 -chiral algebra A is pro-nilpotent if the
inverse system
                                               ch           ch
                                A ↠ A/Ā ⊗ 2 ↠ A/Ā ⊗ 3 ↠ · · ·
                                        ch
is pro-isomorphic to A, where Ā ⊗ 𝑛 denotes the 𝑛-fold chiral tensor power of the augmentation ideal.
     Dually, a coaugmented E1 -chiral coalgebra C is conilpotent if C = 𝑛 ≥0 𝐹𝑛 C where 𝐹𝑛 C is the coradical
                                                                       S
filtration (the largest sub-coalgebra on which the iterated reduced coproduct Δ̄ ( 𝑛 ) vanishes).
Remark 9.5.3 (Convergence role of pro-nilpotence). Pro-nilpotence ensures the cobar differential
𝑑Ω : Ω (C)𝑛 → Ω (C)𝑛−1 is well-defined: the formula involves a sum over all ways to decompose a
tensor factor via the coproduct, which in general is an infinite series. Conilpotence ensures this sum is
finite in each degree. On the algebra side, pro-nilpotence ensures the bar construction is degree-wise
finite-dimensional. See Appendix P for the completion theory.

9.5.2     The bar-cobar equivalence for Assch
Theorem 9.5.4 ( E 1 -chiral Koszul duality; [proved]). [Regime: quadratic on the Koszul locus; filtered-
complete via PBW degeneration (Convention 2.9.2).]
    The bar-cobar adjunction restricts to an equivalence of ∞-categories. For the underlying 𝐸1 bar con-
struction in the ∞-categorical setting, see [43, §5.2.2].
    The equivalence is

                         𝐵¯ ch : Assch -Algaug, pronil ⇄ Assch -CoAlgcoaug, conil : Ωch ,

where:
• Assch -Algaug, pronil is the ∞-category of augmented, pro-nilpotent E1 -chiral algebras on 𝑋 ;
• Assch -CoAlgcoaug, conil is the ∞-category of coaugmented, conilpotent E1 -chiral coalgebras on 𝑋 .
      The unit and counit of the adjunction are quasi-isomorphisms:

                   Ωch ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)) −−→ A for all A ∈ Assch -Algaug, pronil ,
                                    ∼

                                 C −−→ 𝐵¯ ch ( Ωch (C)) for all C ∈ Assch -CoAlgcoaug, conil .

Proof. The proof proceeds in three steps.
     Step 1: Reduction to the classical operadic statement. By Proposition 2.8.5, the chiral associative operad
Assch is the chiral lift of the classical associative operad Ass. The bar-cobar adjunction for a Koszul operad
P in a stable presentably symmetric monoidal ∞-category V is an equivalence P-Algaug,pronil (V) ≃
P ! -CoAlgcoaug,conil (V) whenever P is Koszul [135, Theorem 11.4.1]. We apply this with V = D-mod( 𝑋 )
(the stable ∞-category of D-modules on 𝑋 , equipped with the chiral tensor product) and P = Ass.
     Step 2: Koszulity of Ass in the chiral tensor category. By Lemma 9.5.5 below (applied with P = Ass and
V = D-mod( 𝑋 )), the classical Koszulity of Ass [135, Theorem 7.4.1] transfers to the chiral tensor category:
the operadic bar complex 𝐵 Ass ( 𝑘 ) is quasi-isomorphic to Ass! after base change to V.
9.5. The E 1 -chiral Koszul duality theorem                                                                    597


  Step 3: Geometric realization via conﬁguration spaces. The bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A) has an explicit geometric

                         𝐵¯ 𝑛ch (A) = Γ 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ A ⊠𝑛 ⊗ Ω𝑛−1 (log 𝐷 ) .
