The key difference from the E∞ -chiral case is that the Σ𝑛 -action is not imposed: the 𝑛-th bar component is
indexed by ordered configurations ( 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧𝑛 ), not unordered ones. The differential is the same alternating
sum of face maps (collisions of adjacent points), reflecting the non-Σ nature of the associative operad.
   For the cobar construction, by Corollary 6.3.11, we have 𝑑cobar    2    = 0 via Verdier duality. The counit
        ch  ¯ ch
map Ω ( 𝐵 (A)) → A is a quasi-isomorphism by the acyclicity of the augmented bar complex (a
standard contraction argument using the augmentation 𝜀 , as in Theorem 6.12.1), and the unit map is a
quasi-isomorphism by the dual argument for conilpotent coalgebras.

Lemma 9.5.5 (Operadic Koszulness transfer [135]; [proved]). Let P be a quadratic operad over a
field 𝑘 , and let V be a stable presentably symmetric monoidal ∞-category over 𝑘 . If P is Koszul in the
classical sense (i.e., over the category of 𝑘 -modules), then P is Koszul as an operad internal to V: the
                                      ∼
operadic bar construction 𝐵 P ( 𝑘 ) −−→ P ! is a quasi-isomorphism of cooperads in Σ-objects of V.

Proof. Koszulness of a quadratic operad P = F (𝑉 )/( 𝑅) is equivalent to the acyclicity of the Koszul
complex P ◦𝜅 P ! , where 𝜅 : P ! → P is the universal twisting morphism [135, Theorem 7.4.2]. We explain
why this property, once established over 𝑘 -Mod, holds automatically in V.
    Step 1: The Koszul complex is built from operadic composition. The Koszul complex P ◦𝜅 P ! is defined
as the composition product 𝑛 ≥0 P ( 𝑛) ⊗Σ𝑛 (P ! ) ⊗ 𝑛 equipped with a differential twisted by 𝜅 . Crucially,
                              L
both the composition product and the twisting differential are determined by the quadratic data (𝑉 , 𝑅)–
-the generators 𝑉 , the space of relations 𝑅 ⊂ F (𝑉 ) (3), and the combinatorics of planar trees indexing
operadic compositions [135, §7.4]. No structure of the ambient symmetric monoidal category enters beyond
the tensor product and direct sums indexed by these combinatorial data.
    Step 2: Base change preserves acyclicity. Given a symmetric monoidal functor 𝑘 -Mod → V (the unit
functor 𝑀 ↦→ 𝑀 ⊗ 1 V ), the Koszul complex over V is the image (P ◦𝜅 P ! ) ⊗𝑘 1 V . Since V is 𝑘 -linear
(presentably enriched over 𝑘 ), this base-change functor is exact: it preserves all colimits and finite limits
(being a left adjoint between stable categories), hence preserves quasi-isomorphisms. The acyclicity of the
Koszul complex over 𝑘 -Mod [135, Theorem 7.4.1] therefore implies acyclicity over V.
    Step 3: From Koszul complex to bar-cobar resolution. By [135, Theorem 11.3.3], acyclicity of the Koszul
                                                                                            ∼
complex is equivalent to the bar-cobar resolution being a quasi-isomorphism: Ω (P ¡ ) −     → P as operads.
This equivalence is formal (it holds in any abelian category where the Koszul complex is defined), so it
transfers together with Step 2. The ∞-categorical upgrade follows from [135, Theorem 11.4.1] (see also
[95, §16] for the model-categorical treatment of the bar-cobar adjunction for algebras over Koszul operads
in general symmetric monoidal model categories).

Remark 9.5.6 (Veriﬁcation of hypotheses). Steps 1–2 of the proof invoke [135, Theorem 11.4.1] and
Lemma 9.5.5 with V = D-mod( 𝑋 ) equipped with the chiral tensor product ⊗ch . We verify the required
hypotheses on V:
  (i) Stable presentable ∞-category. The ∞-category D-mod( 𝑋 ) is stable and presentable by [44, Chap-
      ter I.3]; see also [43, Proposition 5.5.3.6] and [43, §1.1].
598                                                                 Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


  (ii) Symmetric monoidal structure. The chiral tensor product endows D-mod( 𝑋 ) with a symmetric
       monoidal structure by [2, 3.4.10]. While ⊗ch does not in general coincide with the !-tensor product,
       it does define a symmetric monoidal structure on the ∞-categorical enhancement, as established in
       [44, Chapter IV.5].
 (iii) Exactness of base change (Lemma 9.5.5, Step 2). The unit functor 𝑘 -Mod → D-mod( 𝑋 ) is exact
       because D-mod( 𝑋 ) is 𝑘 -linear and stable. More concretely, D-mod( 𝑋 ) carries a 𝑡 -structure for
       which ⊗ ch is right-exact on each factor [2, 3.4.12], and the bar filtration produces complexes bounded
       below (in the 𝑡 -structure sense), so the derived tensor product agrees with the underived one on each
       filtered piece.
Example 9.5.7 (Heisenberg specialization). For the Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 , Theorem 9.5.4 simplifies
dramatically: H𝑘 is E∞ -chiral (fully commutative OPE, no ordering dependence), so the E1 bar construction
factors through the E∞ bar–-the Σ𝑛 -quotient on ordered configurations is already an isomorphism, and
the bar components 𝐵¯ 𝑛ch (H𝑘 ) are indexed by unordered configurations. The counit quasi-isomorphism
Ωch ( 𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 )) −
                    ∼
                   → H𝑘 was verified explicitly in Chapter 1: the bar complex (§1.1–§1.3) recovers Symch (𝑉 ∗ ),
and the cobar of this commutative coalgebra reconstructs H𝑘 . The spectral discriminant is trivial
(Δ H𝑘 ( 𝑥 ) = 1, rank 1), reflecting that no non-trivial higher operations arise.
Corollary 9.5.8 ( E 1 – E 1 Self-Duality; [proved]). Since ( Assch ) !  Assch ⊗ sgn (Proposition 2.8.5),
the Koszul dual of an augmented pro-nilpotent E1 -chiral algebra A is a conilpotent E1 -chiral coalgebra
A ! := 𝐵¯ ch (A). Under linear duality (when A has finite-dimensional graded components), this coalgebra
dualizes to an E1 -chiral algebra, and the double-dual map

is a quasi-isomorphism. This is the E1 -chiral manifestation of the classical self-duality Ass!  Ass ⊗ sgn.

                                          ∼                                ∼

Remark 9.5.9 (Comparison with Francis–Gaitsgory). Francis–Gaitsgory [26] establish chiral Koszul duality
for the Liech –Comch pair (mechanism (i) of Remark 2.8.9). Theorem 9.5.4 is the associative counterpart,
operating within the single operadic type Assch . The two results are complementary:

                                             Operadic pair      Algebra ↔ Coalgebra
                      Francis–Gaitsgory      Liech ⊣ Comch      Liech -alg ≃ Comch -coalg
                          This work          Assch ⊣ Assch      Assch -alg ≃ Assch -coalg

The self-dual case is in some sense simpler (the bar and cobar land in the same operadic type) but has not
been treated in the chiral setting in the existing literature.

9.7      Interchange of structures under Koszul duality
9.7.1    Generators and relations
Theorem 9.7.1 (Structure exchange; [proved]). Under Koszul duality between (A1 , A2 ):
  (i) Generators ↔ Relations:
                                                Gen(A1 ) ↔ Rel(A2 ) ⊥
                                                Rel(A1 ) ↔ Gen(A2 ) ⊥
  (ii) Products ↔ Coproducts: Multiplication in A1 corresponds to comultiplication in 𝐵¯ (A2 )
 (iii) Syzygy ladder:
                                      Syz𝑛 (A1 ) ↔ CoSyz𝑛+1 ( 𝐵¯ (A2 ))

Proof. We prove each item from the quadratic duality formalism lifted to the chiral setting.
    (1) Generators ↔ Relations. Suppose A1 is presented as the chiral algebra A (𝑉 , 𝑅) freely generated
by 𝑉 modulo the relation space 𝑅 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉 ⊠ 𝑉 ). By the definition of the chiral Koszul dual (cf. Defi-
nition O.1.2 and the Gui–Li–Zeng framework), A2 = A ( 𝑠 −1𝑉 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑅⊥ ), where 𝑅⊥ is the annihilator
of 𝑅 under the residue pairing:

      ⟨ · , · ⟩res : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉 ⊠ 𝑉 ) ⊗ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉 ∨ ⊠ 𝑉 ∨ ) → ℂ,   ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩res = Res 𝑧1 =𝑧2 𝛼 ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) · 𝛽 ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) .

through the residue duality pairing: Gen(A1 ) ↔ Rel(A2 ) ⊥ .
    The reverse direction Rel(A1 ) ↔ Gen(A2 ) ⊥ follows by applying the same construction with the roles
of A1 and A2 exchanged, using the involutivity of quadratic duality: (A1! ) ! ≃ A1 for Koszul algebras.
    (2) Products ↔ Coproducts. The bar construction 𝐵¯ (A1 ) is a coaugmented dg coalgebra whose comulti-

• Trivial 𝐴∞ (Com) ↔ Maximal 𝐴∞ (Lie)

Proof. We prove each item.
    Item 1. For a commutative chiral algebra A1 = ACom , all higher operations 𝑚𝑘(1) = 0 for 𝑘 ≥ 3 (the

its Koszul dual A2 = A1! carries the Lie operad structure with all brackets 𝑚𝑘(2) potentially non-vanishing.
This is the chiral lift of the classical Com! = Lie duality ([83], Theorem 7.6.5).
    Item 2. The Verdier duality pairing on configuration spaces (Theorem 7.3.2) gives:

dual operation of A2 . Non-degeneracy of the Verdier pairing (Theorem 7.3.2) ensures that 𝑚𝑘(1) ≠ 0 if
and only if the corresponding 𝑛𝑘(2) pairs non-trivially.
    Item 3. Massey products on A1 are defined by the higher 𝐴∞ operations 𝑚𝑘(1) for 𝑘 ≥ 3 (the obstructions
to formality). Under bar-cobar duality, these correspond to comassey products–-the dual obstructions in

A2 –-by the general principle that the bar construction converts algebra operations to coalgebra coopera-

9.8     Filtered and curved extensions
9.8.1    Filtered and curved structures
Physical theories have quantum anomalies—effects that break classical symmetries:
Example 9.8.1 (Central extensions in physics). (i) Virasoro central charge: Conformal anomaly in string
       theory
  (ii) Kac–Moody level: Chiral anomaly in current algebras
 (iii) Yangian deformation: Quantum R-matrix structure
   These require:

Proof. An affine-linear involution 𝜄 ( 𝑘 ) = 𝑎𝑘 + 𝑏 satisfies 𝜄2 ( 𝑘 ) = 𝑎2 𝑘 + 𝑎𝑏 + 𝑏 = 𝑘 for all 𝑘 , giving 𝑎2 = 1

9.8.2    Curved Koszul duality
Theorem 9.8.5 (Curved Koszul pairs; [proved]). [Regime: curved-central (Convention 2.9.2).]
  Filtered algebras (A1 , A2 ) with curvatures 𝜅1 , 𝜅2 form a curved Koszul pair if:
   (i) Associated graded (gr A1 , gr A2 ) are classical Koszul dual
  (ii) Curvatures are dual: 𝜅1 ↔ −𝜅2 under the Koszul pairing
 (iii) The spectral sequence associated to the filtration degenerates at 𝐸2
9.9. Derived chiral Koszul duality                                                                           603


Proof. The filtered bar complex 𝐹• 𝐵¯ (A1 ) has associated graded gr 𝐵¯ (A1 ) = 𝐵¯ (gr A1 ). By condition (1),
Ω ( 𝐵¯ (gr A1 )) ≃ gr A2 at the 𝐸1 level. The curvature condition (2) ensures that the 𝑚0 elements of the
two algebras are related by 𝜅2 = −𝜅1∗ under the Koszul pairing, which is the compatibility condition for
curved 𝐴∞ morphisms (Positselski [171]). The degeneration condition (3) then gives Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A1 )) ≃ A2 as
curved 𝐴∞ algebras. This is the standard criterion for curved Koszul pairs (Loday–Vallette [135], §10.3),
lifted to the chiral setting via Theorem 6.2.69 (geometric bar = operadic bar).

Remark 9.9.3 (Scope). Conjecture 9.9.2 is tagged [conjectured] for two independent reasons:

bar-cobar adjunction for DG chiral algebras. The shadow is the decomposition of the BRST complex into
Koszul dual sectors. (Contributing to the derived/super extension flank adjoining Conjecture 34.9.4, not
to the standard 𝑊∞ /Yangian packet.)

9.10      Counter-examples: when Koszul duality fails
9.10.1    Virasoro algebra: beyond the quadratic setting
Remark 9.10.1 (Virasoro Koszulness requires the PBW framework). The Virasoro algebra with central charge
𝑐 does not admit a Koszul dual in the standard quadratic (uncurved) sense, because its OPE involves a
quartic pole. However, it is chiral Koszul in the PBW sense of Theorem 9.1.35: the PBW filtration yields a
classical Koszul associated graded, and the spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸1 . A completed curved same-
family shadow can be constructed using the techniques of §6.8.2; the stronger H-level infinite-generator
dual object is delegated to the exact 𝑊∞ MC4 package of filtered H-level targets, residue identities, and
finite detection on I𝑁 , whose first live higher-spin stages are already reduced on the theorem surface to the
stage-3 fifteen-coefficient packet and the stage-4 six-coefficient packet organized as three local OPE blocks,
with the genuinely mixed stage-4 frontier reduced to the single mixed (3, 4) triple.
    Why the quadratic framework fails.
  (i) The OPE involves a quartic pole:

9.10.3    Tensor products and Koszulity
Remark 9.10.4 (Tensor products in the algebraic setting). In the classical (non-chiral) setting, tensor products
of Koszul algebras are Koszul: if 𝐴1 and 𝐴2 are Koszul quadratic algebras, then 𝐴1 ⊗ 𝐴2 is Koszul with
( 𝐴1 ⊗ 𝐴2 ) !  𝐴!1 ⊗ 𝐴!2 (Polishchuk–Positselski, Theorem 3.1).
   In the chiral setting, however, the tensor product A1 ⊗ A2 as chiral algebras involves the chiral tensor
product (not the ordinary tensor product of vector spaces), and the Koszul property is no longer automatic.
The bar complex of a chiral tensor product involves configuration spaces with colored points, and the
interaction between colors introduces additional structure beyond the Arnold relations for each color
separately. Whether chiral Koszulity is preserved under chiral tensor products remains open.
Proposition 9.10.5 (Koszul dual of tensor products in the quadratic case; [proved]). Let (A1 , A1! )
and (A2 , A2! ) be quadratic chiral Koszul pairs on a smooth curve 𝑋 . Then the chiral tensor product
A1 ⊗ ch A2 is Koszul, and its Koszul dual is given by:

                                       (A1 ⊗ ch A2 ) !  A1! ⊗ch A2!

as chiral coalgebras. In particular, for Kac–Moody algebras:

                                    𝔤𝑘 ⊗ch 𝔥
                                   (b      bℓ ) !  𝔤
                                                    b− 𝑘 −2ℎ𝔤∨ ⊗ch 𝔥
                                                                   b− ℓ −2ℎ∨
                                                                           𝔥


and the level-shifting involution acts component-wise.

Proof. For quadratic chiral algebras, the bar complex of the chiral tensor product decomposes via the Kün-
neth theorem for configuration spaces. Let A 𝑖 = Freech (𝑉𝑖 )/( 𝑅𝑖 ) with relation spaces 𝑅𝑖 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉𝑖⊠2 ).
The tensor product A1 ⊗ch A2 = Freech (𝑉1 ⊕ 𝑉2 )/( 𝑅1 ⊕ 𝑅2 ) is quadratic with generators 𝑉1 ⊕ 𝑉2 and
relations 𝑅1 ⊕ 𝑅2 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ ((𝑉1 ⊕ 𝑉2 ) ⊠2 ) (the mixed products 𝑉1 ⊠ 𝑉2 and 𝑉2 ⊠ 𝑉1 are free–-no relations
imposed between generators of different colors).
606                                                                     Chapter 9. Chiral Koszul duality


   The orthogonal complement is:

                                            ( 𝑅1 ⊕ 𝑅2 ) ⊥ = 𝑅1⊥ ⊕ 𝑅2⊥

under the direct sum decomposition of (𝑉1 ∗ ⊕ 𝑉2∗ ) ⊗2 , since the mixed components (𝑉1 ∗ ⊗ 𝑉2∗ ) and (𝑉2∗ ⊗
𝑉1 ∗ ) are entirely contained in ( 𝑅1 ⊕ 𝑅2 ) ⊥ (they pair to zero with the pure-color relations 𝑅1 , 𝑅2 ). Therefore:

                       (A1 ⊗ ch A2 ) ! = Freech (𝑉1 ∗ ⊕ 𝑉2∗ )/( 𝑅1⊥ ⊕ 𝑅2⊥ ) = A1! ⊗ch A2!

   The Koszul complex of the tensor product is the tensor product of the Koszul complexes (since the
cross-relations are trivial), and acyclicity of each factor implies acyclicity of the product by the Künneth
theorem. The KM specialization follows from Theorem 20.7.1 applied to each factor.

9.11     Computational methods and verification
9.11.1   Algorithm for checking Koszul pairs
Construction 9.11.1 (Veriﬁcation of Koszul pairs). Given chiral algebras A1 , A2 , one verifies whether they
form a Koszul pair as follows. In the quadratic case, extract generators and relations, check that the residue
pairing is perfect, and verify orthogonality 𝑅1 ⊥ 𝑅2 . In the non-quadratic case, compute 𝐵¯ ≤3 (A 𝑖 ) geo-
metrically, form the Koszul complexes 𝐾∗ (A 𝑖 , A𝑗 ), and check acyclicity in degrees 1, 2, 3. In both cases,
verify bar-cobar quasi-isomorphisms to degree 3.

9.11.2 Complexity analysis
For 𝑛 generators, 𝑚 relations, verification to degree 𝑘 :
• Quadratic case: 𝑂 ( 𝑛2 + 𝑚2 ) for orthogonality
• General case: 𝑂 ( 𝑛𝑘 ) for bar complex dimension
• Configuration integrals: 𝑂 ( 𝑘 ! · 𝑛𝑘 ) worst case

9.12      Summary
Our geometric approach to Chiral Koszul Duality provides:
   (i) Escape from quadratic constraints: Chiral Koszul pairs handle arbitrary OPE structures
  (ii) Complete homological machinery: Derived equivalences, Ext-Tor duality, spectral sequences
 (iii) Chain-level precision: All computations via explicit residues and distributions
 (iv) Physical applications. Yangian-quantum affine duality, holography, mirror symmetry
  (v) Computational algorithms: Verification procedures with complexity bounds

9.12. Summary                                                                                           607


• E1 -chiral Koszul duality (Theorem 9.5.4) –- used by Chapter 24.
   The Koszul pair structure classifies the duality at the algebra level. But a chiral algebra without its
representations is like a group without its actions: the abstract structure exists, but the richest mathemat-
ics–-conformal blocks, fusion rules, the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence–-is inaccessible. The bar-cobar
adjunction extends from algebras to modules, and the Koszul pair structure descends to module categories.
This is the subject of the next chapter.

Chiral Koszul pairs

10.1     Koszul duality
10.1.1 The classical pair on a point
Let 𝑉 be a finite-dimensional vector space. The symmetric algebra Sym(𝑉 ) and the exterior algebra Λ (𝑉 ∗ )
form a Koszul pair (Definition 4.1.5): there is a natural twisting cochain 𝜏 : 𝐵 (Sym(𝑉 )) → Λ (𝑉 ∗ )
that makes the twisted tensor product 𝐵 (Sym(𝑉 )) ⊗𝜏 Λ (𝑉 ∗ ) acyclic. The bar complex 𝐵 (Sym(𝑉 )) =
𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1𝑉¯ ) is a cofree coalgebra with differential built from the commutative product, and 𝜏 identifies
Λ (𝑉 ∗ ) as its linear dual. Priddy’s theorem [58] gives the counit
                                                           ∼
                                       Ω ( 𝐵 (Sym(𝑉 ))) −−→ Sym(𝑉 )
as a quasi-isomorphism. The curvature vanishes: 𝑚0 = 0, so the bar differential satisfies 𝑑 2 = 0 strictly. All
of this is a shadow of the Com! = Lie operadic duality.

10.1.2    The pair on a curve
Now take 𝑋 a smooth algebraic curve and replace Sym(𝑉 ) by the chiral symmetric algebra Comch (𝑉 ⊗ 𝜔 𝑋 )
–- a chiral algebra on 𝑋 whose fiber at each point is a copy of Sym(𝑉 ), but whose 𝑛-point operations are
governed by configuration spaces 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) of colliding points rather than by tensor powers. The Koszul
dual becomes Liech (𝑉 ∗ ⊗ 𝜔 𝑋 ), and the bar construction 𝐵 𝑋 (A) lives on the Fulton–MacPherson com-
pactification FM𝑛 ( 𝑋 ). The chiral twisting cochain (Definition 9.1.14) produces the counit
                                                            ∼
                                            Ω ( 𝐵 𝑋 (A)) −−→ A ,
which is again a quasi-isomorphism when A is chiral Koszul (Theorem A, Theorem 9.1.39). Crucially: the
genus-0 collision differential 𝑑0 still satisfies 𝑑02 = 0. There is no curvature; the only new ingredient is the
integration kernel mediating chiral operations on 𝑋 .
    When 𝑋 = ℙ1 , the BD operadic equivalence recovers the classical pair from the chiral one: the category
of chiral algebras on ℙ1 is equivalent to that of vertex algebras, and the chiral bar construction restricts to
the classical bar construction on generators-and-relations data.

10.1.3   The pair in families: curvature from moduli
Fix a chiral Koszul pair (A , A ! ) on a genus-0 curve and deform the curve to genus 𝑔 ≥ 1. The bar con-
struction 𝐵 𝑔 (A) now lives on M 𝑔 , and the fiberwise differential 𝑑fib becomes curved:
                                               2
                                              𝑑fib = 𝜅 · 𝜔 𝑔 ≠ 0,

where 𝜅 is the level and 𝜔 𝑔 ∈ 𝐻 2 (M 𝑔 ) is the Hodge class. The differential is no longer a differential; it
squares to a curvature term that encodes the central charge.


                                                     609
610                                                                    Chapter 10. Chiral Koszul pairs


   The total corrected differential 𝐷 𝑔 absorbs the curvature into a higher-order correction –- a curved
𝐴∞ -structure in which 𝑚0 ≠ 0 and 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎] –- and satisfies 𝐷 2𝑔 = 0. The passage from 𝑑0 to
𝐷 𝑔 is the passage from classical to quantum: the quantum corrections are controlled by 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)),
and Theorem B (Theorem 8.17.4) shows that bar-cobar inversion persists via 𝐸2 collapse of the associated
spectral sequence. Theorem C (Theorem 8.14.12) identifies the obstruction and deformation spaces as
Lagrangian complements.
Remark 10.1.1 (Three levels of Koszul pair). The construction above exhibits three levels of structure, each
strictly refining the previous:
  (i) Classical (Definition 4.1.5). Input: graded algebras on a point. Bar object: 𝐵 ( 𝐴) = 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 𝐴¯). Cur-
      vature: 𝑚0 = 0. Main result: Priddy [58].
 (ii) Chiral (Definition 9.1.14). Input: chiral algebras on a curve 𝑋 . Bar object: 𝐵 𝑋 (A) on FM𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).
      Curvature: 𝑑02 = 0. Main result: Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39).
(iii) Modular (Definition 8.18.7). Input: chiral algebras + genus tower 𝑔 ≥ 0. Bar object: 𝐵 𝑔 (A) on M 𝑔 .
                   2 = 𝜅 · 𝜔 . Main results: Theorems B–D.
      Curvature: 𝑑fib        𝑔
Each level introduces new phenomena invisible to the previous one: the chiral level brings integration
kernels and OPE poles; the modular level brings curvature, central extensions, and anomalies.

10.1.4    From classical to chiral: the PBW bridge
Classical Koszul duality (Definition 4.1.5, Chapter 4) requires quadratic relations. Chiral algebras are almost
never quadratic: the Virasoro OPE has a quartic pole, 𝑊 -algebras have sixth-order poles, and Yangians
have cubic relations. The PBW filtration (Chapter 9) resolves this by reducing the chiral problem to the
classical one on the associated graded.

10.2     Chiral Hochschild cohomology: construction from
         first principles
10.2.1   The chiral enveloping algebra
Deﬁnition 10.2.1 (Chiral enveloping algebra). For a chiral algebra A on a smooth curve 𝑋 , the chiral
enveloping algebra is:
                                         A 𝑒 = A ⊠ D 𝑋 A op
where ⊠ D 𝑋 is the chiral tensor product over the sheaf of differential operators and A op has the opposite
chiral multiplication 𝑌 op ( 𝑎, 𝑏 ) = 𝑌 ( 𝑏, 𝑎).
Deﬁnition 10.2.2 (Chiral bimodule). An A-bimodule (in the chiral sense) is a D 𝑋 -module M equipped
with a left chiral action 𝜇 𝐿 : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (A ⊠ M) → Δ! M and a right chiral action 𝜇 𝑅 : 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (M ⊠ A) →
Δ! M satisfying the associativity and compatibility conditions:
   (i) Left associativity: 𝜇 𝐿 ◦ (id A ⊠ 𝜇 𝐿 ) = 𝜇 𝐿 ◦ ( 𝜇 A ⊠ id M ) (as chiral operations on A ⊠ A ⊠ M);
  (ii) Right associativity (analogously);
 (iii) Left-right compatibility: 𝜇 𝐿 ◦ (id A ⊠ 𝜇 𝑅 ) = 𝜇 𝑅 ◦ ( 𝜇 𝐿 ⊠ id A ).
Equivalently, M is a module for the chiral enveloping algebra A 𝑒 .
Lemma 10.2.3 (Well-definedness of chiral enveloping algebra; [proved]). The chiral tensor product
A ⊠ D 𝑋 A op is well-defined and carries a natural chiral algebra structure.
10.2. Chiral Hochschild cohomology: construction from first principles                                                    611


Proof. We need to verify:
   (i) Existence: The tensor product exists in the category of D 𝑋 × D 𝑋 -modules.
  (ii) Chiral structure: The diagonal action of D 𝑋 gives a chiral algebra structure.
 (iii) Locality: If A satisfies locality, so does A 𝑒 .
   For (1): We use that D 𝑋 -modules form an abelian category with enough injectives.
   For (2): The chiral multiplication on A 𝑒 is given by:

                       𝑌 𝑒 (( 𝑎1 ⊗ 𝑎2 ) , ( 𝑏1 ⊗ 𝑏2 )) ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑌 ( 𝑎1 , 𝑏1 ) ( 𝑧 ) ⊗ 𝑌 op ( 𝑎2 , 𝑏2 ) ( 𝑧 )

   For (3): Locality of A means ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 𝑁 [𝑌 ( 𝑎, 𝑧 ) , 𝑌 ( 𝑏, 𝑤 )] = 0 for 𝑁 ≫ 0. This property is preserved
under tensor products.
   Associativity: the product 𝑌 𝑒 is associative because it is the tensor product of two associative chiral
products (𝑌 on A and 𝑌 op on A op ), and the tensor product of associative chiral algebras is associative (the
Borcherds identity on A 𝑒 reduces to the tensor product of the Borcherds identities on each factor).

10.3      The chiral Gerstenhaber structure
Hochschild cohomology carries a Gerstenhaber algebra structure [147]: a graded commutative cup product
and a degree −1 Lie bracket, compatible via the Leibniz rule. Both extend to the chiral setting.

10.3.1     The cup product
Deﬁnition 10.3.1 (Cup product on chiral Hochschild cohomology). For 𝑓 ∈ 𝐶 𝐻 𝑝 (A) and 𝑔 ∈ 𝐶 𝐻 𝑞 (A),
define their cup product:

 ( 𝑓 ∪ 𝑔 ) ( 𝑎0 , . . . , 𝑎 𝑝+𝑞 ) = Res 𝑧 𝑝 →𝑤0 𝑓 ( 𝑎0 , . . . , 𝑎 𝑝 ) ( 𝑧0 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝 ) · 𝑔 ( 𝑎 𝑝+1 , . . . , 𝑎 𝑝+𝑞 ) ( 𝑤0 , . . . , 𝑤 𝑞 −1 )

where the residue is taken as the 𝑝-th point approaches the position of the ( 𝑝 + 1)-st point.
Proposition 10.3.2 (Properties of cup product; [proved]). The cup product satisfies:
   (i) Associativity: ( 𝑓 ∪ 𝑔 ) ∪ ℎ = 𝑓 ∪ ( 𝑔 ∪ ℎ)
  (ii) Graded commutativity: 𝑓 ∪ 𝑔 = (−1) | 𝑓 | | 𝑔 | 𝑔 ∪ 𝑓
 (iii) Unit: The identity element 1 ∈ 𝐶 𝐻 0 (A) is a unit for ∪

Proof. Associativity: Both ( 𝑓 ∪ 𝑔 ) ∪ ℎ and 𝑓 ∪ ( 𝑔 ∪ ℎ) involve taking residues at collision points. The
order of residues does not matter by the residue theorem on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).
    Graded commutativity: This requires a homotopy argument: the cup product is defined using a residue
as 𝑧 𝑝 → 𝑤0 , which is not manifestly symmetric. The commutativity up to sign follows from the fact that
the relevant residue pairings on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) are invariant under the permutation exchanging the two groups
of points, together with the Koszul sign arising from reordering the differential forms; this is the chiral
analogue of the classical Eilenberg–Zilber argument for Hochschild cohomology.
    Unit: The identity in 𝐶 𝐻 0 is the identity map A → A, which acts trivially under cup product.

Theorem 10.3.4 (Chiral Gerstenhaber algebra [147, 218]; [proved]). The cohomology 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A)

  (i) Chiral Jacobi identity:

This is the chiral analogue of Gerstenhaber’s classical theorem [147]. The Jacobi identity follows from the
identification of {−, −} 𝑐 with the commutator of coderivations on the bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A): coderivations
form a Lie algebra under the commutator bracket, and the identification 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A)  Coder( 𝐵¯ ch (A)) is
a standard consequence of the bar-cobar adjunction (see [83], Theorem 9.3.2 for the classical case). The
Leibniz rule follows from the fact that coderivations are derivations with respect to the coalgebra structure
on 𝐵¯ ch (A), and the cup product is induced by the coalgebra comultiplication (see Tamarkin [218] for the
𝐸2 -formality approach in the associative setting).

for the complete operadic argument.

complex.

    The passage from 𝐿1 to the full Virasoro at fixed 𝑐 ≠ 0 introduces no new cohomology classes: the

Remark 10.5.2 (Scope). The proof assembles three ingredients: (i) Kac determinant irreducibility at generic
𝑐 ([proved]); (ii) Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral Hochschild comparison ([proved], [2]); (iii) Gel’fand–Fuchs
computation of 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐿1 ; ℂ) ([proved], [205]). The combination is new. For rank 1, Period(Vir𝑐 ) = 2 is
complete; for higher rank, the periodicity profile Π (A) (Remark 10.5.10) is the correct invariant.

Proof. In each case, the Gel’fand–Fuchs computation (Theorem 10.5.3 and the Beilinson–Drinfeld com-

the exponents.

Corollary 10.5.7 (Hochschild ring isomorphism under Koszul duality; [proved]). For any same-
type Koszul pair (A , A ! ), there is an isomorphism of graded rings:

                                           CH∗ (A)  CH∗ (A ! )                                             (10.1)

preserving the number and degrees of polynomial generators. In particular, the number of independent
deformation directions dim CH2 (A) = dim CH2 (A ! ) is a Koszul-duality invariant.

Proof. By Proposition 10.5.6, CH∗ (A) and CH∗ (A ! ) are polynomial rings on generators whose degrees
are determined by the root datum of 𝔤 and the conformal weights of the W-algebra generators, respectively.
Since neither datum changes under the Feigin–Frenkel involution 𝑘 ↦→ 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ (the exponents
of 𝔤 are intrinsic, and the Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction produces generators of the same weights at both
levels), the polynomial rings are abstractly isomorphic.
    The isomorphism (10.1) is induced by the derived Morita equivalence: the bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism
Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −
              ∼
              → A (Theorem 6.12.1) gives a Morita equivalence of bimodule categories in the sense of
Keller [148], which induces an isomorphism on Hochschild cohomology HH∗ ( 𝐴, 𝐴)  HH∗ ( 𝐵, 𝐵 )
for derived-equivalent algebras 𝐴 ≃ 𝐵 . By the Beilinson–Drinfeld comparison, the chiral Hochschild
cohomology reduces to the continuous Lie algebra cohomology, where the Gel’fand–Fuchs computation
produces the polynomial ring structure.

Proposition 10.5.12 (Admissible levels are permuted under Koszul duality; [proved]). Let 𝔤
be a simple Lie algebra. A level 𝑘 is admissible (in the sense of Kac–Wakimoto [160]) if it has the form
𝑘 + ℎ∨ = 𝑝/ 𝑞 with 𝑝, 𝑞 coprime positive integers, 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ if 𝔤 is simply laced ( 𝑝 ≥ ℎ otherwise). Under
the Feigin–Frenkel involution 𝑘 ↦→ 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ :
   (i) The dual level satisfies 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ = −( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) = − 𝑝/ 𝑞 , so | 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ | = 𝑝/ 𝑞 and the denominator is
       preserved. Note that 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ < 0; the Kac–Wakimoto admissibility condition requires 𝑘 + ℎ∨ =
       𝑝/ 𝑞 > 0, but for the Feigin–Frenkel dual the relevant algebra is the Langlands dual 𝔤c∨ 𝑘′ , where
       ℎ∨ (𝔤∨ ) may differ from ℎ∨ (𝔤) in the non-simply-laced case. In the simply-laced case 𝔤 = 𝔤∨ , and
       admissibility of 𝑘 ′ is understood as | 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ | = 𝑝/ 𝑞 with the same Kac–Wakimoto bounds.
  (ii) The set of admissible levels for 𝔤 is mapped bijectively onto the set of admissible levels of opposite
       sign; in the simply-laced case the admissible levels { 𝑘 : 𝑘 + ℎ∨ = 𝑝/ 𝑞, 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ } are sent to { 𝑘 ′ :
       𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ = − 𝑝/ 𝑞 }.

      via the derived equivalence of Theorem 9.6.1.
620                                                                      Chapter 10. Chiral Koszul pairs


Proof. The Feigin–Frenkel involution 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ sends 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ↦→ −( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ), preserving the
absolute value and negating the sign. Since admissibility depends on | 𝑘 + ℎ∨ | being a rational number
 𝑝/ 𝑞 satisfying the Kac–Wakimoto bound 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ (simply-laced) or 𝑝 ≥ ℎ (non-simply-laced), and
 𝑝/ 𝑞 = | − 𝑝/ 𝑞 |, the involution preserves the numerical admissibility condition on | 𝑘 + ℎ∨ |.
     Sign convention. Strictly speaking, the Kac–Wakimoto definition of admissible level requires 𝑘 + ℎ∨ > 0
(i.e., a positive rational number 𝑝/ 𝑞 ), so the dual level 𝑘 ′ with 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ = −( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) < 0 is not admissible
in the literal Kac–Wakimoto sense. The statement is understood in the extended sense: the representation-
theoretic data (admissible weights, fusion rules, modular properties) at level 𝑘 ′ are well-defined via analytic
continuation in the level, as formalized in the Feigin–Frenkel framework [82], where the involution 𝑘 ↦→
−𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ is an equivalence of vertex algebra categories regardless of the sign of 𝑘 + ℎ∨ .
     For part (iii): the derived equivalence of Theorem 9.6.1 applies to Koszul pairs (b         b𝑘′ ). Restricting
                                                                                            𝔤𝑘 , 𝔤
to the admissible subcategory O𝑘adm (the full subcategory of O𝑘 generated by admissible highest-weight
modules 𝐿 𝑘 ( 𝜆) for 𝜆 in the admissible weight set) is compatible with the derived equivalence because
the bar-cobar resolution preserves the weight lattice, and the Koszul dual of an admissible highest-weight
module 𝐿 𝑘 ( 𝜆) is an admissible highest-weight module 𝐿 𝑘′ ( 𝜆′ ) at the dual level (the highest weight is
transported by the duality functor).

Remark 10.5.13 (The critical locus in level space). The level space 𝑘 ∈ ℂ is stratified by Koszul behavior:

              Locus                           Koszul behavior
              Generic 𝑘                       Curved Koszul pair (b      𝔤− 𝑘 −2ℎ∨ )
                                                                    𝔤𝑘 , b
              Critical 𝑘 = −ℎ∨                Self-dual fixed point; bar complex uncurved
              Admissible 𝑘 + ℎ∨ = 𝑝/ 𝑞        Finite-dimensional quotient categories; permuted
              𝑘 ∈ ℤ ≥0 (integrable)           KL equivalence with 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤); 𝑞 ↔ 𝑞 −1
              𝑘 + ℎ∨ ∈ ℤ<0                    Dual integrable: 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ ∈ ℤ ≥0
                                                               FF
The Feigin–Frenkel involution is the reflection 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ↦−−→ −( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ), preserving each stratum with
unique fixed point 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ .

10.6      The transition from quadratic to non-quadratic Koszul
          duality
10.6.1    Limitations of quadratic theory
The Heisenberg algebra is quadratic: a single generator with a single OPE relation (§1.1). Most chiral algebras
of physical interest are not.
Deﬁnition 10.6.1 (Quadratic chiral algebra). A chiral algebra A is quadratic if it admits a presentation:

                                             A = Freech (𝑉 )/( 𝑅)

where 𝑉 is a locally free O 𝑋 -module concentrated in conformal weight 1, and 𝑅 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (𝑉 ⊠ 𝑉 ) consists
of relations among products of two generators.
Example 10.6.2 (The 𝛽𝛾 system is quadratic). Generators: 𝛽 (weight 1), 𝛾 (weight 0)
Relation: [ 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) , 𝛾 ( 𝑤 )] = 𝛿 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )
This is quadratic after shifting 𝛾 to weight 1.
10.7. The Yangian: first non-quadratic example                                                            621


Example 10.6.3 (The Virasoro algebra is non-quadratic). The stress tensor 𝑇 ( 𝑧 ) has weight 2, and the OPE:

                                                    𝑐 /2   2𝑇 (𝑤 )    𝜕𝑇 (𝑤 )
                             𝑇 ( 𝑧 )𝑇 ( 𝑤 ) =            +          +
                                                ( 𝑧 − 𝑤)4 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤)2    𝑧−𝑤
Cannot be expressed with only quadratic relations due to the quartic pole.

10.6.2    The Maurer–Cartan correspondence for quadratic algebras
Following Gui, Li, and Zeng [152], we prove a Maurer–Cartan correspondence for quadratic chiral algebras:
Theorem 10.6.4 (Maurer–Cartan correspondence — quadratic case; [proved]). For a dualizable
quadratic chiral algebra A = A ( 𝑁 , 𝑃 ) with dual A ! = A ( 𝑠 −1 𝑁 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑃 ⊥ ), there is a bijection:

                                   HomChirAlg (A , 𝐵 )  MC(A ! ⊗ 𝐵 )

where MC denotes the set of Maurer–Cartan elements.

Proof. (⇒) Given 𝜙 : A → 𝐵 , set 𝛼 = ( 𝜙 ⊗ id) ( 𝑠 −1 Id 𝑁 ⊗ 𝑁 ∨ ) ∈ (A ! ⊗ 𝐵 ) 1 . Then 𝑑𝛼 = 0 by 𝜙 ( 𝑃 ) = 0
and 𝑃 ⊥ orthogonality, and [ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] = 0 by associativity of 𝜙.
   (⇐) Given 𝛼 = 𝑖 𝑎!𝑖 ⊗ 𝑏 𝑖 ∈ MC(A ! ⊗ 𝐵 ), define 𝜙 ( 𝑛) = 𝑖 ⟨𝑛, 𝑎!𝑖 ⟩ 𝑏 𝑖 . The component 𝑑𝛼 = 0
                       P                                              P
forces 𝜙 ( 𝑃 ) = 0 (so 𝜙 factors through A), and [ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] = 0 forces associativity. The two constructions are
inverse by the universal property of Freech ( 𝑁 ).

10.6.3    Extending to non-quadratic: higher Maurer–Cartan equations
For non-quadratic algebras, the simple Maurer–Cartan equation is insufficient. We need:
Deﬁnition 10.6.5 ( 𝐴∞ Maurer–Cartan equation). Let A be a chiral algebra with 𝐴∞ structure
( 𝑚1 , 𝑚2 , 𝑚3 , . . .). An element 𝛼 ∈ A 1 satisfies the 𝐴∞ Maurer–Cartan equation if:
                                            ∞
                                                 𝑚𝑛 ( 𝛼, . . . , 𝛼 ) = 0
                                           ∑︁
                                           𝑛=1

(There are no factorial prefactors: the 𝑚𝑛 take ordered inputs, unlike the symmetric 𝐿∞ brackets ℓ𝑛 where
the Maurer–Cartan equation 𝑛1! ℓ𝑛 ( 𝛼, . . . , 𝛼 ) = 0 includes 𝑛1! to account for permutation symmetry.)
                               P

Example 10.6.6 (Cubic relations require 𝑚3 ). For the Yangian with RTT relations (cubic), the MC equation
becomes:
                                  𝑚1 ( 𝛼 ) + 𝑚2 ( 𝛼, 𝛼 ) + 𝑚3 ( 𝛼, 𝛼, 𝛼 ) = 0
where 𝑚3 encodes the RTT relation. (In the 𝐿∞ formulation via antisymmetrization, the corresponding
equation is 𝑑𝛼 + 21 [ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] + 61 ℓ3 ( 𝛼, 𝛼, 𝛼 ) = 0.)

10.10     Module categories and resolutions
10.10.1   The derived equivalence
Theorem 10.10.1 (Koszul equivalence of categories [5]; [proved]). If (A , A ! ) form a Koszul pair of
chiral algebras, there is an equivalence of triangulated categories:

                                      𝐷 𝑏 (A-mod) ≃ 𝐷 𝑏 (A ! -mod)

Remark 10.10.2. The equivalence above holds for quadratic, uncurved Koszul pairs with bounded-below
module categories. In the general chiral setting (curved, non-quadratic), the correct statement replaces
𝐷 𝑏 (A-mod) with complete (pro-nilpotent) modules and 𝐷 𝑏 (A ! -mod) with conilpotent comodules; see
Theorem 9.6.2 for the precise formulation and Positselski [171] for the foundational theory.
Theorem 10.10.3 (Positselski comodule-contramodule equivalence; [proved]). For a Koszul chiral
algebra A with curved bar complex 𝐵¯ (A), there is an equivalence of triangulated categories:

                             𝐷 co (A-CoModconil ) ≃ 𝐷 ctr (A ! -ContraMod)

between the coderived category of conilpotent A-comodules and the contraderived category of A ! -
contramodules, extending the module Koszul duality of Theorem 9.6.2 to the proper derived-categorical
setting.

Proof. This is Theorem 6.11.22, which follows from the chiral comodule-contramodule correspondence
(Theorem 6.11.20) applied to the CDG-coalgebra 𝐶 = 𝐵¯ ch (A). The foundational chiral coalgebra homo-
logical algebra is developed in §6.11.
626                                                                             Chapter 10. Chiral Koszul pairs


Remark 10.10.4 (Proof structure). Three layers: (1) 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) is a chiral CDG-coalgebra (Definition 6.11.1);
curvature at 𝑔 ≥ 1 forces the coderived/contraderived framework (Proposition 6.8.7). (2) The functors
Φ𝐶ch , Ψ𝐶ch (Definition 6.11.18) descend to 𝐷 co ≃ 𝐷 ctr (Theorem 6.11.20). (3) Conilpotent CDG-comodules
over 𝐵¯ ch (A) are A-comodules; CDG-contramodules are complete A ! -modules (Theorem 6.11.22).
Theorem 10.10.5 (Full derived module equivalence; [proved]). For a Koszul chiral algebra A with
curved bar complex 𝐵¯ (A), there is a triangulated equivalence:
                               𝐷 𝑏 (Modcompl (A)) ≃ 𝐷 co (CoModconil (A ! ))
where Modcompl (A) denotes the category of complete (pro-nilpotent) A-modules and CoModconil (A ! )
denotes the category of conilpotent A ! -comodules.
    Passing to derived morphisms, the same functor exchanges Ext groups with their coalgebra-side dual
after the global-dimension shift:

10.13     Form degree in higher interaction terms
Proposition 10.13.1 (Quartic expressions on a three-manifold). Let 𝑀 be a smooth three-manifold
and 𝐴 ∈ Ω1 ( 𝑀 ; 𝑊 ) for a finite-dimensional vector space 𝑊 . Any expression obtained by applying a
four-linear map to coefficients of 𝐴 and wedging all four one-form factors is zero. If a vector field 𝑣 and a
four-linear map 𝑇 : 𝑊 ⊗4 → ℂ are specified, the expression

                                        𝑇 ( 𝜄𝑣 𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐴, 𝐴) ∈ Ω3 ( 𝑀 )

is instead a defined three-form. It can be nonzero, but depends on the additional contraction and tensor.

Proof. The first expression belongs to Ω4 ( 𝑀 ) = 0. For the second, 𝜄𝑣 𝐴 has form degree zero, so the total
degree is three. For an explicit local example take 𝑊 = ℂ3 , 𝐴 = 𝑒1 𝑑𝑥 + 𝑒2 𝑑𝑦 + 𝑒3 𝑑𝑧 , 𝑣 = 𝜕𝑥 , and the tensor
whose only nonzero coordinate entry is 𝑇 ( 𝑒1 , 𝑒1 , 𝑒2 , 𝑒3 ) = 1. Then the expression is 𝑑𝑥 ∧ 𝑑𝑦 ∧ 𝑑𝑧 .

     An RTT relation is an algebraic relation on matrix-valued series. To use it as an action term, a map to a
three-form such as the displayed contraction must be defined and its required symmetries proved. A critical
affine level alone does not make the Lie bracket in Ω• ( 𝑀 ) ⊗ 𝔤 vanish. For example, 𝐴 = 𝑒 𝑑𝑥 + 𝑓 𝑑𝑦 in
𝔰𝔩 2 has [ 𝐴, 𝐴]/2 = ℎ 𝑑𝑥 ∧ 𝑑𝑦 ≠ 0, independently of any level parameter.
Proposition 10.13.2 (Integration on a finite quotient). Let a finite group Γ act freely by orientation-
preserving diffeomorphisms on a closed oriented three-manifold 𝑀 . Let 𝜔 be an invariant three-form and
𝜔¯ its descended form on 𝑀 /Γ. Then
                                                     1
                                        ∫              ∫
                                               𝜔¯ =         𝜔.
                                          𝑀 /Γ      |Γ| 𝑀

Proof. The quotient map is an oriented covering of degree | Γ |. An evenly covered coordinate cover and a
partition of unity reduce integration to the sum over its | Γ | sheets. Each sheet has the same integral, giving
the formula.

   For a nonfree finite action, integration on the quotient stack uses the right-hand side as its normalization.
An additional division by | Γ | after taking this quotient integral changes the normalization. Neither a
fractional grading nor a W-algebra specifies an action of Γ on 𝑀 .

Remark 10.13.6 (A chiral Batalin–Vilkovisky comparison). The polynomial operator above is defined on its
displayed finite generator algebra. A residue operator on a chiral configuration complex requires a domain,
a cyclic pairing, its degree and second-order identity, and compatibility with every collision map. The
Arnold relations alone do not specify these data or an interacting master action. An identification with the
polynomial model requires the actual coefficient and operator maps.
10.14. Open questions                                                                                       631


Remark 10.13.7 (Chern–Simons interpretation). The BV antibracket on the bar complex has a natural
interpretation as arising from the Chern–Simons action: for quadratic A, the master action is the CS
functional, and for non-quadratic A the deformation terms 𝑚𝑛−1 contribute higher-order terms. This
identification of the configuration-space BV bracket with the CS-derived bracket requires the Costello–
Gwilliam perturbative quantization formalism [27], which has been verified for specific examples but not
for general non-quadratic chiral algebras.
   Higher interactions on a three-manifold require operations with output in Ω3 ( 𝑀 ), together with a
specified cyclic pairing and differential compatibility. Proposition 10.13.1 constructs a contracted three-form
and distinguishes it from the vanishing fourfold wedge. The ordinary 𝔰𝔩 2 connection 𝑒 𝑑𝑥 + 𝑓 𝑑𝑦 has
curvature ℎ 𝑑𝑥 ∧ 𝑑𝑦 independently of a level parameter. A critical-level abelianization must therefore
change the carrier or construct a comparison that explains this curvature.

10.14     Open questions
Several natural problems remain.
   (i) Classify chiral algebras admitting Koszul duals (the quadratic case is understood; non-quadratic
       algebras require 𝐴∞ structures whose convergence properties are more delicate).
  (ii) Develop a categorified version of chiral Koszul duality, replacing Koszul dual pairs by dual pairs of
       2-categories of modules.
 (iii) Extend the periodicity phenomena (Theorems 10.5.1 and 10.5.3) to non-simply-laced types, where
       the dual Coxeter number and Coxeter number no longer agree.

    The Koszul pair structure developed in this chapter –- the quadratic condition, the periodicity phe-
nomena, the level-shifting involution –- provides the algebraic skeleton on which the examples of Part II
are built. Every explicit computation there begins by verifying the Koszul condition and identifying the
dual; the reward is that the three main theorems then deliver bar cohomology, spectral collapse, and com-
plementarity without further work. The periodicity theorems, in particular, constrain the genus tower:
the Hochschild cohomology ring CH∗ (A) controls deformations of the bar complex at every genus, and
Koszul duality exchanges the periodicity generators of A and A ! with a sign (Corollary 14.6.25).

11.4.1   Quadratic chiral algebras and their duals
Deﬁnition 11.4.1 (Quadratic chiral algebra). A chiral algebra A is quadratic if it admits a presentation

                                             A = 𝑇chiral (V)/( 𝑅)

where:
• V is a locally free O 𝑋 -module of generators
• 𝑇chiral (V) is the free chiral algebra on V
• 𝑅 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (V ⊠ V) consists of quadratic relations
   The free chiral algebra requires care to define. Following Beilinson–Drinfeld:

                                          A ! = 𝑇chiral (V ∗ )/( 𝑅⊥ )

where:
• V ∗ = H 𝑜𝑚 O𝑋 (V , 𝜔 𝑋 ) is the dual shifted by the canonical bundle
• 𝑅⊥ consists of relations orthogonal to 𝑅 under the canonical pairing

Remark 11.4.4 (Three objects). The bar construction 𝐵¯ ch (A) is the Koszul dual coalgebra: a conilpotent
dg coalgebra cogenerated by V ∗ with corelations 𝑅⊥ . The Koszul dual algebra A ! is its graded linear dual:
A ! = 𝐵¯ ch (A) ∨ . The cobar of the bar recovers A itself: Ω ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)) ≃ A (Theorem 6.12.1). What is a
relation in A becomes cofreedom in 𝐵¯ ch (A) and freedom in A ! .

11.5     Example: boson-fermion duality
11.5.1  The free boson chiral algebra
The free boson B on a curve 𝑋 is defined as follows:
   As a chiral algebra. The free boson B is the chiral envelope of the Heisenberg Lie∗ algebra 𝜔 𝑋 (with

11.5.3   Establishing Koszul duality
Theorem 11.5.1 (Boson-fermion correspondence via lattice VOA; [proved] [165]). The free boson
B and free fermion F are related by bosonization through the rank-1 lattice vertex algebra 𝑉ℤ :

                             𝑉ℤ ⊃ B ,               F  𝑉ℤ            (as super vertex algebras)

Remark 11.5.2. This is not Koszul duality in the operadic sense. Koszul duality preserves the dimension of
the generating space: if A has generators in a space 𝑉 , then A ! has generators in 𝑉 ∗ , so dim 𝑉 = dim 𝑉 ∗ .
Here B has one generator ( 𝛼 ) while F has two generators (𝜓 , 𝜓 ∗ ). The Heisenberg algebra is not Koszul
self-dual: H𝜅! ≃ Sym𝑐ℎ (𝑉 ∗ ), a commutative chiral algebra (Part II). The boson-fermion correspondence
is instead a lattice VOA extension: the vertex operators 𝜓 = :𝑒 𝑖𝜙 : and 𝜓 ∗ = :𝑒 − 𝑖 𝜙 : lie in 𝑉ℤ , not in the
Heisenberg subalgebra.

Computation 11.5.3 (Boson Hochschild cohomology; [proved]). Degree 0.

the center of B, consisting of elements whose OPE with every field is regular. An element 𝑎 ∈ B lies in

   Degree 2. A 2-cocycle 𝜙 ∈ 𝐶 2 defines a deformation:

                                     𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) ·𝑡 𝛼 (𝑤 ) = 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛼 (𝑤 ) + 𝑡 𝜙 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 )

                              0

The fermion Hochschild groups are isomorphic to the boson groups (Computation 11.5.3), though the

Remark 11.5.5 (Numerical coincidence). The boson and fermion have isomorphic Hochschild cohomology
groups:
                                 𝐻 𝐻 𝑛 (B) = (ℂ, 0, ℂ) = 𝐻 𝐻 𝑛 (F ) .
In particular the numerical relation 𝐻 𝐻 𝑛 (B)  𝐻 𝐻 2− 𝑛 (F ) ∨ holds. However, this is not an instance
of Theorem 11.4.8: the boson and fermion are not Koszul dual (the Heisenberg has one generator while
the fermion has two; the bosonization correspondence is an isomorphism via lattice VOA extension, not a
Koszul duality). The Koszul dual of H𝑘 is Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) with curvature 𝑚0 = −𝑘𝜔 (equivalently, CE(𝔥− 𝑘 )
since 𝔥 is abelian), not F . The coincidence above reflects the fact that both algebras are ‘‘maximally simple’’
free-field theories with one-dimensional deformation spaces.

construction, which requires a cyclic 𝐿∞ algebra over the modular operad, see Theorem 34.12.3.

Deﬁnition 11.5.11 (Cyclic deformation complex: bar-intrinsic form). Let A be a modular Koszul chiral algebra

b
   This object has four essential properties:
   (i) Filtered-completeness: the bar-length filtration makes Def cyc (A) complete and pronilpotent.

via bar-coalgebra coderivations.

11.5.6    The chiral graph complex and cyclic 𝐿∞ structure
The dg Lie algebra Def cyc (A) of Proposition 11.5.8 is the genus-0 shadow of a richer structure: a full
cyclic 𝐿∞ -algebra whose higher brackets 𝑙𝑛 (𝑛 ≥ 3) are defined by summing over chiral graphs. This is
648                             Chapter 11. Chiral Hochschild cohomology and Koszul duality


the adaptation of the Kontsevich–Soibelman construction [221] to chiral algebras on algebraic curves, via
configuration space integrals on Fulton–MacPherson compactifications.
Deﬁnition 11.5.16 (Chiral graphs). A chiral graph of type ( 𝑛, 𝐿 ) is a datum Γ = (𝑉ext ,𝑉int , 𝐸, 𝜎 ) where:
   (i) 𝑉ext = {𝑣1 , . . . , 𝑣𝑛 } is an ordered set of 𝑛 external vertices (legs);
  (ii) 𝑉int is a finite set of internal vertices, each of valence ≥ 3;
 (iii) 𝐸 is a set of edges connecting vertices in 𝑉 = 𝑉ext ⊔ 𝑉int , with the graph (𝑉 , 𝐸 ) connected;
 (iv) 𝜎 is a cyclic ordering of the half-edges at each internal vertex (ribbon structure);
  (v) the loop number is 𝐿 = | 𝐸 | − |𝑉 | + 1.
The automorphism group Aut( Γ) consists of graph automorphisms preserving the external vertex labeling
and the ribbon structure. Let 𝔊𝑛,𝐿 denote the set of isomorphism classes of chiral graphs of type ( 𝑛, 𝐿 ).

Remark 11.5.23 (Relation to known constructions). (i) On 𝑋 = 𝔸1 , the graph sum reduces to the Kontsevich–
Soibelman 𝐿∞ structure on CoDer( 𝐵 𝐴) [1] [221]. (ii) In the Costello–Gwilliam framework [27, 96], the
graph sum is perturbative quantization of a holomorphic CS-type theory on 𝑋 . (iii) The full graph complex
   𝐿 𝔊𝑛,𝐿 carries Getzler–Kapranov [23] modular-operadic structure; the 𝐿 > 0 part encodes the genus
L
tower. (iv) Both analytic hypotheses are unconditional: Proposition 11.5.20 and Proposition 11.5.19.
Remark 11.5.24 (Physical interpretation). Each chiral graph Γ is a tree-level Feynman diagram: external legs
are deformation inputs, internal edges carry the Szegő propagator 𝑆 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ), and internal vertices carry 𝐴∞
operations. The homotopy Jacobi identity is the Ward identity, mediated by Stokes’ theorem on 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑋 ).
The passage to 𝐿 > 0 (loop level) gives the genus- 𝑔 obstruction from 𝐿 = 𝑔 loop diagrams; the cyclic
pairing ensures the BV QME order by order [168].

11.5.7     The modular deformation complex
The genus-0 cyclic deformation complex Def cyc (A) (Definition 11.5.6) is the tree-level shadow of a modular
convolution dg Lie algebra. The full modular version assembles all genera:
Deﬁnition 11.5.25 (Modular deformation complex). For a chiral algebra A on a smooth projective curve 𝑋 ,
the modular deformation complex is the convolution dg Lie algebra

                       Def mod (A) :=      HomΣ𝑛 𝐶∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) , End A ( 𝑔, 𝑛) ,
                                        Y                                     

where:
• 𝐶∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) denotes chains on the Deligne–Mumford compactification, and the product runs over stable
  pairs ( 𝑔, 𝑛) with 2 𝑔 − 2 + 𝑛 > 0;
• End A ( 𝑔, 𝑛) is the endomorphism space of A ⊗ 𝑛 with genus- 𝑔 curvature;
• the Lie bracket arises from graph gluing: composing endomorphisms along the boundary stratification
  of M 𝑔,𝑛 (separating and non-separating clutching maps).
A Maurer–Cartan element Θ ∈ MC(Def mod (A)) is equivalent to a modular homotopy type on the
underlying graded object of A (Definition 6.15.10). The MC equation 𝑑Θ + 21 [ Θ, Θ] = 0 encodes
clutching compatibility at every genus.
Remark 11.5.26 (Modular versus cyclic). The restriction Def mod (A)| 𝑔 =0  Def cyc (A) recovers the genus-
0 cyclic deformation complex. At 𝑔 ≥ 1, the coefficients are chains on M 𝑔,𝑛 , so stable-graph geometry
enters the convolution algebra itself (Remark 4.1.14).

Remark 11.5.29 (Genus bookkeeping and exhaustiveness). The three components are exactly the
codimension-1 boundary contributions to the modular bar differential–-no others exist. To see this,
classify the codimension-1 boundary strata of M 𝑔,𝑛 : a general boundary divisor 𝐷 Γ is indexed by a stable
graph Γ with one edge. If removing the edge disconnects Γ, the stratum is separating ( 𝑑sep ); if it does not,
the stratum is non-separating ( 𝑑ns ). The third component, 𝑑int , is the ‘‘interior’’ contribution from the
vertex differential on each component.
    The three components act on the genus decomposition 𝑔 = 𝑣 𝑔𝑣 + 𝑏1 ( Γ) as follows: 𝑑int preserves
                                                                     P
the graph (hence preserves 𝑏1 and all 𝑔𝑣 ); 𝑑sep contracts an edge between distinct components (preserving
𝑏1 and total genus); 𝑑ns absorbs a loop edge into a vertex ( 𝑔𝑣 ↦→ 𝑔𝑣 + 1, 𝑏1 ↦→ 𝑏1 − 1, total genus preserved).
The total genus 𝑔 = 𝑣 𝑔𝑣 + 𝑏1 ( Γ) is an invariant of all three.

Proof. The proof extends the Stokes argument of Theorem 11.5.21 from trees to graphs with loops.
    Step 1: Two sources of the QME. The QME has two structurally distinct contributions, corresponding
to the two types of codimension-1 boundary strata of M 𝑔,𝑛 (Definition 12.13.23):

amplitude integrates a form over 𝐶 |𝑉int | ( 𝑋 ) ( Σ). Collision of internal vertices produces codimension-1
boundary strata of the configuration space (Proposition 11.5.20). By Stokes’ theorem, these boundary
contributions give 𝑚 ( 𝑔1 ) ◦ 𝑚 ( 𝑔2 ) compositions with 𝑔1 + 𝑔2 = 𝐺 , exactly as in the tree-level proof of
Theorem 11.5.21.
    Non-separating terms (second sum in (11.8)). These arise not from the boundary of the configuration
space but from the graph structure: contracting a loop edge in Γ (the 𝑑ns component of Definition 11.5.27)

at genus 𝐺 − 1. Analytically, this corresponds to the period integral 𝛾 𝑆 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) 𝑑𝑧 along a homology cycle

Remark 11.5.39 (Three readings of the virtual bar class). The hierarchy (L1)–(L3) reflects the three standard
ways of extracting invariants from a 𝐾 -class–-the same progression that connects the Euler characteristic
to the Chern character to the holonomy representation. In the categorical logarithm paradigm:
• (L1) det 𝑉A = 𝜅 · 𝜆 is the leading coeﬃcient of the logarithm (Theorem Dscal ).
• (L2) ch(𝑉A ) ↔ Δ A ( 𝑥 ) is the Taylor expansion of the logarithm (Theorem DΔ ).
• (L3) Hol(𝑉A ) = Π A is the monodromy of the logarithm–-the ambiguity in choosing a branch (the
  periodicity profile).
This realizes the passage 𝜅 → Δ → Π (scalar → spectral → holonomy) as the natural filtration of informa-
tion in the 𝐾 -class 𝑉A , just as the passage 𝑐1 → ch → ∇ is the natural filtration of information in a vector
bundle with connection. The Heisenberg specialization (Chapter 1, Definition 1.13.1) illustrates all three
levels: 𝜅 = 𝑘 (the level), Δ = 1/(1 − 𝑥 ) (free boson), Π = (ℤ, 𝑘 ℤ, {1}) (abelian periodicity).

11.6     Stratified periodicity framework
11.6.1   Overview: three sources of periodicity
The Hochschild cohomology of chiral algebras can exhibit three types of periodicity: Type I (Modular),
from rational central charge and modular transformations; Type II (Quantum), from quantum groups at
roots of unity; and Type III (Geometric), from the topology of the underlying curve.
Remark 11.6.1. The unconditional core is the quantum periodicity input and the structural theorem that
independent periodicity sources combine by lcm. Explicit modular periods, sharp geometric periods, and
higher-rank closed formulas are conjectural outside the rank-1/minimal-model test cases.

11.6.3.1 The quantum group structure
Proposition 11.6.15 (Quantum periodicity profile under admissible-level KL/DS transport;
[proved]). Let W 𝑘 (𝔤) be the W-algebra at admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 where ℎ∨ is the dual Coxeter
number, 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ , 𝑞 ≥ ℎ∨ , gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1. Then the quantum integers, quantum dimensions, and fusion
coefficients (transported through the KL/DS interface) recur with period dividing

                                        𝑀 = 2ℎ∨ 𝑝𝑞 /gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞, ℎ∨ ) .

This records only the Type II quantum input to the periodicity profile ( 𝑁mod , 𝑁quant ); upgrading to full
bar complex periodicity requires a separate OPE transport theorem.

Proof. At admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 , we write 𝑞KL = exp( 𝜋 𝑖 /( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ )) = exp( 𝜋 𝑖 · 𝑞 / 𝑝) for the
Kazhdan–Lusztig quantum parameter. Since gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1, this 𝑞KL is a root of unity of order dividing
2 𝑝.
    Step 1: Semisimplicity. By Arakawa’s theorem [37], the category O𝑘 (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) at admissible level is
semisimple with finitely many simple objects, indexed by the admissible weights.
    Step 2: Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence and DS reduction. The Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence [184] pro-
vides a braided tensor equivalence O𝑘 (b

11.6.4    Type III: geometric tautological depth
11.6.4.1 Genus dependence and nilpotent depth
The geometric contribution to bar cohomology from higher genus provides bounded tautological depth
rather than periodicity: the Kodaira–Spencer operator is nilpotent and the bar spectral sequence terminates
after finitely many steps.
Theorem 11.6.17 (Geometric tautological depth bound; [proved]). For a chiral algebra A on a genus
𝑔 ≥ 2 curve 𝑋 , the Kodaira–Spencer image of the Hodge class is nilpotent:

                                      𝜅 ( 𝑐1 (𝔼)) 3 𝑔 −2 = 0 in 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A) .

In particular, the geometric direction of the bar spectral sequence has bounded tautological depth: at most
3 𝑔 − 3 nontrivial geometric filtration layers can contribute.
    At 𝑔 = 0, no Hodge bundle contributes; at 𝑔 = 1, the relation 𝑐1 (𝔼) = 121 𝛿 absorbs the Hodge contri-
bution into the modular data.
11.6. Stratified periodicity framework                                                                    667


Proof. The Kodaira–Spencer map (Theorem 8.14.26) provides a ring homomorphism

                                      𝜅 : 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , ℚ) −→ 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A)
whose image controls the geometric contributions to bar cohomology. The geometric operator 𝜎geom acts
via multiplication by 𝜅 ( 𝜆), where 𝜆 = 𝑐1 (𝔼) is the first Chern class of the Hodge bundle 𝔼 → M 𝑔 .
    Since dimℂ M 𝑔 = 3 𝑔 − 3, every cohomology class of degree exceeding 2(3 𝑔 − 3) = 6 𝑔 − 6 vanishes.
In particular,
                               𝜆3 𝑔 −2 = 𝑐1 (𝔼) 3 𝑔 −2 = 0 in 𝐻 2(3 𝑔 −2) (M 𝑔 , ℚ) ,
since 2(3 𝑔 − 2) = 6 𝑔 − 4 > 6 𝑔 − 6 for all 𝑔 ≥ 2. Applying 𝜅 :
                            𝜅 ( 𝜆) 3 𝑔 −2 = 𝜅 ( 𝜆3 𝑔 −2 ) = 𝜅 (0) = 0 in 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A) .
Therefore 𝜎geom is nilpotent of index at most 3 𝑔 − 2, giving at most 3 𝑔 − 3 nontrivial filtration steps. At
𝑔 = 0 there is no Hodge bundle; at 𝑔 = 1, 𝑐1 (𝔼) = 121 𝛿 absorbs into 𝑁mod .
Remark 11.6.18 (Nilpotent depth vs. periodicity). 𝜎geom is nilpotent ( 𝜎 𝑁 = 0), not periodic ( 𝜎 𝑁 = id): the
geometric contribution provides a stabilization threshold (cf. Remark 11.6.30).
Theorem 11.6.19 (Sharp geometric depth on smooth moduli; [proved]). For a chiral algebra A on
a smooth genus 𝑔 ≥ 2 curve, suppose the Kodaira–Spencer map factors through the cohomology of the
smooth moduli space:
                                 𝜅 : 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , ℚ) −→ 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A) .
Then the nilpotency index of 𝜅 ( 𝜆) is at most 𝑔 − 1:
                                     𝜅 ( 𝑐1 (𝔼)) 𝑔 −1 = 0 in 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A) .
In particular:
(a) At genus 2, the Hodge class contribution vanishes entirely: 𝜅 ( 𝜆) = 0.
(b) At genus 3, the geometric depth is at most 2 (compared to 7 from the compactified bound).
(c) In general, the sharp bound 𝑔 − 1 improves the compactified bound 3 𝑔 − 2 by a factor of approxi-
    mately 3.
Proof. The tautological ring 𝑅∗ (M 𝑔 ) of the smooth moduli space satisfies the Graber–Vakil vanishing
theorem [258] (extending Looijenga [259]):
                                      𝑅 𝑑 (M 𝑔 ) = 0 for 𝑑 > 𝑔 − 2.
The Hodge class 𝜆 = 𝑐1 (𝔼) is a tautological class of degree 1. On the smooth moduli space, the Mumford
relation reduces to 𝜆 | M 𝑔 = 𝜅1 /12 (since the boundary class 𝛿 vanishes on M 𝑔 ). Therefore
                                          𝜆 𝑔 −1 ∈ 𝑅 𝑔 −1 (M 𝑔 ) = 0
since 𝑔 − 1 > 𝑔 − 2. Applying 𝜅 :
                                          𝜅 ( 𝜆) 𝑔 −1 = 𝜅 ( 𝜆 𝑔 −1 ) = 0.
    For genus 2: 𝑔 − 1 = 1, so 𝜆1 = 𝜆 ∈ 𝑅1 (M2 ). Since 𝑅 𝑑 (M2 ) = 0 for 𝑑 > 0, we get 𝜆 | M2 = 0, hence
𝜅 ( 𝜆) = 0. This means the Hodge class produces no geometric correction to bar cohomology at genus 2:
the genus-2 bar complex, at the level of the Hodge class contribution, is determined entirely by the genus-0
data.

Remark 11.6.20 (Factorization hypothesis). The factorization through 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 ) holds on smooth curves.
On M 𝑔 , boundary divisor classes 𝛿𝑖 can increase nilpotent depth beyond 𝑔 − 1 (but never beyond 3 𝑔 − 2,
Theorem 11.6.17).
Conjecture 11.6.21 (Geometric amplitude on compactiﬁed moduli; [conjectured]). For a Koszul chiral al-
gebra A on M 𝑔 with factorization extensions to the boundary, the nilpotency index of the geometric
operator 𝜅 ( 𝜆) on M 𝑔 is controlled by the Mumford relation 12𝜆 = 𝜅1 + 𝛿 : the boundary contribution
𝜅 ( 𝛿 ) increases the nilpotency index beyond the interior bound 𝑔 − 1 by at most the depth of the boundary
tautological ring. Precisely, there exists a function nil𝜕 ( 𝑔 ), depending only on the genus, such that:

                          nil( 𝜅 ( 𝜆)) ≤ ( 𝑔 − 1) + nil𝜕 ( 𝑔 ) ,   nil𝜕 ( 𝑔 ) ≤ 2 𝑔 − 1.

The additive structure reflects the Mumford decomposition 12𝜆 = 𝜅1 + 𝛿 , with the interior contributing
at most 𝑔 − 1 (proved) and the boundary contributing nil𝜕 ( 𝑔 ) additional layers.
Remark 11.6.22 (Scope and provenance). The interior bound 𝑔 − 1 is proved (Theorem 11.6.19, Graber–
Vakil); the compactified bound 3 𝑔 − 2 is proved (Theorem 11.6.17). The conjecture interpolates via the
Mumford relation. The geometric contribution is nilpotent ( 𝜎 𝑁 = 0), not periodic ( 𝜎 𝑁 = id); true
periodicity arises from Types I and II only. (Part of the MC2 theorem package; Theorem 8.18.72.)

Example 11.6.23 (Genus 0: the sphere). No geometric tautological depth (simply connected, no moduli).

Example 11.6.25 (Genus 2: Hodge class vanishing). By Theorem 11.6.19, the Hodge class contribution vanishes
entirely at genus 2: 𝜅 ( 𝜆) = 0 in 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A). This follows from the Graber–Vakil vanishing 𝑅 𝑑 (M2 ) = 0
for 𝑑 > 0. The genus-2 bar complex receives no geometric corrections from 𝑐1 (𝔼); any higher-genus
modifications at 𝑔 = 2 must arise from other tautological classes or from boundary contributions on M 2
(which reduce to M1,1 × M1,1 and M1,2 data).

Remark 11.6.30 (Stratiﬁed periodicity). The mature formulation separates periodic from nilpotent con-

radius of 𝑇rec bounds 𝑁mod (Theorem 27.17.41). See §34.12.9, Future 7.

11.7.3   Holographic duality
Conjecture 11.7.3 (Holographic Koszul duality; [conjectured]). A holographic Koszul template for
AdS3 /CFT2 should exchange:
• a suitable bulk gravity package ↔ a boundary CFT package
• Boson-like fields ↔ Fermion-like fields
• the boundary algebra should arise as a Koszul-dual shadow of a suitable bulk package, heuristically
     !
  Abulk  ≃ Aboundary
Remark 11.7.4 (Scope). This conjecture lies outside the present monograph: it is a physical interpretation,
not a theorem. A precise formulation would require specifying the bulk as a factorization algebra on a
3-manifold with boundary (Costello–Li). The relation 𝑐bulk + 𝑐boundary = 26 has no known proof from
Koszul duality alone. (Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.5.)
   The evidence is threefold: the central charges satisfy 𝑐bulk + 𝑐boundary = 26, the Hochschild cohomologies
are Koszul dual, and the twisting morphism exhibits the same formal pattern used by the conjectural
holographic dictionary.

11.8.10    Computational strategy
Remark 11.8.13 (Computing 𝐻 𝐻 ∗ in practice). To compute 𝐻 𝐻chiral    𝑛 (A) for a chiral algebra given by

generators and OPE data, one proceeds as follows: (1) construct the bar complex 𝐵¯ 𝑛 (A) using configuration
space integrals; (2) build the cobar complex Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) by inserting distributional duals; (3) form the
Hom complex Hom( Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) , A); (4) compute cohomology ker( 𝑑 )/im( 𝑑 ) at each degree. For Koszul
algebras, the concentration of the bar coalgebra 𝐵¯ (A) (whose dual is A ! ) reduces the computation to
lower-dimensional complexes.
Remark 11.8.14 (Noncommutative Hodge degeneration). The pole-order filtration on the chiral Hochschild
complex degenerates at 𝐸1 for Koszul algebras (Theorem 6.12.7), giving a mixed structure analogous to
Kaledin’s noncommutative Hodge theory [77]. Theorem C (complementarity) is Verdier duality in this
setting, exchanging the Hodge filtrations of A and A ! .

11.8.11   Summary and outlook
The bar-cobar approach to Hochschild cohomology provides explicit formulas (all 𝐻 𝐻 ∗ groups com-
putable via configuration space integrals), a geometric interpretation ( 𝐻 𝐻 ∗ from topology of configura-
tion spaces), the Gerstenhaber bracket and 𝐿∞ operations, Koszul duality ( 𝐻 𝐻 𝑛 (A) ↔ 𝐻 𝐻 2− 𝑛 (A ! )),
and deformation theory ( 𝐻 𝐻 2 controls deformations, obstructions in 𝐻 𝐻 3 ). We apply this framework
throughout to quantum corrections, W-algebras, level-rank duality, and higher genus contributions.
    The deformation-obstruction theory developed above is universal: it applies to any Koszul chiral algebra.
In Part 2, we make this concrete. For every major family of vertex algebras –- Heisenberg, free fermion,
𝛽𝛾 -𝑏𝑐 , affine Kac–Moody, Virasoro, 𝑊 -algebras, Yangians –- we compute the bar complex, identify the
Koszul dual, determine the obstruction coefficient 𝜅 (A), and verify the complementarity and genus uni-
versality theorems explicitly. The shared discriminant phenomenon (Theorem 27.17.20) and the 𝐴ˆ-genus
appearance in genus expansions emerge as consequences of the modular characteristic package, not as
isolated coincidences.
Chapter 12


Chiral modules and geometric resolutions

The bar-cobar machinery of the preceding chapters operates at the algebra level. This chapter extends it to
modules: for a chiral algebra A and an A-module M, the module bar construction 𝐵 A (M) produces a
comodule over the bar coalgebra, and the resulting functor Φ is an equivalence on appropriate categories.
For the Heisenberg algebra (Chapter 1), this reduces to the classical Fock space duality; for affine Kac–
Moody algebras, it produces the Feigin–Frenkel correspondence on Verma modules.

12.1     Factorization modules: definitions and categories
A module over a factorization algebra is itself a factorization algebra on a pointed space: the marked point
carries the module data, the remaining points carry algebra data (Voronov [122], Costello–Gwilliam [27],
Ayala–Francis [45]). The bar complex 𝐵¯ (A , 𝑀 ) lives on such pointed configuration spaces, and its Verdier
dual is a comodule over 𝐵¯ (A). When A is Koszul, every module 𝑀 admits a bar resolution whose 𝐸2 -
collapse computes Ext groups, and the resulting module Koszul duality exchanges representation categories
under 𝑘 ↔ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ .
Deﬁnition 12.1.1 (Factorization module). Let F be a factorization algebra on a manifold 𝑀 with values in a
symmetric monoidal ∞-category V, and let 𝑥 ∈ 𝑀 be a point. A factorization module over F supported
at 𝑥 is a rule M that assigns:
  (i) To each open disk 𝐷 ∋ 𝑥 : an object M ( 𝐷 ) ∈ V.
 (ii) To each finite collection of pairwise disjoint opens 𝑈1 , . . . , 𝑈𝑛 ⊂ 𝐷 with 𝑈𝑖 ∩ { 𝑥 } = ∅ for all 𝑖 and
      𝑥 ∈ 𝐷 : an action map
                           𝛼𝑈𝐷1 ,...,𝑈𝑛 : F (𝑈1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ F (𝑈𝑛 ) ⊗ M ( 𝐷 ) −→ M ( 𝐷 ) ,
       compatible with the factorization structure of F on 𝑀 \ { 𝑥 }.
These data satisfy associativity and unit axioms parallel to (FA2)–(FA5) of Definition 4.10.3, with M
replacing F at the marked point 𝑥 .
Remark 12.1.2 (The Swiss-cheese picture). When 𝑀 = ℝ𝑛 and 𝑥 = 0, the collection of disks around the
origin with disjoint smaller disks away from the origin defines the Swiss-cheese operad SC𝑛 of Voronov [122].
Algebras over SC𝑛 are pairs ( 𝐴, 𝑀 ) where 𝐴 is an 𝐸𝑛 -algebra and 𝑀 is an 𝐴-module in an appropriate
homotopical sense. Definition 12.1.1 globalizes this to arbitrary manifolds.

Deﬁnition 12.1.5 (Module categories). For a chiral algebra A on 𝑋 , we define the following categories of
modules:
   (i) Mod A : the dg category of chiral A-modules (Definition 12.1.3), with morphisms the D 𝑋 -module
       maps compatible with the chiral action. This is a stable ∞-category when V = Ch(ℂ).
  (ii) ModEA1 : the dg category of E1 -chiral A-modules (Definition 12.1.4), when A is E1 -chiral. There is a
       forgetful functor Mod A → ModEA1 when A is E∞ -chiral.
 (iii) 𝐷 (Mod A ): the derived category, obtained by inverting quasi-isomorphisms. We assume throughout
       that Mod A is compactly generated: i.e., it is generated under filtered colimits by the compact objects
       Mod𝑐A . This holds whenever A is finitely generated as a chiral algebra (the free modules Free A (𝑉 )
       for finite-dimensional 𝑉 are compact generators).
Remark 12.1.6 (Tensor structure on module categories). For a rational vertex algebra 𝑉 , the module category
Mod𝑉 carries a braided tensor structure via the fusion product (Huang–Lepowsky–Zhang [167]), with
braiding from the monodromy of conformal blocks on ℙ1 . For b    𝔤𝑘 at positive integer level, this is identified
with the quantum group tensor product on C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) via the KL equivalence (Theorem 20.11.4).

Remark 12.1.12 (Towards chain-level / evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno). The mechanism above–
-Verdier duality reverses collision cycle orientation, hence inverts the 𝑅-matrix monodromy–-admits a
homotopy-coherent enhancement. Ordered configuration spaces on the line carry the braid group action
(Arnol’d), and bar-cobar duality implements Verdier duality on these configuration spaces. The chain-
level / evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno theorem (Theorems 24.9.3 and 24.9.5) proves that this
mechanism, composed with the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence, yields a chain-level derived equivalence
with braiding reversal 𝑅𝑞 ↦→ 𝑅𝑞 −1 –- both for affine algebras and for Yangians on the evaluation locus.
This is the theorematic DK-0/DK-1 package. The later DK stages –- extension beyond the evaluation
locus, the factorization-level Kazhdan bridge, and the dg-shifted comparison –- remain conjectural; see
Conjecture 34.12.13 and §24.9 for the full treatment.

Deﬁnition 12.1.22 (Bundle of conformal blocks). Let A be a rational chiral algebra and Λ1 , . . . , Λ𝑟 a col-
lection of highest weights. As the pointed curve ( 𝑋 ; 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑟 ) varies over the moduli space M 𝑔,𝑟 , the
spaces of conformal blocks (Definition 12.1.16) assemble into a vector bundle

                                       𝕍 (A; Λ1 , . . . , Λ𝑟 ) → M 𝑔,𝑟

of finite rank, called the bundle of conformal blocks (or bundle of vacua).
   (i) The bundle carries a projective flat connection: the Knizhnik–Zamolodchikov–Bernard (KZB) con-
       nection, whose horizontal sections satisfy the KZB equations.
  (ii) The rank of 𝕍 is independent of the genus- 𝑔 curve 𝑋 and depends only on the algebra A, the weights
       Λ𝑖 , and the genus 𝑔 .
 (iii) The factorization property of A implies a factorization of the bundle under degeneration: when 𝑋
       degenerates to a nodal curve 𝑋0 = 𝑋1 ∪ 𝑝 𝑋2 , the fiber satisfies

12.2     Highest weight modules
Affine Kac–Moody, Virasoro, and W-algebras carry a conformal grading; their module theory is governed
by highest weight representations.
Deﬁnition 12.2.1 (Weight grading and highest weight modules). Let A be a chiral algebra equipped with
a conformal vector (a Virasoro subalgebra generated by 𝑇 ( 𝑧 ) = 𝑛 𝐿𝑛 𝑧 − 𝑛−2 ). A weight grading on an
                                                                   P
A-module M is a decomposition M = ℎ M ℎ into generalized eigenspaces of 𝐿0 .
                                       L
   A module M is highest weight of weight 𝜆 (encoding the 𝐿0 -eigenvalue ℎ together with any additional
Cartan data) if M = A · 𝑣𝜆 is generated by a vector 𝑣𝜆 satisfying:
   (i) A >0 · 𝑣𝜆 = 0 (annihilation by positive modes);
  (ii) 𝐿0 · 𝑣𝜆 = ℎ · 𝑣𝜆 (weight condition);
 (iii) for affine algebras, 𝔥 · 𝑣𝜆 = 𝜆 | 𝔥 · 𝑣𝜆 (Cartan eigenvalue).
692                                      Chapter 12. Chiral modules and geometric resolutions


Deﬁnition 12.2.2 (Verma module). The Verma module M ( 𝜆) is the universal highest weight module of
weight 𝜆: it is induced from the one-dimensional representation of the non-negative subalgebra A ≥0 =
A0 ⊕ A >0 on which 𝑣𝜆 has weight 𝜆 and A >0 acts by zero:

                                 M ( 𝜆) = Ind A
                                              A ≥0 ℂ𝜆 = 𝑈 (A <0 ) ⊗ℂ ℂ𝜆 .

Every highest weight module of weight 𝜆 is a quotient of M ( 𝜆). The unique simple quotient is L ( 𝜆) =
M ( 𝜆)/J ( 𝜆), where J ( 𝜆) is the maximal proper submodule.
Deﬁnition 12.2.3 (Shapovalov form). The Shapovalov form on M ( 𝜆) is the unique symmetric bilinear form
⟨·, ·⟩𝜆 : M ( 𝜆) × M ( 𝜆) → ℂ satisfying ⟨𝑣𝜆 , 𝑣𝜆 ⟩𝜆 = 1 and the contravariance property

                                       ⟨ 𝑎𝑛 · 𝑢, 𝑤 ⟩𝜆 = ⟨𝑢, 𝑎− 𝑛 · 𝑤 ⟩𝜆

for all modes 𝑎𝑛 of generating fields. Equivalently, ⟨𝑢, 𝑤 ⟩𝜆 = 𝜀 ( 𝑢 · 𝜎 (𝑤 )), where 𝜎 is the anti-involution
sending 𝑎𝑛 ↦→ 𝑎− 𝑛 and 𝜀 is the counit M ( 𝜆) → ℂ𝜆 .
    The form is non-degenerate on the weight-( ℎ+𝑛) subspace M ( 𝜆) ℎ+𝑛 if and only if M ( 𝜆) has no
singular vectors of weight ℎ+𝑛. The Kac determinant det⟨·, ·⟩𝜆,𝑛 on this subspace admits a product formula
([76], Theorem 9.1; [90], Lecture 4) whose vanishing locus determines the reducibility of M ( 𝜆).
Proposition 12.2.4 (Generic irreducibility; [proved]). For the affine algebras b             𝔤𝑘 , the Virasoro
algebra Vir𝑐 , and the W-algebras W 𝑘 (𝔤): the Verma module M ( 𝜆) is irreducible for generic values of the

parameters, so its vanishing defines a proper subvariety of the parameter space.
    The reducibility locus includes:
   (i) Minimal model values: 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 = 1 − 6( 𝑝 − 𝑞 ) 2 / 𝑝𝑞 for Vir𝑐 (Feigin–Fuchs [159]);

 (iii) Critical level: 𝑘 = −ℎ for 𝔤
                             ∨    b𝑘 (the Sugawara construction is undefined; see Remark 6.4.12).
Remark 12.2.5 (Connection to Koszul duality). Generic irreducibility is the representation-theoretic coun-
terpart of the Koszul property. At generic level, the Ext groups

                              Ext O (M ( 𝜆) , M ( 𝜇)) = 0,       𝑞 > 0, 𝜆 ≠ 𝜇,

Theorem 12.2.14 (BGG reciprocity for affine algebras [3, 185]; [proved]). In category O𝑘 (b            𝔤) at
generic level, each simple module L ( 𝜆) has a projective cover 𝑃 ( 𝜆) satisfying the BGG reciprocity:

                                       [ 𝑃 ( 𝜆) : M ( 𝜇)] = [M ( 𝜇) : L ( 𝜆)]

where [ 𝑃 : M] denotes the Verma module multiplicity in a Verma flag of the projective, and [M : L]
denotes the composition factor multiplicity.
    Equivalently, the Grothendieck group 𝐾0 (O𝑘 ) has two natural bases: the Verma modules {[M ( 𝜆)]}
and the simple modules {[L ( 𝜆)]}. The transition matrix between them is upper-triangular (with respect
to the partial order on weights), and BGG reciprocity states that the inverse transition matrix is the transpose
of the transition matrix.
    This is proved for finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebras by Bernstein–Gel’fand–Gel’fand [3] and
extended to symmetrizable Kac–Moody algebras by Rocha-Caridi–Wallach and Kashiwara–Tanisaki [185].
Remark 12.2.15 (BGG reciprocity and the bar-cobar resolution). The projective cover 𝑃 ( 𝜆) is the bar res-
olution of L ( 𝜆) by Verma modules (Theorem 12.7.5, Step 1), so [ 𝑃 ( 𝜆) : M ( 𝜇)] counts bar complex
multiplicities. For a Koszul algebra, [ 𝑃 ( 𝜆) : M ( 𝜇)] = dim Ext∗O (L ( 𝜆) , L ( 𝜇)) and BGG reciprocity
becomes self-duality of the bar complex under the Shapovalov form.

ment of BGG reciprocity. The 𝐸2 page 𝐸2 = 𝐻 𝑞 ( 𝐵¯ 𝑝 (A)) of the bar filtration encodes the module
                                              𝑝,𝑞
                                     𝑝,0
multiplicities in each bar degree: 𝐸2 is the space of weight- 𝑝 bar generators, and 𝐸2 for 𝑞 > 0 measures
                                                                                        𝑝,𝑞

syzygies. At admissible levels, the rationality of 𝐿 𝑘 (𝔤) (Theorem 20.11.13) implies finite-dimensionality of
all 𝐸𝑟 (Corollary 20.11.15). A deeper question is whether the BGG multiplicities–-specifically the Kazh-

      the tilting module 𝑇 ( Λ) maps to the indecomposable tilting module 𝑇𝑞 ( Λ) ∈ C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)).
 (iv) Under the module Koszul duality Φ of Theorem 12.1.11, tilting modules are sent to tilting modules:
      Φ (𝑇𝑘 ( Λ)) = 𝑇𝑘′ ( Λ).
Proof. (i) follows from the self-contragredience 𝑇 ( 𝜆) ∨  𝑇 ( 𝜆) (the defining property of tilting modules),
combined with the compatibility of the bar construction with contragredience.
    (ii) is a direct consequence of BGG reciprocity: a projective 𝑃 ( 𝜇) has a Verma flag with multiplicities
[ 𝑃 ( 𝜇) : M ( 𝜈 )] = [M ( 𝜈 ) : L ( 𝜇)], and 𝑇 ( 𝜆), being both Verma-filtered and co-Verma-filtered, has
multiplicities equal to the composition multiplicities by the double-flag property.
    (iii) follows from the uniqueness of indecomposable tilting modules with a given highest weight: the
KL functor preserves highest weights and the Verma flag structure (it sends M ( Λ) to the quantum Verma
module 𝑀𝑞 ( Λ)), so it must send tilting to tilting.
    (iv) The Koszul duality functor preserves the Verma flag structure (since Verma modules are Koszul,
the bar complex of a Verma module is a comodule with the correct filtration). The self-duality of tilting
modules (both Verma-filtered and co-Verma-filtered) maps to the corresponding property at the dual level.
By uniqueness of indecomposable tilting modules, Φ (𝑇𝑘 ( Λ)) = 𝑇𝑘′ ( Λ).

Theorem 12.2.33 (Arakawa’s rationality criterion; [proved]). Let 𝑉 be a vertex algebra satisfying
