Remark 12.2.34 (Associated variety and Koszul duality). The associated variety is not preserved by level-
shifting Koszul duality: e.g., 𝑋𝑉1 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) = {0} but 𝑋𝑉−3 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) = 𝔰𝔩 ∗2 . When 𝑋𝑉 = {0}, the bar spectral sequence
degenerates at a finite page; for 𝑋𝑉 ≠ {0} it may have non-trivial higher differentials–-the passage from
Koszul to curved 𝐴∞ .
Proposition 12.2.35 (Orbit duality for affine vertex algebras; [proved]). Let 𝔤 be a simple Lie
algebra of type 𝐴 (i.e., 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ), and let 𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) be the simple affine vertex algebra at admissible level 𝑘 .
Then the associated varieties of 𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) and its Koszul dual 𝑉𝑘′ (𝔤) ( 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ ) are related by the
Barbasch–Vogan duality 𝑑 : N (𝔤) → N (𝔤):
                                              𝑋𝑉𝑘′ (𝔤) = 𝑑 ( 𝑋𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) )
where 𝑑 (𝕆𝜆 ) = 𝕆𝜆𝑡 is the orbit corresponding to the transpose partition (for type 𝐴, this equals the
Barbasch–Vogan duality of [203]).
Proof. At admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 with gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1 and 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ , Arakawa [126] shows that
𝑋𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) = 𝕆𝜆 where 𝜆 is determined by the denominator 𝑞 of the admissible level. For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 𝑁 : at non-
degenerate admissible level, 𝑋𝑉𝑘 = {0} (trivial orbit, partition (1 𝑁 )); at degenerate admissible level, 𝑋𝑉𝑘 =
𝕆𝜆 for a non-trivial partition 𝜆.
   The Koszul dual level 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −ℎ∨ − 𝑝/ 𝑞 lies outside the admissible regime
(Definition 20.11.12), but the vertex algebra 𝑉𝑘′ (𝔤) is well-defined. The associated variety 𝑋𝑉𝑘′ is
determined by the Feigin–Frenkel involution: the shift 𝑝/ 𝑞 ↦→ − 𝑝/ 𝑞 transposes the partition classifying
the nilpotent orbit (by the interplay between the dual Coxeter number and the admissible weight
classification; cf. Kac–Wakimoto [160]), giving 𝑋𝑉𝑘′ = 𝕆𝜆𝑡 . For type 𝐴, 𝜆 𝑡 is the transpose partition, and
𝕆𝜆𝑡 = 𝑑 (𝕆𝜆 ) by definition of Barbasch–Vogan duality.
Example 12.2.36 (𝔰𝔩 3 orbit duality). For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 3 , there are three nilpotent orbits, classified by partitions
of 3:

                     Partition                  Orbit                    Dimension     𝑑 (𝕆)
                     (1, 1, 1)               {0} (trivial)                  0           𝕆 (3)
                     (2, 1)        𝕆min (minimal = subregular)               4         𝕆 (2,1)
                     (3)                  𝕆prin (principal)                  6          {0}

The minimal orbit is self-dual under BV duality (since (2, 1) 𝑡 = (2, 1)), while the trivial and principal orbits
are exchanged.
    At non-degenerate admissible level 𝑘 = −3 + 𝑝/ 𝑞 ( 𝑝 ≥ 3, gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1): 𝑉𝑘 (𝔰𝔩 3 ) is rational with
𝑋𝑉𝑘 = {0}, while the Koszul dual at 𝑘 ′ = −3 − 𝑝/ 𝑞 has 𝑋𝑉𝑘′ = 𝕆prin = N . This illustrates the general
phenomenon that Koszul duality maps rational vertex algebras to maximally non-rational ones.
    At the ‘‘boundary’’ admissible level 𝑘 = −3 + 3/2 = −3/2, the associated variety is 𝑋𝑉−3/2 = 𝕆min , and
the Koszul dual at 𝑘 ′ = −3 − 3/2 = −9/2 also has 𝑋𝑉−9/2 = 𝕆min : both lie on the self-dual minimal orbit.
12.2. Highest weight modules                                                                                701


12.2.4    Logarithmic modules and non-semisimple tensor categories
When 𝑉 is not rational, the module category is non-semisimple: indecomposable modules need not be
simple, and 𝐿0 may act non-semisimply (with Jordan blocks). This occurs in two distinct situations:
(a) 𝑋𝑉 ≠ {0} (not 𝐶2 -cofinite): infinitely many simples, and the module category has no finiteness
    control;
(b) 𝑋𝑉 = {0} (𝐶2 -cofinite) but not rational: finitely many simples, but the module category is a ﬁnite
    non-semisimple tensor category–-the logarithmic case.
Such modules are called logarithmic because the correlation functions involve log( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) terms arising
from the Jordan block structure.
Deﬁnition 12.2.37 (Logarithmic module). A module M over a vertex algebra 𝑉 is logarithmic if the 𝐿0 -
action on M is not semisimple: there exist generalized eigenvectors 𝑣 ∈ M with ( 𝐿0 − ℎ) 𝑘 𝑣 = 0 but
( 𝐿0 − ℎ) 𝑘 −1 𝑣 ≠ 0 for some 𝑘 ≥ 2.
   The rank of the logarithmic module (at conformal weight ℎ ) is the maximal Jordan block size of 𝐿0 on
M ℎ . A rank-1 logarithmic module is an ordinary (non-logarithmic) module.
Proposition 12.2.38 (Logarithmic modules and bar complex extensions; [proved]). Let 𝑉 be a
vertex algebra that is not rational, and let L1 , L2 be simple 𝑉 -modules. A non-trivial extension

                                         0 → L1 → E → L2 → 0

in the module category corresponds to a class in Ext𝑉1 (L2 , L1 ), which is computed by the bar complex:

                               Ext𝑉𝑛 (L2 , L1 )  𝐻 𝑛 (Hom𝑉 ( 𝐵¯ (L2 ) , L1 )) .                          (12.8)

Proof. The bar construction for modules provides a resolution 𝐵¯ (𝑉 , L2 ) of L2 by 𝑉 -modules built from
the bar complex of 𝑉 ; applying Hom𝑉 (−, L1 ) and taking cohomology computes Ext𝑉∗ (L2 , L1 ).

Remark 12.2.39 (Jordan blocks and spectral sequence differentials). The Jordan block structure of loga-
rithmic modules is reflected in the bar SS: an indecomposable extension E with gr E  L1 ⊕ L2 has
the extension class [E] ∈ Ext1 appearing as a bar 1-cocycle. A length-𝑟 extension chain corresponds to
non-trivial 𝐸𝑟 differentials, analogous to Massey products.

(2, 1) model) is 𝐶2 -cofinite but not rational. By Adamović–Milas [114], W ( 𝑝) has exactly 2 𝑝 simple mod-

Remark 12.2.42 (Ext quiver of W (2)). The Ext quiver of W (2) (restricted to non-projective simples) has
vertices {Λ (1) , Λ (2)} and arrows: two arrows Λ (1) ⇒ Λ (2) and one arrow Λ (2) → Λ (1). The path alge-
bra of this quiver, modulo the relations imposed by the 𝐴∞ structure, recovers the endomorphism algebra
End( 𝑃 (1) ⊕ 𝑃 (2)) controlling the block. This shows how the bar complex encodes the representation-
theoretic data of a non-semisimple module category.
Remark 12.2.43 (Non-semisimple tensor categories and the bar complex). The bar complex detects non-
semisimplicity in three regimes (bar-cobar duality, in the sense of Theorem A, holds fully only in regime (i)):
   (i) Semisimple ( 𝑋𝑉 = {0}, rational): bar SS degenerates at 𝐸2 ; Verlinde exact.
  (ii) Non-semisimple ( 𝑋𝑉 = {0}, 𝐶2 -cofinite, not rational): higher differentials encode extensions; modi-
       fied Verlinde via pseudo-traces (Creutzig–Ridout [115]).
 (iii) Wild ( 𝑋𝑉 ≠ {0}): bar SS need not converge; curved 𝐴∞ regime (§12.8).

12.3     Resolutions and character formulas
For a bounded acyclic resolution 𝑉 • → 𝑀 , the graded character satisfies ch( 𝑀 ) = 𝑖 ≥0 (−1) 𝑖 ch(𝑉 𝑖 );
                                                                                         P
when the resolution terms are free or induced modules, this alternating sum collapses to a closed form. In
the chiral setting, vector spaces are replaced by D 𝑋 -modules, tensor products respect locality (singularities
only on diagonals), and configuration spaces provide the geometric arena.

12.4     Deriving the chiral module resolution
12.4.1   Free chiral modules

                             Free A (𝑉 ) =   Γ ( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (A ⊠𝑛 ⊠ 𝑉 ))

Proof. The 𝑛-th summand accounts for 𝑛 copies of A acting on 𝑉 : on the configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) of
𝑛 distinct points, the 𝑛 copies of A are placed without coincidences, and the extension 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ allows poles
along diagonals to encode OPE singularities. Taking global sections produces the space of allowed fields.

                                            (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝑚𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝑚 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0.

The operations are given by configuration space integrals: 𝑚1 is the bar differential,

is the residue action, and higher 𝑚𝑛 are given by iterated residues on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) weighted by the propagator
forms. The 𝐴∞ relations follow from Stokes’ theorem on the Fulton–MacPherson compactification
together with the Arnold–Orlik–Solomon relations (Theorem 5.1.22), exactly as in the bar nilpotency
proof (Theorem 6.2.27).
Remark 12.6.2. The 𝐴∞ -module structure on the bar resolution is a special case of the general homotopy
transfer theorem (Appendix K; see Keller [148] and Merkulov [149] for the original constructions). In the
chiral setting, the transfer data come from the operad structure on configuration spaces (Definition 12.13.20).

12.6.2    𝐿∞ structure
Theorem 12.6.3 ( 𝐿 ∞ structure on cochains; [proved]). The cochain complex RHom A (P• , P• )
carries an 𝐿∞ -algebra structure with brackets

                                       ℓ𝑛 :            RHom → RHom[2 − 𝑛] .
                                                  V𝑛

The first two brackets are ℓ1 ( 𝑓 ) = [ 𝑑, 𝑓 ] and ℓ2 ( 𝑓 , 𝑔 ) = (−1) | 𝑓 | [ 𝑓 , 𝑔 ] (the graded commutator); the
higher brackets ℓ𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 3 are the Massey-type operations arising from the homotopy transfer of the dg
Lie structure on endomorphisms. This is a consequence of the Kontsevich–Soibelman formality frame-
work [221].

12.6.3    Chiral Gerstenhaber structure
Theorem 12.6.4 (Chiral Gerstenhaber algebra; [proved]). The chiral Hochschild cohomology
𝐻 𝐻ch∗ (A , A) carries a Gerstenhaber algebra structure: a graded-commutative cup product ∪ : 𝐻 𝐻 𝑝 ⊗
𝐻 𝐻 𝑞 → 𝐻 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 and a degree-(−1) Lie bracket {−, −} : 𝐻 𝐻 𝑝 ⊗ 𝐻 𝐻 𝑞 → 𝐻 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 −1 satisfying the
Leibniz rule
                          { 𝑓 , 𝑔 ∪ ℎ } = { 𝑓 , 𝑔 } ∪ ℎ + (−1) ( | 𝑓 | −1) | 𝑔 | 𝑔 ∪ { 𝑓 , ℎ } .
The cup product arises from composition of multilinear chiral operations; the bracket from the commuta-
tor of vertex operators, realized via contraction of vector fields against forms on configuration spaces. The
Gerstenhaber structure on Hochschild cochains of associative algebras is due to Gerstenhaber [147]; the chi-
ral generalization follows from the action of the little discs operad on configuration spaces (Tamarkin [218],
Francis–Gaitsgory).

    Step 2: Vanishing of 𝑑1 at generic level. The 𝑑1 differential maps 𝐸1𝑛,∗ → 𝐸1𝑛+1,∗ , i.e., M ( 𝑤 · 𝜆) →

complex (Theorem 9.1.39) then yields an exact resolution of L ( 𝜆) by Verma modules, indexed by the affine
Weyl group and graded by the length function.
    Step 4: Screening operator differentials. The differentials 𝑑 : M (𝑤 ′ · 𝜆) → M (𝑤 · 𝜆) (for ℓ ( 𝑤 ′ ) =

The fusion ring has three simple objects; the subring generated by 𝐿 (2Λ1 ) is the ℤ/2 group ring

    In the bar complex framework, this corresponds to the 𝐸2 degeneration at generic/integrable

Proposition 12.7.13 (Ext complementarity at dual levels; [proved]). At the Koszul dual level 𝑘 ′ =
−𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −6, the situation reverses: 𝐿 −6 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) is not rational (its associated variety 𝑋 𝐿 −6 = N ≠ {0} by
orbit duality, Proposition 12.2.35), and the module category has non-trivial extensions.
    More precisely, what the rational side sees as semisimplicity (Ext-vanishing), the dual side sees as non-
trivial extensions. This follows from three ingredients already established in this chapter:
   (i) Singular vector locus symmetry (Corollary 12.7.19): the Feigin–Frenkel involution 𝜄 : 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨
       rearranges the zero locus of the Kac–Kazhdan determinant det 𝑆𝑛 ( 𝜆, 𝑘 ), sending the component
       { 𝜆 = 𝑠 −1−𝑟 ( 𝑘 +ℎ∨ )} to { 𝜆 = 𝑠 −1+𝑟 ( 𝑘 +ℎ∨ )}. A Verma module that is irreducible at level 𝑘 (lying
       off Σ𝑛 ) generically acquires singular vectors at level 𝑘 ′ (landing on Σ𝑛 ), and vice versa.
  (ii) Bar resolution (Proposition 12.12.6): Ext𝑛A ( 𝑀 , 𝑁 ) ≃ 𝐻 𝑛 (Hom A ( 𝐵 • (A) ⊗ A 𝑀 , 𝑁 )). Singular
       vectors in M ( 𝜆) 𝑘 produce non-trivial classes in 𝐻 1 of the bar complex, hence non-vanishing Ext1 .
       Their absence yields Ext1 = 0.
 (iii) Associated variety obstruction (Theorem 12.2.33): 𝑋 𝐿𝑘′ = N ≠ {0} implies the module category at
       level 𝑘 ′ is not semisimple, so Ext𝑖 ≠ 0 for some modules and some 𝑖 > 0.
    Concretely, Proposition 12.7.12 gives Ext𝑖O2 = 0 for 𝑖 > 0 at level 𝑘 = 2 (semisimplicity), while at the
dual level 𝑘 ′ = −6 the Kac–Kazhdan determinant acquires new zeros by (i), producing the non-trivial
Ext1 classes detected by (ii). This module-level complementarity is parallel to, but logically independent
of, the global complementarity theorem (Theorem 8.14.12), which decomposes the center cohomology
𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) rather than the module Ext groups.

level-independent.
    The level appears in the representation theory through the set of allowed highest weights: at level 𝑘 , the
dominant integral weights form the level-𝑘 alcove 𝑃+𝑘 = {Λ | ⟨Λ, 𝜃 ∨ ⟩ ≤ 𝑘 }, where 𝜃 is the highest root.
Under 𝑘 ↦→ 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ , the alcove changes (for 𝑘 ′ < 0 the notion of ‘‘integrable’’ module requires
modification; see the admissible modules of Kac–Wakimoto [160]).
    For the same formal highest weight 𝜆 (viewed as a weight of the finite-dimensional 𝔤), the Weyl–Kac
formula produces the same formal power series. This is the character-level manifestation of the Zhu algebra
isomorphism 𝐴 (b   𝔤𝑘 )  𝑈 (𝔤)  𝐴 (b 𝔤𝑘′ ) (Proposition 12.2.26): the Zhu algebra classifies the lowest weight
spaces, and the character is built from the Zhu data by the BGG resolution.

Remark 12.7.15 (Character duality in the bar-cobar framework). The character identity ch( 𝐿 𝑘 ( 𝜆)) =
ch( 𝐿 𝑘′ ( 𝜆)) holds because the bar complexes at levels 𝑘 and 𝑘 ′ have the same graded dimensions (Verma
module spaces depend only on 𝔤); the differentials differ but cancel in the Euler characteristic. This does
not imply O𝑘 ≃ O𝑘′ (e.g., 𝑘 = 1 is semisimple, 𝑘 ′ = −3 is not for 𝔰𝔩 2 ); Koszul duality exchanges categories
via the module-comodule equivalence (Remark 12.1.9).

12.7.6   Virasoro Verma modules under Koszul duality

bar resolution of such a module M satisfies 𝐻 1 ≠ 0, where 𝐻 1 encodes the extension data (the ‘‘logarithmic

12.8.2    Tracking the transition
Theorem 12.8.3 (Deformation of acyclicity; [proved]). Let (P• , 𝑑𝑡 ) be a flat family of bounded
cochain complexes over a smooth connected base 𝑆 , with P• ( 𝑡0 ) acyclic at some 𝑡0 ∈ 𝑆 . Then:
   (i) The Euler characteristic 𝜒 (P• ( 𝑡 )) = 0 for all 𝑡 ∈ 𝑆 .
  (ii) On the smooth locus 𝑆 ◦ ⊂ 𝑆 (complement of the discriminant where homology dimensions jump),
       the homology sheaves H 𝑘 = 𝑅 𝑘 𝜋∗ P• carry the Gauss–Manin connection ∇𝐺 𝑀 , and the graded
       character ch( 𝑡 ) = 𝑘 (−1) 𝑘 ch( 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝑡 )) is a flat section: ∇𝐺 𝑀 ch = 0.
                          P

 (iii) At a point 𝑡1 ∈ 𝑆 \ 𝑆 ◦ where homology appears, the individual 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝑡 ) jump (upper-
       semicontinuously in dimension), but 𝜒 = 0 is preserved: each new 𝐻 𝑘 is balanced by a
       compensating 𝐻 𝑘+1 .

Proof. (1) Constancy of Euler characteristic. For a flat family of bounded complexes, the Euler characteristic
is locally constant on 𝑆 (Grothendieck, EGA III; see also Hartshorne [206], III.12). Since 𝜒 (P• ( 𝑡0 )) = 0
(acyclicity implies all 𝐻 𝑘 = 0, so 𝜒 = 0) and 𝑆 is connected, 𝜒 ( 𝑡 ) = 0 for all 𝑡 .
    (2) Gauss–Manin connection. On the smooth locus 𝑆 ◦ where dim 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝑡 ) is constant, the Katz–Oda
construction ([207]) provides the Gauss–Manin connection ∇𝐺 𝑀 on each H 𝑘 | 𝑆 ◦ : the connecting homo-
morphism in the long exact sequence of the de Rham complex of the family. Flatness (∇𝐺 𝑀 ) 2 = 0 follows
from the integrability of the de Rham differential. The alternating character ch is flat because ∇𝐺 𝑀 acts
on each H 𝑘 and the Euler characteristic is additive.
    (3) Wall-crossing. At a discriminant point 𝑡1 , the nearby cycles functor 𝜓𝑡1 (H 𝑘 ) (Deligne, SGA 7) relates
                                                                           +1
the generic fiber to the special fiber. The exact triangle 𝜓 → 𝑖 ∗ → 𝜙 −→ (where 𝜙 is the vanishing cycles
functor) gives: dim 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝑡1 ) − dim 𝐻 𝑘 ( 𝑡gen ) = dim 𝜙𝑡1 (H 𝑘 ) − dim 𝜙𝑡1 (H 𝑘 −1 ). Summing over 𝑘 with
alternating signs, the vanishing cycle contributions cancel (the Euler characteristic of the vanishing cycles
complex is zero, since it is the mapping cone of a quasi-isomorphism on the generic fiber), confirming
𝜒 ( 𝑡1 ) = 𝜒 ( 𝑡gen ) = 0.
Remark 12.8.4 (Context). In the chiral algebra setting, 𝑆 is the character variety or level space, P• ( 𝑡 ) is
the bar-cobar resolution at level parameter 𝑡 , and the transition from acyclic (generic level) to non-acyclic
(critical/admissible levels) corresponds to the appearance of non-trivial chiral homology. The Gauss–Manin
connection on the smooth locus is the Beilinson–Drinfeld connection on the chiral homology sheaf ([2]),
and the wall-crossing at discriminant points reflects the non-semisimplicity of the representation category
at admissible levels.

12.10.1     Beilinson–Bernstein localization
Theorem 12.10.1 (Beilinson–Bernstein [1]; [proved]). Let 𝔤 be a semisimple Lie algebra, 𝐺 / 𝐵 the
flag variety, and 𝜆 ∈ 𝔥∗ a dominant regular weight. The twisted sheaf of differential operators D𝜆 on 𝐺 / 𝐵
satisfies:
   (i) The global sections functor Γ : Mod(D𝜆 ) → Mod(𝑈 (𝔤) 𝜒 ) is an equivalence of abelian categories,
       where 𝑈 (𝔤) 𝜒 denotes modules with generalized infinitesimal character 𝜒 = 𝜒𝜆+ 𝜌 .
  (ii) The inverse is the localization functor Δ𝜆 : 𝑀 ↦→ D𝜆 ⊗𝑈 (𝔤) 𝑀 .
 (iii) Both functors are exact and preserve the derived categories: 𝐷 𝑏 (Mod(D𝜆 )) ≃ 𝐷 𝑏 (Mod(𝑈 (𝔤) 𝜒 )).

Proof. This is [1, Theorem 1.1]. The key ingredients are: (a) the global sections of D𝜆 are 𝑈 (𝔤)/ker 𝜒𝜆+ 𝜌
(by the Beilinson–Bernstein isomorphism); (b) the higher cohomology 𝐻 𝑖 ( 𝐺 / 𝐵, D𝜆 ⊗ O F ) = 0 for
𝑖 > 0 and 𝜆 dominant (Borel–Weil–Bott vanishing); (c) faithful flatness of D𝜆 over 𝑈 (𝔤) 𝜒 .

12.10.3    Associated variety and singular support
Proposition 12.10.8 (Bar complex and singular support; [proved]). For an integrable 𝔤         b𝑘 -module
𝑀 , the singular support of the localized D-module Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 ) on 𝐺 / 𝐵 is related to the bar complex by:

                                      SS( Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 )) = 𝕆 𝑀 ∩ 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝐺 / 𝐵 )

where 𝕆 𝑀 ⊂ 𝔤∗ is the nilpotent orbit associated to 𝑀 via the Arakawa associated variety construction
(Definition 12.2.32). Under Koszul duality, the Barbasch–Vogan duality 𝑑BV (Proposition 12.2.35) on
nilpotent orbits corresponds to the exchange of singular supports:
                                                       KD
                                     SS( Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 )) ←−→ SS( Δ𝑘′ ( 𝑀 ! )) .

Proof. The localized D-module Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 ) is holonomic when 𝑀 has finite-dimensional associated variety
(which holds for integrable modules by the Arakawa–Moreau theorem [68]). The singular support is the
characteristic variety Ch( Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 )) ⊂ 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝐺 / 𝐵 ), which is a Lagrangian subvariety.
    The Springer resolution 𝜇 : 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝐺 / 𝐵 ) → N (where N ⊂ 𝔤∗ is the nilpotent cone) maps SS( Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 ))
to 𝕆 𝑀 . The fiber 𝜇−1 (𝕆 𝑀 ) ∩ SS( Δ𝑘 ( 𝑀 )) is a union of conormal bundles to Schubert cells, and the
components correspond to the terms of the BGG resolution.
    Under Koszul duality, the level shift 𝑘 ↦→ 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ and the module functor 𝑀 ↦→ 𝑀 ! jointly
transform the singular support. The orbit duality 𝕆 𝑀 ↦→ 𝑑BV (𝕆 𝑀 ) (Proposition 12.2.35) is precisely the
Barbasch–Vogan duality on N , which for type 𝐴 corresponds to partition transpose. This establishes the
claimed exchange of singular supports.

Remark 12.10.9 (Microlocal viewpoint). Via Riemann–Hilbert, D-modules on 𝐺 / 𝐵 with singular support
in 𝕆 ∩ 𝑇 ∗ ( 𝐺 / 𝐵 ) correspond to constructible sheaves microsupported in the same Lagrangian. The bar
complex resolves the corresponding perverse sheaf: terms 𝐵¯ 𝑛ch ( 𝑀 ) on 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) form the Cousin complex.
Both the geometric bar complex and BB localization compute the same cohomology (Proposition 12.10.3),
the former via configuration spaces on any curve 𝑋 , the latter on the flag variety.

12.12.2    Fusion product preservation under bar-cobar
Theorem 12.12.10 (Fusion product preservation; [proved]). For a Koszul chiral algebra A with
Koszul dual A ! , the module-level bar-cobar functor Φ : Mod(A) → CoMod(A ! ) (Theorem 9.6.2) pre-
serves fusion products:
                               Φ ( 𝑀1 ⊠ A 𝑀2 ) ≃ Φ ( 𝑀1 ) ⊠ A ! Φ ( 𝑀2 )                   (12.25)
as objects of the comodule category.
    For Kac–Moody algebras 𝔤 b𝑘 at integrable level:
730                                       Chapter 12. Chiral modules and geometric resolutions


   (i) The fusion product ⊠𝑘 on O𝑘int (b
                                       𝔤) is sent to the tensor product on the semisimplified tilting quotient
       C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)), preserving the braiding up to a sign determined by the level shift.
  (ii) For Heisenberg Fock modules 𝐹𝜆 ⊠𝜅 𝐹𝜇  𝐹𝜆+ 𝜇 , the braiding phase 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖𝜆𝜇/𝜅 is sent to 𝑒 −2𝜋 𝑖𝜆𝜇/𝜅
       under 𝜅 ↦→ −𝜅 .
 (iii) The bar coalgebra coproduct

                                Δ : 𝐵 (A , 𝑀1 ⊠ 𝑀2 ) → 𝐵 (A , 𝑀1 ) ⊗ 𝐵 (A , 𝑀2 )

      is the chain-level realization of the fusion product, induced by the separating degeneration map of
      Theorem 33.4.13(ii).

Proof. This is an immediate consequence of the monoidal module Koszul duality theorem
(Theorem 12.1.11), which proves that Φ is lax monoidal with respect to fusion products and that
the structure map 𝜇 𝑀 ,𝑁 is a quasi-isomorphism for Koszul modules. Concretely:
   Main statement (12.25). Theorem 12.1.11, equation (12.1), constructs the natural transformation

                            𝜇 𝑀1 ,𝑀2 : Φ ( 𝑀1 ⊠ A 𝑀2 ) → Φ ( 𝑀1 ) ⊠ A !,𝑐 Φ ( 𝑀2 )

via the Alexander–Whitney factorization on configuration spaces (Step 1 of that proof), and proves it is a
quasi-isomorphism when 𝑀1 , 𝑀2 are Koszul modules (Step 2, using the Künneth theorem and diagonal
concentration).
    Part (i): braiding reversal. Step 3 of Theorem 12.1.11 proves that the composite equivalence reverses
the braiding ( 𝜎 ! = 𝜎 −1 ), using the Verdier involution on 𝐶 2 (ℙ1 ) to invert the monodromy 𝑅-matrix of
the KZ connection. By the Kohno–Drinfeld theorem, this monodromy is identified with 𝑅𝑞 ∈ 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤),
and inversion gives the 𝑞 → 𝑞 −1 transformation, establishing the ⊠𝑘 ↔ ⊗𝑞 correspondence.
    Part (ii): Heisenberg phase inversion. For the Heisenberg algebra, the braiding on Fock modules 𝐹𝜆 is
the scalar 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖𝜆𝜇/𝜅 . By Step 3(d) of Theorem 12.1.11, orientation reversal sends 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖𝜆𝜇/𝜅 ↦→ 𝑒 −2𝜋 𝑖𝜆𝜇/𝜅 under
𝜅 ↦→ −𝜅 .
    Part (iii): chain-level coproduct. Step 1 of Theorem 12.1.11 identifies the Alexander–Whitney map
with the factorization along separating divisors of M 𝑔,𝑛 : the summand where 𝑝 points cluster near the
first marked point and 𝑞 near the second yields 𝐵¯ 𝑝 ( 𝑀1 ) ⊗ 𝐵¯ 𝑞 ( 𝑀2 ). This is precisely the separating
degeneration map Δsep of Theorem 33.4.13(ii).

Remark 12.12.11 (Non-semisimple lift). At chain level, the KL functor Φ factors through a non-semisimple
category before semisimplification to C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)). A chain-level lift of Theorem 12.12.10(i) to this non-
semisimple intermediate –- the full tilting category before the quotient –- would strengthen the result but
is not needed for the present applications and is deferred.
Remark 12.12.12 (Proof structure). The monoidality of Φ was the hardest part of the Kazhdan–Lusztig
programme [184]. The configuration space proof via the bar complex resolves this: residue maps along
separating divisors of M 𝑔,𝑛 are compatible with the fusion product’s associativity and commutativity
constraints (Theorem 12.1.11, Steps 1–3).

12.12.3    Verification: Heisenberg fusion in the bar complex
We verify Theorem 12.12.10 for the Heisenberg algebra H𝜅 acting on Fock modules 𝐹𝜆 , 𝐹𝜇 .
12.12. Genus-graded module categories                                                                        731


Proposition 12.12.13 (Heisenberg fusion splitting; [proved]). Let H𝜅 be the Heisenberg chiral
algebra at level 𝜅 ≠ 0, and let 𝐹𝜆 , 𝐹𝜇 be Fock modules. Then

                                     Φ ( 𝐹𝜆 ⊠𝜅 𝐹𝜇 )  Φ ( 𝐹𝜆 ) ⊗ Φ ( 𝐹𝜇 )                                (12.26)

as comodules over the Koszul dual coalgebra 𝐵 (H𝜅 ).

Proof. The Heisenberg OPE is 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 𝜅 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 : there is a double pole but no simple pole. By the
pole decomposition (Proposition 6.2.30), the bar differential on any module decomposes as 𝑑 = 𝑑bracket +
𝑑curvature , where 𝑑bracket arises from simple-pole residues and 𝑑curvature from double-pole residues. For H𝜅 ,
the simple-pole residue vanishes identically, so 𝑑bracket = 0.
   Consider the bar complex of the fusion product 𝐵 (H𝜅 , 𝐹𝜆 ⊠ 𝐹𝜇 ). The underlying graded space is
𝐵 (H𝜅 ) ⊗ ( 𝐹𝜆 ⊗ 𝐹𝜇 ). The differential decomposes as 𝑑 = 𝑑𝜆 + 𝑑 𝜇 + 𝑑cross , where 𝑑𝜆 (resp. 𝑑 𝜇 ) acts on
the 𝐹𝜆 (resp. 𝐹𝜇 ) factor through the double-pole curvature, and 𝑑cross encodes interactions between the
two module factors via the configuration space of points distributed between the two components.
   The key observation is that 𝑑cross = 0. Indeed, the cross-term arises from residues of the OPE between
generators acting on 𝐹𝜆 and generators acting on 𝐹𝜇 . In the genus-0 fusion (pants decomposition of M 0,4 ),
these cross-terms are governed by simple-pole residues along the separating divisor. Since the Heisenberg
OPE has no simple pole, all such residues vanish. The vanishing of 𝑑cross gives the Künneth splitting

                              𝐵 (H𝜅 , 𝐹𝜆 ⊠ 𝐹𝜇 )  𝐵 (H𝜅 , 𝐹𝜆 ) ⊗ 𝐵 (H𝜅 , 𝐹𝜇 )

as chain complexes, which descends to the isomorphism (12.26) after applying Φ. The phase inversion
𝜅 ↦→ −𝜅 on the dual side (Proposition 12.1.7) is automatic: 𝑑curvature is linear in 𝜅 , and the Koszul dual acts
at level −𝜅 .

Remark 12.12.14. The Heisenberg case is exceptional: 𝑑cross = 0 because the OPE is purely double-pole. For
non-abelian 𝔤b𝑘 , 𝑑cross ≠ 0 and the bar complex of the fusion product does not split; monoidality requires
the full separating-divisor machinery of Theorem 33.4.13.

12.13     Koszul duality and universal chiral defects
12.13.1  Holographic principle: genus-graded Koszul duality
Remark 12.13.1 (Costello–Li holographic conjecture across genera). For 𝑁 D-branes, the genus-graded bound-
ary operator algebra (at 𝑁 → ∞) and the twisted supergravity bulk algebra are conjecturally related by
genus-graded Koszul duality.
Remark 12.13.2 (Genus-graded Koszul duality). The universal MC class Θ A (Theorem 8.18.36) mediates
genus-graded Koszul duality: Θ A + Θ A ! = 𝐾 · 𝜂 ⊗ Λ gives the Lagrangian polarization of the quantum
corrections across the genus tower.

12.13.2   Universal chiral defects and bar-cobar duality
Deﬁnition 12.13.3 (Universal chiral defect). For a chiral algebra A, the universal chiral defect D (A) is the
chiral algebra satisfying:
   (i) Universality: Any defect coupling to A factors through D (A)
  (ii) Koszul property: D (A) is (quasi-)Koszul dual to A
 (iii) Geometric realization: D (A)  Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) (cobar of bar)
Theorem 12.13.4 (Universal defect = Koszul dual [135, 171]; [proved]). The universal chiral defect
D (A) is characterized as the Koszul dual:

                                   D (A) = A ! := RHom A-mod (ℂ, ℂ)

where the RHom is computed in the derived category of A-modules.
  Explicitly, this is computed by the cobar construction:

                                            D (A) = Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A))

with differential encoding the failure of strict Koszul duality.

𝑈ℏ,𝑐 (Diff (ℂ) ⊗ 𝔤𝔩 𝑁 ). These are conjecturally related by curved Koszul duality with deformation parameter
𝑐.

• The center becomes large (Feigin–Frenkel center)

12.13.8       The prism principle: operadic identification
The geometric bar-cobar duality of chiral algebras is an instance of operadic Koszul duality in the sense of
Ginzburg–Kapranov [32] and Getzler [22].

12.13.8.1 The chiral operad
Deﬁnition 12.13.20 (Chiral operad). The chiral operad Pch is the topological operad with:

                                 Pch ( 𝑛) = Ω∗log 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) ,   𝑛 ≥ 1,
                                                             

the complex of logarithmic differential forms on the Fulton–MacPherson compactification of 𝑛 + 1 points
on the curve 𝑋 . The operad composition maps:

                                ◦𝑖 : Pch ( 𝑚) ⊗ Pch ( 𝑛) → Pch ( 𝑚 + 𝑛 − 1)

are induced by the gluing maps 𝐶 𝑚+1 ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝐶 𝑚+𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) that identify the 𝑖 -th point of the
first configuration with the distinguished point of the second.
    The symmetric group 𝔖𝑛 acts by permuting the non-distinguished points, and the unit is the identity
form in Ω0 ( 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 )) = ℂ.
Proposition 12.13.21 (Genus-zero identification; [proved]). At genus 0 (i.e., 𝑋 = ℙ1 ), the chiral
operad is quasi-isomorphic to the hypercommutative operad:

                                           Pch | 𝑔 =0 ≃ HyCom.

Explicitly, 𝐶 𝑛+1 (ℙ1 )  M 0,𝑛+2 (the Deligne–Mumford compactification of the moduli space of rational
curves with 𝑛 + 2 marked points), and the cohomology operad { 𝐻 ∗ (M 0,𝑛+2 )}𝑛 ≥1 is the hypercommutative
operad HyCom of Getzler [22].

Proof. The identification 𝐶 𝑛+1 (ℙ1 )  M 0,𝑛+2 is classical: the Fulton–MacPherson compactification of
𝑛 + 1 points on ℙ1 with one point fixed at ∞ is isomorphic to the Deligne–Mumford moduli space of
stable rational curves with 𝑛 + 2 punctures [12]. Under this identification, the operad composition maps
of Pch correspond to the clutching maps

                                      M 0,𝑚+1 × M 0,𝑛+1 → M 0,𝑚+𝑛

that glue two rational curves at marked points. The cohomology operad of {M 0,𝑛+2 } is the hypercommu-
tative operad by Getzler’s theorem [22, Theorem 1.5]: the fundamental classes of the boundary strata satisfy
exactly the relations defining HyCom.
    The quasi-isomorphism follows because M 0,𝑛+2 is a smooth projective variety with pure Hodge
structure, hence formal as a dga by Deligne–Griffiths–Morgan–Sullivan [7]. Thus Ω∗ (M 0,𝑛+2 ) is
quasi-isomorphic to 𝐻 ∗ (M 0,𝑛+2 ) as an operad.

    Part (iii): Cobar via Verdier duality. By the intrinsic cobar definition (Definition 6.3.6), Ωch is the

operadic bar-cobar by Parts (ii)–(iii), the result follows.

Deﬁnition 12.13.23 (Modular operad). A modular operad (Getzler–Kapranov [23, §5]) in a symmetric
monoidal category V consists of:
  (i) A collection of objects {M ( 𝑔, 𝑛)}2 𝑔 −2+𝑛>0 in V, each equipped with a Σ𝑛 -action (the stability
      condition 2 𝑔 − 2 + 𝑛 > 0 excludes ( 𝑔, 𝑛) = (0, 0) , (0, 1) , (0, 2)).
 (ii) Separating gluing maps: for each partition {1, . . . , 𝑛} = 𝑆1 ⊔ 𝑆2 and 𝑔 = 𝑔1 + 𝑔2 ,

                           𝜉𝑆1 ,𝑆2 : M ( 𝑔1 , | 𝑆1 | + 1) ⊗ M ( 𝑔2 , | 𝑆2 | + 1) −→ M ( 𝑔, 𝑛) ,

       corresponding to gluing two curves at marked points.
 (iii) Non-separating gluing maps: for each pair of distinguished marked points,

                                      𝜉ns : M ( 𝑔, 𝑛 + 2) −→ M ( 𝑔 + 1, 𝑛) ,

      corresponding to self-gluing (identifying two marked points on the same curve).
These maps satisfy:
• Equivariance: compatibility with the Σ𝑛 -actions;
• Associativity: iterated gluings are independent of the order in which they are performed;
• Commutativity: separating gluing is symmetric in the two factors.
The canonical example is the collection of Deligne–Mumford moduli spaces {M 𝑔,𝑛 }2 𝑔 −2+𝑛>0 with clutch-
ing maps at the boundary strata.

the curvature 𝜇0 for cross-genus terms, and the modular operad boundary relation for pure higher-genus
terms combine to give 𝑑bar2 = 0.


Deﬁnition 12.13.26 (Modular graph coeﬃcient algebra). The modular graph coeﬃcient algebra is the com-

the differential is induced by boundary stratification. Each stable graph Γ contributes the integral over the

deformation complex of A tensored with the modular graph coefficient algebra. This is the correct target
for the full non-scalar genus tower. (Part of the MC2 theorem package; Theorem 8.18.72.)

Lemma 12.13.34 (Sign consistency for bar differential; [proved]). The sign convention above ensures
that for any pair of edges 𝑒1 , 𝑒2 in a tree, the signs arising from contracting 𝑒1 then 𝑒2 versus contracting 𝑒2
then 𝑒1 differ by exactly (−1), ensuring 𝑑 2 = 0.

Proof. This is a standard result in operad theory; see Loday–Vallette [83], Proposition 6.3.2. The key
mechanism: label the edges 1, . . . , 𝐸 . Contracting edge 𝑖 produces a tree with 𝐸 − 1 edges, relabeled
1, . . . , 𝐸 − 1. If 𝑖 < 𝑗 , then contracting 𝑖 first shifts edge 𝑗 to position 𝑗 − 1. The sign for contracting edge
at position 𝑘 in a tree 𝑇 is 𝜖 ( 𝑘, 𝑇 ) = 𝑘 − 1 + ℓ < 𝑘 | 𝑣ℓ | where | 𝑣ℓ | is the degree of the operation at the
                                                        P
vertex below edge ℓ . One checks:

                               𝜖 ( 𝑖, 𝑇 ) + 𝜖 ( 𝑗 − 1, 𝑇 /𝑒 𝑖 ) = 𝜖 ( 𝑗, 𝑇 ) + 𝜖 ( 𝑖, 𝑇 /𝑒𝑗 ) + 1
so that contracting in opposite order introduces a sign of (−1) 1 = −1, giving 𝑑 2 = 0.

12.13.10    Partition complexes and the commutative operad
For the commutative operad Com, the bar construction admits an explicit combinatorial model via partition
lattices:
Deﬁnition 12.13.37 (Partition lattice). The partition lattice Π𝑛 is the poset of all partitions of {1, 2, . . . , 𝑛},
ordered by refinement: 𝜋 ≤ 𝜎 if every block of 𝜋 is contained in some block of 𝜎 . The proper part
Π 𝑛 = Π𝑛 \ {0̂, 1̂} excludes the minimum (discrete partition) and maximum (trivial partition).
Theorem 12.13.38 (Partition complex structure; [proved]). The bar complex 𝐵 ( Com) ( 𝑛) is quasi-
isomorphic to the reduced chain complex 𝐶˜∗ ( Π 𝑛 ) of the proper part of the partition lattice Π𝑛 . More
precisely:
                                 𝐵 ( Com) ( 𝑛) ≃ 𝑠 𝑛−1 𝐶˜∗ ( Π 𝑛 ) ⊗ sgn𝑛
where sgn𝑛 is the sign representation of 𝑆𝑛 .
Proof. Elements of Com◦𝑘 ( 𝑛) (the 𝑘 -fold composition) correspond to ways of iteratively partitioning 𝑛
elements through 𝑘 levels. The simplicial structure is:
• Face maps compose adjacent levels of partitioning (coarsening)
• Degeneracy maps repeat a level (refinement followed by immediate coarsening)
   After normalization (removing degeneracies), we obtain chains on Π 𝑛 . The dimension shift and sign
representation arise from the suspension in the bar construction and the need for 𝑆𝑛 -equivariance.
   The poset Π 𝑛 has the homology of a wedge of ( 𝑛 − 1)! spheres of dimension 𝑛 − 3, with the 𝑆𝑛 -action
on the top homology given by the Lie representation tensored with the sign. This follows from the classical
results of Björner–Wachs [9] and Stanley [14], who computed:
                              𝐻˜ 𝑛−3 ( Π 𝑛 )  Lie ( 𝑛) ⊗ sgn𝑛 as 𝑆𝑛 -representations
and 𝐻˜ 𝑘 ( Π 𝑛 ) = 0 for 𝑘 ≠ 𝑛 − 3.
Remark 12.13.39 (Simplicial model). The simplicial bar for Com literally consists of chains of refinements
𝜋0 ≤ 𝜋1 ≤ · · · ≤ 𝜋𝑘 in Π𝑛 . This is the nerve of the poset Π𝑛 , and the identification with the cooperad
structure follows from taking normalized chains.

  (ii) Residues at collision divisors should model bulk interactions
 (iii) The cobar construction should recover the boundary package from suitable bulk data
 (iv) The bar-cobar adjunction is conjecturally interpreted as the algebraic shadow of holographic duality

Remark 12.13.41 (Physical evidence and scope). This conjecture is supported by matching of partition func-
tions, three-point functions, and conformal blocks between boundary W-algebras and bulk Vasiliev theory
[21]. It is labeled [conjectured] because the holographic identification of the bar construction with bulk
field content, and of the cobar construction with boundary reconstruction, requires physical input from
the AdS3 /CFT2 correspondence that lies outside the algebraic framework of this monograph. The mathe-
matical content is the structural parallel between the bar-cobar adjunction and the holographic dictionary.
Remark 12.13.42 (Scope). Conjecture 12.13.40 is tagged [conjectured] because the claimed dictionary be-
tween the bar-cobar adjunction and the AdS/CFT correspondence requires physics input at two lev-
els: (i) the identification of bar complex generators with bulk higher-spin fields relies on the Gaberdiel–
Gopakumar duality, which is itself a physics conjecture supported by numerical evidence (partition function
matching, three-point function agreement) but without a mathematical proof; (ii) the cobar reconstruction
of boundary correlators from bulk Witten diagrams presupposes the AdS3 /CFT2 correspondence, which
is not a theorem. Within the algebraic framework of this monograph, one can prove that the bar-cobar
adjunction has the same formal structure as the holographic dictionary, but the identification of the two
requires external physical input that we do not attempt to supply. In the repo’s frontier order, the theo-
rematic input here is the completed M-level bar-cobar package and its finite-stage coefficient identities;
any filtered H-level higher-spin bulk target is upstream MC4, and the holographic comparison itself is
downstream MC5.
    Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type VII (physics-dictionary). The conjecture treats the bar-
cobar adjunction as the algebraic shadow of the holographic dictionary, mapping boundary correlators to
bulk Witten-diagram data only after additional physics input. (Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.5.)

Quantum corrections to Arnold relations

Strict genus-0 nilpotence breaks as soon as the propagator remembers the periods of the curve. Curvature
terms, Eisenstein regularizations, and their assembly into a curved 𝐴∞ package are treated here as the explicit
correction mechanism behind the higher-genus theory. The Heisenberg computation of Chapter 1 is the
frame case; the point now is to show that its genus-1 identity already exhibits the universal pattern.

13.1     Braid groups and Arnold relations
13.1.1   Arnold relations and the braid group
Arnold’s relations among differential forms on configuration spaces arise from the topology of the braid
group. Consider three strands in a braid, labeled 1, 2, and 3. Their projections onto a plane trace out paths
𝑧1 ( 𝑡 ), 𝑧2 ( 𝑡 ), and 𝑧3 ( 𝑡 ). The fundamental group of the configuration space of three distinct points in the
plane is the braid group 𝐵 3 .
13.1.1.1 The braid derivation of Arnold relations
Start with a specific braid where strand 1 circles around strand 2, while strand 3 remains fixed. The winding
number of this motion is captured by the integral:
                                             ∮
                                                 𝑑𝑧1 − 𝑑𝑧2
                                                             = 2𝜋 𝑖
                                                   𝑧1 − 𝑧2
   If we compose three such braids–-where 1 circles 2, then 2 circles 3, then 3 circles 1–-we return to the
identity braid. This topological fact translates to an algebraic relation.
   To see this explicitly, consider the logarithmic 1-forms:

                                                               𝑑𝑧1 − 𝑑𝑧2
                                      𝜂12 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) =
                                                                𝑧1 − 𝑧2
                                                               𝑑𝑧2 − 𝑑𝑧3
                                      𝜂23 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) =
                                                                𝑧2 − 𝑧3
                                                               𝑑𝑧3 − 𝑑𝑧1
                                      𝜂31 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) =
                                                                𝑧3 − 𝑧1
   The braid group relation tells us that these forms cannot be independent. The key is the partial fraction
identity: clearing denominators in
                               1                       1                       1
                                           +                       +                        =0
                    ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 )

gives the numerator ( 𝑧3 − 𝑧1 ) + ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) + ( 𝑧2 − 𝑧3 ) = 0.


                                                       745
746                                       Chapter 13. Quantum corrections to Arnold relations


   Computing the wedge product 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 and using the form-level analogue of this identity yields:

                                    𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 + 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = 0

   This is Arnold’s relation: it encodes the fact that the three braiding operations compose to the identity.

flatness of a connection on a graded vector bundle.

13.2     Genus one: theta functions and central extensions
13.2.1   Theta functions on elliptic curves
Riemann’s 1857 treatise introduced the period matrix and theta functions for algebraic curves. The one-loop
string amplitude involves these same theta functions, connecting Riemann surface geometry to quantum
field theory.

13.2.2.3 Computing the quantum correction
The logarithmic forms on the torus are:

   Using the quasi-periodicity of 𝜁 and the Fay trisecant identity on the torus, we find:

    where 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ) is the Eisenstein series of weight 2 and the right-hand side is a (2, 0)-form on 𝐶3 ( Σ𝜏 ).
(Note: this is a holomorphic (2, 0)-form, not a (1, 1)-form; the quasi-periodicity of 𝜁 means the correction

13.2.3   The central extension at genus one
13.2.3.1 The central extension
Consider the Heisenberg vertex algebra H𝜅 with generators 𝑎𝑛 for 𝑛 ∈ ℤ. The commutation relations are:

                                                [ 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑎𝑛 ] = 𝜅 𝑚 𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0

    where 𝜅 is the level. The central extension is present already at genus zero–-it is part of the deﬁnition
of the Heisenberg algebra. What changes at genus one is not the commutation relations themselves, but
the modular properties of the resulting chiral algebra: the partition function acquires 𝜏 -dependence, and
correlation functions must be consistent with the quantum-corrected Arnold relations on the torus.
13.2.3.2 The explicit construction of the central element
The deformation of the Arnold relation at genus 1 encodes the curving obstruction 𝑚0(1) in the genus-1 bar
complex. For the Heisenberg algebra H𝜅 , this obstruction is:

                                                   𝑚0(1) = 𝜅 · 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 )

   The factor 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ) controls the modular dependence of the genus-1 partition function 𝑍 (1) = 𝜂 ( 𝜏 ) − rank ,
consistent with the identity 𝜕𝜏 log 𝜂 ( 𝜏 ) = 𝜋12𝑖 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ). The central charge ( 𝑐 = 1 for rank-1 Heisenberg) is a
genus-0 datum determined by the Sugawara construction, not by this integral.
13.2.3.3 The cocycle condition
The quantum correction satisfies a cocycle condition. Define:

                                                𝜔 ( 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑎𝑛 ) = 𝑚𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0

   This is a 2-cocycle in the Lie algebra cohomology:

                        𝜔 ( [ 𝑎 ℓ , 𝑎𝑚 ] , 𝑎𝑛 ) + 𝜔 ( [ 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑎𝑛 ] , 𝑎 ℓ ) + 𝜔 ( [ 𝑎𝑛 , 𝑎 ℓ ] , 𝑎𝑚 ) = 0

   The central extension is the universal one classified by 𝐻 2 (Heisenberg, ℂ).

13.4     The 𝐴∞ structure
13.4.1 Background
The 𝐴∞ structure was introduced by Stasheff [15] in connection with the associahedron, and was applied
to deformation quantization by Kontsevich [34].
   For chiral algebras, the 𝐴∞ structure encodes all the higher coherences needed for consistency across
genera.

13.4.3       Explicit computations for specific algebras
13.4.3.1 For the Heisenberg algebra
The 𝐴∞ structure simplifies dramatically: 𝑚1 = 0 (the bar complex is already a complex), 𝑚2 is the standard

corrections for 𝑔 ≥ 1 enter not through higher 𝑚𝑛 but through the propagator and the cohomology of
M 𝑔 (cf. Part III).
13.4.3.2 For the 𝛽 𝛾 system

BRST differential (satisfying the curved relation 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎]); 𝑚2 is the standard OPE product; and
𝑚3 = 𝑄 2 ×(triple interaction from composite fields).

13.5     Koszul duality and complementary deformations
13.5.1   The fundamental theorem
Remark 13.5.1 (Koszul complementarity at higher genus). For a Koszul dual pair (A , A ! ) of chiral algebras,
the quantum correction spaces at any genus 𝑔 satisfy:

                                   Q 𝑔 (A) ⊕ Q 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) .

See Theorem 8.14.12 for the full statement and proof (via Kodaira–Spencer map and Verdier involution on
moduli space cohomology).

13.5.2   Examples of Koszul complementarity
13.5.2.1 Example 1: free fermions and free bosons
The free fermion system F with OPE:
                                                                 1

                                                                 1

   At genus 𝑔 , the quantum corrections decompose according to spin structure parity: Q 𝑔 (F ) receives
contributions from the Pfaffian line bundle over odd spin structures, while Q 𝑔 ( 𝛽𝛾 ) receives contributions
from even spin structures. Heuristically, their union covers the spin-structure-dependent part of the moduli
space, though the precise relationship to 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) involves the tautological ring and requires further
analysis.

13.6.1   When does filtering degenerate to curved?
This subsection does not repeat the full filtered/cooperadic analysis of Section 6.10. Its role inside the
quantum-correction chapter is narrower: extract the algebra-side input used by Theorem 6.8.12 and fix the
three calibration regimes that reappear throughout Part II.
Proposition 13.6.1 (Filtered ⇒ curved; [proved]). Let A be a filtered chiral algebra with exhaustive,
separated, complete filtration. Assume:
  (i) each filtration quotient is finite-dimensional:

                                     dim( 𝐹𝑘 A/ 𝐹𝑘 −1 A) < ∞                  for all 𝑘 ;

  (ii) the associated graded algebra gr(A) is generated by gr1 (A) with quadratic defining ideal;
 (iii) every higher relation in A differs from a quadratic consequence by a central filtration-≥ 2 correction.
Then there exists a curved presentation of A with curvature element

                                                          𝜇0 ∈ 𝐹2 A

such that A and this curved model are filtered quasi-isomorphic.

Proof. Write 𝑉 := gr1 (A) and choose splittings 𝑠𝑘 : gr𝑘 (A) → 𝐹𝑘 A. Completeness and separatedness
produce a filtered surjection from the completed free chiral algebra

                                                 𝜋 : 𝑇bch (𝑉 ) ↠ A .

Let 𝐼 = ker( 𝜋 ). Its quadratic part is determined by the defining ideal of gr(A); denote it by 𝐼2 .
   Assumption (3) says that every higher relation class in 𝐼 is a quadratic consequence modulo a central
correction of filtration at least 2. Collect these correction terms by filtration degree:

                                              𝜇0( 𝑘 ) ,       𝜇0( 𝑘 ) ∈ 𝐹𝑘 A/ 𝐹𝑘 −1 A .
                                       ∑︁
                                𝜇0 =
                                       𝑘 ≥2

Assumption (1) guarantees convergence in the filtered topology, so 𝜇0 is well-defined in 𝐹2 A.
   Twist the quadratic model by 𝜇0 . Centrality of the correction terms gives the curved Maurer–Cartan
identity
                                            𝑑 2𝜇0 = [ 𝜇0 , −] .
Quotienting by the closed ideal generated by 𝐼2 yields a curved model Acurv together with a filtered mor-
phism
                                              Acurv → A
that is an isomorphism on associated graded pieces. Hence it is a filtered quasi-isomorphism.

Remark 13.6.2 (Dependencies). This proposition is the algebra-side input for Theorem 6.8.12. The required
convergence control comes from Theorem 6.10 and Theorem 6.8.15; Appendix P supplies the completion
technology in the genuinely filtered regime.
754                                       Chapter 13. Quantum corrections to Arnold relations


Example 13.6.3 (Virasoro: ﬁltering is auxiliary). For the Virasoro algebra, the conformal-weight filtration
records descendants of a single field 𝑇 . The weight-4 quasi-primary
                                                             3 2
                                             Λ = :𝑇 𝑇 : −      𝜕𝑇
                                                            10
is not a new generator on the same footing as 𝑇 ; it is the first place where the central term forces a curved
correction. Proposition 13.6.1 therefore identifies the filtered presentation with a curved model whose
essential datum is the curvature scalar 𝑚0 = 𝑐 · 1.
    In particular, Virasoro belongs to the curved regime rather than the genuinely filtered one: completion
is needed because one has infinitely many descendants, not because new independent generators appear at
each weight.
Example 13.6.4 (𝑊3 : ﬁltering is intrinsic). The 𝑊3 algebra sits on the other side of the boundary. Besides
the fields 𝐿 and 𝑊 , the OPE of 𝑊 with itself produces composite operators such as : 𝐿𝐿 : that are not
descendants of a single generator. The filtration by conformal weight therefore detects genuinely new
pieces rather than bookkeeping for one curved field.
   Thus 𝑊3 does not collapse to a finite-generator curved model. It requires the completed filtered frame-
work of Section 6.10, and later higher-genus calculations must remember this distinction.
Example 13.6.5 (Calibration by the Heisenberg frame). The Heisenberg algebra from Chapter 1 supplies
the quadratic endpoint of the hierarchy: genus-0 bar terms are already finite in each weight, no completion
is needed, and higher-genus corrections enter only through the modular curvature package. Together with
Examples 13.6.3 and 13.6.4, this gives the three regimes used repeatedly later: quadratic, curved, and genuinely
filtered.
Theorem 13.6.6 (Convergence criterion in the filtered/curved regimes; [proved]). Within the
hierarchy
                              quadratic ⊂ curved ⊂ filtered,
no new convergence theorem is needed beyond Theorem 6.10. More precisely:
   (i) quadratic finite-type examples such as Heisenberg converge without completion;
  (ii) filtered presentations that collapse to a curved model, such as Virasoro, are governed by the completed
       curved bar construction;
 (iii) genuinely filtered examples such as 𝑊3 require completion because infinitely many filtration pieces
       contribute non-descendant composites.

Proof. Part (1) is the quadratic finite-type clause of Theorem 6.10. Part (2) combines Proposition 13.6.1 with
the same theorem: once the filtered presentation has collapsed to a curved model, convergence is governed by
the completed curved bar complex. Part (3) is Example 13.6.4: the appearance of non-descendant composites
in arbitrarily high weights forces passage to the completed filtered bar construction.

Remark 13.6.7 (Operational takeaway). When a later chapter invokes higher-genus corrections for a non-
quadratic algebra, one should first answer four questions.
   (i) Are all higher-weight terms descendants of finitely many generators? If yes, the filtration is auxiliary.
  (ii) Does the correction lie in the center? If yes, the curved model carries the relevant modular data.
 (iii) Do genuinely new composites appear in arbitrarily high weights? If yes, completion is intrinsic.
13.6. Summary of the dictionary                                                                          755


 (iv) Does the generating space itself become infinite? If yes, one has moved beyond the finite-type theory
      proved in this volume and into the completed infinite-generator programme.
This checklist is the local decision rule behind the passage from finite-type 𝑊𝑁 algebras to the 𝑊∞ /Yangian
frontier recorded in Chapter 34.

Chiral Hochschild cohomology and deformation
theory

The fiberwise curvature 𝑑fib2 = 𝜅 · 𝜔 at genus 1 (Chapter 1) shows that deformations of the bar complex are

controlled by a cohomological invariant. Hochschild cohomology is the algebraic home of this invariant:
it organizes all infinitesimal deformations and obstructions of a chiral algebra into a single graded object
equipped with a Gerstenhaber bracket. The chiral enhancement incorporates OPE data, the geometry of
the curve, and the 𝐴∞ structure of the bar complex.

mology HH∗ , Hochschild homology HH∗ , cyclic homology HC∗ , negative cyclic homology HC∗ , and

are all defined here and should be cited from here throughout the text. Other chapters that use Hochschild or
cyclic invariants (notably the deformation theory and Poincaré duality chapters) reference these definitions
rather than re-establishing them.

                           𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) = ℂ[Θ1 , . . . , Θ𝑟 ] ,           Θ 𝑖 ∈ 𝐶 𝐻 ℎ𝑖
where ℎ𝑖 = 𝑚𝑖 + 1 are the conformal weights of the W-algebra generators and 𝑚1 , . . . , 𝑚𝑟 are the expo-

(the Virasoro case) this is an isomorphism, yielding periodicity of period ℎ1 = 2.
   For example: 𝔰𝔩 2 gives the Virasoro with period 2 (Theorem 10.5.1). For 𝔰𝔩 3 (W3 , generators of weights
2 and 3), the dimensions dim 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 grow polynomially (not periodically): the ring ℂ[ Θ1 , Θ2 ] has Hilbert
function #{( 𝑎, 𝑏 ) : 2 𝑎 + 3𝑏 = 𝑛}.
Proof. We extend the argument of Theorem 10.5.1 from the Virasoro (𝔰𝔩 2 ) to general 𝔤.
    Step 1 (Spectral sequence degeneration). The bar filtration on 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) induces a spectral sequence
𝐸2 ⇒ 𝐶 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) with 𝐸2 = 0 for 𝑞 > 0 at generic 𝑘 . The vanishing of the internal factor
  𝑝,𝑞                                 𝑝,𝑞

follows from:
• At generic 𝑘 , W 𝑘 (𝔤) is simple as a vertex algebra (Arakawa [37], Theorem 4.1).
• At generic 𝑘 , the Shapovalov form on Verma modules is non-degenerate (no singular vectors), so every
  finitely generated W 𝑘 (𝔤)-module in category O is a direct sum of irreducible highest-weight modules.
  (This is a property of generic level, not of simplicity per se: simplicity of the vertex algebra does not by
  itself imply semisimplicity of the module category.)
• Consequently Ext𝑞 ( 𝑀 , 𝑁 ) = 0 for 𝑞 > 0 and 𝑀 , 𝑁 ∈ O𝑘 , giving 𝐸2 = 0 for 𝑞 > 0.

The spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 : 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) = 𝐸2𝑛,0 .
    Step 2 (Generalized Gel’fand–Fuchs computation). The 𝐸2𝑛,0 page computes the continuous relative
Lie algebra cohomology of the W-algebra Lie algebra. The principal Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction produces

is a topological Lie algebra with 𝑟 generating currents.
    By the generalization of the Gel’fand–Fuchs theorem to Lie algebras of formal differential operators
with 𝑟 generators (Fuchs 1986, Ch. 2; Feigin–Fuchs 1984 for the 𝑟 = 1 case), the continuous relative
cohomology is a polynomial ring:
                               ∗

where Θ𝑖 ∈ 𝐻 ℎ𝑖 is the Gel’fand–Fuchs cocycle associated to the 𝑖 -th generator 𝑊 ( ℎ𝑖 ) . Each Θ𝑖 represents
the universal deformation of 𝑊 ( ℎ𝑖 ) in the chiral Hochschild complex.
   Step 3 (Cup product structure). Combining Steps 1 and 2:
                                      𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) = ℂ[Θ1 , . . . , Θ𝑟 ] .
The cup product maps ∪ Θ𝑖 : 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 → 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛+ℎ𝑖 are injective (multiplication in a polynomial ring) and
jointly surjective (every monomial Θ1𝑎1 · · · Θ𝑟𝑎𝑟 is reached). For 𝑟 = 1 this gives literal periodicity of period
ℎ1 . For 𝑟 ≥ 2, the Hilbert function 𝐻 ( 𝑛) = dim 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 is a quasi-polynomial in 𝑛 of period
                              𝑑 = lcm( ℎ1 , . . . , ℎ𝑟 ) = lcm( 𝑚1 + 1, . . . , 𝑚𝑟 + 1) ,
760                      Chapter 14. Chiral Hochschild cohomology and deformation theory


meaning 𝐻 ( 𝑛) depends polynomially on 𝑛 within each residue class modulo 𝑑 . In particular, dim 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛
grows as 𝑛𝑟 −1 for 𝑟 ≥ 2, so there is no literal periodicity; rather, the growth rate and pattern repeat with
period 𝑑 .
   Concretely: for 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 2 ( 𝑟 = 1, ℎ1 = 2), 𝑑 = 2, recovering the Virasoro periodicity. For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 3 ( 𝑟 = 2,
ℎ1 = 2, ℎ2 = 3), 𝑑 = 6. For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ( ℎ𝑖 = 𝑖 + 1, 𝑖 = 1, . . . , 𝑁 − 1), 𝑑 = lcm(2, 3, . . . , 𝑁 ).
Remark 14.2.4 (Scope). The proof assembles: (i) Arakawa’s simplicity theorem for W-algebras at generic
level ([proved], [37]); (ii) the Beilinson–Drinfeld comparison ([proved], [2]); (iii) the generalized Gel’fand–
Fuchs computation for Lie algebras with multiple generators ([proved], [205]). For non-principal nilpotent
orbits (Remark below), the simplicity hypothesis requires case-by-case verification.
Remark 14.2.5 (Elementary model presentation; Convention 2.9.2). Step A (H-level): 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (A) is the endo-
morphism algebra of the identity functor on factorization A-modules: it classifies 𝐴∞ -deformations of
the chiral algebra A. The polynomial structure 𝐶 𝐻 ∗ (W 𝑘 (𝔤))  ℂ[ Θ1 , . . . , Θ𝑟 ] asserts that the formal
moduli space of deformations is a smooth affine space of dimension 𝑟 = rank(𝔤). Each generator Θ𝑖 is
the universal deformation class of the 𝑖 -th W-generator 𝑊 ( ℎ𝑖 ) ; the polynomial ring structure says all
deformations are unobstructed.
    Step B (M-level): The proof is a chain-level computation: the bar filtration induces a spectral sequence
𝐸2 ⇒ 𝐶 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) that collapses at 𝐸2 by generic Ext-vanishing (Arakawa simplicity [37]), and the
   𝑝,𝑞

surviving 𝐸2𝑛,0 page computes the continuous Gel’fand–Fuchs cohomology of the W-Lie algebra with 𝑟
generating currents (Fuchs [205]).
    Reduction B→A (M-level → H-level): The M-level bar complex 𝐵¯ HH (A) = (A ⊗ 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā) ⊗ A , 𝑑 )
is a dg model for the derived endomorphism object 𝑅End A-A (A). By Proposition 6.2.52, the H-level
endomorphism algebra is recovered from the M-level bar complex up to contractible ambiguity, so the
M-level spectral sequence collapse determines the H-level polynomial structure.
    Step C (S-level): The Hilbert function dim 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 (W 𝑘 (𝔤)) = #{( 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑟 ) : 𝑎𝑖 ℎ𝑖 = 𝑛} grows as
                                                                                              P
𝑛𝑟 −1 /( ℎ1 · · · ℎ𝑟 ) and is quasi-polynomial of period 𝑑 = lcm( ℎ1 , . . . , ℎ𝑟 ). For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 2 : literal period 2. For
𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 3 : 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, . . . with quasi-period 6.
    Reduction B→C (M-level → S-level): The S-level Hilbert function is extracted from the M-level spec-
tral sequence by taking the Euler characteristic of 𝐸2𝑛,0 : the collapse at 𝐸2 ensures dim 𝐶 𝐻 𝑛 = dim 𝐸2𝑛,0 ,
and the Gel’fand–Fuchs computation identifies 𝐸2𝑛,0 with the partition function of 𝑟 generators of

Remark 14.2.6 (Non-principal nilpotent orbits). For general W 𝑘 (𝔤, 𝑓 ) with 𝑓 not necessarily principal,
the conformal weights of the generators are determined by the Kazhdan grading associated to the 𝔰𝔩 2 -
triple ( 𝑒, ℎ, 𝑓 ). The periodicity period is then 𝑑 = lcm( ℎ1 , . . . , ℎ 𝑠 ) where ℎ1 , . . . , ℎ 𝑠 are the resulting
conformal weights. When the generic-level non-coboundary condition can be verified for a given orbit, the
same argument applies; for special orbits this remains an open problem.

14.3      Deformation theory
14.3.1    Infinitesimal deformations
Theorem 14.3.1 (Deformation classification; [proved]). (i) 𝐶 𝐻 1 (A) classifies outer derivations
       Der(A)/Inn(A) (not infinitesimal automorphisms, which are all derivations).
  (ii) 𝐶 𝐻 2 (A) classifies first-order deformations.
 (iii) 𝐶 𝐻 3 (A) contains the primary obstructions to extending deformations.
14.4. Physical applications                                                                           761


 (iv) Unobstructed deformations correspond to marginal operators in CFT.

Remark 14.6.1 (Physical origin). In 2d CFT on a genus 𝑔 surface Σ 𝑔 , the partition function 𝑍 [ Σ 𝑔 ] =

(genus 0) contribution, 𝐸2 incorporates one-loop corrections, and higher pages capture multi-loop effects.
The spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 precisely when the theory is modular invariant.

Remark 14.6.4 (Functoriality). The Hochschild-cyclic spectral sequence is functorial: a morphism
𝑓 : A → B induces 𝑓∗ : 𝐸𝑟 (A) → 𝐸𝑟 (B), tensor products satisfy 𝐸𝑟 (A ⊗ B)  𝐸𝑟 (A) ⊗ 𝐸𝑟 (B) up
to higher structure, and Koszul duality gives 𝐸𝑟 (A ! )  𝐸𝑟 (A) ∨ . The Hochschild complex represents the
functor Bimod A ∋ 𝑀 ↦→ HomBimod (HH(A) , 𝑀 ).

14.6.7     Cyclic homology exchange under Koszul duality
Corollary 14.6.23 (Cyclic homology duality; [proved]). For a Koszul pair (A , A ! ), the Connes
periodicity operator 𝑆 intertwines the Koszul duality on Hochschild homology with a [−2]-shifted duality
on cyclic homology:
                                       HC𝑛 (A)  HC− 𝑛 (A ! ) ∨                                   (14.1)
for all 𝑛, where HC∗ denotes periodic cyclic homology.

Proof. The SBI exact sequence (Corollary 14.6.13) relates HH∗ and HC∗ via the periodicity operator 𝑆 .
The Koszul duality for Hochschild cohomology (Theorem 11.4.8) gives HH𝑛 (A)  HH2− 𝑛 (A ! ) ∨ ⊗ 𝜔 𝑋 .
Inserting this into the SBI sequence for A and comparing with the SBI sequence for A ! : the periodicity
operator 𝑆 shifts degree by −2 on both sides, so the duality on HH∗ descends to periodic cyclic homology
as stated. The shift by 2 in the Hochschild duality is absorbed by the periodicity 𝑆 , yielding the unshifted
duality (14.1) on HP∗ = lim HC∗+2𝑘 .
                           ←− 𝑆

                                               Θ ←→ −Θ′

14.6.8    Summary and future directions
The theoretical arc of Part I is now complete. Algebraic foundations (§4) supplied the operadic language;
configuration spaces (§5) gave it geometric content; the bar-cobar construction realized the adjunction as
Verdier duality on the Ran space; and the higher-genus theory assembled the proved scalar package 𝜅 , the
proved spectral package ( Δ A , Π A ), and the theorematic simple-Lie-symmetry Maurer–Cartan comple-
tion Θ A . The three main theorems –- adjunction (A), inversion on the Koszul locus (B), and Lagrangian
complementarity (C) –- are shadows of a single structure: the modular Koszul object associated to a fac-
torization algebra on curves. Chiral Hochschild cohomology, developed in this chapter, is the infinitesimal
invariant of that structure: it detects periodicities, controls deformations, and exchanges under Koszul
duality via the Connes operator. Part II turns from the abstract theory to its concrete realizations, beginning
with the lattice construction that provides a uniform source for all major families of chiral algebras.
Chapter 15


E 𝑛 Koszul duality and higher-dimensional bar
complexes

Throughout this monograph, the bar differential has been built from configuration spaces of points on
a curve: the propagator 𝜔𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) is a meromorphic 1-form, its singularities are controlled by
Arnold relations, and the bar-cobar adjunction lives over the chiral operad. This chapter asks a different
question: what remains true when one leaves the Beilinson–Drinfeld curve setting and passes to genuine
little-disks factorization on real 𝑛-manifolds? Then the propagator becomes a closed ( 𝑛 − 1)-form, collision
strata are governed by Totaro relations, and the bar-cobar adjunction governs E𝑛 -algebras.
     Two axes must be kept separate. Inside chiral geometry on a fixed curve one has the hierarchy E∞ -chiral ⊂
P∞ -chiral ⊂ E1 -chiral, so the passage from Heisenberg to Yangian changes commutativity and locality, not
manifold dimension. The topological ladder is instead indexed by real manifold dimension: 𝑛 = 1 is the
classical associative/ 𝐴∞ bar-cobar theory on intervals or circles, 𝑛 = 2 is the oriented-surface setting whose
holomorphic refinement recovers the chiral bar complex on a complex curve, and 𝑛 = 3 interfaces with
Chern–Simons theory and Vassiliev invariants (Chapter 32). At 𝑛 = 2 the bar complex governs E2 -algebras–
-the natural algebraic structure on braided monoidal categories–-and connects to Kontsevich’s formality
theorem for the little 2-disks operad.
Convention 15.0.1 (Two axes in this chapter). In this chapter, bare E𝑛 always denotes little-disks/topological
factorization on real 𝑛-manifolds. The earlier hierarchy E∞ -chiral/P∞ -chiral/E1 -chiral remains curve-based.
Hence the chiral bar complex on a complex curve belongs to the topological ladder at 𝑛 = 2, while the
𝑛 = 1 case is the classical associative/ 𝐴∞ bar construction.


15.1    Higher-dimensional configuration spaces

                          𝐶𝑘 ( 𝑀 ) = ( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑘 ) ∈ 𝑀 𝑘 | 𝑥 𝑖 ≠ 𝑥𝑗 for 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 .
                                      

Theorem 15.1.3 (Totaro presentation, general 𝑛 [41]; [proved]). For 𝑛 ≥ 2, the cohomology ring
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ); ℚ) is the graded-commutative algebra generated by classes 𝛼𝑖𝑗 ∈ 𝐻 𝑛−1 , 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 ≤ 𝑘 ,
subject to the relations:
   (i) (Symmetry) 𝛼𝑖𝑗 = (−1) 𝑛 𝛼𝑗 𝑖 ;
  (ii) (Totaro relations) 𝛼𝑖𝑗 · 𝛼𝑗 𝑘 + 𝛼𝑗 𝑘 · 𝛼𝑘𝑖 + 𝛼𝑘𝑖 · 𝛼𝑖𝑗 = 0 for distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 ;
 (iii) (Degree) 𝛼𝑖𝑗2 = 0 when 𝑛 is odd; when 𝑛 is even, 𝛼𝑖𝑗2 is determined by the Euler class.
At 𝑛 = 2, after identifying ℝ2  ℂ and choosing the oriented generator of 𝐻 1 ( 𝐶2 (ℝ2 )), one recovers
Arnold’s three-term relation on 𝐶𝑘 (ℂ). By contrast, 𝑛 = 1 is the degree-0 associative setting of ordered
points on a line, not the chiral curve case.
Proof. See Totaro [102], Theorem 1; also Cohen [41], Theorem A for the formality statement. The key
geometric input is that projection maps 𝐶𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) → 𝐶2 (ℝ𝑛 ) induce pullbacks of the fundamental class of
𝑆 𝑛−1 (the linking sphere), and all relations among these pullbacks are generated by the three-term relation
(ii).
Remark 15.1.4 (Arnold as Totaro at 𝑛 = 2). In the E𝑛 hierarchy, 𝑛 is the real dimension. The classical Arnold
generators on 𝐶𝑘 (ℂ) are Totaro generators at 𝑛 = 2; our chiral bar complex uses 𝑛 = 2:
                           E𝑛 -level       Manifold                 Bar complex
                             𝑛=1        interval/circle      associative bar (classical)
                             𝑛=2        surface/curve       chiral bar (this monograph)
                             𝑛=3          3-manifold            Chern–Simons bar
                           general 𝑛     𝑛-manifold                     E𝑛 bar
Main Theorems A, B, C are the holomorphic refinement of the 𝑛 = 2 chapter of E𝑛 Koszul duality.

15.1.1 Fulton–MacPherson compactification in dimension 𝑛
Deﬁnition 15.1.5 (FM compactiﬁcation of 𝐶𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 )). The Fulton–MacPherson compactiﬁcation 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) is
the real oriented blowup of (ℝ𝑛 ) 𝑘 along all partial diagonals, ordered by reverse inclusion. Equivalently
(Axelrod–Singer, Kontsevich), it is the closure of the image of the map
                                                       Y 𝑛−1 Y
                            𝐶𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) ↩→ (ℝ𝑛 ) 𝑘 ×          𝑆 ×         [0, ∞]
                                                            𝑖 <𝑗          | 𝑆 | ≥2

recording positions, relative directions 𝜃 𝑖𝑗 = ( 𝑥 𝑖 − 𝑥𝑗 )/| 𝑥 𝑖 − 𝑥𝑗 | ∈ 𝑆 𝑛−1 , and relative distances. The result
is a smooth manifold with corners whose boundary strata are indexed by nested partitions of {1, . . . , 𝑘 }–-
the same combinatorial data as the Stasheff associahedron (𝑛 = 1) or the FM operad (𝑛 ≥ 2).
Proposition 15.1.6 (Boundary strata and operadic structure; [proved] [12]). The codimension-1
boundary strata of 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) are indexed by subsets 𝑆 ⊂ {1, . . . , 𝑘 } with | 𝑆 | ≥ 2, and are diffeomorphic to
                                  𝜕𝑆 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 )  𝐶 𝑘 − | 𝑆 |+1 (ℝ𝑛 ) × 𝐶 | 𝑆 | (ℝ𝑛 ) .
This factorization equips {𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 )} 𝑘 ≥0 with the structure of a topological operad–-the Fulton–
MacPherson operad FM𝑛 –-which is a model for the E𝑛 operad (i.e., weakly equivalent to the little 𝑛-disks
operad).
Proof. The operadic structure is due to Getzler–Jones [24] and Salvatore; the equivalence FM𝑛 ≃ E𝑛 is
proved by Salvatore–Longoni for 𝑛 ≥ 2 and follows from Stasheff’s theorem for 𝑛 = 1.

(differential of a constant). Residues along 𝑧1 = 𝑧2 extract OPE data.

Theorem 15.6.2 ( 𝑑 2 = 0 for the E 𝑛 bar complex; [proved]). For any 𝑛 ≥ 1 and any E𝑛 -algebra 𝐴, the
E𝑛 bar differential satisfies 𝑑 2 = 0.

Proof. The argument is identical to the 𝑛 = 2 case (Theorem 15.3.2), with the Arnold/Totaro relations in
                                               2 . For general 𝑛, the Totaro relation holds in degree 2( 𝑛 − 1),
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶3 (ℝ𝑛 )) providing the cancellation of 𝑑res
and the cancellation works in any degree.
    The result also follows from the general formality framework of Idrissi [240]: Poincaré duality on the

𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) and its cohomology algebra (the Totaro algebra), and the propagator differential is compatible
with this quasi-isomorphism.

Remark 15.6.3 (The dimensional ladder). The transition from 𝑛 to 𝑛 + 1 trades algebraic structure for
topological generality:

                  𝑛     Propagator            Relations               Bar complex computes
                  1     𝑑 log | 𝑡1 − 𝑡2 |     Stasheff polytopes      Hochschild cohomology
                  2     𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 )      Arnold (OS)             Chiral Koszul dual
                  3     linking 2-form        graph cohomology        Vassiliev invariants
                  𝑛     ( 𝑛−1)-form           Totaro                  E𝑛 -factorization homology

At each level, the propagator is a closed ( 𝑛 − 1)-form, the relations in 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶3 (ℝ𝑛 )) ensure 𝑑 2 = 0, and the
bar cohomology computes the Koszul dual in the appropriate operadic sense.

15.6.2    Knudsen’s higher enveloping algebras
Theorem 15.6.4 (Higher enveloping algebras; [proved]). (Knudsen [241]) For a Lie algebra 𝔤 and
𝑛 ≥ 1, the 𝑛-th enveloping algebra 𝑈𝑛 (𝔤) is an E𝑛 -algebra satisfying:
   (i) 𝑈1 (𝔤) = 𝑈 (𝔤) is the classical universal enveloping algebra.
  (ii) (PBW) There is an equivalence of graded objects gr 𝑈𝑛 (𝔤) ≃ SymE𝑛 (𝔤[ 𝑛 − 1]), where SymE𝑛 is
       the free commutative E𝑛 -algebra.
 (iii) (Koszul duality) 𝐵 E𝑛 (𝑈𝑛 (𝔤)) is quasi-isomorphic to CEE∗𝑛 (𝔤), the E𝑛 -Chevalley–Eilenberg com-
       plex of 𝔤.
   This result is the higher-dimensional analogue of the PBW theorem and the classical bar-CE comparison.
At 𝑛 = 2, the E2 enveloping algebra 𝑈2 (𝔤) is the topological shadow of the chiral universal enveloping
algebra 𝑈
        b (𝔤𝑘 ) = 𝑉𝑘 (𝔤) (the vacuum module; see Theorem 15.3.2 for the precise E2 statement). Knudsen’s
Koszul duality at 𝑛 = 2 is the topological shadow of our chiral Koszul duality.

15.6.3   Kontsevich formality and deformation quantization
Theorem 15.6.5 (Formality of E 2 ; [proved]). (Kontsevich [133], Tamarkin [218]) The E2 operad is
formal over ℚ: there is a quasi-isomorphism of operads

                                       𝐶∗ ( E2 ; ℚ) ≃ 𝐻∗ ( E2 ; ℚ) .

Consequently, every E2 -algebra structure on a cochain complex 𝐴 is determined up to quasi-isomorphism
by the induced 𝐻∗ ( E2 )-algebra structure on cohomology.
Remark 15.6.6 (Formality and deformation quantization). Kontsevich formality [133] implies star products
on arbitrary Poisson manifolds. In our framework (Chapter 22), E2 Koszul duality exchanges the bar
complex of polyvector fields with that of polydifferential operators–-Poisson brackets with star products.
The explicit Kontsevich star product arises from propagator integrals on 𝐶 𝑘 (H ), a specific E2 bar complex
model with boundary conditions.
Proposition 15.6.7 ( E 𝑛 formality for 𝑛 ≥ 2; [proved]). (Fresse–Willwacher, Idrissi [240]) The
E𝑛 operad is formal over ℝ for all 𝑛 ≥ 2. The formality map is constructed explicitly via configuration
space integrals on 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ) using the propagator of Definition 15.2.1, with the Kontsevich graph expansion
providing the explicit formulas.

15.7     The 𝑛 = 3 case: Chern–Simons theory
The 𝑛 = 3 case of E𝑛 Koszul duality connects directly to perturbative Chern–Simons theory and the
Kontsevich integral of Chapter 32.
Conjecture 15.7.1 (E3 bar complex and Chern–Simons; [conjectured]). For 𝔤 a finite-dimensional Lie algebra
with invariant inner product, the E3 bar complex 𝐵 E3 (𝑈3 (𝔤)) computes the perturbative Chern–Simons
invariants of 3-manifolds:
   (i) The propagator is the Chern–Simons propagator of Example 15.2.4: the Green’s 2-form of the gauge-
       fixed Laplacian on 𝑀 .
  (ii) The Feynman diagrams of Axelrod–Singer are the contributions from individual boundary strata of
       𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑀 ).
 (iii) The bar cohomology 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵 E3 (𝑈3 (𝔤))) should recover the Kontsevich graph complex with Lie algebra
       coefficients.
Remark 15.7.2 (Scope). Part (ii) (Feynman diagrams = boundary strata) is established (Axelrod–Singer,
Kontsevich [34], Cattaneo–Mnev [243]). What is conjectured is the full chain-level identification (iii):
showing the Axelrod–Singer compactification models the E3 bar complex (the 𝑛 = 2 analogue is our Prism
Principle, Theorem 12.13.25). The 𝑛 = 3 case requires modular E3 -operads, not yet developed. (Contributing
to Conjecture 34.9.5.)

15.8     Summary and the dimensional ladder
What is proved.
   (i) The Totaro presentation of 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 )) generalizes Arnold’s presentation from 𝑛 = 2 to all 𝑛
       (Theorem 15.1.3).
  (ii) The E2 bar complex satisfies 𝑑 2 = 0 via the Totaro relations (Theorem 15.3.2).
15.8. Summary and the dimensional ladder                                                                779


 (iii) The chiral bar-cobar duality of Main Theorem A is recovered as the 𝑛 = 2 case of E𝑛 Koszul duality
       (Corollary 15.4.4).
 (iv) Our construction is the chain-level refinement of Ayala–Francis Poincaré–Koszul duality at 𝑛 = 2
       (Proposition 15.5.2).
  (v) E𝑛 Koszul duality, E𝑛 formality, and higher enveloping algebras are established in the literature for
       all 𝑛 (Theorem 15.4.2, Theorem 15.6.4, Proposition 15.6.7).
What remains as computational refinement. The abstract E𝑛 Koszul duality is fully established for
all 𝑛 (formality, Totaro presentation, Knudsen’s higher enveloping algebras; see Theorem 15.4.2 and Re-
mark 34.10.3). The following are concrete calculations beyond the proved theorems:
   (i) Explicit closed-form formulas for the E𝑛 bar differential in terms of Totaro generators at each 𝑛 ≥ 3
       (the propagator and FM compactification exist and 𝑑 2 = 0 is proved, but the individual formulas
       have not been tabulated).
  (ii) The 𝑛 = 3 Chern–Simons identification (Conjecture 15.7.1): connecting the E3 bar complex to
       perturbative CS invariants at the chain level.
 (iii) Higher-genus E𝑛 theory: for 𝑛 ≥ 3, the analogue of genus- 𝑔 quantum corrections would require a
       notion of ‘‘higher-dimensional moduli’’ replacing M 𝑔 . The correct framework may be cobordism
       categories or extended TQFTs, but this is far from the current state of the art.
   The dimensional ladder makes precise the sense in which this monograph’s results–-chiral bar-cobar
duality, quantum complementarity, genus expansions–-are the 𝑛 = 2 chapter of a general story that extends
through all dimensions.
Remark 15.8.1 (The E1 -E2 obstruction). The Yangian is E1 -chiral (Theorem 24.1.5): binary fusion with
braiding ( 𝑅-matrix level). Upgrading to E2 requires coherent many-point transport: an associator Φ ∈
exp( Lie(
      c 𝑡12 , 𝑡23 )) satisfying pentagon and hexagon. The Drinfeld–Kohno theorem (Theorem 24.9.3) is the
E1 -level comparison (KZ monodromy = 𝑅-matrix); full E2 coherence requires associator input, governed
by the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group.
Remark 15.8.2 (The Grothendieck–Teichmüller group). E2 formality (Tamarkin [218]) is not canonical:
it depends on a Drinfeld associator Φ, and the non-uniqueness is governed by GRT. For the Yangian,
the 𝑅-matrix is E1 -level data (braid); the associator Φ provides E2 -level coherence. DK is naturally an
E1 -factorization theorem; full E2 coherence is a separate, GT-dependent upgrade.

At generic level 𝑘 , the bar complex 𝐵 (b                                     𝔤𝑘 ) measures the failure of 𝑑 2 = 0

completed/coderived enlargement beyond the semisimplified target, is a separate outer MC3 problem.
Remark 16.0.1 (Periodicity frontier). The theorematic core of this chapter is asymmetric. The critical-level
bar/oper identification is proved, and the manuscript isolates a rank-1 periodic shadow in Proposition 16.4.5.
The stronger admissible-level statement that the full bar complex carries a periodic CDG structure, especially
in the higher-rank form needed for Kazhdan–Lusztig transport, remains conjectural and belongs to the
MC3/periodicity frontier. Even on the KL side, the ordinary semisimplified target C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) and any larger
non-semisimple or completed/coderived lift must be kept separate.

16.1     Derived algebraic geometry: prerequisites
The exposition follows Lurie [43] and Toën–Vezzosi.
Deﬁnition 16.1.1 (Derived stack). A derived stack (over a field 𝑘 of characteristic zero) is a functor
         op
𝑋 : cdga𝑘 → S from commutative dg-algebras to the ∞-category of spaces, satisfying étale descent. A
derived stack 𝑋 has:
   (i) A classical truncation 𝑡0 ( 𝑋 ), which is an ordinary algebraic stack obtained by restricting to ordinary
       (non-dg) commutative algebras.
  (ii) A cotangent complex 𝕃 𝑋 ∈ QCoh( 𝑋 ), a quasi-coherent sheaf on 𝑋 (in the derived sense) controlling
       deformations and obstructions. For a smooth classical scheme 𝑌 viewed as a derived stack, 𝕃𝑌 =
       Ω𝑌1 [0] is the ordinary sheaf of differentials.
 (iii) A derived structure sheaf O 𝑋der , a sheaf of cdga’s whose cohomology sheaves H 𝑖 (O 𝑋der ) encode the
       derived information beyond the classical truncation.
Deﬁnition 16.1.2 (Formal smoothness). A derived stack 𝑋 is formally smooth if its cotangent complex
𝕃 𝑋 is concentrated in cohomological degree 0 (i.e., 𝕃 𝑋 ≃ Ω1𝑡0 ( 𝑋 ) [0]). Equivalently, 𝑋 has no higher
obstructions: every infinitesimal deformation extends.

16.2      The oper space

given by projecting to 𝐻 0 is a map of algebras: the bar complex at critical level is a dg-algebra (since the

Proof. The bar complex 𝐵 (b 𝔤− ℎ∨ ) carries a product from the coproduct on the bar coalgebra (dual to the

is a genuine dg-algebra. The PBW filtration is compatible with the product, and the identification 𝐻 0 =

the Frenkel–Gaitsgory functor follows from [25], Theorem 9.5: the localization of the vacuum module is
