16.4     Root-of-unity bar complexes
16.4.1    Admissible levels and the quantum group parameter
Deﬁnition 16.4.1 (Admissible level). A level 𝑘 is admissible if 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 where 𝑝, 𝑞 ∈ ℤ>0 ,
gcd( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) = 1, and 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ (for simply-laced 𝔤; the condition is more involved for non-simply-laced types).
                                                              ∨
The associated quantum group parameter is 𝑞QG = 𝑒 𝜋 𝑖 /( 𝑘+ℎ ) = 𝑒 𝜋 𝑖𝑞/ 𝑝 .
    At an admissible level, the current double-pole coefficient is 𝑘𝜅 ( 𝑎, 𝑏 )1, where 𝜅 is the normalized
invariant form. The mode bracket obtained by testing this coefficient is 𝑘𝑚𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0 𝜅 ( 𝑎, 𝑏 ) 𝐾 in (20.2). Its
Chevalley–Eilenberg differential squares to zero at every level (Theorem 20.6.9). Thus this central term
alone does not establish a nonzero square of an unreduced chiral bar differential. Such a conclusion requires
a specified curved carrier and the actual coefficient comparison of Remark 20.6.18. The Sugawara central
charge 𝑘 dim(𝔤)/( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) and a curvature operator are separate constructions from the current central
extension. Meanwhile, the representation category O𝑘int (b  𝔤) is semisimple with |Adm𝑘 | simple objects
(Theorem 20.11.13).

16.4.2    The periodic CDG structure
Deﬁnition 16.4.2 (Curved dg-algebra (CDG)). A curved differential graded algebra (CDG-algebra) is a
triple ( 𝐴, 𝑑, ℎ) where 𝐴 is a graded algebra, 𝑑 : 𝐴 → 𝐴 [1] is a derivation, and ℎ ∈ 𝐴2 is the curvature
element, satisfying:
16.4. Root-of-unity bar complexes                                                                         787


   (i) 𝑑 2 ( 𝑎) = [ ℎ, 𝑎] for all 𝑎 ∈ 𝐴;
  (ii) 𝑑ℎ = 0 (the curvature is closed).
Applying a curved analogue of this definition to a chiral bar object requires the graded coalgebra, its
coderivation, and its curvature map. Proposition 6.2.30 gives only an identity for two operators on a
common graded space; it does not construct these data. In particular, a central element in an algebra has
zero commutator even when it is nonzero, so the level coefficient alone cannot imply a nonzero curvature
operator.
Conjecture 16.4.3 (Periodic CDG structure at admissible level; [conjectured]). At admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ +
𝑝/ 𝑞 , the bar complex 𝐵 (b𝔤𝑘 ) admits a periodic CDG structure: there exists a natural isomorphism of CDG-
coalgebras
                                              𝑛+2 𝑠           𝑛
                                            𝐵       (b
                                                     𝔤𝑘 )  𝐵 (b 𝔤𝑘 )
where 𝑠 = 𝑝 (the numerator of 𝑘 + ℎ∨ = 𝑝/ 𝑞 ), so the bar complex is 2 𝑝-periodic in bar degree.
Remark 16.4.4 (Positselski’s framework). Positselski [171] develops CDG-algebras whose Koszul duality
exchanges coderived and contraderived categories: 𝐷 co ( 𝐴) ≃ 𝐷 ctr ( 𝐵 ). For periodic CDG-algebras, the
coderived category reduces to the stable category of a finite-dimensional quotient (the passage from 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)
to 𝑢𝑞 (𝔤)). Conjecture 16.4.3 asserts that the bar complex at admissible level is periodic in this sense; up-
grading it requires understanding the quantum group center action on the bar complex at a root of unity.
(Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.3.)

16.4.3    Evidence for periodicity
Proposition 16.4.5 (Affine sl2 periodicity; [proved]). For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 2 , the bar cohomology
         b 2,𝑘 )) at generic level satisfies the periodicity

Proof. See the proof in Chapter 20 (Theorem 10.5.3): the periodicity follows from the rank-1 structure of

Remark 16.4.6 (Periodicity and quantum group). At admissible level 𝑘 = −2 + 𝑝/ 𝑞 , the period 2ℎ =
4 divides 2 𝑝 when 𝑝 is even. The 4-periodicity of the bar cohomology dimensions is a shadow of the
representation-theoretic periodicity of the quantum group 𝑈𝑞 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) at 𝑞 = 𝑒 𝜋 𝑖𝑞/ 𝑝 . For the small quantum
group 𝑢𝑞 , the representation category is 2 𝑝-periodic, and Conjecture 16.4.3 asserts that the bar complex
‘‘sees’’ this periodicity via CDG structure.
Remark 16.4.7 (Scope boundary for periodicity). Only rank-1 strict periodicity is proved in this chapter
(Proposition 16.4.5). For higher-rank affine algebras, strict periodicity is not established and can fail; the
active statement remains the periodic CDG conjecture (Conjecture 16.4.3) together with growth/profile
control. In particular, periodicity does not transfer automatically across Koszul duality or level-shift invo-
lutions without additional rank-sensitive input.

16.5.1 Roadmap: from critical level to KL
Remark 16.5.7 (The critical-admissible deformation). As 𝑘 deforms from −ℎ∨ to −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 , the bar com-
plex interpolates: uncurved at critical level (computes oper functions, Theorem 16.3.1); CDG-coalgebra at
generic perturbation; conjecturally periodic CDG at rational 𝑝/ 𝑞 (recovering the semisimplified KL tar-
get). This connects geometric Langlands (opers) to representation-theoretic Langlands (quantum groups)
through bar-cobar duality.

16.6     Connections to the geometric Langlands programme
16.6.1   The Frenkel–Gaitsgory programme
Theorem 16.6.1 (Frenkel–Gaitsgory localization; [proved]). (Frenkel–Gaitsgory [25]) There is a
localization functor
                       Δ: 𝐷 𝔤b− ℎ∨ -mod −→ 𝐷 QCoh(Op𝔤∨ ( 𝐷 ))
                                                                  

that is an equivalence on the subcategory of modules on which the center 𝑍 (b
                                                                            𝔤− ℎ∨ ) acts locally finitely.
Remark 16.6.2 (Bar-cobar as localization). The bar complex is a chain-level model for the localization
functor Δ: the vacuum module maps to OOp (Theorem 16.3.1), a Verma module 𝑀𝜆 maps to the skyscraper
at the corresponding oper, and the full derived structure is computed by Theorem 16.3.11.

16.6.2    From opers to Hecke eigensheaves
Remark 16.6.3 (The Langlands path). The Frenkel–Gaitsgory programme factors geometric Langlands

16.7     Summary
What is proved.
   (i) Full derived oper identiﬁcation (Theorem 16.3.11): 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵 (b  𝔤− ℎ∨ ))  Ω𝑛 (Op𝔤∨ ( 𝐷 )) for all 𝑛 ≥ 0.
       Proof: bar-Ext (Corollary 6.9.17) + Frenkel–Teleman [233]. Independent PBW confirmation at 𝑛 = 0
       (Theorem 16.3.1), 𝑛 = 1 (Proposition 16.3.2), 𝑛 = 2 (Proposition 16.3.3), 𝑛 = 3 (Corollary 16.3.10).
  (ii) The bar complex at critical level is a chain-level model for the Frenkel–Gaitsgory localization functor
       (Proposition 16.3.13).
 (iii) Five of six ingredients for the semisimplified KL-from-bar-cobar conjecture are proved
       (Conjecture 16.5.3).
 (iv) Bar cohomology periodicity at rank 1 (Proposition 16.4.5).
  (v) Whitehead spectral decomposition (Proposition 16.3.4): the 𝐸1 page factors as Fun(Op) ⊗ 𝐻 ∗ (𝔤; 𝑘 ),
       reducing the PBW spectral sequence to finitely many transgression differentials.
 (vi) The PBW spectral sequence analysis at 𝑛 = 3 identifies the 𝑑4 transgression differential
       (Proposition 16.3.6, Proposition 16.3.7).
What remains.
  (i) The periodic CDG structure at admissible levels (Conjecture 16.4.3): this is the single remaining
      ingredient for a bar-cobar proof of the semisimplified KL target.
 (ii) The semisimplified KL equivalence from bar-cobar (Conjecture 16.5.3): depends on the periodic
      CDG structure.
16.7. Summary                                                                                       791


 (iii) Any non-semisimple or completed/coderived KL lift beyond C(𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)): this is a separate outer MC3
       extension and is not implied by the semisimplified KL step.
 (iv) Higher-rank periodicity: extending Proposition 16.4.5 beyond rank 1 to establish periodicity for
       general 𝔤.
   The critical-level bar complex sits at the intersection of three programmes: geometric Langlands
(Programme I), the KL equivalence (Programme II), and fusion product preservation (Programme III).
Bar-cobar duality provides a single algebraic object–-the bar complex–-that unifies these apparently
disparate research directions.
      Part II

Complete Portraits




        793
                                                                                                            795


In Chapter 1, we computed the bar complex, Koszul dual, curvature tower, and 𝐴ˆ-genus for the Heisenberg
algebra. Part II applies the same programme to every major family of chiral algebras. These chapters should
be read as complete portraits rather than as subordinate examples: each family reveals a structural feature
that is invisible in the Heisenberg frame alone. The constructions of Part I–-the bar complex, the genus
tower, the Koszul pair structure–-are defined for any augmented chiral algebra satisfying mild finiteness
conditions. The question driving Part II is: what do these constructions produce when applied to the
algebras that arise in practice?
    The answer is unexpectedly structured. The bar cohomology dimensions of apparently unrelated alge-
bras–-the Kac–Moody algebra 𝔰𝔩       b 2 , the Virasoro algebra, the 𝛽𝛾 -system–-share a common discriminant
Δ ( 𝑥 ) = (1 − 3 𝑥 ) (1 + 𝑥 ). The genus expansion of every Koszul algebra is controlled by a single obstruction
invariant 𝜅 , and 𝜅 transforms predictably under Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction. The complementarity sums
𝑐 + 𝑐 ′ are root-datum invariants. These are not coincidences; they are the fingerprints of the general theory
made visible in specific examples. Each family of chiral algebras reveals a distinct face of the modular Koszul
structure: the Feigin–Frenkel involution 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ is Koszul duality for Kac–Moody algebras; Drin-
feld–Sokolov reduction is a Koszul functor; the 𝐴ˆ-genus in the Heisenberg genus expansion witnesses a
family index theorem; the Yangian forces a departure from 𝐸∞ -chiral to 𝐸1 -chiral Koszul duality.
    The examples are organized along the axis from the E∞ -commutative atom (Heisenberg) to the E1 -
associative atom (Yangian). Kac–Moody algebras, Virasoro, and W-algebras are E∞ -chiral with increas-
ingly complex OPE pole structures. Lattice vertex algebras carry an E1 sublattice structure visible through
screening operators. The Yangian is purely E1 -chiral: its bar complex uses ordered configuration spaces and
Verdier duality acts by 𝑅-matrix inversion, not type exchange.
Chapter 17


The lattice construction

The constructions of Part I take as input a chiral algebra A and produce its Koszul dual, its genus corrections,
its modular characteristic package. Part II supplies the input. Every chiral algebra in this monograph arises
from a common source: the lattice vertex algebra 𝑉𝐿 associated to an even lattice 𝐿 . The Heisenberg algebra
of Chapter 1 is 𝑉𝐿 for 𝐿 = ℤ; affine Kac–Moody at level 1 is 𝑉𝑄 for the root lattice 𝑄 ; the free fermion is
a subalgebra of a rank-1 lattice VOA; W-algebras are obtained by quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction.
The lattice construction is therefore the universal entry point for Part II.

17.1     Even lattices and root systems
Deﬁnition 17.1.1 (Lattice). A lattice is a free abelian group Λ of finite rank equipped with a symmetric
bilinear form ⟨·, ·⟩ : Λ × Λ → ℤ. The lattice is:
   (i) integral if ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ ∈ ℤ for all 𝛼, 𝛽 ∈ Λ;
  (ii) even if ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛼 ⟩ ∈ 2ℤ for all 𝛼 ∈ Λ (this implies integrality);
 (iii) positive-deﬁnite if ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛼 ⟩ > 0 for all 𝛼 ≠ 0;
 (iv) non-degenerate if the map Λ → Λ∗ := Hom( Λ, ℤ) given by 𝛼 ↦→ ⟨ 𝛼, ·⟩ is injective;
  (v) unimodular if this map is an isomorphism, i.e., Λ = Λ∗ .
Deﬁnition 17.1.2 (Discriminant group). For a non-degenerate lattice Λ, the dual lattice is Λ∗ = { 𝜆 ∈
Λ ⊗ℤ ℚ : ⟨𝜆, 𝛼 ⟩ ∈ ℤ ∀ 𝛼 ∈ Λ}. The discriminant group is the finite abelian group 𝐷 ( Λ) = Λ∗ /Λ, whose
order equals | det(⟨𝑒 𝑖 , 𝑒𝑗 ⟩)| for any basis { 𝑒 𝑖 } of Λ. The bilinear form on Λ induces a ℚ/ℤ-valued bilinear
form on 𝐷 ( Λ).
Example 17.1.3 (Root lattices). The ADE root lattices provide the fundamental examples.

                             Lattice    Rank     det        ℎ∨      Unimodular?
                             𝐴𝑛          𝑛       𝑛+1       𝑛+1          No
                             𝐷𝑛          𝑛        4       2𝑛 − 2        No
                             𝐸6          6        3         12          No
                             𝐸7          7        2         18          No
                             𝐸8          8        1         30          Yes
For each simply-laced root system Φ, the root lattice ΛΦ = ℤΦ is even and positive-definite. The Cartan
matrix 𝐴𝑖𝑗 = ⟨ 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛼𝑗 ⟩ encodes the bilinear form on simple roots.
Remark 17.1.4 (Uniqueness of 𝐸8 ). By Mordell’s theorem (1938), 𝐸8 is the unique even unimodular positive-
definite lattice of rank 8. In rank 16, there are exactly two such lattices: 𝐸8 ⊕ 𝐸8 and 𝐷16
                                                                                           + (the latter being the

overlattice of 𝐷16 by its spinor class). This classification is the lattice-theoretic origin of the two heterotic
string theories.

798                                                                      Chapter 17. The lattice construction


Deﬁnition 17.1.5 (Lattice operations). We record the operations that will become functorial on vertex algebras
in Section 17.7.
   (i) Direct sum. For lattices Λ1 , Λ2 , the orthogonal direct sum Λ1 ⊕ Λ2 has ⟨( 𝛼1 , 𝛼2 ) , ( 𝛽1 , 𝛽2 )⟩ =
       ⟨ 𝛼1 , 𝛽1 ⟩ + ⟨ 𝛼2 , 𝛽2 ⟩.
  (ii) Sublattice. A sublattice Λ′ ↩→ Λ of finite index gives rise to 𝐷 ( Λ′ ) ↠ 𝐷 ( Λ).
 (iii) Overlattice (gluing). For an isotropic subgroup 𝐼 ⊂ 𝐷 ( Λ) (meaning ⟨ 𝛾, 𝛾 ′ ⟩ ≡ 0 mod ℤ for all
       𝛾, 𝛾 ′ ∈ 𝐼 ), the preimage Λ 𝐼 = { 𝜆 ∈ Λ∗ : [ 𝜆] ∈ 𝐼 } is a lattice with Λ ⊂ Λ 𝐼 ⊂ Λ∗ .
 (iv) Orbifold. For 𝜎 ∈ Aut( Λ), the fixed sublattice Λ 𝜎 and the coinvariants Λ/(1 − 𝜎 ) Λ both carry
       induced bilinear forms.

17.2     Cocycle theory
The vertex algebra structure on 𝑉Λ requires a choice of 2-cocycle on Λ. Different cocycles produce genuinely
different algebraic structures, ranging from honest vertex algebras (E∞ -chiral) to nonlocal E1 -chiral algebras.
The cocycle theory controls this distinction.
Deﬁnition 17.2.1 (2-cocycle on a lattice). A 2-cocycle on a lattice Λ is a function 𝜀 : Λ × Λ → ℂ× satisfying:

                                   𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝜀 ( 𝛼 + 𝛽, 𝛾 ) = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 + 𝛾 ) 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛾 )                         (17.1)

for all 𝛼, 𝛽, 𝛾 ∈ Λ. The cocycle is:
   (i) normalized if 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 0) = 𝜀 (0, 𝛼 ) = 1 for all 𝛼 ;
  (ii) bimultiplicative if 𝜀 ( 𝛼 + 𝛼 ′ , 𝛽 ) = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝜀 ( 𝛼 ′ , 𝛽 ) and similarly in the second argument;
 (iii) symmetric (in the sense of Borcherds) if

                                                𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 )                             (17.2)

       for all 𝛼, 𝛽 ∈ Λ.
Remark 17.2.2. The symmetry condition (17.2) is the Borcherds axiom: it is precisely the condition needed
for the vertex operator skew-symmetry 𝑌 ( 𝑎, 𝑧 ) 𝑏 = 𝑒 𝑧𝜕 𝑌 ( 𝑏, − 𝑧 ) 𝑎 to hold. Note that for an even lattice,
(−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ is well-defined. For an odd lattice, one would need (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛼 ⟩ ⟨ 𝛽,𝛽 ⟩/4 corrections; we restrict to
even lattices throughout.
Deﬁnition 17.2.3 (Commutator map). The commutator of a cocycle 𝜀 is

                                                𝑐 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) :=              .

Lemma 17.2.4 (Cocycle classification; [proved]). Let Λ be an even lattice. Then:
   (i) For any normalized bimultiplicative 2-cocycle 𝜀 , the commutator satisfies 𝑐 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ if
       and only if 𝜀 is symmetric.
  (ii) The set of symmetric cocycles on Λ is a torsor for Hom( Λ ⊗ Λ, ℂ× ) sym , the group of symmetric
       bicharacters.
 (iii) The cohomology group 𝐻 2 ( Λ, ℂ× ) classifies cocycles up to coboundary equivalence. Two cocycles
       𝜀, 𝜀 ′ are cohomologous if there exists 𝑓 : Λ → ℂ× with 𝜀 ′ ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = 𝑓 ( 𝛼 ) 𝑓 ( 𝛽 ) 𝑓 ( 𝛼 + 𝛽 ) −1 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ).

versely, if 𝑐 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ , then 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 ) is the Borcherds axiom.

Remark 17.2.7 (Non-symmetric deformations via roots of unity). More generally, given a symmetric cocycle
𝜀0 and an antisymmetric bilinear form 𝑞 : Λ × Λ → ℤ/ 𝑁 ℤ, the product 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = 𝜀0 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) · 𝜁 𝑞 ( 𝛼,𝛽 )
(where 𝜁 = 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖 / 𝑁 ) is a non-symmetric cocycle whenever 𝑞 is not identically zero. Such deformations
interpolate between the commutative (E∞ ) and noncommutative (E1 ) worlds.

Theorem 17.3.2 ( E 1 vs. E ∞ classification; [proved]). The lattice vertex algebra 𝑉Λ𝜀 is:
   (i) an E∞ -chiral algebra (a vertex algebra in the sense of Borcherds) if and only if 𝜀 is symmetric;
  (ii) an E1 -chiral algebra for any cocycle 𝜀 ;
 (iii) strictly E1 (not E∞ ) when 𝜀 is not symmetric.

Proof. (ii) The cocycle condition (17.1) on 𝜀 ensures associativity of the vertex operator products
𝑌 (𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼 , 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 𝑒 𝛽 , 𝑤 ) = 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼 , 𝑧 ) 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛽 , 𝑤 ). Hence 𝑉Λ𝜀 is always at least E1 -chiral.
   (i) and (iii). The skew-symmetry axiom for vertex algebras requires 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼 , 𝑧 ) 𝑒 𝛽 = 𝑒 𝑧𝜕 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛽 , − 𝑧 ) 𝑒 𝛼 .
Computing both sides:

               LHS = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝑧 ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 + · · · ,
               RHS = 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 ) (− 𝑧 ) ⟨ 𝛽,𝛼 ⟩ 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 + · · · = 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 ) (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝑧 ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 + · · · .

Equality of the leading terms requires 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = (−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ 𝜀 ( 𝛽, 𝛼 ), which is the Borcherds symmetry
condition (17.2). Hence skew-symmetry holds if and only if 𝜀 is symmetric. When 𝜀 is not symmetric, the
OPE exchange picks up a phase 𝑐 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 )/(−1) ⟨ 𝛼,𝛽 ⟩ ≠ 1, so the algebra is strictly E1 .

Example 17.3.3 (Heisenberg as a lattice vertex algebra). The Heisenberg vertex algebra H𝜅 at level 𝜅 is the
𝛼 = 0 sector of 𝑉Λ𝜀 for any lattice Λ:

                                     H𝑑 := 𝑉0 = H ⊗ 𝑒 0  ℂ[ 𝛼−𝑖 𝑛 : 𝑖, 𝑛 ≥ 1] ,

with 𝑑 = rank( Λ) free bosons. The cocycle 𝜀 does not enter the 𝛼 = 0 sector. This is the simplest output
of the lattice engine, and the base case for all bar complex computations.
Remark 17.3.4 (Lattice specialization to the frame example). The case Λ = ℤ (with standard form ⟨1, 1⟩ = 2,
giving an even rank-1 lattice) recovers the Heisenberg algebra H𝑘 of Chapter 1; the bar complex computed
there (§1.3) is the Λ = ℤ specialization of the lattice bar complex developed in §17.5.

Remark 17.4.3 (Non-simply-laced algebras). For non-simply-laced 𝔤 (types 𝐵 𝑛 , 𝐶𝑛 , 𝐹4 , 𝐺2 ), the Frenkel–

17.5     Bar complexes of lattice vertex algebras
The lattice grading decomposes the bar complex into orthogonal summands indexed by Λ, since the bar
differential preserves the total lattice degree.
Construction 17.5.1 (Bar complex of 𝑉Λ𝜀 ). The geometric bar complex B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) has:
Generators. Elements of the form

where 𝛼𝑖 ∈ Λ \ {0} and 𝜔 is a logarithmic form on 𝐶 𝑝 ( 𝑋 ). (We suppress Heisenberg descendants 𝛼−𝑖 𝑛 |0⟩
for notational clarity; they contribute additional tensor factors.)
Grading. The total lattice degree is 𝑖 =1 𝛼𝑖 ∈ Λ, and the bar degree is 𝑝.
                                     P𝑝
Differential. The bar differential 𝑑 = 𝑑res sums residues over collision divisors. For a degree-2 element
[ 𝑒 𝛼 | 𝑒 𝛽 ] ⊗ 1:
                                   𝑑 ( [ 𝑒 𝛼 | 𝑒 𝛽 ] ⊗ 1) = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) [ 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 ] ⊗ 1                (17.4)
when ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ = −1 (simple pole in the OPE), and 𝑑 = 0 when ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ ≥ 0 (no pole) or ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ ≤ −2 (higher

Theorem 17.5.2 (Lattice bar complex structure; [proved]). The bar complex B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) satisfies:
   (i) Lattice grading. The differential preserves the total lattice degree 𝑖 𝛼𝑖 ∈ Λ, decomposing the bar
                                                                             P
       complex as B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) = 𝛾 ∈ Λ B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) 𝛾 .
                             L

  (ii) Residue criterion. Simple poles occur only when ⟨ 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛼𝑗 ⟩ = −1 for some pair, and these are the only
       contributions to the differential.
 (iii) Cocycle dependence. The cocycle 𝜀 appears explicitly in the bar differential via (17.4). Different cocycles
       give non-isomorphic bar complexes.

Proof. (i) The OPE 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼 , 𝑧 ) 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛽 , 𝑤 ) produces vertex operators of lattice degree 𝛼 + 𝛽 . The residue
operation preserves this degree, since Res 𝑧 =𝑤 does not change the total lattice weight 𝛼 + 𝛽 .
    (ii) The OPE (17.3) has a pole of order −⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ at 𝑧 = 𝑤 . Pairing with the logarithmic form 𝜂𝑖𝑗 =
𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) extracts exactly the order-1 residue: Res 𝑧 =𝑤 [( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) − 𝑚 𝑑 log( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )] = 𝛿𝑚,1 . Hence the
differential is nonzero only for a simple pole (order 1, i.e., ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ = −1). For ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ ≥ 0 there is no pole and
the residue vanishes. For ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛽 ⟩ ≤ −2 the pole of order ≥ 2 pairs trivially with 𝑑 log.
17.5. Bar complexes of lattice vertex algebras                                                                  803


   (iii) To show that different cocycles give non-isomorphic bar complexes, note that the differential 𝑑 ( [ 𝑒 𝛼 |
𝑒 𝛽 ] ⊗ 1) = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) [ 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 ] ⊗ 1 in (17.4) carries the sign 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) ∈ {±1} explicitly. A change of cocycle
𝜀 ↦→ 𝜀 ′ with 𝜀 ′ ( 𝛼, 𝛽 )/ 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) = 𝑐 ( 𝛼 ) 𝑐 ( 𝛽 )/𝑐 ( 𝛼 + 𝛽 ) (a coboundary, 𝑐 : Λ → {±1}) corresponds to
rescaling each basis vector 𝑒 𝛼 ↦→ 𝑐 ( 𝛼 ) 𝑒 𝛼 , hence to an isomorphism of bar complexes. However, if 𝜀 ′ and
𝜀 differ by a non-trivial class in 𝐻 2 ( Λ; {±1}), no such coboundary exists: the two bar complexes have
differentials that cannot be related by any diagonal change of basis, so they are non-isomorphic as chain
complexes.

Proposition 17.5.5 ( 𝐷 4 bar complex and triality; [proved]). For the 𝐷4 root lattice, the bar complex

algebra at level 1.

Proof. The 𝐷4 root lattice has 24 roots, all of the form ±𝑒 𝑖 ± 𝑒𝑗 ( 𝑖 ≠ 𝑗 ). These form a single orbit under

of the 𝐷4 Dynkin diagram, permuting the three ‘‘legs’’ and hence permuting the three nontrivial cosets of

spinor vectors lie in 𝐷4∗ \ 𝐷4 , not in the root lattice itself.
    Step 1. Triality action on bar complex. The triality automorphism 𝜎 acts on the lattice as a graph au-
tomorphism of the 𝐷4 Dynkin diagram, permuting the three ‘‘legs.’’ This extends to an automorphism

of 𝑉𝐷4 via 𝜎 ( 𝑒 𝛼 ) = 𝑒 𝜎 ( 𝛼 ) . Since the bar construction is functorial (any algebra automorphism induces a
coalgebra automorphism of the bar complex), 𝜎 acts on B̄(𝑉𝐷4 ).
     Step 2. Action on homology. In bar degree 1, the generators are [ 𝑒 𝛼 ] for each of the 24 roots 𝛼 . The

coboundary).
     Step 3. Conclusion. The 𝑆3 -action on 𝐻∗ ( B̄(𝑉𝐷4 )) is the representation-theoretic manifestation of

17.6      Koszul duality for lattice algebras
Deﬁnition 17.6.1 (Inverse cocycle). For a cocycle 𝜀 : Λ × Λ → ℂ× , the inverse cocycle is 𝜀 −1 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) :=
𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) −1 . The cocycle condition is preserved under inversion, and the commutator satisfies 𝑐 𝜀 −1 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) =
𝑐 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) −1 . In particular, if 𝜀 is symmetric, so is 𝜀 −1 .
Theorem 17.6.2 (Koszul dual of lattice vertex algebra; [proved]). The Koszul dual of the lattice
E1 -chiral algebra 𝑉Λ𝜀 is:
                                     (𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ! = (𝑉Λ𝜀 ) 𝑐 ,
                                                    −1



the coalgebra structure on the lattice vertex algebra with inverse cocycle. More precisely:
   (i) The underlying graded vector space of (𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ! is 𝑉Λ∗ .
  (ii) The coalgebra structure is determined by 𝜀 −1 : the coproduct Δ : 𝑉Λ∗ → 𝑉Λ∗ ⊗ 𝑉Λ∗ has structure
       constants 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) −1 .
 (iii) For symmetric 𝜀 , the Koszul dual is again a (co)lattice vertex algebra with the same symmetry type.

Proof. The Koszul dual is computed via the bar-cobar adjunction. The product 𝜇 : 𝑉Λ ⊗ 𝑉Λ → 𝑉Λ has
structure constants 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) from the group algebra multiplication 𝑒 𝛼 · 𝑒 𝛽 = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 . The Koszul
dual coalgebra is extracted from the bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (𝑉Λ𝜀 ). In the bar construction, each tensor factor
is desuspended by 𝑠 −1 , and the bar differential involves the product 𝜇 composed with Koszul signs from
the desuspension. For the lattice algebra, where 𝜇 ( 𝑒 𝛼 ⊗ 𝑒 𝛽 ) = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 with | 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 )| = ±1, the
desuspension introduces a sign (−1) | 𝛼 | | 𝛽 | that, combined with the bilinearity of 𝜀 , produces the cocycle
inversion: the bar-complex coproduct has structure constants 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) −1 . Since 𝜀 −1 is again a valid cocycle,
     −1
(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) 𝑐 is a valid coalgebra, and the Koszul duality exchanges the two.

Theorem 17.6.3 (Koszul morphism for lattice algebras; [proved]). The canonical twisting mor-
phism 𝜏 : B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) → 𝑉Λ𝜀 is a Koszul morphism: the twisted complex

                                                 B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ⊗𝜏 𝑉Λ𝜀

is acyclic.

Proof. The proof uses the lattice weight filtration.
    Step 1: Filtration setup. Filter the twisted complex by total lattice weight: define 𝐹 𝑝 ( B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ⊗𝜏 𝑉Λ𝜀 ) to
consist of elements whose total lattice weight 𝑖 | 𝛼𝑖 | 2 ≥ 𝑝 (where | 𝛼 | 2 = ⟨ 𝛼, 𝛼 ⟩ for the inner product on
                                                  P
Λ, which is positive-definite by assumption). Since Λ is positive-definite, each total degree 𝑛 contains only
finitely many lattice vectors of bounded weight, so the filtration is bounded below and convergent.
    Step 2: 𝐸1 identiﬁcation. The differential 𝑑0 on the associated graded 𝐸0 is the bar differential for the
Heisenberg subalgebra H𝑑 ⊂ 𝑉Λ𝜀 (the zero-weight sector, generated by the oscillator modes 𝑎𝑛𝑖 , 𝑛 < 0).
This is because the leading-order OPE at weight 𝑝 is between a weight- 𝑝 vertex operator and the unit: the
lattice exponentials are constant on gr and only the Heisenberg structure contributes to 𝑑0 .
806                                                                              Chapter 17. The lattice construction


   Step 3: Acyclicity at 𝐸1 . By the Heisenberg bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism (Theorem 18.6.10, applied to
H𝑑 ), the twisted complex for the Heisenberg algebra is acyclic: 𝐻 ∗ ( B̄(H𝑑 ) ⊗𝜏 H𝑑 ) = 0 in positive degree.
Hence 𝐸1 = 0 for 𝑝 + 𝑞 > 0, and the spectral sequence collapses at 𝐸1 .
           𝑝,𝑞

   Step 4: Cocycle phases. The cocycle 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) ∈ {±1} appears as a sign in the differential of the twisted
complex, but the underlying graded vector spaces depend only on Λ (not on the choice of 𝜀 ). Since the
acyclicity at 𝐸1 is established for all choices of 𝜀 simultaneously (the Heisenberg part 𝑑0 is 𝜀 -independent),
the twisted complex is acyclic for every valid 2-cocycle.
   Step 5: Convergence. Since the filtration is bounded below in each total degree and 𝐸1 = 0 for 𝑝 + 𝑞 > 0,
                                                                                         𝑝,𝑞

the spectral sequence converges to zero in positive total degree, establishing acyclicity of B̄(𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ⊗𝜏 𝑉Λ𝜀 as
required.

Remark 17.6.4 (Self-duality for unimodular lattices). When Λ is unimodular (Λ = Λ∗ ) and the cocycle 𝜀
satisfies 𝜀 −1 ∼ 𝜀 (cohomologous), the Koszul dual (𝑉Λ𝜀 ) ! is isomorphic to 𝑉Λ𝜀 itself (as a coalgebra). This
is the case for 𝐸8 : the lattice vertex algebra 𝑉𝐸8 is Koszul self-dual. (Note: the Heisenberg algebra H𝜅 is
Koszul but not self-dual: H𝜅! ≃ Sym𝑐ℎ (𝑉 ∗ ) by Theorem 18.6.10. Self-duality is a special feature of the 𝐸8
lattice structure.)

17.7        Functorial properties and lattice operations
Each lattice operation from Definition 17.1.5 lifts to a functorial operation on vertex algebras, and these
lifts are compatible with the bar construction.

17.7.1      Direct sum
Theorem 17.7.1 (Tensor product from direct sum; [proved]). For even lattices Λ1 , Λ2 with cocycles
𝜀1 , 𝜀2 :
                                   𝑉Λ𝜀11 ⊕⊗Λ𝜀22  𝑉Λ𝜀11 ⊗ 𝑉Λ𝜀22                             (17.5)
where ( 𝜀1 ⊗ 𝜀2 ) (( 𝛼1 , 𝛼2 ) , ( 𝛽1 , 𝛽2 )) = 𝜀1 ( 𝛼1 , 𝛽1 ) 𝜀2 ( 𝛼2 , 𝛽2 ).

Proof. The state space decomposes as HΛ1 ⊕Λ2 ⊗ ℂ[ Λ1 ⊕ Λ2 ]  (HΛ1 ⊗ ℂ[ Λ1 ]) ⊗ (HΛ2 ⊗ ℂ[ Λ2 ]). The
vertex operator for 𝑒 ( 𝛼1 ,𝛼2 ) factors as 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼1 , 𝑧 ) ⊗ 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛼2 , 𝑧 ) since the oscillators for Λ1 and Λ2 commute
(orthogonality of the direct sum).
17.7. Functorial properties and lattice operations                                                                    807


Corollary 17.7.2 (Künneth for bar complexes [135]; [proved]). Under the isomorphism (17.5):

                                        B̄(𝑉Λ1 ⊗ 𝑉Λ2 ) ≃ B̄(𝑉Λ1 ) ⊗ B̄(𝑉Λ2 ) .

Proof. The bar construction of a tensor product of vertex algebras is quasi-isomorphic to the tensor product
of bar constructions, by the Eilenberg–Zilber/Künneth theorem for the bar construction (cf. Chapter 4).
The lattice grading ensures the relevant spectral sequence converges.

17.7.2     Sublattice embedding
Proposition 17.7.3 (Sublattice maps; [proved]). An embedding of even lattices 𝜄 : Λ′ ↩→ Λ induces:
                                                     ∗
   (i) An embedding of vertex algebras 𝜄∗ : 𝑉Λ𝜄 ′ 𝜀 ↩→ 𝑉Λ𝜀 (restriction of the cocycle).
  (ii) A map of bar complexes B̄( 𝜄∗ ) : B̄(𝑉Λ′ ) → B̄(𝑉Λ ).
 (iii) On homology, the induced map respects the lattice grading: the 𝛾 -sector of 𝐻∗ ( B̄(𝑉Λ′ )) maps to
       the 𝜄 ( 𝛾 )-sector of 𝐻∗ ( B̄(𝑉Λ )).

Proof. (i) The inclusion 𝜄 : Λ′ ↩→ Λ induces an embedding of group algebras ℂ[ Λ′ ] ↩→ ℂ[ Λ] (sending
𝑒 𝛾 ↦→ 𝑒 𝜄 ( 𝛾 ) ) and of Heisenberg algebras HΛ′ ↩→ HΛ (the lattice is a subspace of the target space). The
cocycle on Λ′ is the restriction 𝜄∗ 𝜀 ( 𝛾, 𝛾 ′ ) = 𝜀 ( 𝜄 ( 𝛾 ) , 𝜄 ( 𝛾 ′ )). The vertex algebra structure is preserved
because the state–field correspondence 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝛾 , 𝑧 ) = 𝑉𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) restricts to 𝑌 ( 𝑒 𝜄 ( 𝛾 ) , 𝑧 ), and the OPE singularities
are determined by the inner product which is preserved by 𝜄.
     (ii) The bar construction B̄ is a functor from chiral algebras to chiral coalgebras. The embedding 𝜄∗
is a morphism of chiral algebras, so B̄( 𝜄∗ ) is a well-defined coalgebra map. Concretely, the configuration
space integrals defining the bar differential on B̄(𝑉Λ′ ) are computed using the OPE of 𝑉Λ′ , which is the
restriction of the OPE of 𝑉Λ , so B̄( 𝜄∗ ) commutes with differentials.
     (iii) The lattice grading is defined by total lattice charge 𝛾tot = 𝑖 𝛾𝑖 for a bar element 𝑠 −1 𝑒 𝛾1 ⊗ · · · ⊗
                                                                               P
𝑠 −1 𝑒 𝛾𝑛 . Since 𝜄 maps Λ′ -elements to Λ-elements via a group homomorphism, 𝜄 ( 𝛾tot ) = 𝑖 𝜄 ( 𝛾𝑖 ) = 𝜄 ( 𝛾 )tot ,
                                                                                                        P
so the 𝛾 -sector of B̄(𝑉Λ′ ) maps into the 𝜄 ( 𝛾 )-sector of B̄(𝑉Λ ). The differential preserves lattice charge (the
product 𝑒 𝛼 · 𝑒 𝛽 = 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) 𝑒 𝛼+ 𝛽 preserves total charge), so the grading is compatible on homology.

Remark 17.7.8 (The derivation chain). The four operations –- direct sum, sublattice embedding, overlattice
extension, and orbifold –- generate the following derivation chain that produces every example in Part 2:
                             FKS                  BRST                       orbifold
                 Lattice Λ −−−→ Kac–Moody −−−−→ 𝑊 -algebras −−−−−→ non-simply-laced
17.8. Chiral Hochschild cohomology of lattice algebras                                                             809


More precisely:
 (1) Start with an even positive-definite lattice Λ.
(2) The Frenkel–Kac–Segal theorem (Theorem 17.4.1) gives the level-1 affine algebra 𝐿 (b𝔤, 1).
                                                     √
(3) Higher levels arise from sublattice embeddings 𝑘 Λ ↩→ Λ (rescaling the bilinear form by 𝑘 ).
(4) 𝑊 -algebras arise by quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction (BRST cohomology of the affine algebra
     with respect to a nilpotent subalgebra).
(5) Non-simply-laced algebras arise from orbifolds of simply-laced lattice constructions.
(6) Tensor products of these give further examples (direct sum of lattices).
At each step, the bar complex transforms functorially, so the Koszul duality theory of Part 1 applies through-
out.

Theorem 17.9.2 (Modular invariance; [proved]). For an even unimodular lattice Λ of rank 𝑑 , the
partition function 𝑍 1 (𝑉Λ , 𝜏 ) is 𝑆 -invariant: 𝑍 1 (𝑉Λ , −1/ 𝜏 ) = 𝑍 1 (𝑉Λ , 𝜏 ). Under 𝑇 : 𝜏 ↦→ 𝜏 + 1, the

𝑑 ≡ 0 (mod 24).
Proof. By Poisson summation, ΘΛ (−1/ 𝜏 ) = ( 𝜏 / 𝑖 ) 𝑑/2 | Λ∗ /Λ | 1/2 ΘΛ√︁∗ ( 𝜏 ). For unimodular Λ = Λ∗ , this

𝜂 ( 𝜏 + 1) = 𝑒 𝜋 𝑖 /12 𝜂 ( 𝜏 ), giving 𝑍 1 ( 𝜏 + 1) = 𝑒 − 𝜋 𝑖𝑑/12 𝑍 1 ( 𝜏 ). For 𝑑 ≡ 0 (mod 24) this is exact invariance;
in general, 𝑍 1 transforms as a modular function of the appropriate level.
     For 𝑑 = 8 ( 𝐸8 ): the 𝑇 -phase is 𝑒 −8𝜋 𝑖 /12 = 𝑒 −2𝜋 𝑖 /3 ≠ 1, so 𝑍 1 ( 𝜏 + 1) = 𝑒 −2𝜋 𝑖 /3 𝑍 1 ( 𝜏 ): the partition
function is 𝑆 -invariant but not 𝑇 -invariant. Equivalently, 𝑍 1 = 𝐸4 ( 𝜏 )/ 𝜂 ( 𝜏 ) 8 = 𝑗 ( 𝜏 ) 1/3 transforms under
𝑇 with a cube-root-of-unity multiplier, making it a modular function for the congruence subgroup Γ (3)
but not for the full SL2 (ℤ). Full modular invariance holds only for 𝑑 ≡ 0 (mod 24) (e.g., the Leech lattice
with 𝑑 = 24).

17.9.1   The three theorems for lattice algebras
Remark 17.9.4 (Main theorems for lattice VOAs). The computations of this chapter provide an abelian
verification of the main theorems of Part 1:
  (i) Theorem A (Geometric Bar-Cobar Duality, Theorem 9.1.39; A0 /A1 /A2 decomposition in
                                              ch
       Remark 9.1.11). The bar complex 𝐵 (𝑉Λ𝜀 ) is computed explicitly in §17.5, and the Koszul dual
       is identified as the lattice algebra with inverse cocycle (Theorem 17.6.2). The lattice grading
       decomposes the bar complex into finite-dimensional sectors (Theorem 17.5.2), making the bar-cobar
       adjunction concrete and computable.
  (ii) Theorem B (Bar-Cobar Inversion, Theorem 8.17.4). For unimodular lattices, the self-duality of Theo-
       rem 17.5.7 ensures spectral sequence collapse: the bar complex resolves 𝑉Λ by free Heisenberg modules.
 (iii) Theorem C (Complementarity, Theorem 8.14.12; C0 /C1 decomposition in Remark 8.14.11). The
       central charge of 𝑉Λ equals the rank 𝑑 . By Theorem 2.4.1, 𝑐 (𝑉Λ ) + 𝑐 ((𝑉Λ ) ! ) = 2 𝑑 when both algebras
       exist with distinct cocycles. The genus universality theorem (Theorem 8.13.16) predicts obs 𝑔 = 𝜅 · 𝜆 𝑔 ;
       the lattice Hochschild cohomology (Theorem 17.8.1) identifies the obstruction parameter 𝜅 = 𝑑 /2
       for the Heisenberg sector.
   The lattice construction provides the simplest non-trivial test of the general framework: the abelian
structure makes the bar complex explicitly computable, yet the cocycle twist introduces genuine duality
phenomena absent in the free-field case. The functorial properties (§17.7) show that bar-cobar duality
intertwines lattice-theoretic operations (direct sum, overlattice, orbifold) with algebraic operations on
chiral algebras.

17.11      E1 -chiral algebras from cocycle deformations
The preceding sections compute bar complexes of lattice algebras with symmetric cocycles, obtaining E∞ -
chiral algebras. Theorem 17.3.2 guarantees that any 2-cocycle produces an E1 -chiral algebra; non-symmetric
cocycles produce strictly E1 structures. This section develops the E1 theory systematically: the bar complex
moves from unordered to ordered configurations, the bar cohomology acquires new classes, and the re-
sulting Koszul pairs provide a rich family of E1 -chiral algebras complementing the Yangian construction of
Chapter 24.

Remark 17.11.5 (The deformation parameter space). For a rank- 𝑑 lattice Λ, the space of antisymmetric
bilinear forms Λ × Λ → ℤ/ 𝑁 ℤ is 2 ( Λ∗ / 𝑁 Λ∗ )  (ℤ/ 𝑁 ℤ) ( 2 ) . The number of non-zero forms is
                                       V                              𝑑


𝑁 ( 2 ) − 1. For each such form, the deformed cocycle gives a distinct E1 -chiral algebra (distinct in the sense
    𝑑


that different non-cohomologous deformations give non-isomorphic E1 bar complexes).
    For rank 2: the space of antisymmetric forms is ℤ/ 𝑁 ℤ, with generator 𝑞 ( 𝑒1 , 𝑒2 ) = 1. This gives 𝑁 − 1
distinct deformations for each 𝑁 .
    For rank 𝑑 ≥ 3: the space is multi-dimensional, and the deformations form a ( 𝑑 − 1)-parameter family.

Remark 17.11.11 (Pattern across examples). The three computations exhibit a universal structure:

   (i) In each adjacent-pair sector 𝛾 = 𝛼𝑖 + 𝛼𝑗 , the E1 bar complex 0 → ℂ2 −
                                                                                                      𝑑
                                                                                → ℂ → 0 has dim ker( 𝑑 ) = 1,
       producing exactly one ordering cycle.
  (ii) The ordering cycle coefficient is always 𝜁𝑁−1 , regardless of the specific value of 𝑞 on that edge (only
       the normalization and overall phase depend on 𝑞 ).
 (iii) The number of ordering cycles equals the number of edges in the Dynkin diagram: 1 for 𝐴2 , 3 for
       𝐷4 . These are not the number of positive roots (which is 3 for 𝐴2 , 12 for 𝐷4 ), but rather the number
       of adjacent simple root pairs. At higher bar degrees, the remaining positive roots contribute to the
       bar cohomology through longer chains of collisions.

 (iv) The E∞ bar complex has 𝐻 2 = 0 in every sector considered above: all ordering cycles are strictly E1
      classes that vanish under symmetrization.
  (v) Koszul duality inverts the deformation parameter: 𝑞 → − 𝑞 , with the dual braiding being the trans-
      pose of the original.

17.11.7    The E1 inversion principle
The following principle unifies the Koszul duality for lattice E1 -chiral algebras (Theorem 17.6.2), Yangians
(Theorem 24.2.2), and the abstract E1 theory (Theorem 9.5.4).
Theorem 17.11.15 ( E 1 inversion principle; [proved]). Let A be an E1 -chiral algebra whose non-
commutativity is controlled by a defining datum 𝛿 (an 𝑅-matrix, a 2-cocycle, or a deformation parameter).
Then the Koszul dual A ! is the same algebra with the inverted datum 𝛿 −1 :
                                                    A !,ch  A 𝛿ch−1 .
The three instances proved in this monograph are:

              E1 algebra A                   Datum 𝛿                     Koszul dual A !   Reference
              Lattice 𝑉Λ𝜀                    Cocycle 𝜀               𝑉Λ    𝜀 −1            Thm 17.6.2
              Yangian 𝑌𝑅 (𝔤)                 𝑅-matrix 𝑅 ( 𝑢)         𝑌𝑅 −1 (𝔤)             Thm 24.2.2
                                                                       𝑁 ,− 𝑞
              Quantum lattice 𝑉Λ             Phase 𝜁 𝑞                                     Thm 17.11.13(iv)
                                𝑁 ,𝑞

In each case, the inversion arises from the self-duality of the chiral associative operad: Assch  Assch ⊗ sgn
(Proposition 2.8.5). The sign twist sgn is realized geometrically as the orientation reversal on ordered
configuration spaces, which inverts the defining non-commutativity datum.

Proof. The abstract statement follows from the E1 -chiral Koszul duality (Theorem 9.5.4) and the self-duality
                                                                                           !
of Assch : the bar construction on an E1 -chiral algebra A produces a coalgebra over Assch  Assch ⊗ sgn,
which is again an associative coalgebra but with the sign-twisted structure. This sign twist is realized in
each instance as:
• For lattice algebras: the bar differential carries the cocycle value 𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ), and the sign twist inverts it to
  𝜀 ( 𝛼, 𝛽 ) −1 .
• For Yangians: the bar differential encodes the RTT relation via the 𝑅-matrix, and the sign twist inverts
  𝑅 ( 𝑢) → 𝑅 −1 ( 𝑢), equivalently ℏ → −ℏ for the Yang 𝑅-matrix.
• For quantum lattice algebras: the deformation datum 𝜁 𝑞 ( 𝛼,𝛽 ) is inverted to 𝜁 − 𝑞 ( 𝛼,𝛽 ) .
                                                                                                                        ord
In each case, the geometric mechanism is that the Verdier involution on ordered configurations 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
reverses the ordering, which transposes the defining relation and hence inverts the non-commutativity
data.

Remark 17.11.16 (Relation to Feigin–Frenkel duality). The E1 inversion principle is the ordered-
configuration analog of the Feigin–Frenkel level shift 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ for E∞ -chiral algebras. In the E∞
theory, Verdier duality on unordered configurations inverts the level; in the E1 theory, Verdier duality on
ordered configurations inverts the defining datum. Both are instances of the same geometric mechanism
(the Verdier involution on FM compactifications), applied in different operadic contexts.
   The parallel extends to the classical limit: the Feigin–Frenkel shift has a classical limit 𝑘 → ∞ in which
the duality becomes trivial; the E1 inversion has a classical limit ℏ → 0 (for Yangians) or 𝑁 → ∞ (for
quantum lattice algebras) in which the datum becomes the identity and the duality becomes the E∞ Koszul
duality of Sym ↔ (Corollary 24.2.3).

Remark 17.11.21 (Quantum group identiﬁcation programme). The screening algebra of Construction 17.11.19
is the primary tool for establishing Conjecture 17.11.18(ii). Three complementary routes are available.
826                                                                 Chapter 17. The lattice construction


Route A: Screening algebra via Nichols algebras. The nilpotency 𝑄 𝑖2 = 0 (part (ii) above) and the
off-diagonal braiding (17.11) determine the screening algebra as a quotient of the Nichols algebra B (𝑉 )
of the Yetter–Drinfeld module 𝑉 = 𝑟𝑖=1 ℂ 𝑥 𝑖 with braiding matrix 𝑞𝑖𝑗 = 𝑐 𝜀 𝑁 ,𝑞 ( 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛼𝑗 ) [256]. The trivial
                                        L
self-braiding ( 𝑞𝑖𝑖 = 1) places the screening algebra in the ‘‘super-type’’ regime where nilpotency is order 2
                                                         2 𝑞 ( 𝛼𝑖 ,𝛼𝑗 )
on each generator; the off-diagonal entries 𝑞𝑖𝑗 = − 𝜁𝑁        carry the deformation data. The quantum
group identification requires matching the resulting Nichols algebra with 𝑢 𝜁 (𝔤) + .
Route B: Module category comparison. The vertex tensor category structure on 𝑉Λ𝔤 -modules [167]
                                                                                            𝑁 ,𝑞

carries a braiding whose monodromy involves the deformed commutator 𝑐 𝜀 𝑁 ,𝑞 (Proposition 17.11.4(ii)).
For braided fusion categories, the monoidal structure is determined by the 𝑆 -matrix and twist data [74].
Matching the 𝑆 -matrix of 𝑉Λ𝔤 -mod with that of Rep( 𝑢 𝜁 (𝔤)) establishes the braided equivalence by
                             𝑁 ,𝑞

rigidity.
Route C: Zhu algebra. Zhu’s theorem provides a bijection between simple modules of a vertex algebra
and simple modules of its Zhu algebra. An explicit computation of 𝐴 (𝑉Λ𝔤 ) and comparison with the
                                                                       𝑁 ,𝑞

center of 𝑢 𝜁 (𝔤) controls the module categories on both sides.
  Route A provides the functor (embedding of the quantum group into the endomorphism algebra),
while Route B provides the equivalence criterion. A complete verification requires the vertex tensor category
machinery of [167] extended to the strictly E1 setting –- an active area connected to [256, 257].
Remark 17.11.22 (Screening nilpotency as logarithm of quantum group periodicity). The nilpotency 𝑄 𝑖2 = 0
(Proposition 17.11.20(ii)) is the logarithmic (nilpotent, infinitesimal) datum of the lattice programme, while
the 𝑁 -periodic representation theory of the quantum group 𝑢 𝜁 (𝔤) at 𝜁 = 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖 / 𝑁 is the exponential
(periodic, global) datum. The nilpotence-periodicity correspondence (Remark 6.0.1) predicts that the
module category equivalence of Conjecture 17.11.18(ii) should be provable by matching the logarithmic
data: the screening algebra (generated by nilpotent elements 𝑄 𝑖2 = 0 with braiding 𝑐 𝜀 𝑁 ,𝑞 ( 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛼𝑗 )) encodes
the same information as the nilpotent part 𝑢 𝜁 (𝔤) + of the small quantum group. Exponentiating both
sides via the categorical exp/log correspondence would promote the nilpotent matching to a module
category equivalence–-just as, in Lie theory, an isomorphism of nilpotent Lie algebras exponentiates to an
isomorphism of the corresponding unipotent groups.
   This provides a fourth route to the quantum group identification, complementing Routes A–C
of Remark 17.11.21: match the logarithmic (screening) data, then exponentiate to obtain the periodic
(representation-theoretic) equivalence. The advantage is that the nilpotent data (braiding matrix 𝑞𝑖𝑗 and
nilpotency orders) are computable, while the periodic data (full fusion category structure) are harder to
access directly. The inversion principle 𝑞 ↦→ − 𝑞 under Koszul duality (Theorem 17.11.15) is the statement
that the logarithm changes sign under duality: log(A ! ) = − log(A), which exponentiates to 𝜁 ↦→ 𝜁 −1 .
Remark 17.11.23 (The two E1 construction methods). This monograph constructs E1 -chiral algebras by two
complementary methods:
(a) Lattice cocycle deformation (this section): start with an E∞ -chiral lattice VOA and deform the cocycle
    to break symmetry. This is a ‘‘top-down’’ method: the state space is fixed, and the OPE acquires phases.
    The deformation is controlled by a finite parameter ( 𝑁 , 𝑞 ).
(b) RTT/R-matrix presentation (Chapter 24): start with the RTT relations and build the E1 -chiral algebra
    from generators and relations. This is a ‘‘bottom-up’’ method: the algebra is presented by generators
    with an 𝑅-matrix-valued OPE.
17.12. Factorization bar-cobar for lattice algebras                                                                              827


The two methods are unified by the E1 inversion principle (Theorem 17.11.15): in both cases, Koszul duality
inverts the non-commutativity datum.
     The bridge between the two constructions is the Frenkel–Kac–Segal theorem: method (a) produces
E1 -chiral algebras from lattices (the ‘‘abelian’’ source), while method (b) produces them from quantum
groups (the ‘‘non-abelian’’ source). At level 1 with symmetric cocycle, FKS identifies the two; the deformed
FKS construction (Remark 17.11.17) extends this identification to the E1 world, connecting lattice cocycle
phases to quantum group deformation parameters.

17.12       Factorization bar-cobar for lattice algebras
The general bar-cobar equivalence (Theorem 9.1.39) is stated for any chiral Koszul pair. For lattice vertex
algebras, the lattice grading provides a decomposition that makes the factorization structure explicitly
828                                                                Chapter 17. The lattice construction


computable. The goal of this section is to establish a factorization-level bar-cobar equivalence for lattice
VOAs that bypasses the thick-generation arguments required in the Yangian setting (Chapter 24, §24.9).

Remark 17.12.2 (Sectorwise ﬁniteness: the key structural advantage). Property (iii) is the critical feature
that distinguishes the lattice setting from the general Yangian setting. For Yangians, the bar complex has
infinitely many generators in each internal degree (the RTT generators 𝑇𝑖𝑗( 𝑟 ) for all levels 𝑟 ≥ 0), and
establishing factorization-level results requires thick-generation arguments (DK-2, Proposition 24.8.8). For
lattice algebras, sectorwise finiteness means that the twisted tensor products 𝐾𝜏𝐿 and 𝐾𝜏𝑅 are direct sums
of finite-dimensional complexes, one per lattice sector. Acyclicity of each sector can be checked directly.

Remark 17.12.4 (Why thick generation is unnecessary). The proof of Theorem 17.12.3 does not use any
thick-generation argument. Compare with the Yangian DK ladder (Chapter 24):
• DK-2 (Proposition 24.8.8) requires showing that evaluation modules thickly generate the finite-
  dimensional representation category. For lattice algebras, the lattice sectors replace thick generation: the
  direct sum decomposition (17.12) is exact, not a thick-closure approximation.
• DK-3 (Proposition 24.9.9) requires lifting the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence to factorization categories.
  For lattice algebras, both sides of the Koszul duality live in the same lattice-VOA family (cocycle 𝜀 vs.
  𝜀 −1 ), so no external bridge is needed.
The lattice setting thus provides the first unconditional (Tier T1) factorization bar-cobar equivalence in the
monograph.

Remark 17.12.6 (The factorization DK programme from lattices). Corollary 17.12.5 is unconditional: it
does not depend on thick generation, the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalence, or the Latyntsev factorization
quantum group construction. It is an intrinsic statement about the lattice vertex algebra, proved entirely
within the bar-cobar framework of Part I.
   The relationship to the Yangian DK programme (MC3, Conjecture 34.9.3) is as follows:
(a) At level 1 with symmetric cocycle, the lattice factorization DK reduces to the self-duality of unimodular
    lattice VOAs (Theorem 17.5.7), which is proved.
(b) At level 1 with non-symmetric cocycle, the E1 lattice factorization DK gives a proved instance of the E1
    inversion principle (Theorem 17.11.15) at the factorization level.
                                                           √
(c) For general level 𝑘 : by the sublattice embedding 𝑘Λ ↩→ Λ (Proposition 17.7.3), the level-𝑘 KM
    algebra embeds into the level-1 lattice VOA. Whether the factorization bar-cobar equivalence for the
    sublattice implies the equivalence for the full level-𝑘 theory is a tractable extension of the present
    methods.
(d) For the full MC3 conjecture: identifying the module category of 𝑉Λ𝔤 with quantum group repre-
                                                                            𝑁 ,𝑞

     sentations at 𝜁 = 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖 / 𝑁 would upgrade the lattice factorization DK to the full Kazhdan–Lusztig
     factorization equivalence. This identification is Conjecture 17.11.18, currently conjectural.
    Thus the lattice chapter should be read as proving DK-1 21 and its level/ 𝑞 variants by an independent
factorization route, not as closing the full MC3 enlargement beyond the theorematic evaluation-generated
core. The exact remaining MC3 input here is the quantum-group identification above. Only after that

standard infinite towers.

17.13     Homotopy-level factorization DK via E1 lattices
The factorization bar-cobar equivalence of Theorem 17.12.3 is an M-level statement: a quasi-isomorphism
of factorization dg-algebras on Ran( 𝑋 ). This section lifts the equivalence to H-level, constructing an
equivalence of E1 -factorization ∞-categories for lattice vertex algebras. The sectorwise finiteness of Propo-
sition 17.12.1(iii) is the mechanism that makes the lift possible without the thick-generation arguments
needed in the Yangian setting (DK-2/3 of Remark 24.9.11).

and a finite filtration maps to a finite filtration. On each filtration piece (a finite-dimensional dg vector
space), the quasi-isomorphism is a quasi-isomorphism of chain complexes, hence an equivalence in the dg
nerve.
    Therefore the induced functor on compact objects is an equivalence, and by Schwede–Shipley the full
functor is an equivalence of stable ∞-categories.

Remark 17.13.11 (Summary: the lattice DK programme). The results of §17.12–17.13 establish:
 (1) Unconditional factorization bar-cobar for all even positive-definite lattices, symmetric or not
     (Theorem 17.12.3).
(2) Homotopy-level E1 -factorization category equivalence for all lattice VOAs (Theorem 17.13.3).
(3) Level-𝑘 extension via sublattice embeddings (Proposition 17.13.5, Theorem 17.13.6).
(4) Full quantum lattice factorization DK (Theorem 17.13.7).
(5) Bridge to Yangian DK at level 1 (Proposition 17.13.8).
(6) Conditional full MC3 via quantum group identification (Conjecture 17.13.9).
The lattice route is the most complete factorization DK programme in this monograph: steps (1)–(5)
are unconditional (proved here), and the only remaining hypothesis for the full MC3 is (6), which is a
representation-theoretic statement independent of the bar-cobar/factorization framework.
   Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type II (equivalence). Steps (1)–(5) are M-level proved, H-level
proved. Step (6) is M-level conditional, H-level conditional.

18.1      Free fermion
The free fermion replaces the Heisenberg double pole with a fermionic simple pole; the bar complex
collapses.

fermionic field 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) of conformal weight ℎ = 21 with OPE:

forces many components of the bar complex to vanish.

Remark 18.1.4 (Vanishing mechanism). The vanishing in degree ≥ 2 reflects the antisymmetry of the
Clifford algebra: one cannot have multiple fermions at the same point, which translates to the impossibility
of non-trivial higher bar complex elements respecting antisymmetry.

Theorem 18.2.3 ( 𝛽 𝛾 bar complex rank; [proved]). For all 𝑛 ≥ 1, rank( 𝐵¯ geom
                                                                           𝑛   ( 𝛽𝛾 )) = 2 · 3𝑛−1 , where

position (the residue along each collision divisor 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 in the NBC spanning tree).
    Independence. The type sectors carry distinct quantum numbers under the bigrading by generator parity
and leading conformal weight: 𝛽 -type has parity 𝛽 and leading weight ℎ 𝛽 = 1; 𝛾 -type has parity 𝛾 and
leading weight ℎ 𝛾 = 0; 𝜕 -type has parity 𝛾 and leading weight ℎ 𝛾 + 1 = 1 ≠ 0. Since the 𝛽 - and 𝛾 -parities
are orthogonal, and 𝜕 -type is distinguished from 𝛾 -type by weight, the sectors are linearly independent.
    Exhaustion. Every element of 𝐵¯ geom   𝑛    belongs to a unique type sector, since the PBW basis of the 𝛽𝛾
vertex algebra provides a weight-graded decomposition of ( 𝑠 −1 𝐴¯) ⊗ 𝑛 , and each PBW basis element tensored
with an NBC form belongs to a unique type assignment via its parity and weight at each position.
    Count. | 𝑡1 | = 2 and | 𝑡𝑖 | = 3 for 𝑖 > 1 gives rank( 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ) = 2 · 3𝑛−1 .

18.2.3    Verifying orthogonality
Proposition 18.2.5 ( 𝑏 𝑐 – 𝛽 𝛾 orthogonality; [proved]). The relations 𝑅𝑏𝑐 ⊥ 𝑅 𝛽𝛾 under the residue
pairing: the Clifford relation of the 𝑏𝑐 system is orthogonal to the Weyl relation of the 𝛽𝛾 system.

Proof. The generators pair via the residue pairing ⟨𝑏, 𝛽 ⟩ = 1, ⟨𝑐, 𝛾 ⟩ = 1, ⟨𝑏, 𝛾 ⟩ = 0, ⟨𝑐, 𝛽 ⟩ = 0 (dual bases).
   The quadratic relations are 𝑅𝑏𝑐 = 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑏 (Clifford/symmetric) and 𝑅 𝛽𝛾 = 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛾 − 𝛾 ⊗ 𝛽
(Weyl/antisymmetric).
   Computing:

                            ⟨ 𝑅𝑏𝑐 , 𝑅 𝛽𝛾 ⟩ = ⟨𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑏, 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛾 − 𝛾 ⊗ 𝛽 ⟩
                                         = ⟨𝑏, 𝛽 ⟩⟨𝑐, 𝛾 ⟩ − ⟨𝑏, 𝛾 ⟩⟨𝑐, 𝛽 ⟩
                                            + ⟨𝑐, 𝛽 ⟩⟨𝑏, 𝛾 ⟩ − ⟨𝑐, 𝛾 ⟩⟨𝑏, 𝛽 ⟩
                                         = (1) (1) − (0) (0) + (0) (0) − (1) (1) = 0.

     The cancellation is exact: the symmetric relation (+) and antisymmetric relation (−) are orthogonal
complements under the residue pairing. This is the quadratic data underlying the Koszul duality ( 𝛽𝛾 ) ! 
𝑏𝑐 .

18.2.4  Cohomology and duality
Theorem 18.2.6 ( 𝛽 𝛾 – 𝑏 𝑐 Koszul duality; [proved]). The 𝛽𝛾 system (two bosonic generators with
antisymmetric relation) and the 𝑏𝑐 ghost system (two fermionic generators with symmetric relation) are
Koszul dual:
                                         ( 𝛽𝛾 ) !  𝑏𝑐    and    ( 𝑏𝑐 ) !  𝛽𝛾 .
At the level of bar complexes:

                     𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝑏𝑐 ))  Symch ( 𝛽, 𝛾 ) ,   𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ geom ( 𝛽𝛾 ))  Λch ( 𝑏, 𝑐 ) .

Remark 18.2.7. This is a two-generator duality: 𝛽𝛾 has dim 𝑉 = 2 (bosonic) and 𝑏𝑐 has dim 𝑉 ∗ = 2
(fermionic). It should not be confused with the single-generator duality Λch ( 𝜓 ) ↔ Symch ( 𝛾 ) between
one free fermion and one free boson.

Proof. The key computation uses the Gui–Li–Zeng quadratic duality framework. The quadratic datum
for 𝛽𝛾 has generators 𝑁 = ℂ 𝛽 ⊕ ℂ 𝛾 (dim 𝑁 = 2, bosonic) and relation 𝑃 = span{ 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛾 − 𝛾 ⊗ 𝛽 } ⊂
Λ2 ( 𝑁 ) (antisymmetric).
   The dual datum ( 𝑠 −1 𝑁 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑃 ⊥ ) is computed via the residue pairing:

                                           ⟨ 𝑃 ⊗ 𝜔 𝑋 2 , 𝑃 ⊥ ⊗ 𝑠2 𝜔 𝑋 2 ⟩ = 0

   Under this pairing, the antisymmetric relation dualizes to:

                                    𝑃 ⊥ = span{𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑏 } ⊂ Sym2 ( 𝑁 ∗ )

which is the anticommutation relation for the 𝑏𝑐 ghost system (two fermionic generators 𝑏 = 𝛽 ∗ , 𝑐 = 𝛾 ∗ ).
   Therefore A ( 𝑠 −1 𝑁 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑃 ⊥ ) = 𝑏𝑐 , establishing ( 𝛽𝛾 ) ! = 𝑏𝑐 .
   The geometric manifestation is that Verdier duality on configuration spaces exchanges symplectic pair-
ings with Clifford pairings. Here ‘‘symplectic’’ means antisymmetric ( 𝛽𝛾 − 𝛾 𝛽 = 1), while ‘‘Clifford’’
means anticommuting (𝑏𝑐 + 𝑐𝑏 = 1). See Section 19.3.3 for the full NAP perspective.

Remark 18.2.8 (The twisting morphism for free-ﬁeld dualities). The Koszul duality ( 𝛽𝛾 ) !  𝑏𝑐 is mediated
by the universal twisting morphism 𝜏 : 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) → 𝛽𝛾 , which takes a concrete form for free fields.
    For the 𝛽𝛾 system, 𝜏 acts on a single-insertion bar element by returning the corresponding current:
𝜏 ([ 𝛽 ∗ ]) = 𝛽 , 𝜏 ( [ 𝛾 ∗ ]) = 𝛾 . The Maurer–Cartan equation 𝑑𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 encodes the free-field OPE:
the convolution ( 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 ) ( [ 𝛽 ∗ ⊗ 𝛾 ∗ ⊗ 𝜂12 ]) = Res 𝑧1 =𝑧2 [ 𝛽 ( 𝑧1 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑧2 ) 𝜂12 ] = 1 recovers the contraction
𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 (𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ), and the MC equation states that this is the only obstruction to exactness of the
bar complex.
    Dually, the twisting morphism for the 𝑏𝑐 system 𝜏𝑏𝑐 : 𝐵¯ ( 𝑏𝑐 ) → 𝑏𝑐 satisfies the same MC equation
with the Clifford OPE 𝑏 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑐 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ). Verdier duality on 𝐶 2 ( 𝑋 ) exchanges the two: the propa-
gator 𝜂12 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) is Verdier self-dual, so 𝔻Ran ( 𝜏𝛽𝛾 ) = 𝜏𝑏𝑐 (Theorem 9.1.39, Theorem A2 ). The
Koszul duality ( 𝛽𝛾 ) !  𝑏𝑐 is the statement that Verdier duality intertwines the two twisting morphisms.
Acyclicity of the twisted tensor product 𝐾 ( 𝜏 ) = 𝛽𝛾 ⊗𝜏 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) follows from the quadratic Koszulness of
the antisymmetric relation 𝛽𝛾 − 𝛾 𝛽 = 1, confirming the Koszul property via the fundamental theorem
(Theorem 9.1.8).

Example 18.3.6 (Physical interpretation). In string theory, this extended system describes:
• 𝜓 (0) : Matter fermions
• 𝜓 (1) : Faddeev–Popov ghosts for local supersymmetry
• 𝜓 (−1) : Ghosts for ghosts in higher string field theory
The derived Koszul duality becomes the field-antifield correspondence in the BV formalism.
Remark 18.3.7 (Scope). A complete proof requires assembling the jet bundle structure, stratified residue
pairing, and cobar reconstruction into a single functorial argument. This is a derived/super extension
problem, not one of the standard MC4 finite-packet lanes; no analogue of I𝑁 or Δ 𝑎,0 ( 𝑁 ) is yet identified
here.

Remark 18.6.7 (Physical meaning of curvature). The curvature 𝑚0 = 𝑘 · 𝑐 is the homological manifestation
of the Heisenberg algebra’s central extension. The level 𝑘 appears as the coefficient of the curvature: central
charges correspond to curvatures in homological algebra, and quantum anomalies manifest as obstructions
to strict associativity.
Remark 18.6.8. (Energy-Momentum Tensor). The curvature 𝑚0 = 𝑘 · 𝑐 arises geometrically from the
Heisenberg energy-momentum tensor: 𝑇 = 21𝑘 : 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) : The normal ordering prescription creates
the central term through point-splitting regularization, which geometrically corresponds to approaching
the diagonal in 𝐶2 ( 𝑋 ) along a specific direction determined by the complex structure.

Remark 18.6.11 (Level-shifting vs Koszul duality). Two distinct phenomena must be distinguished. Koszul

shifting: Rep(H𝑘 ) ≃ Rep(H− 𝑘 ) (an equivalence of representation categories). The former is algebraic;
the latter is representation-theoretic.

18.6.6     Twisted modules: Ramond and Neveu–Schwarz sectors
The free fermion and Heisenberg algebras possess twisted modules arising from automorphisms of the
chiral algebra. Module Koszul duality interacts non-trivially with these twisted sectors.
Deﬁnition 18.6.22 (Ramond and Neveu–Schwarz sectors). Let F be the free fermion chiral algebra with
generator 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) and automorphism 𝜎 : 𝜓 ↦→ −𝜓 (the fermion parity involution).

Proposition 18.6.23 (Twisted module Koszul duality for fermions; [proved]). Under the fermion–
boson Koszul duality F ! ≃ Symch ( 𝛾 ):
   (i) The NS sector of F corresponds to the vacuum module of Symch ( 𝛾 ).
  (ii) The Ramond sector of F corresponds to the 𝜎 ! -twisted module of Symch ( 𝛾 ), where 𝜎 ! : 𝛾 ↦→ − 𝛾
       is the dual involution.
 (iii) The spectral flow 𝑈1/2 on F dualizes to a shift functor 𝛾𝑛 ↦→ 𝛾𝑛+1/2 on Symch ( 𝛾 )-modules.

Proof. The automorphism 𝜎 : 𝜓 ↦→ −𝜓 induces an automorphism 𝜎 ! of the Koszul dual via the bar-
cobar functor. Since the bar construction is functorial for algebra automorphisms (Theorem 9.1.39), and
since 𝜎 acts on the generator space 𝑉 = Span{ 𝜓 } by −1, the induced automorphism 𝜎 ! = 𝐵¯ ( 𝜎 ) ∨ acts
on 𝑉 ∗ = Span{ 𝛾 } by −1 as well (the Koszul pairing ⟨𝜓 , 𝛾 ⟩ = 1 is preserved under the simultaneous sign
change).
   For (i): the NS sector is the vacuum module of F , and module Koszul duality (Theorem 9.6.2) sends
the vacuum module to the vacuum module.

    For (ii): a 𝜎 -twisted module 𝑀 of F is, by definition, a module where the monodromy around the

flat connection on 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) \ 𝐷 ; the twist by 𝜎 on the algebra side becomes a twist by 𝜎 ! on the dual side.
    For (iii): spectral flow shifts the mode index by 1/2. Since the Koszul pairing identifies 𝜓𝑟 with 𝛾𝑟 (at
the level of generator modes), the shift 𝜓𝑟 ↦→ 𝜓𝑟 +1/2 induces 𝛾𝑟 ↦→ 𝛾𝑟 +1/2 .

Remark 18.12.2 (Scope: conjectural table entries). A same-family central-charge reflection does not compute
bar or semi-infinite cohomology. For the actual critical Virasoro vacuum charge, Corollary 30.5.3 gives abso-

states. Any other proposed semi-infinite growth formula requires its own differential and a cohomology
calculation.
Remark 18.12.3 (Heisenberg vs Yangian: self-duality contrast). The Heisenberg algebra is not self-dual:
H ! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) ≇ H , since the central extension and non-commutative oscillator modes dualize to the
commutative chiral algebra on the dual space (Lie ↔ Com duality, not to be confused with the boson-
fermion correspondence). By contrast, the Yangian satisfies 𝑌 (𝔤) !  𝑌𝑅 −1 (𝔤) (Theorem 24.2.2): the RTT
presentation is quadratic in the E1 -chiral sense, the dual relations use the inverse R-matrix 𝑅 −1 ( 𝑢), and at
the classical level (ℏ = 0) this reduces to exact self-duality (Corollary 24.2.3), visible in 3d mirror symmetry
(Higgs ↔ Coulomb).
   The Heisenberg OPE 𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛼 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2 has a double pole that produces symmetric (bosonic)
coproduct structure in the bar construction. By contrast, the Yangian’s RTT relations have built-in 𝑅-
matrix self-duality that preserves the structure under bar-cobar.

This is the standard Feynman rule interpretation: graphs are Feynman diagrams, edges are propagators
( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ), vertices carry fields (W𝑣 ), and the differential implements Wick contraction.

18.21      Comparison of free-field examples
Geometric complexity correlates inversely with algebraic simplicity: the free fermion (one generator) van-
ishes above degree 1; the 𝛽𝛾 system grows as 2 · 3𝑛−1 ; the Heisenberg gains a central charge class; the Virasoro
connects to M 0,𝑛 ; W-algebras link to flag varieties.
Remark 18.21.1 (Main theorems for free ﬁelds). Free fields verify all three main theorems in the abelian
case. Theorem A: fermion! = Symch ( 𝛾 ), ( 𝑏𝑐 ) ! = 𝛽𝛾 , H𝑘! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) with 𝑚0 = −𝑘 𝜔; dualities are
exact ( 𝑐 + 𝑐 ′ = 0). Theorem B: genus-0 inversion via Theorem 6.12.1; genus-1 inputs from Theorems 18.11.1
and 18.22.6. Theorem C: obs 𝑔 (H𝑘 ) = 𝑘 · 𝜆 𝑔 with 𝜅 (H𝑘 ) + 𝜅 (H𝑘! ) = 0.

18.22.1    Failure of self-duality
Theorem 18.22.1 (Heisenberg is not self-dual; [proved]). For any level 𝑘 ≠ 0, the Heisenberg algebra
H𝑘 is not Koszul self-dual. Instead:

                                     Koszul(H𝑘 ) = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) ≠ H𝑘

   The algebras have different structure:

                                Heisenberg H𝑘          Symmetric Symch (𝑉 ∗ )
                               Non-commutative              Commutative
                                [ 𝛼, 𝛼 ] = 𝑘 ≠ 0       𝛼 · 𝛼 = 𝛼 2 (commutes)
                               Central extension        No central extension
                               Double pole OPE              Regular OPE
                                 Nontrivial 𝜋1                Trivial 𝜋1

Proof. By Theorem 18.6.2, the bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 ) has cocommutative coproduct: the Heisenberg OPE
𝛼 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛼 (𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑘 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2 produces only the double-pole term, whose residue gives a symmetric (primitive)
coproduct Δ ( 𝛼 ) = 𝛼 ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ 𝛼 . Cocommutative coalgebras are Koszul dual to commutative algebras
(coLie! = Com, see [83], Theorem 7.6.5), so H𝑘! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ). This is commutative with regular OPE,
while H𝑘 is non-commutative with singular OPE, so H𝑘 ≇ H𝑘! .

18.22.2    Three different “dualities” for Heisenberg
Three separate mathematical structures govern Heisenberg, and confusing them is a reliable source of error.
  (i) Koszul duality (algebra → dual coalgebra → dual algebra).
                                             ¯                 ∨
                                      H𝑘 −−→ 𝐵¯ ch (H𝑘 ) −−−−−→ Symch (𝑉 ∗ )
                                           𝐵               (−)



       The first arrow is the bar construction: extraction of OPE residues along collision divisors in 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
       produces the Koszul dual coalgebra coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ), a conilpotent factorization coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ).
       The second arrow is Verdier/linear duality, producing the Koszul dual algebra Symch (𝑉 ∗ ). The
       cobar construction is not involved: Ω ( 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 )) ≃ H𝑘 recovers the original algebra, not its dual
       (Theorem 6.12.1).
       The distinction is mediated by the convolution Lie algebra Hom( 𝐵¯ (H𝑘 ) , H𝑘 ): the canonical twist-
       ing morphism 𝜏 : coLiech (𝑉 ∗ ) → H𝑘 , 𝑣 ∗ ↦→ 𝐽𝑣 , is its Maurer–Cartan element. The convolution
       product 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 because the cogenerator 𝑣 ∗ is primitive (Δ̄ ( 𝑣 ∗ ) = 0), so the MC equation
       𝜕 𝜏 + 𝜏 ★ 𝜏 = 0 holds on generators for degree reasons (cf. Remark 1.5.2).
       Level behavior: 𝑘 appears as curvature 𝑚0 ∝ 𝑘 ; it does not change the duality type.
       Structure exchanged: Lie (non-commutative) ↔ Com (commutative).
  (ii) Level-shifting/rank-level duality (representation categories).

                                                 Rep(H𝑘 ) ≃ Rep(H− 𝑘 )

      Level behavior: 𝑘 ↔ −𝑘 (for Heisenberg, ℎ∨ = 0).
      Structure exchanged: Representation categories (not algebras themselves).
874                                                                       Chapter 18. Free field atoms


 (iii) Boson-fermion correspondence (categorical equivalence).

                                             Rep(H𝑘 ) ≃ Rep(F ⊗2 )

      where F is the free fermion algebra.
      Level behavior: Relates Heisenberg to fermions, not to itself.
      Structure exchanged: Module categories have equivalent structure.
    Only (1) is the subject of this manuscript. The three dualities act on different mathematical categories:
(1) on algebras and coalgebras (via the bar-cobar adjunction on Ran( 𝑋 )), (2) on representation categories
(via autoequivalences), (3) on module categories (via bosonization). The bar construction is the engine
of (1); it has no direct role in (2) or (3).

18.22.4    BV quantization and the bar complex for free fields
Proposition 18.22.3 (Bar complex as BV complex; [proved]). Let A be a free field chiral alge-
bra (Heisenberg, free fermion, 𝛽𝛾 , or 𝑏𝑐 ghost system). Then the reduced bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A) is quasi-
isomorphic, as a curved differential graded coalgebra, to the chain-level BV complex of the corresponding
free bosonic or fermionic field theory on a Riemann surface 𝑋 .

Proof. By the Prism Principle (Theorem 9.1.39), the genus-0 bar complex is computed by configuration
space integrals on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) with the Fulton–MacPherson propagator. For free fields, the only nonvanishing
OPE poles are of order ≤ 2 (double poles for Heisenberg; simple poles for 𝛽𝛾 , fermions, and 𝑏𝑐 ghosts),
so the bar differential decomposes as 𝑑 = 𝑑bracket + 𝑑curvature (Proposition 6.2.30). Since the OPE data are
quadratic (no cubic or higher terms), the resulting configuration space integrals are exactly those of Wick’s
theorem for Gaussian path integrals, which compute the BV complex.

Remark 18.22.4 (Curvature and one-loop determinants). The bar curvature 𝑚0 is the one-loop determi-

nant: 𝑚0 = 𝑘 /2 for H𝑘 , 𝑚0 = −13 for 𝑏𝑐 . Anomaly cancellation (Theorem 34.10.8): 𝐵 (H 26 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 ) is
uncurved (26 · 21 − 13 = 0), yielding the BV quantization of the bosonic string. The formula 𝑚0 = 𝜅 /2
(Proposition 6.2.30) matches the QME coefficient.

Remark 18.22.8 (Physical interpretation: quantum complementarity). At genus 1, Koszul duality is electro-
magnetic duality on 𝑇 2 : A-cycle winding (position) exchanges with B-cycle winding (momentum), and
the S-transformation Ω → −1/Ω acts as Fourier transform on Jac(𝑇 2 ). The level shift 𝑘 → −𝑘 is the
quantum manifestation of this classical symplectic duality.

18.22.7     From Fourier duality to chiral Koszul duality
Remark 18.22.9 identified the chiral bar construction as a nonlinear generalization of the classical Fourier
transform. We now develop this identification in three stages of increasing nonlinearity: the classical abelian
transform, its higher-dimensional extension to Jacobians of curves, and the genuinely non-abelian general-
ization to configuration space integrals with non-factorizing kernel. The passage between stages is governed
by a single datum: the order of the OPE pole.
18.22.7.1 Stage I: pairwise factorization and the abelian kernel

       (𝔰𝔩 2 ⊗ 𝔰𝔩 2 )𝔰𝔩 2 . These five elements are bar cocycles–-the ‘‘harmonic modes’’ that survive the non-
       abelian Fourier transform.
  (ii) Abelian limit ( 𝑘 = 0): rank( 𝑑bar ) = 3 (row 1 vanishes). The kernel gains one dimension: the Casimir
       class 𝜅 = 𝐽 𝐻 ⊗ 𝐽 𝐻 /2 + 𝐽 𝐸 ⊗ 𝐽 𝐹 + 𝐽 𝐹 ⊗ 𝐽 𝐸 becomes a cocycle, since its image under 𝑑 is 3𝑘 · 1 = 0.
       This extra mode is the zero-frequency Fourier coefficient of the Killing form.
The Heisenberg algebra at the same degree has a 1 × 1 matrix ( 𝑘 ), with 0-dimensional kernel for 𝑘 ≠ 0. The
passage from a 1 × 1 scalar to the 4 × 9 matrix (27.6) is the passage from abelian Fourier (one frequency,
one coefficient) to non-abelian Fourier (dim(𝔤) 2 = 9 frequency channels, dim(𝔤) + 1 = 4 coefficient slots,
and a 5-dimensional kernel of harmonic modes governed by the representation theory of 𝔤).

18.22.7.3 Stage III: non-abelian Fourier symmetry and spectral measure
Remark 18.22.16 (The Weyl group as non-abelian Poisson summation). The Weyl–Kac character formula
(Theorem 20.11.17) replaces the dual-lattice sum in classical Poisson summation with an alternating sum
over 𝑊aff = 𝑊 ⋉ 𝑄 ∨ . The bar spectral sequence realizes this: 𝐸1 is indexed by Verma modules M ( 𝑤 · 𝜆),
collapsing at generic level and reducing to a finite Weyl orbit at admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 .

                                                                                                     Q
𝜆𝑖 𝑥 ) (Theorem 27.17.20) is the chiral Plancherel density: Δ H = 1 (uniform, partition growth), Δ 𝛽𝛾 =

18.22.7.4 Stage IV: the homotopy-theoretic uplift

18.22.9    Curved duality under level inversion 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘
Theorem 18.22.24 (Heisenberg level inversion: curved duality; [proved]). The Heisenberg algebras
at levels 𝑘 and −𝑘 form a curved/ﬁltered dual pair (distinct from standard Koszul duality) with:
   (i) Curvature terms: 𝑚0( 𝑘 ) = 𝑘 · 𝑐 where 𝑐 is the central element
  (ii) Modified pairing: ⟨ 𝐽 ⊗ 𝐽 , 𝐽 ⊗ 𝐽 ⟩𝑘 = 𝑘 · 𝛿 (2) ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )
 (iii) Curved bar complexes related by: 𝐵¯ 𝑛curved (H𝑘 )  𝐵¯ 𝑛curved (H− 𝑘 ) as vector spaces with opposite dif-
       ferentials
   This is not the same as the standard Koszul duality H ! = Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) established above; it is an additional
duality structure that exists in the curved/filtered category.

Proof. The double pole prevents standard residue extraction: the literal residue Res 𝑧 =𝑤 [ 𝑘 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 · 𝜂 𝑧𝑤 ]
vanishes since the integrand has a triple pole with zero residue (cf. the clarification at Theorem 18.22.21).
Instead, the Borcherds identity extracts the OPE coefficient directly, giving the boundary pairing

                                             ⟨ 𝐽 ⊗ 𝐽 , 𝐽 ⊗ 𝐽 ⟩𝑘 = 𝑘

(the level appears as the second-order pole coefficient, not as a residue).
   Under 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 , this pairing changes sign, establishing curved self-duality. The curved bar complex has
chain groups:
• 𝐵¯ 0 = ℂ, 𝐵¯ 1 = currents, 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ≠ 0 for all 𝑛 ≥ 1
• The bracket differential 𝑑bracket = 0 (the double pole has zero residue)
                                                2 ≠ 0 and the bar complex is curved: it does not have
• The curvature 𝑚0(1) = −𝑘 · 𝑐 is nonzero, so 𝑑fib
  well-defined cohomology in the usual sense
The curvature controls the failure of the bar differential to square to zero.

18.24      String theory and holographic dualities
18.24.1    The algebraic string theory dictionary
Proposition 18.24.1 (State complexes, central coefficients, and insertion maps). The following
statements use separate, specified carriers.
  (i) On a nonzero restricted Virasoro module tensored with the conformal ghost module, the full charge
      is nilpotent exactly at matter central charge 26.
18.24. String theory and holographic dualities                                                               887


  (ii) The parameter reflection of Proposition 30.6.1 negates the affine scalar 𝑎 ( 𝑘 ), while its Sugawara
       central charges sum to 2 dim 𝔤. For principal Virasoro parameters the reflected half-central charges
       sum to 13 by Proposition 30.6.2.
 (iii) The polynomial reduction admits the explicit associative bar quasi-isomorphisms of Theorem 30.5.1.
 (iv) Insertion integrals defined by Proposition 30.1.6 descend to cohomology and retain multilinear
       dependence on the insertion classes.

Proof. Part (i) follows from the operator identity and its detecting vector in Theorem 30.3.5. Part (ii) is the
direct substitution in the two scalar propositions. Part (iii) uses the explicitly defined maps 𝑖, 𝑝 and their
tensorwise bar maps. Part (iv) is the chain identity for the insertion map followed by Stokes’ theorem.

   A chiral string comparison still requires a unital collision target, a relative sheaf carrier, and compatible
symbol and correction maps. Theorem 30.3.13 states the filtered chain criterion. For an affine comparison
the full hypotheses of Theorem 30.4.3 also remain necessary. Quantum reduction further requires the
equivariance and totalization data of Theorem 30.5.2. Maps over moduli require compatible connections,
pairings, and clutching operations.

For smooth de Rham forms one may take 𝐼 = 𝑍 . For logarithmic forms with regularization, existence

and closedness of 𝐼 are additional hypotheses.

Proof. Apply (18.3) to the closed insertion cycle 𝑥 . The difference of its two image forms is 𝑑 𝐸 ℎ ( 𝑥 ), whose
image under 𝐼 is zero by hypothesis. For smooth forms on the compact oriented manifold 𝑍 , Stokes’
theorem gives the required closedness of integration. For a regularized functional the same conclusion uses
its stated closedness; sharing a compactification does not establish that property. A chain quasi-isomorphism
without (18.3) does not identify pairings. For example, on one-dimensional complexes in degree zero the
identity map is a quasi-isomorphism, while the functionals 𝑥 ↦→ 𝑥 and 𝑥 ↦→ 2 𝑥 differ.

    The augmentation-kernel bar for 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 cannot supply 𝑇𝑛 by Proposition 30.3.11. A different unital
chiral target requires its own construction, relative descent, insertion maps, and pairing homotopy before
this corollary applies.

18.25     Complete classification of extensions
Theorem 18.25.1 (Classification of extendable algebras [163]; [proved]). A chiral algebra A on
ℂℙ1 extends to a consistent string background on all genera if and only if:
   (i) Anomaly cancellation. The total central charge satisfies 𝑐total = 𝑐matter + 𝑐ghost = 0, giving 𝑐 = 26
       (bosonic) or 𝑐 = 15 (superstring).
  (ii) Modular invariance. The partition function 𝑍 ( 𝜏 ) = tr H 𝑞 𝐿0 − 𝑐 /24 is invariant under SL2 (ℤ).
 (iii) Rationality or integrability. The algebra has finitely many irreducible modules, with fusion rules
       satisfying the Verlinde formula.
 (iv) BRST cohomology. There exists a nilpotent BRST operator 𝑄 with 𝑄 2 = 0, and A = 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝑄, Vstring ).
18.26. Quantum corrections and deformed Koszul duality                                                      889


Proof. Necessity.
     (1) Anomaly cancellation: The integrand on M 𝑔,𝑛 involves det(Im Ω) − 𝑐 /2 ; for the Belavin–Knizhnik
anomaly to cancel, 𝑐total = 0. Hence 𝑐matter = 26 (bosonic, 𝑐ghost = −26) or 𝑐matter = 15 (super, 𝑐ghost = −15).
     (2) Modular invariance: 𝑍 ( 𝜏 ) must be SL2 (ℤ)-invariant; otherwise the genus-1 bar complex integrand
is ill-defined on ℍ/SL2 (ℤ).
     (3) Rationality: Conformal blocks V ( Σ 𝑔 , 𝑉® ) must be finite-dimensional, guaranteed by rationality
(Zhu’s theorem). The Verlinde formula ensures consistency with the OPE.
     (4) BRST structure: Nilpotency 𝑄 2 = 0 ensures gauge-invariant amplitudes (independence of Beltrami
differentials on Σ 𝑔 ).
     Suﬃciency. Given (1)–(4), the genus- 𝑔 extension is constructed via Segal’s sewing axioms, and the
spectral sequence of Theorem I.7.1 converges by (3).

Remark 18.25.2 (Provenance). Each condition is classical in the string theory literature: (1) anomaly cancel-
lation via the Belavin–Knizhnik theorem [200]; (2) modular invariance of the partition function (Friedan–
Martinec–Shenker); (3) the Verlinde formula and finite-dimensionality of conformal blocks (Zhu [89]);
(4) BRST nilpotency (Kato–Ogawa, Borcherds [201]). The sufficiency argument via Segal’s sewing axioms
is due to Segal [202].

   The function 𝐺𝜏 is a meromorphic expression on the covering plane with the stated transformation
law. A propagator on an elliptic curve requires its additional periodicity, coefficient bundle, and differential
equation. The character, this kernel, and a chiral chain complex are separate objects.
Conjecture 18.28.5 (Chiral realization of modular transformation laws). For a conformal chiral algebra with
a specified convergent character space and a compatible family of elliptic chiral chain complexes, there is a
modular-equivariant chain-level realization of its character transformation law. Such a realization includes
descent maps on the family of elliptic curves and a trace map compatible with those descent maps. The
scalar character identities above do not construct these maps.
894                                                                                Chapter 18. Free field atoms


    A pole of residue one cannot be the only singularity of a meromorphic differential on a compact torus.
A Cauchy kernel therefore requires a correction that removes the constant mode. The correction below
is smooth away from the pole, respects changes of lattice basis, and gives an explicit homotopy for the
Dolbeault differential.

   This construction concerns the scalar smooth Dolbeault complex on a compact complex torus. It
supplies neither a conformal-character trace on chiral chains nor a comparison with a vertex-algebra BRST
complex. Such a comparison must specify its coefficient objects and its compatibility with collision maps
and with the displayed contraction.
Proposition 18.31.2 (Fiber data and genus-one cohomology). Isomorphism of the fibers of two flat
complexes does not imply isomorphism of their genus-one cohomology. In particular, a diskwise bar/BRST
comparison without transition compatibility does not determine genus-one cohomology or a modular
transformation law.

Proof. Example 30.6.5 gives rank-one local systems on the torus with identical fibers and cohomology
dimensions (1, 2, 1) or (0, 0, 0). The missing condition is the compatibility with transitions, or equivalently
horizontality in Proposition 30.6.4.

   For a conformal matter module, the ghost square is still governed by ( 𝑐 − 26)/12 in Theorem 30.3.5. A
modular weight requires its own determinant line and automorphy factor. The scalar 𝑐 /24 in a vacuum
energy does not construct that line or its transformation law.

   All results match the predictions of Theorem 9.1.39.

19.1     Setup and conventions
The 𝛽𝛾 system is the simplest nontrivial chiral algebra.

19.1.1   Algebraic structure
Fields: 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) of conformal weight ℎ 𝛽 = 𝜆, 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) of weight ℎ 𝛾 = 1 − 𝜆.
