19.1.2    Mode algebra and stress tensor
Proposition 19.1.1 (Mode algebra [10]; [proved]). Expand in modes:
                              ∑︁                        ∑︁
                     𝛽 ( 𝑧) =    𝛽𝑛 𝑧 − 𝑛− 𝜆 , 𝛾 ( 𝑧) =    𝛾𝑛 𝑧 − 𝑛− (1− 𝜆 ) .

The commutation relations are [ 𝛽𝑚 , 𝛾𝑛 ] = 𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0 .
Theorem 19.1.2 (Stress tensor and central charge [10]; [proved]). The stress-energy tensor is:

                                 𝑇 𝛽𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) = (1 − 𝜆):𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜕 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ): − 𝜆:𝜕 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ):

                                     𝑐 𝛽𝛾 = +2(6𝜆2 − 6𝜆 + 1)            (bosonic 𝛽𝛾 )

For the fermionic 𝑏𝑐 system with the same conformal weights, the sign reverses: 𝑐𝑏𝑐 = −2(6𝜆2 − 6𝜆 + 1).
Computation 19.1.3 (Central charges for special cases). Fermionic 𝑏𝑐 system ( 𝑐𝑏𝑐 = 1 − 3(2𝜆 − 1) 2 ):
𝜆 = 2: 𝑐 = −26 (string theory ghosts); 𝜆 = 1: 𝑐 = −2; 𝜆 = 1/2: 𝑐 = 1 (complex fermion pair); 𝜆 = 0: 𝑐 = −2.
Bosonic 𝛽𝛾 system ( 𝑐 𝛽𝛾 = +2(6𝜆2 − 6𝜆 + 1)): 𝜆 = 1: 𝑐 = +2; 𝜆 = 0: 𝑐 = +2; 𝜆 = 1/2: 𝑐 = −1 (symplectic
bosons).

19.2     Bar complex computation
Unlike the Heisenberg bar complex (§1.3), where 𝑑bracket = 0 because the abelian OPE has no simple pole,
the 𝛽𝛾 system has a nontrivial bar differential: the mixed OPE 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) kills every element
containing both a 𝛽 and a 𝛾 factor (via the residue Res[ 𝛽𝛾 · 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ] = 1), while pure 𝛽 ⊗ 𝑛 and pure 𝛾 ⊗ 𝑛
tensors are cocycles. This is the chain-level mechanism behind the 3𝑛 growth: at each tensor position, the
differential acts on the mixed pair but not on the pure types or their conformal descendants.

Proof. The explicit computation for degrees 1–3 proceeds as follows.
    Degree 1: 𝐵¯ 1 = 𝑉𝛽 ⊕ 𝑉𝛾 (2 types).
    Degree 2: There are 22 = 4 pure tensor types (choosing 𝛽 or 𝛾 at each of 2 positions) plus 2 derivative
types (𝑉𝜕 𝛽 and 𝑉𝜕 𝛾 ), giving 4 + 2 = 6 types.
    Degree 3: There are 23 = 8 pure tensor types. Derivative terms arise when one or both of positions 2,
3 are replaced by conformal descendants: substituting 𝜕 𝛾 at position 2 (with any of 𝛽, 𝛾 at positions 1, 3)
gives 2 · 2 = 4 types, substituting at position 3 gives another 4, and substituting at both positions 2 and 3
gives 2, for a total of 8 + 4 + 4 + 2 = 18 types. These match 2 · 30 = 2, 2 · 31 = 6, 2 · 32 = 18.

                                                              (

                                                               0 𝑛≥1

This is the Koszul property: the bar complex is acyclic above degree 0.
Proof. By the Koszul duality ( 𝛽𝛾 ) !  F (Theorem 19.3.1) and the bar-cobar adjunction (Theorem 9.1.39),
the bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) is quasi-isomorphic to the Chevalley coalgebra of the free fermion system. Since
the 𝛽𝛾 –fermion pair is Koszul (the underlying operadic duality is Comch –Liech , which is Koszul by Theo-
rem 9.3.7), acyclicity follows from the general inversion theorem (Theorem 8.17.4).
   Alternatively, one verifies directly: in degree 0, 𝐻 0 = ℂ (vacuum). In degree 1, ker( 𝑑 1 ) = 𝑉𝛽 ⊕ 𝑉𝛾
and im( 𝑑 0 → 𝐵¯ 1 ) surjects onto both summands by the 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) OPE, giving 𝐻 1 = 0.
The pattern continues: each cocycle in degree 𝑛 ≥ 1 is exact by the residue calculus of the bar differential
(Definition 6.1.13).

19.3      Koszul dual
19.3.1
     Main result: Koszul duality with free fermions
Theorem 19.3.1 (Koszul dual of 𝛽 𝛾 ; [proved]). The Koszul dual of the 𝛽𝛾 system is the 𝑏𝑐 ghost
system:
                                     ( 𝛽𝛾 ) !  𝑏𝑐   and      ( 𝑏𝑐 ) !  𝛽𝛾
   This is a two-generator duality (dim 𝑉 = 2: one bosonic pair 𝛽, 𝛾 dualizes to one fermionic pair 𝑏, 𝑐 ),
not to be confused with the single-generator duality Λch ( 𝜓 ) ↔ Symch ( 𝛾 ). The 𝑏𝑐 system has:
   (i) Generators. 𝑏 with conformal weight ℎ𝑏 = 𝜆 and 𝑐 with conformal weight ℎ𝑐 = 1 − 𝜆
  (ii) Statistics. Fermionic (𝑏 and 𝑐 are odd/anticommuting)
                               1
 (iii) OPE. 𝑏 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑐 ( 𝑤 ) ∼     , 𝑏 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑏 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 0, 𝑐 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑐 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 0
                              𝑧−𝑤
Proof. This is the chiral analog of the classical Koszul duality between Sym(𝑉 ) and Λ (𝑉 ∗ ) for associative
algebras. The proof follows from the Gui–Li–Zeng framework [91].
   Step 1: Quadratic Data
   For 𝛽𝛾 system:
• Generators: 𝑁 = O 𝑋 · 𝛽 ⊕ O 𝑋 · 𝛾
• Relations: 𝑃 ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ ( 𝑁 ⊠ 𝑁 ) encode symplectic pairing:
                                            1
                              ⟨ 𝛽, 𝛾 ⟩ =         , ⟨ 𝛽, 𝛽 ⟩ = 0,        ⟨ 𝛾, 𝛾 ⟩ = 0
                                         𝑧1 − 𝑧2
   For the 𝑏𝑐 ghost system F :
• Generators: 𝑁 ′ = O 𝑋 · 𝑏 ⊕ O 𝑋 · 𝑐 (two fermionic generators, dual to 𝛽, 𝛾 )
• Relations: 𝑃 ′ ⊂ 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ ( 𝑁 ′ ⊠ 𝑁 ′ ) encode anticommutation:
                                                  1

                                               𝑧1 − 𝑧2
   Step 2: Dual Quadratic Data
   The Koszul dual is constructed via:
                                             ( 𝑠 −1 𝑁 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑃 ⊥ )
   For F : The dual of the Clifford relation 𝑏 ⊠ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊠ 𝑏 is the Weyl/symplectic pairing 𝛽 ⊠ 𝛾 − 𝛾 ⊠ 𝛽 ,
recovering 𝛽𝛾 .
   For 𝛽𝛾 : The dual of the Weyl pairing is the Clifford relation, recovering F .

19.3.2.1 Bar complex of the 𝑏 𝑐 ghost system

                                   𝐵¯ 𝑛 (F ) = Sym𝑛𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 F̄ )

Proof. The 𝑏𝑐 ghost system has OPEs 𝑏 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑐 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑧 −1 𝑤 , 𝑏 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑏 (𝑤 ) ∼ 0, 𝑐 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑐 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 0 (Definition in

19.4      Relationship to special cases
19.4.1  Understanding the 𝜆 parameter
Remark 19.4.1 (Conformal weights). The 𝛽𝛾 system has fields with conformal weights:

                                             ℎ 𝛽 = 𝜆,    ℎ𝛾 = 1 − 𝜆

where 𝜆 is a parameter.
    When 𝜆 = 1, 𝛽 has weight 1 and 𝛾 has weight 0. The system remains bosonic (commuting fields) for
all values of 𝜆. The 𝑏𝑐 ghost system is the fermionic counterpart with anticommuting fields of the same
weights.

19.4.2     The 𝑏𝑐 ghost system and Koszul duality
Proposition 19.4.2 (Central charge complementarity for 𝛽 𝛾 / 𝑏 𝑐 ; [proved]). The Koszul duality
( 𝛽𝛾 ) ! ≃ 𝑏𝑐 of Theorem 19.3.1 has a sharp central charge consequence:

                𝑐 𝛽𝛾 = +2(6𝜆2 − 6𝜆 + 1) ,        𝑐𝑏𝑐 = −2(6𝜆2 − 6𝜆 + 1) ,          𝑐 𝛽𝛾 + 𝑐𝑏𝑐 = 0.

Proof. The central charge of the 𝛽𝛾 system is computed from the stress tensor (Theorem 19.1.2). Replacing
bosonic statistics by fermionic statistics negates the Virasoro central term: the commutator [ 𝐿𝑚 , 𝐿𝑛 ] picks
up a sign from the fermion loop, so 𝑐𝑏𝑐 = −𝑐 𝛽𝛾 .
   This exact cancellation is specific to the Sym/Ext exchange. For general Koszul dual pairs the central
charges need not sum to zero: affine Kac–Moody algebras satisfy 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ) + 𝑐 (−𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ ) = 𝑐crit instead
(Remark 20.4.2).

Remark 19.4.3 (Statistics exchange as a general principle). The 𝛽𝛾 ↔ 𝑏𝑐 duality illustrates a general prin-
ciple: chiral Koszul duality exchanges bosonic and fermionic statistics. At the operadic level, this reflects
the classical duality Com! = Lie (commutative ↔ Lie), which at the level of enveloping algebras becomes
Sym(𝑉 ) ! = Λ (𝑉 ∗ ) (symmetric ↔ exterior). The chiral lift preserves this exchange because the quadratic
duality functor ( 𝑁 , 𝑃 ) ↦→ ( 𝑠 −1 𝑁 ∨ 𝜔 −1 , 𝑃 ⊥ ) sends symmetric pairings to exterior relations and vice versa.

19.4.3    Boson-fermion correspondence
Theorem 19.4.4 (Physical bosonization [10]; [proved]). There is a physics ‘‘bosonization’’ map
relating 𝛽𝛾 and free fermions at the level of correlation functions:
                                                    Bosonization
                                Correlators[ 𝛽𝛾 ] ←−−−−−−−→ Correlators[F ]

    This is different from Koszul duality: bosonization equates correlation functions, while Koszul duality
is an algebraic relationship between chiral algebras via bar-cobar.

19.4.4 Symplectic bosons ( 𝜆 = 1/2)
At 𝜆 = 1/2, both fields have weight 1/2:
                                               1
                                            𝑇 = ( 𝛽𝜕 𝛾 − 𝜕 𝛽 · 𝛾 )
                                               2
   At this value the OPE with the stress tensor is logarithmic, the representation theory is non-semisimple
(logarithmic CFT), and the Koszul dual remains F .

19.5.1   Bundle data on curves

   Special cases.

       at 𝜆 = 2 provides the BRST ghosts of the bosonic string

Remark 19.5.2 (Bundle pairing as bar differential). The Serre duality residue pairing 𝐾𝑋𝜆 ⊗ 𝐾𝑋1− 𝜆 →

Theorem 19.5.5 (Universal property of 𝛽 - 𝛾 [10]; [proved]). The 𝛽 - 𝛾 system is the free vertex algebra
generated by two fields 𝛽, 𝛾 of weights 𝜆, 1 − 𝜆 with the single relation 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ). For any
vertex algebra 𝑉 with fields 𝛽 ′ , 𝛾 ′ satisfying this OPE, there exists a unique homomorphism Free[ 𝛽, 𝛾 ] →
𝑉 sending 𝛽 ↦→ 𝛽 ′ , 𝛾 ↦→ 𝛾 ′ .

19.6.3    Degree 5 and the acyclicity pattern
At degree 5, the 32 pure tensor types follow the same pattern: [ 𝛽 5 ] and [ 𝛾 5 ] have 𝑑 = 0, while all 30 mixed
types have nontrivial differentials. The derivative types (130 of them) similarly split into exact and boundary
components.
Proposition 19.6.4 (Acyclicity of the 𝛽 𝛾 bar complex; [proved]). For all 𝑛 ≥ 1, 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 )) = 0.

Proof. We construct an explicit contracting homotopy ℎ : 𝐵¯ 𝑛 → 𝐵¯ 𝑛+1 satisfying 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 = id on 𝐵¯ 𝑛
for 𝑛 ≥ 1.
    Define ℎ on a pure tensor element 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔 by inserting a 𝛾 (respectively 𝛽 ) at the first tensor

                         ℎ ( 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = 𝛾 ( 𝑧0 ) ⊗ 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜂01 ∧ 𝜔

where 𝑧0 is a new point on 𝑋 and 𝜂01 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧0 − 𝑧1 ).
   The key identity is:

 ( 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 ) ( 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = Res𝐷01 𝛾 ( 𝑧0 ) 𝑎1 ( 𝑧1 ) · 𝜂01 ⊗ 𝑎2 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔 + (other terms).
                                                                    


When 𝑎1 = 𝛽 , the residue Res 𝑧0 =𝑧1 [ 𝛾 ( 𝑧0 ) 𝛽 ( 𝑧1 ) · 𝜂01 ] = −𝟙 (from 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛽 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ −1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )), producing
the identity on the summand. When 𝑎1 = 𝛾 , the 𝛾 𝛾 OPE is regular and this residue vanishes; however, the
912                                                            Chapter 19. Complete example: the 𝛽 𝛾 system


term ℎ𝑑 applied first contracts a 𝛽 – 𝛾 pair elsewhere in the tensor, reducing the problem to a lower-degree

   More precisely, decompose 𝐵¯ 𝑛 by the number 𝑘 of 𝛾 factors among 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑛 . The homotopy ℎ
increases the 𝛾 count by 1, and the differential 𝑑 (via 𝛽𝛾 contraction) decreases it by 1 when it acts on a 𝛽 – 𝛾

one 𝛾 (and the pure 𝛾 𝑛 element maps under 𝑑 to zero, but also lies in the image of 𝑑 from degree 𝑛 + 1 via
the element 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛾 𝑛 ), the homotopy covers all cases.
   Thus 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 )) = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 1, and 𝐻 0 = ℂ (the vacuum).

19.8     Spectral sequence for 𝛽𝛾 Koszulness
The Koszulness of the 𝛽𝛾 system (Theorem 19.2.2) can be established systematically via a spectral sequence
associated to the conformal weight filtration on 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ). The argument parallels the non-abelian preview
of §1.15, with the symplectic pairing ⟨ 𝛽, 𝛾 ⟩ = 1 replacing the Killing form.

19.8.1   Conformal weight filtration
Deﬁnition 19.8.1 (Conformal weight ﬁltration). Define the decreasing filtration 𝐹 𝑝 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ( 𝛽𝛾 ) by total con-
formal weight:

                    𝐹 𝑝 𝐵¯ 𝑛 = 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔 ∈ 𝐵¯ 𝑛 ℎ ( 𝑎1 ) + · · · + ℎ ( 𝑎𝑛 ) ≥ 𝑝
                              


where ℎ ( 𝑎𝑖 ) is the conformal weight of the generator 𝑎𝑖 (so ℎ ( 𝛽 ) = 𝜆, ℎ ( 𝛾 ) = 1 − 𝜆, ℎ ( 𝜕 𝑘 𝛽 ) = 𝜆 + 𝑘 ,
etc.).
   The bar differential preserves the filtration: since the OPE 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) has conformal
weight 0 on the right-hand side, the residue operation does not increase the total conformal weight. There-
fore ( 𝐹 𝑝 𝐵¯ ∗ , 𝑑 ) is a filtered complex and the associated spectral sequence converges to 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 )).

Proposition 19.8.4 (Spectral sequence collapse; [proved]). The conformal weight spectral sequence
for 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) collapses at 𝐸2 for all values of the conformal weight parameter 𝜆.

Proof. By Proposition 19.8.2, the 𝐸1 page is computed by the classical Koszul complex of the 2-dimensional
symplectic vector space (𝑉 , ⟨·, ·⟩) with ⟨ 𝛽, 𝛾 ⟩ = 1. This complex is exact in positive degrees (the pairing is
nondegenerate), so 𝐸1 = 0 for 𝑝 + 𝑞 ≥ 1 at the leading filtration level.

yond the simple pole. Since the 𝛽𝛾 OPE has no regular terms (the full OPE is exactly 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) = 1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )
with no subleading corrections), the 𝑑1 differential on conformal descendants is entirely determined by the

    The Virasoro module structure on conformal descendants is semisimple for generic 𝜆 (the Verma
module 𝑀ℎ,𝑐 is irreducible for generic ℎ and 𝑐 ). Semisimplicity implies that the higher Koszul differentials

19.9       Symplectic boson 𝜆 = 1/2 specialization
At 𝜆 = 1/2, both fields 𝛽 and 𝛾 have conformal weight 1/2, the central charge is 𝑐 𝛽𝛾 = −1, and the stress
tensor takes the antisymmetric form 𝑇 = 21 (:𝛽𝜕 𝛾: − :𝜕 𝛽 · 𝛾:). This is the symplectic boson (or ‘‘symplectic
fermion’’) system, which plays a distinguished role in logarithmic conformal field theory.

19.9.1    ℤ2 symmetry of the bar complex
Deﬁnition 19.9.1 (ℤ2 action). At 𝜆 = 1/2, the 𝛽𝛾 system admits the involution 𝜎 : 𝛽 ↔ 𝛾 (exchange of
the two fields), which is a vertex algebra automorphism since ℎ 𝛽 = ℎ 𝛾 = 1/2 and the OPE 𝛽 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛾 ( 𝑤 ) ∼
1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) is antisymmetric under 𝜎 (one has 𝛾 ( 𝑧 ) 𝛽 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ −1/( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ), consistent with 𝜎 acting by −1 on
the pairing).
      This ℤ2 acts on the bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) by exchanging tensor factors:

                             𝜎 ( 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑛 ⊗ 𝜔) = 𝜎 ( 𝑎1 ) ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜎 ( 𝑎𝑛 ) ⊗ 𝜔,
19.9. Symplectic boson 𝜆 = 1/2 specialization                                                                   917


where 𝜎 ( 𝛽 ) = 𝛾 and 𝜎 ( 𝛾 ) = 𝛽 . The bar differential commutes with 𝜎 (since 𝜎 is a vertex algebra auto-
morphism), so 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) decomposes into 𝜎 -eigenspaces 𝐵¯ = 𝐵¯ + ⊕ 𝐵¯ − .

On the − eigenspace:

                                       𝑑 ( 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛽 − 𝛾 ⊗ 𝛾 ) = 0.

Thus 𝑑 maps ( 𝐵¯ 2 ) − surjectively onto ( 𝐵¯ 0 ) − (the vacuum, which is 𝜎 -invariant, so lies in the + eigenspace;
more precisely, the element 𝛽 ⊗ 𝛾 − 𝛾 ⊗ 𝛽 maps to 2 · 𝟙 ∈ ( 𝐵¯ 0 ) + , showing the ℤ2 decomposition interacts
nontrivially with the bar differential).

Proof. The full bar cohomology satisfies 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 )) = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 1 and 𝐻 0 = ℂ by Proposition 19.6.4

Remark 19.9.4 (Connection to logarithmic CFT). The symplectic boson at 𝜆 = 1/2 is a prototypical example
of a logarithmic conformal field theory: the 𝐿0 operator is not diagonalizable on the full module category,
and indecomposable but reducible modules (Jordan blocks for 𝐿0 ) appear. The ℤ2 orbifold ( 𝛽𝛾 ) ℤ2 is
the triplet vertex algebra W (2) at 𝑐 = −2 (cf. Example 12.2.40), whose representation category is non-
semisimple with finitely many simple objects.
    The bar complex detects this non-semisimplicity: while 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 )) is concentrated in degree 0 (the sys-
tem is Koszul), the equivariant bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) ℤ2 carries additional structure. The chain-level ℤ2 action
on 𝐵¯ is nontrivial (Computation 19.9.2), and the resulting equivariant derived category 𝐷 𝑏 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝛽𝛾 ) ⋊ ℤ2 )
encodes the non-semisimple tensor structure of the triplet algebra modules. This is a bar-complex-level
manifestation of the general principle that logarithmic CFTs correspond to non-Koszul (or ‘‘logarithmic
Koszul’’) phenomena in homological algebra.
   The 𝛽𝛾 /𝑏𝑐 duality is the two-generator chiral lift of Com! = Lie; the equivariant structure at 𝜆 = 1/2
foreshadows the logarithmic phenomena of the W-algebra chapters.

Remark 19.10.12 (Genus-2 vs genus-1: structural differences). The genus-2 computation reveals three features
invisible at genus 1:
   (i) Multi-dimensional Hodge bundle. At genus 1, 𝔼 is a line bundle and 𝜆1 = 𝑐1 (𝔼). At genus 2, 𝔼
       has rank 2, and 𝜆2 = 𝑐2 (𝔼) is a determinantal class involving the interaction of both B-cycle mon-
       odromies.
  (ii) Off-diagonal periods. The period matrix entry 𝑧 = Ω12 encodes the interaction between the two
       handles of Σ2 . This interaction contributes to 𝜆2 through the cross-term in 𝑐2 (𝔼) = 21 ( 𝑐1 (𝔼) 2 −
       2 ch2 (𝔼)).
 (iii) Function-valued monodromies. The genus-1 B-cycle monodromy is the constant −2 𝜋 𝑖 ; the genus-2
       monodromies −2 𝜋 𝑖 · 𝜔𝑗 ( 𝑤 ) are sections of 𝜔Σ2 . This explains why 𝜆2 lives in 𝐻 4 (not 𝐻 2 ): each
       B-cycle defect contributes a 2-form on moduli space, and the two defects combine multiplicatively.
Remark 19.10.13 (Degeneration behavior). As Σ2 degenerates, the obstruction class obs2 = 𝜅 · 𝜆2 restricts
to the boundary divisors of M 2 :
• Separating degeneration ( 𝛿1 : Σ2 → 𝐸𝜏1 ∪ 𝐸𝜏2 via a node): 𝜆2 | 𝛿1 = 𝜆1 ( 𝐸𝜏1 ) · 𝜆1 ( 𝐸𝜏2 ), the product of
  genus-1 Hodge classes. The two B-cycle monodromies decouple, recovering two independent genus-1
  obstructions.
• Non-separating degeneration ( 𝛿0 : Σ2 → nodal genus-1): the period matrix entry 𝑧 = Ω12 → 0, the Hodge
  bundle acquires a rank-1 sub-bundle, and 𝜆2 | 𝛿0 = 0. The vanishing reflects the fact that a non-separating
  node reduces the effective genus without producing a separating obstruction.
This degeneration behavior is consistent with the recursive structure of the genus expansion
(Theorem 19.10.15).

Proof. The Heisenberg algebra is a free (Gaussian) theory: Wick’s theorem reduces all correlation func-
tions to products of two-point functions. Therefore the genus- 𝑔 two-point function is exactly the Green
function 𝐺Ω 𝑔 ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) = 𝜕𝑧1 log 𝐸 ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ; Ω 𝑔 ), the chiral derivative of the prime form on Σ 𝑔 .
     Step 1: Genus expansion.
     The full partition function sums over genera: 𝑍 = 𝑔 ≥0 ℏ2 𝑔 −2 𝑍 𝑔 . For the Heisenberg algebra (a free
                                                                 P
theory), each genus- 𝑔 contribution is exact–-it is not a perturbative loop correction. Rather, 𝑍 𝑔 encodes
the propagator on Σ 𝑔 through the period matrix Ω 𝑔 .
     Step 2: Modular weight.
     At genus 𝑔 , the correlation function is a modular form whose weight is determined by the number of
insertions and the genus.
     Step 3: Modular constraints on expansion coeﬃcients.
     The coefficient 𝑐𝑘 ( Ω 𝑔 ) in the Laurent expansion 𝐺Ω 𝑔 ( 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 ) = ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) −1 + 𝑘 ≥0 𝑐𝑘 ( Ω 𝑔 ) ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) 𝑘
                                                                                             P
is a function of the period matrix Ω 𝑔 ∈ H 𝑔 , holomorphic on the Siegel upper half-space. Since the partition
function must transform as a section of a line bundle on M 𝑔 (i.e. as a Siegel modular form), each coefficient
𝑐𝑘 ( Ω 𝑔 ) must be a Siegel modular form of the appropriate weight under 𝑆 𝑝2 𝑔 (ℤ). The weight is fixed by
the requirement that the product ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) −1 · 𝑐𝑘 ( Ω 𝑔 ) ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) 𝑘 be an ( 𝑟, 𝑠 )-form of total weight zero on
Σ 𝑔 × Σ 𝑔 ; each additional factor of ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) has conformal weight (1, 0), so 𝑐𝑘 must have modular weight
𝑘 + 1.
     Step 4: Generation by explicit modular forms.
     For 𝑔 = 1: The graded ring 𝑘 𝑀𝑘 ( 𝑆 𝐿2 (ℤ)) is generated by 𝐸4 and 𝐸6 ; by Eisenstein’s theorem, every
                                    L
even-weight modular form is a polynomial in these two. The quasi-Eisenstein series 𝐸2 appears in 𝐺𝜏 at
weight 2 as the unique quasi-modular form (Theorem 19.10.18).
     For 𝑔 = 2: The ring of Siegel modular forms for 𝑆 𝑝4 (ℤ) is classically known (Igusa [139]): it is generated
by cusp forms 𝜒10 , 𝜒12 and Eisenstein series 𝐸4 , 𝐸6 (of degrees 10, 12, 4, 6 respectively). The genus-2 Green
function expansion has coefficients in this ring, as verified explicitly in Theorem 19.10.8.
926                                                          Chapter 19. Complete example: the 𝛽 𝛾 system


    For general 𝑔 : The structure of the Siegel modular forms ring 𝑀∗ (Sp2 𝑔 (ℤ)) is finitely presented for
𝑔 ≤ 3 by classical results [141], and the generators of the ring are known explicitly in those cases. The
concrete expansion claimed in this theorem is therefore complete and rigorous for 𝑔 ≤ 3. For 𝑔 ≥ 4, the ring
of Siegel modular forms is not fully described, and the assertion about the coefficient ring means that the
expansion coefficients lie in the finitely generated subalgebra of 𝑀∗ (Sp2 𝑔 (ℤ)) determined by the modular
weight constraints of Step 3.

Proposition 19.10.16 (Modular weight formula [139]; [proved]). At genus 𝑔 , the Green function
                                               ( 𝑔)
expansion involves Siegel Eisenstein series 𝐸𝑘 ( Ω) for even weights 𝑘 > 𝑔 + 1 (by Klingen’s conver-
gence bound). For 𝑔 ≤ 3, the leading (lowest weight) series contributing to the propagator expansion has
weight 2 𝑔 ; for 𝑔 ≥ 4, the minimum converging even weight is ⌈ 𝑔 + 2⌉ even , which is strictly less than 2 𝑔 .
The ring of Siegel modular forms at genus 𝑔 ≥ 3 is more complex than the Eisenstein series alone; for 𝑔 = 2,
the full ring includes cusp forms 𝜒10 and 𝜒12 (Igusa’s generators) in addition to Eisenstein series.

Proof. The Green function on a genus- 𝑔 surface expands in Siegel modular forms of Sp(2 𝑔, ℤ). The
                                                                                                 ( 𝑔)
period matrix Ω ∈ ℌ 𝑔 has 𝑔 ( 𝑔 + 1)/2 independent entries. By Klingen’s convergence theorem, 𝐸𝑘 ( Ω)
converges absolutely for even 𝑘 > 𝑔 + 1. For 𝑔 ≤ 3, the minimum converging even weight is 2 𝑔 (since
𝑔 + 2 ≤ 2 𝑔 when 𝑔 ≥ 2, and 𝑔 = 1 uses the quasi-modular 𝐸2 ). For 𝑔 ≥ 4, the minimum converging
even weight drops below 2 𝑔 : at genus 4, 𝐸6(4) already converges (weight 6 > 5 = 𝑔 + 1), though 2 𝑔 = 8.
Whether the Green function expansion at genus 𝑔 ≥ 4 genuinely begins at weight 2 𝑔 (for reasons beyond
convergence) is a question we do not address here.

Remark 19.10.17 (Scope). Every claim in this proposition is established in the literature: (i) Klingen’s conver-
gence bound for Siegel Eisenstein series ([proved], [42]); (ii) the leading weight 2 𝑔 follows from (i); (iii) the
structure of the ring of Siegel modular forms at genus 2 (Igusa’s generators 𝜒10 , 𝜒12 ) is classical ([proved],
Igusa [139]). The precise expansion coeﬃcients at genus 𝑔 ≥ 3 (beyond what is stated here) depend on open
problems in the theory of Siegel modular forms; these are not claimed by this proposition.

20.4      Koszul duality: abstract theory
The level shift 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ is Verdier duality on configuration spaces: the Serre dual of the level-𝑘
invariant form on 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) is the level-(−𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ ) form, with the shift 2ℎ∨ arising from the adjoint
Casimir eigenvalue.

20.4.1    The general pattern
Theorem 20.4.1 (Level-shifting duality, abstract form; [proved]). For the Heisenberg algebra,
Koszul duality sent the Lie-type H𝑘 to the Com-type Symch (𝑉 ∗ ) (§1.5); in the abelian case, the dual algebra
has a different type. For non-abelian Kac–Moody algebras, Koszul duality instead shifts the level: the dual
has the same type 𝔤b but at level 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ .
   For any simple Lie algebra 𝔤 and level 𝑘 ≠ −ℎ∨ , there exists a quasi-isomorphism of complexes:
                                               𝐵¯ geom (b
                                                        𝔤𝑘 ) ∨ ≃ 𝔤
                                                                 b− 𝑘 −2ℎ∨

This is the chiral analog of the classical Koszul duality between symmetric and exterior algebras, but curved
by the level parameter.

Proof. This is proved as Theorem 20.7.1 below: the bar complex of 𝔤
                                                                  b𝑘 is computed via residues on FM
compactifications (Step 1), the curvature 𝑚0 = ( 𝑘 + ℎ ) 𝜅 /(2ℎ ) is identified from the double-pole
                                                        ∨      ∨

OPE (Step 2), the cobar OPE recovers the level −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ structure constants (Step 3), and the result is
characterized by functorial uniqueness (Step 4).

Remark 20.5.6 (What 𝔰𝔩b 2 reveals). The 𝔰𝔩 2 computation exhibits all three structural features of Kac–
Moody Koszul duality in their simplest form:
   (i) Level shift as curvature. The double pole 𝑘 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 in 𝑒 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑓 ( 𝑤 ) creates curvature 𝑚0 ∝ ( 𝑘 +
       ℎ∨ ) 𝜅 in the bar complex. The cobar construction inverts this curvature, producing the dual level
       −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −𝑘 − 4. This is the chain-level mechanism behind the Feigin–Frenkel involution.
  (ii) Critical level as curvature-free locus. At 𝑘 = −2, the curvature vanishes (𝑚0 = 0), the bar complex
       becomes an honest dg coalgebra, and the Koszul dual is 𝔰𝔩   b 2, −2 itself –- self-duality. Simultaneously,
       the Sugawara construction degenerates and the center enlarges to the oper algebra.
 (iii) Central charge non-cancellation. Unlike the 𝛽𝛾 /𝑏𝑐 pair (Proposition 19.4.2), the central charges satisfy
       𝑐 ( 𝑘 ) + 𝑐 (−𝑘 − 4) = 𝑐crit rather than zero: curvature prevents cancellation.

20.6.5    Level dependence, current modes, and filtrations
The level occurs in the current OPE as 𝑘 , whereas the Sugawara denominator contains 𝑘 + ℎ∨ . A filtration
of a differential must use the coefficient of the actual operator. We first compute that coefficient, then
construct the complex of Laurent current modes and its two filtrations. A comparison with the geometric
chiral bar complex requires further coefficient maps.

Lemma 20.6.8 (The central cocycle). The form 𝜈 is alternating and satisfies

                               𝜈 ( [ 𝑢, 𝑣 ] , 𝑤 ) − 𝜈 ( [ 𝑢, 𝑤 ] , 𝑣 ) + 𝜈 ( [𝑣, 𝑤 ] , 𝑢) = 0.

Consequently (20.2) defines a Lie bracket for every 𝑘 .

Proof. Since a Laurent derivative has zero residue, Res( 𝑔 𝑑𝑓 ) = − Res( 𝑓 𝑑 𝑔 ). For 𝑢 = 𝑥 𝑓 , 𝑣 = 𝑦 𝑔, 𝑤 =
𝑧ℎ, invariance and symmetry of 𝜅 make its three cyclic coefficients equal to 𝜅 ( [ 𝑥, 𝑦 ] , 𝑧 ). The cyclic sum
of their differential factors is

                                ℎ 𝑑 ( 𝑓 𝑔 ) + 𝑓 𝑑 ( 𝑔ℎ) + 𝑔 𝑑 ( ℎ𝑓 ) = 2 𝑑 ( 𝑓 𝑔ℎ) ,

whose residue vanishes. This proves the cocycle identity. The noncentral part of Jacobi is Jacobi in 𝐿 , and
the central part is the identity just proved.

Proof. For three inputs, applying (20.3) twice gives
                                 [[ 𝑢, 𝑣 ] 𝑘 , 𝑤 ] 𝑘 − [[ 𝑢, 𝑤 ] 𝑘 , 𝑣 ] 𝑘 + [[𝑣, 𝑤 ] 𝑘 , 𝑢] 𝑘 = 0.
For two disjoint pairs of inputs, opposite contraction orders produce the two brackets in opposite exterior
order. Their contributions cancel. For any larger wedge, move the three overlapping inputs, or the four
disjoint inputs, to the front; both contraction orders acquire the same permutation sign, so the preceding
cancellations apply with the remaining wedge unchanged. These exhaust the terms of 𝐷 𝑘2 , hence 𝐷 𝑘2 = 0.
Every input involves finitely many pairs. Expanding this identity as a polynomial in 𝑘 therefore proves (20.4).
    The operator 𝑃 replaces two 𝐿 factors by one, so ( 𝑟, 𝑠 ) changes to ( 𝑟 − 1, 𝑠 ). The operator Δ replaces
two 𝐿 factors by 𝐾 , so ( 𝑟, 𝑠 ) changes to ( 𝑟 − 2, 𝑠 + 1); it vanishes if 𝑠 = 1. These changes give exactly the
displayed bidegrees. They also prove closure of every stated source and target. No totalization sign is added:
the two operators already anticommute.

Corollary 20.6.15 (A smaller complex for nonzero level). For 𝑘 ≠ 0, the inclusion

                                        (ker 𝜈 ⊆ Λ𝐿, 𝑑 𝐿 ) −→ ( 𝐶 • , 𝐷 𝑘 )

is a quasi-isomorphism, with Λ𝑛 𝐿 placed in degree −𝑛. The spectral sequence of Proposition 20.6.13 has
only its zeroth row on 𝐸1 and converges at 𝐸2 for this Laurent mode algebra.

Proof. The relation 𝜈𝑑 𝐿 = 𝑑 𝐿 𝜈 makes the source a complex and its inclusion a chain map. Given a cycle
𝛼 + 𝐾 ∧ 𝛽 , choose 𝛾 with 𝜈 𝛾 = 𝛽 /𝑘 by the lemma. Subtracting 𝐷 𝑘 𝛾 leaves 𝛼 − 𝑑𝐿 𝛾 , a cycle in ker 𝜈 .
This proves surjectivity on cohomology. If a cycle in ker 𝜈 is a boundary 𝐷 𝑘 ( 𝛾 + 𝐾 ∧ 𝜂 ), its zero central
component gives 𝑘𝜈 𝛾 = 𝑑 𝐿 𝜂 . Choose 𝜃 with 𝜈𝜃 = 𝜂 /𝑘 . Then 𝛾 − 𝑑 𝐿 𝜃 lies in ker 𝜈 and has the same 𝑑 𝐿
boundary, which proves injectivity. Finally, the cokernel row in the displayed 𝐸1 page is zero by the lemma,
so all differentials beyond 𝑑1 vanish.

20.6.5.3 The critical pair and the formal parameter
Theorem 20.6.16 (Obstruction to a critical-pair bigrading). Let 𝔤 be simple and 𝑐 ≠ 0. No bigrading
refining the total grading of the algebraic complex 𝐶 • makes 𝐷 𝑐 have bidegree (1, 0) and Δ have bidegree
(0, 1). In particular this obstruction applies at 𝑐 = −ℎ∨ .

Proof. First, 𝐻1 ( 𝐴𝑘 ) = 𝐴𝑘 /[ 𝐴𝑘 , 𝐴𝑘 ] by the explicit differential in lengths one and two. The algebra 𝐿 is
perfect: if 𝑥 = 𝑖 [ 𝑎𝑖 , 𝑏 𝑖 ] in 𝔤, then 𝑥𝑡 𝑚 = 𝑖 [ 𝑎𝑖 , 𝑏 𝑖 𝑡 𝑚 ] 𝑘 , since the first mode is zero and contributes no
                P                                P
central term. For 𝑘 ≠ 0, choose ℎ with 𝜅 ( ℎ, ℎ) ≠ 0; the bracket [ ℎ𝑡, ℎ𝑡 −1 ] 𝑘 = 𝑘𝜅 ( ℎ, ℎ) 𝐾 also generates
the central line. Thus
                                   𝐻1 ( 𝐴0 ) = C 𝐾 ,      𝐻1 ( 𝐴𝑘 ) = 0 ( 𝑘 ≠ 0) .
Suppose the proposed bigrading existed. For 𝑧 ≠ 0, multiplying 𝐶 𝑝,𝑞 by 𝑧 𝑞 defines an automorphism 𝑇𝑧
of the algebraic direct sum. It satisfies 𝑇𝑧 𝐷 𝑐 𝑇𝑧−1 = 𝐷 𝑐 and 𝑇𝑧 Δ𝑇𝑧−1 = 𝑧Δ. Consequently all complexes
𝐷 𝑐 + 𝜆Δ with 𝜆 ≠ 0 would be isomorphic. But 𝜆 = −𝑐 gives 𝐷0 and 𝜆 = −2𝑐 gives 𝐷 − 𝑐 , whose degree-
minus-one cohomology groups have just been shown to differ. This contradiction proves the assertion,
without requiring the bigrading to preserve individual modes or the central-factor decomposition.

Corollary 20.6.17 (Formal comparison about a nonzero level; [proved]). Fix 𝑐 ≠ 0, and let 𝜆
have degree zero. On the formal completion 𝐶 • [[ 𝜆]] = 𝑎 ≥0 𝜆 𝑎 𝐶 • , use 𝐷 = 𝐷 𝑐 + 𝜆Δ and the 𝜆-adic
                                                       Q
filtration. Its spectral sequence has

                         𝐸1𝑎,𝑏 = 𝜆 𝑎 𝐻 𝑎+𝑏 ( 𝐶, 𝐷 𝑐 )   ( 𝑎 ≥ 0) ,       𝑑𝑟 = 0     ( 𝑟 ≥ 1) ,

and converges to 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶, 𝐷 𝑐 ) [[ 𝜆]] with its complete, separated 𝜆-adic filtration. This applies in particular
to the critical value 𝑐 = −ℎ∨ .

Proof. Define 𝑇𝜆 to be the identity on Λ𝐿 and multiplication by 1 + 𝜆/𝑐 on 𝐾 ∧ Λ𝐿 . The formulas for
𝑃 and Δ give
                                        ( 𝐷 𝑐 + 𝜆Δ)𝑇𝜆 = 𝑇𝜆 𝐷 𝑐 .
The factor 1 + 𝜆/𝑐 is invertible as a formal power series, so this is a filtered chain isomorphism from the
constant complex to the deformed one. Its map on the associated graded is the identity. For the constant
complex, every cohomology class on every graded piece has a constant-coefficient cycle lift; hence every
page differential vanishes. Coefficientwise splitting of a complex of vector spaces into its cohomology
and contractible pairs shows directly that 𝐻 𝑗 ( 𝐶 [[ 𝜆]] , 𝐷 𝑐 ) = 𝐻 𝑗 ( 𝐶, 𝐷 𝑐 ) [[ 𝜆]]: choose complements to
boundaries in cycles and to cycles in each 𝐶 𝑗 , and apply the resulting linear contraction to every coefficient.
The same splitting identifies the induced filtration with the power-series filtration, proving the stated
convergence and completeness. The filtered isomorphism transports all these conclusions to 𝐷 .

    The formal statement is not evaluation of arbitrary power series at a nonzero complex number. For a
fixed 𝑘 ≠ 0, a separate algebraic chain isomorphism from ( 𝐶, 𝐷 𝑐 ) to ( 𝐶, 𝐷 𝑘 ) is the identity on Λ𝐿 and
multiplication by 𝑘 /𝑐 on 𝐾 ∧ Λ𝐿 . It becomes singular at 𝑘 = 0, exactly where the preceding homology
jump occurs. For the three-mode example, the central-factor spectral sequence has its only nonzero 𝑑1 from
𝑥 ∧ 𝑦 to 𝑘𝐾 ; its kernel and cokernel recover the dimensions calculated in Example 20.6.10.
Remark 20.6.18 (Comparison with chiral coeﬃcients). The mode construction retains 𝐾 as an exterior
generator of degree −1, and 𝐷 𝑘2 = 0 for every level. The chiral bar construction instead uses state sheaves on
configuration strata, geometric residues, and their grading shifts. A comparison must define maps on those
948                                                    Chapter 20. Explicit Kac–Moody Koszul duals


full carriers and intertwine their differentials and filtrations. The smearing calculation above supplies the
current bracket, but not that comparison. The current-only tensors tensored with top logarithmic forms
do not by themselves provide all composite states or the vacuum outputs of collisions. Example 20.6.7
also prevents inferring an affine-linear family on all states merely from the current OPE. Thus the native
critical-first and central-first spectral sequences require additional filtered coefficient constructions. The
two mode filtrations and the formal completion above specify exactly the results available on their stated
carriers.
    A central extension is also distinct from a curved differential. If a degree-one derivation 𝑑 of a graded
algebra satisfies 𝑑 2 = [ 𝑚0 , −], then a nonzero central 𝑚0 still has zero commutator. Thus a nonzero level
or a central Casimir does not alone prove 𝑑 2 ≠ 0. Identifying a particular curved chiral model and its
curvature requires its actual derivation, graded commutator, and coefficient comparison.

Remark 20.6.20 (Degreewise exceptional sets). No finite exceptional set uniform in all degrees follows from
this argument. For example, put 𝑀 2𝑛 = 𝑀 2𝑛+1 = C for 𝑛 ≥ 0, set 𝑑𝑘2𝑛 = 𝑘 − 𝑛, and set every other
differential to zero. This is a polynomial complex, finite-dimensional in each degree, but its exceptional
values over all degrees include every nonnegative integer. For the affine mode complex, the explicit central
rescaling instead gives an isomorphism at all nonzero levels, with the specific failure at zero proved above.
Neither conclusion supplies a Hilbert series or a finite exceptional set for an unconstructed native chiral
complex.

20.11.6    Admissible level representations
At positive integer levels, the category O𝑘int (b
                                                𝔤) is semisimple with finitely many simples. At admissible levels,
the representation theory is richer: the category is no longer semisimple, but retains finiteness properties
that make the bar complex tractable.
Deﬁnition 20.11.12 (Admissible level and admissible weights). A level 𝑘 ∈ ℂ for b
                                                                                𝔤 is admissible if 𝑘 =
−ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 where 𝑝, 𝑞 are coprime positive integers satisfying 𝑝 ≥ ℎ∨ (and for non-simply-laced 𝔤, 𝑞 is
coprime to 𝑟 ∨ = max𝑖 𝑎∨𝑖 , the lacing number).
   A weight Λ of level 𝑘 is admissible if:
   (i) ⟨Λ + 𝜌, 𝛼 ∨ ⟩ ∉ {0, −1, −2, . . . } for all positive real roots 𝛼 ∈ Δ+re ;
  (ii) ⟨Λ + 𝜌, 𝛼 ∨ ⟩ ∈ ℤ>0 for a specific subset of positive real roots determined by 𝑝 and 𝑞 .
The set of admissible weights at level 𝑘 is denoted Adm𝑘 . It is a finite set: |Adm𝑘 | < ∞ (Kac–
Wakimoto [160]).
960                                                  Chapter 20. Explicit Kac–Moody Koszul duals


Theorem 20.11.13 (Representation theory at admissible level [126, 160]; [proved]). Let 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ +
𝑝/ 𝑞 be an admissible level.
   (i) (Kac–Wakimoto [160]) For each Λ ∈ Adm𝑘 , the simple module L ( Λ) is the unique irreducible quo-
       tient of the Verma module M ( Λ). These are all the simple highest weight modules in the admissible
       category.
  (ii) (Arakawa [126]) The simple affine vertex algebra 𝐿 𝑘 (𝔤) at admissible level is rational if and only if the
       admissible level is non-degenerate, meaning 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 (𝔤) = {0} (Definition 12.2.32). At non-degenerate
       admissible levels, 𝐿 𝑘 (𝔤) has finitely many simple modules, all admissible.
 (iii) (Arakawa [126]) At degenerate admissible level, 𝐿 𝑘 (𝔤) has infinitely many simple modules. The
       associated variety 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 (𝔤) = 𝕆 is a non-trivial nilpotent orbit closure, and the module category has
       logarithmic (non-semisimple) structure.
Proposition 20.11.14 (Bar complex at admissible level; [proved]). Let 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 be an
admissible level forb
                    𝔤. The bar complex exhibits the following behavior, controlled by the associated variety
𝑋 𝐿𝑘 (𝔤) :
   (i) Non-degenerate admissible: 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 = {0}. The bar spectral sequence 𝐸𝑟 degenerates at a finite page
                                                                                 𝑝,𝑞

       (bounded by the dimension of the Zhu algebra 𝐴 ( 𝐿 𝑘 )), and the bar complex computes exact char-
       acter formulas (the Kac–Wakimoto character formula replaces the Weyl–Kac formula).
  (ii) Degenerate admissible: 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 = 𝕆 ≠ {0}. The bar spectral sequence has non-trivial differentials 𝑑𝑟 for
       𝑟 ≤ 𝑟0 (𝕆), where 𝑟0 (𝕆) depends on the orbit 𝕆. The higher cohomology groups 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ (b     𝔤𝑘 ) , 𝑛 >

 (iii) Koszul dual level: the admissible level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 maps under the Feigin–Frenkel involution
       to 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −ℎ∨ − 𝑝/ 𝑞 . Note that 𝑘 ′ does not satisfy Definition 20.11.12 (since 𝑘 ′ + ℎ∨ =
       − 𝑝/ 𝑞 < 0); the vertex algebra 𝐿 𝑘′ (𝔤) lies outside the admissible regime. Nonetheless, the central
       charge complementarity (Theorem 2.4.1) applies, and the orbit duality (Proposition 12.2.35) predicts
       𝑋 𝐿𝑘′ = 𝑑 (𝕆) where 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 = 𝕆.
Proof. For (i): when 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 = {0}, the algebra 𝐿 𝑘 (𝔤) is 𝐶2 -cofinite (Theorem 12.2.33(i)). The Li filtration
{ 𝐹𝑝 } on 𝐿 𝑘 has finite-dimensional associated graded, so the induced filtration on the bar complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝐿 𝑘 )
has a spectral sequence whose 𝐸1 page is computable from gr 𝐹 𝐿 𝑘 (a finite-dimensional commutative
algebra). The spectral sequence thus degenerates at a finite page bounded by dim gr 𝐹 𝐿 𝑘 (= dim 𝐴 ( 𝐿 𝑘 ),
the Zhu algebra dimension).
     For (ii): when 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 = 𝕆 ≠ {0}, the associated graded gr 𝐹 𝐿 𝑘 is a positive-dimensional Poisson variety.
The bar spectral sequence inherits non-trivial differentials from the Poisson bracket on gr 𝐹 𝐿 𝑘 : these are
the curved 𝐴∞ operations 𝑚𝑘 for 𝑘 ≥ 2. The higher cohomology 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝐿 𝑘 ) , 𝑛 > 0) classifies extensions
0 → 𝑀1 → 𝐸 → 𝑀2 → 0 in the module category; for admissible modules, these extensions are the
logarithmic couplings.
     For (iii): the level shift 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ + 𝑝/ 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑘 ′ = −ℎ∨ − 𝑝/ 𝑞 is the Feigin–Frenkel involution. The
orbit duality prediction 𝑋 𝐿𝑘 ↔ 𝑑 ( 𝑋 𝐿𝑘′ ) follows from Proposition 12.2.35 (proved for type 𝐴; expected for
all types). The vertex algebra 𝐿 𝑘′ (𝔤) is well-defined but not admissible in the sense of Definition 20.11.12;
its representation theory is governed by the Koszul dual bar complex.

Remark 20.12.2 (Critical level). At 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ = −2, the curvature 𝑑fib      2 = 0 vanishes (Convention 8.0.2),

so the genus-1 bar complex becomes a genuine differential graded coalgebra. This is consistent with the
enhanced algebraic structure at critical level (Theorem 20.5.2): the Feigin–Frenkel center provides ex-
tra flat sections, and the bar differential is strictly nilpotent. In the language of the universal MC class
(Theorem 8.18.36), the critical level is the unique point where Θ A = 0: the entire genus tower collapses
because 𝜅 (−ℎ∨ ) = 0. The Feigin–Frenkel center then becomes an uncurved Koszul algebra, and the
bar-cobar adjunction is an honest equivalence at every genus.

Remark 20.13.7 (Rank-2 features). The passage from 𝔰𝔩 2 (rank 1) to 𝔰𝔩 3 (rank 2) introduces three structural
novelties, all of which the genus-1 pipeline handles:
  (i) Serre relations. The degree-3 bar complex encodes the Serre relation (ad 𝐸1 ) 2 ( 𝐸2 ) = 0
      (Computation 27.2.2). These are invisible at rank 1 (where the Serre relations are vacuous)
                                                                  (1) ,3
       but contribute non-trivially to the cohomology of 𝐵 .
  (ii) Two-dimensional weight lattice. The Cartan subalgebra 𝔥 = span{ 𝐻1 , 𝐻2 } introduces a 2-
       dimensional weight lattice, so the genus-1 Shapovalov non-degeneracy must be checked on the full
       𝐴2 weight system (not just a single weight line as for 𝔰𝔩 2 ).
 (iii) Non-diagonal Cartan OPE. The Cartan matrix 𝐴𝑖𝑗 for 𝔰𝔩 3 has off-diagonal entries 𝐴12 = −1, so
       the Cartan-Cartan OPE 𝐻𝑖 ( 𝑧 ) 𝐻𝑗 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑘 𝐴𝑖𝑗 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 mixes the two Cartan directions. The
       curvature computation contracts over all 8 generators (not just 3), but the universal formula 𝐶2ad =
       2ℎ∨ = 6 absorbs this complexity.
    Despite these rank-2 features, the genus-1 answer depends only on 𝑘 + 3 (the shifted level) and dim(𝔰𝔩 3 ) =
8 (the number of currents). This confirms the universality principle: the genus-1 pipeline for any simple 𝔤   b𝑘
is controlled by 𝑘 + ℎ∨ and dim(𝔤), with all root system dependence absorbed into the Casimir identity
𝐶2ad = 2ℎ∨ .

20.14.3    The oper space at critical level: summary
The bar complex of the affine algebra at critical level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ occupies a distinguished position in the
theory. By Corollary 8.13.25, the bar complex 𝐵 (b 𝔤− ℎ∨ ) is uncurved: the curvature 𝑚0 vanishes because
the Sugawara construction degenerates at the critical level. The first two cohomology groups have been
identified:
• 𝐻 0 ( 𝐵 (b
           𝔤− ℎ∨ ))  Fun(Op𝔤∨ ( 𝐷 )) (Theorem 20.14.9): the zeroth bar cohomology recovers the algebra
  of functions on the space of 𝔤∨ -opers on the formal disc.
• 𝐻 1 ( 𝐵 (b
           𝔤− ℎ∨ ))  Ω1 (Op𝔤∨ ( 𝐷 )) (Proposition 20.14.10): the first bar cohomology recovers Kähler differ-
  entials on the oper space.
   These are the first two terms of the identification 𝐵 (b𝔤− ℎ∨ ) ≃ O der (Op𝔤∨ ( 𝐷 )) (Theorem 20.14.11),
which establishes that the full bar complex provides a vertex-algebraic model of the derived geometry of
the oper space. The full derived identification, including the DAG prerequisites, root-of-unity periodic
CDG structure, and the Kazhdan–Lusztig programme, is developed in Chapter 16.

20.14.4  Fusion monoidality for Kac–Moody modules
The module bar-cobar functor Φ : Mod(A) → CoMod(A ! ) (Theorem 9.6.2) preserves fusion products
(Theorem 12.12.10). For Kac–Moody algebras the evidence comes from three sources.
    Heisenberg Fock modules. For the Heisenberg algebra H𝜅 , the fusion of Fock modules satisfies
𝐹𝜆 ⊠𝜅 𝐹𝜇  𝐹𝜆+ 𝜇 , and one verifies Φ ( 𝐹𝜆 ⊠ 𝐹𝜇 )  Φ ( 𝐹𝜆 ) ⊗ Φ ( 𝐹𝜇 ) with phase inversion 𝜅 ↦→ −𝜅
(Proposition 12.1.7). The proof relies on the purely double-pole nature of the Heisenberg OPE; see §12.12.3
for the explicit bar-level computation.
    Integrable Kac–Moody modules. For b    𝔤𝑘 at positive integral level, the separating-divisor coproduct of
the chain-level modular functor (Theorem 33.4.13) provides the chain-level fusion map

                       Δsep : 𝐵 (b
                                 𝔤𝑘 , 𝑀1 ⊠𝑘 𝑀2 ) −→ 𝐵 (b
                                                       𝔤𝑘 , 𝑀1 ) ⊗ 𝐵 (b
                                                                      𝔤𝑘 , 𝑀2 ) .

In genus 0, the pants decomposition of M 0,4 yields a natural isomorphism Φ ( 𝑀1 ⊠ A 𝑀2 )  Φ ( 𝑀1 ) ⊠ A !
Φ ( 𝑀2 ) as an exact sequence, which is the genus-0 case of monoidality.
    Genus-1 obstruction. At genus 1, the curvature 𝑚0 ≠ 0 prevents strict monoidality. The obstruction is
controlled by 𝜅 (A) · [M 1,1 ], the curvature times the fundamental class of the genus-1 moduli space: this
is the same invariant that governs the genus-1 quantum correction in Theorem 8.14.12. The full conjecture
and its relation to the Kazhdan–Lusztig programme appear in Theorem 12.12.10.
20.15. Open questions                                                                                   979


20.15     Open questions
Question 20.15.1. The genus-1 pipeline (§20.12) shows that modular forms enter through 𝐸2 via the 𝐵 -cycle
quasi-periodicity of the propagator. What is the complete structure at genus 𝑔 ≥ 2, where the propagator
has 2 𝑔 quasi-periodicity defects? Does the genus- 𝑔 partition function involve Siegel modular forms on
ℌ𝑔 ?
Question 20.15.2. Can we extend beyond simple 𝔤 to affine algebras of twisted type, super Lie algebras, or
exceptional cases?
Question 20.15.3. What is the categorification? Is there a 2-categorical Koszul duality for affine Kac–Moody
categories, lifting the module-level duality of Theorem 9.6.2 to a 2-functor on the 2-category of module
categories?
Question 20.15.4. How does the bar-cobar framework interact with the quantum geometric Langlands
program? The critical-level bar complex provides a chain-level oper resolution (Theorem 20.14.11), and the
admissible-level bar complex is conjectured to recover the KL equivalence (Conjectures 20.14.2–20.14.4).
Does the full genus-graded bar complex (Theorem 31.6.2) provide a chain-level refinement of the quantum
Langlands kernel?

W-algebra Koszul duals

Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction [48, 51] sends the Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤      b𝑘 to the W-algebra W 𝑘 (𝔤, 𝑓 ) by
BRST reduction along a nilpotent element 𝑓 ∈ 𝔤. The result is no longer generated by weight-1 currents
alone. Principal reduction has generator weights at least two, while the subregular 𝔰𝔩 3 reduction retains a
weight-one current. The charged subregular generators have weight 3/2 and even parity.
   The principal 𝔰𝔩 2 and subregular 𝔰𝔩 3 reductions admit explicit unital maps into their full affine–ghost
complexes (Theorems 21.5.2 and 21.9.2). Their proofs preserve the vacuum terms of every binary collision.
Compatibility with a reflected Koszul dual requires a further comparison between levels, as specified in
Remark 21.9.6.

21.2     Reduction parameters and finite Batalin–Vilkovisky
         complexes
Proposition 21.2.1 (Conformal obstruction to parameter reflection). Let 𝑡 ∈ ℂ∗ and put 𝑐 ( 𝑡 ) =
13 − 6( 𝑡 + 𝑡 −1 ). A conformal vertex algebra isomorphism between the universal Virasoro algebras at charges
𝑐 ( 𝑡 ) and 𝑐 (−𝑡 ) exists if and only if 𝑡 = ± 𝑖 .
Proof. A conformal isomorphism preserves the vacuum and conformal vector 𝑇 . It therefore preserves
𝑇(3) 𝑇 = ( 𝑐 /2)1, so the two charges must agree. Since their sum is 26, equality is equivalent to 𝑐 ( 𝑡 ) = 13, or
𝑡 + 𝑡 −1 = 0. This gives 𝑡 = ± 𝑖 . Conversely both universal algebras then have charge 13, and the map sending
their conformal generators to one another is an isomorphism by their identical universal presentation.

   At 𝑡 = −2/3, reflection gives 𝑐 ( 𝑡 ) = 26 and 𝑐 (−𝑡 ) = 0, whereas the reciprocal partner 𝑡 −1 = −3/2
has charge 26. This distinguishes reflection from conformal Feigin–Frenkel duality by an actual vertex

requirements.

    The Virasoro relation for 𝐿 constructs a map 𝜄 𝐿 : Vir𝐶 ( 𝑘 ) → 𝐶𝑘− . Filter its source by assigning degree
two to all derivatives of 𝜔. The PBW basis of the universal Virasoro vacuum module consists of the ordered
products of 𝐿 − 𝑛 , 𝑛 ≥ 2, acting on the vacuum. Its associated graded algebra is ℂ[ 𝜕 𝑟 𝜔 : 𝑟 ≥ 0]. The
associated graded of 𝜄 𝐿 sends 𝜕 𝑟 𝜔 to 𝑤 𝑟 /𝑡 and is a quasi-isomorphism by (21.11). The associated graded of
its mapping cone is acyclic. For a cone cycle, solve its boundary equation in its highest filtration quotient
and subtract that boundary. Induction terminates because the filtration is bounded below. Hence 𝜄 𝐿 is a
quasi-isomorphism.
    Equation (21.8) identifies [𝑇 ] = [ 𝐿 ] in 𝐻 0 ( 𝐶𝑘 ). The two induced vertex homomorphisms agree on
the universal generator, hence agree everywhere. Thus 𝜄𝑇 is a quasi-isomorphism as well. Since its source
has zero differential, an element in its kernel has zero cohomology class in the source and must be zero.
This proves injectivity.

    Theorem 21.5.2 concerns the universal vacuum carrier. It agrees with the PBW and reduction statements
in [272, Theorem 5.8, p. 32; §5.3, p. 33; Example 5.22, p. 39]. No vanishing statement on an unrestricted
category of affine modules is used in the proof. The sign of the character in (21.2) differs from the 𝑒 + 1
convention of [272, §5.1]; the substitution ( 𝑒, 𝑓 , 𝑏, 𝑐 ) ↦→ (−𝑒, − 𝑓 , −𝑏, −𝑐 ) identifies the two conventions.

Proof. Parity preservation sends 𝑏, 𝑐 to zero. The identity 𝑏 (0) 𝑐 = 1 would then send 1 to zero, contradicting

Corollary 21.7.1. The componentwise map

                                         𝐾2 (Vir𝐶 ( 𝑘 ) ) −→ 𝐾2 ( 𝐶𝑘 )

defined by I𝑋 ⊠ I𝑋 on 𝑃 [1] and Δ! I𝑋 on 𝑅 is a quasi-isomorphism.

products of complexes over ℂ preserve quasi-isomorphisms. The localization O 𝑋 2 → O 𝑋 2 (∗Δ) is flat, so

the total map has a two-step filtration with these two acyclic cones as quotients. It is acyclic by the long
exact sequence of cohomology.

    The complex (21.16) retains the unit and is explicitly defined on 𝑋 2 . Its comparison does not require
an augmentation of 𝐶𝑘 . An identification with a reduced chiral bar defined using an augmentation kernel
would require such an augmentation, which is excluded by 𝑏 (0) 𝑐 = 1. An infinite totalization over configu-
ration spaces requires its own definition and convergence theorem; the two-step argument above contains
no such limit.

and 𝐿𝑛 lowers weight by 𝑛 > 0. The orbit of a weight- 𝑁 state lies in the span of the finitely many words in
𝐿1 , . . . , 𝐿 𝑁 with total weight loss at most 𝑁 . The positive part therefore integrates to formal coordinate
changes, and integral 𝐿0 integrates to 𝔾𝑚 . The action is locally finite despite the infinite-dimensional
weight-zero subspace.

Proposition 21.8.1. For every smooth complex algebraic curve 𝑋 and 𝑘 ≠ −2, the map 𝜄𝑇 descends to
a unital quasi-isomorphism of differential chiral algebras

                                            AVir𝐶 ( 𝑘 ) ,𝑋 −→ A𝐶DS𝑘 ,𝑋 .

The local binary collision comparison of Corollary 21.7.1 descends to 𝑋 2 .

Proof. The conformal map 𝜄𝑇 intertwines all 𝐿𝑛 and hence their integrated coordinate actions. Proposi-
tion 21.4.1 says that 𝐷 commutes with the same action. Thus both the sheaf map and its differential are
defined on the associated sheaves. Translation compatibility gives horizontality. The coordinate covariance
of the vertex operation, equivalently the chiral construction in Lemma 21.6.1, glues the collision identity
on overlaps. Its unit is preserved before descent. Locally in an étale coordinate, the underlying complex is
O 𝑋 ⊗ 𝐶𝑘 , so Theorem 21.5.2 proves the quasi-isomorphism. The same local argument applies to the two
terms of (21.16); quasi-isomorphism is local.

    The superscript DS specifies the coordinate action, which uses 𝑇 . For example, 𝑒 and 𝑏 have weight zero,
𝑓 has weight two, and ℎ has third-order conformal pole −2𝑘 1. These are not the three weight-one primary
currents of the Sugawara coordinate action. The proposition therefore does not identify this associated
sheaf with a separately prescribed affine-current bundle using other coordinate transitions. Nor does it
construct compatibility with clutching at nodal curves, a completed chiral bar, or a second semi-infinite
differential. Each such comparison has an additional carrier and an additional intertwining equation.

21.9     An explicit subregular reduction of 𝔰𝔩 3
The subregular reduction has a nonzero weight-one current and two even charged fields. Their vacuum
products determine both the reduction map and its normalization. An integral good grading gives a complex
with two charged ghost pairs and no neutral ghosts.

Proof. Let 𝐶𝑅+ be generated by 𝑎 − 1, 𝑒, 𝑏1 , 𝑏2 . Its vertex products are commutative and its differential is
preserved. Normally ordered multiplication gives a linear map of complexes

                                   𝐶𝑅− ⊗ 𝑅 𝐶𝑅+ −→ 𝐶𝑅 ,              𝑠 ⊗ 𝑡 ↦−→ 𝑠 (−1) 𝑡.

The tensor differential is 𝐷 ( 𝑠 ⊗ 𝑡 ) = 𝐷𝑠 ⊗ 𝑡 + (−1) | 𝑠 | 𝑠 ⊗ 𝐷𝑡 . To prove bijectivity, assign filtration degrees
zero to derivatives of 𝑎, 𝑒, 𝑏 𝑖 , one to derivatives of ℎ, 𝑗, 𝑢, 𝑣, 𝑐 𝑖 , and two to derivatives of 𝐴, 𝐵 . All singular
brackets lower total filtration degree by at least one. The associated graded is the polynomial algebra in the
even jets tensored with the exterior algebra in the odd jets. The changes 𝑎 ↦→ 𝑎 − 1 and (21.18), including
all derivatives, are polynomial and invertible there. Thus multiplication induces a bijection on associated
graded modules. Induction on the nonnegative filtration degree proves the stated linear bijection. The
filtration need not have finite-dimensional pieces. Every individual state has finite degree. This is a tensor
decomposition of complexes, not of vertex algebras.

symbols, which proves linear independence. Given a degree-zero closed state, subtract a linear combination
of these monomials with the same leading symbol. The filtration degree decreases. Repeating terminates
and proves that these monomials span ker( 𝐷 | ( 𝐶𝑅− ) 0 ). There are no degree-minus-one states in 𝐶𝑅− . Thus

                                                              (1)

proves all brackets. They agree with the universal presentation in [278, §2, p. 2]. The PBW theorem proves
that this presentation introduces no further relations.
Corollary 21.9.4 (Special levels and reflection). The current vacuum coefficient is 𝜅 𝐽 = (2𝑘 + 3)/3.
The 𝐺 + , 𝐺 − cubic coefficient is ( 𝑘 + 1) (2𝑘 + 3), and the 𝑇 , 𝑇 quartic coefficient is 𝑐 /2. All three vanish
simultaneously at 𝑘 = −3/2. At 𝑘 = −1/2 they are 2/3, 1, 1/5, respectively. For 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 6 and 𝑘 ≠ −3, the
reflected conformal charges obey
                                               𝑐 ( 𝑘 ) + 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ′ ) = 50.
Equality 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ) = 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ′ ) holds precisely when ( 𝑘 + 3) 2 = −4. Hence a conformal vertex isomorphism at
reflected levels is impossible for all other noncritical parameters.
Proof. The common root follows from the first coefficient and direct substitution in the other two. At
𝑘 = −1/2, the charge is 2/5. Writing 𝑡 = 𝑘 + 3 gives 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ) = 25 − 6𝑡 − 24/𝑡 and 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ′ ) = 25 + 6𝑡 + 24/𝑡 . Their
equality is equivalent to 𝑡 2 = −4. A conformal unital map preserves 𝑇(3) 𝑇 = ( 𝑐 /2)1. At the two exceptional
parameters, this calculation states only equality of charges. It does not construct an isomorphism.

Remark 21.9.6 (The chiral dual after quantum reduction). For a simple Lie algebra 𝔤 and principal nilpotent
𝑓 , the proposed curved chiral comparison is

                                       W 𝑘 (𝔤, 𝑓 ) ! ≃ W − 𝑘 −2ℎ (𝔤, 𝑓 ) .
                                                                 ∨




Its construction requires the affine–ghost collision complex, a unital reduced target, and a comparison that
commutes with the reduction differential and all collision maps. No such map is supplied by replacing a
free-field state space with its cohomology. The actual polynomial comparison is Theorem 30.5.1. Proposi-
tion 21.2.1 excludes a conformal vertex isomorphism under reflection for generic Virasoro parameters. The
curved chiral comparison above therefore needs a separately specified notion of equivalence and preserved
structures. At critical level the Sugawara conformal vector is undefined, so a limiting assertion additionally
requires a construction over the level parameter.
Remark 21.9.7 (Reduction maps and twisting morphisms). A differential 𝑄 DS on the affine–ghost complex
is a degree-one operator, rather than a degree-zero map from the reduced algebra to the affine algebra. It
therefore cannot define an arrow 𝐵¯ (W) → 𝐵¯ (b 𝔤𝑘 ) by bar functoriality. For the polynomial reduction, the
degree-zero maps are the explicit 𝑖, 𝑝 of Theorem 30.5.1. Their associative bar maps preserve tensor length
and commute with the two components of the bar differential. A chiral twisting morphism after quantum
reduction requires the corresponding maps on the full collision complexes.

Remark 21.9.9 (Scope). A proof requires: (1) DS reduction for arbitrary nilpotent 𝑓 (non-standard BRST
complexes); (2) Barbasch–Vogan duality [203] relating O 𝑓 to O 𝑓 𝐷 with component group compatibility;
(3) a level-shift formula 𝑘 ′ = 𝑘 ′ ( 𝑘, 𝑓 ) generalizing 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ . The principal comparison requires the
maps in Remark 21.9.6; the first non-principal family is hook-type; the 𝔰𝔩 3 subregular computation is the
seed. The remaining frontier splits into three exact packets: dual-orbit input (BV/Spaltenstein dictionary),
orbit-indexed level shift, and paired DS seed transport/globalization.

Proposition 21.9.12 (Subregular reduction and reflected parameters; [proved]). For the universal

21.10.4    Coset construction

the Drinfeld–Sokolov approach.

                       Com(𝑉 ′ ,𝑉 ) = {𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 : 𝑎 ( 𝑛 ) 𝑣 = 0 for all 𝑎 ∈ 𝑉 ′ , 𝑛 ≥ 0} .

21.12      Bar complex for W-algebras
21.12.1    The curved differential
The Heisenberg bar complex had a single generator of weight 1 and purely quadratic OPE (§1.1); the Kac–
Moody bar complex had multiple generators but still weight 1 (§20.4). For W-algebras, the generators have
conformal weights ≥ 2, the OPE poles are higher-order, and the bar differential is genuinely non-quadratic
–- this is where the filtered (not merely curved) framework of Theorem 6.9.3 becomes essential.

21.13     Koszul duality for W-algebras: statement and strategy
21.13.1   The main theorem
Remark 21.13.1 (Reﬂected and critical W-algebra comparisons). The parameter reflection 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨
specifies a proposed curved chiral comparison, as in Remark 21.9.6. The reflected central-charge sum for 𝔰𝔩 3
is 100 by Proposition 30.6.2. For 𝔰𝔩 2 , Theorem 21.5.2 and Proposition 21.8.1 construct the actual noncritical
reduction map into the full affine–ghost complex, with its specified coordinate action. Neither this reduc-
tion quasi-isomorphism nor the scalar reflected sum identifies a Koszul dual at the reflected parameter.
Such an identification requires a specified chiral bar construction and a map compatible with its reduction
and collision differentials. At critical level the displayed conformal vector has a pole; specialization requires
a family of complexes over the level parameter and a base-change argument. Feigin–Frenkel reciprocity of
shifted parameters is a different transformation from reflection.

21.13.2    Obstructions to naive Koszul duality
Remark 21.13.2 (Obstructions to naive Koszul duality). The standard bar-cobar construction fails for W-
algebras because:
   (i) Non-quadratic relations. Relations are of degree ≥ 3, so the naive Koszul dual does not close
  (ii) Curvature. 𝑚12 ≠ 0 (the bar differential 𝑑𝐵 always satisfies 𝑑𝐵2 = 0, but the internal differential is
       curved), requiring curved 𝐴∞ technology
 (iii) Higher operations. The 𝐴∞ operations 𝑚3 , 𝑚4 , . . . are all non-zero
 (iv) Convergence. Must verify the infinite series of 𝐴∞ operations converges
1006                                                                     Chapter 21. W-algebra Koszul duals

21.14.4Koszul dual at critical level
Theorem 21.14.4 (Virasoro self-duality at 𝑐 = 0; [proved]). At central charge 𝑐 = 0 (the unique

The Virasoro algebra is Koszul self-dual.

Proof. We give a direct proof via the bar complex, avoiding the Wakimoto realization and its attendant

   Step 2 (Quadratic presentation). The OPE (21.26) is quadratic: the singular terms involve 𝑇 itself (not

generator 𝑇 (conformal weight 2) subject to the quadratic relation 𝑇 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑇 ( 𝑤 ) − 2𝑇 (𝑤 ) ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2 −

                                                                           𝑖,𝑗

the bigrading is by bar degree and weight. This is verified: the bar complex has 𝐵¯ 𝑛 supported in weight
≥ 2𝑛 (from 𝑛 copies of 𝑇 , each of weight 2), with equality achieved only on the diagonal 𝑗 = 2 𝑖 . The

21.14.5   Genus-1 pipeline for the Virasoro algebra
The genus-0 bar complex 𝐵¯ (Vir𝑐 ) (Computation above) has curvature 𝑚0 = 𝑐 /2 from the quartic pole
𝑇(3) 𝑇 = 𝑐 /2, giving a curved 𝐴∞ structure for 𝑐 ≠ 0. The genus-1 pipeline lifts the bar complex to the
torus 𝐸𝜏 and computes all three main-theorem invariants, paralleling the 𝔰𝔩  b 2 pipeline (§20.12).
   Unlike the Kac–Moody bar complex, which is uncurved at genus 0 ( 𝑑02 = 0, reflecting the Jacobi
identity) with genus-1 curvature 𝑚0(1) = ( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) · 𝜔1 arising entirely from the 𝐵 -cycle monodromy, the
Virasoro bar complex is already curved at genus 0 (𝑚0 = 𝑐 /2, reflecting the quartic pole). The 𝐵 -cycle
monodromy at genus 1 promotes this scalar curvature to a cohomology class on M 1,1 .

Remark 21.14.10 (Bosonic string interpretation). The special role of 𝑐 = 26 in bosonic string theory receives
a structural explanation from complementarity. The BRST complex of the bosonic string requires 𝑐matter +
𝑐ghost = 0, i.e., 𝑐 + (−26) = 0, which selects 𝑐 = 26. In the bar-cobar framework: Vir!26 ≃ Vir0 is the
uncurved self-dual algebra, so the genus-1 bar complex of Vir26 has its curvature ‘‘absorbed’’ by the exactness
of the dual–-the obstructions of Vir26 are precisely the deformations of Vir0 .

21.15.6   Koszul dual of W3
Remark 21.15.7 (The reﬂected W-three comparison). The parameter reflection 𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ specifies a
proposed curved chiral comparison, as in Remark 21.9.6. The reflected central-charge sum for 𝔰𝔩 3 is 100 by
Proposition 30.6.2. For𝔰𝔩 2 , Theorem 21.5.2 and Proposition 21.8.1 construct the actual noncritical reduction
map into the full affine–ghost complex, with its specified coordinate action. Neither this reduction quasi-
isomorphism nor the scalar reflected sum identifies a Koszul dual at the reflected parameter. Such an
identification requires a specified chiral bar construction and a map compatible with its reduction and
collision differentials. At critical level the displayed conformal vector has a pole; specialization requires a
family of complexes over the level parameter and a base-change argument. Feigin–Frenkel reciprocity of
shifted parameters is a different transformation from reflection.

21.15.7   Genus-1 pipeline for the W3 algebra
The genus-0 bar complex of W3𝑘 has curvature from two independent channels: 𝑚0(𝑇 ) = 𝑐 /2 (quartic pole
of 𝑇 𝑇 ) and 𝑚0(𝑊 ) = 𝑐 /3 (sixth-order pole of 𝑊𝑊 ); see Computation 21.27.29. The genus-1 pipeline
lifts the bar complex to the torus 𝐸𝜏 and verifies the three main theorems, paralleling the Virasoro pipeline
(§21.14.5) and the 𝔰𝔩
                   b 2 pipeline (§20.12).
    Unlike the Virasoro algebra, which has a single generator 𝑇 , giving a single curvature channel 𝜅 = 𝑐 /2.
The W3 algebra has two generators 𝑇 (weight 2) and 𝑊 (weight 3), producing two independent vacuum
leakages whose sum gives the total obstruction coefficient 𝜅 = 𝑐 /2 + 𝑐 /3 = 5𝑐 /6. The cross-terms 𝑇 ⊗ 𝑊
and 𝑊 ⊗ 𝑇 contribute no vacuum leakage (the 𝑇𝑊 OPE has at most a double pole), so the curvature
is purely ‘‘diagonal’’ in the generator space. This two-channel split is the chain-level manifestation of
Θ W3 (Theorem 8.18.36): the genus-1 component 𝜃 1 = (5𝑐 /6) · 𝜇𝑊3 ⊗ 𝜆1 carries both the 𝑇 -channel ( 𝑐 /2)
and the 𝑊 -channel ( 𝑐 /3) as separate coderivation components, but their sum 𝜅 = 5𝑐 /6 is the unique
scalar controlled by 𝐻cyc2  ℂ. Dually, the complementarity sum 𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 500/6 reflects Θ + Θ! =

(500/6) · 𝜂 ⊗ Λ, the Lagrangian splitting of the quantum corrections.

Remark 21.15.10 (W3 minimal model levels). At W3 minimal model levels ( 𝑘 such that 𝑐 = 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 with

with 𝑐 = −22/5, where non-trivial null vectors appear.

Proof. Since 𝜅 = 𝑐 · ( 𝐻𝑁 − 1) and 𝜅 ′ = 𝑐 ′ · ( 𝐻𝑁 − 1): 𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = ( 𝐻𝑁 − 1) ( 𝑐 + 𝑐 ′ ). The complementarity

21.16.3    Orbit duality
Deﬁnition 21.16.5 (Dual nilpotent orbits). For a nilpotent orbit O ⊂ 𝔤, the Barbasch–Vogan dual orbit

   For classical groups:
• Partition 𝜆 of 𝑛 ↔ partition 𝜆𝑇 (transpose)
• Principal ( 𝑛) ↔ trivial (1𝑛 )
• Subregular ( 𝑛 − 1, 1) ↔ minimal (2, 1𝑛−2 )

Example 21.16.6 (Orbit duality for 𝔰𝔩 𝑛 ). For 𝔰𝔩 3 :

                                      Orbit type      Partition     Dual partition
                                       Principal         (3)           (1, 1, 1)
                                      Subregular        (2, 1)          (2, 1)
                                         Zero          (1, 1, 1)         (3)
   For 𝔰𝔩 3 , the principal and zero orbits are exchanged by partition transpose. The minimal nonzero orbit
equals the subregular orbit (2, 1) and is self-dual.
   For 𝔰𝔩 4 :

                                      Orbit type      Partition     Dual partition
                                      Principal          (4)          (1, 1, 1, 1)
                                        (3, 1)          (3, 1)         (2, 1, 1)
                                        (2, 2)         (2, 2)           (2, 2)
   Here partition duality is no longer trivial: (3, 1) and (2, 1, 1) are exchanged.

21.17      Curved 𝐴∞ structures
21.17.1 Necessity of 𝐴∞ structures
Remark 21.17.1 (Necessity of 𝐴∞ ). For W-algebras, the following all force us beyond DG algebras:
   (i) 𝑚12 ≠ 0: Curvature element 𝑚0 prevents 𝑚1 from being a differential
  (ii) Non-quadratic relations: products of generators do not close in low degrees
 (iii) High-order poles: OPEs have poles of order > 2
 (iv) Homotopy coherence: Must satisfy higher associativity up to homotopy
   The minimal structure capturing this is a curved 𝐴∞ algebra.
Deﬁnition 21.17.2 (Curved 𝐴∞ algebra). A curved 𝐴∞ algebra is a ℤ-graded vector space 𝐴 with:
• Operations: 𝑚𝑛 : 𝐴⊗ 𝑛 → 𝐴 of degree 2 − 𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 0
• Curvature: 𝑚0 ∈ 𝐴 (degree 2 element)
• Differential: 𝑚1 : 𝐴 → 𝐴 with 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎]
• Product: 𝑚2 : 𝐴 ⊗ 𝐴 → 𝐴
• Higher operations: 𝑚𝑛 for 𝑛 ≥ 3
   Satisfying the curved 𝐴∞ relations:
                                    (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝑚𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝑚 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0
                              ∑︁
                                  𝑛=𝑟 + 𝑠 +𝑡

for all 𝑛 ≥ 0 (where the 𝑛 = 0 relation encodes curvature as a cocycle).
Remark 21.17.3 (Decoding the relations). The first few relations are (with 𝑛 = 𝑟 + 𝑠 + 𝑡 ):
          𝑛 = 0 : 𝑚1 ( 𝑚0 ) = 0
          𝑛 = 1 : 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = 𝑚2 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎) − 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚0 )
          𝑛 = 2 : 𝑚1 ( 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑏 )) = 𝑚2 ( 𝑚1 ( 𝑎) , 𝑏 ) + (−1) | 𝑎 | 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚1 ( 𝑏 )) + 𝑚3 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎, 𝑏 ) + · · ·

   These encode that curvature is a cocycle, the differential squares to curvature, and the Leibniz rule holds
up to higher homotopy.

21.18     Applications and physical interpretations
21.18.1   4d gauge theory and AGT correspondence
Conjecture 21.18.1 (AGT correspondence –- W-algebra version; [conjectured]). For 4d N = 2 gauge theory
with gauge group 𝐺 on ℝ2 × 𝐶 𝑔 in Ω-background ( 𝜖1 , 𝜖2 ), the Nekrasov partition function equals a
W 𝑘 ( 𝐺 ) conformal block:
                                  𝐺,𝐶 𝑔
                                ZNek ( 𝜖1 , 𝜖2 ; 𝑎®, 𝑞 ) = ⟨𝑉1 | 𝑞 𝐿0 |𝑉2 ⟩ W 𝑘 ( 𝐺 )
where 𝑘 is determined by ( 𝜖1 , 𝜖2 ). W-algebra Koszul duality corresponds to S-duality in the gauge theory.
(Part of the MC2 theorem package; Theorem 8.18.72.)
Remark 21.18.2 (Scope: AGT correspondence). A proof requires localization on the instanton moduli space
and identification of contributions with W-algebra matrix elements; see Alday–Gaiotto–Tachikawa [107].
The gauge-theory comparison requires a map from its observable complex to the stated chiral target.

21.19     The three theorems for W-algebras
Remark 21.19.1 (Main theorems for W-algebras). This chapter verifies Theorems A, B, and C for principal
W 𝑘 (𝔤). The proposed chiral equivalence in Remark 21.9.6 requires a Wakimoto resolution with its full
ghost complex and equivariant collision maps. The scalar level reflection alone does not construct this
equivalence. Theorem B gives strict inversion at 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ (Theorem 20.1.2) and spectral sequence collapse
at genus 1 for Vir𝑐 and W3𝑘 . Theorem C gives complementarity 𝑄 1 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 1 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 1,1 ) with
𝜅 (W𝑁 ) = 𝑐 · ( 𝐻𝑁 − 1) (Theorem 21.15.14).

Example 21.20.8 (Logarithmic Virasoro modules at 𝑐 = 25). At the Ising model value 𝑐 = 1/2 ( 𝑘 = −2 + 4/3,
𝑝 = 4, 𝑞 = 3 for 𝔰𝔩 2 ), the Koszul dual central charge is 𝑐 ′ = 51/2 = 25 21 . The Vir𝑐 ′ algebra is non-rational at
𝑐 ′ > 25: the module category is non-semisimple.
    More precisely, for the general Virasoro minimal model 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 with Koszul dual 𝑐 ′𝑝,𝑞 = 26 − 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 :
   (i) At 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 : rational, with ( 𝑝 − 1) ( 𝑞 − 1)/2 simple modules (the Kac table).
  (ii) At 𝑐 ′𝑝,𝑞 : non-rational. The module category contains indecomposable modules with logarithmic
       couplings (rank-2 Jordan blocks for 𝐿0 ). The extension groups are controlled by the bar complex at
       the dual level, which has non-trivial higher differentials corresponding to the curved 𝐴∞ structure
       (§21.20).
As a conjectural extension ([conjectured]) of the complementarity theorem (Theorem 8.14.12), which is
proved for Koszul pairs at generic level, we posit that the obstructions to rationality at 𝑐 ′𝑝,𝑞 are dual to the
deformations at 𝑐 𝑝,𝑞 : the logarithmic structure at the Koszul dual level is conjecturally controlled by the
rational structure at the original level.
Remark 21.20.9 (Modiﬁed Verlinde formula for logarithmic W-algebras). For 𝐶2 -cofinite non-rational
vertex algebras (triplet W ( 𝑝), singlet M ( 𝑝)), the classical Verlinde formula (Theorem 12.1.24) is replaced
by the modified formula of Creutzig–Ridout [115]: the 𝑆 -matrix acts on pseudo-trace functions (traces over
projective modules). In the bar framework, this corresponds to using indecomposable projective modules;
the higher bar spectral sequence differentials–-trivial in the rational case–-encode logarithmic fusion rules.

and the Higgs bundle moduli space?

21.22.3    Central charge dependence
                                                                                    16
Theorem 21.22.5 (Central charge scaling; [proved]). The OPE coefficient 𝛼 ( 𝑐 ) = 22+5 𝑐 multiplying
Λ in the 𝑊 –𝑊 OPE has the following properties:
   (i) Pole at 𝑐 = −22/5 = −4.4. The composite field diverges
  (ii) 𝑐 → ∞ limit. 𝛼 ( 𝑐 ) → 0 (classical limit, no quantum correction)
                             16
 (iii) 𝑐 = 2 (Toda). 𝛼 (2) = 32 = 21
                                            4
 (iv) 𝑐 = −2 (minimal model). 𝛼 (−2) = 16
                                       12 = 3
                                     16
  (v) 𝑐 = 100 (large 𝑐 ). 𝛼 (100) = 522 ≈ 0.0307
Physical interpretation. Case 1: 𝑐 = −22/5 (pole).
   At this value, the denominator 22 + 5𝑐 = 0, so 𝛼 → ∞. This is a critical central charge where the 𝑊3
algebra degenerates.
   The coefficient 𝛼 diverges, indicating a degeneration of the 𝑊3 algebra structure.
   Case 2: 𝑐 → ∞ (classical limit).
   As 𝑐 → ∞, 𝛼 → 0, so the full ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2 coefficient in the 𝑊 –𝑊 OPE becomes:
                                        3 2             𝑐 →∞
                                       10 𝜕 𝑇 + 𝛼 Λ    −−−−−→ 103 𝜕 2𝑇
   The : 𝑇 𝑇 : contribution (contained in Λ) vanishes, leaving only the derivative term. This is the classical
Poisson bracket limit.
   Case 3: 𝑐 = 2 (Toda ﬁeld theory).
   For 𝔰𝔩 3 Toda theory, 𝑐 = 2 gives 𝛼 (2) = 1/2. The full ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2 coefficient is:
                        3 2      1       1         3      1
                                                             2        1          3 2
                       10 𝜕 𝑇 + 2 Λ = 2 :𝑇 𝑇 : + 10 1 − 2 𝜕 𝑇 = 2 :𝑇 𝑇 : + 20 𝜕 𝑇

   Both terms have comparable magnitude.
   Physically: This is the free field realization of 𝑊3 using two free bosons.
   Case 4: 𝑐 = −2.
   At 𝑐 = −2 (which arises from the DS formula at 𝑘 = −3/2 or 𝑘 = −7/3):
                                                       4
                                                 𝛼 (−2) =
                                                       3
   The composite field coefficient is LARGER than in the Toda case, indicating strong quantum effects.
   Physically: Minimal models are highly quantum, with finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces.
   Case 5: 𝑐 = 100 (large 𝑐 ).
   At 𝑐 = 100:
                                         𝛼 (100) ≈ 0.0307 ≪ 1
   The composite field is small, approaching the classical limit.
   Physically: Large 𝑐 CFTs are weakly coupled, nearly classical.

         16

Both values are convention-independent: they depend only on 𝑐 and the Virasoro algebra structure, not
on the normalization of 𝑊 . Different normalizations of 𝑊 (e.g., Fateev–Lukyanov vs. Zamolodchikov)
change the overall coefficient of Λ in the 𝑊𝑊 OPE, but not Λ itself or the ratio 𝛼 .

21.22.7    Computational verification: Jacobi identity
Computation 21.22.9 (Jacobi identity check). We verify the Jacobi identity:
                      [ 𝐿𝑚 , [𝑊𝑛 ,𝑊𝑝 ]] + [𝑊𝑛 , [𝑊𝑝 , 𝐿𝑚 ]] + [𝑊𝑝 , [ 𝐿𝑚 ,𝑊𝑛 ]] = 0
   explicitly for low modes 𝑚, 𝑛, 𝑝 ∈ {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2}.
   Example: 𝑚 = 0, 𝑛 = 1, 𝑝 = −1.
   Since [𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ] has mode number 0 and Λ has conformal weight 4, we have [ 𝐿0 , Λ0 ] = 0 (the zero
mode of a primary field of weight ℎ satisfies [ 𝐿0 , Φ𝑛 ] = −𝑛Φ𝑛 ). Thus [ 𝐿0 , [𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ]] = 0.
   For the remaining terms: [ 𝐿0 ,𝑊−1 ] = (0 − (−1))𝑊−1 = 𝑊−1 (using [ 𝐿𝑚 ,𝑊𝑛 ] = (2𝑚 − 𝑛)𝑊𝑚+𝑛
at 𝑚 = 0), so [𝑊−1 , 𝐿0 ] = −𝑊−1 and [𝑊1 , [𝑊−1 , 𝐿0 ]] = −[𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ]. Similarly [ 𝐿0 ,𝑊1 ] = −𝑊1 , so
[𝑊−1 , [ 𝐿0 ,𝑊1 ]] = −[𝑊−1 ,𝑊1 ] = [𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ].
   The sum is 0 − [𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ] + [𝑊1 ,𝑊−1 ] = 0, confirming the Jacobi identity.
   For non-trivial checks (e.g., 𝑚 = 1, 𝑛 = 2, 𝑝 = −3), the Jacobi identity constrains the coefficient of
𝐿𝑚+𝑛 in the 𝑊 –𝑊 OPE to be:
                                              ( 𝑚 − 𝑛) (2𝑚2 − 𝑚𝑛 + 2𝑛2 − 8)
                                𝛾 ( 𝑚, 𝑛) =
                                                            30
   With this complete formula, the Jacobi identity holds for all modes.

21.22.12    Null vectors and degenerate 𝑊3 representations
At special values of the conformal weight ℎ, the 𝑊3 charge 𝑤 , and the central charge 𝑐 , the 𝑊3 Verma

Remark 21.22.19 (Comparison with Virasoro null vectors). In the Virasoro algebra, the level-1 null vector
𝐿 −1 | ℎ⟩ = 0 requires only ℎ = 0 (one condition). For 𝑊3 , the level-1 null vector imposes one condition
relating ℎ, 𝑤 , and 𝑐 (equation (21.27)), reflecting the extra quantum number 𝑤 . The null vector curve in
the ( ℎ, 𝑤 )-plane is a non-trivial algebraic curve depending on 𝑐 , in contrast with the Virasoro case where
the null conditions are discrete points in the ( ℎ, 𝑐 )-plane.
Proposition 21.22.20 (Null vectors and bar complex relations; [proved]). A null vector | 𝜒ℓ ⟩
at level ℓ in the 𝑊3 Verma module M𝑊3 ( 𝑐, ℎ, 𝑤 ) corresponds to a relation in the bar complex 𝐵¯ (W3 )
restricted to the ( 𝑐, ℎ, 𝑤 )-sector. Specifically, if 𝑑𝐵¯ denotes the bar differential, then the element 𝜉ℓ ∈ 𝐵¯ 1
corresponding to | 𝜒ℓ ⟩ satisfies 𝑑𝐵¯ ( 𝜉ℓ ) = 0 and is exact: 𝜉ℓ = 𝑑𝐵¯ ( 𝜂 ) for some 𝜂 ∈ 𝐵¯ 0 .
    In particular, the bar cohomology 𝐻 1 ( 𝐵¯ (W3 )) at weight ℎ + ℓ has strictly lower dimension for degen-
erate representations (where null vectors exist) than for generic representations.

Proof. The bar complex 𝐵¯ 1 (W3 ) at weight ℎ + ℓ is spanned by elements of the form 𝑠 −1 𝜙 where 𝜙 runs
over weight-( ℎ + ℓ ) states in the augmentation ideal W 3 (cf. Construction 21.15.5). A null vector | 𝜒ℓ ⟩
in the Verma module is, by definition, a state annihilated by all positive modes. In the bar complex, this
translates to an element 𝜉ℓ ∈ 𝐵¯ 1 for which 𝑑1 ( 𝜉ℓ ) = 0 (the component of 𝑑𝐵¯ from the linear part of the
OPE).
21.22. The 𝑊3 composite field: all coefficients explicit                                                         1037


    The element is exact because the null vector is a descendant: | 𝜒ℓ ⟩ = 𝑃 ( 𝐿 − 𝑛 ,𝑊− 𝑚 )| ℎ, 𝑤 ⟩ for some
polynomial 𝑃 in the negative modes. This polynomial 𝑃 corresponds to an element 𝜂 ∈ 𝐵¯ 0 (the degree-0
bar complex at weight ℎ + ℓ , which records the descendants) such that 𝑑𝐵¯ ( 𝜂 ) = 𝜉ℓ .
    The consequence for bar cohomology follows: each null vector at level ℓ converts a potential cohomology
class in 𝐻 1 ( 𝐵¯ ℎ+ℓ ) into an exact element, reducing dim 𝐻 1 by one. For minimal model representations
(where the maximal number of null vectors occur), this reduction is responsible for the finite-dimensionality
of the bar cohomology (cf. Example 21.20.5).

21.22.13   The 𝑊3 Kac determinant
The Kac determinant for the 𝑊3 algebra generalizes the Virasoro Kac determinant (Kac [76]) to a two-
parameter family indexed by ( ℎ, 𝑤 ). Its vanishing locus determines the degenerate representations.

Remark 21.22.25 (Kac determinant and bar complex ﬁltration). The 𝑊3 Kac determinant controls the bar
complex of W3 as follows. The bar complex 𝐵¯ • (W3 ) has a weight filtration by 𝐿0 eigenvalue; at weight
ℎ + ℓ , the rank of the Gram matrix 𝑀ℓ determines the dimension of the non-degenerate part of 𝐵¯ 1 in that
weight sector. When det 𝑀ℓ = 0 (i.e., a null vector appears), the bar cohomology changes:
  (i) At det 𝑀ℓ ≠ 0 (generic): the bar complex at weight ℎ + ℓ is acyclic in degree 1, and the spectral
      sequence from Theorem 6.12.6 has 𝐸11,ℓ = 0.
 (ii) At det 𝑀ℓ = 0 (degenerate): the bar complex acquires non-trivial cohomology 𝐻 1 ( 𝐵¯ ℎ+ℓ ) ≠ 0,
      and the spectral sequence has additional generators at 𝐸11,ℓ corresponding to the null vectors
      (Proposition 21.22.20).
   For the 𝑊3 minimal models, the Kac determinant vanishes at infinitely many levels (all ℓ = 𝑟 𝑠 with
1 ≤ 𝑟 ≤ 𝑞 − 1, 1 ≤ 𝑠 ≤ 𝑝 − 1), and the resulting bar complex has finite-dimensional cohomology groups,
consistent with the rationality of these models.

21.23     Minimal model fusion rules via Verlinde formula
21.23.1   Recollection: Verlinde formula
Theorem 21.23.1 (Verlinde formula, general form [29]; [proved]). For a rational conformal field
theory with modular-invariant partition function, the fusion coefficients 𝑁𝑖𝑗𝑘 are given by:

                                        𝑟 −1 𝑆 𝑆 ( 𝑆 −1 )          𝑟 −1 𝑆 𝑆 𝑆 ∗
                                        ∑︁    𝑖ℓ 𝑗 ℓ      ℓ𝑘       ∑︁    𝑖ℓ 𝑗 ℓ ℓ 𝑘
                               𝑁𝑖𝑗𝑘 =                          =
                                        ℓ =0
                                                  𝑆0ℓ              ℓ =0
                                                                              𝑆0ℓ

where:
• 𝑆 is the modular S-matrix: 𝑆𝑖𝑗 = ⟨ 𝑖 | 𝑆 : 𝜏 → −1/ 𝜏 | 𝑗 ⟩
• 𝑟 is the number of primary fields
• 𝑁𝑖𝑗𝑘 counts the number of times primary 𝑘 appears in 𝑖 × 𝑗 OPE
Remark 21.23.2 (Witten’s interpretation). Witten showed that the Verlinde formula can be understood via
Chern–Simons theory on 𝑆 3 , moduli spaces of flat connections, and geometric quantization of character
varieties.

Remark 21.23.6 (W3 primary labeling). The single-pair labeling Φ𝑟,𝑠 is a simplification. Properly, 𝑊3

dimensions and fusion rules require the Fateev–Lukyanov Kac formula for 𝑊3 .

21.23.7    Fusion matrices for M (4, 3)
Theorem 21.23.13 (Virasoro fusion rules for M (4 , 3) [46]; [proved]). After the identification
Φ𝑟,𝑠 ∼ Φ𝑞 − 𝑟, 𝑝 − 𝑠 , the three Virasoro primaries of M (4, 3) are 𝕀 = Φ1,1 (identity, ℎ = 0), 𝜎 = Φ1,2 ( ℎ =
1/16), and 𝜀 = Φ1,3 ( ℎ = 1/2). Their fusion rules are:

                                      𝕀×Φ=Φ           for all primaries Φ
                                      𝜎 ×𝜎 =𝕀+𝜀
                                      𝜎×𝜀=𝜎
                                       𝜀×𝜀 =𝕀

This is the Ising model fusion algebra, which is commutative, associative, and generated by 𝜎 with relation
𝜎 2 = 𝕀 + 𝜀 and 𝜀 = 𝜎 2 − 𝕀.
Remark 21.23.14 (Virasoro vs. 𝑊3 fusion rules). These are Virasoro fusion rules; the 𝑊3 (4, 3) rules require
𝐴2 weight labeling (Section 21.23.3).

Remark 21.23.24 (Golden ratio structure). The appearance of 𝜑 = (1 + 5)/2 in the quantum dimensions
and fusion rules of M (5, 4) is a manifestation of the 𝐴4 Dynkin diagram structure: the quantum dimen-
sions of 𝕀, 𝜀 ′ , 𝜀 ′′ , 𝜀 ′′′ are 1, 𝜑, 𝜑, 1, which are the components of the Perron–Frobenius eigenvector of the
𝐴4 adjacency matrix. This pattern extends: for M ( 𝑝, 𝑝−1), the quantum dimensions of the first-row fields
Φ1,𝑠 are 𝑈𝑠 −1 ( 𝜑 𝑝 /2) where 𝜑 𝑝 = 2 cos( 𝜋 / 𝑝).
