Strategy III: Reduction to the Kazhdan–Lusztig problem.
Proposition 24.8.28 (Thick generation via projective resolutions; [proved]). Let O be a highest-
weight category with finite global dimension, and let Ceval ⊂ 𝐷 𝑏 (O) be the thick subcategory generated
24.8. Yangian representation theory and bar modules                                                         1161


by evaluation modules. Then Ceval = 𝐷 𝑏 (O) if and only if every projective indecomposable 𝑃 ( 𝜆) of O
admits a finite resolution
                            0 → 𝐹𝑛 → · · · → 𝐹1 → 𝐹0 → 𝑃 ( 𝜆) → 0                               (24.10)
with each 𝐹𝑖 ∈ Ceval .

Proof. (⇒): If Ceval = 𝐷 𝑏 (O), then 𝑃 ( 𝜆) ∈ 𝐷 𝑏 (O) = Ceval and such a resolution exists by definition of
thick closure.
    (⇐): Suppose every 𝑃 ( 𝜆) admits a finite evaluation resolution (24.10). Then 𝑃 ( 𝜆) ∈ Ceval . Since O
has finite global dimension, every object 𝑀 ∈ O admits a finite projective resolution. Each projective term
lies in Ceval , so 𝑀 ∈ Ceval by iterated cones. Every object of 𝐷 𝑏 (O) is a bounded complex of objects of O,
hence lies in Ceval .

Remark 24.8.29 (Kazhdan–Lusztig input for Yangian category O). For 𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ), Proposition 24.8.28
reduces thick generation to two inputs:
(a) Finite global dimension. For truncated shifted Yangians, this follows from the Brundan–Kleshchev
    equivalence [55] with parabolic BGG category O for 𝔤𝔩 𝑀 , which has finite global dimension. For
    the full Yangian 𝑌 (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ), the corresponding finiteness remains conjectural and is motivated by the
    analogous structure of Hernandez’s category Oℤ [53].
(b) Projective modules in evaluation thick closure. The projective covers 𝑃 ( 𝜆) in O have Verma flags
    with multiplicities ( 𝑃 ( 𝜆) : 𝑀 ( 𝜇)) given by Kazhdan–Lusztig polynomials (via BGG reciprocity:
    ( 𝑃 ( 𝜆) : 𝑀 ( 𝜇)) = [ 𝑀 ( 𝜇) : 𝐿 ( 𝜆)]). The combinatorial data is accessible from the KL theory for
    Yangians developed by Brundan–Kleshchev [55] and Kang–Kashiwara–Kim–Oh [56]. The remaining
    step is to show that the Verma modules appearing in these flags lie in Ceval , connecting to Strategy I.
This is the most classical approach: the combinatorial structure is provided by the KL theory, and the
analytical input reduces to resolvability of Verma modules. For type 𝐴, the Brundan–Kleshchev equivalence
makes the finite global dimension unconditional.

Strategy II: t-structure argument.
    This is now proved: Lemma 24.8.11 and Theorem 24.8.12 implement Strategy II completely. The key
insight (Remark 24.8.13) is that thick generation reduces to the finite-dimensionality of simples, which
holds unconditionally for 𝔰𝔩 2 and for the polynomial subcategory Opoly at all 𝑁 .
Remark 24.8.30 (Residual obstruction beyond polynomial category O). The remaining question at 𝑁 ≥ 3
(Remark 24.8.13(iii)) is whether the polynomial subcategory Opoly exhausts the DK-relevant category O. If
not, the infinite-dimensional simples 𝐿 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) at non-polynomial ℓ -weights are the precise obstruction.
   In the classical setting (without the Yangian spectral parameter), infinite-dimensional simples
at non-integral weight are orthogonal to all finite-dimensional modules (different blocks of BGG
category O). The Yangian spectral parameter creates inter-block extensions: the 𝑅-matrix poles at
𝑎 − 𝑏 ∈ {0, ±1, . . . , ±( 𝑁 − 1)} produce nontrivial Ext𝑌1 (𝑉𝑛 ( 𝑏 ) , 𝐿 ( 𝜆, 𝑎)) connecting finite-dimensional
and infinite-dimensional modules. Whether these extensions suffice for thick generation beyond Opoly is
the residual content of the generation problem at 𝑁 ≥ 3.

Strategy I: Highest-weight filtration and BGG resolution.
1162                                                         Chapter 24. Yangians and shifted Yangians


Proposition 24.8.31 (BGG resolution criterion for thick generation; [proved]). Thick generation
of 𝐷 𝑏 (O𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) ) by evaluation modules holds if every Verma module 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) ∈ O𝑌ℏ admits a finite
resolution
                               0 → 𝐸𝑚 → · · · → 𝐸1 → 𝐸0 → 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) → 0                         (24.11)
with each 𝐸𝑖 a finite direct sum of evaluation modules 𝑉𝜇 ( 𝑏 ) (𝑉𝜇 finite-dimensional).

Proof. If (24.11) holds, then 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) ∈ Ceval by iterated cones. Every simple 𝐿 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) is a quotient of
𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎); the kernel is a module of O of strictly shorter composition length. By induction on length, all
simples lie in Ceval . Lemma 24.8.11 then gives Ceval = 𝐷 𝑏 (O).

Remark 24.8.32 (BGG resolution via spectral parameter extensions). For dominant integral 𝜆, the Verma
module 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) surjects onto the finite-dimensional evaluation module 𝐿 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) with kernel 𝑀 ( 𝜇, 𝑎)
at lower weight 𝜇 = 𝑠 𝛼 · 𝜆. Iterating along the Weyl group orbit produces the classical BGG resolution, all
of whose terms are Verma evaluation modules at the same spectral parameter 𝑎.
    For non-dominant 𝜆, the classical BGG resolution is unavailable: 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) is simple at fixed 𝑎. The
Yangian structure opens a new channel: evaluation at different spectral parameters. The 𝑅-matrix inter-
twiner
                             𝑅𝑉 ,𝑊 ( 𝑎 − 𝑏 ) : 𝑉 ( 𝑎) ⊗ 𝑊 ( 𝑏 ) → 𝑊 ( 𝑏 ) ⊗ 𝑉 ( 𝑎)
has poles at 𝑎 − 𝑏 ∈ {0, ±1, . . . , ±( 𝑁 − 1)} (for fundamental representations of 𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ). At these poles, the
residues create nontrivial extensions between evaluation modules at distinct spectral parameters.
    For 𝔰𝔩 2 : the 𝑅-matrix pole at 𝑎 − 𝑏 = ±1 produces extensions

                                     0 → 𝑉𝑛 ( 𝑎) → 𝐸 → 𝑉𝑚 ( 𝑎 + 1) → 0

for appropriate 𝑛, 𝑚. Iterating such extensions along a chain of spectral parameters 𝑎, 𝑎 + 1, 𝑎 + 2, . . .
builds complexes whose totalization approaches Verma-type modules. Whether this process terminates in
a ﬁnite resolution (24.11) is the key analytical question. For 𝔰𝔩 2 , the Ext groups Ext𝑛O (𝑉𝑚 ( 𝑏 ) , 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎)) are
computable from the 𝑞 -character theory of Hernandez [53], and finiteness of the resolution would follow
from eventual vanishing of these Ext groups at large spectral parameter separation | 𝑎 − 𝑏 |.

Proposition 24.8.34 (Heart-capture criterion; [proved]). Let A be a finite-length abelian category
and T ⊂ 𝐷 𝑏 (A) a thick triangulated subcategory. If every simple object of A lies in T , then T = 𝐷 𝑏 (A).

Proof. By induction on Jordan–Hölder length, every object of A lies in T : if 0 → 𝐾 → 𝑀 → 𝑆 → 0
is exact with 𝑆 simple and length( 𝐾 ) < length( 𝑀 ), then 𝐾 ∈ T by the inductive hypothesis and 𝑆 ∈ T
by assumption, so the cone of 𝐾 → 𝑀 places 𝑀 in T . For the full derived category, every bounded
complex 𝑋 • is built from its cohomology objects by canonical truncation triangles: 𝜏≤ 𝑛−1 𝑋 → 𝜏≤ 𝑛 𝑋 →
𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) [−𝑛], so by induction on cohomological amplitude, 𝑋 • ∈ T .
Proposition 24.8.35 (Standard-capture criterion; [proved]). Let A be a finite-length highest-
weight category with finite weight poset Λ and standard objects {Δ ( 𝜆)} 𝜆 ∈ Λ . Let T ⊂ 𝐷 𝑏 (A) be a thick
subcategory. If every standard object Δ ( 𝜆) ∈ T , then T = 𝐷 𝑏 (A).

Proof. Induct on the weight poset. For a maximal 𝜆, Δ ( 𝜆) = 𝐿 ( 𝜆), so 𝐿 ( 𝜆) ∈ T . For general 𝜆, the
quotient Δ ( 𝜆) ↠ 𝐿 ( 𝜆) has kernel filtered by simples 𝐿 ( 𝜇) with 𝜇 > 𝜆, all of which lie in T by induc-
tion. Since Δ ( 𝜆) ∈ T and the kernel is in T , the cone construction places 𝐿 ( 𝜆) ∈ T . Heart-capture
(Proposition 24.8.34) then gives T = 𝐷 𝑏 (A).

    The theorematic part of Strategy IV is already settled on the evaluation-generated core by Theo-

Remark 24.8.48 (Corrected MC3 frontier). Theorem 24.8.41 closes the thick generation problem:
                                    Dℏeval = 𝐷 𝑏 (Repfd ) ⊊ 𝐷 𝑏 (O𝑌ℏ ) .
The left equality is the theorem; the strict inclusion follows from Lemma 24.8.22 whenever O𝑌ℏ contains
infinite-dimensional objects (Verma or asymptotic modules). No further enlargement of the thick closure
is possible within ordinary 𝐷 𝑏 (O).
    The remaining MC3 frontier therefore splits into two layers. Within ordinary 𝐷 𝑏 (O), thick generation
by evaluation modules is completely resolved: it yields exactly 𝐷 𝑏 (Repfd ). Extending DK beyond Repfd
requires a completed or coderived enhancement and reopens the generation problem in that enlarged
setting.
(a) If the factorization DK conjecture (Conjecture 24.9.8) targets the evaluation-generated core, then
    DK-2/3 is unconditionally proved for all 𝑁 in type 𝐴 by (24.13), and the DK ladder proceeds directly
    to DK-4.

    modules in the sense of Hernandez–Zhang [262]), then a completed, coderived, or ind-completed
    enhancement 𝐷  b (O) is required (Remark 24.8.23(b)), and the generation mechanism shifts from thick
    closure to localizing subcategories with compact generation. The structural input for this extension

24.9       Chain-level and evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–
           Kohno
The classical Drinfeld–Kohno theorem [182, 183] identifies the monodromy representation of the KZ
                                                                                                 ∨
connection on 𝔤b𝑘 conformal blocks with the 𝑅-matrix representation of 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤) at 𝑞 = 𝑒 𝜋 𝑖 /( 𝑘+ℎ ) . The
24.9. Chain-level and evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno                                             1169


constructions of this chapter and Part I yield a derived enhancement in a staged ladder. DK-0 is the chain-
level equivalence reversing braiding; DK-1 is the factorization statement on the evaluation locus. The later
stages DK-2 through DK-5 concern extension beyond evaluation objects, factorization-level Kazhdan trans-
port, and the dg-shifted/RTT-complete comparison package. The classical Kazhdan–Lusztig and Kazhdan
equivalences translate the DK-0 part into the 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 involution on quantum group representations.
Remark 24.9.1 (Three-layer Yangian triage). The Yangian content of this chapter separates into three layers
of decreasing certainty:
(A) Proved. Chain-level E1 bar-cobar duality (Theorem 24.2.2), evaluation-locus factorization comparison
    (Theorem 24.9.7), DK-2/3 on the evaluation-generated core at all simple types (Corollary 24.9.15),
    and finite-stage packet reductions.
(B) Conjectural but well-posed. The filtered H-level dg target W ht , RTT-adapted finite-quotient package,
    coefficientwise RTT completion comparison, and compact-generator packet (Conjecture 34.9.4).
(C) Downstream physics. The dg-shifted Yangian realization, full DK-4/5 bridge, and module-category
    enhancement (Chapter 30).
Layer (A) is the proved DK core. Layer (B) is the live algebraic frontier. Layer (C) is downstream of (B)
and of MC5.
Remark 24.9.2 (DK as genus-0 E1 -factorization theorem). The correct ontological ladder for the DK com-
parison is not ‘‘E1 → E2 ’’ as if E2 were ‘‘more commutative Yangian.’’ Rather:
(1) E1 -chiral Yangian: ordered fusion, 𝑅-matrix, DK monodromy. This is Layers (A)–(B) above.
(2) Associator/GT layer: the coherence upgrade problem from E1 to E2 requires a Drinfeld associator
    (Remark 15.8.1).
(3) Modular layer: genus and periods deform the entire E1 -factorization package. This is the content of
    modular homotopy theory (Definition 2.5.1).
DK compares geometric braid monodromy (from KZ/configuration space) with algebraic braid data
(from 𝑅-matrix/quantum group). Both are realizations of the same E1 -factorization transport on ordered
configurations. DK is the genus-0 face; modular homotopy theory asks what happens when the curve
acquires genuine moduli.

where the vertical arrows are the Kazhdan–Lusztig equivalences (Theorem 12.2.9), the top arrow is the

Proof. We verify commutativity of the diagram on objects, morphisms, tensor products, and braiding.
    Step 1: Objects. The top arrow Φ sends the integrable module 𝐿 ( Λ) at level 𝑘 to the Koszul dual module
at level 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ (Theorem 20.7.1). The left vertical sends 𝐿 ( Λ) to the tilting module 𝑇𝑞 ( Λ)
(Theorem 12.2.9). Traversing the diagram in both directions: ΦKL ◦ Φ sends 𝐿 ( Λ) to 𝑇𝑞 −1 ( Λ) (since
𝑞 ′ = 𝑞 −1 ), which is ΦKL ( 𝐿 ( Λ)) in the 𝑞 −1 -category. This equals the image under ( 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 ) ◦ ΦKL , since
the 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 functor sends 𝑇𝑞 ( Λ) to 𝑇𝑞 −1 ( Λ) (the labeling by dominant weights Λ is independent of the
sign of 𝑞 ).
    Step 2: Braiding. The braiding on O𝑘int is the monodromy of the KZ connection on conformal blocks.
By the classical Kohno–Drinfeld theorem [182, 183], ΦKL sends this monodromy to the quasi- 𝑅-matrix
R 𝑞 ∈ 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤) b⊗ 2 . The top arrow Φ reverses the braiding: 𝜎 ↦→ 𝜎 −1 (Theorem 12.1.11, step 3). On the quantum
group side, this corresponds to R 𝑞 ↦→ R 𝑞−1 = R 𝑞 −1 , which is precisely the bottom arrow.
    Step 3: Tensor structure. The top arrow preserves the monoidal structure up to braiding reversal
(Theorem 12.1.11, step 2): the bar complex of the fusion product 𝑀 ⊠ 𝑁 decomposes via the Alexander–
Whitney map into the cotensor product of the individual bar complexes. The KL equivalence identifies
the fusion product with the quantum group tensor product [184], and the 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 functor preserves the
tensor product structure (the underlying fusion rules depend only on 𝔤, not on the sign of 𝑞 ).
Remark 24.9.4 (The DK square as geometry). The four arrows of the DK square (24.14) have distinct
geometric origins:

                Top:             Verdier duality on 𝐶 𝑛 (ℙ1 ) reverses collision cycles
                Left/Right:      KZ monodromy = quasi- 𝑅-matrix (analytic continuation)
                Bottom:          𝑅𝑞 ↦→ 𝑅𝑞 −1 = 𝑅𝑞−1 (Hopf algebra involution)
The commutativity of the square is the statement that bar-cobar duality geometrically implements the quan-
tum group involution: the algebraic operation 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 is realized by orientation reversal on configuration
spaces.

24.9.4    The staged ladder beyond the evaluation locus
The evaluation-module results above establish the derived Drinfeld–Kohno correspondence at the chain
level and on the evaluation locus. The remaining work is not one undifferentiated conjectural jump: it is
the staged passage from DK-2 through DK-5 of Remark 24. First one enlarges the theorematic evaluation-
generated core to the natural ordinary-derived/completed/coderived ambient; only after that enlargement
is fixed does the standard-tower MC4 comparison begin. The first H-level bridge targets all modules:
Conjecture 24.9.8 (Factorization-categorical DK/KL bridge (DK-3); [conjectured]). The equivalence of
Theorem 24.9.7 extends to the full E1 -factorization category:

                                    FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) ≃ FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) op ,

where Y (𝔤) is the Yangian E1 -chiral algebra and 𝑈𝑞 (𝔤) is the quantum group, viewed as an E1 -factorization
algebra via the construction of Latyntsev [212]. This is the factorization-level Kazhdan bridge beyond the
evaluation subcategories; it separates the ordered Yangian factorization problem from the later dg-shifted
comparison of Conjecture 24.9.43. (Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.3.)
Proposition 24.9.9 (DK-3 reduction to evaluation-generated factorization cores; [proved]). Let
                      gen                                     gen
                 FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) ⊂ FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) ,        FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) ⊂ FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤))

be the smallest full stable idempotent-complete braided monoidal subcategories containing all ordered
tensor products of evaluation objects. Assume there exist exact braided monoidal functors
                                   gen       gen                    gen
                              𝐾 𝑍 fact : FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) → FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) op ,
                                   gen      gen                       gen

whose restrictions to the evaluation generators recover the evaluation-locus comparison of Theorem 24.9.7
after transport to the quantum-group evaluation side, and such that both composites are isomorphic to
the identity on those generators. Then the two functors are quasi-inverse braided monoidal equivalences
on the generated cores. If, in addition,
                      gen                                      gen
                 FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) = FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) ,         FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) = FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) ,

then Conjecture 24.9.8 holds.

Proof. The generated cores are obtained from the evaluation generators by finite iterates of shifts, cones,
direct summands, and ordered tensor products. Exact braided monoidal functors preserve each of these
operations. Therefore any natural transformation between exact braided monoidal functors that is an
isomorphism on the evaluation generators remains an isomorphism on the full generated cores. Applying
this to the two composites shows that they are naturally isomorphic to the identity on the generated cores,
hence the two functors are quasi-inverse equivalences there. The final sentence is immediate.

Remark 24.9.10 (Exact extra inputs for DK-2/DK-3). Propositions 24.8.8 and 24.9.9 make the remaining
Yangian DK inputs exact. After the evaluation-locus theorem, the live extra packets are:
   (i) preservation or replacement resolution theory on the completed Yangian categories O;
  (ii) thick generation of those derived categories by evaluation modules –- proved in type A
       (Proposition 24.8.9);
 (iii) construction of the ordered factorization Kazhdan transport on the evaluation-generated factoriza-
       tion core –- a natural candidate is identified (Proposition 24.8.14); what remains is strict factorization-
       monoidal enhancement (Remark 24.8.15); and
 (iv) a reconstruction argument, Barr–Beck style or equivalent, producing the quasi-inverse pair on that
       core.
For finite-dimensional representations in type 𝐴, items (ii)–(iv) are resolved by Theorem 24.8.17: thick
generation (Proposition 24.8.9) eliminates (ii), and the monoidal thick extension (Lemma 24.8.16) re-
solves (iii)–(iv) by extending the evaluation-level data to the thick closure. The live extra packets are
therefore: (i) preservation for category O and thick generation beyond Repfd . None of these is a new
residue computation on evaluation modules. The residue/RTT identities begin only at the downstream
DK-4/MC4 boundary.
Remark 24.9.11 (DK ladder: what is proved and what remains). DK-0/1: chain-level braided
bar-cobar (Theorems 9.5.4–24.9.5) and evaluation-locus factorization DK (Theorem 24.9.7) –-
proved. DK-2/3: evaluation-generated core, all simple types –- proved by thick generation in type 𝐴
(Theorem 24.8.17) and sectorwise convergence for all types (Corollary 24.9.15); category-O extension
conjectural (Conjecture 24.9.8, reduces to thick generation by Corollary 24.8.18). DK-4/5: conjectural
(Conjecture 24.9.43; see Remark 24.9.10 for exact inputs). Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.3.

24.9.5    ∞-categorical factorization Koszul duality
The DK ladder as formulated in Remark 24.9.11 decomposes the factorization Koszul duality problem
into five stages, with DK-0/1/2/3 proved on the evaluation-generated core at all simple types and DK-4/5
conjectural. From first principles, the entire ladder is a single ∞-categorical statement: Koszul duality for
E1 -algebras in the symmetric monoidal stable ∞-category of factorization coalgebras on Ran( 𝑋 ). We make

this precise and show that DK-2/3 extends to the evaluation-generated core at all types via sectorwise con-
vergence, bypassing thick generation, and that DK-4/5 reduces to a formal deformation theory comparison
within the same framework.

does not require thick generation: the sectorwise convergence argument works for all simple types without

the RTT Yangian (Proposition 24.2.6), whose proof uses Molev’s PBW theorem [72] as external input.

Remark 24.9.16 (H/M/S semantic levels for DK-2/3). Step A (H-level): Theorem 24.9.13 asserts an equiva-
                                  gen          gen
lence of stable ∞-categories FactE1 (A) ≃ FactE1 (A ! ) op on the evaluation-generated cores, with braiding
reversal 𝑅 ↦→ 𝑅 −1 . This is the theorem.
    Step B (M-level): The proof is a dg chain-level argument: sectorwise convergence of the bar spectral
sequence on each Ran-stratum, extended to the full factorization cosheaf by descent. Concretely, the mod-
ule bar functor is exact and braided monoidal (Theorem 12.1.11), and the quasi-isomorphism on evaluation
generators extends to the generated core by functoriality (Proposition 24.9.9).
    Reduction B→A (M-level → H-level): The dg descent implies the ∞-categorical equivalence: a map of
factorization cosheaves that is a quasi-isomorphism on every basis open is a global quasi-isomorphism in
the ∞-categorical sense (Lurie [43, Proposition 5.5.2.2]). Thus the M-level sectorwise quasi-isomorphisms
determine the H-level equivalence of stable ∞-categories.
    Step C (S-level): The shadow is the equality of graded dimensions dim Ext𝑖A (𝑉𝜆 ,𝑉𝜇 ) =
dim Ext𝑖A ! (𝑉𝜆! ,𝑉𝜇! ) across evaluation modules, together with the Kazhdan–Lusztig multiplicity
formula transported to the Koszul dual side.
    Reduction B→C (M-level → S-level): Taking cohomology of the M-level module bar complex 𝐵¯ mod ( 𝑀 )
extracts the S-level Ext groups. The sectorwise spectral sequence (Theorem 24.9.12) converges at each
tridegree, so the M-level quasi-isomorphism on evaluation generators yields isomorphisms of Ext groups.
Remark 24.9.17 (Two proofs in type 𝐴; scope comparison). For 𝔤 = 𝔰𝔩 𝑁 , there are now two independent
proofs of DK-2/3 on the evaluation-generated core:
(a) Thick generation (Theorem 24.8.17): uses the Drinfeld polynomial classification to show that eval-
    uation modules generate all finite-dimensional simples, then the composition-length argument of
    Lemma 24.8.11. This proof is representation-theoretic and specific to type 𝐴.
(b) Sectorwise convergence (Corollary 24.9.15): uses the root lattice grading and loop filtration to bypass
    thick generation entirely. The proof is operadic/factorization-theoretic and works for all types.
Proof (b) is strictly more general (all types 𝐴–𝐺 ), but proof (a) is more explicit: it identifies the generated
core as 𝐷 𝑏 (Repfd ) via the Drinfeld classification. Proof (b) identifies the generated core as the thick closure
of evaluation objects in the factorization category, without naming the individual simples. The two proofs
agree on type 𝐴: thick generation by evaluation modules (Proposition 24.8.9) identifies the two generated
cores.
24.9. Chain-level and evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno                                             1177


Remark 24.9.18 (Interaction with the four-conjecture package). Theorem 24.9.13 and Corollary 24.9.15 resolve
DK-2/3 for the evaluation-generated core at all types. The four conjectures of Remark 24.8.48(b) –- Baxter
exact triangles (Conjecture 24.8.42), shifted-prefundamental generation (Conjecture 24.8.43), pro-Weyl
recovery (Conjecture 24.8.45), and DK on compacts (Conjecture 24.8.46) –- concern the extension beyond
this core to infinite-dimensional modules via a completed or coderived enhancement.
    The two programmes are complementary:
(a) The sectorwise convergence theorem gives the strongest factorization equivalence on the natural
    domain (evaluation-generated core) at all types.
(b) The four-conjecture package enlarges the domain to include prefundamental and asymptotic modules,
    requiring new input (Baxter TQ-lifts, pro-Weyl limits) beyond Koszul duality.
(c) The formal moduli framework below provides the categorical home for both programmes: the
    evaluation-generated core is the compact part of the formal moduli problem, and the four-conjecture
    package extends to the completed/ind-completed part.

Remark 24.9.26 (The RTT relation as Koszul duality datum). The entire proved DK ladder (DK-0 through
DK-3, unconditional at all simple types) rests on a single structural observation:

The RTT relation 𝑅12 ( 𝑢 − 𝑣 ) 𝑇1 ( 𝑢) 𝑇2 ( 𝑣 ) = 𝑇2 ( 𝑣 ) 𝑇1 ( 𝑢) 𝑅12 ( 𝑢 − 𝑣 ) is simultaneously the deﬁning relation
                                of the algebra and the input to Koszul duality.

Three consequences, each one sentence, give the full result:
(a) Quadratic ⇒ 𝑅-matrix inversion. The RTT relation is quadratic in 𝑇 ; the orthogonal complement
    𝑅⊥ of the 𝑅 ( 𝑢)-relations is the 𝑅 −1 ( 𝑢)-relations, so 𝑌 (𝔤) ! = 𝑌−ℏ (𝔤) (Theorem 24.2.2).
(b) PBW ⇒ Koszulness. Molev’s PBW basis gives a flat deformation to Sym(𝑉 ); Sym is classically Koszul;
    flatness transfers Koszulness to 𝑌 (𝔤), giving bar-cobar recovery for free (Proposition 24.2.6, Corol-
    lary 24.2.7).
(c) Root grading ⇒ sectorwise convergence. The root lattice 𝑄 (𝔤) decomposes the bar complex into sectors
    with dim 𝑉𝑟 = (dim 𝑉0 ) 2 uniformly; a non-increasing sequence of non-negative integers stabilizes;
    the factorization bar complex is therefore a genuine coalgebra on Ran( 𝑋 ), and Künneth + cosheaf
    descent extend the diagonal quasi-isomorphism to all strata (Theorem 24.9.12, Theorem 24.9.13).
These are logically independent inputs; together they give DK-2/3 for every simple 𝔤 without any thick-
generation argument.
   The deeper unity: all three are consequences of the fact that the RTT presentation expresses the Yangian
as a quadratic algebra whose deﬁning relations encode the 𝑅-matrix. The bar construction extracts the
𝑅-matrix and inverts it; PBW guarantees this extraction is lossless; the root grading guarantees it converges
sector by sector. Geometrically: bar-cobar duality is Verdier duality on ordered configuration spaces, and
Verdier duality reverses the orientation of ordered collisions –- which inverts the 𝑅-matrix. The RTT
presentation is, in this precise sense, the Yangian presenting itself as a Koszul duality problem.
   For the conjectural levels: DK-4 adds no new idea. The same PBW–Koszul–root-grading package gives
surjective transition maps 𝑛 (𝑉≤∗𝑁 +1 ) ↠ 𝑛 (𝑉≤∗𝑁 ) on the associated graded of bar cohomology, hence
                            V                 V
Mittag-Leffler for the RTT tower (Theorem 24.9.34) and a well-behaved completed bar-cobar equivalence
                                                                                  dg
(Corollary 24.9.35). What remains is a structure identification: lim 𝔤 𝑁  YA (Maurer–Cartan element,
                                                                  ←−   𝑁
translation, coproduct). DK-5 adds only the ∞-categorical PBW exponential Mod(𝔤 A ) ≃ Rep(exp(𝔤 A )).
Coderived factorization duality off the Koszul locus
On the Koszul locus (generic levels, evaluation-generated core), Theorem 24.9.13 provides an equivalence
in the ordinary derived sense. Off the Koszul locus –- at admissible affine levels, minimal-model central
charges, or for infinite-dimensional modules beyond the generated core –- the bar-cobar object persists
as a curved factorization coalgebra, and the correct framework is the coderived/contraderived category of
Positselski [171].

Remark 24.9.28 (The coderived category as the natural ambient). The equivalence (24.17) is the correct
categorical context for the full MC3 programme:
(a) On the Koszul locus (generic level), DK-0 through DK-3 live in the ordinary derived category, and
    the coderived category adds nothing new. This is the domain of Theorem 24.9.13.
(b) Off the Koszul locus (admissible levels, minimal-model central charges), the bar-cobar object Ω ( 𝐶 )
    is curved: 𝑑 2 = ℎ ≠ 0. The ordinary derived category is trivial (every module is contractible via
    ℎ ), but the coderived category retains the full categorical information. The four conjectures of Re-
    mark 24.8.48(b) naturally live here: Baxter exact triangles, shifted-prefundamental generation, pro-
    Weyl recovery, and DK on compacts are all statements about the coderived/contraderived equiva-
    lence (24.17).
(c) The passage from the evaluation-generated core (compact objects in 𝐷 𝑏 ) to the full category O
    (possibly non-compact objects in 𝐷 co ) is controlled by the ind-completion of the coderived category:
    see Theorem 24.9.29 below.

The extension from the evaluation-generated core (compact objects) to the full Yangian category O (ind-
completed) is a standard categorical construction once the compact part is established. The key input is
the compactness of evaluation objects in the factorization category.

Remark 24.9.32 (Tangent Lie algebra controls the extension programme). The formal moduli reformulation
(Conjecture 24.9.31) reveals the organizing role of the tangent Lie algebra 𝔤 A : all four MC3 extension
conjectures are consequences of a single structural property of 𝔤 A , namely that it is algebraizable –- that
the formal moduli problem 𝔉A is the formal completion of a global (algebraic) moduli problem.
    In the DK-4 framework (Conjecture 24.9.22), algebraizability is the content of the RTT-adapted fil-
tration: the formal group 𝐺 A admits a filtration whose finite quotients are the finite RTT stages, and the
transition maps are the RTT truncations. If this filtration is Mittag-Leffler on cohomology (the concrete
form of algebraizability), all four conjectures follow by the MC4 reduction principle (Conjecture 6.8.20).
    This reduces the four MC3 conjectures to a single input: the Mittag-Leﬄer property of the RTT tower
on bar cohomology.

Proof. Under Corollary 24.3.15, the local DK-4 packet is already closed, so only DK-5 remains. Assumptions

evaluation objects is the whole finite-dimensional Yangian factorization category.

Corollary 24.9.76 closes DK-5 via ind-extension (Proposition 24.9.48).

Remark 24.9.93 (Rational vs. trigonometric DK). The DK square takes different forms depending on the
𝑅-matrix type:
   Rational DK (Theorem 24.9.5). The Yangian 𝑅-matrix 𝑅 ( 𝑢) = 1 − ℏ 𝑃 /𝑢 is rational in the additive
spectral parameter 𝑢. Koszul duality sends ℏ → −ℏ, i.e., 𝑅 ( 𝑢) → 𝑅 −1 ( 𝑢). The bar complex uses the
propagator 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) on the FM compactification of ℂ.
24.9. Chain-level and evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno                                            1215


    Trigonometric DK (Remark 24.7.3). The quantum loop algebra 𝑈𝑞 (b        𝔤) has trigonometric 𝑅-matrix
𝑅 ( 𝑢/𝑣 ) in the multiplicative parameter. Koszul duality sends 𝑞 → 𝑞 −1 . The bar complex uses the propa-
gator 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 / 𝑧𝑗 ) on the FM compactification of ℂ× .
    The Kazhdan functor Φ 𝐾 intertwines the rational and trigonometric pictures via the exponential map
𝑢 ↦→ 𝑒 𝑢 , ℂ → ℂ× . The DK square (24.15) encodes the commutativity of this intertwining with bar-cobar
duality.
    The Yangian chapter reveals the E1 -chiral face of the theory. The chain-level / evaluation-locus derived
Drinfeld–Kohno theorem (Theorems 24.9.3 and 24.9.5) proves that bar-cobar duality geometrically imple-
ments the quantum group involution 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 , via orientation reversal on ordered configuration spaces.
The E∞ -chiral examples of the preceding chapters all have commutative factorization structure; the Yangian
is the first object whose Koszul duality intertwines genuinely noncommutative (braided) monoidal data.
The theorematic endpoint is DK-2/3 for finite-dimensional type 𝐴 (Theorem 24.8.17), which extends the
evaluation-locus factorization comparison (Theorem 24.9.7) to all finite-dimensional representations via
thick generation. The remaining frontier is the extension to category O and other types, followed by the
staged passage through DK-4/DK-5 (dg-shifted/triple-bridge comparison), which is the natural E1 -chiral
bridge to the modular Koszul programme (§34.12).
Chapter 25


Toroidal and elliptic algebras

Two directions extend the curve-based theory: (a) replacing the logarithmic propagator by an elliptic one
on 𝐸𝜏 , yielding E1 -chiral structures; (b) seeking surface-factorization or double-affine objects on ℂ∗ × ℂ∗ .
Only direction (a) fits the curve-chiral hierarchy. The bar complex acquires Eisenstein-series corrections
controlled by 𝜏 , and the Fay trisecant identity replaces the Arnold relation.
Remark 25.0.1 (Two programme tracks). Track (a) keeps the base an algebraic curve and asks for an elliptic E1 -
chiral realization on 𝐸𝜏 . Track (b) seeks a genuine surface-factorization or double-affine object on ℂ∗ × ℂ∗
or related two-parameter spaces. Only track (a) is described in this chapter with curve-chiral language;
track (b) is a separate higher-dimensional programme target.
Remark 25.0.2 (The generalization principle: Arnold to Fay). The Arnold relation (Theorem 5.1.22), which
governs the genus-0 bar differential, admits two distinct generalizations. Direction (a): via clutching mor-
phisms and the universal Maurer–Cartan class Θ 𝐴 , one passes to the modular regime on stable curves,
recovering the higher-genus bar complex of Part I (Remark 2.7.1). Direction (b): via the Fay trisecant
identity (Theorem 25.3.2), one replaces the additive (logarithmic) propagator 𝜔 = 𝑑𝑧 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) by the
elliptic (multiplicative) propagator built from the Weierstrass 𝜎 -function, entering the toroidal regime.
The present chapter develops direction (b): the systematic passage from logarithmic to elliptic propagators
and its consequences for bar-cobar duality.
Remark 25.0.3 (Rational, trigonometric, elliptic: curve geometry). The three quantum group families arise
from the geometry of the underlying curve:

                     𝑅-matrix type       Quantum group                 Spectral parameter          Curve
                     Rational            Yangian 𝑌 (𝔤)                 𝑢 = 𝑧1 − 𝑧2                 ℙ1
                     Trigonometric       Quantum loop 𝑈𝑞 ( 𝐿𝔤)         𝑞 = 𝑒 2𝜋 𝑖 ( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 )/ 𝛽   ℂ∗
                     Elliptic            Elliptic QG 𝐸𝑞, 𝑝 (𝔤)         𝑢 ∈ 𝐸𝜏                      𝐸𝜏

The passage from rational to trigonometric to elliptic parallels additive → multiplicative → modular
spectral parameter; this chapter develops the elliptic face.

the algebra is associative but not commutative, hence strictly E1 .
     Step 2: Associativity (gap). The 𝑅-matrix 𝑅𝑖𝑗 ( 𝑢) = 𝑔𝑖𝑗 ( 𝑢) · Id satisfies the Yang–Baxter equation
trivially (being scalar-valued). The genuine content of associativity lies in verifying that the full matrix-
valued OPE structure–-including the Serre-type relations of Definition 25.1.1–-defines an algebra over Assch
(Definition 2.8.4). This requires an explicit verification that triple OPEs are consistent, which we do not
carry out here.
     Step 3: Realization on 𝐸𝜏 . Set 𝜏 = log 𝑡 /log 𝑞 and let 𝐸𝜏 = ℂ∗ / 𝑞 ℤ . The generating currents 𝑒 𝑖 ( 𝑧 ),

define sections of line bundles on 𝐸𝜏 . The OPE of Proposition 25.1.2 has poles at 𝑧 /𝑤 ∈ 𝑞 ℤ , which descend
to a single point on 𝐸𝜏 . This defines a candidate E1 -chiral algebra structure on 𝐸𝜏 , pending verification of
Step 2.
     Step 4: Surface-factorization horizon on ℂ∗ × ℂ∗ . The horizontal modes 𝑥 𝑖,𝑛          ± depend on the spectral

parameter 𝑢 and the vertical modes 𝑒 𝑖 ( 𝑧 ) depend on 𝑧 . Together they give fields on ℂ∗𝑢 × ℂ∗𝑧 with the two
independent gradings (by horizontal and vertical mode number) providing the doubly-graded structure.

     Conditional on Step 2–-i.e., the verification that the toroidal OPE defines an associative Assch -algebra

Theorem 25.3.2 (Fay identity at genus 1 [136]; [proved]). For any four points 𝑢1 , 𝑢2 , 𝑢3 , 𝑢4 on an
elliptic curve 𝐸𝜏 , the theta function satisfies the Fay trisecant identity:

                𝜃 ( 𝑢1 − 𝑢2 ) 𝜃 ( 𝑢3 − 𝑢4 ) − 𝜃 ( 𝑢1 − 𝑢3 ) 𝜃 ( 𝑢2 − 𝑢4 ) + 𝜃 ( 𝑢1 − 𝑢4 ) 𝜃 ( 𝑢2 − 𝑢3 ) = 0

This is a bilinear identity (each term is a product of two theta functions), which at genus 1 is the degenerate
case of the general Fay trisecant identity on higher-genus curves. The identity is equivalent to the Riemann
addition formula and reduces to the Ptolemy relation sin( 𝛼 − 𝛽 ) sin( 𝛾 − 𝛿 ) − sin( 𝛼 − 𝛾 ) sin( 𝛽 − 𝛿 ) +
sin( 𝛼 − 𝛿 ) sin( 𝛽 − 𝛾 ) = 0 in the rational limit 𝜏 → 𝑖 ∞.
   This identity underlies the Yang–Baxter equation for elliptic R-matrices: the star-triangle relation is a
consequence of the Fay identity applied to the structure functions of the elliptic algebra.

Remark 25.3.7 (Scope). The proof assembles three ingredients: (i) the Laurent expansion of the Weierstrass
𝜁 -function in terms of Eisenstein series ([proved], classical); (ii) the convergence of the correction-order
spectral sequence (bounded filtration at each bar degree); and (iii) Zhu’s modular invariance theorem for
genus-1 𝑛-point functions of rational vertex algebras [89] ([proved]). The combination and the identifica-
tion of the splitting mechanism (Step 5) are new to this work. The Heisenberg verification uses the explicit
computations of §19.10.

of H𝜅 at degree 𝑛 admits the decomposition:

       𝐵¯ 𝑛ell (H𝜅 ) = 𝐵¯ 𝑛rat (H𝜅 ) ⊕ 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ) · 𝐵¯ 𝑛(1) ⊕ 𝐸4 ( 𝜏 ) · 𝐵¯ 𝑛(2) ⊕ · · · ⊕ 𝐸2𝑛−2 ( 𝜏 ) · 𝐵¯ 𝑛( 𝑛−1)     (25.4)

with only finitely many nonzero terms. Specifically, 𝐵¯ 𝑛( 𝑘 ) = 0 for 𝑘 ≥ 𝑛.

Proof. Step 1 (Finite propagator expansion). The elliptic bar complex at degree 𝑛 involves 𝑛2 propagator

factors 𝜔ell

𝜖𝑖𝑗 + 𝑘 ≥1 𝑐𝑘 ( 𝜏 ) 𝜖𝑖𝑗2𝑘 −1 . The bar differential at degree 𝑛 extracts the residue at the diagonal 𝜖𝑖𝑗 = 0; since

the OPE of the Heisenberg current 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) has a double pole ( 𝑎 ( 𝑧1 ) 𝑎 ( 𝑧2 ) ∼ 𝜅 /( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) 2 ), the residue
at each pair involves at most the coefficient of 𝜖𝑖𝑗−1 in the integrand. This means the Laurent coefficient
𝑐𝑘 ( 𝜏 ) 𝜖𝑖𝑗2𝑘 −1 contributes to the residue only if 2𝑘 − 1 ≤ 1, i.e., 𝑘 ≤ 1, for each individual propagator factor.
However, when multiple propagator factors are combined in the degree-𝑛 bar element (𝑛 − 1 propagators
appear in a degree-𝑛 element), the correction terms from different propagator pairs may accumulate. The
total correction order is bounded by 𝑛 − 1 (one correction per propagator), giving 𝐵¯ 𝑛( 𝑘 ) = 0 for 𝑘 ≥ 𝑛.
     Step 2 (Eisenstein coeﬃcient identiﬁcation). The correction term 𝐵¯ 𝑛( 𝑘 ) arises from choosing exactly 𝑘 of
the 𝑛 − 1 propagator factors to contribute their leading correction 𝑐1 ( 𝜏 ) 𝜖𝑖𝑗 (or, more precisely, assigning
a total correction weight of 𝑘 distributed among the propagators, with correction of weight 𝑗 from a
single propagator contributing 𝑐𝑗 ( 𝜏 )). By the computation of (25.3), the leading correction at degree 2 is
𝑐1 ( 𝜏 ) ∝ 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ). At degree 𝑛, the correction of total weight 𝑘 lies in the subspace of (quasi-)modular forms
of weight 2𝑘 , which is spanned by monomials in 𝐸2 , 𝐸4 , 𝐸6 . Since the Heisenberg algebra is free (Gaussian),
the only contributing terms are the single-propagator corrections (there are no interaction terms between
different propagator pairs), so the coefficient of 𝐵¯ 𝑛( 𝑘 ) is precisely 𝑐𝑘 ( 𝜏 ) = (−1) 𝑘 𝐺2𝑘+2 ( 𝜏 ) ∝ 𝐸2𝑘+2 ( 𝜏 ) for
𝑘 ≥ 2, and 𝑐1 ( 𝜏 ) ∝ 𝐸2 ( 𝜏 ).
     Step 3 (Direct sum splitting). The corrections 𝐸2 , 𝐸4 , 𝐸6 , . . . have distinct modular weights 2, 4, 6, . . .
and are therefore linearly independent over ℂ. The decomposition (25.4) is a direct sum, not merely a
filtration.

25.5      Dynamical Yang–Baxter equation for 𝔰𝔩 2
We verify the dynamical Yang–Baxter equation for the 𝔰𝔩 2 elliptic 𝑅-matrix of Definition 25.2.2, and show
that the key identity reduces to the Fay trisecant (Theorem 25.3.2). The connection to bar nilpotency is
made precise: the dynamical YBE encodes 𝑑 2 = 0 for the elliptic bar complex with dynamical parameter.

25.5.1    The dynamical Yang–Baxter equation
Deﬁnition 25.5.1 (Dynamical Yang–Baxter equation). The dynamical Yang–Baxter equation (DYBE) for
an 𝑅-matrix 𝑅 ( 𝑢, 𝜆) ∈ End(𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 ) depending on spectral parameter 𝑢 and dynamical parameter 𝜆 ∈ 𝔥∗
is:
   𝑅12 ( 𝑢, 𝜆) 𝑅13 ( 𝑢 + 𝑣, 𝜆 − ℎ (2) ) 𝑅23 ( 𝑣, 𝜆) = 𝑅23 ( 𝑣, 𝜆 − ℎ (1) ) 𝑅13 ( 𝑢 + 𝑣, 𝜆) 𝑅12 ( 𝑢, 𝜆 − ℎ (3) ) (25.5)
where ℎ ( 𝑖 ) denotes the action of ℎ ∈ 𝔥 on the 𝑖 -th tensor factor of 𝑉 ⊗3 , and 𝜆 − ℎ ( 𝑖 ) means that the
dynamical parameter 𝜆 is shifted by the weight of the state in factor 𝑖 .

Proposition 25.5.3 (DYBE reduces to Fay; [proved]). The dynamical Yang–Baxter equation (25.5)

       for appropriate specializations of 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐, 𝑑 depending on 𝑢, 𝑣, 𝜆, 𝜂 .

Remark 25.7.1 (Degeneration limits). The three regimes degenerate via
                                          𝜏 →𝑖 ∞                           𝑞 →1
                                Elliptic −−−−−−→ Trigonometric −−−−→ Rational.

As 𝜏 → 𝑖 ∞, 𝜃 1 ( 𝑧 | 𝜏 ) → 2 sin( 𝜋 𝑧 ) and the Eisenstein corrections collapse to constants; as 𝑞 → 1, the
trigonometric propagator becomes 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧 and 𝑅𝑞 ( 𝑢) → 1 − ℏ 𝑃 /𝑢. The bar complex degenerates accord-
ingly: 𝐵¯ ell (A) → 𝐵¯ trig (A) → 𝐵¯ rat (A), consistent with the spectral sequence of Theorem 25.3.6.

26.4.4     Explicit genus-2 bar differential
The genus-1 curvature of 𝔰𝔩 b 2,𝑘 was computed in Theorem 20.12.1 by extracting the B-cycle monodromy
of the elliptic propagator. The analogous computation at genus 2 yields the first non-abelian genus-2
bar differential. The Heisenberg case (Theorem 19.10.10; see also the frame computation in §1.10) serves
as template; the new content is the interplay between the double-pole coefficient 𝑘 and the structure
constants 𝑓 𝑎𝑏 𝑐 , which produces the dual Coxeter correction ℎ∨ = 2 in the curvature.

Remark 26.4.7 (Genus-1 vs genus-2 monodromies). At genus 1, the single B-cycle monodromy of 𝐾 (1) is the

by which the level 𝑘 enters the genus-2 curvature directly, in addition to the dual Coxeter correction from
the structure constants.

elements. The cancellation with ( 𝑑 (1) ) 2 is a genuine constraint that is not visible in any abelian example.

Remark 26.4.13 (Non-abelian features at genus 2). The 𝔰𝔩
                                                      b 2 genus-2 computation reveals three features
invisible in the abelian case:
   (i) Two-channel curvature. 𝜅 = 3( 𝑘 + 2)/4 receives contributions from both the double-pole channel
       (∝ 𝑘 ) and the simple-pole channel (∝ ℎ∨ ). For the Heisenberg, only the double-pole is active.

       nonzero–-a genuine cancellation encoding OPE-central extension compatibility.
 (iii) Root vs Cartan sectors. Root pairs receive both channels (26.7); Cartan pairs only double-pole (26.8);
       mixed pairs only simple-pole (26.9)–(26.10).
Remark 26.4.14 (Degeneration limits). As Σ2 degenerates:
   (i) Separating ( 𝛿1 ): Ω = diag( 𝜏1 , 𝜏2 ), monodromies decouple, and obs2 | 𝛿1 = 𝜅 · 𝜆1 ( 𝐸𝜏1 ) · 𝜆1 ( 𝐸𝜏2 ) fac-
       torizes into two genus-1 curvatures.
  (ii) Non-separating ( 𝛿0 ): Ω12 → 0, 𝜆2 | 𝛿0 = 0, and the bar differential reduces to genus 1.
These limits are identical to the Heisenberg degeneration (Remark 19.10.13): the non-abelian structure does
not alter boundary behavior.

Remark 26.4.22 (What genus-2 complementarity reveals). Two structural features emerge:
   (i) Free energy ≠ dimension. 𝐹2 = 𝜅 · 7/5760 is a single scalar, while dim 𝑄 2 is the full bar cohomol-
       ogy rank. At genus 1, dim 𝐻 ∗ (M 1,1 ) = 2 forces 𝐹1 to determine dim 𝑄 1 ; at genus 2 (dim = 8), 𝐹2
       constrains but does not determine the 𝜎 -eigenspace dimensions.
  (ii) Algebra-dependence of 𝜎 . Self-dual algebras give a universal 4 + 4 splitting (Theorem 8.14.47); non-
       self-dual algebras have asymmetric 𝜎 -eigenspaces encoding OPE data. This is a genus-2 phenomenon:
       at genus 1, dim 𝐻 ∗ = 2 forces 1 + 1.

26.5      Virasoro duality and the bosonic string at all genera
The Virasoro algebra provides the second key showcase for the three main theorems. Unlike the Heisenberg
(§1.12) and Kac–Moody cases (where 𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 0 and complementarity is exact cancellation), the Virasoro
has a nonzero complementarity sum 𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 13, reflecting the conformal anomaly of the bosonic string.
Moreover, the Virasoro exhibits a trichotomy at 𝑐 = 0 (uncurved), generic 𝑐 (curved), and 𝑐 = 26 (dual to
the uncurved algebra) that has no Kac–Moody analog.

26.5.1    Setup
Recall from the Master Table (Table 27.1) and the genus-1 pipeline (§21.14.5):

                  Algebra     Same-family partner / dual datum        𝑐 (A)     𝑐 + 𝑐′   𝜅 (A)

Corollary 26.11.2 (Koszul complementarity of genera; [proved]). For a Koszul pair (A , A ! ):
                                                                              𝑥 /2

The right-hand side depends only on the root datum (Theorem 26.8.2). For affine Kac–Moody algebras
(𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 0), the complementary genera cancel: 𝜙 A = − 𝜙 A ! . For Virasoro (𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 13), the sum is
13 · ( 𝑥 /2)/sin( 𝑥 /2).

Proof. Immediate from 𝜙 A = 𝜅 · ( 𝑥 /2)/sin( 𝑥 /2) and linearity in 𝜅 .

Remark 26.11.3 (Relation to index theory). The appearance of the modified Todd class ( 𝑥 /2)/sin( 𝑥 /2)
(rather than the 𝐴ˆ-genus ( 𝑥 /2)/sinh( 𝑥 /2)) reflects the positive Faber–Pandharipande coefficients: all
𝜆FP                                                                  ˆ
  𝑔 > 0 (Remark 26.4.28). In the Atiyah–Singer framework, the 𝐴-genus governs the Dirac operator and
has alternating signs. The Wick rotation 𝑥 ↦→ 𝑖 𝑥 relates the two generating functions, but the underlying
geometry is distinct: the genus expansion operates on the algebraic moduli space M 𝑔 (with tautological
intersection theory), while the 𝐴ˆ-genus operates on smooth manifolds (with characteristic classes of the
tangent bundle).

26.11.1  Koszul duality as duality of genera
The multiplicative genus 𝜙 A packages the genus expansion into a single algebro-geometric invariant. The
duality pairing on genera induced by Koszul duality is not visible in the Frenkel–Gaitsgory or Costello–
Gwilliam frameworks; it is specific to the bar-cobar approach.
Proposition 26.11.4 (Koszul duality as genus involution; [proved]). The assignment A ↦→ 𝜙 A
defines a homomorphism from the Grothendieck group 𝐾0 (KCA) of Koszul chiral algebras (under tensor
product) to the additive group of multiplicative sequences:

                                                𝜙 A⊗ B = 𝜙 A + 𝜙 B .                                        (26.20)

The Koszul duality functor A ↦→ A ! induces an involution on genera:

                      𝜙 A! ( 𝑥 ) = −𝜙 A ( 𝑥 )      for Kac–Moody algebras (𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 0),                     (26.21)

and more generally
                                                                 𝑥 /2
                                   𝜙 A! ( 𝑥 ) = (𝜅 + 𝜅 ′) ·              − 𝜙A ( 𝑥)                          (26.22)
                                                              sin( 𝑥 /2)
for arbitrary Koszul pairs.
26.12. From genus expansions to knot invariants                                                         1263


Proof. Equation (26.20) follows from the additivity 𝜅 (A ⊗ B) = 𝜅 (A) + 𝜅 (B) (Corollary 8.13.22)
and the linearity of the generating function in 𝜅 (Proposition 26.11.1). Equations (26.21)–(26.22) restate
Corollary 26.11.2.

Theorem 26.11.5 (Genus duality determines the Koszul pair; [proved]). [Regime: curved-central
on the Koszul locus (Convention 2.9.2).]
   For a Koszul chiral algebra A with obstruction coefficient 𝜅 ≠ 0, the genus expansion determines:
   (i) The obstruction coefficient 𝜅 (A) (from 𝐹1 = 𝜅 /24);
  (ii) The central charge 𝑐 (A) whenever 𝜚 (𝔤) is known (from 𝜅 = 𝑐 · 𝜚, Corollary 21.15.16);
 (iii) The Feigin–Frenkel dual level 𝑘 ′ for affine algebras (from 𝜅 + 𝜅 ′ = 0);
 (iv) The radius of convergence | 𝑥 | = 2 𝜋 (independent of A, Theorem 26.4.26).

Proof. Part (i): 𝐹1 (A) = 𝜅 · 𝜆1FP = 𝜅 /24 (Theorem 8.13.16), so 𝜅 = 24 𝐹1 . Part (ii): 𝜅 = 𝑐 · 𝜚 (𝔤) with 𝜚
tabulated (Remark 21.15.17), so 𝑐 = 𝜅 / 𝜚. Part (iii): The Feigin–Frenkel involution gives 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨
with 𝜅 ( 𝑘 ′ ) = −𝜅 ( 𝑘 ) (antisymmetry of the complementarity sum for Kac–Moody algebras), determining
𝑘 ′ from 𝜅 . Part (iv): Theorem 26.4.26 (the convergence ratio 𝐹𝑔 +1 / 𝐹𝑔 → 1/(2 𝜋 ) 2 is 𝜅 -independent).
Remark 26.11.6 (The genus expansion as a complete invariant). The genus expansion { 𝐹𝑔 (A)} determines
𝜅 , 𝑐 , and 𝑘 ′ (hence A ! abstractly) but not A itself: e.g., H1 and Vir2 share 𝜅 = 1. The bar cohomology
generating function 𝑃A ( 𝑥 ) provides the additional data.

26.12      From genus expansions to knot invariants
The genus tower { 𝐹𝑔 (A)} 𝑔 ≥0 connects to finite-type knot invariants through the Fulton–MacPherson
propagator integrals that underlie both constructions.
1264                                                            Chapter 26. Explicit genus expansions


Remark 26.12.1 (Genus-0 bar complex and weight systems). The genus-0 bar complex of a Koszul chiral
algebra A produces weight systems via the same configuration space integrals on 𝐶 𝑛 (ℙ1 ) that compute
the genus-0 expansion 𝐹0 . Concretely, the FM propagator 𝜔 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) on the boundary strata of
𝐶 𝑛 (ℙ1 ) assigns to each chord diagram an element of 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)), yielding finite-type knot invariants
(Theorem 32.2.1, Chapter 32).
Proposition 26.12.2 (Loop expansion interpretation; [proved]). Let 𝔤ˆ 𝑘 be a Koszul affine
Kac–Moody algebra with obstruction coefficient 𝜅 = 𝜅 (𝔤ˆ 𝑘 ). In the genus tower 𝐹𝑔 (𝔤ˆ 𝑘 ) = 𝜅 · 𝜆FP
                                                                                                   𝑔
(Theorem 8.13.16):
   (i) At genus 0: 𝐹0 produces weight systems, i.e., finite-type knot invariants in the sense of Vassiliev–
       Kontsevich.
  (ii) At genus 1: 𝐹1 = 𝜅 /24 produces the writhe correction (framing anomaly).
 (iii) At genus 𝑔 ≥ 2: 𝐹𝑔 produces the 𝑔 -loop term of perturbative Chern–Simons theory on 𝑆 3 , where
       the bar complex curvature 𝜅 plays the role of the coupling constant 1/( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ).
The full development appears in Chapter 32.

Proof. Parts (i) and (ii) follow from the identification of the genus-0 and genus-1 FM integrals with,
respectively, the Kontsevich integral configuration space integrals and the Dedekind eta regularization
(Theorem 8.13.16). Part (iii): the genus- 𝑔 contribution 𝐹𝑔 = 𝜅 · 𝜆FP𝑔 is computed by integration over
M 𝑔 , which is precisely the 𝑔 -loop Feynman integral of Chern–Simons theory after gauge fixing (Axelrod–
Singer). The curvature 𝜅 (𝔤ˆ 𝑘 ) enters as the overall coupling constant of the Chern–Simons action at
level 𝑘 .

    Three regimes.
• 𝑐 = 0: Uncurved. The bar complex is a genuine cochain complex ( 𝐷 2 = 0 on 𝑉¯ ). The Koszul dual is
  Vir!0 ≃ Vir0 (Theorem 21.14.4). The 𝑇 𝑇 OPE is purely quadratic (2𝑇 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 + 𝜕𝑇 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 )), and
  the Koszul duality is of classical type.
• 𝑐 ≠ 0, generic: Curved 𝐴∞ . The completed bar construction is needed (Appendix P). The Koszul dual
  is Vir!𝑐 ≃ Vir26− 𝑐 (Example 6.8.18), where the shift 𝑐 ↦→ 26 − 𝑐 arises from the Verdier duality pairing on
  𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) interacting with the quartic pole data.
• 𝑐 = 26: The dual Virasoro Vir!26 ≃ Vir0 is the uncurved algebra. Equivalently, the bosonic string BRST
  complex at 𝑐 = 26 is governed by the bar complex of Vir26 (Theorem 18.16.3).
    The curvature–central charge dictionary: the curvature 𝑚0 = 𝑐 /2 is an invariant of the chiral algebra
that determines the qualitative structure of the bar complex. For the Virasoro, it is the only such invariant
(since 𝑇 is the sole generator), so the full bar complex structure is controlled by 𝑐 alone. This is the simplest
instance of the general principle that curvature = quantum correction (Theorem 8.13.16).

Computation 27.3.9 (W3 curvature and dual level verification). The W3 bar complex has vacuum
leakage from two independent channels:
  (i) Virasoro sector: 𝑇(3) 𝑇 = 𝑐 /2 (quartic pole), contributing 𝑚0(𝑇 ) = 𝑐 /2.
  (ii) 𝑊 -sector: 𝑊(5)𝑊 = 𝑐 /3 (sixth-order pole), contributing 𝑚0(𝑊 ) = 𝑐 /3.
The ratio 𝑚0(𝑊 ) /𝑚0(𝑇 ) = 2/3 is independent of the level and equals the ratio of central term normalizations
in the 𝑊𝑊 and 𝑇 𝑇 OPEs ( 𝑐 /3 vs. 𝑐 /2).
    Both leakages vanish simultaneously if and only if 𝑐 = 0. The full W3 curvature is proportional to
( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) = ( 𝑘 + 3) (Theorem 21.12.2), which vanishes at the critical level 𝑘 = −3. These are distinct
conditions:
• 𝑐 = 0 occurs at rational levels 𝑘 = −5/3 and 𝑘 = −9/4 (from solving 12( 𝑘 + 2) 2 = 𝑘 + 3, i.e., 12𝑢2 − 𝑢 −
  1 = 0 where 𝑢 = 𝑘 + 2).
1276                                                                         Chapter 27. Detailed computations


• 𝑘 = −3 is the critical level where the Sugawara tensor is undefined and the DS construction degenerates.
Similarly, for the Virasoro (𝔰𝔩 2 ), 𝑐 = 0 occurs at 𝑘 = −1/2 and 𝑘 = −4/3 (both rational), while critical level
is 𝑘 = −2. See Theorem 21.12.2 for the full discussion.
    At the dual level 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 6, the dual central charge is 𝑐 ′ = 𝑐 ( 𝑘 ′ ) = 2 − 24( 𝑘 ′ + 2) 2 /( 𝑘 ′ + 3) =

The curvature of one algebra determines the curvature of its dual. When 𝑐 = 0 (uncurved at 𝑘 = −5/3

the critical level itself.

5(100 − 𝑐 )) = 16/(522 − 5𝑐 ). These differ (the dual algebra has a different OPE structure), but both are
determined by a single parameter 𝑐 . In the large-level limit 𝑘 → ∞ (where 𝑐 → −∞), both 𝛼 ( 𝑐 ) → 0−
and 𝛼 ( 𝑐 ′ ) → 0+ : both algebras become classical simultaneously.

    Method. The chiral bracket differential is built as a matrix of size dim 𝐵¯ 𝑛 × dim 𝐵¯ 𝑛−1 , where dim 𝐵¯ 𝑛 =

in the FM compactification.

quadratic approximation (Computation 27.4.10), suggesting a structural origin for this number in the
beyond-quadratic OPE data.

27.5      Non-simply-laced example: 𝔰𝔬
                                    b 5 (type 𝐵 2 )
All Kac–Moody computations in the manuscript so far treat simply-laced types ( 𝐴𝑛 , 𝐷𝑛 , 𝐸𝑛 ), where roots
have a single length and ℎ∨ = h (Coxeter number equals dual Coxeter number). Here we compute the bar
complex for 𝔰𝔬b 5,𝑘 (type 𝐵 2 ), the simplest non-simply-laced affine Kac–Moody algebra. The key difference:
the dual Coxeter number ℎ∨ = 3 is not equal to the Coxeter number h = 4, and the level-shifting duality
𝑘 ↦→ −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −𝑘 − 6 uses ℎ∨ , not ℎ.

27.6      Geometric-algebraic bar comparison
A central claim of this monograph is that the geometric bar complex (constructed from configuration space
integrals on Fulton–MacPherson compactifications) agrees with the algebraic bar complex (constructed
from OPE residues). This agreement is proved abstractly as Theorem 6.2.69 (bar_cobar_construction.tex),
but the term-by-term verification has not been exhibited. We carry it out here for 𝔰𝔩
                                                                                   b 2,𝑘 , the simplest algebra
where both curvature and bracket data are visible.

   (i) Arnold ⇒ Jacobi: the bar differential squares to zero because the forms satisfy the Arnold relations.

       𝑑02 = 0 is equivalent to the Arnold relation via the residue dictionary.
This is Theorem 6.2.69 made completely explicit.

   Formality. The homotopy transfer theorem applied to this SDR shows that 𝔰𝔩 2 is formal: all transferred
𝐿∞ operations 𝑙𝑛 vanish for 𝑛 ≥ 3, since the homotopy ℎ is concentrated in degree 2 and the cohomology
gap ( 𝐻 1 = 𝐻 2 = 0) prevents the tree formula from producing nonzero contributions. This is consistent
with the general result that semisimple Lie algebras are formal as dg Lie algebras (cf. Deligne–Griffiths–
Morgan–Sullivan [7]).
   The SDR conditions ( 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 = id − 𝜄 ◦ 𝑝, ℎ2 = 0, 𝑝 ◦ ℎ = 0, ℎ ◦ 𝜄 = 0) are verified by direct matrix
computation on the 10-dimensional complex Λ∗ (𝔰𝔩 ∗2 ).

27.7      BGG resolution of 𝔰𝔩
                            b 2 via bar complex
The bar complex of 𝔰𝔩
                   b 2,𝑘 at generic level geometrically realizes the Bernstein–Gel’fand–Gel’fand resolution
(Theorem 12.7.2): the bar differential produces the BGG differential, and the bar cohomology groups are
the Verma modules. At genus 0, this realization is strict ( 𝑑 2 = 0). At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the bar complex acquires
curvature 𝑚0 = 𝜅 (𝔰𝔩b 2,𝑘 ) · 𝜆 𝑔 controlled by the universal MC class Θ of Theorem 8.18.36, deforming
the BGG differential into a curved 𝐴∞ resolution whose genus- 𝑔 corrections encode the moduli-space
cohomology 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , ZA ).

                                     b2 (type 𝐺2 )
After the 𝐵 2 computation of §27.5, we treat the most exceptional non-simply-laced simple Lie algebra: 𝐺2 .
This algebra has lacing number 𝑟 ∨ = 3 (the ratio of long to short root squared lengths), the largest among
simple Lie algebras. Its Coxeter and dual Coxeter numbers differ: ℎ = 6 ≠ ℎ∨ = 4.

Remark 27.8.9 (The 𝐺2 computation in context). The 𝐵 2 (§27.5) and 𝐺2 computations together demonstrate
that the framework handles all lacing numbers 𝑟 ∨ ∈ {1, 2, 3}:

                            Type        dim      ℎ       ℎ∨   𝑟∨       Level shift       Max Serre deg.
                            𝐴1            3      2        2    1            −𝑘 − 4                  3

                            𝐵2           10      4        3    2            −𝑘 − 6                  4
                            𝐺2           14      6        4    3            −𝑘 − 8                  5
As the lacing number increases, the bar complex requires higher degrees to encode all the algebraic structure.
The universal formulas (Theorems 20.7.1 and 8.13.16) hold uniformly, but the complexity of the bar complex
grows with 𝑟 ∨ .

27.12       Structure theorems from bar complex computations
We collect the principal structural results established by the preceding computations, stated as formal
propositions.
Proposition 27.12.1 (Heisenberg bar complex: maximal-form cycles; [proved]). For the Heisen-
berg algebra H𝜅 at any level 𝜅 , every element of 𝐵¯ 𝑛 (H𝜅 ) with maximal form degree (i.e., tensored with a
form 𝜔 ∈ Ω𝑛−1 ( 𝐶 𝑛 )) is a cycle of the bar differential, for all 𝑛 ≥ 2.

Proof. The bar differential has two components: the residue differential 𝑑res (from OPE singularities at
collision divisors) and the de Rham differential 𝑑dR (from exterior differentiation on configuration spaces).
    The de Rham component. For maximal-degree forms 𝜔 ∈ Ω𝑛−1 ( 𝐶 𝑛 ), 𝑑dR ( 𝜔) = 0 since logarithmic
forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) are closed on 𝐶 𝑛 \ 𝜕 .
    The residue component. The Heisenberg OPE 𝑎 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎 ( 𝑤 ) = 𝜅 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 2 has a double pole and no simple
pole: 𝑎 (1) 𝑎 = 𝜅 (scalar) and 𝑎 (0) 𝑎 = 0. At each collision divisor 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 , we must evaluate Res𝐷 𝑖𝑗 ( 𝜅 /( 𝑧 𝑖 −
𝑧𝑗 ) 2 · 𝜔). Two cases arise:
1304                                                                     Chapter 27. Detailed computations


   (i) If 𝜔 contains the factor 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )/( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ), then the integrand is 𝜅 𝑑 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )/( 𝑧 𝑖 −
       𝑧𝑗 ) 3 ∧ (other factors). This triple pole has zero residue (the residue extracts the coefficient of ( 𝑧 𝑖 −
       𝑧𝑗 ) −1 𝑑 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ), which is absent).
  (ii) If 𝜔 does not contain 𝜂𝑖𝑗 , then the integrand 𝜅 /( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) 2 · 𝜔 has a double pole with no 𝑑 ( 𝑧 𝑖 −
       𝑧𝑗 )/( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) factor; the contour integral around 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 vanishes.
In both cases the residue is zero, so 𝑑res = 0 on maximal-form elements. Computations 27.1.1 and 27.1.2
verify this explicitly at 𝑛 = 3 and 𝑛 = 4.

Remark 27.12.2. The vanishing mechanism is specific to the Heisenberg: the OPE has only a double pole
and no simple pole. For the Virasoro (quartic pole 𝑇(3) 𝑇 = 𝑐 /2), the maximal-form bar differential does
not vanish in general–-the quartic pole produces curvature (Computation 27.3.4). For affine Kac–Moody
algebras (b
          𝔤𝑘 with double pole 𝜅𝑖𝑗 and simple pole 𝑓 𝑎𝑏 𝑐 𝐽 𝑐 ), the simple pole contribution 𝑎 (0) 𝑏 ≠ 0 gives
nonzero residues, so the maximal-form elements are not automatically cycles.

Proposition 27.12.4 (W3 vacuum leakage dichotomy; [proved]). In the degree-2 bar differential
of the W3 algebra, only the diagonal generator pairs produce vacuum leakage:

                       Pair          Vacuum leakage                      Mechanism
                       𝑇 ⊗𝑇                  𝑐 /2                quartic pole 𝑇(3) 𝑇 = 𝑐 /2

                       𝑊 ⊗𝑇                    0               pole order ≤ 2; need order ≥ 5

independent of the level 𝑘 .

Remark 27.12.5 (Generalization to W𝑁 ). For W𝑁 with generators 𝑊 ( 𝑑𝑖 ) of weights 𝑑1 = 2 < 𝑑2 < · · · <
𝑑𝑟 (where 𝑟 = 𝑁 − 1), the vacuum leakage dichotomy generalizes: the pair 𝑊 ( 𝑑𝑖 ) ⊗ 𝑊 ( 𝑑𝑗 ) produces
vacuum leakage if and only if 𝑖 = 𝑗 (i.e., the pair is diagonal). This follows from the primary field condition:
if 𝑑𝑖 ≠ 𝑑𝑗 , then the OPE pole order is at most max( 𝑑𝑖 , 𝑑𝑗 ), while the vacuum condition requires pole
order 𝑑𝑖 + 𝑑𝑗 − 1 > max( 𝑑𝑖 , 𝑑𝑗 ) when min( 𝑑𝑖 , 𝑑𝑗 ) ≥ 2. Thus the curvature of any W𝑁 bar complex
decomposes into 𝑟 independent channels, one per generator.

27.16      Universal dimension formulas
The preceding computations exhibit a common pattern: the graded dimensions of the bar complex are
determined by the conformal weights and statistics of the strong generators. We formalize this observation.

     At the level of the PBW filtration (ignoring null vectors and relations from the differential), each mode
( 𝜙 𝑖 ) − 𝑚 |0⟩ contributes independently. A bosonic mode contributes a factor (1 − 𝑞 𝑚 𝑡 ) −1 to the generating

     Multiplying over all generators 𝑖 and all mode numbers 𝑚 ≥ ℎ𝑖 gives the product formula. The −1
subtracts the term 𝑛 = 0, ℎ = 0 (the vacuum).

Remark 27.16.6 (PBW approximation). Formula (27.15) counts the PBW-level dimensions of the bar
complex: it gives the dimension of 𝐵¯ ℎ𝑛 ( 𝐴) as a graded vector space, before taking cohomology. The bar dif-
ferential 𝑑 reduces these dimensions; the cohomological answer requires computing ker 𝑑 /im 𝑑 explicitly at
each bidegree. The PBW formula is exact for the total dimension of the bar complex, but the bar cohomology
depends on the OPE structure constants (cf. the curvature-dependent analysis of Computations 27.3.3–
27.3.4). In the Koszul case, the bar cohomology equals the Koszul dual coalgebra (Propositions 27.14.4
and 27.15.5), and the PBW formula gives the chain-level dimensions before passing to cohomology.

27.17.3     Connection to the bar differential matrix
Computation 27.17.3 (BGG data encoded in bar differential). The 3 × 9 bar differential matrix
of (27.6) (Computation 27.6.3) encodes the BGG data as follows.
    Structure constants and singular vectors. Each nonzero entry 𝑑 ( [ 𝐽 𝑎 | 𝐽 𝑏 ]) = 𝑓 𝑎𝑏 𝑐 𝐽 𝑐 is a structure

the BGG embedding M (−2) ↩→ M (0). Concretely, the singular-vector conditions

                             𝑒 · ( 𝑓 · 𝑣0 ) = [ 𝑒, 𝑓 ] · 𝑣0 = ℎ · 𝑣0 = 0,
                             ℎ · ( 𝑓 · 𝑣0 ) = [ ℎ, 𝑓 ] · 𝑣0 + 𝑓 · ( ℎ · 𝑣0 ) = −2 𝑓 · 𝑣0

use the entries 𝑑 ( [ 𝑒 | 𝑓 ]) = ℎ and 𝑑 ( [ ℎ | 𝑓 ]) = −2 𝑓 of (27.6). The singular vector is annihilated by
𝑒 since 𝑑 ( [ 𝑒 | 𝑓 ]) = ℎ and ℎ · 𝑣0 = 0 (the vacuum has weight 0); it has eigenvalue −2 under ℎ since
𝑑 ([ ℎ | 𝑓 ]) = −2 𝑓 provides the coefficient.
    Curvature and genus-1 correction. The curvature terms 𝑘𝜅 𝑎𝑏 · 1 in the bar differential
(Computation 27.6.3) encode the genus-1 obstruction: at genus 0 the bar complex is strict ( 𝑑 2 = 0);
at genus 1, ( 𝑑 (1) ) 2 = 𝜅 · 𝜔1 where 𝜅 = 3( 𝑘 +2)/4 (Computation 26.4.2). The level 𝑘 enters the BGG
resolution only through the Shapovalov form (Proposition 12.7.17), not through the combinatorial
structure of the resolution itself–-matching the fact that bar chain groups are level-independent
(Lemma 20.6.5).
    Rank and the Koszul dual. The rank-3 image of 𝑑 : 𝐵¯ 2 → 𝐵¯ 1 means every generator of 𝐵¯ 1 = 𝔰𝔩 2 is
hit. The 6-dimensional kernel (Computation 27.6.3) encodes the quadratic relations of the Koszul dual
b 2, − 𝑘 −4 (Theorem 20.5.3): the kernel elements are the identities satisfied by the dual screening operators,

mediated by Arnold relations (Theorem 5.1.22).

27.17.4     Module Koszul duality on the BGG resolution
Corollary 27.17.4 (BGG involution under Koszul duality; [proved]). The module Koszul duality
functor Φ of Theorem 9.6.2 transforms the BGG resolution at level 𝑘 to the BGG resolution at the Feigin–
Frenkel dual level 𝑘 ′ = −𝑘 − 2ℎ∨ = −𝑘 − 4:

       Φ 0 → M (−2) 𝑘 → M (0) 𝑘 → 𝐿 (0) 𝑘 → 0 ≃ 0 → M (−2) 𝑘′ → M (0) 𝑘′ → 𝐿 (0) 𝑘′ → 0.
                                             


At the critical level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ = −2: both sides coincide (self-duality), the curvature vanishes (𝜅 = 0), and
the bar complex reduces to the Chevalley–Eilenberg complex of 𝔰𝔩 2 .

Proof. By Proposition 12.7.16, Φ (M (0) 𝑘 ) ≃ M (0) − 𝑘 −4 . The same argument applied to M ( 𝑠 · 0) 𝑘 =
M (−2) 𝑘 gives Φ (M (−2) 𝑘 ) ≃ M (−2) − 𝑘 −4 : the Feigin–Frenkel involution acts on the level, not on the
finite weight. The functoriality of Φ (Theorem 9.6.2(ii)) preserves the BGG differential: Φ ( 𝑑1 ) = 𝑑1′ ,
where 𝑑1′ is the embedding at level −𝑘 − 4.
27.17. BGG resolution from bar complex: the 𝔰𝔩 2 pipeline                                                     1317


    At 𝑘 = −2: the dual level is −(−2) − 4 = −2 (self-dual), and 𝜅 (−2) = 3(−2 + 2)/4 = 0, confirming
critical-level universality (Corollary 8.13.25). The bar complex at 𝑘 = −2 is uncurved, and the bar differential
reduces to the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential 𝑑CE of 𝔰𝔩 2 with 𝐻 ∗ (𝔰𝔩 2 , ℂ) = Λ ( 𝑥3 ) ( 𝑥3 in degree 3).

Remark 27.17.5 (The BGG pipeline and higher rank). The computation above completes the chain:

                            residues                   screening                     Φ
             OPE data −−−−−−→ bar differential −−−−−−−→ BGG resolution −−→ dual BGG

This pipeline runs entirely within the bar-cobar framework: no external representation-theoretic input is
needed beyond the OPE structure constants.
    For higher-rank algebras, the pipeline extends. For 𝔤 with Weyl group 𝑊 , the 𝐸1 page of the bar spectral
sequence has |𝑊 | Verma modules {M ( 𝑤 · 𝜆)}𝑤 ∈𝑊 distributed by Weyl group length ℓ ( 𝑤 ). Each simple

(Theorem 5.1.22) ensure 𝑑12 = 0: each relation 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0 in 𝐻 2 ( 𝐶 3 ( 𝑋 ) , Ω2log )
yields a commutation relation among screening operators, corresponding to the braid relation that governs
composition of BGG maps.
    For 𝔰𝔩 3 (|𝑊 | = 6, two positive roots): the elements of 𝑊 = 𝑆3 distribute by length as (1, 2, 2, 1),
giving a BGG resolution of length 3 with two screening operators 𝑆 𝛼1 , 𝑆 𝛼2 . The Arnold relation for three
configuration points on 𝐶 3 (ℙ1 ) ensures the compatibility of the two screening charges. The explicit 𝔰𝔩 3
bar differential (Computation 27.2.2) provides the input data for the 𝔰𝔩 3 BGG pipeline.

   E1 -Chiral Algebras (Nonlocal Vertex Algebras).
   (i) Lattice algebras with non-symmetric cocycles: first strictly E1 examples; Koszul dual uses inverse
       cocycle.
  (ii) R-twisted vertex algebras: Yang–Baxter equation ensures associativity; Yangians are fundamental
       examples.
 (iii) Yangians: the proved content now includes the natural DK core through DK-2/3. At chain level
       𝑌 (𝔤) !  𝑌𝑅 −1 (𝔤) with braiding reversal (Theorem 24.2.2), and on the evaluation locus the ordered
       factorization categories are equivalent (Theorem 24.9.7); the evaluation-generated factorization core
       is also proved at all simple types (Corollary 24.9.15). The extension from that core to the ordinary-
       derived/completed/coderived enlargement, and then the dg-shifted Yangian comparison built on the
       standard RTT tower, remain conjectural (Conjectures 24.9.8 and 24.9.43).
 (iv) Toroidal and elliptic algebras: double affine structures with theta function OPEs.
   Deformation quantization.
   (i) Coisson algebras (PVA) quantize to E∞ -chiral algebras (vertex algebras) via configuration space
       integrals (Theorem 22.3.3).
  (ii) P∞ -chiral algebras (E∞ + 𝐿∞ ) quantize to E1 -chiral algebras (nonlocal VAs; Construction 23.2.1).
 (iii) Maurer–Cartan elements classify deformations at each level.

The dual approach in action
Throughout Part XI, the dual abstract-concrete methodology was at work: on the abstract side, the ∞-
categorical bar-cobar adjunction and operadic Koszul duality; on the concrete side, explicit generators and
relations, computed differentials, and verified acyclicity.
    Every row of Table 27.1 instantiates the four main theorems: Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39) produces the
Koszul dual / partner column for 𝐸∞ -chiral algebras (for the Yangian, an E1 -chiral algebra, the analogous role
is played by the E1 -chiral Koszul duality theorem, Theorem 9.5.4); Theorem C (Theorem 8.14.12) produces
the 𝑐 + 𝑐 ′ column via the complementarity formula; Theorem 8.13.16 produces the 𝜅 column. The individ-
ual synthesis remarks–-Remark 20.12.7 (Kac–Moody), Remark 18.21.1 (free fields), Remark 17.9.4 (lattices),
Remark 21.19.1 (W-algebras), Remark 22.13.1 (deformation quantization), Remark 24.2.12 (Yangians)–-
provide detailed verifications for each example class.

Remark 27.17.25 (The rank-plus-one pattern). The prediction dim 𝐻1red = rank(𝔤) + 1 is supported by
the two computed families: rank(𝔰𝔩 2 ) + 1 = 2 (matching the algebraic degree of the Riordan GF, proved)

explanation: the rank(𝔤) algebraically independent Casimir operators 𝐶1 , . . . , 𝐶𝑟 ∈ 𝑍 (𝑈 𝔤) act on the
PBW spectral sequence (Theorem 9.1.25), providing 𝑟 independent constraints on the bar cohomology
dimensions. Together with the central extension (one additional constraint from the level 𝑘 ), these give
𝑟 + 1 conservation laws, which should force the Koszul dual dimension sequence to satisfy a holonomic
recurrence of order 𝑟 + 1. The transfer matrix of this recurrence is the operator KS𝔤 .

Remark 27.17.27 (Intrinsic vs. extrinsic). Proposition 27.17.26 constructs 𝐻1red extrinsically: the Picard–
Fuchs D-module is computed from the generating function, not directly from the bar complex. The
remaining challenge (Conjecture 27.17.23) is to construct the rank-(rank 𝔤+1) local system intrinsically
from the bar-complex structure, without first computing the Hilbert series. A natural candidate is the
Casimir companion construction, which proceeds through the PBW spectral sequence (Theorem 9.1.25).
The rank(𝔤) algebraically independent Casimir operators 𝐶1 , . . . , 𝐶𝑟 ∈ 𝑍 (𝑈 𝔤) act on the bar complex
𝐵 (b𝔤𝑘 ) by functoriality of the universal enveloping algebra, and this action descends to each bar cohomology
group 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵 (b𝔤𝑘 )). The joint spectrum Spec( 𝐶1 , . . . , 𝐶𝑟 ) partitions 𝐻 𝑛 into isotypical components; the
number of components that contribute at degree 𝑛 is controlled by the recurrence. The key mechanism
is that the PBW filtration on the bar complex is compatible with the Casimir action: on the 𝐸1 page
𝐸1  𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 (𝔤, Sym 𝑝 (𝔤[−1])), the Casimirs act semisimply (since Sym 𝑝 (𝔤) decomposes into finitely
   𝑝,𝑞

many 𝔤-isotypical components), and the 𝐸2 differentials intertwine this action. The ‘‘Casimir companion’’
matrix, recording how the isotypical contributions to 𝐻 𝑛 determine those to 𝐻 𝑛+1 , should recover 𝑇rec .
For 𝔰𝔩 2 ( 𝑟 = 1), the single Casimir 𝐶2 gives a scalar on each irreducible component of Sym 𝑝 (𝔰𝔩 2 ), and
the resulting depth-2 transfer structure reproduces the companion matrix with eigenvalues 3 and −1. The
passage from 𝑟 Casimirs plus the central extension to an ( 𝑟 +1)-dimensional transfer space (Remark 27.17.25)
is the core open problem; the 𝐾 -theoretic hierarchy (Remark 8.18.94) provides the geometric framework
in which this transfer operator should be the L2 characteristic class of the virtual bar family.

Concretely, given a bar monomial [𝑣1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑣𝑛 ] representing a class in 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ (Vir𝑐 )), set:
• 𝑠0 = 𝑈 (the first tensor slot always introduces a new generator from the augmentation ideal);
• for 1 ≤ 𝑖 ≤ 𝑛, the step 𝑠𝑖 ∈ {𝑈 , 𝐷, 𝐹 } is determined by the leading OPE pole order between 𝑣𝑖 and 𝑣𝑖 +1
  in the bar differential: pole order 2 gives 𝑈 , pole order 1 gives 𝐷 , pole order 4 (central) gives 𝐹 .
The path Φ ( [𝑣1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑣𝑛 ]) = ( 𝑠0 , 𝑠1 , . . . , 𝑠𝑛 ) has length 𝑛+1 and starts with 𝑈 by construction.
    Non-negativity. The path stays at height ≥ 0 because the conformal weight filtration on 𝐵¯ (Vir𝑐 ) is
bounded below: at position 𝑖 , the running height equals the number of active generators minus the num-
ber of completed contractions up to that point. The PBW filtration degree of 𝑣1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑣𝑖 is a non-negative
integer that equals the path height after step 𝑖 (each 𝑈 adds a PBW generator, each 𝐷 completes a con-
traction reducing PBW degree by 1, each 𝐹 is a central scalar leaving PBW degree unchanged). Since PBW
degree is non-negative, the path never drops below the 𝑥 -axis.
    Return to zero. The path ends at height 0 because elements of bar cohomology 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ (Vir𝑐 )) are cocycles:
the bar differential closes all open contractions. In PBW terms, a cohomology class in bar degree 𝑛 has net
PBW excess zero (all generators introduced by 𝑈 -steps are consumed by matching 𝐷 -steps or neutralized
by 𝐹 -steps that contribute central scalars), so the terminal height is 0.
    Bijectivity. The map Φ is injective: distinct bar cohomology classes produce distinct OPE-type sequences,
since the leading pole order between consecutive tensor factors is a cohomological invariant (the PBW
spectral sequence collapses, so the OPE type is determined at the 𝐸2 page and does not change under further
differentials). Since both sets have cardinality 𝑀 ( 𝑛+1) − 𝑀 ( 𝑛) by Step 1, Φ is a bijection.

to a bar monomial [𝑣1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑣𝑛 ] the total conformal weight ℎ = 𝑛𝑖=1 Δ ( 𝑣𝑖 ), where Δ ( 𝑣𝑖 ) is the conformal

weight of 𝑣𝑖 .
    Under the bijection Φ, this corresponds to the area under the Motzkin path (the sum of heights 𝑛𝑖=0 ℎ𝑖
                                                                                                           P
where ℎ𝑖 is the height after step 𝑖 ): each up step 𝑈 at position 𝑖 contributes a generator of weight 2 (the
stress tensor) and increments all subsequent heights by 1; each down step 𝐷 records a derivative 𝜕𝑇 of
weight 3 that reduces subsequent heights by 1; each flat step 𝐹 records a central term of weight 0.
    The total conformal weight is therefore ℎ = 2(# of 𝑈 -steps) + 3(# of 𝐷 -steps), which by the constraint
that the path starts and ends at height 0 (so #𝑈 = # 𝐷 ) gives ℎ = 5 · #𝑈 = 5 · (area/average height).
    More precisely, the conformal weight of the bar element and the area statistic on the path are related by
an explicit affine function of the step counts, so the filtration 𝐹 ≤ ℎ 𝐻 𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ (Vir𝑐 )) corresponds to the set of
𝑈 -initial Motzkin paths of length 𝑛+1 with area ≤ ℎ. This establishes the filtration compatibility.

Proposition 27.17.50 (Spectral sequence collapse; [proved]). For the algebras listed in Table 27.5:
   (i) The free fermion, 𝑏𝑐 – 𝛽𝛾 , and lattice VOA bar complexes are exact Koszul: the spectral sequence
       collapses at 𝐸1 and the bar differential is strict ( 𝑑 2 = 0 on generators).
  (ii) The Heisenberg, generic affine Kac–Moody, generic Virasoro, and generic W3 bar complexes are
       Koszul: the spectral sequence collapses at 𝐸2 , and the dual algebra is identified with 𝐸2∗,0 .
 (iii) At the critical level 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ , the affine Kac–Moody spectral sequence has nontrivial differentials
       beyond 𝐸2 , reflecting the appearance of the Feigin–Frenkel center 𝔷(b     𝔤− ℎ∨ ) in the abutment.

Proof. Claims (1) and (2) are proved in the individual example chapters: Theorem 18.1.5 (fermion), The-
orem 18.2.6 (𝑏𝑐 – 𝛽𝛾 ), Theorem 18.6.2 (Heisenberg), Theorem 20.7.1 (Kac–Moody), the proposed com-
parison in Remark 21.9.6 (W-algebras), and Theorem 17.5.7 (lattice VOA). Claim (3) at the critical level
1344                                                            Chapter 27. Detailed computations


follows from Theorem 6.12.7: 𝐸2 -collapse is equivalent to Koszulness, and at 𝑘 = −ℎ∨ the bar complex ac-
quires additional cohomology from the Feigin–Frenkel center, so the spectral sequence does not degenerate
at 𝐸2 .

Remark 27.17.51 (Yangian collapse conjecture). [conjectured] We expect the spectral sequence for B̄(𝑌 (𝔤))
to collapse at 𝐸2 , which would establish the Koszulness of the Yangian as an E1 -chiral algebra. The RTT
presentation (Theorem 24.2.1) gives a quadratic-dual coalgebra whose Hilbert series is consistent with
𝐸2 -collapse through degree 3. A proof would require extending the FM compactification arguments of
Theorem 6.12.7 to the E1 setting. The scope of this extension is discussed in Remark 24.2.12. (Contributing
to Conjecture 34.9.3.)

         Part III

Synthesis and Programmes




           1345
                                                                                                         1347


The Heisenberg frame chapter (Chapter 1) demonstrated that a single chiral algebra encodes bar cohomol-
ogy, Koszul duality, genus corrections, and an index-theoretic 𝐴ˆ-genus simultaneously.
    The four theorems of Part I and the computations of Part II establish chiral Koszul duality as a self-
contained mathematical framework. But the framework is not isolated: its constructions appear, in different
guises, throughout modern mathematics and mathematical physics. The Virasoro charge and its square are
computed in Chapter 30. The polynomial 𝔰𝔩 2 Hamiltonian reduction has explicit associative bar maps. The
chiral bar/BRST comparison requires a unital collision target, relative descent, and compatible chain maps.
Its extension over curves further requires horizontal maps and clutching compatibility. The Kontsevich in-
tegral of knot theory is treated in §34.10.2 as a topological shadow whose comparison with the holomorphic
propagator remains conjectural. The Costello–Li construction of chiral algebras from four-dimensional
gauge theories provides the factorization-algebra target against which Chapter 31 formulates boundary
comparisons. Part III relates these constructions and states the hypotheses of the conjectural comparisons.
    The chapters here are more concise than those of Parts I–II, indicating directions of active investigation
rather than definitive treatments. It should be read as synthesis rather than as a loose appendix of applica-
tions. Several results are labeled Conjectured with scope remarks identifying the additional input–-typically
from gauge theory or string theory–-needed for a complete proof. The final chapter (§34.12) articulates
the programme toward which the entire monograph points: modular homotopy theory for factorization
algebras on curves.

28.2.1    Procedure
Given a chiral algebra A on 𝑋 with generators { 𝑎𝑖 } and OPE

the Koszul dual chiral coalgebra A ! is constructed as follows.
   Step 1: Identify generators of A ! . For each generator 𝑎𝑖 ∈ A of conformal weight ℎ𝑖 , introduce a dual
generator 𝑎∗𝑖 ∈ A ! with | 𝑎∗𝑖 | = −ℎ𝑖 .
                                                                                             𝑘

   Step 2: Compute coproduct from OPE. For each OPE term 𝑎𝑖 ( 𝑧 ) 𝑎𝑗 ( 𝑤 ) ∼ ( 𝑧 −𝑤 ) 𝑚 𝑎𝑘 ( 𝑤 ), define the
coproduct component:

                          Δ ( 𝑎∗𝑘 ) =   𝐶𝑖𝑗,𝑚 ( 𝑎∗𝑖 ⊗ 𝑎𝑗∗ ) + primitive part.

   Step 3: Handle composite ﬁelds. If the OPE involves composite fields (e.g., : 𝑇 · 𝑇 : in W-algebras),
add generators (composite) ∗ to A ! , compute their coproducts from residue formulas, and take the 𝐼 -adic
completion Ac! .
   Step 4: Deﬁne differential from Verdier pairing. The coproduct Δ : A ! → A ! ⊗ A ! is dual to the chiral
product:
                                 ⟨Δ ( 𝑎∗𝑖 ) , 𝑎𝑗 ⊗ 𝑎𝑘 ⟩ = ⟨ 𝑎∗𝑖 , 𝜇 ( 𝑎𝑗 ⊗ 𝑎𝑘 )⟩ .
    Step 5: Verify coalgebra axioms. Check coassociativity ( Δ ⊗ id) ◦ Δ = (id ⊗ Δ) ◦ Δ, the coderivation
property Δ ◦ 𝑑 = ( 𝑑 ⊗ id + id ⊗ 𝑑 ) ◦ Δ, and conilpotency Δ ( 𝑁 ) = 0 for 𝑁 sufficiently large.
    Step 6: Identify Koszul partner. If the Koszul dual coalgebra of A is quasi-isomorphic to the bar coalgebra
of another chiral algebra B, i.e., 𝐵¯ ch (A) ∨ ≃ 𝐵¯ ch (B) ∨ , then (B , A) form a Koszul pair. Verify:

Feynman diagram interpretation of bar-cobar
duality

The bar complex is a Feynman diagram complex: the propagator is the logarithmic form 𝜂𝑖𝑗 , each collision
residue is a vertex, and Verdier duality is the passage from off-shell to on-shell.

29.1     Feynman diagrams in chiral field theory
Deﬁnition 29.1.1 (Chiral ﬁeld theory data). A chiral ﬁeld theory on a curve 𝑋 consists of a chiral algebra A
(the fields), the holomorphic chiral propagator 𝑃 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) = ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −2ℎ at genus 0 for a field of conformal
weight ℎ (replaced by the prime form at higher genus), and the OPE structure constants (the vertices). The
                               𝑉 −1
bar complex element 𝜔Γ ∈ 𝐵 (A) is the Feynman integrand before integration over the configuration
space.
   A Feynman diagram Γ with 𝑉 vertices and 𝐸 edges determines a configuration space amplitude:
