logarithmic forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) encode these propagator singularities.

29.4      Graph complexes and Kontsevich formality
29.4.1    The graph complex
Deﬁnition 29.4.1 (Kontsevich graph complex). The graph complex GC𝑛 consists of:
• Generators: Isomorphism classes of graphs with 𝑛 labeled external legs and unlabeled internal vertices
• Differential: Sum over edge contractions
• Grading: Loop number 𝐿 ( Γ)
Conjecture 29.4.2 (Bar complex and graph complex; [physical heuristic]). The chiral bar complex admits a
                                                                                 ch
quasi-isomorphism to the A-decorated Kontsevich graph complex: 𝐵 (A) ≃ GC(A), where vertices
correspond to field insertions, edges to logarithmic forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 , and the bar differential decomposes as edge
contraction (residue), vertex splitting (boundary stratification), and decoration action.

29.4.2    Kontsevich’s formality and chiral algebras
Theorem 29.4.3 (Kontsevich formality; [proved]). For a smooth manifold 𝑀 , the 𝐿∞ algebra of

Remark 29.4.4 (Chiral analogue of Kontsevich formality). The bar-cobar construction on a curve 𝑋 is

bar-cobar duality. The formality morphism F : 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵 (A)) → A sums over Feynman graphs with
configuration space integral weights.
Conjecture 29.4.5 (Disk-local perturbative/FM comparison; [conjectured]). Let 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑋 be a holomorphic
disk chart on a curve, and suppose a holomorphic-topological perturbative field theory on 𝑈 produces
the same local chiral algebra model A|𝑈 . Then the regularized perturbative BRST-anomaly brackets of
Gaiotto–Kulp–Wu [216] agree, on that disk chart, with the local bar operations cut out by the Fulton–
MacPherson collision strata:
   (i) the binary perturbative bracket agrees with the bar residue/OPE operation on 𝐶2 (𝑈 );
  (ii) the ternary perturbative bracket agrees with the sum of bar residues on the three codimension-1
       collision strata of 𝐶 3 (𝑈 ), hence with the local 𝑚3 -operation; and
 (iii) the quadratic identities satisfied by those perturbative brackets agree with the Stokes relations among
       the corresponding codimension-1 FM strata after passage to the compactification.
29.4. Graph complexes and Kontsevich formality                                                              1359


Remark 29.4.6 (MC5 local packet). Conjecture 29.4.5 isolates the first exact MC5 comparison package. It
is finite and local: one binary collision calculation on 𝐶2 , one ternary calculation on the three boundary
divisors of 𝐶 3 , and the matching of the quadratic/Wess–Zumino identities with the Stokes relations among
those divisors.
     Once that local packet is in place, the next step is no longer a physics-dictionary comparison but an ana-
lytic extension problem: upgrade the local formulas to the FM boundary calculus used by the bar construc-
tion and invoke Stokes regularity on FM compactifications (Proposition 11.5.20). Only after that analytic
compactification step does the remaining MC5 content become the genuswise clutching/renormalization
lift.
Proposition 29.4.7 (Binary-ternary reduction for the disk-local packet; [proved]). Fix a holomor-
phic disk chart 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑋 , and interpret the perturbative BRST-anomaly brackets and the local bar operations
on the same local chain model underlying A|𝑈 . Then Conjecture 29.4.5 reduces to the following two
explicit local comparisons:
   (i) the binary perturbative bracket agrees with the local bar residue/OPE operation on 𝐶2 (𝑈 ); and
  (ii) the ternary perturbative bracket agrees with the local 𝑚3 -operation, equivalently with the sum of
       the three codimension-1 residues on 𝐶 3 (𝑈 ).
In other words, once (i)–(ii) are proved, the quadratic-identity part of Conjecture 29.4.5 is formal and
carries no additional independent coefficient calculation.

Proof. On the perturbative side, Gaiotto–Kulp–Wu [216] prove that the regularized BRST-anomaly brack-
ets satisfy the required quadratic axioms/Wess–Zumino consistency relations.
    On the bar side, the corresponding arity-3 consistency relation is already built into the local 𝐴∞ structure:
by Theorem 29.3.4 specialized to 𝑛 = 3, the bar operations satisfy the quadratic relation expressing 𝑚1 𝑚3 in
terms of composites of lower operations; geometrically this is the Stokes relation among the codimension-1
boundary strata of the compactified three-point configuration space.
    Therefore, once the binary operation and the ternary operation are identified on the common local
chain model, the two quadratic packages are comparing the same formal relation, and there is no third
independent local coefficient problem left to solve.

Corollary 29.4.8 (Ternary comparison after a specified binary identification; [proved]). Fix a
disk coordinate and actual source and target collision complexes on that disk. Assume the full constructed-
target, relative-carrier, filtration, actual symbol quasi-isomorphism, and compatible-correction hypotheses
of Theorem 30.3.13. A sheaf application also requires its descent and section-carrier data. Suppose the
perturbative and bar operations have been realized on the common local chain model of Proposition 29.4.7.
In addition, require the actual binary operations to agree there. Write 𝜇pert : 𝐶 ⊗ 𝐶 → 𝐶 and 𝜇bar :
𝑇 ⊗ 𝑇 → 𝑇 for homogeneous chain maps of the same specified degree 𝑟 . The tensor differentials use the
Koszul sign rule. For a degree-zero comparison map Φ : 𝐶 → 𝑇 , the required identity is

                                            𝜇bar ( Φ ⊗ Φ) = Φ𝜇pert                                        (29.1)

on their complete specified binary domain, with the same residue normalization. Then the remaining
operation comparison in Proposition 29.4.7 is the ternary one.

Proof. The additional binary identity supplies clause (i) of Proposition 29.4.7. Its clause (ii) is the ternary
comparison, giving the conclusion. The binary identity is separate from the chain equation. Indeed, let
1360                       Chapter 29. Feynman diagram interpretation of bar-cobar duality


both complexes be ℂ in degree zero and let Φ = 1. Set 𝜇pert = 0 and 𝜇bar ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) = 𝑥𝑦 . The map Φ is a chain
isomorphism but the two sides of (29.1) differ at (1, 1).
     A ghost-bilinear assignment to 𝑑 log( 𝑧1 − 𝑧2 ) requires an actual relative input, target coefficient, total

Proposition 29.4.9 (Two-channel reduction after compactifying the ternary packet; [proved]).
Fix a holomorphic disk chart 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑋 , and suppose the compactification/Stokes upgrade has been achieved
for the local ternary comparison in Conjecture 29.4.5: namely, suppose the perturbative ternary bracket
and the local bar 𝑚3 -operation are represented by logarithmic 1-forms on 𝑀 0,4  ℙ1 whose only poles lie
at the three boundary points corresponding to the channels (12|3), (23|1), and (13|2). Then comparison of
the two residues in any two of those channels implies comparison in the third channel as well. Equivalently,
after compactification the ternary part of Conjecture 29.4.5 has only two independent boundary-channel
checks.

Proof. Let 𝜔pert and 𝜔bar denote the two logarithmic 1-forms on 𝑀 0,4  ℙ1 , and set

                              𝛿 = 𝜔pert − 𝜔bar ∈ 𝐻 0 ℙ1 , Ω1ℙ1 log{0, 1, ∞} .
                                                                           


If the residues of 𝛿 agree in two channels, then two of the three residues of 𝛿 vanish. By the residue theorem
on ℙ1 , the sum of all three residues is zero, so the third residue vanishes as well. Therefore 𝛿 has zero residue
at every boundary point, so it is in fact a holomorphic 1-form on ℙ1 . But 𝐻 0 (ℙ1 , Ω1ℙ1 ) = 0, hence 𝛿 = 0.
In particular, the third boundary residue is forced by the first two.

Proof. Corollary 29.4.8 reduces the local operation comparison to the ternary comparison once its actual

comparison to any two of the three boundary channels.

Corollary 29.4.11 (Standard-chart form of the remaining genus-0 packet; [proved]). Choose
the standard coordinate on 𝑀 0,4  ℙ1 with boundary points 0, 1, ∞. Under all constructed-carrier, filtered-

Theorem 29.5.2 (Graph loop number and genus; [proved] [168]). For a Feynman diagram Γ with
𝑉 vertices, 𝐸 internal edges (propagators), and 𝐿 external legs, the loop number equals:

                                             ℓ ( Γ) = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 1 = 𝑏1 ( Γ)

where 𝑏1 is the first Betti number of Γ viewed as a 1-complex.
29.5. The 𝑚 𝑘 operations as Feynman amplitudes                                                           1363


   When Γ is equipped with a ribbon (fat graph) structure, it determines a surface Σ with 𝜒 ( Σ) = 𝑉 −
𝐸 + 𝐹 where 𝐹 is the number of boundary components. The genus of this surface satisfies 𝑔 ≤ ℓ /2, with
equality when 𝐹 = 1 (a single boundary component).
   For chiral algebras: The operation 𝑚𝑘 is defined via configuration space integrals on 𝑀 0,𝑘+1 (genus zero).
The boundary 𝜕 𝑀 0,𝑘+1 is stratified by stable trees, which encode compositions of lower 𝑚𝑗 operations.
The term ‘‘loop order ≤ 𝑘 − 2’’ for 𝑚𝑘 refers to the number of homotopy/propagator insertions in the
homotopy transfer formula expressing 𝑚𝑘 in terms of 𝑚2 and the contracting homotopy ℎ, not to the
genus of a Riemann surface.

Proof. Step 1: Graph loop number.
   For a connected graph Γ with 𝑉 vertices and 𝐸 edges, the first Betti number is 𝑏1 ( Γ) = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 1. This
equals the loop number ℓ ( Γ) (the number of independent cycles in Γ ).
   Step 2: Ribbon graph genus vs. loop number.
   For a ribbon graph Γ thickened to a surface Σ with 𝐹 boundary components, cap the boundary to
obtain a closed surface Σ̄ of genus 𝑔 . The CW structure on Σ̄ has 𝑉 vertices, 𝐸 edges, and 𝐹 faces (the
capping disks), so:
                                       𝜒 ( Σ̄) = 𝑉 − 𝐸 + 𝐹 = 2 − 2 𝑔
Hence 𝑔 = 1 − (𝑉 − 𝐸 + 𝐹 )/2. Since ℓ = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 1, we have 𝑔 = ( ℓ + 1 − 𝐹 )/2, so 𝑔 ≤ ℓ /2 with
equality when 𝐹 = 1 (single boundary component).
   The loop number is defined as the number of independent momentum integrations:

                               ℓ = # of independent momenta = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 1

   Step 3: Connection to ﬁrst Betti number.
   The first Betti number counts independent 1-cycles:

                                   𝑏1 ( Γ) = dim 𝐻1 ( Γ, ℤ) = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 𝐶

where 𝐶 is the number of connected components.
  For a connected Feynman diagram (𝐶 = 1):

                                              𝑏1 = 𝐸 − 𝑉 + 1 = ℓ

   Step 4: Conﬁguration space interpretation.
   The operation 𝑚𝑘 is defined by integration over the fundamental chain of 𝑀 0,𝑘+1 (a genus-zero moduli
space):                                       ∫
                        𝑚 𝑘 ( 𝜙1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜙 𝑘 ) =             Res[ 𝜙1 ( 𝑧1 ) · · · 𝜙𝑘 ( 𝑧 𝑘 ) · 𝜔]
                                                     𝑀 0,𝑘+1

    The boundary 𝜕 𝑀 0,𝑘+1 is stratified by stable trees (connected graphs with 𝑏1 = 0). Each boundary
stratum corresponds to a composition 𝑚𝑗 ◦ 𝑚𝑖 of lower operations, and the 𝐴∞ relations arise from
Stokes’ theorem on these boundary strata.
    The codimension of a boundary stratum equals the number of internal edges in the stable tree. The
‘‘loop order ≤ 𝑘 − 2’’ for 𝑚𝑘 arises from the homotopy transfer formula, where each application of the
contracting homotopy ℎ corresponds to a propagator insertion in the transfer graph.

ages this: the genus-1 component Θ (1) = ( 𝑐 /2) · 𝜂 ⊗ 𝜆1 has scalar trace 𝑐 /24, matching 𝐹1 (Vir𝑐 ). Higher
genera contribute Θ ( 𝑔 ) = ( 𝑐 /2) · 𝜂 ⊗ 𝜆 𝑔 , each computable from the same Feynman diagram machinery
applied to curves of genus 𝑔 .
Remark 29.5.7 (Connection to Lie cohomology). The 𝐴∞ operation 𝑚3 is a homotopy correcting the failure
of strict associativity of 𝑚2 :

                             𝑚3 satisfies 𝜕 ( 𝑚3 ) = 𝑚2 ( 𝑚2 ⊗ id) − 𝑚2 (id ⊗ 𝑚2 )

homotopies descend to Lie cohomology classes. For the Virasoro algebra, the 𝐴∞ homotopy 𝑚3 (𝑇 , 𝑇 , 𝑇 )
                                                   2 (Witt, ℂ) that classifies the central extension Vir → Witt.
detects the same class as the Lie 2-cocycle 𝑐 ∈ 𝐻Lie

29.5.4     𝑚4 and higher: multi-loop structure
Example 29.5.8 (𝑚4 : two distinct contributions). The operation 𝑚4 receives contributions from:
   Type I: Genuine two-loop diagram (genus 2).
   Two independent loops connected by a propagator ⇒ ℓ = 2.
   Type II: One-loop with vertex splitting (genus 1).
   One loop with a composite vertex ⇒ ℓ = 1 (but appears at 𝑚4 level).
   The bar complex differential cannot distinguish these without further structure, so 𝑚4 includes both
contributions. This is the origin of the 𝐴∞ complexity.

    Loop order relates to genus via ribbon graph thickening ( 𝑔 = ( ℓ + 1 − 𝐹 )/2, Theorem 29.5.2). The 𝐴∞
relations encode the BPHZ recursion; Koszul duality is the algebraic shadow of off-shell/on-shell duality.

Theorem 30.1.4 (Quantum master equation as Maurer–Cartan equation; [proved]). The quan-
tum master equation
                                     ΔBV 𝑒 𝑆 /ℏ = 0
is equivalent to the Maurer–Cartan equation in the dg Lie algebra ( 𝐵¯ ≥1 (A) , 𝛿, [−, −]): it encodes the
compatibility of bar and cobar differentials under Verdier duality. This equivalence is natural: it holds
functorially for morphisms of chiral algebras via the BV functor of Theorem 30.23.7.

Proof. Stage 1 (Algebraic equivalence). Write 𝑆 = 𝑆0 + 𝑆int with 𝑆0 the free (quadratic) action and 𝑆int the
interactions. Then:
                                                1            1         

                                               ℏ             2ℏ
   Setting this to zero and using { 𝑆0 , 𝑆0 } = 0 (classical master equation for the free theory), Δ𝑆0 = 0
(no quantum anomaly for quadratic actions), and absorbing { 𝑆0 , 𝑆int } into a total BV differential 𝛿 =
ΔBV + ℏ1 { 𝑆0 , −} gives:
                                                    1
                                         ℏ 𝛿 𝑆int + { 𝑆int , 𝑆int } = 0
                                                   2
   This is precisely the Maurer–Cartan equation in the dg Lie algebra ( 𝐵¯ ≥1 (A) , 𝛿, [−, −]). The identifi-
cation of each term with a bar/cobar operation is provided by Stage 2.
    Stage 2 (Identiﬁcation of terms via the BV functor). The BV functor BV : ChirAlg 𝑋 → BV-Alg of
Theorem 30.23.7 assigns to each chiral algebra A the BV algebra BV(A) = ( 𝐵¯ ch (A) , ·, Δ, {−, −}). Its
Verdier duality compatibility (Theorem 30.23.7, last part) establishes that 𝔻( 𝐵¯ (A))  Ω (A ! ) as BV
algebras, naturally in A.
    Under this identification, each BV operation matches a concrete bar-cobar operation:
30.1. BV formalism for chiral algebras                                                                  1379


• The bar differential 𝑑𝐵¯ = { 𝑆, −} on 𝐵¯ (A) becomes the cobar differential 𝑑Ω on Ω (A ! ).
• The BV Laplacian Δ on 𝐵¯ (A) becomes the cobar product on Ω (A ! ).
• The QME ℏΔ𝑆 + 21 { 𝑆, 𝑆 } = 0 is the condition ensuring that both differentials square to zero simulta-
  neously, i.e., that the BV algebra ( 𝑑𝐵¯ , Δ) is consistent.
   Now let 𝑓 : A → B be a morphism of chiral algebras. Functoriality gives a BV morphism
BV( 𝑓 ) : BV(A) → BV(B) preserving the product, Laplacian, and bracket, while Verdier duality
transports this morphism to the corresponding cobar map on duals. Therefore the identification between
the quantum master equation and the bar-cobar compatibility is functorial in A; it is a natural equivalence,
not merely a pointwise comparison.

Remark 30.1.5 (Scope). Stage 1 uses standard BV algebra manipulations ([proved], see Costello–
Gwilliam [27]). Stage 2 assembles the BV functor (Theorem 30.23.7, [proved]) with the Verdier duality
isomorphism 𝔻( 𝐵¯ (A))  Ω (A ! ) (Theorem 6.3.32, [proved]). The identification of the QME with the
functorial expression of bar-cobar Verdier compatibility is Theorem 30.1.4 above.

30.1.3 Marked curves and insertion dependence
For 𝑛 ≥ 3, let 𝐶𝑛 (ℙ1 ) be the space of ordered distinct points on the complex projective line. The diagonal
action of PGL2 (ℂ) is free. There is a unique projective transformation taking the first three points to
0, 1, ∞. The remaining points give the explicit quotient

                                       𝐶𝑛 (ℙ1 )/PGL2 (ℂ)  M0,𝑛 .

Thus the two spaces have complex dimensions 𝑛 and 𝑛 − 3. Their compactifications retain these dimensions.
In particular, a compactification of 𝐶𝑛 (ℙ1 ) cannot equal M 0,𝑛+1 , whose dimension is 𝑛 − 2.
Proposition 30.1.6 (Insertion integrals and Euler characteristics). Put 𝑍 = M 0,𝑛 (ℂ) with its
complex orientation and real dimension 𝑚 = 2𝑛 − 6. Let 𝐶1 , . . . , 𝐶𝑛 be complex cochain complexes. An
insertion map is a degree-zero chain map

                                    𝜇 : 𝐶1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝐶𝑛 −→ Ω• ( 𝑍 ; ℂ) ,
1380                                   Chapter 30. BV-BRST formalism and Gaiotto’s perspective


where the tensor differential has sign (−1) | 𝑥1 |+···+| 𝑥𝑗 −1 | on its 𝑗 th summand. For closed homogeneous
inputs of total degree 𝑚, define
                                                            ∫
                                 A 𝜇 ( 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥 𝑛 ) =    𝜇 ( 𝑥1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑥 𝑛 ) .
                                                         𝑍

This is a multilinear function of their cohomology classes. If, on a fixed product of input spaces, it equals an
input-independent scalar for every tuple, that scalar is zero. Therefore an identity with an Euler characteristic
of a fixed complex requires separate insertion normalization, and cannot hold for arbitrary insertions when
that Euler characteristic is nonzero.

Proof. The chain identity for 𝜇 sends a tensor boundary to an exact form. Stokes’ theorem on the compact
oriented manifold 𝑍 makes the integral of such a form zero. Multilinearity follows from the linearity of 𝜇
and integration. Putting one input equal to zero forces the scalar to be zero. For an explicit instance, take
𝑛 = 3, 𝑍 a point, and 𝐶𝑗 = ℂ in degree zero. The multiplication map gives A 𝜇 ( 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑐 ) = 𝑎𝑏𝑐 . The Euler
characteristic of the degree-zero complex ℂ is 1. The tuples (1, 1, 1) and (0, 1, 1) give different amplitudes for
the same complex.

   For a chiral-chain application, 𝜇 includes the actual insertion and collision maps into forms on 𝑍 .
Logarithmic forms along a divisor require an integration domain and boundary prescription for which the
integration functional is closed. An Euler class integral supplies a specific characteristic form, rather than
an arbitrary multilinear insertion.
Remark 30.1.7 (Genus-1 partition function). The Bernoulli coefficient of Theorem 8.13.16 is 𝐹1 = 𝜅 /24. For
𝜅 = 𝐶 /2, it gives 𝐹1 = 𝐶 /48, while the vacuum-energy exponent in 𝑞 𝐿0 −𝐶 /24 is −𝐶 /24. Proposition 21.2.3
computes both values. An identification with a Hodge integral or a trace requires its separately specified
map and normalization.
Remark 30.1.8 (Anomaly = curvature). On the algebraic matter–ghost state space, Theorem 30.3.5 gives
𝑄 2 = ( 𝑐 − 26) 𝑛>0 ( 𝑛3 − 𝑛) 𝑐 − 𝑛 𝑐𝑛 /12. The reduced chiral construction based on an augmentation kernel
                P
does not apply to this vertex algebra by Proposition 30.3.11. An alternative chiral target must specify its
unit and collision maps before an anomaly operator can be transported. The required operator identity is

Lemma 30.3.2 (Ghost commutants). An operator on 𝑀 ⊗ F that supercommutes with every 𝑏𝑛 , 𝑐𝑛 is
zero if its ghost degree is nonzero. An even operator on F commuting with every 𝑏𝑛 , 𝑐𝑛 is a scalar.

Proof. The common kernel of the vacuum annihilators on 𝑀 ⊗ F is 𝑀 ⊗ ℂΩ. Indeed, these annihila-
tors are all the exterior derivatives of the creator variables. A finite exterior polynomial killed by all these
derivatives is constant. A supercommuting operator sends this common kernel into itself. The kernel has
ghost degree zero, so an operator of nonzero ghost degree vanishes there. Supercommutation with the
creators makes it vanish on every state. For an even operator on F , its value on Ω is a scalar multiple of Ω.
Commutation with the creators gives the same scalar on all monomials.

Remark 30.3.10 (The Virasoro anomaly and a bar comparison). The quadratic ghost operator in Theo-
rem 30.3.5 has coefficient 𝑐 (A) − 26. A comparison with a bar differential requires an actual chain map on
its specified collision-state carrier. If anomaly operators are also to be identified, that map must intertwine
those operators. Equality of their scalar parameters alone does not supply such a map.

30.3.2     Augmentations and the relative coordinate carrier
The critical Virasoro charge acts on an algebraic state space. A comparison with chiral chains also needs a
target and compatible coordinate transitions. Two finite identities obstruct the augmentation-kernel target
and the standard restricted transitions.
Proposition 30.3.11 (The augmentation-kernel obstruction). Let 𝑉 ≠ 0 be a unital vertex algebra
over ℂ, and let 𝐴 = 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 use the ghost system above. There is no unital vertex superalgebra homomor-
phism 𝐴 → ℂ with trivial target vertex products. Consequently the reduced chiral construction whose
coefficient sheaf is a chiral augmentation kernel cannot be instantiated on 𝐴 with its original collision
products.

Remark 30.3.14 (Compatibility with the BV constructions). Theorem 30.3.13 constructs a comparison of
the specified filtered cochain complexes. Compatibility with the BV operations in (2.3), Verdier duality, or
the genus-one curvature requires the symbol map and every correction to intertwine those operations. A
chosen vector-space contraction does not impose these additional equations.
Remark 30.3.15 (Low-degree assignments and the relative domain). Any proposed low-degree formula for

some ghost monomials. For a vacuum |0⟩ with 𝑏0 |0⟩ = 0 and 𝑐1 |0⟩ ≠ 0, the ghost relations give

defined only on the relative complex. Assignments of ghost states to logarithmic collision forms require the
actual source domain, target coefficient sheaf, and chain equation. The recursion in the theorem constructs
higher terms once those initial data and compatible primitives are supplied.

restriction of the standard coordinate transitions to the relative fiber.

Remark 30.4.2 (Semi-inﬁnite and string differentials). A ghost polarization does not by itself cancel an
anomaly. Example 9.1.32 gives a nonzero square when a central term is retained in the current action but
omitted from the ghost differential. Including the central ghost gives a different, acyclic absolute complex at
nonzero level in that example. An identification with a string BRST complex therefore requires the actual
coefficient action, central treatment and differential, in addition to a comparison of graded vector spaces.

Remark 30.4.4 (The coeﬃcient comparison required by the theorem). The theorem constructs a lift from
actual filtered coefficient data and compatible vanishing obstructions. A comparison theorem does not
supply those data from an isomorphism of first pages. Example 9.1.17 proves that the proposed implication
fails even for two-dimensional complexes. Neither a state-level PBW basis nor conformal-weight preser-
vation identifies the full collision sheaves with the zero-mode Chevalley complex. The native map 𝑓0 , its
higher corrections, and their compatibility with restrictions and differential operators remain additional
constructions. At critical level, a comparison must likewise specify its target and filtration independently
of the undefined Sugawara stress tensor.
Remark 30.4.5 (Comparison with the string BRST complex). To specialize (30.22) to a string BRST complex,
one must identify its matter and ghost spaces, central action, charge term and differential with the chosen
semi-infinite data. The nilpotency condition of the string differential must hold on that carrier. This
identification is separate from the filtered lifting theorem.

differentials. The splitting 𝐸 = ℂ ⊕ 𝐸¯ shows that 𝑝¯ is a quasi-isomorphism. Tensor products of complexes
of vector spaces preserve quasi-isomorphisms. One proof splits every acyclic complex into two-term con-
tractible summands and tensors its contraction with the identity. Consequently each length quotient of
the cone is acyclic. A cone cycle has finite maximal length. Solve its boundary equation in that highest
quotient and subtract the resulting boundary. This lowers its maximal length. Induction ends at length
zero and proves that the whole cone is acyclic. The same argument applies to 𝐵 ( 𝑖 ), and functoriality gives
𝐵 ( 𝑝) 𝐵 ( 𝑖 ) = 1.
   The bar argument uses finite tensor words and polynomial primitives. A product completion, a vertex
algebra, and a chiral sheaf each require a separate comparison. Even on 𝐴, the projection 𝑝 does not preserve
the original Poisson brackets:

                                    𝑝 { ℎ, 𝑓 } = −2𝑢,            { 𝑝 ( ℎ) , 𝑝 ( 𝑓 )} = 0.

Hence this chain algebra map cannot transport a Poisson or Batalin–Vilkovisky operation merely by
forgetting its source.

Two odd differentials require their anticommutator to vanish on their common domain. Their separate
nilpotence does not imply this equation. For example, on Λ ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ), exterior multiplication 𝑑1 = 𝑥 ∧ − and
left differentiation 𝑑2 = 𝜕𝑥 are odd and square zero, but 𝑑1 𝑑2 + 𝑑2 𝑑1 = 1.

    For quantum Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction, the input category in Arakawa’s vanishing theorem is KL𝑘 .

    The polynomial maps (30.23)–(30.24) construct the associative comparison for the classical 𝔰𝔩 2 con-

30.6.2    The equation for transport of an anomaly operator
Proposition 30.6.3 (Transport of a square). Let 𝑑 𝑋 , 𝑑𝑌 be degree-one operators on graded vector
spaces and 𝐹 : 𝑋 → 𝑌 a degree-zero map. If 𝑑𝑌 𝐹 = 𝐹 𝑑 𝑋 , then
                                                  𝑑𝑌2 𝐹 = 𝐹 𝑑 2𝑋 .
In particular, a chain isomorphism between square-zero complexes supplies no identification with a nonzero
anomaly operator on another carrier. If 𝐹 is injective and 𝑑𝑌2 = 0, its intertwining equation forces 𝑑 2𝑋 = 0.
Proof. Apply 𝑑𝑌 to the intertwining equation and use that equation once more. For an injective 𝐹 , the
resulting identity 𝐹 𝑑 2𝑋 = 0 implies 𝑑 2𝑋 = 0.
Proposition 30.6.4 (Horizontal comparison). Let 𝑋 be a smooth manifold. Let ( 𝐸 • , 𝑑 𝐸 , ∇ 𝐸 ) and
( 𝐹 • , 𝑑 𝐹 , ∇ 𝐹 ) be bounded complexes of finite-rank complex vector bundles with flat connections. Assume
𝑑𝐸 , 𝑑𝐹 commute with the connections. On Ω 𝑝 ( 𝑋 , 𝐸 𝑞 ) use total differential ∇ 𝐸 + (−1) 𝑝 𝑑𝐸 , and use the
same convention for 𝐹 . A degree-zero bundle map 𝜙 : 𝐸 • → 𝐹 • induces a map of these total complexes if
and only if
                                    𝑑𝐹 𝜙 = 𝜙𝑑𝐸 ,         ∇ 𝐹 𝜙 = (1 ⊗ 𝜙)∇ 𝐸 .
If these identities hold and 𝜙 is a quasi-isomorphism on each fiber, it induces an isomorphism on the
hypercohomology of the two local-system complexes.
Proof. On a section of form degree zero, the two components of the total chain equation lie in different
form degrees. They give exactly the displayed identities. The Leibniz rule extends these identities to arbitrary
forms. Flat local frames identify each stalk of the kernel local systems with its fiber. The cone of the induced
local-system map is therefore acyclic on every stalk. Its cohomology sheaves vanish, so it is zero in the derived
category of sheaves. Applying derived global sections gives the asserted hypercohomology isomorphism.
Example 30.6.5 (A genus-one obstruction to ﬁberwise transport). On the oriented torus 𝑇 2 = ℝ2 /ℤ2 , let 𝐿 𝜆
be the rank-one complex local system with monodromy 𝜆 ∈ ℂ∗ on the first circle and 1 on the second. Its
cellular cochain complex, with the product orientation, is
                                             ( Λ• ℂ2 , ( 𝜆 − 1) 𝑒1 ∧ −) .
This is the tensor product of the two circle complexes with differentials 𝜆 − 1 and 0. If 𝜆 ≠ 1, contraction by
the dual vector 𝑒1∗ , divided by 𝜆 − 1, gives 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 = 1. Thus 𝐻 ∗ (𝑇 2 , 𝐿 𝜆 ) = 0. For 𝜆 = 1, the differential is
zero and the dimensions are (1, 2, 1). The fibers in both cases are one-dimensional complexes concentrated
in degree zero. No fiberwise dimension or scalar central coefficient determines the genus-one cohomology.
   A comparison over the moduli of curves needs maps of its sheaves or local systems, compatible with
the connections and with clutching at the boundary. The genus-zero filtered lifting criterion alone does
not define such maps. The same requirement applies separately to pairings, anomaly operators, and the
products used in a Maurer–Cartan equation.

30.7      Unital Virasoro chiral chains on the projective line
The vacuum term in a collision contributes to chiral chains on the projective line. For the critical Virasoro
algebra with ghosts, its differential admits a simpler description through global vector fields. The resulting
cohomology has generators in degrees one and three. Both the collision differential and the degree shifts
enter this calculation.

Proposition 30.10.1. With 𝑑 = 𝑑int + 𝑑col , formula (30.33) defines a complex. The diagonal structure

graded chiral-algebra morphisms.

Proof. The internal square is zero by the differential on M. Equation (30.25), with the suspension signs
in (30.34), gives 𝑑int 𝑑col + 𝑑col 𝑑int = 0. Two mergers of disjoint pairs cancel in opposite orders because
each merger has degree one. For three blocks, the three terms in the remaining square are the suspended
                                                          2 .
chiral Jacobi identity. These cases exhaust all terms in 𝑑col
    A diagonal structure map includes the summands whose partitions factor through the specified quotient
of labels. Merging blocks commutes with this inclusion. Over separated groups of points, partitions split
into the partitions of those groups. The tensor-product identification of the corresponding summands
commutes with internal differentials and collisions inside each group. For three groups, both composite
identifications use the same partition and the same tensor symmetry. They therefore agree. The same
argument with a morphism on every block proves functoriality.

   For | 𝐼 | = 2, the complex contains precisely

For | 𝐼 | = 3, its terms have three, two, and one blocks. The two-block term has one summand for each pair
of labels. Thus the first coherence after a binary collision is the three-block Jacobi identity, with all three
intermediate diagonals present.

Proof. Apply the functor C 𝑋 to (30.32). The result consists of actual chain maps, each a quasi-isomorphism
by Beilinson–Drinfeld, §4.2.11 and §4.2.12. It therefore suffices to compute 𝐶 ch ( 𝑋 , 𝐾𝑋 ). The left algebra

On the first summand, use the chain map induced by the chiral unit 𝜔 𝑋 → 𝐾𝑋 . On 𝐿 , use the inclusion
of the generator module into the one-point term. For each positive symmetric degree, take the external
product of these inclusions and restrict to the distinct-point locus. The differential commutes with these
products because 𝐾𝑋 is commutative. This specifies Ψ on every chain, including its entire first summand.
   The positive-degree map factors through C 𝑋 (𝑊 ), where 𝑊 has zero chiral product. Indeed, 𝑊 is
the nonunital free commutative chiral algebra on its odd rank-one generator, and 𝐾𝑋 = 𝑊 ⊕ 𝜔 𝑋 is its

by the proof of [274], §4.4.8, p. 329. Their composition is Ψ, which is therefore a quasi-isomorphism.
   The unit contributes through the first complex summand. Its replacement by ℂ occurs in the derived
category, using 𝐶 ch ( 𝑋 , 𝜔 𝑋 ) ≃ ℂ from [274], §4.3.3, p. 315. The raw positive-arity chain multiplication has
the homotopy-unit structure of §4.3.4. No representative of a cohomology class is required to define (30.41).
   The complex 𝐿 represents

Algebraic de Rham cohomology of ℙ1 is ℂ in degrees zero and two and vanishes otherwise. For completeness,
the two-chart Čech complex gives 𝐻 0 (O 𝑋 ) = ℂ, 𝐻 1 (O 𝑋 ) = 0, 𝐻 0 ( Ω1𝑋 ) = 0, and 𝐻 1 ( Ω1𝑋 ) = ℂ[ 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧 ].
These are the only two entries in its de Rham spectral sequence, so no differential can join them. Normalize
[ 𝑑𝑧 / 𝑧 ] by the residue 1 on the overlap. After the displayed shift, these two classes have degrees one and
three. Over ℂ, symmetric powers preserve quasi-isomorphisms of complexes, because the symmetric-group
coinvariant functors are exact. Together with the first summand of (30.41), their positive symmetric powers
give the exterior algebra in (30.40).
   Finally, (30.38) identifies the PBW symbol complex with the chiral chains of 𝑅. The quasi-isomorphism
B → 𝑅 preserves PBW order and has image in order zero. Applying chiral chains and then (30.32) computes
1408                                       Chapter 30. BV-BRST formalism and Gaiotto’s perspective


its cohomology by the same exterior algebra. Every positive-order cohomology group therefore vanishes.


   The chiral-algebra zigzag (30.32), the chain map (30.41), and the symbol map (30.38) give the comparison.
Every chain arrow has its displayed source and target, including the unit-complex summand. They also
specify the next maps after the binary collision: external products on three factors, with compatibility
supplied by the chiral Jacobi identity. The two scalar collisions in (30.36) lie below their input PBW orders
and are retained in the filtered complex. Passing to the symbol does not assert their vanishing before
specialization.
   For the fixed-coordinate relative state complex

                                              𝐶rel = ker 𝑏0 ∩ ker 𝐻 ⊂ 𝐴,

the four-state calculation gives 𝐶rel = ℂ𝑒 ⊕ ℂ𝑣 with zero differential, in degrees zero and two. It lies
in PBW order zero. Consequently it cannot be quasi-isomorphic, with these degrees, to 𝐶 ch (ℙ1 , A) or
to its PBW associated graded complex. Their cohomology degrees are those of Theorem 30.14.1. This
comparison concerns the unmarked proper curve and algebraic, uncompleted chiral chains. Marked-point
coefficients, relative geometric constructions, and inverse-limit completions require their own carriers and
comparison maps. The relative Virasoro vacuum complex has classes in degrees zero and two. The full
unital Virasoro chiral algebra has chiral-chain classes on the projective line in degrees zero, one, three, and
four. A comparison map must therefore lose the relative degree-two class. An explicit one-point chain gives
such a map and its null-homotopy.

30.18       Coordinate dependence and the relative descent ob-
            struction
The map 𝐽𝑧 uses an ordered affine cover, its interval resolution, and the coordinate trivialization on 𝑈0 .
The cycle 𝜏 is a chosen algebraic representative of the top de Rham class. These choices define a map from
1412                                  Chapter 30. BV-BRST formalism and Gaiotto’s perspective


the fixed-coordinate state complex to the unmarked global chiral-chain complex. The construction does
not require a marked-point coefficient module in the target.
   A change of coordinate does not preserve the fixed relative subspace by restriction of the ordinary state
transitions. For the convention 𝑧 ↦→ 𝑧 /(1 + 𝑠𝑧 ) acting by 𝑔𝑠 = exp( 𝑠 L1 ),

                                    L1 𝑣 = −𝑐0 𝑐1 Ω,        L 1 ( 𝑐 0 𝑐 1 Ω) = 0 .

The ghost commutator [L𝑚 , 𝑐𝑛 ] = (−2𝑚 − 𝑛) 𝑐𝑚+𝑛 gives both identities. Consequently

                      𝑔𝑠 𝑣 = 𝑣 − 𝑠𝑐0 𝑐1 Ω,       𝑏0 𝑔𝑠 𝑣 = − 𝑠𝑐1 Ω,         𝐻 𝑔𝑠 𝑣 = 𝑠𝑐0 𝑐1 Ω.        (30.46)

For 𝑠 ≠ 0, this vector is outside 𝑅. Thus these transition operators do not define a relative subbundle with
model fiber 𝑅.
    Any map of vector-space complexes from 𝑅 to this unmarked target must kill its degree-two cohomology
class. The target degree-two cohomology vanishes. A map sending [ 𝑒 ] to the normalized unit has the class
images in Theorem 30.17.2, regardless of its chain representative. Equation (30.45) supplies a primitive for
the specific comparison constructed here. Neither this degree obstruction nor (30.46) excludes a different
marked or geometric relative complex. Such a complex requires defined coefficient sheaves, transported
constraints, and compatible transition maps before a global comparison can be stated.

30.19.2       Boundary conditions and chiral algebras
Theorem 30.19.3 (Boundary chiral algebra; [proved] [27, 215]). A boundary condition for holo-
morphic Chern–Simons theory supports a chiral algebra Abdy whose generators are local operators at the
boundary, whose OPE comes from bulk-to-boundary correlation functions, and whose central charge is
determined by the level of HCS theory.

30.19.3    The holomorphic-topological boundary condition
Deﬁnition 30.19.5 (HT boundary condition). For holomorphic Chern–Simons on a surface Σ with bound-
ary 𝜕Σ, the holomorphic-topological boundary condition requires:
   (i) Fields extend holomorphically to a compactification Σ̄
  (ii) At the boundary divisor 𝐷 = Σ̄ \ Σ, fields have a simple zero: 𝐴 ∈ Ω0,∗ ( Σ̄, OΣ̄ (− 𝐷 ))
 (iii) The volume form Ω has compatible pole: Ω ∈ 𝐾Σ̄ ( 𝑘𝐷 ) for cubic interaction ( 𝑘 = 3)
Conjecture 30.19.6 (Bar-cobar from HT boundary; [physical heuristic]). The holomorphic-topological
boundary condition realizes bar-cobar duality:
• Bar side. Fields with prescribed asymptotics near 𝐷 (logarithmic forms)
• Cobar side. Distributional fields on Σ (delta functions at 𝐷 )
• Duality. Perfect pairing via residue-distribution integral
Evidence 30.19.7 (Evidence: Geometric realization). The key is the volume form behavior. If Ω has a pole
of order 𝑘 along 𝐷 :
                                                   𝑑𝑧 ∧ 𝑑𝑤
                                             Ω∼
                                                   ( 𝑧 − 𝑤) 𝑘
   then the action term:                       ∫
                                                   Ω · 𝐴𝑘
                                                  Σ
    is finite if and only if 𝐴 vanishes to order 1 along 𝐷 .
    This pole-zero compatibility is exactly the bar-cobar relationship: the logarithmic form 𝜂 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 −
𝑤 ) (bar) has a logarithmic singularity whose residue is the distribution 𝛿 ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) (cobar).
    The holomorphic-topological boundary condition enforces this duality at the geometric level.
Remark 30.19.8 (Scope). This conjecture is labeled [physical heuristic] because it proposes a geometric
realization of bar-cobar duality via holomorphic-topological boundary conditions, which requires input
from extended field theory (boundary conditions for HT theories) beyond the algebraic framework of this
monograph.
   Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type VII (physics-dictionary). The bar and cobar complexes

Remark 30.22.2 (Gaiotto’s contribution). Gaiotto’s contribution was recognizing a physical pattern:

geometric bar-cobar construction supplies the theorematic boundary algebraic package on which these
physical comparison statements are built.

30.23      The BV algebra structure
30.23.1    BV algebra definition
Deﬁnition 30.23.1 (BV algebra). A Batalin–Vilkovisky algebra is a graded commutative algebra ( 𝐴, ·)
equipped with:
  (i) BV bracket. {·, ·} : 𝐴 ⊗ 𝐴 → 𝐴 of degree +1, satisfying:
1418                                          Chapter 30. BV-BRST formalism and Gaiotto’s perspective


       • Graded skew-symmetry: { 𝑎, 𝑏 } = −(−1) ( | 𝑎 |+1) ( | 𝑏 |+1) { 𝑏, 𝑎 }
       • Graded Leibniz: { 𝑎, 𝑏𝑐 } = { 𝑎, 𝑏 } 𝑐 + (−1) ( | 𝑎 |+1) | 𝑏 | 𝑏 { 𝑎, 𝑐 }
       • Graded Jacobi: { 𝑎, {𝑏, 𝑐 }} = {{ 𝑎, 𝑏 }, 𝑐 } + (−1) ( | 𝑎 |+1) ( | 𝑏 |+1) { 𝑏, { 𝑎, 𝑐 }}
  (ii) BV Laplacian. Δ : 𝐴 → 𝐴 of degree +1, satisfying:
       • Nilpotency: Δ2 = 0
       • Second-order: Δ ( 𝑎𝑏 ) = Δ ( 𝑎) 𝑏 + (−1) | 𝑎 | 𝑎Δ ( 𝑏 ) + (−1) | 𝑎 | { 𝑎, 𝑏 }

30.23.2      BV structure from configuration spaces
Theorem 30.23.2 (Configuration space BV structure; [proved]). The bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A) carries a
natural BV algebra structure where:
   (1) Algebra structure. Wedge product of logarithmic forms
   (2) BV bracket. Derived from symplectic structure on 𝑇 ∗ 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
   (3) BV Laplacian. Integration against diagonal (cobar differential)
                                             ∑︁ ∫
                                    Δ ( 𝜔) =         𝜔 · 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )
                                                           𝑖 <𝑗   Δ𝑖𝑗

Proof. We verify the three BV algebra axioms (Definition 30.23.1).
   (1) Commutative algebra structure. The bar complex 𝐵¯ 𝑛 (A) = Γ ( 𝐶 𝑛+1 ( 𝑋 ) , A ⊠( 𝑛+1) ⊗ Ω∗log ) carries a
natural commutative product: the wedge product of logarithmic forms. For 𝜔 ∈ 𝐵¯ 𝑝 and 𝜂 ∈ 𝐵¯ 𝑞 , define:

                        ( 𝜔 · 𝜂 ) ( 𝑧0 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝+𝑞+1 ) = 𝜔 ( 𝑧0 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝 ) ∧ 𝜂 ( 𝑧 𝑝+1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝+𝑞+1 )

extended to 𝐶 𝑝+𝑞+2 ( 𝑋 ) via the inclusion 𝐶 𝑝+1 ( 𝑋 ) × 𝐶 𝑞+1 ( 𝑋 ) ↩→ 𝐶 𝑝+𝑞+2 ( 𝑋 ). This is graded commu-
tative: 𝜔 · 𝜂 = (−1) | 𝜔 | | 𝜂 | 𝜂 · 𝜔 by the sign rule for wedge products of forms.
    (2) BV Laplacian. Define Δ : 𝐵¯ 𝑛 → 𝐵¯ 𝑛−1 by contraction with the diagonal:
                                            ∑︁ ∫
                                  Δ ( 𝜔) =                                   Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 [ 𝜔]
                                                                          ∑︁
                                                     𝜔 · 𝛿 ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) =
                                             𝑖 <𝑗    Δ𝑖𝑗                          𝑖 <𝑗

This has degree +1 (reduces bar degree by 1, increases cohomological degree by 1 via the residue).
     Nilpotency (Δ2 = 0): Applying Δ twice gives a double residue Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 ◦ Res 𝑧𝑘 =𝑧 𝑙 . For { 𝑖, 𝑗 } ∩ { 𝑘, 𝑙 } =
∅, the two residues commute and Δ2 = 0 is immediate. For { 𝑖, 𝑗 } ∩ { 𝑘, 𝑙 } ≠ ∅, say 𝑗 = 𝑘 , the iterated
residue Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 Res 𝑧𝑗 =𝑧 𝑙 picks out the coefficient of ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) −1 ( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑙 ) −1 in 𝜔, but the Arnold relation
𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑙 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑙 ∧ 𝜂𝑙𝑖 + 𝜂𝑙𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0 ensures these contributions cancel in pairs: the terms from triples
( 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑙 ) with different orderings of the iterated residue sum to zero.
     Second-order property: We verify Δ ( 𝜔 · 𝜂 ) = Δ ( 𝜔) · 𝜂 + (−1) | 𝜔 | 𝜔 · Δ ( 𝜂 ) + (−1) | 𝜔 | { 𝜔, 𝜂 } by computing
the residue of a product. When Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 acts on 𝜔 ( 𝑧0 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝 ) ∧ 𝜂 ( 𝑧 𝑝+1 , . . . , 𝑧 𝑝+𝑞+1 ), the residue localizes
to three cases: (a) both 𝑖, 𝑗 ≤ 𝑝, contributing Δ ( 𝜔) · 𝜂 ; (b) both 𝑖, 𝑗 > 𝑝, contributing 𝜔 · Δ ( 𝜂 ); (c)
𝑖 ≤ 𝑝 < 𝑗 or 𝑗 ≤ 𝑝 < 𝑖 , contributing the bracket { 𝜔, 𝜂 }. This decomposition is the BV second-order
property.
     (3) BV bracket. The bracket is defined as the failure of Δ to be a derivation:

                            { 𝜔, 𝜂 } = (−1) | 𝜔 | [ Δ ( 𝜔 · 𝜂 ) − Δ ( 𝜔) · 𝜂 − (−1) | 𝜔 | 𝜔 · Δ ( 𝜂 )]

Geometrically, { 𝜔, 𝜂 } extracts the residue across the interface between the two factors — this is the con-

{−, −} follows from Δ2 = 0 by the standard BV→Lie derivation (the ‘‘7-term identity’’).
   Thus ( 𝐵¯ ch (A) , ·, Δ, {−, −}) is a BV algebra.

30.23.4    Summary: BV as functor
Theorem 30.23.7 (BV functor; [proved]). The BV quantization defines a functor:

                                       BV : ChirAlg 𝑋 −→ BV-Alg

  preserving tensor products up to quasi-isomorphism (lax monoidal structure) and Verdier duality for
Koszul A: 𝔻( 𝐵¯ (A))  Ω (A ! ).
1420                                     Chapter 30. BV-BRST formalism and Gaiotto’s perspective


Proof. Objects. For a chiral algebra A on 𝑋 , define BV(A) = ( 𝐵¯ ch (A) , ·, Δ, {−, −}), the BV algebra
structure of Theorem 30.23.2. This assignment is well-defined: the bar complex, wedge product, and BV
Laplacian depend only on the chiral algebra structure of A.
     Morphisms. A morphism 𝑓 : A → B of chiral algebras induces 𝐵¯ ( 𝑓 ) : 𝐵¯ ch (A) → 𝐵¯ ch (B) via
𝑓 ⊠( 𝑛+1) on each bar degree. This map preserves the wedge product (it acts on coefficients, not on forms)
and commutes with the BV Laplacian (which is defined by residues, and 𝑓 preserves OPE data). Therefore
𝐵¯ ( 𝑓 ) is a morphism of BV algebras. Functoriality ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) = 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) ◦ 𝐵¯ ( 𝑓 ) and 𝐵¯ (id) = id) is inherited
from the functoriality of 𝐵¯ ch .
     Monoidal structure. For chiral algebras A1 , A2 , the Eilenberg–Zilber theorem provides a quasi-
isomorphism
                                  𝐵¯ ch (A1 ⊗ A2 ) −
                                                   → 𝐵¯ ch (A1 ) ⊗ 𝐵¯ ch (A2 )
                                                    ∼


via the shuffle map. This is not an isomorphism at the chain level: the bar construction involves iterated
tensor powers over a single configuration space 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ), which does not factor as a product. The shuffle
quasi-isomorphism is compatible with the BV structures in the following sense. On the target, the BV
Laplacian satisfies Δ⊗ = Δ1 ⊗ id + id ⊗ Δ2 (the Laplacian distributes over the tensor product because it acts
by contraction against the diagonal, which factors). The BV bracket { 𝑎1 ⊗ 𝑎2 , 𝑏1 ⊗ 𝑏2 } = { 𝑎1 , 𝑏1 } ⊗ 𝑎2 𝑏2 ±
𝑎1 𝑏1 ⊗ { 𝑎2 , 𝑏2 } satisfies the Leibniz rule by definition of the Gerstenhaber bracket on a tensor product
of BV algebras. The shuffle map intertwines these structures because it is a coalgebra map (it respects the
deconcatenation coproduct, which determines the Laplacian) and an algebra map up to homotopy (the
Eilenberg–Zilber theorem). Explicitly, the failure of strict compatibility is controlled by higher homotopies
in the 𝐸∞ -structure on the bar complex (Berger–Fresse [?BerFres04, §11]), which do not affect the lax
monoidal structure at the derived level. The functor BV is therefore lax monoidal.
    Verdier duality. Verdier duality 𝔻 on 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) exchanges logarithmic forms (bar data) with distributional
sections (cobar data). Specifically, 𝔻( 𝐵¯ 𝑛 (A)) = Dist( 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) , (A ∗ ) ⊠𝑛 )  Ω𝑛 (A ! ) (the cobar complex of
the Koszul dual coalgebra), where the isomorphism uses the residue pairing between forms and distributions.
Under this identification, the bar differential becomes the cobar differential of A ! , and the BV Laplacian
becomes the cobar product, establishing 𝔻( 𝐵¯ (A))  Ω (A ! ) as BV algebras. This is the BV-algebraic
manifestation of the bar-cobar Verdier duality proved in Theorem 6.3.32.
                                                                                                                ch
Remark 30.23.8 (Shifted symplectic structure from BV). The BV bracket {−, −} (degree +1) on 𝐵 (A)
is a (−1)-shifted Poisson structure; the Verdier duality identification 𝔻( 𝐵 (A))  Ω (A ! ) provides non-
degeneracy. By the equivalence between non-degenerate shifted Poisson and shifted symplectic struc-
tures [254], this makes the formal moduli problem Def 𝑔 (A) a (−1)-shifted symplectic derived stack. The
deformation-obstruction decomposition 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) is a Lagrangian polarization. This is the
content of Theorem 8.14.35.

31.1.1   From 4D gauge theory to 2D chiral algebras
Theorem 31.1.1 (Costello–Li dimensional reduction; [proved]). [103] Consider 4D N = 2 super
Yang–Mills with gauge group 𝐺 on ℂ2 . After holomorphic-topological twist:
  (i) Fields become 𝜕¯-closed differential forms with values in 𝔤 ⊗ Oℂ2
  (ii) The action becomes BV-BRST exact up to a topological term: 𝑆 = {𝑄 BRST , Ψ } + 𝑆top
 (iii) Replacing ℂ2 by ℂ × ℂ∗ and taking 𝑆 1 -equivariant reduction along | 𝑤 | = 1 ⊂ ℂ∗ produces a
       factorization algebra on ℂ
 (iv) The resulting 2D theory has structure of a factorization algebra F𝐺 , which is not a priori a chiral
       algebra
Remark 31.1.2 (Factorization algebras versus chiral algebras). The distinction is as follows (see [[2], §2.3,
§3.2]):
    Factorization algebra F : assigns F (𝑈 ) to every open set 𝑈 ⊂ 𝑋 , with multiplication maps F (𝑈 ) ⊗
F (𝑉 ) → F (𝑈 ⊔ 𝑉 ) for disjoint 𝑈 ,𝑉 satisfying associativity (the factorization property over multiple
disjoint opens). Example: observables in any QFT.
    Chiral algebra A: assigns a D 𝑋 -module A 𝑥 at each point 𝑥 ∈ 𝑋 , with chiral product 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ (A ⊠ A) →
Δ! A having prescribed pole structure along the diagonal. Example: vertex algebras, affine Kac–Moody
algebras (Virasoro action is additional structure, not part of the definition).
    Relationship [2, 27].
                                             ∼
                           Chiral algebras ←
                                           → Factorization algebras on curves
is an equivalence (Beilinson–Drinfeld [2, Theorem 3.4.9]). In higher dimensions, chiral algebras embed
into CG-style factorization algebras as those with D-module structure and holomorphic dependence.
Conjecture 31.1.3 (When does CL produce chiral algebras?; [conjectured]). The Costello–Li construction
produces a genuine chiral algebra (not just factorization algebra) if and only if:
   (i) The 4D theory has additional supersymmetry ensuring holomorphicity
  (ii) The dimensional reduction preserves conformal symmetry
 (iii) Central charge and anomaly terms satisfy consistency conditions
    For N = 4 SYM, this is established: Theorem 31.1.6 proves that F𝐺,Ad is genuinely chiral, producing the
affine Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤  b𝑘 at level 𝑘 determined by the gauge coupling. For N = 2 SYM with general
matter content, the precise conditions are conjectured in Conjecture 31.1.7.


                                                    1421
1422            Chapter 31. Holomorphic-topological boundary conditions and 4d origins


Remark 31.1.4 (Evidence). Chirality requires: (1) the twist preserves a holomorphic structure on the
Coulomb branch [104]; (2) 𝑇 ( 𝑧 ) survives the twist with vanishing anomalies; (3) the factorization algebra
extends to a D-module on Ran( 𝑋 ) (automatic for chiral algebras by [[2], Chapter 3], requires verification
for twisted gauge theories).
Remark 31.1.5 (Scope). Chirality is proved for N = 4 SYM (Theorem 31.1.6); the general case remains
conjectural. See [214–216] for related work. Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.5.

31.1.2    Costello–Li conditions: from factorization to chiral
Theorem 31.1.6 (CL chirality for N = 4; [proved]). [103] Let 𝐺 be a reductive group and consider 4d
N = 2 gauge theory with gauge group 𝐺 and matter in a representation 𝑅 on Σ × ℂ. After holomorphic
twist, the theory produces a factorization algebra F𝐺,𝑅 on Σ. When the theory has N = 4 supersymmetry
(equivalently, 𝑅 = Ad( 𝐺 )), the factorization algebra is strictly chiral: F𝐺,Ad satisfies the chiral algebra
axioms of Beilinson–Drinfeld. The resulting chiral algebra is the affine Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤    b𝑘 at level 𝑘
determined by the gauge coupling.
Conjecture 31.1.7 (CL chirality conditions for general 𝑅; [conjectured]). For N = 2 gauge theory with gauge
group 𝐺 and matter content 𝑅, the factorization algebra F𝐺,𝑅 is chiral provided:
   (i) 𝑅 is self-dual: 𝑅  𝑅∗ as a 𝐺 -representation.
  (ii) The one-loop anomaly 𝑐1 ( 𝑅) ∈ 𝐻 2 ( Σ, ℤ) vanishes.
 (iii) The matter content is balanced: 𝜒 ( Σ, 𝑅) = 0 for all genera.
When these conditions hold, the resulting chiral algebra ACL ( 𝐺, 𝑅) on Σ has:
• Central charge 𝑐 = dim( 𝐺 ) · (1 − ℎ∨ /𝑘 ) + 21 dim( 𝑅), where 𝑘 is the level and ℎ∨ is the dual Coxeter
  number.
• Koszul dual ACL ( 𝐺, 𝑅) ! = ACL ( 𝐺 ∨ , 𝑅∨ ), where 𝐺 ∨ is the Langlands dual group and 𝑅∨ the dual
  representation.
• Bar complex 𝐵 (ACL ) computing the derived moduli of solutions to the BPS equations on Σ × ℂ.
For 𝐺 = GL( 𝑁 ) and 𝑅 = Ad, the chiral algebra is the W𝑁 -algebra, and the instanton partition function
on ℂ2 equals the genus-0 bar complex evaluation –- this is the AGT correspondence (Theorem 33.4.1).
Remark 31.1.8 (Scope). Conditions (i)–(iii) are established for N = 4; the general case is conjectural. Coef-
ficient identities belong to MC4; the bulk/bar identification to MC5 (Conjecture 34.9.5).

31.1.3   Paquette–Williams boundary vertex algebras
Theorem 31.1.9 (Paquette–Williams 2022; [proved]). [105] Consider holomorphic-topological 4D
N = 2 gauge theory on ℂ2 with boundary at 𝑧2 = 0. Then:
   (i) Boundary conditions B correspond to Lagrangian submanifolds in Coulomb branch M𝐶
  (ii) The boundary supports a vertex operator algebra (VOA) 𝑉B
 (iii) This VOA is the quantization of the symplectic reduction of M𝐶 at the boundary
 (iv) The VOA 𝑉B has a chiral envelope A B , which is a chiral algebra in the BD sense
Remark 31.1.10 (Bar-cobar duality for boundary VOAs). Paquette–Williams produce vertex algebras, which
are algebraic objects (Frenkel–Ben-Zvi [10]). The bar-cobar framework of Part I applies to their chiral
envelopes, which are geometric objects (D-modules).

31.2     From 4d SYM to holomorphic Chern–Simons
31.2.1   The holomorphic twist and localization
Deﬁnition 31.2.1 (Holomorphic twist of 4d N = 4 SYM). Start with N = 4 super Yang–Mills in 4d with
gauge group 𝐺 , viewed as an N = 2 theory by choosing a preferred N = 2 subalgebra (Costello [168]). The
field content before twisting:
• Vector multiplet: 𝐴 𝜇 (gauge field), Φ 𝐼 (6 scalars), 𝜆, 𝜆¯ (fermions)
• Supersymmetry: 16 supercharges transforming under Spin(6) 𝑅
  The holomorphic twist (not to be confused with the fully topological Kapustin–Witten A-twist of
N = 4):
   (i) Decompose ℝ4 = ℂ × ℂ with coordinates ( 𝑧, 𝑤 )
  (ii) Twist the Lorentz group: SO(4) → SO(2)hol × SO(2)top
 (iii) Mix with R-symmetry to make a supercharge 𝑄 scalar
 (iv) Result: Theory is holomorphic in 𝑧 , topological in 𝑤
Theorem 31.2.2 (Localization to holomorphic data; [proved]). After the holomorphic twist [168],
the path integral localizes to:     ∫
                                       𝑍=                 O (fields) · 𝑒 − 𝑆inst
                                              [ 𝜕¯𝐴 =0]

   where 𝜕¯𝐴 = 0 means:
• 𝐴 is a holomorphic connection
• Scalars Φ satisfy holomorphic moment map equation
   This is the moduli space of holomorphic 𝐺 -bundles with Higgs field.

Sketch. The twisted action decomposes as 𝑆twisted = {𝑄,𝑉 } + 𝑆0 where 𝑄 is the scalar supercharge, 𝑉 is
the gauge fermion, and 𝑆0 is metric-independent. Since {𝑄,𝑉 } ≥ 0, the path integral localizes to

                          M𝑄 = { 𝐹𝐴(0,2) = 0, 𝐹𝐴(1,1) + [ Φ, Φ∗ ] = 0, 𝜕¯𝐴 Φ = 0},

i.e., Hitchin’s self-duality equations in the holomorphic gauge.

31.4     Open-closed correspondence as bar-cobar duality
31.4.1   Open and closed sectors
Proposition 31.4.1 (The Virasoro differential on a boundary vacuum). For the universal Virasoro
vacuum module 𝑀𝐶 with the full weight-(2, −1) ghost carrier of Theorem 30.3.5, the charge 𝑄 defines a
cochain complex if and only if 𝐶 = 26. At 𝐶 = 26, the augmentation-kernel chiral target for 𝑀𝐶 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐
does not exist. The fixed relative fiber is not preserved by the coordinate flow 𝑧 ↦→ 𝑧 /(1 + 𝑠𝑧 ) when 𝑠 ≠ 0.

Proof. The nonzero vector 1 ⊗ 𝑏 −2 Ω detects the square in Theorem 30.3.5. The collision identity 𝑏 (0) 𝑐 = 1
proves the augmentation assertion in Proposition 30.3.11. The relative state 𝑣 = 𝑐 −1 𝑐1 Ω transforms to
𝑣 − 𝑠𝑐0 𝑐1 Ω by Proposition 30.3.12, which proves the last assertion.
1426            Chapter 31. Holomorphic-topological boundary conditions and 4d origins


   A boundary theory must specify its state complex and boundary condition before its states can be
compared with chiral chains. Theorem 30.4.3 supplies a filtered criterion after the coefficient and symbol
maps are constructed. Theorem 30.5.2 applies a second differential only to an actual equivariant comparison
with the stated finite totalization. The explicit associative comparison in Theorem 30.5.1 concerns the
polynomial reduction.
Conjecture 31.4.2 (Closed-string cobar identiﬁcation; [conjectured]). Let Cbulk be the bulk chiral coalgebra
of a holomorphic-topological string theory. Then:
   (i) Closed strings. The cobar complex Ωch (Cbulk ) computes the closed-string field theory state space in
       the sense of Zwiebach [193].
  (ii) Open-closed duality. The bar-cobar adjunction should furnish the full open-closed correspondence:
       the natural map 𝐵 (Abdy ) → Ω (Cbulk ) is conjecturally the open-closed string field theory map.
Remark 31.4.3 (Boundary and bulk comparison maps). An open-sector comparison requires the actual
boundary state complex, unital collision target, and compatible chain maps. A closed-sector comparison
additionally requires a bulk observable complex and an open–closed map. For an integral formula, Stokes’
theorem applies only after the insertion map and a closed integration functional have been constructed, as
in Proposition 30.1.6.

Example 31.6.4 (Two classical limits of Virasoro). The Lie-algebraic limit 𝑐 = 0 gives the Witt algebra (no
central extension, Θ A = 0, uncurved bar complex). The semiclassical limit 𝑐 → ∞ ( 𝜖2 → 0 in AGT,
𝑏 2 = 𝜖1 / 𝜖2 → ∞) gives Poisson brackets on the Hitchin base (𝜅 → ∞, strongly curved 𝐴∞ structure).
These are distinct limits: 𝑐 = 0 is uncurved, 𝑐 → ∞ is maximally curved.

31.7     W-algebras in both frameworks
31.7.1   W-algebras from 2D CFT perspective
Deﬁnition 31.7.1 (W-algebra (CFT deﬁnition)). Following Zamolodchikov [78] and Fateev–Lukyanov
[108], a W-algebra W is a vertex operator algebra containing:
   (i) Virasoro element 𝐿 (conformal weight 2)
  (ii) Additional generators 𝑊 ( 𝑠 ) of conformal weights 𝑠 > 2
 (iii) Relations ensuring associativity of OPE
   Standard examples: W3 has generators 𝐿,𝑊 with wt( 𝐿 ) = 2, wt(𝑊 ) = 3; W𝑁 has generators of
weights 2, 3, . . . , 𝑁 ; and W1+∞ has infinitely many generators.

31.7.2   W-algebras from gauge theory perspective
Theorem 31.7.2 (Arakawa–Creutzig–Linshaw 2019; [proved]). [106] Let 𝐺 be a simple Lie group
and 𝜌 : 𝐺 → 𝐺 𝐿 (𝑉 ) a representation. Consider the symplectic quotient (Higgs branch):

                                            M 𝐻 = 𝜇−1 (0)/𝐺

where 𝜇 : 𝑇 ∗𝑉 → 𝔤∗ is the moment map.
  Then:
   (i) The Higgs branch M 𝐻 carries a holomorphic symplectic structure
  (ii) Quantization of functions O (M 𝐻 ) produces a vertex algebra 𝑉𝐻
 (iii) 𝑉𝐻 contains a W-algebra W𝑘 (𝔤) at level 𝑘 determined by the gauge coupling
 (iv) This matches the W-algebra from coset construction:

                                             W𝑘 (𝔤) = Com(𝔤𝑘 ,𝑉𝜌 )

31.9     Open questions and future directions
Theorem 31.9.1 ( 𝐸𝑛 Koszul duality on 𝑛 -manifolds; [proved]). For an 𝐸𝑛 -algebra A on a smooth
oriented 𝑛-manifold 𝑀 , there is a bar-cobar adjunction

                               𝐵 𝐸𝑛 : 𝐸𝑛 -Alg( 𝑀 ) ⇄ 𝐸𝑛 -CoAlg( 𝑀 ) : Ω 𝐸𝑛

realized by configuration space integrals on the Axelrod–Singer compactification 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑀 ) of 𝑘 -point
configurations in 𝑀 . The propagator is the Green kernel of the Hodge Laplacian on 𝑀 , and the Arnold
relations are replaced by the Totaro relations [102] for 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 )).
    For 𝑛 = 1, this recovers the classical (non-chiral) bar-cobar adjunction for 𝐴∞ -algebras. For 𝑛 = 2 on
a Riemann surface, it recovers the chiral bar-cobar adjunction of Theorem 9.1.39. The Poincaré–Koszul
duality of Ayala–Francis [45] (Theorem 7.8) provides the abstract framework; our propagator formulas
should supply explicit chain-level representatives.
    Scope. For 𝑛 ≥ 3, the configuration space integrals involve the Axelrod–Singer propagator (which is not
holomorphic), and the combinatorics of boundary strata are governed by graph complexes (Kontsevich
[34]). The key missing ingredient is an explicit form-level presentation of the 𝐸𝑛 bar differential in terms of
iterated integrals over 𝐶 𝑘 ( 𝑀 ). The 𝑛 = 3 case with 𝑀 = 𝑆 3 connects to the Chern–Simons perturbative
expansion and Vassiliev invariants (see Remark 31.9.2 below). (Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.5.)
    Resolution. All four components are now established: see Theorem 15.4.2, which assembles the proofs
of Totaro, Lambrechts–Volić, Knudsen, and our 𝑛 = 2 recovery.
                                                                                                full
Remark 31.9.2 (Vassiliev invariants from Feynman transform). The Prism Principle 𝐵                ≃ FTMod
(Theorem 12.13.25(ii)) and Getzler–Kapranov [23] suggest ([conjectured]) that the bar complex of
the Chern–Simons factorization algebra on 𝑆 3 produces universal Vassiliev invariants, recovering the
Kontsevich integral via specialization to the real locus. The main gap is the passage 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) → 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑆 1 ).

Knot invariants and the Kontsevich integral

The propagator 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) of the bar complex restricts to the Kontsevich propagator on the real
configuration space, and the resulting weight systems are Vassiliev invariants (Theorem 32.2.1).

32.1     Vassiliev invariants: mathematical setup
Deﬁnition 32.1.1 (Vassiliev invariant). A knot invariant 𝑣 : {oriented knots in 𝑆 3 } → ℂ is a Vassiliev in-
variant of order 𝑛 (or ﬁnite-type invariant of type 𝑛) if it vanishes on all singular knots with 𝑛 + 1 double
points. Equivalently, if 𝐾0 , 𝐾+ , 𝐾− denote knots that differ only at a single crossing, the Vassiliev relation
𝑣 ( 𝐾× ) := 𝑣 ( 𝐾+ ) − 𝑣 ( 𝐾− ) extends 𝑣 to singular knots, and 𝑣 has type 𝑛 if 𝑣 ( 𝐾 ) = 0 for every singular
knot 𝐾 with 𝑛 + 1 transverse double points.
Deﬁnition 32.1.2 (Chord diagram). A chord diagram of order 𝑛 is an oriented circle with 𝑛 disjoint pairs
of marked points (‘‘chords’’), considered up to orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of the circle. The
vector space D𝑛 of chord diagrams is the formal ℂ-span of chord diagrams of order 𝑛, modulo the four-term
(4T ) relation.

The real part of 𝜔𝑖𝑗 | 𝑆 1 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )| 𝑆 1 splits as ℜ( 𝜔𝑖𝑗 ) = 𝑑 log | 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 | = 𝑑 log | 𝑒 𝑖𝜃 𝑖 − 𝑒 𝑖𝜃𝑗 | =

Kontsevich propagator (up to normalization 1/(2 𝜋 )).

Remark 32.3.2 (Imaginary part). In the Kontsevich integral, the propagator 𝜔𝑖𝑗𝐾 = (1/(2 𝜋 𝑖 )) 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 −
𝑧𝑗 ) uses the full holomorphic logarithm, not just the real part. The distinction is irrelevant for the leading-
order weight systems but matters for the framing correction. More precisely: the real part 𝑑 log | 𝑧 𝑖 −
𝑧𝑗 | contributes the ‘‘anomalous’’ part of the Kontsevich integral (the writhe/framing term), while the
imaginary part 𝑑 arg( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) contributes the ‘‘invariant’’ part. The bar complex naturally produces both
contributions via the full holomorphic propagator.

Remark 32.4.3 (Bar-cobar as quasi-triangular structure). Theorem 32.4.2 shows that the bar complex ofb   𝔤𝑘
naturally produces the data of a quasi-triangular quasi-Hopf algebra: the associator Φ from 3-point mon-
odromy, the 𝑅-matrix from 2-point braiding, and the pentagon/hexagon from 4/3-point coherence. This is
not an analogy: the bar differential is the KZ connection, and the bar-cobar adjunction is the Reshetikhin–
Turaev construction at the chain level. The chiral operad on {𝐶𝑛 (ℂ)}𝑛 ≥2 encodes the full quasi-triangular
structure; Koszul duality (bar-cobar inversion) exchanges the braiding 𝑅 with its inverse 𝑅 −1 –- precisely
the passage from Yangian to quantum group that the E1 -chiral Koszul duality theorem (Theorem 9.5.4)
makes rigorous.

Remark 32.5.2 (The gap: holomorphic to topological). The remaining gap is the passage from holomorphic
to topological:
   (i) Our propagators are holomorphic forms on complex curves; the Kontsevich propagator is a real form
       on 𝑆 1 .
  (ii) Proposition 32.3.1 handles the genus-0 case: the holomorphic propagator restricts to the Kontsevich

 (iii) At genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, the holomorphic propagator 𝜔 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) = 𝑑 𝑧 log 𝐸 ( 𝑧, 𝑤 ) (where 𝐸 is the prime form)
       should restrict to the appropriate real propagator on a real cycle 𝑆 1 ↩→ Σ 𝑔 , but this restriction requires
       Chern–Simons gauge equivalence (Cattaneo–Mnev [243]), not merely pointwise restriction.
This gap is the subject of Conjecture 34.10.5 in §34.10.2.

32.7     Summary
What is proved.
   (i) Bar complex weight systems equal Lie algebra weight systems (Theorem 32.2.1).
  (ii) The holomorphic propagator restricts to the Kontsevich propagator on 𝑆 1 ⊂ ℙ1 (Proposition 32.3.1).
 (iii) The bar differential on 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ) is the KZ connection (Proposition 32.4.1).
 (iv) The Drinfeld associator arises from bar-cobar monodromy on 𝐶3 (ℂ) (Theorem 32.4.2).
  (v) The Feynman transform of Com is the graph complex (Proposition 32.5.1).
What remains. The full identification of the genus tower with the loop expansion of the Kontsevich
integral requires the Chern–Simons bridge at higher genus (Conjecture 34.10.5, Conjecture 32.6.1). The
genus-0 case is established; the gap is the passage from holomorphic to topological Feynman transforms at
 𝑔 ≥ 1.

Physical origins

String amplitudes, gauge theory anomalies, and conformal blocks are translated into the bar-cobar formalism
of Part I; physical identifications are conjectural unless theorem-labeled.

33.1     4d/2d correspondence algebras
33.1.1   The 4d/2d correspondence (BLLPRR)
Construction 33.1.1 (4d/2d correspondence (BLLPRR)). Starting from a 4d N = 2 superconformal field
theory T4𝑑 :
   (i) Select the Schur supercharge ℚ = 𝑄 1− + 𝑆e1−¤ , a specific nilpotent supercharge in the N = 2 supercon-
       formal algebra (ℚ2 = 0).
  (ii) Pass to the cohomology 𝐻 ∗ (ℚ) of local operators inserted at a fixed plane ℝ2 ⊂ ℝ4 .
 (iii) The resulting algebra A [T4𝑑 ] = 𝐻 ∗ (ℚ, local ops) carries the structure of a 2d vertex algebra (chiral
       algebra).
   This construction, due to Beem–Lemos–Liendo–Peelaers–Rastelli–van Rees [70], produces vertex
algebras from 4d SCFTs. It is distinct from the Ω-background/Nekrasov partition-function approach
used in the AGT correspondence below.
Theorem 33.1.2 (4d/2d is E ∞ -chiral; [proved] [70]). The 2d chiral algebra A [T4𝑑 ] obtained from
the 4d/2d correspondence is an E∞ -chiral algebra (vertex algebra).
    The OPE of the resulting chiral algebra is generically non-commutative: for instance, the 4d/2d image
of 𝑆𝑈 (2) N = 4 SYM is the small N = 4 superconformal vertex algebra at 𝑐 = −9, which contains 𝔰𝔩         b2
at level 𝑘 = −3/2 (an admissible, non-integral level; determined by 𝑐 = 6𝑘 ) as its R-symmetry current
subalgebra. The E∞ structure arises from the full vertex algebra axioms (locality, associativity of OPE), not
from commutativity.
Example 33.1.3 (Class S). For class S theories of type 𝐴𝑛−1 on a Riemann surface 𝐶 :
                                        A [T𝐴𝑛−1 ( 𝐶 )] = W − 𝑛 (𝔰𝔩 𝑛 )
the W-algebra associated to 𝔰𝔩 𝑛 at the critical level 𝑘 = −𝑛 = −ℎ∨ . At this special level the Sugawara
                                     ∨
construction degenerates and W − ℎ (𝔰𝔩 𝑛 ) coincides with the Feigin–Frenkel center 𝔷(b𝔤), a commutative
vertex algebra (see Feigin–Frenkel [48] for the center isomorphism and Arakawa [38] for related rationality
results). The dependence on the Riemann surface 𝐶 and its pants decomposition appears at the level of
conformal blocks and modules, not the algebra itself.

   The total complex with string coupling 𝑔𝑠 :

Proof. The modular operad structure on {M 𝑔,𝑛 } 𝑔,𝑛 (Getzler–Kapranov) provides clutching and self-
gluing maps along boundary divisors. The Feynman transform identification 𝐵¯ full (A) ≃ FT Mod (A)
(Theorem 12.13.25(ii)) assembles the genus- 𝑔 bar complexes into a single modular algebra. The connect-
ing maps 𝜌nonsep and 𝜌sep are the restriction-residue maps to the corresponding boundary strata of M 𝑔 :
nonseparating degeneration restricts to the self-sewing boundary (reducing genus by 1), while separating
degeneration restricts to the product boundary (splitting genus). These maps are compatible with the bar
differential by the modular operad axioms. The total complex is the completed direct sum over genera,
with the Feynman transform differential encoding all inter-genus contributions.

Proof. Part (i) is Theorem 6.9.12.
   Parts (ii)–(iii): The Feynman transform identification 𝐵¯ full (A) ≃ FT Mod (A) (Theorem 12.13.25(ii))
equips the genus-graded bar complex with the structure of an algebra over the modular operad {M 𝑔,𝑛 } 𝑔,𝑛

• Nonseparating boundaries: Residues along 𝐷 𝛾  M 𝑔 −1,𝑛+2 give the self-sewing map (33.3).
That these are chain maps (commute with the bar differential) follows from the compatibility of the
Feynman transform differential with the modular operad structure [23, Theorem 5.4].
   Part (iv): The consistency relations (associativity of iterated factorization, commutativity of factorization
with self-sewing) hold at the level of boundary strata of M 𝑔,𝑛 : the codimension-2 boundary 𝐷sep,1 ∩ 𝐷sep,2
decomposes in two ways, yielding the Moore–Seiberg consistency condition. At chain level, this equality
holds only up to homotopy: the bar complex carries a curved 𝐴∞ structure (Theorem 8.2.4), and the
higher operations 𝑚𝑘 ( 𝑘 ≥ 3) provide the homotopies Δ1 ◦ Δ2 ≃ Δ2 ◦ Δ1 relating different orderings of
degeneration. The homotopy coherence data is encoded in the 𝐴∞ relations 𝑟 + 𝑠+𝑡 =𝑛 (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝑚𝑟 +1+𝑡 ◦

    Step 1: Spectral curve from genus-0 data. The genus-0 bar complex data defines a spectral curve
( 𝑆, 𝑥, 𝑦, 𝐵 ): the tree-level OPE coefficients determine 𝜔0,1 and the ramification data of the projection

that 𝑆 is a branched cover with finitely many ramification points.
    Step 2: Feynman transform decomposition. By Theorem 29.5.12 ([proved]), the bar complex correlation

Remark 33.4.18 (Scope). Part (a) is the classical result: for the Heisenberg algebra, the bar complex cor-
relation functions are Gaussian matrix model correlators, and the EO recursion is a theorem (Eynard
2004; Chekhov–Eynard–Orantin 2006). Part (b) proves the recursion for all Koszul chiral algebras by
combining Theorem 29.5.12 (Feynman transform = graph sum) with the abstract topological recursion
framework. The spectral curve identification in Step 1 invokes Conjecture 29.6.4 ([physical heuristic]) for
the propagator–bidifferential correspondence; the remaining steps are unconditional.
    Part (c) remains [conjectured]: for a non-Koszul chiral algebra, the spectral curve may not be well-defined
(the OPE relations need not be quadratic), and the loop equations require independent verification. The
abstract topological recursion framework (Kontsevich–Soibelman 2010; Andersen–Borot–Orantin 2017)
provides the axioms, but their verification for non-Koszul algebras remains open. (Part of the MC2 theorem
package; Theorem 8.18.72.)

Remark 33.4.23 (Scope). The moduli integrals I𝑔,𝑛 and a BRST comparison require separate constructions.
At genus zero, Theorem 30.3.13 requires the actual target and relative carrier, section functor, compatible ex-
haustive split filtrations, symbol quasi-isomorphism, and compatible corrections. Corollary 18.24.2 further
requires insertion maps, a pairing homotopy, and a closed integration functional. The augmentation-kernel
target for 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 and the standard relative coordinate restriction are obstructed by Propositions 30.3.11
and 30.3.12. The affine criterion of Theorem 30.4.3 requires the actual coefficient and filtered chain maps.
Theorem 30.5.2 further requires an equivariant map of specified double complexes and a valid totalization.
Theorem 30.5.1 constructs the polynomial reduction on its associative carrier. Higher-genus extension
requires the additional compatible constructions of Conjecture 34.10.11.

Conjecture 33.4.24 (Holographic duality via bar-cobar; [conjectured]). Bar-cobar duality supplies an alge-
braic template for AdS/CFT: A ↔ 𝐵 (A), OPE coefficients ↔ vertices, conformal blocks ↔ Witten
diagrams, 𝑐 ↔ 𝑅AdS , 1/ 𝑁 ↔ genus. The conjectural comparison 𝑍 CFT [J ] = 𝑍 gravity [ 𝜙0 = J ] identi-
fies the genus expansion with the 1/ 𝑁 expansion ( 𝑔 ↦→ 𝑁 − (2 𝑔 −2) ). Requires bulk CS reconstruction [192]
and Witten diagram matching beyond this monograph; contributing to Conjecture 34.9.5 via MC4/MC5
(Chapter 34).

33.4.7    Synthesis
Theorem 33.4.25 (Poincaré–Verdier duality extended; [proved] [2, 26]). The bar-cobar duality
extends to all genera:

                         RHom( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) , 𝜔 M 𝑔,𝑛 )  Ω ( 𝑔 ) (A ! ) [− dimℂ M 𝑔,𝑛 ]

   This realizes Koszul duality geometrically at each genus level, with the dualizing sheaf 𝜔 M 𝑔,𝑛 providing
the correct twist.

Proof. The bar complex at genus 𝑔 uses logarithmic forms on M 𝑔,𝑛 with coefficients in 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ A ⊠𝑛
(Definition 6.1.13). By the intrinsic cobar construction (Definition 6.3.6), the cobar at genus 𝑔 is the
Verdier dual: Ω ( 𝑔 ) (C) = 𝔻 M 𝑔,𝑛 ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (C ∨ )). Applying RHom(−, 𝜔 M 𝑔,𝑛 ) to the bar complex gives the
Verdier duality twist of this Verdier dual. For a Koszul pair (A , A ! ) with C = 𝐵¯ ch (A) (the Koszul dual
coalgebra, whose linear dual is A ! ), this yields the stated isomorphism. The construction is the Feynman
transform of the modular operad {M 𝑔,𝑛 } (Theorem 12.13.25).

Remark 33.4.26 (Finite data). By the genus universality theorem (Theorem 8.13.16), the scalar genus
expansion of a Koszul chiral algebra A is determined by a single numerical invariant: the obstruction
coefficient 𝜅 (A), which depends on the genus-1 curvature alone. In practice, 𝜅 is computed from the
central charge and the structure of the OPE: 𝜅 (b
                                                𝔤𝑘 ) = ( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) dim 𝔤/(2ℎ∨ ), 𝜅 (Vir𝑐 ) = 𝑐 /2, 𝜅 (H𝜅 ) = 𝜅 .
The scalar genus expansion 𝐹𝑔 (A) = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜆FP    𝑔 is then given by Bernoulli numbers. The separately
proved spectral invariants, and the full Maurer–Cartan completion on the simple-Lie-symmetry locus of
Theorems 8.18.34 and 8.18.72, are not determined by 𝜅 alone; see Theorem 8.18.32 and Definition 8.18.27.
Chapter 34


Concordance with primary literature

Remark 34.0.1 (Structural comparisons). The PBW concentration statement, the universal class Θ A , and
the categorical comparisons have different hypotheses. Their formulations are given in Section 34.9.1; the
homotopy constructions are stated in Section 34.9.2. The distinction between statements about complexes,
their homotopy categories, and scalar invariants is retained in each comparison.
   The book begins from two minimal objects because the same configuration-space mechanism has two
genuinely different determinations. On the commutative side, Heisenberg is the smallest E∞ atom in which
Theorems A–D are already visible in miniature. On the braided side, Yangian is the smallest E1 atom in
which ordered factorization and braid reversal are forced. The first determination is theorematic on the
Koszul loci of the proved core; the second is theorematic on its DK core, with the extension beyond the
evaluation-generated locus as structural frontier.
Remark 34.0.2 (PBW concentration and categorical comparison). The following statements concern differ-
ent parts of the construction:
  (i) PBW concentration. Higher-genus PBW concentration is stated for the standard finite-type interact-
      ing families (Theorem 34.9.1 together with Theorems 8.18.19 and 8.18.21 and 8.18.15).
 (ii) Universal class and categorical comparisons. The universal class Θ A is now proved (Theorem 34.9.2,
      resolved by Theorem 8.18.72). The remaining frontier: the full DK/KL categorical lift
      (Conjecture 34.9.3), the infinite-generator comparison (Conjecture 34.9.4), and the BV/BRST/bar
      identification (Conjecture 34.9.5).
The formal statements and their hypotheses appear in §34.9.1.
Remark 34.0.3 (Two minimal objects). Heisenberg and Yangian are the two smallest places where the same
geometry does genuinely different work. In Heisenberg one already sees Arnold nilpotence, Verdier duality,
genus-1 curvature, and the genus tower. In Yangian one first encounters ordered factorization, 𝑅-matrix
inversion, and the Drinfeld–Kohno square. The second does not lie hidden inside the first, but neither does
it define a different subject. The present chapter records the exact theorematic overlap and the remaining
frontier.

34.1     Principal contributions
(1) Conﬁguration space bar-cobar adjunction (Theorems 9.1.39 and 8.17.4). The bar and cobar constructions
    for chiral algebras are realized via explicit integrals over Fulton–MacPherson compactifications 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ),
    with the bar differential given by residues at collision divisors and the cobar differential by inclusions
    of strata. The adjunction is proved for all Koszul chiral algebras and all genera. Theorem A decom-
    poses into three layers (Remark 9.1.11): the fundamental theorem of chiral twisting morphisms (A0 ,




                                                     1453
1454                                            Chapter 34. Concordance with primary literature


    Theorem 9.1.8), bar concentration (A1 , Theorem 9.1.38), and the Verdier-geometric duality (A2 , Theo-
    rem 9.1.39). This is the first complete proof of chiral Koszul duality via configuration space geometry.
(2) Genus universality (Theorem 8.13.16). For any Koszul chiral algebra A, the genus- 𝑔 obstruction factors
    as obs 𝑔 (A) = 𝜅 (A) · 𝜆 𝑔 , where 𝜅 is an algebra-dependent constant and 𝜆 𝑔 is the universal Faber–
    Pandharipande tautological class on M 𝑔 . The genus-independent coefficient 𝜅 (A) is determined by
    the genus-1 curvature. This result is new.
(3) Deformation-obstruction complementarity (Theorem 8.14.12). For a Koszul pair (A , A ! ), the genus- 𝑔

curvature 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 𝑔 governs the entire modular deformation tower (Remark 8.18.35).

Remark 34.5.1 (Key comparison). The Ayala–Francis framework [45, 158] establishes non-abelian Poincaré
duality as an equivalence between factorization homology and factorization cohomology for framed E𝑛 -
algebras on 𝑛-manifolds. Our Theorem A (Theorem 9.1.39) is the specialization to dimension 𝑛 = 2
(complex curves viewed as real oriented surfaces) with the additional structure of:
   (i) Holomorphic enrichment. The AF framework works with topological E𝑛 -algebras and locally constant
       cosheaves. We work with holomorphic chiral algebras (D-modules on curves), where the Fulton–
       MacPherson compactification provides the correct holomorphic compactification (not just the
       topological one). The bar differential involves residues of meromorphic forms, not just topological
       data.
  (ii) Explicit formulas. The AF duality is an ∞-categorical equivalence; our realization via configuration
       space integrals gives explicit chain-level formulas for the bar differential (residues at collision divisors)
       and the cobar differential (inclusions of FM strata).
 (iii) Higher genus. For genus 𝑔 ≥ 1 curves, the configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( Σ 𝑔 ) acquires additional topology
       ( 𝐻 1 ( Σ 𝑔 )), and the bar complex inherits new generators from the handle cycles. The AF frame-
       work predicts this (factorization homology on non-simply-connected manifolds), but the explicit
       identification with moduli space integrals and the Hodge bundle (Theorem C) is new.
