Remark 34.7.1 (Key comparison). The Costello–Gwilliam factorization algebra framework [27] relates to
ours through the Beilinson–Drinfeld equivalence between chiral algebras and factorization algebras on
curves (BD, Chapter 3). The precise comparison:
   (i) Factorization homology. The CG factorization homology 𝑋 A computes the same object as our
                                                                      ∫

       chiral homology 𝐻∗ ( 𝐵¯ ch (A)). Our explicit realization via configuration space integrals provides
       chain-level formulas that the CG framework treats abstractly.
  (ii) Koszul duality. The CG framework includes Koszul duality for factorization algebras (CG, Vol. 2,
       Chapter 5), specialized to holomorphic factorization algebras on curves. Their Koszul duality, re-
       stricted to this setting, recovers our chiral Koszul duality. Our contribution is the explicit identifica-
       tion of the Koszul dual for all standard families (Kac–Moody, Virasoro, W𝑁 , etc.) via the bar-cobar
       adjunction on Fulton–MacPherson spaces.
 (iii) Quantum corrections. The CG perturbative quantization framework produces 𝐴∞ structures from
       Feynman diagram expansions (CG, Vol. 2, Chapter 3). Our curved 𝐴∞ structure on the bar complex
       is the chiral-algebraic counterpart: the curvature 𝑚0 = 𝜅 · 1 arises from the highest-order OPE
       pole (quartic for Virasoro, double for Heisenberg), not from a Feynman diagram sum. The genus
       universality theorem shows that these two perspectives produce the same genus- 𝑔 obstruction class.
 (iv) BV-BRST. Theorem 21.2.4 constructs a polynomial BV differential and its Koszul quotient map
       under a regular-sequence hypothesis. A comparison between field-theory observables and a chiral
       bar complex requires the actual observable complex, collision target, coefficient maps, coordinate
       descent, and a chain morphism. The filtered criterion of Theorem 30.3.13 applies only after these
       data are supplied. The polynomial quotient map alone does not construct those curvewise data.
  (v) Monoidal bar-cobar. Booth–Lazarev [239] construct monoidal model structures on categories of
       coalgebras, providing the homotopical infrastructure for the bar-cobar adjunction to be a Quillen
       equivalence in the monoidal setting. This is realized by the fusion product preservation theorem
       (Theorem 12.12.10): the bar construction is a monoidal functor from the tensor category of chiral
       algebra modules to the comodule category over the bar coalgebra.

Remark 34.8.1 (Convention for Koszul dual isomorphisms). In Loday–Vallette [135], §7.1–7.2, the Koszul
dual includes the sign representation: Ass! = Ass ⊗ sgn and Com! = Lie{1} (with operadic suspension). In
this manuscript, we absorb the sign twist into the bar desuspension: our bar construction uses the shifted
generators 𝑠 −1 A whose sign already accounts for the sgn-twist. Concretely, our convention Ass!  Ass
means that the dual cooperad is isomorphic to Ass as a graded cooperad after this shift. All bar-cobar
computations in the text use the desuspended convention consistently, so no sign errors propagate. See
Appendix G for the explicit translation between conventions.
Remark 34.8.2 (Chiral enhancement). We lift the entire LV framework to the chiral setting, replacing
vector spaces with D-modules and tensor products with chiral tensor products.
Remark 34.8.3 (Synthesis). The common thread running through the comparisons above is that each
framework–-Beilinson–Drinfeld’s chiral algebras, Francis–Gaitsgory’s chiral Koszul duality, Costello–
Gwilliam’s factorization algebras, Loday–Vallette’s operadic Koszul theory–-captures one projection of
a single underlying phenomenon: the duality between commutative and Lie structures, mediated by con-
ﬁguration spaces. The contribution of the present monograph is the explicit chain-level realization of this
duality via configuration space integrals, which makes all projections simultaneously computable. The
bar complex 𝐵¯ ch (A) is the meeting point: it is BD’s chiral homology, FG’s Koszul dual coalgebra, CG’s
factorization homology on the Ran space, and LV’s bar construction–-all incarnated as a single cochain
complex with an explicitly computable differential.

34.9     Conjecture stratification
The ∼150 conjectured claims in this monograph are not peers. We stratify them into three tiers by the nature
and difficulty of the missing input.
Tier 1 — Foundational. Conjectures whose resolution would extend the proved theorems to new structural
levels. These require substantial new mathematics:
• Coderived Ran formalism for non-Koszul chiral algebras: the categorical extension of Theorem B off
  the Koszul locus.
• Virasoro and W∞ Koszul duals: explicit identification of the dual chiral algebras.

The former higher-genus PBW concentration conjecture is now resolved for the standard finite-type inter-
acting families by Theorems 8.18.19, 8.18.21, and 8.18.15.
1460                                         Chapter 34. Concordance with primary literature


Tier 2 — Consequence. The following conjectures concern computations or extensions of the stated
constructions:
• Derived Drinfeld–Kohno ladder beyond the theorematic evaluation-generated core: ordered
  E1 -factorization with 𝑅-matrix inversion, factorization-level Kazhdan transport, and dg-shifted
  comparison.
• Kazhdan–Lusztig from bar-cobar: the remaining stages beyond the proved chain-level framework.
• Shifted-symplectic enhancement: upgrading the Lagrangian complementarity to a shifted symplectic
  structure on the moduli of Koszul pairs.
• Fusion preservation under Koszul duality.

Tier 3 — Physics horizon. Physics-facing conjectures that require input from quantum field theory or
string theory. These are correctly conjectural within a mathematics monograph:
• BV = bar identification for general field theories (beyond the holomorphic setting).
• Path integral = bar-cobar: the full Feynman–Koszul dictionary at all genera.
• Holographic Koszul duality: AdS/CFT via the bar-cobar template.
• E𝑛 extension to higher-dimensional field theories.
• AGT comparison via bar-cobar/Koszul duality.

34.9.1 PBW concentration and categorical comparison problems
The PBW concentration theorem and the universal class Θ A concern different constructions. The DK/KL
enlargement and the infinite-generator comparison require further categorical data; the BV/BRST com-
parison depends on those data. Periodicity is a separate assertion from this chain of implications.
Theorem 34.9.1 (Higher-genus PBW concentration for the standard finite-type interacting fam-
ilies). [proved] The genus- 𝑔 PBW spectral sequence concentrates at all genera for the three standard
finite-type interacting families treated in the proved core: affine Kac–Moody (Theorem 8.18.19), Virasoro
(Theorem 8.18.21), and principal finite-type W-algebras, including higher W𝑁 (Theorem 8.18.15).
    This resolves MC1 for the standard ﬁnite-type interacting families. Theorem 8.18.24 isolates the common
unique-weight-2 𝑑2 mechanism behind the Virasoro and principal ﬁnite-type W arguments; for chiral al-
gebras with semisimple Lie symmetry satisfying hypotheses (a)–(c), the enrichment-killing is unconditional
via Whitehead vanishing plus 𝐿0 invertibility. The resolved status of MC1 for the named families rests on
the family theorems above; the universal semisimple statement extends MK3 beyond those families without
further family-speciﬁc input.
Theorem 34.9.2 (Cyclic 𝐿 ∞ deformation algebra and universal Θ A (MC2)). [proved] For a
modular Koszul chiral algebra A on a smooth projective curve with non-degenerate invariant form and
simple Lie symmetry, there exists a cyclic 𝐿∞ -algebra Def cyc (A) and a universal Maurer–Cartan element

recovers sewing, and whose Verdier duality recovers complementarity.
   Resolved by Theorem 8.18.72. See Deﬁnition 8.18.27.

to an ordinary-derived/completed/coderived enlargement carrying the natural DK-relevant subcategories.

Conjecture 34.9.5 (BV/BRST/bar identiﬁcation). [conjectured] For a holomorphic field theory on a Rie-
mann surface, the BV/BRST complex coincides with the bar complex of the associated chiral algebra, at all
genera.
    This is the mathematical-physics bridge. It is downstream of Theorem 34.9.1, Theorem 34.9.2, and Con-
jectures 34.9.3–34.9.4, and should not be placed on the same logical level. The genus-zero comparison in
Theorem 30.3.13 and Corollary 18.24.2 requires its constructed target, relative descent, symbol map, compatible
corrections, and pairing data. The augmentation and relative-transition obstructions are Propositions 30.3.11
and 30.3.12.
Remark 34.9.6 (Master conjecture hierarchy). Theorem 34.9.1 is the entry theorem: together with Theo-
rems 8.18.19, 8.18.21, and 8.18.15, it resolves MC1 for the standard finite-type interacting families. Theo-
rem 8.18.24 packages the common unique-weight-2 𝑑2 mechanism used in the Virasoro and principal finite-
type W proofs; under hypotheses (a)–(b) alone, it should be read as a criterion requiring separate later-page
and extension control. Under the additional semisimple symmetry hypothesis (c), the enrichment-killing
is unconditional. Theorem 34.9.2 (by Theorem 8.18.72) constructs the H-level completion of the modular
characteristic hierarchy. Conjectures 34.9.3 and 34.9.4 are staged structural extensions: the DK/KL enlarge-
ment beyond the theorematic evaluation-generated core and the filtered H-level comparison problem for
the standard infinite towers. The exact dependency chain is:

Remark 34.9.9 (Completion frontier crystallization). The completion frontier (Appendix P) extends the
strict finite-type core under three explicit hypotheses:
(H1) finite D 𝑋 -generation and polynomial growth of structure constants (verified for all Master Table
     families);
(H2) finite-dimensional Hochschild cohomology (verified for finite-type families by standard
     BGG/Shapiro arguments);
(H3) finite-stage bar-cobar compatibility: each truncation A/ 𝐼 𝑛 lies on the Koszul locus (verified for
     finite-type families where the truncations are finite-dimensional, but not yet established in general).
The proof-density remarks in that appendix (Remarks P.2.4, P.3.3, P.3.5) identify the compressed steps.
Expanding (H3) to a general finite-stage compatibility lemma is the open problem separating the completion
frontier from full theorematic standing.

Remark 34.9.15 (Shared completed environment for MC3 and MC4). MC3 beyond Repfd and MC4 stabi-
lization both require working in completed or pro-nilpotent categories: MC3 needs a coderived enhance-
ment to accommodate prefundamental and asymptotic modules, while MC4 needs separated completions
of the infinite-generator towers W∞ and 𝑌 (𝔰𝔩 ∞ ). The pro-nilpotent formalism of Francis–Gaitsgory [26]
provides the common categorical framework for both programmes.
    MC5 (BV/BRST at all genera): The Virasoro charge and its square are given in Theorem 30.3.5. The
genus-zero comparisons of Theorem 30.3.13 and Corollary 18.24.2 and Theorem 30.4.3 require their con-
structed targets, coefficient actions, relative descent, section carriers, filtrations, actual symbol maps, and
compatible corrections. For 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 , the augmentation-kernel target is excluded by Proposition 30.3.11. The
standard relative transitions also fail in Proposition 30.3.12.
    The genus-zero question therefore includes construction of a different unital chiral target, its relative
coordinate carrier, and its symbol comparison. Binary operations require (29.1); integration requires (18.3)
and a closed functional. Higher genus adds renormalization, anomaly-operator compatibility, and clutching
equations.
    The recent perturbative holomorphic-topological papers sharpen only the local end of this route.
Gaiotto–Kulp–Wu [216] construct regularized BRST-anomaly brackets in flat holomorphic-topological
theories, prove their quadratic/Wess–Zumino identities, and point toward a compactified configuration-
space formulation; in the present book that is M-level local coefficient input, not yet a proof that the
curvewise bar differential has been recovered. Costello–Dimofte–Gaiotto [215] supply boundary chiral
algebras as source examples, while Dimofte–Niu–Py [217] supply the dg-shifted Yangian target on the
line-operator side; constitutionally, the latter belongs upstream to MC4 whenever it is used to build the
Yangian H-level target.
    The disk-local comparison of Conjecture 29.4.5, reduced by Proposition 29.4.7 to explicit binary
and ternary local checks. Under the full constructed-carrier and filtered-comparison hypotheses and the
additional binary identity (29.1), Corollary 29.4.8 leaves the ternary comparison; compactification and
Stokes compatibility upgrading those local amplitudes to the FM boundary calculus, after which Propo-
sition 29.4.9 reduces the ternary packet on 𝑀 0,4 to two independent boundary channels, canonically
realizable as the residues at 0 and 1 in the standard 0, 1, ∞ chart by Corollary 29.4.11, equivalently as the
two coefficients of 𝑑 log 𝑡 and 𝑑 log(1 − 𝑡 ) by Corollary 29.4.13, i.e. as the named equalities apert = abar and
bpert = bbar packaged in Corollary 29.4.15; and only then clutching-compatible genuswise lifting. These
comparisons require the categorical constructions in MC3/MC4.

   34.9.2     Homotopy templates for conjectures
   The stratification above classifies conjectures by diﬃculty. The following classification is orthogonal: it
   sorts conjectures by homotopy type–-what kind of mathematical object each conjecture asserts the existence
   or properties of. Every conjecture in this monograph fits one of seven templates (Convention 2.9.1).
   Convention 34.9.18 (Homotopy templates). Type I. Existence of a homotopy object. A filtered cyclic 𝐿∞ -
           algebra, MC element, or factorization (co)algebra is asserted to exist with specified compatibility.
           Example: Θ A (Theorem 34.9.2).
  Type II. Equivalence of homotopy categories. Two ∞-categories (or stable/E1 -monoidal variants) are equiv-
           alent; current chain models give a presentation on a dense sublocus. Examples: full coderived
           bar-cobar (Conjecture 34.9.3), full DK, KL from bar-cobar.
 Type III. Shifted-symplectic / Lagrangian enhancement. A pairing already constructed at the model level
           upgrades to an 𝑛-shifted symplectic structure on a formal moduli problem. Examples: complemen-
           tarity upgrades, moduli of Koszul pairs.
 Type IV. Trace / index statement. A scalar invariant is the image of a universal deformation object under a
           trace or pushforward functor. Examples: genus generating series ( 𝐴ˆ-genus), GRR for modular
           deformations.
  Type V. Periodicity / autoequivalence. A finite homotopy action, graded autoequivalence, or periodic filtra-
           tion operator exists on a homotopy object; numerical periods are its shadow. Examples: reflected
           modular periodicity, quantum group periodicity at roots of unity.
 Type VI. Filtered / pro-object comparison. A theorematic completed model exists stagewise, and the remaining
           problem is to identify the intended H-level target by compatible finite quotients and finite-detection
           criteria. Examples: W∞ duals (Conjecture 34.9.4), Yangian towers.
Type VII. Physics-dictionary conjecture. Two deformation problems–-one algebraic, one field-theoretic–-are
           controlled by quasi-isomorphic dg Lie or 𝐿∞ -algebras. Examples: BRST = bar (Conjecture 34.9.5),
           BV = bar-cobar, path integral = factorization.
   Remark 34.9.19 (Using the templates). Each individual conjecture in the monograph carries a scope remark
   identifying its tier (Foundational / Consequence / Physics). The homotopy template provides the com-
   plementary structural information: what kind of homotopy-theoretic statement the conjecture makes. The
   resolved PBW theorem and the four remaining master conjectures above are respectively of Types I, II, II,
   VI, and VII.

Remark 34.10.4 (Proof assembly for part (iii)). Part (iii) of Theorem 15.4.2 is proved by assembling the
following known ingredients into the abstract chain-level construction.
    Step 1: Formality. The E𝑛 operad is formal over ℚ for all 𝑛 ≥ 2: Kontsevich [35] and Tamarkin [218]
proved this for 𝑛 = 2; Lambrechts–Volić [242] established the general case via configuration space integrals
                                                                                                     ∼
on semi-algebraic models for 𝐶 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ). Formality provides a quasi-isomorphism 𝐶∗ ( E𝑛 ) −          → 𝐻∗ ( E𝑛 ) of
operads, so the bar-cobar adjunction can be studied at the level of homology.
    Step 2: Totaro’s presentation. For 𝑛 ≥ 3, the cohomology ring 𝐻 ∗ (Conf 𝑘 (ℝ𝑛 ); ℚ) is generated by degree-
( 𝑛 − 1) classes 𝜔𝑖𝑗 (1 ≤ 𝑖 < 𝑗 ≤ 𝑘 ) subject to: (a) 𝜔𝑖𝑗 = (−1) 𝑛 𝜔𝑗 𝑖 ; (b) 𝜔2𝑖𝑗 = 0; (c) the generalized Arnold
relation 𝜔𝑖𝑗 𝜔𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜔𝑗 𝑘 𝜔𝑘𝑖 + 𝜔𝑘𝑖 𝜔𝑖𝑗 = 0 [41, 102]. These replace the classical Arnold relations (which
govern 𝑛 = 1, 2) with their higher-dimensional analogues; the key difference is that the generators sit in
odd degree when 𝑛 is even and even degree when 𝑛 is odd.
    Step 3: Graph complex connection. Kontsevich’s graph complex GC𝑛 computes 𝐻 ∗ (Aut( E𝑛 )), and the
bar differential on E𝑛 -algebras factors through GC𝑛 . The passage from 𝑛 = 2 to 𝑛 ≥ 3 is governed by the
transition from the Lie graph complex (𝑛 = 1) through the associative graph complex (𝑛 = 2) to the
commutative graph complex (𝑛 → ∞); the obstruction theory at each stage is controlled by the parity of
the generators.
    Step 4: Synthesis. The abstract construction is complete: formality (Step 1) transfers the bar-cobar adjunc-
tion to homology; the Totaro presentation (Step 2) provides explicit generators; Knudsen’s higher envelop-
ing algebras [241] identify the bar cohomology with E𝑛 -operadic Koszul duality; and Idrissi’s Part (i) [240]
ensures 𝑑 2 = 0 at the chain level. What remains as a computational reﬁnement is writing down the explicit
bar differential formula in Totaro generators at each 𝑛 ≥ 3–-the natural candidate propagator is the Lam-
brechts–Volić propagator [242], and the parity of the generators (odd for even 𝑛) produces sign patterns
that must be tracked through the differential.

                             full
and our identification 𝐵 ≃ FT (Theorem 12.13.25) extends this to Koszul chiral algebras. The gap at

requires the actual coefficient and filtered chain maps. Theorem 30.5.2 further requires an equivariant map

on its associative carrier.

comparison and a bulk observable complex. The boundary comparison still needs its unital chiral car-

additional horizontal chain equation.
Remark 34.10.15 (Chiral comparison data). The affine criterion of Theorem 30.4.3 requires the actual
coefficient and filtered chain maps. Theorem 30.5.2 further requires an equivariant map of specified double

coordinate descent, and section carrier. It must then supply compatible exhaustive split filtrations, a genuine

filtration order. These requirements remain at genus zero.

vacuum, the standard relative transition restriction and the proposed replacement by absolute states fail

calculation. After a chain comparison is constructed, binary operations still require (29.1); insertion pair-
ings require (18.3) and a closed integration functional. Higher genus additionally requires compatible
renormalization and clutching maps.

34.10.5    3d mirror symmetry from E1 -chiral Koszul duality
Conjecture 34.10.16 (3d mirror symmetry; [conjectured]). For 3d N = 4 gauge theories with Coulomb and
Higgs branches, E1 -chiral Koszul duality provides the algebraic mechanism:
   (i) The Coulomb branch algebra (in the sense of Braverman–Finkelberg–Nakajima [156]) is the E1 -chiral
       bar complex of the Higgs branch algebra.
  (ii) The curved 𝐴∞ structure on the bar complex encodes mass and FI parameter deformations.
 (iii) Symplectic duality (Braden–Licata–Proudfoot–Webster) is the module-level avatar of E1 -chiral
       Koszul duality (Theorem 9.5.4).
Remark 34.10.17 (Scope). This is highly speculative. The mathematical ingredients –- E1 -chiral Koszul
duality (Theorem 9.5.4), Yangian bar complexes (§24.6), and the Coulomb branch construction of [156] –-
exist independently. However, connecting them requires: (a) identifying the Coulomb branch ring with
a specific E1 -chiral bar complex; (b) showing that symplectic duality (exchange of Coulomb and Higgs
branches) corresponds to bar-cobar inversion; (c) relating the mass/FI deformations to the curvature of
the bar complex. Each of these steps requires substantial new work combining 3d gauge theory, symplectic
geometry, and the E1 -chiral framework.
    Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type II (equivalence of homotopy categories). The conjecture
asserts an equivalence of E1 -monoidal ∞-categories (Coulomb branch factorization vs. Higgs branch bar-
cobar). (Contributing to Conjecture 34.9.3.)

34.10.7    The nine programmes: synthesis and interdependence
Programmes I (higher-dimensional Koszul duality, §34.10.1) and II (Vassiliev invariants, §34.10.2) share
the critical-level bar complex as common foundation, but diverge in application: Programme I computes
E𝑛 -operadic Koszul duals via configuration space integrals on 𝑛-manifolds, while Programme II specializes
from complex curves to real circles, extracting knot invariants via the Kontsevich integral. At 𝑛 = 3, the
two programmes converge: the E3 -bar complex on a 3-manifold computes perturbative Chern–Simons
invariants, and the restriction to configuration spaces of circles in 𝑆 3 produces precisely the Vassiliev weight
systems of Programme II (Proposition 34.10.6).
    The anomaly cancellation programme (§34.10.3) is the physical interpretation of the curvature theory:
𝜅tot = 0 is both the mathematical condition 𝑑bar2 = 0 and the physical condition for consistent quantization

(Theorem 34.10.8). This feeds directly into the AdS3 /CFT2 programme (§34.10.4), where the curvature
𝑚0 = 𝜅 · 1 plays the role of the cosmological constant: the bar-cobar adjunction 𝐵 (A) ⊣ Ω ( 𝐵 (A)) models
the boundary-to-bulk and bulk-to-boundary maps of holographic duality. The 3d mirror symmetry pro-
gramme (§34.10.5) extends this physical circle from 2d to 3d, with E1 -chiral Koszul duality (Theorem 9.5.4)
replacing the E2 -chiral theory and Coulomb–Higgs exchange replacing bar-cobar inversion.
    The noncommutative Hodge programme (§34.10.6) reinterprets the entire genus tower as a twistor
family: the genus expansion variable 𝑔𝑠 plays the role of the Kontsevich–Soibelman twistor parameter, and
the chiral Hodge numbers ℎ 𝑔 (A) provide the Hodge-theoretic data. This programme depends on the
                                𝑝,𝑞

complementarity theorem (Theorem 8.14.12), which supplies the Hodge symmetry ℎ 𝑔 (A) = ℎ 𝑔 (A ! ).
                                                                                           𝑝,𝑞           𝑞, 𝑝


Remark 34.10.24 (Unifying vision: modular Koszul duality for factorization algebras). All of the pro-
grammes above are facets of a single conjecture: for a factorization algebra F on an oriented 𝑛-manifold 𝑀 ,
the Feynman transform FT(F ) computes the Koszul dual factorization algebra on 𝑀 with reversed
orientation. The evidence is the following hierarchy of established and conjectural instances:
   (i) At 𝑛 = 1 ( 𝐴∞ -algebras): classical bar-cobar duality (Loday–Vallette [135]). This is the foundational
       case, with the bar and cobar constructions as mutual inverses on the Koszul locus.
  (ii) At 𝑛 = 2 with complex structure (chiral algebras): the Main Theorems A, B, C of this monograph
       (Theorems 9.1.39, 8.17.4, 8.14.12). The Feynman transform is realized by Verdier duality on FM
       compactifications, and the genus expansion provides the quantum corrections.
 (iii) At 𝑛 = 2 topological (E2 -algebras): Kontsevich formality [36], which identifies the E2 -bar complex
       with the deformation complex of the associative operad.
 (iv) At 𝑛 = 3 (E3 -algebras): perturbative Chern–Simons invariants, with Vassiliev weight systems ex-
       tracted from the E3 -bar complex (Conjecture 34.10.5).
  (v) At 𝑛 = ∞ (E∞ -algebras): factorization homology duality of Ayala–Francis [45], which provides the
       ∞-categorical framework for Poincaré–Koszul duality on arbitrary manifolds.
This monograph provides case (ii) in full detail; the passage from (ii) to the general conjecture is the content
of §34.12 below. For the individual comparison statements, see §34.12.9.

34.12.1   The coderived Ran-space formalism
The bar-cobar adjunction is most naturally an equivalence of ∞-categories–-the categorical exp/log corre-
spondence (Remark 6.0.1):

                         𝐵¯ 𝑋 : Algaug (Fact( 𝑋 )) ⇄ CoAlgconil (Fact( 𝑋 )) : Ω 𝑋 ,
1492                                              Chapter 34. Concordance with primary literature


where Fact( 𝑋 ) denotes factorization algebras on Ran( 𝑋 ) (cf. Appendix O).
    On the Koszul locus this is an equivalence: exp ◦ log = id on the convergence domain. When curvature
is present–-that is, when the categorical logarithm acquires non-trivial monodromy–-the correct ambient
category is not the ordinary derived category but the coderived category in the sense of Positselski [171]: the
analytic continuation that extends the exp/log correspondence past the convergence radius.
    Curved objects produce acyclic-but-not-contractible complexes that the derived category erases too
brutally; the coderived category retains the monodromy data that the ordinary derived category discards,
just as the multi-valued logarithm retains branch information that a single-valued determination loses.
    The provisional coderived category Dco prov ( 𝑋 ) (Definition P.11.10, Proposition P.11.11) provides a work-
ing substitute within the scope of this monograph. The Koszul locus–-where bar-cobar inversion holds
unconditionally (Theorem 8.17.4)–-is the locus where the coderived and derived categories agree.
    What is established. Appendix O compares the strict, completed, and literature existence paradigms
for bar-cobar on Ran( 𝑋 ). Theorem 9.1.39 provides the adjunction; Theorem 8.17.4 provides inversion on
the Koszul locus. Appendix P.11, §P.11.4 develops the coderived and contraderived categories on Ran( 𝑋 ):
curved factorization coalgebras with CDG-factorization compatibility (Definition P.11.15), coacyclic fac-
torization objects (Definition P.11.19), stratified conservative restriction via the injective characterization
(Theorem P.11.21), and the factorization co-contra correspondence (Theorem P.11.24). The provisional
coderived category embeds fully faithfully (Proposition P.11.22).
    What remains. A single conjecture: off-Koszul bar-cobar inversion on Ran( 𝑋 ) (Conjecture P.11.26)–-
the statement that Ω 𝑋 𝐵 𝑋 (A) → A is an isomorphism in 𝐷 co (CoFact( 𝑋 )) without Koszulness. The
abstract precedent (Positselski [171, Theorem 7.2]), the on-Koszul case (Theorem 8.17.4), and the completed
Yangian case (Corollary 24.9.35) provide evidence.

34.12.2    The Lagrangian form of complementarity
Theorem C (Theorem 8.14.12) establishes the direct-sum decomposition 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕ 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) =
𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , Z(A)) via the eigenspace decomposition of the Verdier involution. The natural strengthening
is a Lagrangian-polarization theorem, now proved:
Theorem 34.12.1 (Lagrangian complementarity; [proved]). For a modular Koszul pair (A , A ! ),
the complex 𝐶 𝑔 := 𝑅Γ (M 𝑔 , ZA ) carries two shifted symplectic structures, each admitting 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and
𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) as complementary Lagrangians in the sense of Pantev–Toën–Vaquié–Vezzosi [253]:
   (i) a (−(3 𝑔 −3))-shifted symplectic structure from Verdier duality on the center local system
       (Proposition 8.14.36);
  (ii) a (−1)-shifted symplectic structure on the formal moduli Def 𝑔 (A) from the BV antibracket
       (Theorem 8.14.35).
Remark 34.12.2 (Degree clariﬁcation). The original formulation of this result stated a single (−1)-shifted
symplectic structure on 𝐶 𝑔 . The proved version reveals two structures of different degrees: the Verdier
pairing gives (−(3 𝑔 −3))-shifted on 𝐶 𝑔 itself, while the BV antibracket gives (−1)-shifted on the formal
moduli. Both support the same Lagrangian polarization. See Remark 8.14.37 for the compatibility.

34.12.4   The discriminant as spectral invariant
The shared discriminant Δ ( 𝑥 ) = (1 − 3 𝑥 ) (1 + 𝑥 ) across 𝔰𝔩 2 , Virasoro, and 𝛽𝛾 systems (Theorem 27.17.20)

class of the modular Koszul object: where 𝜅 (A) is a scalar measuring the curvature of 𝑑 2 , the discriminant

their local operator content is entirely different. The underlying reason is functorial: Drinfeld–Sokolov
reduction changes the growth pole (i.e. the leading OPE data) while preserving the discriminant family.
This is compatible with the observation that Δ A depends only on the quadratic OPE data, which is the
Koszul-dual-determining datum.

Deﬁnition 34.12.8 (Spectral branch object). A spectral branch object for a modular Koszul chiral algebra A is
a finite-rank perfect complex 𝑉Abr together with a branch transport operator 𝑇br, A : 𝑉Abr → 𝑉Abr such that
                                       Δ A ( 𝑥 ) = det 1 − 𝑥 𝑇br, A .                                  (34.2)
                                                                     

The pair (𝑉Abr , 𝑇br, A ) satisfies:
   (i) Δ A ! = Δ A (the spectral discriminant is self-dual);
  (ii) exact factorization functors preserving quadratic OPE data preserve 𝑇br, A ;
 (iii) rank(𝑉Abr ) equals the degree of algebraicity of the Koszul-dual Hilbert series.
Status. In the verified cases (Theorem 34.12.5), 𝑉Abr is constructed as the span of the companion-matrix
eigenvectors of 𝑇rec , and (34.2) is proved. The general construction of 𝑉Abr from the bar complex (rather
than from the recurrence) remains open; see Conjecture 27.17.23 for the conjectural identification with a
subquotient of 𝐻 1 . (Part of the MC2 theorem package; Theorem 8.18.72.)

Remark 34.12.10 (The punchline). The content of the theorem is not the generating function identity
(which was already proved as Theorem 26.4.29), but its origin: the genus expansion of a Koszul chiral
algebra is the Grothendieck–Riemann–Roch pushforward of the Todd class of the universal curve, scaled
by the bar-complex curvature. The 𝐴ˆ-genus appears not by accident but because 𝐴ˆ is the multiplicative
genus associated to the formal group law 𝐹 ( 𝑥, 𝑦 ) = 𝑥 + 𝑦 –- the trivial (additive) formal group –- and
the bar-complex genus expansion is additive in 𝜅 . Equivalently, the Bernoulli numbers governing both the
Todd class and the 𝜓 -𝜆 𝑔 integrals are the same Bernoulli numbers because both are computed by the same
GRR calculation on the universal curve.
    In physical terms: the genus expansion of a chiral algebra is an index. The ‘‘partition function’’
   𝐹𝑔 ℏ2 𝑔 −2 is the family index of the modular deformation complex on M 𝑔 , and anomaly cancellation
P
(𝜅tot = 0) is the vanishing of this index.
    The explicit universal class Θmin
                                   A = 𝜅 · 𝜂 ⊗ Λ (Theorem 8.18.36) gives this a precise homotopy-algebraic
              ˆ
meaning: 𝐴 is the character of Θ A –- it computes how the universal MC element distributes its weight
across genera. The Bernoulli numbers appear because they are the Taylor coefficients of tr( Θ), not because
of any formal group coincidence. The formal group is additive because 𝜅 itself is additive under tensor
product (Corollary 8.13.22), which in turn follows from Θ A⊗ B = Θ A + Θ B in the factorization algebra
sense.
Remark 34.12.11 (Scope). Steps 1–3 of the proof use only results established in this monograph (genus
universality, Theorem 8.13.16) and imported results (Mumford’s GRR formula [150]; Faber–Pandharipande
                                                                              ( 𝑔)
[47]). Step 4 is classical generating function analysis. The identification D A = 𝜅 (A) · 𝔼 is canonical
given the genus universality theorem; the functoriality of the construction follows from the functoriality
of 𝜅 (determined by genus-1 curvature) and 𝔼 (determined by the universal curve).
                                              ( 𝑔)
   What remains. The theorem identifies D A via its top Chern class (the obstruction). A stronger result
                      ( 𝑔)
would construct D A as a sheaf on M 𝑔 (not just a 𝐾 -theory class) and identify its full Chern character
with the genus expansion at all intermediate degrees, not just the top. This would require the coderived
Ran-space formalism of §34.12 and is the subject of Theorem 34.12.3.
Remark 34.12.12 (The GRR theorem as horizon). In the Chriss–Ginzburg tradition, a foundational mono-
graph builds toward a single theorem that justifies the entire development. For this monograph, that
theorem is Theorem 34.12.9: the genus expansion of a Koszul chiral algebra is a GRR pushforward. The
master diagram (2.3) is the engine; the modular characteristic hierarchy is the protagonist: the scalar genus
tower and spectral invariants are proved, while the full quintuple CA = ( Θ A , 𝜅 (A) , Δ A , Π A , H A ) now
has its H-level component Θ A proved (Theorem 8.18.72, resolving Theorem 34.12.3); and the family index
theorem is the punchline. What remains beyond this monograph –- 𝐶mod (shifted-symplectic complemen-
tarity), derived Drinfeld–Kohno, the elliptic extension –- are further consequences of the same master
diagram in richer geometric settings.

34.12.6    The spectral discriminant as characteristic class
The discriminant Δ A ( 𝑥 ) = det(1 − 𝑥 𝑇 ) deserves promotion from a shared generating-function curiosity
to the ﬁrst genuinely nontrivial non-scalar characteristic class of the modular Koszul object. Where the scalar
invariant 𝜅 (A) measures the curvature of 𝑑 2 , the polynomial Δ A records the full branch geometry of the
dual Hilbert series (Theorem 27.17.20).
    Distinct chiral theories can lie on the same modular spectral sheet –- sharing the same discriminant –-
even when their local operator content differs entirely. Drinfeld–Sokolov reduction changes the growth
pole (the leading OPE data) while preserving the discriminant family; this is a functorial consequence of
the modular structure, not a numerical accident. The 𝐾 -theoretic framework that organizes the scalar
invariant 𝜅 (L1), the spectral discriminant Δ (L2), and the periodicity profile Π (L3) into a hierarchy of
characteristic classes of the virtual bar family VA ∈ 𝐾0 (M 𝑔 ) is developed in Remark 8.18.94; the intrinsic
construction of the L2 operator from Casimir actions on bar cohomology is Conjecture 27.17.23.

34.12.7    Chain-level / evaluation-locus derived Drinfeld–Kohno
The Yangian theory (Chapter 24) establishes bar-cobar recovery for the E1 -chiral Yangian and the 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1
transformation of the quantum parameter. The chain-level derived Drinfeld–Kohno theorem is now
proved (Theorems 24.9.3 and 24.9.5): the E1 -chiral Koszul duality functor, composed with the Kazhdan–
Lusztig (resp. Kazhdan) equivalence, yields a derived equivalence with braiding reversal 𝑅𝑞 ↦→ 𝑅𝑞 −1 for
both affine algebras and Yangians. The factorization-level statement on the evaluation locus is also proved
(Theorem 24.9.7).
   The full factorization-categorical statement remains conjectural, but the remaining work is staged rather
than monolithic:
Conjecture 34.12.13 (Factorization-categorical DK/KL bridge (DK-3); [conjectured]). There exists an equiv-
alence of E1 -factorization categories

                                     FactE1 (Y (𝔤)) ≃ FactE1 (𝑈𝑞 (𝔤)) op

extending the chain-level equivalence of Theorem 24.9.5 from evaluation modules to all objects of Yangian
category O, and identifying the Yangian E1 -factorization structure with the factorisation quantum group
structure of Latyntsev [212].
Remark 34.12.14 (Scope and ladder). The Yangian frontier is best read as a DK ladder:
(a) DK-0 (proved): braided monoidal bar complexes, Verdier = 𝑅-matrix inversion, and the chain-level
    DK square (Theorem 12.1.11; Proposition 24.2.10(iii); Theorem 24.9.5).
(b) DK-1 (proved): the factorization-level statement on the evaluation locus (Theorem 24.9.7).
(c) DK-2/3 (proved, evaluation-generated core, all simple types, domain: Opoly ): The domain is the
    polynomial subcategory Opoly (Corollary 24.8.19), not the full Category O. Two independent proofs.
    Both rely on Yangian Koszulness (Proposition 24.2.6), which uses Molev’s PBW theorem [72] as
    external input. Type 𝐴 thick generation: Theorem 24.8.17 resolves DK-2/3 for Repfd of 𝑌 (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) via
    thick generation (Proposition 24.8.9). Sectorwise convergence (all types): Corollary 24.9.15 resolves DK-
    2/3 for the evaluation-generated core at all simple types, via the ∞-categorical sectorwise convergence
    theorem (Theorem 24.9.13), bypassing thick generation. The remaining gap to Conjecture 34.12.13 is
    the completed/coderived extension beyond the generated core (Corollary 24.8.18).
(d) DK-4/DK-5 (conjectural): the dg-shifted Yangian and full triple-bridge completion (Conjecture 24.9.43).
34.12. Towards modular homotopy theory                                                                     1501


The key control point is that the evaluation-locus theorem is already theorematic; the category-O extension
and the dg-shifted comparison are downstream stages, not hidden inside the same claim. See §24.9 for the
full treatment and Remark 24.9.11 for the precise decomposition. The exact extra DK-2/DK-3 packets are
recorded in Remark 24.9.10.
    Homotopy template (Convention 2.9.1): Type II (equivalence of homotopy categories). At H-level:
an equivalence of E1 -monoidal ∞-categories. The M-level model is the braided monoidal bar-cobar dg
category; the S-level shadow is the classical DK equivalence on evaluation modules. (Contributing to
Conjecture 34.9.3.)
    DK is naturally an E1 -factorization theorem: it compares two E1 -level objects (KZ monodromy and
𝑅-matrix data). The step from E1 to full E2 coherence requires Drinfeld associator input and is governed by
the Grothendieck–Teichmüller group (Remarks 15.8.1 and 15.8.2). The modular layer (genus deformation
of E1 -factorization) is the content of the modular homotopy theory programme (Definition 2.5.1).

34.12.8    Summary
The historical rhyme is this. Classical operadic Koszul duality says: quadratic presentation plus bar-cobar
formalism produces homotopy theory. The theory sought here says: factorization presentation on curves
plus Verdier duality on modular compactifications produces modular homotopy theory. Just as Drinfeld–
Kohno related KZ monodromy to quantum groups, the theory sought here would relate configuration-
space/Deligne–Mumford monodromy to curved chiral Koszul duality. And just as étale cohomology
supplied the correct ambient cohomology theory for Frobenius and zeta functions, factorization homology
on Ran( 𝑋 ) together with Verdier duality on M 𝑔,𝑛 is the correct ambient cohomology theory for OPE,
monodromy, and bar-cobar duality on curves. The following comparisons distinguish possible parameter
spaces, categorical constructions, and their scalar consequences (Definition 34.12.15; Remark 34.12.19).

34.12.9    Parameter spaces and categorical comparisons
A proposed comparison may fail because its parameter space vanishes, or may require a categorical con-
struction beyond an identity of scalar invariants. The examples below distinguish these possibilities.

(Theorem 24.9.34), yielding the completed bar-cobar equivalence for Yangians (Corollary 24.9.35). DK-4
is thereby reduced to the algebraic identification of the tangent Lie algebra with the dg-shifted Yangian
(Conjecture 24.9.36).
Remark 34.12.18 (The category O generation obstruction: precise structure). The blocking issue beyond
the proved DK-2/3 theorematic core is no longer another evaluation-level comparison. DK-2/3 is now
resolved on the evaluation-generated core at all simple types (Corollary 24.9.15). What remains before the
full Conjecture 24.9.8 is the domain-enlargement problem: in ordinary derived categories, Corollary 24.8.18
asks whether 𝐷 𝑏 (O𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) ) is thickly generated by evaluation modules; in completed/coderived form, the
same enlargement appears as the four conjectural extension packages of Remark 24.8.48(b). We record the
precise mathematical content, known partial results, and candidate strategies.
    The problem and its natural domain. Let Ceval ⊂ 𝐷 𝑏 (O𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) ) denote the thick triangulated subcate-
gory generated by the evaluation modules 𝑉𝜆 ( 𝑎) (the pullback of 𝑉𝜆 ∈ Repfd (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) along ev 𝑎 : 𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 ) →
𝑈 (𝔰𝔩 𝑁 )). By Lemma 24.8.22, the thick closure of finite-length objects in 𝐷 𝑏 (A) equals 𝐷 𝑏 (A fd ): it
captures exactly the complexes with finite-length total cohomology. Therefore, if O contains genuine
infinite-length objects, the literal question Ceval = 𝐷 𝑏 (O) has a negative answer.
    The correct generation question is therefore:
                                                   ?
                                             Ceval = 𝐷 𝑏 (Opoly )
where Opoly is the polynomial subcategory (all simples finite-dimensional). This holds for 𝑁 = 2 uncon-
ditionally and for Opoly at all 𝑁 . For Repfd in place of Opoly , the answer is yes (Proposition 24.8.9): every
finite-dimensional irreducible is a subquotient of a tensor product of fundamental evaluation modules.
    For modules beyond Opoly , the correct framework is localizing (not thick) generation in a
completed/Ind-enhanced category, or enlargement of the generator set to include prefundamental or
asymptotic modules.
    What is known.
(a) Finite-dimensional type 𝐴: resolved (Theorem 24.8.17). Every finite-dimensional simple module lies
    in Ceval .
(b) 𝑁 = 2 (Yangian of 𝔰𝔩 2 ): resolved (Theorem 24.8.12). Category O for 𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 2 ) is controlled by the
    Kirillov–Reshetikhin modules and their limits: every module has a finite composition series with
    finite-dimensional factors [52]. Since every finite-dimensional simple lies in Dℏeval (Proposition 24.8.9),
    Lemma 24.8.11 yields 𝐷 𝑏 (O𝑌ℏ (𝔰𝔩 2 ) ) = Dℏeval . More generally, thick generation holds for the polynomial
    subcategory Opoly at all 𝑁 (Remark 24.8.13).
(c) Lattice bypass: for lattice vertex algebras, DK-1 21 (Theorem 17.12.3) gives the factorization equiva-
    lence without any thick generation argument, via sectorwise finiteness of the Λ-graded bar complex.
    At simply-laced level 1, the FKS identification yields an unconditional factorization DK statement
    (Corollary 17.12.5).
   Candidate strategies. All four are developed in detail in §24.8.1 of the Yangian chapter.
1508                                          Chapter 34. Concordance with primary literature


   (i) Highest-weight ﬁltration + resolution (Proposition 24.8.31). If every Verma module 𝑀 ( 𝜆, 𝑎) admits
       a finite resolution by finite-dimensional evaluation modules, thick generation follows. The classical
       BGG resolution handles dominant integral 𝜆; for non-dominant 𝜆, the Yangian 𝑅-matrix poles
       create inter-spectral-parameter extensions that may yield resolutions (Remark 24.8.32).
  (ii) t-structure argument (Theorem 24.8.12). Proved for 𝔰𝔩 2 and Opoly at all 𝑁 . The generation problem
       reduces to finite-dimensionality of simples via Lemma 24.8.11.
 (iii) Reduction to the Kazhdan–Lusztig problem (Proposition 24.8.28). Thick generation is equivalent to:
       every projective indecomposable has a finite evaluation resolution. The KL multiplicities provide
       the combinatorial data; the remaining input is that Verma modules lie in Ceval (Remark 24.8.29).
 (iv) Sectorwise ﬁniteness generalization (Proposition 24.8.24). The factorization bar complex has a (root
       weight, loop degree) bifiltration with finite-dimensional bigraded pieces. The associated spectral
       sequence has 𝐸1 page given by the bar cohomology of the current algebra 𝑈 (𝔤[ 𝑡 ]). Unlike the lattice
       case, the 𝐸1 page is nontrivial (Remark 24.8.25). This strategy is now theorematic on the evaluation-
       generated core: sectorwise convergence plus factorization descent resolve DK-2/3 for all simple types
       (Theorem 24.9.13 and Corollary 24.9.15).
    Assessment. The generation problem is now resolved for the natural domain Opoly (Theorem 24.8.12):
thick generation holds for 𝑁 = 2 unconditionally and for Opoly at all 𝑁 , by the composition-length argu-
ment (Lemma 24.8.11) combined with finite-dimensionality of all polynomial simples. By Lemma 24.8.22,
this is the strongest possible thick-generation statement: the thick closure of finite-dimensional evaluation
modules in 𝐷 𝑏 (O) equals 𝐷 𝑏 (Opoly ) and cannot reach infinite-length modules.
    Theorem 24.8.41 sharpens the type- 𝐴 picture to an exact identification: the evaluation-generated core
equals 𝐷 𝑏 (Repfd ), and the DK-2/3 equivalence extends to this entire core at all 𝑁 in type 𝐴. Outside
type 𝐴, Corollary 24.9.15 still gives the theorematic endpoint: DK-2/3 on the evaluation-generated core at all
simple types. The remaining MC3 frontier therefore splits into two layers. First comes the ordinary-derived
domain question: does the DK-relevant category stop at the evaluation-generated / polynomial core, or is
there a larger ordinary-derived domain worth naming?
    Second comes the genuine completion step: if one wishes to include infinite-dimensional modules,
generation reopens in a completed/coderived setting:
(a) If the factorization DK conjecture targets the evaluation-generated core, DK-2/3 is unconditionally
    proved at all simple types, and the DK ladder proceeds directly to DK-4 (Remark 24.8.48(a)).
(b) If one wishes to include infinite-dimensional modules (prefundamental, asymptotic), a com-
    pleted/coderived enhancement is required, with generation via Baxter-type exact triangles relating
    prefundamental and evaluation modules (Remark 24.8.48(b)).
   Strategy (iv) is now the proved bypass for the evaluation-generated core, and its residual rôle
                                                                                              √︁ is di-
agnostic rather than frontier: the 𝐸1 page is proved to have sub-exponential growth ∼ exp( 𝜋 𝑟 𝑝/12)
(Proposition 24.8.39, Computation 24.8.40); the convergence problem has been discharged by Theo-
rem 24.9.12, so what remains is to understand whether and how the completed/coderived enlargement
packages should be attached beyond the generated core.

Comparison 7: Periodicity and tautological depth.
    Proposed statement. Modular, quantum, and geometric periodicities unify into a single coherent classi-
fication, with clean reciprocity laws under Koszul duality.
34.12. Towards modular homotopy theory                                                                     1509


    Geometric, quantum, and modular contributions. The principal correction is that the ‘‘geometric peri-
odicity’’ of the original formulation is not periodic at all: the geometric operator 𝜎geom = 𝜅 ( 𝜆) is nilpotent
( 𝜎 𝑁 = 0, providing bounded tautological depth) rather than periodic ( 𝜎 𝑁 = id). The corrected framework
has two genuine periodic sources and one nilpotent stabilization mechanism:
(a) Modular periodicity (Type I). Conjectured for minimal models (Conjecture 11.6.3) and WZW models
    at all positive integer levels (Conjecture 11.6.9), with 𝑇 -matrix periodicity proved unconditionally
    in both cases; conjectured for general rational chiral algebras (Conjecture 11.6.7). Natural next cases:
    W-algebra minimal models and rational orbifolds.
(b) Quantum periodicity (Type II). Proved: the quantum-profile input coming from quantum integer,
    quantum-dimension, and fusion-data periodicity is unconditional at admissible level. Its transport
    under Koszul duality is governed by 𝑞 ↦→ 𝑞 −1 (Proposition 11.6.31).
(c) Geometric tautological depth (Type III). Proved: the Kodaira–Spencer image of the Hodge class is
    nilpotent with index ≤ 𝑔 − 1 on smooth moduli (Theorem 11.6.19, via Graber–Vakil vanishing [258]),
    and ≤ 3 𝑔 − 2 on M 𝑔 (Theorem 11.6.17). At genus 2, the Hodge class contribution vanishes entirely.
    The boundary-extended amplitude is bounded by the Mumford relation (Conjecture 11.6.21). The
    geometric contribution controls the stabilization threshold–-the conformal weight beyond which
    modular/quantum periodicity holds–-not a periodic factor.
The stratified periodicity package (page 668) therefore gives Period(A) | lcm( 𝑁mod , 𝑁quant ), with the
geometric tautological depth bounding the stabilization threshold. The modular input remains the sole
conjectural periodic ingredient. The reflected periodicity conjecture (Conjecture 11.6.12), which would
express how modular periods transform under Koszul duality via the dual central charge, depends on
Conjecture 11.6.7. Within the monograph itself, the only explicit periodic bar calculation at theorem level
beyond the general exchange theorem is the rank-1 𝔰𝔩  b 2 pattern of Proposition 16.4.5; higher-rank periodic
CDG packages remain frontier statements and should not be used as already proved transport data in MC3.
    What replaces the original ‘‘unified doctrine’’ is a stratiﬁed periodicity framework organized by the
nilpotence-periodicity correspondence (Remark 6.0.1): every periodic phenomenon in bar cohomology arises
as the exponential of a nilpotent datum, and conversely. The geometric contribution is correctly classified
as nilpotent depth (proved): the operator 𝜅 ( 𝜆) is nilpotent with index ≤ 𝑔 − 1 (Theorem 11.6.19), and
its exponential exp( 𝜅 ( 𝜆)) is unipotent, not periodic–-geometry provides a stabilization threshold, not a
period.
    The quantum periodicity is unconditional: the screening operators 𝑄 𝑖2 = 0 (nilpotent) exponentiate
to the periodic representation theory of quantum groups at roots of unity. The modular periodicity
of bar cohomology remains conjectural even for the flagship rational families, but the T-matrix period
formula 𝑁 = 24 𝑞 ′ /gcd( 𝑝′ , 24) for 𝑐 = 𝑝′ / 𝑞 ′ is the direct consequence of exp(2 𝜋 𝑖 𝑁 𝑐 /24) = 1: the
period is determined by when the exponential of the central charge (the scalar nilpotent datum) returns to
identity. The sharp modular formula 𝑁mod is the remaining modular-periodicity conjecture; the nilpotence-
periodicity correspondence predicts that it will be derived from 𝜅 (A) via exponentiation.

    Proposed statement. The shared discriminant Δ ( 𝑥 ) = (1 − 3 𝑥 ) (1 + 𝑥 ) across 𝔰𝔩

braic cases. The spectral radius of 𝑇rec equals dim(𝔤) for Kac–Moody algebras (Theorem 27.17.41). The

Drinfeld–Sokolov invariance of the discriminant (Theorem 27.17.20) shows that distinct chiral theories
on the same modular spectral sheet share the same Δ, even when their operator content differs entirely.
    The discriminant’s role is now precise: 𝜅 (A) is the ﬁrst scalar characteristic number of the universal
class Θ A (Theorem 34.12.3), and Δ A ( 𝑥 ) is the ﬁrst non-scalar characteristic class–-the spectral determinant
of the transfer matrix governing the recurrence of bar-cohomology dimensions. The spectral branch object

Comparison 9: BV/BRST/path-integral/holography completion.
    Proposed statement. The entire BV-BRST formalism, path integrals, anomalies, holographic duality, and
higher-dimensional extensions would all eventually be read through the Koszul-duality machine.
    Genus zero and the higher-genus conjectures. At genus zero, Theorem 30.3.13 is a filtered comparison
criterion with a separately constructed target and relative carrier, a prescribed section functor, compatible
exhaustive split filtrations, an actual graded chain quasi-isomorphism, and compatible corrections. The
affine criterion of Theorem 30.4.3 requires the actual coefficient and filtered chain maps. Theorem 30.5.2
further requires an equivariant map of specified double complexes and a valid totalization. Theorem 30.5.1
constructs the polynomial reduction on its associative carrier. For 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑏𝑐 , Proposition 30.3.11 obstructs
the augmentation-kernel target. Proposition 30.3.12 obstructs the standard relative coordinate transitions
for the universal Virasoro vacuum. These genus-zero obstructions require a different constructed chiral
carrier before a symbol comparison can be posed.
    Corollary 18.24.2 transfers amplitudes only with actual 𝑛-point insertion maps, their pairing homotopy,
and a closed integration functional on a declared form domain. Corollary 29.4.8 reduces the local com-
parison to arity three only after the separate binary-intertwining identity is supplied. The algebraic string
dictionary of Theorem 30.3.13 and Corollary 18.24.2 uses these conditions; equality of scalar anomalies does
not replace them.
    The higher-genus programme (Conjectures 30.23.5, 29.8.3, 18.27.2) requires Costello’s renormaliza-
tion framework at all genera and remains correctly conjectural. The holographic duality programme
(Conjectures 11.7.3, 22.10.1) and the E𝑛 extension (Theorem 15.4.2; proved) illustrate Comparison 3’s higher-
dimensional shadow.

The proposed modular homotopy theory for factorization algebras on curves is the global completion of the
nilpotence-periodicity correspondence (Remark 6.0.1) from genus 0 to all genera. Its structural identity is
the principle that nilpotence is the logarithm of periodicity: the bar construction is the categorical logarithm
whose single-valued regime is classical Koszul duality (genus 0) and whose multi-valued regime is the
modular theory (genus 𝑔 ≥ 1); the curvature 𝜅 (A) is the infinitesimal generator of the monodromy; the
coderived category is the analytic continuation; the characteristic hierarchy (Remark 8.18.29) organizes the
logarithmic data (𝜅 , Δ, Θ) from which the periodic data ( 𝑁 , Π , modular automorphy) are derived via
exponentiation.
   The GRR genus theorem (Comparison 5), the spectral characteristic statements (Comparisons 4 and 8),
and the derived Drinfeld–Kohno comparisons beyond the evaluation locus (Comparison 6) give distinct
consequences. All-genus corrections parametrized by 𝐻 1 (M 𝑔 ) are excluded by the vanishing in Compari-
son 1; sharp global periodicity is a separate assertion from the geometric nilpotence in Comparison 7. The
nilpotence-periodicity framework classifies the geometric contribution as nilpotent depth (not period),
derives modular periodicity from the scalar characteristic via exponentiation, and identifies the Koszul
locus as the convergence domain of the categorical logarithm.

V6: Higher-genus BV/BRST. Costello renormalization compatibility: the genus- 𝑔 bar complex should
be compatible with the Costello–Gwilliam BV quantization framework at all genera, not just genus 0
(Conjecture 30.23.5). The genus-zero statement requires the full target, relative-descent, filtration, symbol-
map, correction, operation, and pairing data of Comparison 9. Propositions 30.3.11 and 30.3.12 obstruct
the specified augmentation-kernel and standard relative constructions. Higher genus requires the further
compatible extension.
V7: Pro-nilpotent topology. Completed bar-cobar convergence in the Francis–Gaitsgory pro-nilpotent
framework [26]: finite-stage bar-cobar compatibility (Remark 34.9.9(H3)) for the 𝐼 -adic completion. Scope:
structural framework in place (Appendix P); finite-stage compatibility open (Stratum II).
V8: Braided monoidal compatibility. Factorization-level Kazhdan equivalence: Theorem 24.8.17 gives
braided monoidal equivalences on Repfd ; the upgrade to category 𝑂 requires DK-4/5 (Conjectures 20.14.2–
20.14.4) and the compact generation of Conjecture 24.8.46. Scope: DK-2/3 proved; braided upgrade open.

Appendix A


Geometric dictionary

Each entry represents a precise mathematical correspondence–-not merely an analogy–-between three lan-
guages: the physical (conformal field theory and operator products), the algebraic (operads and homological
algebra), and the geometric (configuration spaces and residues).

                   Algebraic Structure             Geometric Realization
                   Chiral multiplication           Residues at collision divisors
                   Central extensions              Curved 𝐴∞ structures
                   Conformal weights               Pole orders in residue extraction
                   Normal ordering                 NBC basis choice
                   BRST cohomology                 Spectral sequence pages
                   Operator product expansion      Logarithmic form singularities
                   Jacobi identity                 Arnold–Orlik–Solomon relations
                   Module categories               D-module pushforward
                   Koszul duality                  Orthogonality under residue pairing
                   Vertex operators                Sections over configuration spaces
                   Screening charges               Exact forms modulo boundaries
                   Conformal blocks                Flat sections of connections

Remark A.0.1 (Reading the dictionary). Each entry represents a precise functor or natural transformation
between categories. For instance, the correspondence ‘‘Chiral multiplication ↔ Residues at collision
divisors’’ is the content of Theorem 6.2.70, establishing that the multiplication map factors through the
residue homomorphism. Similarly, ‘‘Central extensions ↔ Curved 𝐴∞ structures’’ reflects Theorem 18.6.2,
showing how the failure of strict associativity due to central charges is precisely captured by the curvature
term 𝑚0 .

Sign conventions

                                                 𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗

• Transposition: 𝜂𝑗 𝑖 = 𝜂𝑖𝑗 as forms (since 𝑑 log(−1) = 0; the antisymmetry 𝑒𝑗 𝑖 = −𝑒 𝑖𝑗 is an Orlik–
  Solomon algebra convention, not a property of the forms)
• Residues: Res 𝑧 𝑖 =𝑧𝑗 [ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ] = 1

• Koszul sign rule: Moving degree 𝑝 past degree 𝑞 introduces (−1) 𝑝𝑞
• Differential grading: deg( 𝑑 ) = 1, deg( 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ) = 1
• Suspension: 𝑠 has degree 1, desuspension 𝑠 −1 has degree −1

Appendix F


Arnold relations

F.1     Arnold relations: historical development and attribu-
        tion
F.1.1  Historical context
Arnold [97] proved that 𝐻 ∗ (Conf 𝑛 (ℂ) , ℤ) is generated by classes 𝜔𝑖𝑗 subject to

                                       𝜔𝑖𝑗 𝜔𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜔𝑗 𝑘 𝜔𝑘𝑖 + 𝜔𝑘𝑖 𝜔𝑖𝑗 = 0

for distinct 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 . Brieskorn [98] extended this to arbitrary hyperplane arrangements via the deletion-
restriction exact sequence. The Orlik–Solomon theorem [13] gives the definitive algebraic form:
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝑀 (A) , ℤ)  𝐴 (A), the exterior algebra on arrangement generators modulo Arnold relations.
    The connection to chiral algebras runs through Kontsevich’s formality theorem [101] (configuration
space integrals satisfying 𝑑 2 = 0 via Arnold relations), Beilinson–Drinfeld [2] (Arnold relations in the
chiral bar construction), Costello–Gwilliam [27] (Arnold relations as locality in factorization algebras),
and recent extensions to derived categories and higher genus [26, 91].

F.2     The Arnold relation and its proofs
Theorem F.2.1 (Arnold relations [127]; [proved]). For any configuration of points 𝑧1 , . . . , 𝑧𝑛 in ℂ,
define the logarithmic 1-forms:

                                                                   𝑑𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑑𝑧𝑗
                                     𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) =
                                                                    𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗

   Then for any three distinct indices 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 ∈ {1, . . . , 𝑛}:

                                   𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0

These three-term relations generate the complete ideal of relations in 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ) , ℂ), which is therefore
the Orlik–Solomon algebra of the braid arrangement.

F.2.1   Examples
For three points, the Arnold relation reads 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0, proved by the partial
fractions identity ( 𝑧 𝑘 − 𝑧 𝑖 ) + ( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ) + ( 𝑧𝑗 − 𝑧 𝑘 ) = 0. For four points, the 43 = 4 Arnold relations
                                                                                           

generate all relations in 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶4 (ℂ)); higher-degree relations are consequences of the quadratic ones by the
Orlik–Solomon theorem.

F.4       The operadic proof
Deﬁnition F.4.1 (Conﬁguration space operad). The collection {C𝑛 = 𝐶 𝑛 (ℂ)}𝑛 ≥0 forms an operad with:
• C𝑛 represents ‘‘𝑛-ary operations’’
• Composition 𝛾𝑖 : C𝑛 × C𝑚 → C𝑛+𝑚 −1 given by inserting configurations
• Unit 1 ∈ C1 is the identity operation
Proposition F.4.2 (Operadic equivalence: Arnold relations ⇔ 𝑑 2 = 0; [proved]). The Arnold
relations for the forms 𝜂𝑖𝑗 are equivalent to the condition 𝑑 2 = 0 on the configuration space operad.

Proof. The configuration space operad has a natural differential 𝑑 = 𝑖 <𝑗 𝜕𝑖𝑗 where 𝜕𝑖𝑗 corresponds to
                                                                            P
taking the residue at the collision divisor 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 . Computing:

                    𝑑2 =
                         ∑︁ 2           ∑︁                   ∑︁
                             𝜕𝑖𝑗 +                 𝜕𝑖𝑗 𝜕𝑘𝑙 +    ( 𝜕𝑖𝑗 𝜕𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜕𝑖𝑗 𝜕𝑖𝑘 + 𝜕𝑗 𝑘 𝜕𝑖𝑘 )
                              𝑖 <𝑗           ( 𝑖,𝑗 )≠( 𝑘,𝑙 )              𝑖 <𝑗 < 𝑘
                                          { 𝑖,𝑗 }∩{ 𝑘,𝑙 }=∅

The first sum vanishes ( 𝜕𝑖𝑗2 = 0: a simple pole has no iterated residue). For disjoint index pairs, 𝜕𝑖𝑗 and 𝜕𝑘𝑙
have degree 1 (cohomological) and act on independent factors, so they anticommute: 𝜕𝑖𝑗 𝜕𝑘𝑙 + 𝜕𝑘𝑙 𝜕𝑖𝑗 = 0.
The remaining triple-index terms give 𝑑 2 = 0 if and only if 𝜕𝑖𝑗 𝜕𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜕𝑗 𝑘 𝜕𝑘𝑖 + 𝜕𝑘𝑖 𝜕𝑖𝑗 = 0 for all triples
{ 𝑖, 𝑗, 𝑘 }.
     Under the correspondence 𝜕𝑖𝑗 ↔ Res𝐷 𝑖𝑗 and composition ↔ wedge product, this triple condition is
equivalent to the Arnold relation 𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0. In one direction, assuming the
Arnold relation, the triple residue terms vanish and 𝑑 2 = 0 follows. In the other direction, 𝑑 2 = 0 applied
to appropriate test forms forces the Arnold relation.

F.5.1     Higher coherences
Remark F.5.2. The Arnold relations with larger | 𝑆 | ensure higher coherences: | 𝑆 | = 2 gives associativity,

F.6        Arnold relations: deletion-restriction sequence
Proof of Theorem F.2.1 via deletion-restriction. Proof 1: Combinatorial (à la Arnold).
   Arnold’s original proof [97] uses the Orlik–Solomon algebra.
Deﬁnition F.6.1 (Orlik–Solomon algebra). For the braid arrangement A = { 𝐻𝑖𝑗 } where 𝐻𝑖𝑗 = { 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 },
the Orlik–Solomon algebra is:
                                     OS(A) = ℂ⟨𝑒 𝑖𝑗 | 𝑖 < 𝑗 ⟩/ 𝐼
where 𝐼 is the ideal generated by:
  (i) 𝑒 2𝑖𝑗 = 0
 (ii) 𝑒 𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝑒𝑗 𝑘 + 𝑒𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝑒 𝑘𝑖 + 𝑒 𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝑒 𝑖𝑗 = 0 (Arnold relation)
Lemma F.6.2 (OS computes cohomology [13]; [proved]).

                                            𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐶𝑛 (ℂ) , ℂ) ≃ OS(A)

F.6.1   Attribution
Arnold [97] discovered the relations (1969); Brieskorn [98] generalized to hyperplane arrangements; Or-
lik–Solomon [13] gave the definitive algebraic presentation; Beilinson–Drinfeld [2] recognized their role
in the chiral bar construction. This work extends to all genera (Theorem 8.5.9) with quantum correc-
tions (Theorem 8.5.9). Higher-genus corrections are computed explicitly at genus 1 (Theorem 8.8.10),
genus 2 (Section 8.9), and genus 3 (Section 8.10). We follow Beilinson–Drinfeld in using the name ‘‘Arnold
relations.’’

F.7.4    Physical interpretation: operator product associativity
Remark F.7.5 (OPE associativity). In conformal field theory, the Arnold relations encode associativity of
the operator product expansion: the three ways of computing a three-point function by successive OPEs
must agree up to monodromy. On logarithmic forms, this reads ( 𝜙 𝑖 × 𝜙𝑗 ) × 𝜙𝑘 = 𝜙 𝑖 × ( 𝜙𝑗 × 𝜙𝑘 ), and
the Arnold relations ensure that the correlation function ⟨ 𝜙 𝑖 ( 𝑧 𝑖 ) 𝜙𝑗 ( 𝑧𝑗 ) 𝜙𝑘 ( 𝑧 𝑘 )⟩ is single-valued after
accounting for all branch cuts.

F.8     Global boundary relations on configuration spaces
The local Arnold relations of the preceding sections control the cancellation of codimension-2 contributions
one triple at a time. The global version follows: a systematic accounting of all codimension-2 strata of 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
and their signed contributions. This provides the rigorous foundation for 𝑑res    2 = 0 as a consequence of the
                                      2
boundary-of-boundary identity 𝜕 = 0 on the stratified space 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ).

F.8.1   Stratification of the Fulton–MacPherson compactification
Theorem F.8.1 (Configuration space boundary relations; [proved]). Let 𝑋 be a smooth algebraic
curve and 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) the Fulton–MacPherson compactification of the configuration space 𝐶𝑛 ( 𝑋 ). The
boundary 𝜕𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is a normal crossings divisor whose strata are indexed by nested partitions (equivalently,
rooted trees with 𝑛 labeled leaves). The following hold:
1546                                                                           Appendix F. Arnold relations


  (i) Codimension-1 strata. For each subset 𝑆 ⊆ {1, . . . , 𝑛} with | 𝑆 | ≥ 2, there is a boundary divisor 𝐷 𝑆
      parametrizing configurations where the points labeled by 𝑆 have collided. As a variety,

                                         𝐷 𝑆  𝐶 | 𝑆 | (𝑇𝑥 𝑋 ) × 𝐶 𝑛− | 𝑆 |+1 ( 𝑋 )

       where 𝑇𝑥 𝑋  𝔸1 is the tangent space at the collision point.
  (ii) Codimension-2 strata. Each codimension-2 stratum arises from one of two configurations:
        (a) Nested collisions. 𝑆 ′ ⊂ 𝑆 with | 𝑆 ′ | ≥ 2, | 𝑆 | ≥ 3. The stratum 𝐷 𝑆 ′ ∩ 𝐷 𝑆 parametrizes a two-
            stage collision: the points in 𝑆 ′ collide first within the group 𝑆 , then 𝑆 collides as a whole.
        (b) Disjoint collisions. 𝑆1 ∩ 𝑆2 = ∅ with | 𝑆1 | , | 𝑆2 | ≥ 2. The stratum 𝐷 𝑆1 ∩ 𝐷 𝑆2 parametrizes two
            independent collision events.
 (iii) The boundary-of-boundary identity. Let 𝜕 = 𝑆 𝜖 𝑆 Res𝐷 𝑆 denote the signed boundary operator,
                                                           P
       where 𝜖 𝑆 = (−1) 𝜎 ( 𝑆 ) is the orientation sign from the normal crossings structure (determined by the
       ordering of boundary divisors). Then:
                                                          𝜕 2 = 0.
       Concretely: for every codimension-2 stratum 𝑍 , the two codimension-1 divisors 𝐷1 , 𝐷2 containing
       𝑍 contribute opposite signs,
                                             𝜖𝐷1 → 𝑍 + 𝜖𝐷2 → 𝑍 = 0,
       and the contributions cancel in pairs.

Proof. Step 1: Normal crossings structure. The Fulton–MacPherson compactification 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 ) is a smooth
variety with boundary a normal crossings divisor [12]. The irreducible components of the boundary are
the divisors 𝐷 𝑆 for | 𝑆 | ≥ 2, and distinct components 𝐷 𝑆 , 𝐷 𝑆 ′ meet transversally if and only if either
𝑆 ⊂ 𝑆 ′ , 𝑆 ′ ⊂ 𝑆 , or 𝑆 ∩ 𝑆 ′ = ∅. When 𝑆 and 𝑆 ′ are ‘‘crossing’’ ( 𝑆 ∩ 𝑆 ′ ≠ ∅, neither contained in the
other), 𝐷 𝑆 ∩ 𝐷 𝑆 ′ = ∅. This is the key property that distinguishes the FM compactification from the naive
closure.
   Step 2: Orientation conventions. We fix a total ordering on the set of boundary divisors (e.g., lexicographic
on the subsets 𝑆 ). The normal crossings condition provides, for each codimension-𝑘 stratum 𝐷 𝑆1 ∩ · · · ∩
𝐷 𝑆𝑘 , an orientation determined by the outward normal vectors to 𝐷 𝑆1 , . . . , 𝐷 𝑆𝑘 in that order. Reordering
introduces a sign (−1) sgn( 𝜎 ) from the permutation.
   Step 3: Codimension-2 cancellation. We verify 𝜕 2 = 0 by showing that each codimension-2 stratum
contributes zero. There are two cases.
   Case (a): Nested collisions ( 𝑆 ′ ⊂ 𝑆 ). The stratum 𝐷 𝑆 ′ ∩ 𝐷 𝑆 is reached via two paths:
• First restrict to 𝐷 𝑆 (the group 𝑆 collides), then restrict further to 𝐷 𝑆 ′ within 𝐷 𝑆 (the subgroup 𝑆 ′
  collides within the already- collapsed cluster).
• First restrict to 𝐷 𝑆 ′ (the subgroup 𝑆 ′ collides), then restrict to 𝐷 𝑆 (the remaining points of 𝑆 join the
  collapsed subgroup).
In the normal crossings chart with coordinates ( 𝑡𝑆 , 𝑡𝑆 ′ , . . .), the first path gives Res𝑡𝑆 ′ =0 ◦ Res𝑡𝑆 =0 and
the second gives Res𝑡𝑆 =0 ◦ Res𝑡𝑆 ′ =0 . The two orderings of the normal directions differ by a transposition,
hence contribute with opposite signs. When combined with the local Arnold relation (Theorem F.7.1),
which controls the algebraic content of each residue, the contributions cancel:

                          Res𝐷 𝑆 ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆 ′ + Res𝐷 𝑆 ′ ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆 = 0        on 𝐷 𝑆 ′ ∩ 𝐷 𝑆 .
F.8. Global boundary relations on configuration spaces                                                          1547


   Case (b): Disjoint collisions ( 𝑆1 ∩ 𝑆2 = ∅). Since 𝐷 𝑆1 and 𝐷 𝑆2 involve disjoint sets of points, the residues
along 𝐷 𝑆1 and 𝐷 𝑆2 act on independent tensor factors of A ⊠𝑛 . The two orderings give:

                               Res𝐷 𝑆1 ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆2 = (−1) | 𝑆1 | · | 𝑆2 | Res𝐷 𝑆2 ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆1

by the Koszul sign rule (the residue maps have degrees determined by the codimension). In the boundary
operator 𝜕 , the orientation signs 𝜖 𝑆1 and 𝜖 𝑆2 are chosen so that this Koszul sign precisely compensates the
reordering, giving:
                           𝜖 𝑆1 𝜖 𝑆2 Res𝐷 𝑆1 ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆2 + 𝜖 𝑆2 𝜖 𝑆1 Res𝐷 𝑆2 ◦ Res𝐷 𝑆1 = 0.
   Case (c): Non-transversal strata. When 𝑆 ∩ 𝑆 ′ ≠ ∅ and neither 𝑆 ⊂ 𝑆 ′ nor 𝑆 ′ ⊂ 𝑆 , we have 𝐷 𝑆 ∩ 𝐷 𝑆 ′ =
∅ by the FM compactification structure. These pairs contribute nothing to 𝜕 2 .
   Step 4: Conclusion. Every codimension-2 stratum falls into case (a), (b), or (c), and in each case the
contribution to 𝜕 2 vanishes. Therefore 𝜕 2 = 0, completing the proof.

Appendix G


Sign conventions and shifts

The sign conventions used throughout this monograph are chosen for compatibility with Lo-
day–Vallette [135] (operadic structures), Beilinson–Drinfeld [128] (chiral algebras), and Lurie [43]
(∞-categorical foundations).

G.1       The Koszul sign rule
Convention G.1.1 (Koszul sign rule). Let C be a graded category (chain complexes, differential graded
algebras, graded vector spaces, etc.). When two homogeneous elements 𝑎 and 𝑏 of degrees | 𝑎 | and | 𝑏 |
respectively are interchanged in any formula, a sign (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | must be introduced:

                                                       𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ↦−→ (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑎.

This rule applies universally: to tensor products, compositions, evaluations, and any operation where the
order of graded objects matters.
Deﬁnition G.1.2 (Graded commutator). For homogeneous elements 𝑎, 𝑏 in a graded algebra 𝐴, the graded
commutator is:
                                 [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] := 𝑎 · 𝑏 − (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | 𝑏 · 𝑎.
An algebra is graded commutative if [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] = 0 for all homogeneous 𝑎, 𝑏 , which is equivalent to 𝑎 · 𝑏 =
(−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | 𝑏 · 𝑎.
Proposition G.1.3 (Graded Jacobi identity; [proved]). For any graded Lie algebra ( 𝐿, [−, −]), the
bracket satisfies the graded Jacobi identity:

                     (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑎, [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ]] + (−1) | 𝑏 | · | 𝑎 | [ 𝑏, [ 𝑐, 𝑎]] + (−1) | 𝑐 | · | 𝑏 | [ 𝑐, [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ]] = 0.

This is equivalent to requiring that the adjoint action ad 𝑎 = [ 𝑎, −] is a derivation of the bracket:

                                        [ 𝑎, [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ]] = [[ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] , 𝑐 ] + (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | [ 𝑏, [ 𝑎, 𝑐 ]] .

Proof. The equivalence follows from expanding the graded Jacobi identity and applying graded antisym-
metry [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ] = −(−1) | 𝑏 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑐, 𝑏 ]. The cyclic sum becomes:

              0 = (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑎, [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ]] + (−1) | 𝑏 | · | 𝑎 | [ 𝑏, [ 𝑐, 𝑎]] + (−1) | 𝑐 | · | 𝑏 | [ 𝑐, [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ]]
                 = (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑎, [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ]] − (−1) | 𝑏 | · | 𝑎 | (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑏, [ 𝑎, 𝑐 ]] + (−1) | 𝑐 | · | 𝑏 | [ 𝑐, [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ]]
                 = (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑐 | [ 𝑎, [ 𝑏, 𝑐 ]] − (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | [ 𝑏, [ 𝑎, 𝑐 ]] − [[ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] , 𝑐 ] ,
                                                                                                               


using [[ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] , 𝑐 ] = −(−1) ( | 𝑎 |+| 𝑏 | ) | 𝑐 | [ 𝑐, [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ]] and simplifying exponents.

Convention G.1.4 (Sign in differential graded structures). In a differential graded algebra ( 𝐴, 𝑑, ·):
   (i) The differential has degree | 𝑑 | = +1 (cohomological convention) or | 𝑑 | = −1 (homological conven-
       tion).
  (ii) The Leibniz rule incorporates the Koszul sign:

                                              𝑑 ( 𝑎 · 𝑏 ) = ( 𝑑𝑎) · 𝑏 + (−1) | 𝑎 | 𝑎 · ( 𝑑𝑏 ) .

 (iii) For a differential graded Lie algebra, the bracket-differential compatibility is:

                                               𝑑 [ 𝑎, 𝑏 ] = [ 𝑑𝑎, 𝑏 ] + (−1) | 𝑎 | [ 𝑎, 𝑑𝑏 ] .

Throughout this monograph, we use the cohomological convention | 𝑑 | = +1 unless explicitly stated other-
wise.
Lemma G.1.5 (Sign rule for compositions [83]; [proved]). Let 𝑓 : 𝑉 → 𝑊 and 𝑔 : 𝑊 → 𝑋 be

                                            ( 𝑔 ◦ 𝑓 ) ( 𝑣 ) = 𝑔 ( 𝑓 ( 𝑣 ))   (no sign).

where 𝜏 denotes the graded twist map.

G.2       Cohomological versus homological grading
Deﬁnition G.2.1 (Grading conventions). Let ( 𝐶, 𝑑 ) be a differential graded object.
  (i) Homological grading. 𝐶 = 𝑛 ∈ℤ 𝐶𝑛 with 𝑑 : 𝐶𝑛 → 𝐶𝑛−1 . The differential lowers degree by 1.
                               L

 (ii) Cohomological grading. 𝐶 = 𝑛 ∈ℤ 𝐶 𝑛 with 𝑑 : 𝐶 𝑛 → 𝐶 𝑛+1 . The differential raises degree by 1.
                                 L

The translation is 𝐶 𝑛 = 𝐶− 𝑛 , which exchanges upper and lower indices.
Convention G.2.2 (Standard conventions by context). In this monograph:
   (i) Chain complexes of modules. Homological convention ( 𝐶• , 𝜕 ).
  (ii) Cochain complexes (de Rham, singular cochains). Cohomological convention ( 𝐶 • , 𝑑 ).
 (iii) Operadic bar/cobar. Cohomological convention (translated from the homological convention of
       Loday–Vallette [135] via 𝐶 𝑛 = 𝐶− 𝑛 ; see Definition G.2.1).
 (iv) Hochschild (co)homology. Homological for homology 𝐻 𝐻∗ , cohomological for cohomology 𝐻 𝐻 ∗ .
  (v) D-modules. Cohomological convention, with de Rham complex DR(M) in non-negative degrees.
 (vi) ∞-categories. Cohomological convention following Lurie [43, 131].
Proposition G.2.3 (Duality and grading reversal; [proved]). For a finite-dimensional chain com-
plex ( 𝐶• , 𝜕 ), the dual complex 𝐶 ∗ = Hom( 𝐶, 𝑘 ) naturally carries a cohomological grading:
                                            ( 𝐶 ∗ ) 𝑛 := Hom𝑘 ( 𝐶𝑛 , 𝑘 ) = ( 𝐶𝑛 ) ∗ .
The dual differential 𝜕 ∗ : ( 𝐶 ∗ ) 𝑛 → ( 𝐶 ∗ ) 𝑛+1 is defined by:
                                               ⟨ 𝜕 ∗ 𝜙, 𝑐 ⟩ := (−1) | 𝜙 |+1 ⟨ 𝜙, 𝜕 𝑐 ⟩
for 𝜙 ∈ ( 𝐶 ∗ ) 𝑛 and 𝑐 ∈ 𝐶𝑛+1 .
Proof. The sign ensures ( 𝜕 ∗ ) 2 = 0. Indeed:
                     ⟨( 𝜕 ∗ ) 2 𝜙, 𝑐 ⟩ = (−1) | 𝜙 |+2 ⟨ 𝜕 ∗ 𝜙, 𝜕𝑐 ⟩ = (−1) | 𝜙 |+2 (−1) | 𝜙 |+1 ⟨ 𝜙, 𝜕 2 𝑐 ⟩ = 0.
The sign (−1) | 𝜙 |+1 is precisely the convention that makes ( 𝐶, 𝐶 ∗ ) into a duality pairing of chain complexes.


Deﬁnition G.2.4 (Connective and coconnective). A chain complex 𝐶 (in homological grading) is:
   (i) Connective if 𝐶𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 < 0 (concentrated in non-negative degrees).
  (ii) Coconnective if 𝐶𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 > 0 (concentrated in non-positive degrees).
 (iii) Bounded if both conditions hold with finitely many nonzero terms.
In cohomological grading, connective means 𝐶 𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 > 0, and coconnective means 𝐶 𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 < 0.
Remark G.2.5 (Filtrations and spectral sequences). The grading convention affects the indexing of spectral
sequences. For a filtered complex with cohomological grading and increasing filtration 𝐹 𝑝 𝐶 ⊆ 𝐹 𝑝+1 𝐶 , the
spectral sequence has:
                                           𝐸𝑟 ⇒ 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 ( 𝐶 ) .
                                             𝑝,𝑞

For homological grading with decreasing filtration 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 ⊇ 𝐹𝑝+1 𝐶 :
                                                        𝑟
                                                      𝐸 𝑝,𝑞 ⇒ 𝐻 𝑝+ 𝑞 ( 𝐶 ) .
The bidegree conventions ( 𝑝, 𝑞 ) versus ( 𝑝, 𝑛 − 𝑝) also vary by author.

G.3      Suspensions and desuspensions
Deﬁnition G.3.1 (Suspension and desuspension). For a graded object 𝑉 =                          𝑛:
                                                                                      L
                                                                                          𝑛𝑉

  (i) The suspension 𝑠𝑉 (also denoted 𝑉 [−1] in the cohomological convention or 𝑉 [1] in the homological
      convention; see Remark G.3.2) is defined by:

                                                       ( 𝑠𝑉 ) 𝑛 := 𝑉 𝑛−1 .

       An element 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 𝑛−1 corresponds to 𝑠𝑣 ∈ ( 𝑠𝑉 ) 𝑛 with | 𝑠𝑣 | = | 𝑣 | + 1.
  (ii) The desuspension 𝑠 −1𝑉 (also denoted 𝑉 [1] in the cohomological convention or 𝑉 [−1] in the homo-

                                               ( 𝑠 −1𝑉 ) 𝑛 := 𝑉 𝑛+1 .
       An element 𝑣 ∈ 𝑉 𝑛+1 corresponds to 𝑠 −1 𝑣 ∈ ( 𝑠 −1𝑉 ) 𝑛 with | 𝑠 −1 𝑣 | = | 𝑣 | − 1.
These are inverse operations: 𝑠 ◦ 𝑠 −1 = 𝑠 −1 ◦ 𝑠 = id.
   The two constructions that produce the Koszul dual use opposite shifts, for a precise reason:
• Bar construction (desuspension): 𝐵¯ (A) = 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā , 𝑑 ). Desuspension lowers generators by one degree
  because the bar differential 𝑑res extracts a residue–-an integration operation that lowers form degree–-and
  the shift compensates so that | 𝑑 | = +1.
• Koszul dual coalgebra (suspension): A ! ↩→ Cofree( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ ) (Appendix J). Suspension raises the dual
  generators 𝑉 ∗ by one degree because dualizing reverses the grading, and the shift restores it.
These are consistent: when A is Koszul, 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ (A)) concentrates in bar degree 1, and the desuspension-
then-suspension cancels, recovering the Koszul dual generators in their natural degree.
Remark G.3.2 (Shift notation ambiguity). The notation 𝑉 [ 𝑛] is used with two incompatible conventions
in the literature:
   (i) Homological convention. (𝑉 [ 𝑛]) 𝑘 = 𝑉𝑘 − 𝑛 , so 𝑉 [1] shifts up (increases indices).
  (ii) Cohomological convention. (𝑉 [ 𝑛]) 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘+𝑛 , so 𝑉 [1] shifts down (decreases indices in the sense that
       degree-𝑘 elements come from degree-( 𝑘 + 1) elements of 𝑉 ).
We follow the cohomological convention: 𝑉 [ 𝑛] 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘+𝑛 . Under this convention, 𝑠𝑉 = 𝑉 [−1] (since
(𝑉 [−1]) 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘 −1 = ( 𝑠𝑉 ) 𝑘 ) and 𝑠 −1𝑉 = 𝑉 [1] (since (𝑉 [1]) 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘+1 = ( 𝑠 −1𝑉 ) 𝑘 ).
   Warning. Many references in algebraic topology use the opposite convention where 𝑠𝑉 = 𝑉 [1]; this
corresponds to (𝑉 [ 𝑛]) 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘 − 𝑛 (the homological convention). When importing results from such refer-
ences, all shift indices must be negated.

where 𝑘 𝐼 is the vector space with basis indexed by 𝐼 . Concretely, if 𝐼 = { 𝑖1 , . . . , 𝑖𝑛 }:

                                           Det( 𝐼 ) = 𝑘 · ( 𝑒 𝑖1 ∧ · · · ∧ 𝑒 𝑖𝑛 )

is 1-dimensional, and permuting the order of 𝐼 introduces signs according to the permutation’s signature.
Lemma G.4.4 (Determinant and ordering [110]; [proved]). For a finite set 𝐼 with total orderings <
and <′ , let 𝜎 ∈ Σ 𝐼 be the permutation taking the <-ordering to the <′ -ordering. Then:

                                 𝑒 𝑖1 ∧ · · · ∧ 𝑒 𝑖𝑛 = sgn( 𝜎 ) · 𝑒 𝑖𝜎 (1) ∧ · · · ∧ 𝑒 𝑖𝜎 (𝑛) .

The determinant line Det( 𝐼 ) is canonically independent of ordering, but a choice of generator (i.e., orien-
tation) depends on ordering.
Deﬁnition G.4.5 (Orientation local system). For a real smooth manifold 𝑀 of dimension 𝑑 , the orientation
local system is the rank-one 𝑘 -local system associated to its frame bundle by 𝑔 ↦→ sgn(det 𝑔 ). Its integral
form has fiber 𝐻𝑑 ( 𝑀 , 𝑀 \ { 𝑝 }; ℤ) at 𝑝. An orientation chooses a generator in each integral fiber, locally
consistently. The real line bundle 𝑑 𝑇 𝑀 instead has transition functions det 𝑔 . These objects have the
                                    V
same orientability obstruction, but only the former is defined as a local system. A complex manifold has its
canonical real orientation.
