Construction G.4.7 (Determinant line in the ordered bar complex). For an augmented differential graded
associative algebra 𝐴, the length-𝑛 bar term is ( 𝐴 [1]) ⊗ 𝑛 , with 𝐴 replaced by its augmentation ideal. The

                                      V
symbols to the left. The determinant has degree −𝑛 and comes before the algebra factors. For a normal-
crossing product chart with divisor labels 𝐸 , equation (6.11) identifies the direct sum of determinant terms
over all 𝑆 ⊆ 𝐸 with the subcomplex of normal logarithmic forms on all product strata. The source has the

is required for closure. It does not identify all logarithmic forms with a line bundle. The full residue sheaf
has strict coordinate pullbacks by Proposition 6.2.10. The chosen normal image can move under a unit
change; its fixed-coefficient overlap comparison is Theorem 6.2.14, and ordered bar coefficients carry the
additional sign (6.28). For state-changing adjacent collisions, the coefficient maps and their exact domains
are (6.29)–(6.31). Their local logarithmic comparison is (6.34); the ℂ∗ counterexamples exclude a general
unfiltered or filtered transfer without the respective hypotheses.

H.1.1    Key differences explained
1. Differential degree. Loday–Vallette use homological grading (| 𝑑 | = −1); this manuscript uses cohomo-

    Translation. If ( 𝐶∗ , 𝑑 ) is a chain complex in LV convention ( 𝑑 : 𝐶𝑛 → 𝐶𝑛−1 ), set 𝐶 𝑛 := 𝐶− 𝑛 with the
same underlying map 𝑑 , which now raises cohomological degree by 1. No sign change is needed: 𝑑us = 𝑑LV
(as linear maps).
    2. Suspension. Loday–Vallette treat suspension 𝑠 as an explicit operator; this manuscript uses the degree
shift 𝑠𝑉 = 𝑉 [−1], so | 𝑠𝑣 | = | 𝑣 | + 1.
    Translation. 𝑠𝑉 (LV) corresponds to 𝑉 [−1] (us), i.e., our 𝑠𝑉 . Both raise degree by 1: LV’s convention
( 𝑠𝑉 ) 𝑘 = 𝑉𝑘 −1 translates via degcoh = − deghom to ( 𝑠𝑉 ) 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘 −1 = (𝑉 [−1]) 𝑘 .
    3. Bar/cobar formulas. Loday–Vallette include explicit suspension in the formula; this manuscript
absorbs it into the D-module structure.
    Translation. Our 𝐵¯ 𝑛 (A) corresponds to LV’s 𝐵 (A) in degree 𝑛 after removing the suspension 𝑠 .

H.4.1    Key differences explained
Kontsevich’s formality.
• Classical: Poisson manifolds → deformation quantization
• Configuration spaces in ℝ𝑑 (no compactification)
• Smooth forms (no poles)
• Graph complex (combinatorial)
   Our chiral formality.
• Coisson algebras (PVA) → vertex algebras (OPE) via chiral configuration spaces
• Configuration spaces on curves (compactified)
• Logarithmic forms (poles at collisions)
• Genus-stratified complex (geometric)
  Relation. Kontsevich’s formality is the genus-0 part of chiral formality. The bar-cobar framework extends
Kontsevich to include all genera (higher-loop corrections).

H.6      Practical guide: how to translate
H.6.1    From Loday–Vallette to our conventions
Rule 1. Replace | 𝑑 | = −1 with | 𝑑 | = +1.
  Rule 2. Replace LV’s suspension 𝑠 with our degree shift [−1]: 𝑠𝑉 = 𝑉 [−1].
  Rule 3. Our geometric forms Ω𝑛 (log 𝐷 ) correspond to LV’s suspended generators 𝑠 𝑛𝑉 .

H.6.2     From Beilinson–Drinfeld to our conventions
Rule 1. BD’s 𝑗!∗ (factorization pushforward) = our explicit configuration space integral.
  Rule 2. BD’s Ran space Ran( 𝑋 ) = our 𝑛 𝐶 𝑛 ( 𝑋 )/∼ (colimit).
                                          S
   Rule 3. BD’s ‘‘chiral product’’ = our ‘‘OPE residue’’

H.6.3    From Costello–Gwilliam to our conventions
Rule 1. CG’s ‘‘1-loop’’ = our ‘‘genus 1’’
  Rule 2. CG’s ‘‘renormalization’’ = our ‘‘ 𝐼 -adic completion’’
  Rule 3. CG’s BV bracket = our bar differential (when specialized to curves).

H.7      Examples of translation
Example H.7.1 (Translating a bar differential formula from LV). Loday–Vallette writes.

                        𝑑𝐿𝑉 ( 𝑠𝑎1 ⊗ 𝑠𝑎2 ⊗ 𝑠𝑎3 ) = (−1) | 𝑎1 | ( 𝑠 [ 𝑎1 , 𝑎2 ] ⊗ 𝑠𝑎3 ) + · · ·

   Our notation.
                       𝑑 ( 𝑎1 ⊗ 𝑎2 ⊗ 𝑎3 ⊗ 𝜔2 ) = ( [ 𝑎1 , 𝑎2 ] ⊗ 𝑎3 ⊗ Res[ 𝜔2 ]) + · · ·
   Translation.
• Remove explicit suspension 𝑠 (implicit in form degree)
• Change sign convention: (−1) | 𝑎1 | becomes automatic from Koszul rule
• Add geometric form 𝜔2 ∈ Ω2 (log 𝐷 )
Example H.7.2 (Translating a BD factorization formula). Beilinson–Drinfeld writes.

                                 𝑗!∗ (A ⊠ A)|𝑈 ⊔𝑉 ≃ 𝑗!∗ A|𝑈 ⊠ 𝑗!∗ A|𝑉

   Our notation.
                                     ∫
                   𝐵¯ 1 (A)|𝑈 ⊔𝑉 =                     A ⊠2 ⊗ Ω1log ≃ 𝐵¯ 1 (A)|𝑈 ⊗ 𝐵¯ 1 (A)|𝑉
                                     𝐶2 (𝑈 )⊔𝐶2 (𝑉 )

   Translation.
• 𝑗!∗ (pushforward) = configuration space integral
• Factorization isomorphism = bar complex splitting
• Add explicit forms Ω1log

H.8      Sign rules for this manuscript
For easy reference, here are ALL sign rules used in this manuscript in one place:
1564                                                        Appendix H. Dictionary of sign conventions


H.8.1     Koszul signs
Rule. When permuting two graded objects 𝑎 and 𝑏 :
                                             𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 = (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 | 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑎
   Application. Moving a form 𝜔 of degree | 𝜔 | = 𝑛 past fields 𝜙1 , . . . , 𝜙𝑘 :
                      ( 𝜙1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜙𝑘 ) ⊗ 𝜔 = (−1) 𝑛 ( | 𝜙1 |+···+| 𝜙𝑘 | ) 𝜔 ⊗ ( 𝜙1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝜙𝑘 )

H.8.2     Collision divisor signs
Rule. Collision divisors are always written with indices in increasing order: 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 means 𝑖 < 𝑗 .
   Convention. We write 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 with 𝑖 < 𝑗 . Geometrically 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 = 𝐷𝑗 𝑖 (same subvariety 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 ). The
sign convention 𝐷𝑗 𝑖 = − 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 applies to the oriented divisor (i.e., to the associated residue forms, not the
subvariety itself).

H.8.3     Arnold relation signs
3-term Arnold relation.
                                     𝜂𝑖𝑗 ∧ 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 + 𝜂𝑗 𝑘 ∧ 𝜂𝑘𝑖 + 𝜂𝑘𝑖 ∧ 𝜂𝑖𝑗 = 0
    Higher-degree consequences. All higher-degree relations in the OS algebra follow from the 3-term Arnold
relations by repeated application. There is no independent ‘‘general Arnold relation’’ beyond the 3-term
version.

H.8.4     Residue signs
The sign arising from the residue at 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 is determined by the Koszul sign rule: the residue operation
(cohomological degree 1) must commute past the preceding tensor factors. For elements 𝑠 −1 𝑎1 P ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑠 −1 𝑎𝑛
                                                                                                        −1
in the bar complex, the residue at 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 (colliding factors 𝑖 and 𝑗 ) picks up the sign (−1) 𝑘 < 𝑖 | 𝑠 𝑎𝑘 | . In
particular, when all generators have even desuspended degree, all residue signs are positive.
    For the explicit sign computations relevant to the bar differential, see the proof of 𝑑 2 = 0 in §6.2.17.

H.9      Common pitfalls and how to avoid them
H.9.1   Pitfall 1: forgetting Koszul signs
Wrong. 𝑑 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔) = 𝑑𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔 + 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑑𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔
  Right. 𝑑 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔) = 𝑑𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔 + (−1) | 𝑎 | 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑑𝑏 ⊗ 𝜔
  The sign (−1) | 𝑎 | comes from moving 𝑑 (degree +1) past 𝑎 (degree | 𝑎 |).

H.9.2    Pitfall 2: confusing hat notations
       b could mean ‘‘omit factors 𝑖 and 𝑗 ,’’ or ‘‘the set { 𝑖, 𝑗 },’’ or something else entirely.
Wrong. 𝑖𝑗
  Right. Use our convention: 𝑖𝑗
                             b always means ‘‘omit both 𝑖 and 𝑗 ’’ with no ambiguity.

H.9.3      Pitfall 3: collision divisor ordering
Convention. We write collision divisors with 𝑖 < 𝑗 : 𝐷13 rather than 𝐷31 . Since 𝐷 𝑖𝑗 = { 𝑧 𝑖 = 𝑧𝑗 } is an
unordered locus, 𝐷31 = 𝐷13 (no sign). Likewise, the logarithmic forms satisfy 𝜂𝑗 𝑖 = 𝜂𝑖𝑗 since 𝑑 log( 𝑧𝑗 −
𝑧 𝑖 ) = 𝑑 log(−( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 )) = 𝑑 log( 𝑧 𝑖 − 𝑧𝑗 ).
     The sign convention 𝑒𝑗 𝑖 = −𝑒 𝑖𝑗 applies only to Orlik–Solomon algebra generators (an algebraic con-
vention for exterior algebra presentations), not to the geometric forms or divisors.
H.10. Summary and recommendations                                                                      1565


H.9.4     Pitfall 4: Arnold relation orientation
Wrong. Assuming Arnold relations hold without signs.
  Right. The cyclic sum includes signs from wedge product antisymmetry:

                                   𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 + 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = 0

   Note: Each term has a + sign in the cyclic sum, but the individual forms anticommute.

H.10      Summary and recommendations
For readers unfamiliar with sign conventions.
   (i) Start with Remark 6.2.68 (Loday–Vallette comparison, in Chapter 6)
  (ii) Consult this appendix when reading other sources
 (iii) Work through the examples in §18.6.2 (Heisenberg explicit calculations)
 (iv) Verify signs match in low-degree computations
   For experts. Our conventions match:
• Kontsevich’s graph complex (lexicographic ordering)
• Costello–Gwilliam’s factorization algebras (cohomological grading)
• Beilinson–Drinfeld’s D-module perspective (implicit signs)
   The main difference from Loday–Vallette is grading direction (| 𝑑 | = +1 vs −1); the translation is a
global sign reversal on the grading.

H.11.1    Conversion formulas
Proposition H.11.1 (Loday–Vallette conversion; [proved]). To convert from our conventions to
Loday–Vallette:
   (i) Replace | 𝑑 | = +1 with | 𝑑 | = −1 (flip grading direction)
  (ii) Replace bar complex 𝐵¯ 𝑛 with 𝐵¯ − 𝑛 (decreasing filtration)
 (iii) Keep Koszul sign rule unchanged (all four conventions agree on the Koszul sign rule)
 (iv) Keep composition order unchanged: ( 𝑓 ◦ 𝑔 )LV = 𝑓 ◦ 𝑔 (the degree reversal affects signs in the
       Leibniz rule, not the order of function composition)

Veriﬁcation. The key identity is that homological grading (LV) relates to cohomological grading (ours) by
deghom = − degcoh .
   For a differential 𝑑 :
• Our convention: 𝑑 : 𝐶 𝑛 → 𝐶 𝑛+1 , so | 𝑑 | = +1
• LV convention: 𝑑 : 𝐶𝑛 → 𝐶𝑛−1 , so | 𝑑 | LV = −1
   The Koszul sign rule in the Leibniz formula is the same in both conventions:

                                    𝑑 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ) = 𝑑𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 + (−1) | 𝑎 | 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑑𝑏

(The degree | 𝑎 | is taken in whichever grading is active.) The sign difference between conventions manifests
in the bar differential, where LV uses explicitly suspended elements 𝑠𝑎: the bar differential sign (−1) | 𝑠𝑎 | =
(−1) | 𝑎 |+1 in LV’s homological convention (where | 𝑠𝑎 | = | 𝑎 | + 1) differs from (−1) | 𝑎 | in ours.

H.11.2    Explicit sign calculations
Example H.11.2 (Three-point Arnold relation). For three points 𝑧1 , 𝑧2 , 𝑧3 , the Arnold relation is:

                                    𝜂12 ∧ 𝜂23 + 𝜂23 ∧ 𝜂31 + 𝜂31 ∧ 𝜂12 = 0

   Sign veriﬁcation.
   (i) Each 𝜂𝑖𝑗 has degree 1
  (ii) Wedge product: 𝜂 ∧ 𝜂 ′ has degree 2
 (iii) Moving forms: 𝜂 ∧ 𝜂 ′ = (−1) 1·1 𝜂 ′ ∧ 𝜂 = − 𝜂 ′ ∧ 𝜂
   All signs are explicit and match BD conventions.
Remark H.11.3 (Fermionic vs bosonic). For fermionic fields 𝜓 : 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜓 ( 𝑤 ) = −𝜓 ( 𝑤 ) 𝜓 ( 𝑧 ) (Koszul sign
with | 𝜓 | = 1).
   For bosonic fields 𝜙: 𝜙 ( 𝑧 ) 𝜙 ( 𝑤 ) = 𝜙 ( 𝑤 ) 𝜙 ( 𝑧 ) (degree | 𝜙 | = 0).
   The bar complex treats both uniformly via suspension 𝑠 : 𝑉 → 𝑉 [−1].

H.12.1     Detailed conversion formulas
H.12.1.1 Koszul signs
Deﬁnition H.12.1 (Koszul sign rule). When permuting graded elements 𝑎 and 𝑏 in a tensor product:
  BD, CG, Us convention.
                                𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ↔ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑎 with sign (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 |
   LV convention.

                         𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ↔ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑎 with sign                      (−1) | 𝑎 | · | 𝑏 |   (same Koszul rule)

      Key difference. LV works in homological grading (| 𝑑 | = −1), using suspended elements 𝑠𝑎 with | 𝑠𝑎 | =
| 𝑎 | + 1. The apparent sign differences in bar complex formulas arise from the shifted degrees of 𝑠𝑎, not
from a different Koszul rule. Specifically, swapping 𝑠𝑎 ⊗ 𝑠𝑏 gives (−1) | 𝑠𝑎 | | 𝑠𝑏 | = (−1) ( | 𝑎 |+1) ( | 𝑏 |+1) , which
differs from (−1) | 𝑎 | | 𝑏 | by the factor (−1) | 𝑎 |+| 𝑏 |+1 .
Example H.12.2 (Koszul sign in bar construction). For 𝑎 ∈ A 𝑚 , 𝑏 ∈ A 𝑛 , 𝑐 ∈ A 𝑝 :
   Us/BD/CG.

               𝑑 ( 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 ) = 𝑑 ( 𝑎) ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + (−1) 𝑚 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑑 ( 𝑏 ) ⊗ 𝑐 + (−1) 𝑚+𝑛 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑑 ( 𝑐 )

   LV (on suspended elements 𝑠𝑎, 𝑠𝑏, 𝑠𝑐 ).

      𝑑 ( 𝑠𝑎 ⊗ 𝑠𝑏 ⊗ 𝑠𝑐 ) = 𝑑 ( 𝑠𝑎) ⊗ 𝑠𝑏 ⊗ 𝑠𝑐 + (−1) 𝑚+1 𝑠𝑎 ⊗ 𝑑 ( 𝑠𝑏 ) ⊗ 𝑠𝑐 + (−1) 𝑚+𝑛+2 𝑠𝑎 ⊗ 𝑠𝑏 ⊗ 𝑑 ( 𝑠𝑐 )

  Explanation. The sign differences arise because | 𝑠𝑎 | = 𝑚 + 1, | 𝑠𝑏 | = 𝑛 + 1, | 𝑠𝑐 | = 𝑝 + 1, and the standard
Koszul rule is applied to these shifted degrees. The LV Koszul sign rule itself is the same (−1) | 𝑥 | | 𝑦 | .

H.12.2      Quick translation table

                             Table H.5: Translation formulas between conventions

       To convert from                                         Apply this transformation
       LV → Us/BD/CG                  Multiply internal terms by (−1) | 𝑎 | , add chiral product
       CG → Us              Shift notation: CG’s 𝑉 [1] (convention 𝑉 [ 𝑛] 𝑘 = 𝑉 𝑘 − 𝑛 ) equals our 𝑉 [−1]
       BD → Us                                 Split 𝑑 ′′ into 𝑑residue and 𝑑correction
       Us → BD                                Combine 𝑑residue + 𝑑correction into 𝑑 ′′
       Us → LV                              Remove chiral product, multiply by (−1) | 𝑎 |

H.12.3      Recommendations for readers
• Reading BD. Our conventions match closely; main difference is we separate out quantum corrections
  explicitly.
• Reading CG. The conventions match exactly; use their formulas directly.
• Reading LV. Add extra (−1) | 𝑎 | signs and remember to include chiral product which LV does not have.
• Writing papers. We recommend the CG conventions (used here) as they are most explicit about quantum
  corrections.
Remark H.12.3 (Origins of different conventions). The conventions reflect different origins: BD developed
for D-modules (orientation from holomorphic structure), CG optimized for BV formalism and factor-
ization algebras, LV for pure operadic theory (no geometric residues), and ours emphasizing geometric
realization and explicit calculations. All conventions are mathematically equivalent–-they are different
presentations of the same underlying structures.

Appendix I


Spectral sequences

Three spectral sequences are central to chiral Koszul duality: the bar spectral sequence (computing bar
complex homology), the Chevalley–Cousin spectral sequence (relating D-module cohomology to con-
figuration space geometry), and the genus spectral sequence (organizing quantum corrections by loop
order).

I.1      Filtered complexes and spectral sequences
Deﬁnition I.1.1 (Filtered chain complex). A ﬁltered chain complex is a chain complex ( 𝐶, 𝑑 ) together with
a sequence of subcomplexes:
                                     · · · ⊆ 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 ⊆ 𝐹𝑝+1 𝐶 ⊆ · · · ⊆ 𝐶
such that 𝑑 ( 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 ) ⊆ 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 for all 𝑝.
    The filtration is:
   (i) Exhaustive if 𝐶 = 𝑝 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 .
                          S

  (ii) Complete (or Hausdorff) if 𝑝 𝐹𝑝 𝐶 = 0.
                                    T

 (iii) Bounded below if for each degree 𝑛, there exists 𝑝0 ( 𝑛) such that 𝐹𝑝 𝐶𝑛 = 0 for 𝑝 < 𝑝0 ( 𝑛).
 (iv) Bounded above if for each degree 𝑛, there exists 𝑝1 ( 𝑛) such that 𝐹𝑝 𝐶𝑛 = 𝐶𝑛 for 𝑝 > 𝑝1 ( 𝑛).
  (v) Bounded if both bounded below and bounded above.

I.2    Convergence criteria
Refined convergence criteria for pro-nilpotent and completed settings follow.
Deﬁnition I.2.1 (Regular spectral sequence). A spectral sequence is regular if for each bidegree ( 𝑝, 𝑞 ), the

                      𝑝,𝑞                                                                                  𝑝,𝑞
                            → 𝐸𝑟                                                                   → 𝐸𝑟

Deﬁnition I.2.3 (Strongly convergent). A spectral sequence 𝐸𝑟                   ⇒ 𝐻 𝑝+𝑞 is strongly convergent if:

   (i) The spectral sequence is regular.
  (ii) The filtration on 𝐻 ∗ is exhaustive and complete.

Theorem I.2.4 (Zeeman comparison theorem; [proved]). Let 𝑓 : 𝐶 → 𝐷 be a filtered chain map be-
tween filtered complexes, inducing 𝑓𝑟 : 𝐸𝑟 ( 𝐶 ) → 𝐸𝑟 ( 𝐷 ) on spectral sequences. If both spectral sequences
converge strongly and 𝑓𝑟 : 𝐸𝑟 ( 𝐶 ) 𝑝,𝑞 → 𝐸𝑟 ( 𝐷 ) 𝑝,𝑞 is an isomorphism for some 𝑟 and all ( 𝑝, 𝑞 ), then:

                                                 𝑓∗ : 𝐻∗ ( 𝐶 ) → 𝐻∗ ( 𝐷 )

is an isomorphism.

Proof. If 𝑓𝑟 is an isomorphism, then so is 𝑓𝑟 +1 = 𝐻 ( 𝑓𝑟 ), and by induction 𝑓∞ : 𝐸∞ ( 𝐶 ) → 𝐸∞ ( 𝐷 ) is an iso-
morphism. Strong convergence implies gr 𝑓∗ : gr 𝐻∗ ( 𝐶 ) → gr 𝐻∗ ( 𝐷 ) is an isomorphism. Completeness
and exhaustiveness imply 𝑓∗ itself is an isomorphism.

I.6     Multiplicative spectral sequences
Deﬁnition I.6.1 (Multiplicative spectral sequence). A spectral sequence ( 𝐸𝑟∗,∗ , 𝑑𝑟 ) is multiplicative if:
   (i) Each 𝐸𝑟∗,∗ is a bigraded algebra.
  (ii) The differential 𝑑𝑟 is a derivation: 𝑑𝑟 ( 𝑥𝑦 ) = ( 𝑑𝑟 𝑥 ) 𝑦 + (−1) | 𝑥 | 𝑥 ( 𝑑𝑟 𝑦 ).
 (iii) The product on 𝐸𝑟 +1 = 𝐻 ( 𝐸𝑟 , 𝑑𝑟 ) is induced from 𝐸𝑟 .
Proposition I.6.2 (Bar spectral sequence is multiplicative [83]; [proved]). The bar spectral se-
quence for an algebra 𝐴 is multiplicative with product:

                                                          𝜎 ∈Sh( 𝑚,𝑛 )
1578                                                                        Appendix I. Spectral sequences


where { 𝑐1 , . . . , 𝑐𝑚+𝑛 } = { 𝑎1 , . . . , 𝑎𝑚 , 𝑏1 , . . . , 𝑏𝑛 } and Sh( 𝑚, 𝑛) is the set of ( 𝑚, 𝑛)-shuffles.
   The shuffle product gives 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴) an algebra structure; together with the deconcatenation comultiplica-
tion, 𝐵¯ ( 𝐴) becomes a differential graded bialgebra.

tive spectral sequence 𝐸𝑟 ⇒ 𝐻 converges strongly, then:

a finite range (the bar complex at each genus has bounded cohomological amplitude, determined by the
conformal weights of the finitely many irreducibles). A spectral sequence with 𝐸2 page bounded in a finite
rectangle necessarily converges: all differentials 𝑑𝑟 for 𝑟 exceeding the width of the rectangle are zero.

Theorem I.7.3 (Degeneration at 𝐸2 [10, 176]; [proved]). For special values of central charge:
• 𝑐 = 0: Topological theory, degenerates at 𝐸1 (the bar complex carries no quantum corrections).
• 𝑐 = 26: Critical bosonic string, degenerates at 𝐸2 (by the no-ghost theorem of Frenkel–Garland–
  Zuckerman).
Conjecture I.7.4 (Superstring degeneration; [conjectured]). For 𝑐 = 15 (critical superstring, matter sector),
the bar spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 . This would follow from a ‘‘no-ghost theorem’’ in the superstring
setting, which remains open. Master conjecture parent: Conjecture 34.9.5 (MC5: BV/BRST = bar).

   The filtration on 𝐵¯ (A) by pole order along collision divisors corresponds to the loop expansion: order-0

Remark I.7.6 (Scope and relation to established results). The page-by-page genus correspondence stated
above is a heuristic physical interpretation, not a theorem. What has been proved rigorously in this mono-
graph is the following:
   (i) The Prism Principle (Corollary 12.13.28) establishes that the bar complex decomposes a chiral algebra
       into its operadic spectrum, with genus-0 structure governed by HyCom ↔ Grav Koszul duality and
       higher-genus structure by the Feynman transform of the modular operad {M 𝑔,𝑛 } (Theorem 12.13.25).
  (ii) The genus filtration (Theorem 6.9.12) ensures 𝐷 𝑔2 = 0 (the total corrected differential, Conven-
       tion 8.0.2) at all genera via the modular operad axioms.
 (iii) The Koszul complementarity theorem (Theorem 8.14.12) gives the precise decomposition 𝑄 𝑔 (A) ⊕
       𝑄 𝑔 (A ! )  𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) of quantum corrections at each genus.
What remains conjectural is the identiﬁcation of the spectral sequence page 𝐸𝑟 with genus-( 𝑟 − 1) contributions
speciﬁcally. The rigorous Feynman transform framework organizes all genera simultaneously rather than
page-by-page; making the page-genus dictionary precise would require an explicit comparison between the
pole-order filtration and the genus grading in the Feynman transform, which has not been carried out in
general.

I.7.5   Computational tools
The differentials can be computed via:
   (i) Čech cohomology. Cover M 𝑔,𝑛 by affine opens
  (ii) Dolbeault cohomology. Use 𝜕¯-operator techniques
 (iii) Combinatorial models. Jenkins–Strebel differentials
 (iv) Topological recursion. Eynard–Orantin formalism

Remark J.0.1 (Relationship to §8.18). The genus-graded Koszul duality theory is developed in §8.18. This

J.1    Genus-graded Koszul duality
Theorem J.1.1 (Extended Koszul duality; [proved]). If (A , A ! ) form a genus-0 Koszul dual pair
with central curvature at all genera, then under suitable finiteness and convergence conditions:
                                                                   !

where ℏ tracks the genus.

Proof. This is the content of Theorem 8.18.3 (the canonical version in §8.18), proved via the Prism Principle
(Theorem 12.13.25), strict nilpotence at all genera (Theorem 6.9.12), and the universal extension tower
(Theorem 6.5.7). See the proof there for full details.

Remark J.2.2 (Classical vs chiral Koszulness). The criterion above is classical algebraic Koszulness (BGS [5]).
In the chiral setting, classical Koszulness of the enveloping algebra does not imply chiral Koszulness of the
corresponding vertex algebra, because the chiral bar construction uses all OPE poles (Borcherds locality),
not just the leading term.
    Concrete illustration. The enveloping algebra 𝑈 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) is Koszul in the classical sense: Ext𝑈 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) (𝕜 , 𝕜) = 0

the affine algebra 𝔰𝔩
                    b 2 at level 𝑘 , the OPE of currents has both a simple pole (the structure constants 𝑓𝑐𝑎𝑏 )

including the double pole, so additional cancellations must be verified: specifically, the PBW spectral

(proved in Chapter 20), not a corollary of the classical statement.

J.2.4    Physical interpretation across genera
In physics, genus-graded Koszul duality appears as electric-magnetic duality with genus corrections (abelian
case), open-closed string duality with modular forms (topological strings), holographic duality with genus
expansion (AdS/CFT), mirror symmetry with period integrals (A-model/B-model), and string amplitudes
with genus-graded corrections.

J.2.6    Koszul duality at higher genus: the tower structure
The genus 0 Koszul duality:
                                                 Ω𝐶•(0) (A) ≃ A
extends to all genera by the modular operad structure.
J.2.6.1 The genus 𝑔 statement
For each 𝑔 ≥ 0, there is a duality:
                                                        ( 𝑔)
                                              Ω ( 𝑔 ) 𝐶• (A) ≃ A ( 𝑔 )
where:
• Ω ( 𝑔 ) is the genus 𝑔 cobar construction
• A ( 𝑔 ) is the genus 𝑔 component of A
J.2.6.2 Compatibility
The genus stratification satisfies:
                                                        ( 𝑔)          ( 𝑔 −1)

(boundary/degeneration maps) compatible with:

                                               𝜄 : A ( 𝑔 −1) → A ( 𝑔 )

(restriction maps).
    This gives a tower of Koszul dualities:

                                               Acomplete = lim A ( 𝑔 )

                                                        ( 𝑔)

for 𝜎 ∈ Γ 𝑔 .

J.4.5   Curvature and centrality
Theorem J.4.9 (Curvature must be central; [proved]). Let C
                                                         b be a curved coalgebra with curvature:

                                                         b2
                                                    𝜇0 ∈ C
      b = A ! for some algebra A, then 𝜇0 must be central in the sense:
   If C

                                    𝜇0 commutes with all operations in A
                              b = A!?
J.4. Essential image: when is C                                                                              1591


Proof. We verify centrality directly from the curved 𝐴∞ relations (cf. Positselski [171]).
   The key point is that a curved 𝐴∞ -algebra carries two differentials that must be carefully distinguished:
• The bar differential 𝑑𝐵 on the tensor coalgebra 𝐵¯ (A) = (𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā) , 𝑑𝐵 ), which encodes all the oper-
  ations 𝑚0 , 𝑚1 , 𝑚2 , . . . simultaneously. The condition 𝑑𝐵2 = 0 is equivalent to the full system of curved
  𝐴∞ relations; it holds unconditionally.
• The internal differential 𝑚1 on the algebra A itself. In the curved case, 𝑚12 ≠ 0 in general: 𝑚1 fails to be
  a differential, and the failure is measured by the curvature 𝑚0 .
We now make this precise.
    Step 1. Arity-0 relation (cocycle condition). The curved 𝐴∞ relation at arity 𝑛 = 0 has a single term
( 𝑟, 𝑠, 𝑡 ) = (0, 0, 0), giving 𝑚1 ( 𝑚0 ) = 0. Thus 𝑚0 is a cocycle for 𝑚1 .
    Step 2. Arity-1 relation (curvature identity). At arity 𝑛 = 1, the three terms ( 𝑟, 𝑠, 𝑡 ) with 𝑟 + 𝑠 + 𝑡 = 1
are:

                              (0, 1, 0) : (−1) 0·1+0 𝑚1 ( 𝑚1 ( 𝑎)) = 𝑚12 ( 𝑎) ,
                              (0, 0, 1) : (−1) 0·0+1 𝑚2 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎) = −𝑚2 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎) ,
                              (1, 0, 0) : (−1) 1·0+0 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚0 ) = 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚0 ) .

Setting the sum to zero:

                        𝑚12 ( 𝑎) = 𝑚2 ( 𝑚0 , 𝑎) − 𝑚2 ( 𝑎, 𝑚0 ) = [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎] 𝑚2     for all 𝑎.                (J.1)

This is the curvature identity: 𝑚1 squares not to zero but to the inner derivation [ 𝑚0 , −].
  Step 3. Centrality implies strictness. From (J.1), two regimes emerge:
   (i) Curved (𝑚0 not central): [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎] 𝑚2 ≠ 0 for some 𝑎, so 𝑚12 ≠ 0, and A has no internal differential.
       The bar differential 𝑑𝐵 on 𝐵¯ (A) nonetheless satisfies 𝑑𝐵2 = 0; this is guaranteed by the full system
       of curved 𝐴∞ relations (including the arity-1 relation above), which are equivalent to 𝑑𝐵2 = 0. So the
       bar complex is always a well-defined dg coalgebra, even when the algebra itself is not a dg algebra.
  (ii) Uncurved / strict (𝑚0 central): [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎] 𝑚2 = 0 for all 𝑎, so 𝑚12 = 0 and 𝑚1 is an honest differential.
       The algebra (A , 𝑚1 ) is then a genuine dg algebra.
   Step 4. Examples.
• Heisenberg at level 𝜅 . The curvature is 𝑚0 = −𝜅 · 𝜔, a scalar multiple of the symplectic pairing. Scalars
  commute with everything: [−𝜅𝜔, 𝑎] 𝑚2 = 0 for all 𝑎. So H𝜅 is strict (uncurved) at every level, and 𝑚1 is
  a genuine differential.
• Kac–Moody at level 𝑘 . The curvature is 𝑚0 = ( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) · 𝐶 , where 𝐶 is the Casimir element. By Schur’s
  lemma for the adjoint representation, 𝐶 is central in the enveloping algebra 𝑈 (𝔤): [𝐶, 𝑥 ] = 0 for all
  𝑥 ∈ 𝔤. Hence [ 𝑚0 , 𝑎] 𝑚2 = ( 𝑘 + ℎ∨ ) [𝐶, 𝑎] = 0 for all 𝑎, and 𝔤
                                                                   b𝑘 is strict at every level. At the critical
  level 𝑘 = −ℎ the curvature vanishes entirely (𝑚0 = 0), and the algebra is uncurved in the stronger sense
               ∨

  of having no curvature term at all.
   Step 5. Summary. In the bar construction 𝐵¯ (A), the curvature 𝜇0 is the image of 𝑚0 under the desus-
pension 𝑠 −1 : A → 𝑠 −1 A. The bar condition 𝑑𝐵2 = 0 always holds and encodes all curved 𝐴∞ relations
simultaneously: arity 0 gives Step 1, arity 1 gives Step 2. Centrality of 𝑚0 is the additional condition under
which the internal differential 𝑚1 itself squares to zero, i.e., the algebra is uncurved.
1592                                                      Appendix J. Koszul duality reference tables


Example J.4.10 (Virasoro central charge). The Virasoro algebra provides a third illustration of curvature
centrality. The central extension is determined by the Lie algebra 2-cocycle 121 ( 𝑚3 − 𝑚) 𝛿𝑚+𝑛,0 , so the
central charge 𝑐 is a curvature term. Centrality is immediate: [ 𝑐, 𝐿𝑛 ] = 0 for all 𝑛, so 𝑐 generates 𝑍 (Vir) =
ℂ · 𝑐 . In the bar coalgebra, 𝑐 appears as the curvature element 𝜇0 in the coalgebra differential, and the
curvature identity (J.1) gives 𝑚12 = [ 𝑐, −] = 0: the Virasoro algebra is strict at every value of 𝑐 . This
confirms Theorem J.4.9.

Remark J.4.14 (Non-uniqueness at the strict level). The theorem only guarantees quasi-isomorphism, not
strict isomorphism. Different presentations of the same chiral algebra (e.g., different choices of generators
and relations) give strictly different algebras that are quasi-isomorphic.
    Example. The Heisenberg algebra can be presented as:
• H1 = Free( 𝑎, 𝑎∗ )/( [ 𝑎, 𝑎∗ ] − 1)
• H2 = Free( 𝑥, 𝑝)/( [ 𝑥, 𝑝] − 𝑖 ℏ)
   These are different presentations (different generators), but H1 ≃ H2 as chiral algebras, and both have
the same Koszul dual.
Appendix K


Homotopy transfer

The homotopy transfer theorem transports algebraic structures along quasi-isomorphisms at the cost of
introducing higher operations.

K.1     Historical origins
𝐴∞ algebras were introduced by Stasheff [15] to encode the homotopy-coherent associativity of loop space
multiplication. The operadic viewpoint identifies them as algebras over the homology of the little intervals
operad. For the role of bar-cobar duality in the chiral setting, see Chapter 8.

K.2     The homotopy transfer theorem
Theorem K.2.1 (Homotopy transfer theorem [83, 180]; [proved]). Let (𝑉 , 𝑑𝑉 ) and (𝑊 , 𝑑𝑊 ) be
chain complexes with:
   (i) A chain map 𝑝 : 𝑉 → 𝑊 (projection).
  (ii) A chain map 𝜄 : 𝑊 → 𝑉 (inclusion).
 (iii) A chain homotopy ℎ : 𝑉 → 𝑉 [−1] satisfying id𝑉 − 𝜄 𝑝 = 𝑑𝑉 ℎ + ℎ𝑑𝑉 .
 (iv) The side conditions (compatibility of ℎ with 𝑝, 𝜄 ): 𝑝𝜄 = id𝑊 , ℎ𝜄 = 0, 𝑝ℎ = 0, ℎ2 = 0.
Such data is called a strong deformation retract (SDR).
   If 𝑉 carries a P∞ -algebra structure (for P a Koszul operad), then 𝑊 inherits a P∞ -algebra structure
such that 𝑝 and 𝜄 extend to ∞-quasi-isomorphisms of P∞ -algebras.

Proof. The transferred structure on 𝑊 is constructed via the tensor trick ([83] §10.3). For an A∞ -algebra
structure on 𝑉 with operations 𝑚𝑛 : 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑛 → 𝑉 , define 𝑇𝑛 : 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑛 → 𝑉 recursively by:

                                              𝑚𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ ℎ 𝑇𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) .
                                         ∑︁
                            𝑇𝑛 = 𝑚𝑛 +
                                             𝑟 + 𝑠 +𝑡 =𝑛
                                                𝑠 <𝑛

This converges since 𝑇𝑠 with 𝑠 < 𝑛 is already defined and ℎ absorbs the degree. The transferred operations
are 𝑚˜ 𝑛 := 𝑝 ◦ 𝑇𝑛 ◦ 𝜄 ⊗ 𝑛 . Explicitly:

                       𝑚˜ 1 = 𝑝 𝑑𝑉 𝜄 = 𝑑𝑊 ,
                       𝑚˜ 2 = 𝑝 𝑚2 𝜄 ⊗2 ,
                       𝑚˜ 3 = 𝑝 𝑚3 𝜄 ⊗3 + 𝑝 𝑚2 ( ℎ𝑚2 ⊗ id) 𝜄 ⊗3 + 𝑝 𝑚2 (id ⊗ ℎ𝑚2 ) 𝜄 ⊗3 .

   Veriﬁcation of A∞ -relations. The A∞ -relation at arity 𝑛 for {𝑚˜ 𝑘 } requires:

                                     (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝑚˜ 𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝑚˜ 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0.                (K.1)
                                ∑︁
                               𝑟 + 𝑠 +𝑡 =𝑛

1596                                                                        Appendix K. Homotopy transfer


Substituting 𝑚˜ 𝑘 = 𝑝 ◦ 𝑇𝑘 ◦ 𝜄 ⊗ 𝑘 and using the SDR identity 𝜄 𝑝 = id𝑉 −( 𝑑𝑉 ℎ + ℎ𝑑𝑉 ), each internal
composition 𝜄 𝑝 between an outer 𝑇𝑟 +1+𝑡 and inner 𝑇𝑠 decomposes as:
• a term id𝑉 , which together with the A∞ -relations for { 𝑚𝑘 } gives cancelling contributions;
• a term − 𝑑𝑉 ℎ − ℎ𝑑𝑉 , which telescopes by the side conditions ℎ2 = 0, 𝑝ℎ = 0, ℎ𝜄 = 0.
Concretely, the terms involving id𝑉 reassemble into 𝑝 ◦ ( A∞ relation for { 𝑚𝑘 }) ◦ 𝜄 ⊗ 𝑛 = 0, while the terms
involving 𝑑𝑉 ℎ + ℎ𝑑𝑉 cancel pairwise: ℎ2 = 0 prevents double homotopy insertions, and 𝑝ℎ = ℎ𝜄 = 0
kill boundary terms. Thus {𝑚˜ 𝑛 } satisfies the A∞ -relations.
    The maps 𝑝 and 𝜄 extend to ∞-morphisms 𝑝˜𝑛 and 𝜄˜𝑛 by the same tree formula with 𝑝 (resp. 𝜄 ) at the
root (resp. leaves), and the composite 𝑝˜ ◦ 𝜄˜ = id𝑊 by 𝑝𝜄 = id𝑊 , while 𝜄˜ ◦ 𝑝˜ ∼ id𝑉 via the homotopy built
from ℎ.

Remark K.3.3 (Tree-level only). A fundamental feature of the homotopy transfer theorem is that only
tree-level graphs contribute: the sum in Theorem K.3.2 runs over trees (acyclic connected graphs), never
over graphs with loops. This is because the three side conditions ℎ2 = 0, 𝑝ℎ = 0, and ℎ𝜄 = 0 together
ensure that any graph with a cycle vanishes: ℎ2 = 0 kills paths with consecutive homotopies, 𝑝ℎ = 0 kills
graphs where ℎ appears at the output edge, and ℎ𝜄 = 0 kills graphs where ℎ appears at an input edge. In
the chiral algebra setting, this means the transferred operations are algebraic (finite sums), not analytic, and
no renormalization issues arise.

K.4      Applications to minimal models
Deﬁnition K.4.1 (Minimal model). A minimal model of a dg-algebra 𝐴 is an A∞ -algebra 𝑀 with:
   (i) 𝑀 has zero differential: 𝑚1 = 0.
                                           ∼
  (ii) There is an A∞ -quasi-isomorphism 𝑀 −
                                           → 𝐴.
A minimal model is unique up to A∞ -isomorphism.
Theorem K.4.2 (Existence of minimal models [180]; [proved]). Every A∞ -algebra over a field admits
a minimal model. Explicitly, if 𝐴 is an A∞ -algebra:
   (i) Take 𝑀 = 𝐻∗ ( 𝐴) as a graded vector space.
  (ii) Choose an SDR ( 𝐴, 𝐻∗ ( 𝐴) , 𝑝, 𝜄, ℎ).
 (iii) Apply the homotopy transfer theorem to get { 𝑚𝑛 }𝑛 ≥2 on 𝑀 .
 (iv) The resulting ( 𝑀 , 0, 𝑚2 , 𝑚3 , . . .) is the minimal model.
Corollary K.4.3 (Formality [7, 35]; [proved]). An A∞ -algebra 𝐴 is formal if its minimal model has
𝑚𝑛 = 0 for all 𝑛 ≥ 3, i.e., the minimal model is a graded associative algebra with trivial differential and no
higher operations.
    Equivalently, 𝐴 is formal if 𝐴 ≃ 𝐻∗ ( 𝐴) as A∞ -algebras, where 𝐻∗ ( 𝐴) has the trivial A∞ -structure from
its product.
Example K.4.4 (Minimal model of de Rham complex). For 𝑋 = 𝑆 1 (circle), the de Rham complex is:

   (i) 𝑀 = 𝑘 · 1 ⊕ 𝑘 · 𝑥 with |1| = 0, | 𝑥 | = 1.

 (iii) 𝑚𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 3 (the circle is formal).
Application K.4.5 (Minimal model for chiral algebras). For a chiral algebra A, the homotopy transfer
theorem provides:
   (i) A minimal A∞ -chiral structure on 𝐻∗ch (A).
  (ii) The higher operations { 𝑚𝑛 }𝑛 ≥3 encode obstructions to formality.
 (iii) For Koszul chiral algebras, the minimal model simplifies (higher operations vanish).

Theorem K.4.6 (Homotopy transfer for operadic algebras [83]; [proved]). Let P be a Koszul
operad and ( 𝐴,𝑊 , 𝑝, 𝜄, ℎ) an SDR with 𝐴 a P-algebra. The transferred P∞ -structure on 𝑊 satisfies:
   (i) The P∞ -relations hold strictly (not just up to homotopy).
  (ii) The maps 𝜄 and 𝑝 extend to ∞-morphisms.
 (iii) If 𝐴 is already P∞ (not just P), the transfer still works.

K.6     Applications to chiral algebras
Theorem K.6.1 (Chiral homotopy transfer; [proved]). Let A be an E1 -chiral algebra on a curve 𝑋
and suppose we have an SDR of the underlying D-module:

                                          (A , 𝐻 , 𝑝, 𝜄, ℎ)   with 𝐻 = 𝐻∗ch (A) .

Then:
   (i) 𝐻 inherits an A∞ -chiral algebra structure.
  (ii) The higher operations { 𝑚𝑛ch }𝑛 ≥3 are ‘‘Massey products’’ for the chiral structure.
 (iii) If A is Koszul, then 𝑚𝑛ch = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 3.

Proof. We apply the general homotopy transfer theorem (Theorem K.2.1) to the E1 -chiral operad.
   Step 1 (D-module compatibility). Since A is a chiral algebra, it carries a D 𝑋 -module structure. The SDR
maps ( 𝑝, 𝜄, ℎ) must be morphisms of D 𝑋 -modules (i.e., commute with the action of D 𝑋 ). This holds
because chiral homology 𝐻 = 𝐻∗ch (A) is defined as a derived functor in the category of D 𝑋 -modules,
K.6. Applications to chiral algebras                                                                           1601


so 𝑝 and 𝜄 are automatically D 𝑋 -linear, and ℎ can be chosen D 𝑋 -linearly by the splitting argument of
Lemma K.2.3(i) applied within the D 𝑋 -module category (which is abelian with enough projectives over a
smooth curve 𝑋 ).
    Step 2 (Transferred binary operation). The transferred product is 𝑚˜ 2 = 𝑝 ◦ 𝜇ch ◦ ( 𝜄 ⊗ 𝜄), exactly as in
Construction K.3.1. Since 𝜇ch is a chiral product (defined via the 𝑗∗ 𝑗 ∗ functor on 𝑋 × 𝑋 ), 𝑚˜ 2 inherits
D 𝑋 -linearity from Step 1.
    Step 3 (Higher operations via trees). The transferred operations 𝑚˜ 𝑛ch for 𝑛 ≥ 3 are sums over planar
rooted trees with 𝑛 leaves (as in Construction K.3.1), where each internal edge contributes a factor of ℎ and
each internal vertex contributes the chiral product 𝜇ch . Since only tree-level graphs contribute (no loops;
cf. Remark K.3.3), each 𝑚˜ 𝑛ch is a finite sum.
    Step 4 (A∞ -relations). The transferred operations { 𝑚˜ 𝑛ch } satisfy the A∞ -relations by the same algebraic
argument as in the general theorem: the identity 𝑟 + 𝑠+𝑡 =𝑛 (−1) 𝑟 𝑠+𝑡 𝑚˜ 𝑟 +1+𝑡 (id⊗ 𝑟 ⊗ 𝑚˜ 𝑠 ⊗ id⊗ 𝑡 ) = 0 follows
                                                   P
from substituting the tree formulas and using the E1 -relations on A together with the SDR identities
𝑝𝜄 = id, id − 𝜄 𝑝 = 𝑑ℎ + ℎ𝑑 , ℎ2 = 0.
    Koszulness (iii). If A is Koszul, the bar spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 with 𝐸∞ concentrated on
the Koszul line 𝑞 = 0 (Proposition I.3.4). This means Ext A ( 𝑘, 𝑘 ) = 0 for 𝑞 ≠ 0: the bar resolution is
                                                                 𝑝,𝑞

minimal. One may therefore choose the SDR for 𝐵¯ (A) → 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ (A)) compatible with the bigrading,
so that the homotopy ℎ preserves bar degree and shifts internal degree. Every tree contributing to 𝑚˜ 𝑛ch for
𝑛 ≥ 3 would produce an operation of bar-degree shift incompatible with the Koszul line concentration,
forcing 𝑚˜ 𝑛ch = 0. Equivalently, for a minimal resolution all Massey products vanish.

       𝑘 ≠ −ℎ∨ ).

K.7      Homotopy transfer and the main theorems
The apparatus of this appendix is not auxiliary to the main theory; it is the mechanism by which classical
Koszul duality acquires quantum corrections. We make this precise.

K.7.1    The bar-cobar counit as HTT output
Theorem K.7.1 (Bar-cobar inversion via homotopy transfer; [proved]). Let A be a chiral Koszul
algebra on a smooth curve 𝑋 . The bar-cobar counit
                                           𝜓 : Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) → A
of Theorem 9.1.39 is the canonical A∞ -quasi-isomorphism produced by the homotopy transfer theorem
(Theorem K.2.1), applied to the SDR
                                  Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) , A , 𝜓 , 𝜄counit , ℎHodge
                                                                         

where 𝜄counit is the canonical inclusion and ℎHodge is the contracting homotopy from the Hodge decompo-
sition of Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) relative to the bar filtration.
                                                                                             !
Proof. By construction, the cobar complex Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) is the cofree chiral algebra on 𝑠 A with differential
𝑑cobar = 𝑑coop + 𝑑tw , where 𝑑tw encodes the twisting morphism 𝜏 : 𝐵¯ (A) → A.
    Step 1 (SDR from bar filtration). The bar filtration 𝐹𝑝 Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) gives a spectral sequence with 𝐸1 =
                                                                                                         𝑝,𝑞

𝐻 𝑞 (gr 𝐹𝑝 Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A))). By Koszulness, 𝐸1 is concentrated on 𝑞 = 0 (Proposition I.3.4). The 𝐸1 -degeneration
produces an SDR: the projection 𝜓 to 𝐸∞  A and the inclusion 𝜄 from A back to the cobar complex,
with contracting homotopy ℎ lowering the 𝑞 -degree. The side conditions 𝜓 𝜄 = id, ℎ2 = 0, 𝜓 ℎ = 0, ℎ𝜄 = 0
follow from the bigrading.
    Step 2 (HTT produces the same map). Applying Theorem K.2.1 to the strict E1 -chiral algebra structure
on Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) and the SDR from Step 1 produces transferred operations {𝑚˜ 𝑛 }𝑛 ≥2 on A and an A∞ -quasi-
isomorphism 𝑓∞ : A → Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)). The component 𝑓1 = 𝜄 and the binary product 𝑚˜ 2 = 𝜓 ◦ 𝜇 ◦ ( 𝜄 ⊗ 𝜄) =
𝜇 A (the original product on A, since 𝜓 𝜄 = id).
    Step 3 (Koszulness forces vanishing). For 𝑛 ≥ 3, each tree 𝑇 contributing to 𝑚˜ 𝑛 (Construction K.3.1)
inserts at least one homotopy ℎ on an internal edge. Since ℎ lowers the filtration degree by 1 and the Koszul-
line concentration forces all non-trivial cohomology to live on 𝑞 = 0, the composition 𝜓 ◦ (tree) ◦ 𝜄 ⊗ 𝑛
vanishes: the output lives in 𝑞 < 0, which is empty. Therefore 𝑚˜ 𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 3, and 𝑓∞ = 𝜓 is a strict
quasi-isomorphism of dg algebras, not merely of A∞ -algebras.
    This is the chain-level content of the bar-cobar inversion (Theorem 9.1.39): on the Koszul locus, the bar-
cobar counit is the HTT quasi-isomorphism, and Koszulness is the vanishing of all Massey products.
Remark K.7.2 (Koszulness as formality). The preceding proof identifies three equivalent conditions (cf.
Remark 8.17.6):
   (i) A is chiral Koszul (bar spectral sequence degenerates at 𝐸2 , Koszul-line concentration).
  (ii) The transferred A∞ -structure on 𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ (A)) is formal: 𝑚˜ 𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 3.
 (iii) The bar-cobar counit 𝜓 is a strict quasi-isomorphism (not merely A∞ ).
The equivalence (i) ⇔ (ii) is the homotopy-algebraic meaning of Koszulness: a Koszul algebra is one whose
derived structure contains no hidden higher information beyond the binary product. Condition (iii) is the
geometric meaning: the configuration space integrals computing 𝜓 collapse to residue extraction alone,
with no contributions from higher-codimension boundary strata.

Remark K.7.4 (Feynman diagrams as transferred operations). Proposition K.7.3 establishes the following
dictionary between the algebraic HTT and the physical Feynman diagram expansion:
1604                                                                      Appendix K. Homotopy transfer


               HTT (algebraic)                  ←→ Feynman (geometric)
               Planar rooted tree 𝑇         ←→ Tree-level Feynman diagram
               Internal edge of 𝑇           ←→ Propagator insertion 𝜔𝑖𝑗
               Vertex of valence 𝑘          ←→ 𝑘 -valent interaction vertex (OPE)
               Homotopy ℎ                   ←→ Integration over loop momentum (fiber)
               SDR projection 𝑝             ←→ External state projection
               Transferred 𝑚˜ 𝑛             ←→ 𝑛-point tree-level amplitude
               Massey product 𝑚˜ 3 ≠ 0      ←→ Non-trivial 3-point function
               Koszulness (𝑚˜ 𝑛 = 0, 𝑛 ≥ 3) ←→ Free field theory (Gaussian)

The identification ‘‘Koszulness = free theory’’ has precise content: for a Koszul chiral algebra, the bar
complex is a minimal resolution, all Massey products vanish, and the Feynman expansion truncates at tree
level with only 2-valent vertices (propagators). Non-Koszul algebras have non-trivial Massey products,
corresponding to genuine higher-point interactions that cannot be reduced to pairwise propagation.

Remark K.7.6 (Higher genus: moduli cohomology as transferred operations). At genus 𝑔 ≥ 2, the bar
complex 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A) is a family over M 𝑔 with fiberwise differential 𝑑fib satisfying 𝐷 2𝑔 = 0 (Theorem 8.7.3).
The HTT applied fiberwise produces a curved A∞ -algebra over M 𝑔 whose operations are sections of
bundles over moduli space. The key identification is:
                                       ( 𝑔)
   The 𝑛-ary transferred operation 𝑚˜ 𝑛 is a section of

                                    H 𝑜𝑚 (A ⊠𝑛 , A) ⊗ 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 , ℚ) .

The dependence on 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔,𝑛 ) is the ‘‘quantum correction’’ from the genus- 𝑔 moduli geometry.
This gives a homotopy-algebraic interpretation of Theorem C (Deformation-Obstruction Complemen-
tarity, Theorem 8.14.12): the quantum obstruction 𝑄 𝑔 (A) and the dual obstruction 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) together
span 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) because they are the complementary components of the transferred A∞ -structure on
𝐻 ∗ ( 𝐵¯ ( 𝑔 ) (A)), restricted to the center and projected along the Koszul line and its complement. The com-
plementarity 𝑄 𝑔 (A) + 𝑄 𝑔 (A ! ) = 𝐻 ∗ (M 𝑔 , 𝑍 (A)) is the statement that the full transferred structure
exhausts the moduli cohomology, with nothing left over.
    This interpretation elevates Theorem C from a numerical identity to a structural statement: the bar-
cobar machine, viewed through HTT, decomposes moduli-space cohomology into the piece controlled by
A and the piece controlled by A ! , with the Koszul duality functor as the sorting mechanism.
Remark K.7.7 (Physical content: renormalization vs. homotopy transfer). There is a profound analogy
between homotopy transfer and perturbative renormalization in quantum field theory, which becomes an
identification in the chiral algebra setting:
   (i) Tree-level HTT = classical field theory. The tree formula (Theorem K.3.2) sums over tree-level
       Feynman diagrams. The condition ℎ2 = 0 in the SDR (the ‘‘no-loop’’ condition from Remark K.3.3)
       ensures that only trees contribute, not graphs with loops. This is the algebraic counterpart of the
       statement that classical field theory is determined by its tree-level amplitudes.
  (ii) Genus- 𝑔 curvature = 𝑔 -loop quantum corrections. The curvature 𝜅 (A) · 𝜔 𝑔 at genus 𝑔 is the
       analogue of the 𝑔 -loop counterterm in perturbative renormalization. The perturbation lemma that
       extends HTT to the curved setting (Proposition K.7.5) corresponds to absorbing the counterterm
       into the effective action, order by order in ℏ ∼ 𝜅 (A).
 (iii) Koszulness = absence of anomalies. A Koszul chiral algebra has 𝑚˜ 𝑛 = 0 for 𝑛 ≥ 3
       (Theorem K.6.1(iii)), meaning no higher-point interactions are generated by integrating
       out degrees of freedom. In physics, this is the statement that the theory is anomaly-free at the level of
       OPE structure: the classical OPE data determine the quantum theory completely, with no need for
       higher-order counterterms. The genus- 𝑔 curvature 𝜅 (A) is the only quantum correction, and it is
       universal (Theorem 8.13.16).
Appendix L


Dual abstract-concrete methodology

Every major result is established via two complementary approaches: an abstract ∞-categorical proof using
universal properties and functorial characterizations, and a concrete geometric proof using explicit chain-
level constructions.

L.1     Philosophy and benefits
Convention L.1.1 (Dual proof methodology). For fundamental theorems in derived algebra and geometry,
we provide two proofs:
   (i) an abstract proof establishing existence, uniqueness, and functoriality through categorical methods;
  (ii) a concrete proof providing explicit formulas and computations.
The agreement of both proofs validates the constructions.
Remark L.1.2 (Dual proofs). The dual methodology serves multiple purposes.
    Validation: Agreement between abstract and concrete approaches confirms correctness. Errors in one
approach are often caught by the other.
    Computation: Abstract proofs establish what exists; concrete proofs show how to compute it. For
applications, explicit formulas are essential.
    Generalization: Abstract proofs often generalize more directly (to derived settings, higher categories,
etc.), while concrete proofs may reveal special structures visible only with explicit formulas.
    Understanding: Different readers approach mathematics differently. Some prefer categorical elegance;
others prefer explicit calculations. Providing both serves the full mathematical community.
Example L.1.3 (Duality of approaches). Consider proving that the bar-cobar adjunction is an equivalence:
    Abstract. In a pro-nilpotent symmetric monoidal ∞-category, the bar and cobar functors are adjoint
equivalences by the general theory of Koszul duality for operads (Francis–Gaitsgory, Lurie).
    Concrete. The bar-cobar complex has an explicit filtration by total degree. The associated spectral se-
quence has acyclic 𝐸1 -page (via the contracting homotopy ℎ [ 𝑎1 | · · · | 𝑎𝑛 ] = [1| 𝑎1 | · · · | 𝑎𝑛 ]). Convergence
follows from bounded-below filtration.
    Both proofs establish the same theorem; together they provide both the ‘‘why’’ (categorical necessity)
and the ‘‘how’’ (explicit acyclicity argument).

L.2      Key instances: bar-cobar and Riemann–Hilbert
L.2.1    Bar-cobar equivalence
Theorem L.2.1 (Abstract bar-cobar equivalence [43, 130]; [proved]). In the ∞-category

Abstract proof. The chiral tensor structure on D-Mod (Ran( 𝑋 )) is pro-nilpotent in the sense of Francis–

L.2.3    ∞-operads
Deﬁnition L.2.5 (∞-operad). An ∞-operad is a functor O ⊗ → Fin∗ satisfying the Segal conditions (Lurie,
HA Definition 2.1.1.10), where Fin∗ is the category of pointed finite sets. A symmetric monoidal ∞-category
is the special case where O ⊗ → Fin∗ is additionally a coCartesian fibration; this is strictly more restrictive
than the general notion of ∞-operad.
Theorem L.2.6 (Geometric models for ∞-operads; [proved]). The geometric bar and cobar con-
structions provide explicit models for the ∞-operadic bar-cobar theory:
   (i) The bar complex 𝐵¯ geom (A) is a model for the ∞-categorical bar construction 𝐵¯ ∞ (A).
  (ii) The cobar complex Ωgeom (C) is a model for the ∞-categorical cobar construction Ω∞ (C).
 (iii) Quasi-isomorphisms of geometric models correspond to equivalences of ∞-categorical objects.

Proof. The key is that the geometric constructions are ‘‘strictly’’ models for the derived constructions:
   For bar. The geometric bar complex 𝐵¯ geom (A) is computed as sections of a factorization algebra on
configuration spaces. By factorization homology (Ayala–Francis), this computes the ∞-categorical tensor
product:                                       ∫
                                     geom
                                  𝐵¯ 𝑛 (A) =
                                                                      !
                                                          A ⊠ 𝑛 = A ⊗∞ 𝑛
                                                     FM𝑛 ( 𝑋 )
1610                                         Appendix L. Dual abstract-concrete methodology


where ⊗∞! is the derived !-tensor product of factorization D-modules.

   For cobar. Similarly, the distributional cobar complex computes the ∞-categorical cofree coalgebra on
the suspended cogenerators.

Corollary L.2.7 (Derived Koszulness [83]; [proved]). A chiral algebra A is derived Koszul if:

                                            Ω∞ ( 𝐵¯ ∞ (A)) ≃ A

in the ∞-category of E1 -chiral algebras.

Proof. The concrete bar-cobar quasi-isomorphism (Theorem L.2.2) establishes derived Koszulness for all
Koszul E1 -chiral algebras.

where 𝐶𝑖𝑗𝑘 is the OPE coefficient at the simple pole. The residue extracts the ( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) −1 term of the OPE,
which contributes when:

(simple pole condition). Higher-order poles ( ℎ𝑖 + ℎ𝑗 − ℎ𝑘 > 1) contribute to higher-order terms in the

Appendix N


The combinatorial frontier of chiral bar
cohomology

This appendix consolidates all known enumerative data arising from the chiral bar-cobar theory and orga-
nizes the computational frontier. The sequences, generating functions, and numerical invariants below are
the shadow-level (S-level) output of the algebraic machinery developed in Parts 1–3; each entry records the
theorem or conjecture from which it derives, its current verification status, and the obstruction to further
computation.
Principle. For a Koszul chiral algebra A, the bar cohomology dimensions dim 𝐻 𝑛 ( B̄(A)) coincide with the
Hilbert function of the Koszul dual A ! (Corollary 9.1.36). These dimensions are the central enumerative
invariants of the theory. Their generating functions encode, in compact form, the full structure of the bar
complex: growth rates, analytic singularities, and (conjecturally) the spectral data of a finite-rank transfer
operator.

Remark N.1.1 (Reading the table). The zeroth column (𝑛 = 0) is always 1: the augmentation A → ℂ
contributes a one-dimensional class in bar degree zero. The first column (𝑛 = 1) equals dim A [1] , the
dimension of the weight-1 augmentation ideal. For Kac–Moody algebras 𝔤         b𝑘 , this is dim 𝔤; for the Virasoro
algebra, it is 1 (the single generator 𝑇 ); for W3 , it is 2 (generators 𝑇 and 𝑊 ).
   The data is level-independent. For every algebra in the table, the bar cohomology dimensions are in-
dependent of the level 𝑘 (or central charge 𝑐 ) at generic values. This is a deep consequence of the PBW
spectral sequence structure: the 𝐸1 page is a Lie algebra cohomology computation that depends only on
the underlying finite-dimensional data (𝔤, dim 𝔤, ℎ∨ ), not on the level (this follows from the PBW spectral
sequence: at generic level the 𝐸2 page is level-independent, and concentration at 𝐸2 gives the result; see
Theorem 34.9.1). The level enters only through the curvature term 𝜔 𝑔 at genus 𝑔 ≥ 1, which affects the
genus expansion (Theorem 8.13.16) but not the bar cohomology dimensions themselves.

 (iii) Virasoro at low degree. The first few Virasoro bar cohomology dimensions (1, 2, 5, 12, 30) begin with

       Motzkin-difference count.

expansion 𝑔 𝐹𝑔 (A) 𝑥 2 𝑔 for all finite 𝜅 (Proposition 26.4.5).

• dim 𝐻 0 = 1 (connected);
• dim 𝐻 1 = 𝑛2 (Arnold generators 𝜂𝑖𝑗 );

The generating functions of bar cohomology dimensions fall into a strict hierarchy of algebraic complexity.
This hierarchy reflects the interaction structure of the underlying chiral algebra.

        {1, . . . , 𝑛 + 3}; restricted lattice paths with three step types and a non-touching constraint.

N.8.3    Structural questions
LR-1. Intrinsic construction of the Kodaira–Spencer operator. Conjecture 27.17.23 predicts a rank-(rank 𝔤 +
      1) transfer operator KS𝔤 whose characteristic polynomial recovers the discriminant. An intrinsic
      construction (from the Casimir operators on the bar complex, without first computing the Hilbert
      series) would reduce the bar cohomology computation to a finite-dimensional eigenvalue problem.
LR-2. Uniformization of the algebraic hierarchy. Is there a structural reason why rank-1 algebras have
      algebraic (degree 2) bar GFs while rank-2 algebras have rational GFs? A possible framework: the
      Picard–Fuchs D-module of the bar GF has holonomic rank rank 𝔤 + 1; for rank 1 this is a second-
      order Fuchsian ODE (with algebraic solutions), while for rank 2 it is third-order (and the solution
      space may contain only rational functions if the monodromy is trivial).
LR-3. Non-simply-laced discriminant structure. For non-simply-laced 𝔤, the DS reduction 𝔤    b𝑘 ↠ W 𝑘 (𝔤)
      involves the dual Coxeter number ℎ∨ ≠ ℎ. The discriminant should     √ reflect this discrepancy. For
      𝐵2 = 𝔰𝔭4 : ℎ = 4, ℎ∨ = 3, dim = 10. Does Δ𝔰𝔭4 factor over ℚ( 𝑑 ) for some discriminant 𝑑
      involving both ℎ and ℎ∨ ?
LR-4. Periodicity and the Coxeter number. The Kac–Moody periodicity theorem gives period 2ℎ for 𝔰𝔩      b2
      (the 𝐸2 -page has period 4 in conformal weight). Whether this periodicity manifests as a functional
      equation for the bar GF –- of the form 𝑃 ( 𝑥 ) = rational + 𝑥 2ℎ 𝑃 ( 𝑥 ), analogous to a modular
      relation –- is unknown.
LR-5. 𝑊∞ and inﬁnite-rank limits. The MC4 tower W𝑁 as 𝑁 → ∞ should converge to 𝑊1+∞ . The
      bar cohomology dimensions dim(W𝑁! )𝑛 form a two-parameter array ( 𝑁 , 𝑛). Is there a closed-
      form bivariate generating function 𝑁 ,𝑛 dim(W𝑁! )𝑛 𝑡 𝑁 𝑥 𝑛 ? For fixed 𝑛, the 𝑁 -dependence is
                                           P
      polynomial (the number of generators grows linearly in 𝑁 ), so the bivariate GF should be rational
      in 𝑡 .

N.9       Computational verification results
We record the results of systematic computational verification of the bar cohomology data. The two methods
are direct rank computation of the chiral bracket differential (with Orlik–Solomon forms), and algebraic
generating function fitting (rational and holonomic recurrence detection). A finite rank computation
concerns the displayed finite complex; it does not by itself identify that complex with a geometric bar
construction.

property that bar cohomology is concentrated in low degrees.
Remark N.9.1 (CE vs. chiral: the string correction). The difference rkchiral − rkCE = 63 − 56 = 7 at degree 3
measures the string correction to the bar differential: seven additional directions in 𝐵¯ 2 become coboundaries
when the full configuration-space geometry is incorporated. This difference is entirely due to the non-trivial
OS algebra structure at degree ≥ 3, where the Arnold relations begin to impose constraints.
   The CE bracket is the 𝐸0 page of the PBW spectral sequence (ignoring the conformal weight grading),
while the chiral bracket incorporates the full Borcherds OPE data. The string correction measures the
contribution of the higher spectral sequence differentials at the level of total rank.

   Computational consequence. The near-rationality means that automated GF solvers applied to Virasoro
data with ≤ 8 terms will find a spurious rational fit. This does not occur with ≥ 9 terms, where the
verification step detects the failure. The lesson is general: any constant-coeﬃcient recurrence hypothesis for
an algebraic sequence must be validated against suﬃciently many terms –- specifically, beyond the Padé
horizon.

N.9.3     GF type classification
The bar cohomology generating functions fall into a hierarchy of algebraic complexity. Automated analysis
confirms and refines the classification of §N.3:

               Algebra     GF type              Recurrence type                       Status

               H, 𝜓        transcendental       none (modular)                        proved
               𝑏𝑐          rational              𝑎𝑛 = 2 𝑎𝑛−1 + 1                      proved
               𝛽𝛾          algebraic (deg 2)    holonomic (order 2, poly deg 1)       proved
               𝔰𝔩
               b2          algebraic (deg 2)    holonomic (order 2, poly deg 1)       proved
               Vir𝑐        algebraic (deg 2)    holonomic (order 2, poly deg 1)       proved
               𝔰𝔩
               b3          rational (conj.)     constant (depth 3)                    conjectured
               W3          rational (conj.)     constant (depth 3)                    conjectured
               𝑌 (𝔰𝔩 2 )   rational (conj.)     constant (depth 2)                    conjectured

     The proved algebras in the𝔰𝔩 2 family all have holonomic recurrences –- linear recurrences with polynomial
coefficients in 𝑛 –- reflecting the algebraic degree 2 of their generating functions. The conjectured algebras
in the 𝔰𝔩 3 family have constant-coefficient recurrences, reflecting rationality.
     The algebraic–rational transition. The qualitative shift from algebraic (degree 2) to rational when
passing from rank 1 (𝔰𝔩 2 ) to rank 2 (𝔰𝔩 3 ) is the central mystery of the combinatorial frontier. If the rank-
plus-one pattern (§N.3.4) holds, then 𝔰𝔩       b 𝑁 for all 𝑁 ≥ 3 should have rational bar GFs, with the 𝔰𝔩 2 family
being the sole algebraic exception. The PBW spectral sequence provides a heuristic: for rank 1, the single
Casimir operator gives a depth-2 recurrence with polynomial coefficients (because the invariant subalgebra
𝑆 ∗ (𝔤[ 𝑡 −1 ] 𝑡 −1 ) 𝔤 has a single generator); for rank ≥ 2, the multiple Casimir operators interact to produce a
deeper recurrence whose polynomial coefficients may ‘‘linearize’’ (become constant) due to cancellations
among the Casimir eigenvalues on different weight spaces.

jectured recurrence 𝑎𝑘 = 4 𝑎𝑘 −1 − 2 𝑎𝑘 −2 − 𝑎𝑘 −3 (from the rational GF 𝑃 ( 𝑥 ) = 𝑥 (2 − 3 𝑥 )/((1 − 𝑥 ) (1 −
3 𝑥 − 𝑥 2 )); see §N.9.6) gives 171, 564, 1862, 6149, . . .; this would be a new entry. Similarly, the 𝔰𝔩
                                                                                                       b 3 sequence
8, 36, 204, . . . (if confirmed through higher degrees) would be new.
   A naturality observation. The known bar cohomology sequences –- partition numbers, Riordan num-
bers, Motzkin numbers, central Delannoy numbers –- all belong to the class of lattice path counts (with
varying step sets and boundary conditions). This is not a coincidence: the PBW spectral sequence, which
computes bar cohomology via iterated Lie algebra cohomology, can be reformulated as a lattice path enu-
meration problem, where each conformal weight level corresponds to a horizontal coordinate and each
cohomological degree to a vertical coordinate. The step set is determined by the OPE singularity structure:
simple poles give rise to ‘‘up’’ and ‘‘down’’ steps, higher-order poles to ‘‘flat’’ steps, and the boundary
condition (non-negativity of height) reflects the unitarity of the underlying vertex algebra. A precise for-
mulation of this lattice-path / bar-cohomology correspondence, extending the Motzkin path model of
Theorem 27.17.45 to all Koszul chiral algebras, would constitute a significant structural advance.
Appendix O


Comparison of existence paradigms for Koszul
duals

                                                    Abstract

            Strict finite-type existence theorems for Koszul duals and the completion construction of Ap-
        pendix P have different hypotheses. This appendix compares them with quadratic and curved existence
        criteria. No single necessary-and-sufficient condition for all these constructions is asserted.


O.1      The existence problem
O.1.1    Motivation and setup
Question O.1.1 (Central question). Given a chiral algebra A on 𝑋 , when does there exist a Koszul dual
coalgebra A ! such that:
   (i) The bar construction resolves the dual coalgebra: 𝐵¯ (A) −
                                                                     ∼
                                                                → A!
  (ii) The cobar of the bar recovers A: Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −
                                                    ∼
                                                    →A
 (iii) The module and comodule categories are equivalent (with completeness/conilpotence conditions):

                                         Modcompl (A) ≃ CoModconil (A ! )

When conditions (1)–(3) hold, the Koszul dual algebra is obtained by linear dualization: (A ! ) ∨ = 𝐵¯ (A) ∨ .

O.1.2     Preliminary definitions
Deﬁnition O.1.2 (Koszul dual –- quadratic case (Priddy)). Let A = 𝑇D (𝑉 )/( 𝑅) be a quadratic chiral
algebra, where 𝑉 is a graded D 𝑋 -module of generators and 𝑅 ⊆ 𝑉 ⊗ D 𝑉 is a subspace of quadratic
relations. The Koszul dual of A is the quadratic coalgebra

                                           A ! ↩→ Cofree D ( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ ) ,

defined as the maximal sub-coalgebra of Cofree D ( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ ) cogenerated by 𝑠𝑅⊥ , where:
• 𝑉 ∗ = Hom D (𝑉 , D 𝑋 ) is the D-linear dual,
• 𝑅⊥ = { 𝑓 ∈ (𝑉 ∗ ) ⊗2 : ⟨ 𝑓 , 𝑟 ⟩ = 0 for all 𝑟 ∈ 𝑅 } is the annihilator of 𝑅 under the natural pairing
  (𝑉 ∗ ) ⊗2 ⊗ 𝑉 ⊗2 → ℂ,
• 𝑠 denotes the cohomological suspension (degree shift by +1).
This definition is intrinsic: A ! is constructed directly from the presentation (𝑉 , 𝑅) without reference to
the bar construction or any resolution. In the chiral setting, the quadratic dual is defined analogously: for a
chiral algebra A presented by generators and chiral OPE relations, A ! is generated by the dual generators
with orthogonal complement relations.


                                                       1633
1634                        Appendix O. Comparison of existence paradigms for Koszul duals


Remark O.1.3 (Relationship to the bar construction). The bar construction 𝐵¯ (A) is defined independently
of the Koszul dual: it is the cofree coalgebra on the desuspension of the augmentation ideal Ā = ker( 𝜀 ),

                                          𝐵¯ (A) = 𝑇 𝑐 ( 𝑠 −1 Ā) , 𝑑 ,
                                                                     

equipped with the differential 𝑑 induced by the multiplication of A. No knowledge of A ! is required to
define 𝐵¯ (A).
    The Koszulness condition (Definition O.1.4 below) is precisely the statement that the natural projection
𝐵¯ (A) ↠ A ! is a quasi-isomorphism of dg coalgebras. Thus the bar construction provides a dg coalge-
bra resolution of A ! when A is Koszul, not its definition. To obtain the Koszul dual algebra from the
coalgebra A ! , one takes the graded linear dual (A ! ) ∨ ; this requires finite-dimensionality of each graded
component of A ! .
Deﬁnition O.1.4 (Koszul property). Let A = 𝑇D (𝑉 )/( 𝑅) be a quadratic chiral algebra with Koszul dual
A ! as in Definition O.1.2. Then A is Koszul if:
  (i) The natural projection from the bar coalgebra to the Koszul dual coalgebra is a quasi-isomorphism
      of dg coalgebras:
                                               𝐵¯ (A) −−→ A !
                                                        ∼


      (Dualizing both sides then gives 𝐵¯ (A) ∨ ≃ (A ! ) ∨ , recovering the Koszul dual algebra as the linear
      dual of the Koszul dual coalgebra; see Remark O.1.3.)
 (ii) Equivalently, the cobar of the bar recovers A:

                                                Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −−→ A
                                                              ∼


 (iii) The module-comodule categories are equivalent (with appropriate completeness/conilpotence):

                                        Modcompl (A) ≃ CoModconil (A ! )

Conditions (1) and (2) are equivalent for conilpotent coalgebras (see [135], Theorem 2.3.3). Note that A !
always exists for quadratic algebras; the content of the Koszul property is that the bar construction provides
a resolution of A ! , rather than merely surjecting onto it.

O.2      Quadratic case: constructive existence proof
O.2.1    Statement of result
Theorem O.2.1 (Quadratic algebras have duals [58, 83]; [proved]). Let A = Free D (𝑉 )/( 𝑅) be a
quadratic chiral algebra, meaning:
   (i) 𝑉 is a graded vector space (the generators)
  (ii) 𝑅 ⊆ 𝑉 ⊗2 (the relations are quadratic)
 (iii) 𝑅 satisfies certain regularity conditions (specified below)
   Then A admits a Koszul dual coalgebra A ! , which can be constructed explicitly.

Proof Strategy. The proof is constructive and has four steps:
   Step 1. Construct the dual space. Define:

                                            𝑉 ∗ = Hom(𝑉 , ℂ)

with dual grading: | 𝑣 ∗ | = −| 𝑣 |.

defined by:
                                𝑅⊥ = { 𝑓 ∈ (𝑉 ∗ ) ⊗2 : 𝑓 ( 𝑟 ) = 0 for all 𝑟 ∈ 𝑅 }
   Step 3. Build the dual coalgebra. Define A ! as the maximal sub-coalgebra of Cofree D ( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ ) cogenerated
by 𝑠𝑅⊥ :
                                           A ! ↩→ Cofree D ( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ )
where 𝑠 denotes suspension (degree shift by 1). (Note: the dual coalgebra is a sub-object of the cofree
coalgebra, not a quotient; the quotient construction Free( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ )/( 𝑠𝑅⊥ ) gives the dual algebra.)
   Step 4. Verify the Koszul property. Check that:
• A ! has a well-defined coalgebra structure
• The bar coalgebra resolves the dual coalgebra: 𝐵¯ (A) −
                                                        ∼
                                                        → A ! (quasi-isomorphism of dg coalgebras)
• The cobar of the bar Ω ( 𝐵¯ (A)) −

  (ii) A is Koszul

O.4      Algorithmic existence test
O.4.1    The algorithm
Construction O.4.1 (Existence test for Koszul duals). Given a chiral algebra A = Free(𝑉 )/( 𝑅), one deter-
mines whether the Koszul dual exists as follows.
   Step 1: Quadratic test. If all relations in 𝑅 lie in 𝑉 ⊗2 , proceed to Step 2; otherwise pass to Step 4 (non-
quadratic case).
   Step 2: Regularity. Compute the dual space 𝑉 ∗ and dual relations 𝑅⊥ ⊆ (𝑉 ∗ ) ⊗2 . If ( 𝑅⊥ ) ⊥ = 𝑅 and
the pairing 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 ∗ → ℂ is non-degenerate, proceed; otherwise the dual does not exist.
   Step 3: Construction and conilpotency. Form the candidate dual A ! ↩→ Cofree( 𝑠𝑉 ∗ ) as the maximal
sub-coalgebra cogenerated by 𝑠𝑅⊥ . The dual exists if and only if A ! is conilpotent.
   Step 4: Non-quadratic case. Compute max𝑖 deg( 𝑟𝑖 ). If relations have bounded degree, define a filtration
by order and check the convergence criteria of Theorem O.3.6. The dual exists (after completion) if and
only if convergence holds.

O.4.2     Examples of algorithm application
Example O.4.2 (Algorithm applied to Heisenberg). Input: H = Free( 𝑎, 𝑎∗ )/( [ 𝑎, 𝑎∗ ] − 1)
   Step 1. Check quadratic. The Heisenberg relation [ 𝑎, 𝑎∗ ] = 1 is inhomogeneous quadratic; the homo-
geneous part of the relation space is:

                                       𝑅 = { 𝑎 ⊗ 𝑎∗ − 𝑎∗ ⊗ 𝑎 } ⊆ 𝑉 ⊗2

Quadratic (in the inhomogeneous sense of Positselski). Proceed to Step 2.
  Step 2. Check regularity.
                                      𝑉 ∗ = span{ 𝑎† , ( 𝑎∗ ) † }
             𝑅⊥ = Sym2 (𝑉 ∗ ) = span{ 𝑎† ⊗ 𝑎† , ( 𝑎∗ ) † ⊗ ( 𝑎∗ ) † , 𝑎† ⊗ ( 𝑎∗ ) † + ( 𝑎∗ ) † ⊗ 𝑎† }
   Check: ( 𝑅⊥ ) ⊥ = 𝑅? Yes. Check: 𝑉 ⊗ 𝑉 ∗ → ℂ non-degenerate? Yes.
   Regular. Proceed to Step 3.
   Step 3. Construct dual.

                     H ! = sub-coalgebra of Cofree( 𝑠𝑎† , 𝑠 ( 𝑎∗ ) † ) cogenerated by 𝑠𝑅⊥

   Step 4. Verify conilpotency.
                                          Δ ( 𝑎† ) = 𝑎† ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ 𝑎†
   This is primitive, hence conilpotent.

Example O.4.3 (Running algorithm on W∞ ). Input: W∞ (W-algebra with infinitely many generators of
all weights)
    Step 1. Check quadratic. Relations include terms of all orders (quadratic, cubic, quartic, .. . ). Not
quadratic. Proceed to Step 4.
    Step 4. Non-quadratic case: bar construction and Koszul property. Check: Are relations bounded
degree?
    NO. W∞ has relations of arbitrarily high degree.
    Output. The bar construction 𝐵¯ (W∞ ) exists as a dg coalgebra, but it does not satisfy the Koszul property
(the counit Ω ( 𝐵¯ (W∞ )) → W∞ is not a quasi-isomorphism), even after completion.
    Explanation. The unbounded complexity of W∞ (relations of arbitrarily high degree among infinitely
many generators) prevents the bar spectral sequence from degenerating at any finite page.

O.5.2    Detailed analysis: W-algebras
Proposition O.5.3 (W -algebra Koszul property [59, 125]; [proved]). For the W-algebra W𝑁 at
central charge 𝑐 :
   (i) W3 at admissible level (e.g., 𝑐 = 2 − 24( 𝑘 + 2) 2 /( 𝑘 + 3) for integer 𝑘 ≥ 0): Koszul, dual exists
  (ii) W3 at generic 𝑐 : Not strictly Koszul, but completed Koszul dual exists (via nilpotent completion,
       Appendix P)
 (iii) W𝑁 for 𝑁 > 3: Rarely strictly Koszul (only special ( 𝑁 , 𝑐 ) pairs); completed duals may exist
 (iv) W∞ : Not Koszul in any sense

Proof Idea. W-algebras have increasingly complex relations as 𝑁 grows:
• W3 : Quadratic and cubic relations
• W4 : Up to quartic relations
• W𝑁 : Up to degree- 𝑁 relations
  The Koszul property holds only when these higher relations ‘‘degenerate’’ to effective quadratic relations,
which happens only at special values of 𝑐 related to minimal models and rational CFTs.
  See Arakawa [37] for complete classification.

Example O.6.2 (Free fermion (𝑏𝑐 ghost) system). The free fermion (𝑏𝑐 ghost) system is:

                                           F = Free( 𝑏, 𝑐 )/( 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑏 )

    Generators. 𝑉 = span{𝑏, 𝑐 } with | 𝑏 | = 𝜆, | 𝑐 | = 1 − 𝜆.

  This is 3-dimensional (codimension 1 in (𝑉 ∗ ) ⊗2 ). Check: ⟨𝑏 ∗ ⊗ 𝑐 ∗ − 𝑐 ∗ ⊗ 𝑏 ∗ , 𝑏 ⊗ 𝑐 + 𝑐 ⊗ 𝑏 ⟩ = 1 − 1 = 0.

coalgebra:

   with the cocommutative shuffle comultiplication. This is the 𝛽𝛾 system (cf. Theorem 19.3.1), consistent
with the Lie↔Com duality: the 𝑏𝑐 system has antisymmetric (Lie-type) relations, so its Koszul dual has
symmetric (Com-type) relations.

    Hence the free fermion (𝑏𝑐 ghost) system is Koszul with symmetric coalgebra dual ( 𝛽𝛾 system).

Remark O.7.1 (Comparison of existence paradigms [83, 171]). Three existence paradigms appear in and
around the monograph:
   (i) Strict quadratic/conilpotent paradigm. In the classical and quadratic literature, regularity plus conilpo-
       tence give an explicit strict dual and bar-cobar resolution (Construction O.2.2).
  (ii) Completed/ﬁlter-complete paradigm. In the non-quadratic setting one seeks a completed dual under
       explicit convergence and inverse-limit hypotheses; Appendix P records this frontier package and its
       standard towers.
 (iii) Negative or comparison statements. Claims that no dual exists depend on the ambient category, the
       allowed completion, and the level at which one asks for inversion. They should therefore be read as
       regime-specific comparison statements, not as a single monograph theorem overriding the family-by-
       family theorem surface.
Accordingly this appendix explains how the paradigms fit together; it does not supply a single constitutional
‘‘if and only if’’ criterion for the whole monograph.

O.7.1    Practical recommendations
Remark O.7.2 (Alternatives when the dual does not exist). If a chiral algebra A does not have a Koszul dual,
alternatives include:
    Option 1: Weaken to 𝐴∞ . Even without Koszul dual, A may have an 𝐴∞ ‘‘quasi-dual’’ with bar-cobar
structures up to homotopy.
    Option 2: Work with derived category. The derived category D 𝑏 (A-mod) exists even without explicit
dual.
    Option 3: Use factorization homology. Factorization homology 𝑋 A can be computed without Koszul
                                                                   ∫

dual (Costello–Gwilliam framework).
1644                      Appendix O. Comparison of existence paradigms for Koszul duals


   Option 4: Restrict to nice subcategory. Sometimes a subcategory of A-mod has better properties.
Appendix P


Nilpotent-completion frontier for non-quadratic
Koszul duality

                                                      Abstract

            This appendix develops a frontier completion package extending the finite-type geometric Koszul
        formalism to a larger class of filtered chiral algebras under finite-generation and polynomial-growth
        hypotheses. For non-quadratic chiral algebras such as Virasoro and W-algebras, the bar construction
        produces an infinite coalgebra that requires completion to yield a usable completed curved bar model
        and dual shadow data. The appendix records the 𝐼 -adic framework, the finite-stage infrastructure, and
        the exact missing lemmas that separate the standard completed examples from a universal completion
        theorem.

Remark P.0.1 (Dependency warning). The theorematic core of the monograph remains the finite-type
Koszul-locus theory of Chapters 9 and 8. The present appendix records the leading extension of that
core, not a replacement of it. Every result below should be read as belonging to the completion frontier
(Stratum II), and its validity is conditional on the finite-generation and polynomial-growth hypotheses
stated in Theorem P.2.3.

P.1      The problem: why completion is necessary
P.1.1    Quadratic vs. non-quadratic
Observation P.1.1 (Classical Koszul theory limitation). Classical Koszul duality applies to quadratic alge-
bras—those presented by generators and quadratic relations. Examples:
• Symmetric algebra: Sym(V) with relations 𝑥𝑦 = 𝑦𝑥
• Exterior algebra: Λ (𝑉 ) with relations 𝑥𝑦 = −𝑦𝑥 , 𝑥 2 = 0
• Polynomial ring: 𝑘 [ 𝑥1 , . . . , 𝑥𝑛 ]
    However, many chiral algebras require completion beyond the quadratic setting: the Virasoro OPE
𝑇 ( 𝑧 )𝑇 (𝑤 ) ∼ 𝑐 /( 𝑧 − 𝑤 ) 4 + · · · is inhomogeneous quadratic (bilinear plus central term), requiring curved
Koszul duality (à la Positselski) and, in the manuscript’s main line, producing only the same-family shadow
Vir26− 𝑐 rather than an H-level infinite-generator dual object; W-algebras ( 𝑁 ≥ 3) involve cubic and higher-
order OPE relations; and the affine Yangian has relations involving spectral parameters.
    For these, the bar construction 𝐵¯ (A) remains a perfectly well-defined dg coalgebra–-it is the Koszul
dual coalgebra in the derived sense (Convention 6.0.3)–-but its cohomology does not concentrate in a
single degree, so the classical Koszul dual algebra A ! is not directly visible. 𝐼 -adic completion resolves this:
the completed bar coalgebra b̄  𝐵 (A) recovers A ! as a graded piece of a filtered inverse limit.




                                                        1645
1646        Appendix P. Nilpotent-completion frontier for non-quadratic Koszul duality

                                        𝐵 (A) := lim 𝐵¯ (A)/ 𝐼 𝑛

Remark P.2.4 (Frontier status). Step 3 above compresses a non-trivial claim: that the obstruction groups
𝐻 2 (A , 𝐹 𝑛 / 𝐹 𝑛+1 ) are eventually zero under the polynomial growth hypothesis. The argument invokes
the finite Hochschild cohomology assumption to control the total obstruction space, and the polynomial
growth bound to show each graded piece 𝐹 𝑛 / 𝐹 𝑛+1 becomes negligible for large 𝑛. A fully expanded proof
would require an explicit filtration-degree estimate showing that the polynomial bound on OPE coefficients
forces 𝐻 2 (A , 𝐹 𝑛 / 𝐹 𝑛+1 ) = 0 for 𝑛 ≫ 0. This places the result in the completion frontier regime of
Remark 2.8.13(ii), not in the strict finite-type core.

P.3     Koszul duality via completion
P.3.1   The main construction
Construction P.3.1 (Completed Koszul dual). For non-quadratic chiral algebras, the intrinsic Definition O.1.2
does not apply. Define the completed Koszul dual coalgebra as:

                                                 A ! := b̄

the 𝐼 -adic completion of the geometric bar complex. This is a completed dg coalgebra; the Koszul dual

differential induced by the coproduct of A ! .

P.5     Physical interpretation: renormalization
P.5.1   Witten’s QFT perspective
Interpretation P.5.1 (Completion as renormalization). In quantum field theory, the I-adic completion
corresponds to renormalization:
   Bare theory. The finite truncations 𝐵¯ (A)/ 𝐼 𝑛 represent the theory with UV cutoff at scale Λ𝑛 .
   Renormalization. Taking 𝑛 → ∞ removes the cutoff:

                           Renormalized theory = lim (Bare theory at scale Λ𝑛 )
                                                 ←−
                                                        𝑛

    Counterterms. The terms in 𝐼 𝑛 correspond to n-loop quantum corrections, which must be summed to
get the full quantum theory.

P.5.2    Feynman diagram expansion
Remark P.5.2 (Feynman diagrams and conilpotent degree). Elements of 𝐼 𝑛 / 𝐼 𝑛+1 in the bar complex corre-
spond to Feynman graphs with specific complexity:
• 𝐼 0 = 𝑘 : Vacuum (no particles)
• 𝐼 1 / 𝐼 2 : Single-particle states
• 𝐼 2 / 𝐼 3 : Two-particle connected graphs
1652        Appendix P. Nilpotent-completion frontier for non-quadratic Koszul duality


• 𝐼 𝑛 / 𝐼 𝑛+1 : n-particle irreducible graphs
   The completion sums over all Feynman diagrams:
                                          ∞
                                                1
                                                      × (n-loop amplitude)
                                         ∑︁
                                   𝑍=
                                         𝑛=0 symmetry

   This is a formal power series requiring completion.

P.7     Computational methods
P.7.1   Computing the completion
Remark P.7.1 (Computing the truncation b̄
                                       𝐵 (A)/ 𝐼 𝑁 ). Given a chiral algebra A and truncation level 𝑁 ,
the quotient 𝐵¯ (A)/ 𝐼 is computed as follows.
                      𝑁

   (i) Generate basis. Degree 0: vacuum; degree 1: generators of A; degree 𝑘 : 𝑘 -fold tensor products.
  (ii) Compute differential. Use the OPE to compute 𝑑 ( 𝑎1 ⊗ · · · ⊗ 𝑎𝑘 ) by extracting residues at collisions
       and summing over all collision patterns.
 (iii) Filter by conilpotent degree. Compute the coproduct iteratively, determine which elements lie in 𝐼 𝑛
       for each 𝑛, and truncate at level 𝑁 .

P.7.2    Convergence criteria in practice
Proposition P.7.2 (Convergence of the completion [2, 130]; [proved]). For a chiral algebra A graded
by conformal weight, the completion b̄
                                    𝐵 (A) is well-defined (the projective limit stabilizes in each total
weight) whenever:
1654       Appendix P. Nilpotent-completion frontier for non-quadratic Koszul duality


  (i) A is ﬁnitely generated; the bar complex at bar degree 𝑛 has total weight ≥ 𝑛 · ℎmin where ℎmin =
      min𝑖 ℎ𝑖 > 0, so each weight space is automatically finite-dimensional. No completion is needed
      beyond finite truncation.
 (ii) A has countably many generators of weights ℎ1 ≤ ℎ2 ≤ · · · → ∞; the completion converges if the
      weights grow fast enough that each total-weight subspace of the bar complex is finite-dimensional.
   Examples.
• Virasoro ( ℎ = 2), 𝑊3 ( ℎ = 2, 3): finitely generated, completion automatic.
• W1+∞ : generators in all integer weights ℎ = 1, 2, 3, . . .; completion requires care but converges since
  ℎ𝑛 → ∞.
